stories.title: From one generation to the next: London gathers to remember Canada’s fallen
stories.summary: Residents, veterans, students, and local officials gathered at Vimy Ridge Park in London’s east end for a Remembrance Day ceremony honouring those who served and sacrificed their lives for Canada.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Residents, veterans, students, and local officials gathered at Vimy Ridge Park in London’s east end for a Remembrance Day ceremony honouring those who served and sacrificed their lives for Canada.

The annual service included the playing of the Last Post, two minutes of silence, and the laying of wreaths at the memorial.

Now in its third year, the ceremony was organized to give residents in the Argyle community an opportunity to participate in Remembrance Day closer to home, particularly those who May not be able to attend the larger service at Victoria Park.

Organizer David Daugharty said the event is made possible through the support of the Argyle Community Association, the Argyle Business Improvement Association, and community volunteers.

“We have the troops; we have the students who make the wreaths. It’s a good ceremony to honour the fallen,” Daugharty said.

He added that remembering those who served is especially important given the sacrifices made by generations of military personnel, including members of his own family.

London Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis says the involvement of local young people helps ensure the importance of Remembrance Day carries on through future generations.

“What’s special about today is the wreaths that are being laid have been put together by our elementary schools and our secondary school in the east end, and they will be laid by young cadets and school representatives,” Lewis said.

Retired air force captain Sam Newman also attended the ceremony to speak with students about the significance of remembering Canada’s veterans.

For some attendees, the service also carried a deeply personal connection.

Lt.-Col. Joe Murray, who grew up in the neighbourhood, said his father was among the veterans who served during the Second World War.

“He was a D-Day veteran. Landed at D-Day, fought through Normandy, was wounded by German aid, went back and fought through the Scheldt and came back. Long story short, with one lung and he never worked again. So, this means a lot to me,” said Lt. Murray.

The ceremony concluded with a reminder of the lasting importance of remembrance and the value of peace.

“Remembrance Day is a solemn reminder of the cost of freedom and the enduring importance of peace,” said Capt (ret’d) Sam Newman.

stories.title: Too young to drive yet, but Perth County teen tearing up junior drag racing circuit
stories.summary: Levi Dill can’t legally drive yet, but he’s one of the best up and coming drag racers in all of Ontario.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Levi Dill can’t legally drive yet, but he’s one of the best up and coming drag racers in all of Ontario.

“It’s a lot of fun. My family’s been doing it for a long time. We know a lot of people at the racetrack, and I enjoy being around them,” said Dill.

The 15-year-old from the Stratford area has racing in his blood. His dad, Mike, has been racing since he was a teenager, so when Levi was just 7, he bought him his first dragster. Levi’s been racing ever since.

“We got my brother and my cousin involved as well, and my twins have been going to the track, since they were four weeks old. So, we’ve always had racing in our blood, and we really enjoy it,” said Levi’s mother, Kirsten.

Levi has taken his racing to the next level the past few years, filling his trophy case and finishing second in the Junior Dragster Racing Program in Grand Bend for the third year in a row. In junior racing, it’s not about who’s the fastest, it’s about reaching a preset time. Still fast, but within limits.

“You have to be really good on the tree, get a good reaction time, and you have to try not to go faster than your dial, or else you’ll lose,” said Levi.

But the youngster still goes fast, reaching 130 km/h, hitting 7.99 seconds on the 1/8th mile track.

“Oh, yeah, the adrenaline is definitely going. I’ve definitely got my fingers crossed in my pockets and stuff. Safety wise though, I am not worried,” said Kirsten.

“There is so much safety equipment on these cars. Kill switches, seatbelts, everything about the safety part of it never worries me, but I’m in it for the win, as we all are.”

Once he gets his actual driving license next year, Levi can start driving the big racecars, while still honing his skills in the junior ranks through age 17. His goals are simple, to be the best dragracer in the world.

“To go to a world final and be the track champion or class champion at the track that I’m racing at,” said Dill.

The sky is the limit for the 15-year-old from Perth County, recently named Junior Dragster Rookie of the Year.

“It’s not a cheap sport, but it’s our sport. And we’re going to keep doing i because he’s passionate about it,” said Kirsten.

stories.title: Quebec confirms infected cow as outbreak of raccoon rabies continues
stories.summary: Coaticook - Quebec has confirmed its first case of raccoon rabies in a cow as the disease continues to spread in an ongoing outbreak.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Quebec ministry of agriculture, fisheries and food says the cow died on Oct. 30, the day the first symptoms appeared, and the rabies infection was confirmed on Wednesday.

It adds that the animal was a young, unvaccinated heifer in the town of Coaticook, in the Estrie region.

Article continues below

Three cats in the Montérégie region previously tested positive for raccoon rabies over the summer.

The provincial government has confirmed 329 cases of the variant of rabies this year in an outbreak that started in 2024.

While raccoon rabies is mostly infecting racoons, cases have also been confirmed in several skunks and foxes.

Quebec, which is conducting surveillance and vaccination operations in at-risk areas, notes that cases of raccoon rabies have increased significantly in the Montérégie region since March.

The disease can affect all mammals, including humans. It is transmitted primarily through the saliva of an infected animal, particularly through a bite.

The government says it is providing financial aid for livestock producers who want to vaccinate their animals against rabies and urges people to vaccinate their pets.

The ministry reiterates the importance of remaining vigilant and taking the necessary precautions to avoid contact with wild, domestic, or farm animals that May be infected with rabies.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 7, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Two dead, including infant, in Ontario tractor-trailer crash
stories.summary: Ontario Provincial Police say they are investigating a fatal collision involving a tractor-trailer that left two people, including an infant, dead.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Ontario Provincial Police say they are investigating a fatal collision involving a tractor-trailer that left two people, including an infant, dead.

Officers first responded to reports of a collision between a tractor-trailer and a passenger vehicle at around 8 p.m. Friday on Highway 69 north of Key River.

Police say the driver of the passenger vehicle, a 30-year-old resident of York, Ont., was pronounced dead at the scene.

They say an infant who was also in the passenger vehicle was brought to the hospital by first responders, but did not survive.

Investigators say the driver of the tractor-trailer did not sustain any life-threatening injuries.

They say the investigation remains ongoing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 7, 2026.

Sadeen Mohsen, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Justin Trudeau steps into new role at Oxford University
stories.summary: He joins an international network of former heads of government at Blavatnik School of Government
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
Former prime minister Justin Trudeau has joined England’s Oxford University in a new role.

Trudeau, 54, joined the Blavatnik School of Government as a distinguished fellow and member of the World Leaders Circle, the school said in a news release Friday.

The release says the former Liberal leader joins an international network of former heads of government, which includes former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern and former U.K. prime minister Rishi Sunak.

From 2015 to 2025, Trudeau served as Canada’s prime minister before stepping down.

The Blavatnik school, founded in 2010, says it is focused on public policy education and inspiring students to improve the “quality of government and public policy-making worldwide.”

Trudeau says in the news release that he is looking forward to “contributing his experience” and working with other leaders to “consider how governments can respond to change and build a more hopeful, inclusive and prosperous future for everyone.”

“In the decade that I was prime minister, the world went through profound change both geopolitically and technologically, which fundamentally reshaped our world,” Trudeau said.

Blavatnik School dean Ngaire Woods said Trudeau brings “a wealth of experience, forged through a decade of public service” which will be beneficial to students.

“Our students are the public leaders of tomorrow, and the opportunity to learn directly from those who have navigated the complexities of government … is invaluable,” Woods said in the release.

Trudeau is expected to visit the school later this month.

stories.title: Canadians choosing pricier destinations over Cuba amid crisis: travel agents
stories.summary: The U.S. oil blockade against Cuba triggered severe fuel shortages in the country prompting Canadian airlines to suspend flights to the island destination earlier this year.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan
stories.content:
As the winter holiday season approaches, one of the most popular sunny destinations for Canadian travellers remains out of reach.

The United States’ oil blockade against Cuba triggered severe fuel shortages in the country and prompted Canadian airlines to indefinitely suspend flights to the island destination earlier this year.

Travel agents say Canadians looking to escape the cold weather this year will have to pay more than what they’re used to for affordable all-inclusive packages in Cuba.

Ashley Harold, a travel agent at Flight Centre Canada, said Mexico, Dominican Republic and several other Caribbean countries and territories such as Aruba, Barbados and Jamaica seem to be getting most of the diversions.

“There isn’t one new Cuba, if you will. Canadians, they’re really spreading their winter travel across a much wider mix of destinations and trip types,” she said in a recent interview.

“We’re also seeing some travellers consider Caribbean cruises or tours to still-warm places like Costa Rica or Peru.”

Domestic tourism is also gaining traction as some Canadians are choosing to visit “fantastic” winter destinations, from Alberta to the West Coast, she said.

“Folks, now more than ever, are wanting to explore their own backyard and keep their dollar within Canada,” she said.

Even though advance bookings have become a new normal after COVID-19, the lack of Cuban vacations has led Canadians to make reservations in other destinations much earlier for best pricing and choice, Harold said.

Cuba welcomed more than a million Canadians annually before the pandemic but that number has been steadily declining in recent years, with visits dropping to around 700,000 in 2025, according to Statistics Canada. The agency recorded 127,000 Canadian visits to Cuba in the first quarter of this year.

Those numbers dropped significantly after U.S. President Donald Trump imposed the oil blockade on Cuba early this year, and the Canadian government subsequently issued a travel advisory due to the shortage of medicine, food and fuel in the country. It still advises Canadians to avoid all non-essential travel to Cuba.

After airlines suspended flights and major hotel chains pulled out of Cuba, the country’s tourism industry and the local economy that heavily depended on it were further devastated. The country of around 11 million people is facing a humanitarian crisis caused by the latest sanctions and the decades-long U.S. trade embargo.

Cuba’s tourism market was dominated by Canadians who relished its affordable winter vacation options. Now, they need to spend hundreds of dollars more to explore other destinations or cut down the number of trips they are making each year, travel agents say.

John Wood, president of Durham Travel east of Toronto, said Cuba visitors are “value conscious” and want to travel as often as they can within their budgets.

Some of Durham Travel’s clients used to go to Cuba “three, four or five times a year … because they could go for a very reasonable price, get away and enjoy the sun and beautiful beaches,” he said in a recent interview.

“And now they can’t do that anymore.”

Wood said his travel agency’s sales to Cuba dropped from more than $389,000 last year to just $24,000 so far into 2026.

Meanwhile, travel sales for the Dominican Republic increased from about $1 million in 2025 to nearly 1.3 million so far this year, he said.

“The Dominican Republic appears to have absorbed most of the difference from Cuba,” he said, noting travellers’ concerns about crime and large seaweed blooms in Mexico.

At Flight Centre Canada, however, Mexico remains the top destination — even if it’s pricier, Harold said.

A seven-day package at a four-star resort in Varadero, Cuba with a flight from Toronto cost under $1,400 per person around the last holiday season, she said. Comparable trips to Mexico, Dominican Republic and Jamaica cost around $1,800 this year, according to Flight Centre data.

“So, for travellers that are used to Cuba pricing, there may need to be a reset in expectations before they start shopping,” Harold said.

But that means tourists can “get creative” with their vacation plans this holiday season, she said.

“I think this is a great opportunity for Canadians to branch out a little bit more with their travels and experience something new.”

stories.title: Aid sector calls out omission of foreign aid in federal budget
stories.summary: The budget tabled Thursday by Prime Minister Mark Carney's government makes no mention of international assistance, foreign aid or international development.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Canada’s aid sector is expressing dismay over the first federal budget in more than 15 years to make no mention of foreign aid, and is calling on Ottawa to outline its vision in an upcoming foreign policy review.

“The budget is largely silent on issues of international development co-operation and humanitarian action,” said Co-operation Canada head Kate Higgins, whose coalition includes most Canadian aid groups operating abroad.

She argued this is the wrong approach “at a time when the stakes around and the world are very high.”

The budget tabled Thursday by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government makes no mention of international assistance, foreign aid or international development.

The Canadian Press reviewed all budgets tabled since 2010 and found references to those terms in each of those documents.

Thursday’s budget mentions Ukraine only in reference to drone production. It mentions aid workers only in passing, in a section on an existing permit program for aid organizations operating in areas under the control of groups Ottawa lists as terrorist entities.

Higgins said the sector assumes Ottawa will stick with its plan announced last year to cut $2.7 billion in foreign aid over four years.

She and other advocates said they were relieved the government did not announce further cuts. She also said Ottawa should acknowledge the important role development funding plays in addressing crises abroad, such as the humanitarian plight of Palestinians in Gaza and the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“International development co-operation addresses the very challenges that the government is seeking to prioritize around defence, around stability, around diplomacy, around economic partnerships, around trade diversification, around a rules-based order that upholds democracy and human rights,” Higgins said.

She said she hopes Ottawa offers more details of its plans for “international development assistance and humanitarian action” in a foreign policy review expected later this month.

In a news conference Friday, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said the foreign policy update will come in “in a matter of weeks” and will include “our approach on development.”

“Rest assured, development assistance is a priority for Global Affairs Canada. It is the reason why we have come forth with humanitarian assistance for Cuba, for Lebanon, for Gaza, for Sudan, among others, this year alone,” she said on Parliament Hill.

The budget’s lack of any mention of foreign aid came just days after the United Nations’ global head of humanitarian issues, Tom Fletcher, praised Canada as a “humanitarian superpower” for the world’s most vulnerable.

“I really hope that Canada continues to hold the line,” he said four days before the budget.

Results Canada, an anti-poverty advocacy group, posted a photo Thursday of a deflated balloon on social media shortly after the budget’s release. The group’s policy director Lindsay Sheridan said her team searched the document in vain for terms relevant to her sector.

“International assistance, foreign aid, vaccines, tuberculosis — just seeing what was in it. And then continuously nothing came up. There was nothing on famines, either. And so, we were just surprised,” she told a video conference with supporters on Thursday.

“We thought that this might be the moment where we would get a little bit more context, a little more understanding of maybe the direction we would be going.”

Unicef Canada also expressed its disappointment in the budget. It said in a news release Ottawa should at least mention international development when it talks about its response to global threats and volatility.

“International assistance helps children survive and thrive while strengthening the health, education and protection systems on which peaceful, stable societies depend,” the group wrote.

The One Campaign, which advocates for African partnerships, says Ottawa should commit to spending $5.5 billion on development annually in the interest of “safeguarding global health and humanitarian investments that underpin long-term economic stability.”

The group also wrote in a news release that Ottawa should align its “development, trade and investment institutions to support co-ordinated, mutually beneficial partnerships with African countries.”

The House of Commons finance committee had urged Ottawa to use the budget to provide more transparency on where Canada’s aid dollars are going, and to focus funding on the world’s most vulnerable.

Critics have argued the Carney government should outline clearer priorities in aid spending, and spearhead initiatives with peer countries.

Sheridan cited the Harper government’s focus on maternal health and the Trudeau government’s work on providing education to children in conflict zones. Canada led both initiatives with support from G7 peers and global financing institutions.

“It seems like a missed opportunity to make a really well-rounded, robust strategy,” she said. “It seems confusing. Not even a mention.”

The One Campaign, which advocates for African partnerships, says Ottawa should commit to spending $5.5 billion on development annually in the interest of “safeguarding global health and humanitarian investments that underpin long-term economic stability.”
The group also wrote in a news release that Ottawa should align its “development, trade and investment institutions to support co-ordinated, mutually beneficial partnerships with African countries.”
The House of Commons finance committee had urged Ottawa to use the budget to provide more transparency on where Canada’s aid dollars are going, and to focus funding on the world’s most vulnerable.
Critics have argued the Carney government should outline clearer priorities in aid spending, and spearhead initiatives with peer countries.

Sheridan cited the Harper government’s focus on maternal health and the Trudeau government’s work on providing education to children in conflict zones. Canada led both initiatives with support from G7 peers and global financing institutions.
“It seems like a missed opportunity to make a really well-rounded, robust strategy,” she said. “It seems confusing. Not even a mention.”

content_blocks.text: Canada’s aid sector is expressing dismay over the first federal budget in more than 15 years to make no mention of foreign aid, and is calling on Ottawa to outline its vision in an upcoming foreign policy review.

“The budget is largely silent on issues of international development co-operation and humanitarian action,” said Co-operation Canada head Kate Higgins, whose coalition includes most Canadian aid groups operating abroad.
She argued this is the wrong approach “at a time when the stakes around and the world are very high.”
The budget tabled Thursday by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government makes no mention of international assistance, foreign aid or international development.
The Canadian Press reviewed all budgets tabled since 2010 and found references to those terms in each of those documents.

Thursday’s budget mentions Ukraine only in reference to drone production. It mentions aid workers only in passing, in a section on an existing permit program for aid organizations operating in areas under the control of groups Ottawa lists as terrorist entities.
Higgins said the sector assumes Ottawa will stick with its plan announced last year to cut $2.7 billion in foreign aid over four years.

She and other advocates said they were relieved the government did not announce further cuts. She also said Ottawa should acknowledge the important role development funding plays in addressing crises abroad, such as the humanitarian plight of Palestinians in Gaza and the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“International development co-operation addresses the very challenges that the government is seeking to prioritize around defence, around stability, around diplomacy, around economic partnerships, around trade diversification, around a rules-based order that upholds democracy and human rights,” Higgins said.
She said she hopes Ottawa offers more details of its plans for “international development assistance and humanitarian action” in a foreign policy review expected later this month.
In a news conference Friday, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said the foreign policy update will come in “in a matter of weeks” and will include “our approach on development.”

“Rest assured, development assistance is a priority for Global Affairs Canada. It is the reason why we have come forth with humanitarian assistance for Cuba, for Lebanon, for Gaza, for Sudan, among others, this year alone,” she said on Parliament Hill.

stories.title: Premier Scott Moe calls federal budget ‘best in a decade’
stories.summary: Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe says he plans to work with the federal government on a cost sharing model for infrastructure projects lacking from the federal budget.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe is praising Prime Minister Mark Carney’s latest federal budget , calling it one of the best in recent years.

Speaking at a panel event on the province’s economic future in Saskatoon on Friday, Moe said he’s optimistic about several budget promises he believes will benefit businesses and communities.

“I would say it’s probably the best budget we’ve had in a decade, but that isn’t saying much,” Moe said, adding Canada likely has “the strongest prime minister” in the last decade or two.

“I’m not standing up here stumping for the Liberal Party or anything like that, but I do appreciate when good non-partisan work is being done.”

Moe has spoken openly about having a more collaborative relationship with Carney than with former prime minister Justin Trudeau, with whom he often clashed over policies such as the federal carbon tax.

Moe pointed to a new exemption for up to $15 million in capital gains from eligible investments in Canadian companies. He called Ottawa’s 10-year plan to end homelessness a “bold commitment” and said he plans to work with the federal government on that goal.

Saskatchewan’s finance minister says the province will work with the federal government on the newly announced productivity mega deduction, which will allow companies to write off certain capital expenses upfront.

Jim Reiter says he expects it to cost Saskatchewan’s treasury around $400 million a year, but says it will be worth it.

“We’re happy to participate. We think it’s going to be a big incentive for business,” Reiter told reporters after the panel. On the budget’s shortcomings, Moe said he had hoped for more infrastructure funding, particularly for municipalities, and plans to keep working with Ottawa on shared funding commitments.

“I met with a number of federal ministers on trying to work together to put together a long-term infrastructure funding program that might be a third federal, third provincial, third municipal. We don’t have that yet,” he said.

Another major Saskatchewan request, giving helium the same tax treatment as oil and gas, was addressed in the budget.

The province’s energy and resource minister said helium companies are looking to build Saskatchewan’s first liquefiers in the Swift Current, Sask., area in as little as two years.

Pam Schwann, president of the Saskatchewan Mining Association, said the budget is good news for mineral exploration and production. She noted that a five-year extension of the Mineral Exploration Tax Credit and the Critical Minerals Exploration Tax Credit gives junior exploration companies more long-term security as they seek financing.

Schwann said the budget also reaffirms Canada’s support for the province’s mineral industry, particularly as it advances its nuclear strategy.

“For Saskatchewan in particular, that’s very exciting. All the way from our upstream exploration and production into supplier opportunities, and then ultimately into supporting nuclear reactor development for our own power in Saskatchewan,” Schwann told Global News in an interview.

However, Schwann says the budget lacked other commitments, such as investment in trade-enabling infrastructure, reforms to the Impact Assessment Act to reduce red tape around project approvals and securing zinc as a federal critical mineral, which would significantly help the province’s McIlvenna Bay project, which is producing copper and zinc and listed as a project of national importance by the federal government last year.

“We were looking for federal recognition in terms of a more narrowed focus on critical minerals and we didn’t see that. So that was a little disappointing, not just for production in Saskatchewan, but also for refining of zinc elsewhere in Canada as well,” Schwann said.

stories.title: Carson Harmer scores winner against former team as London Knights beat Saginaw Spirit
stories.summary: Carson Harmer scored two third period goals including the game winner against his former team as the London Knights held off the Saginaw Spirit 5-3 Friday at Canada Life Place.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Tied at two apiece in the third period, Harmer scored his sixth goal of the season to put the Knights ahead, but after the Spirit tied the game again at three, Harmer scored the eventual winner at 17:25.

Back on Sept. 13, the Knights acquired Harmer to be a two-way center but had to give up Brady Wassilyn in exchange.Wassilyn has become the Ontario Hockey League’s leading scorer with 27 points, including his 13th goal of the season Friday and adding an assist.

Ryan Brown and Evan Van Gorp also scored for the Knights with Cohen Bidgood icing the contest with an empty net goal.

The Knights remain four points behind the Midwest Division leading Guelph Storm who have won five in a row.

London will head to Sarnia Sunday night for a matinee before hosting the Storm in a rare Wednesday night game.

stories.title: What the data says about Indigenous voting in Alberta’s referendum
stories.summary: The Globe analyzed data from 61 polling stations on First Nations reserves and Métis settlements. Here’s how people there voted
stories.author: Joy SpearChief-Morris, Yang Sun
stories.content:
Indigenous people in Alberta turned out in massive numbers in last month’s provincial referendum, voted overwhelmingly in favour of remaining a part of Canada and fiercely rejected the other nine questions on immigration and constitutional issues, according to a Globe and Mail analysis.

The Globe looked at 61 polling stations located on First Nations reserves and Métis settlements from the Oct. 19 vote and found that Indigenous voters cast ballots nearly four times more than were cast in the same voting areas in the 2023 Alberta provincial election. Some nations saw a voter increase of 500 per cent to more than 1,200 per cent.

Nearly 95 per cent of Indigenous people voted to remain in Canada, about 20 percentage points higher than for the rest of Alberta.

“[The province] underestimated what the response was going to be from our communities, and it showed at the polls,” said Kainai Nation Chief Travis Plaited Hair.

“They had something to say, and they said it loud and clear that they were not in favour.”

The Globe’s analysis does not take into account Indigenous people who voted at stations off reserves, nor any advance polling or mail-in voting for both 2023 and the referendum.

Months before voters went to the polls, First Nations in Alberta challenged the legality of provincial separation in court, arguing that it would violate treaties with the Crown and breach the government’s duty to consult Indigenous peoples on matters affecting their rights.

Two Alberta judges ruled that First Nations must be considered in the decision to call a referendum on provincial independence. In a December decision, Court of King’s Bench Justice Colin Feasby ruled that “First Nations, as founding partners in the creation of Alberta, cannot be ignored or bypassed as Alberta contemplates its future whether that is as part of Canada or not.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith appealed a May court ruling that also went against her government. Days later, she called the referendum, wording the independence question in a way that sidestepped the court ruling. Albertans were asked whether the province should remain a part of Canada or begin the process for a binding referendum on independence.

Ahead of last month’s vote, a number of First Nations raised concerns that their members were not given the opportunity to vote in advance polls because of staff shortages. Some First Nations, including Kainai Nation, also known as the Blood Tribe, took part in get-out-the-vote campaigns, along with the Blackfoot Confederacy, which also includes Siksika Nation and Piikani Nation.

Kainai held an information rally the week before the referendum, including a vehicle parade from Cardston to Moses Lake, to show support for treaty rights.

“That’s what really boosted the interest in the referendum, and at the end of the day, influenced the vote too,” Mr. Plaited Hair said.

Kainai saw the number of ballots cast at its polling stations increase about 554 per cent, in comparison with the 2023 provincial election.

Siksika Nation, located about an hour east of Calgary, saw a ballot increase of about 715 per cent on referendum day.

“We know that in the past, some of our nation’s leaders and even our elders would actually discourage voting in provincial elections,” said Siksika Chief Samuel Crowfoot.

“A lot of them were told this, do not vote because it validates a system, a colonial system that we don’t necessarily have full faith and credit in.”

Matthew Wildcat, director of Indigenous Governance and Partnership at the University of Alberta, said strong opposition by First Nations to Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party was the “number one explanation” for such high Indigenous turnout.

“The far-right political circles are very hostile to the rights and distinctiveness of Indigenous peoples,” Mr. Wildcat said.

“People came out because it was an opportunity to vote against, or to show, a political demonstration against this government and the things that they stand for.”

Mr. Wildcat is a member of Ermineskin Cree Nation, which as one of the four nations of Maskwacis saw a voter increase of about 293 per cent.

On the first half of the referendum questions, regarding immigration, 75 to 85 per cent of Indigenous people voted No compared with 42 to 48 per cent in the rest of the province.

Both Blackfoot chiefs said they believe that their members voted according to strong traditional values, adding that their nations and families extend “beyond the Canada-U.S. border.”

“Anything that has to do with immigration has the ability to affect the treaty rights,” Mr. Crowfoot said.

For question five, ON proof of Canadian citizenship being needed to vote in future elections, about 79 per cent of Indigenous voters rejected the idea, versus 42 per cent in the province overall.

Mr. Wildcat said that while the idea wouldn’t necessarily hurt Indigenous people specifically, it would affect marginalized and vulnerable communities.

“Whenever a government puts additional obstacles, and they are obstacles, in the name of secure voting or whatever, it disenfranchises our people,” Mr. Crowfoot said.

Mr. Plaited Hair said not every member “has a passport, and not everyone has a provincial ID or government ID,” adding that many members carry band membership or Indian status cards.

In a statement from the Ministry of Indigenous Relations, the province said the government “will carefully consider how we work to implement the results of the referendum, including proof of citizenship.”

The government did not respond to any of The Globe’s other referendum-related questions for this story.

Mr. Crowfoot and Mr. Plaited Hair see the referendum turnout as setting the table for the next provincial election, scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027.

“I told our nation’s voters the referendum’s a warm-up,” Mr. Crowfoot said.

“They’re going to respect us, and they’re going to give us more attention now.”

Mr. Plaited Hair said not only has membership “woken up to the idea that their voice really does matter,” so has the province.

Mr. Crowfoot said he is proud that his peoples’ voices were heard and remains hopeful his members will continue to be more politically engaged.

“150 years ago, when the treaties were signed, and helped form Alberta, they were instrumental in the building of Canada, and 150 years later, our people fought on behalf of Canada to keep it united.”

Election results don’t show whether a ballot was cast by an Indigenous voter. The Globe looked at results from polling stations on First Nations reserves and Métis settlements. These stations mostly serve people who live in those communities, but some of their voters May not be Indigenous, and they don’t capture the many Indigenous voters who live off reserve.

To identify the stations, The Globe overlaid Elections Alberta’s 2026 voting-area boundaries on the province’s map of First Nations reserves and Métis communities. A station was included if at least 75 per cent of its voting area lies within the Indigenous land. The analysis covers 61 stations and counts only election-day ballots, because Elections Alberta does not report advance votes by station.

In a December decision, Court of King’s Bench Justice Colin Feasby ruled that “First Nations, as founding partners in the creation of Alberta, cannot be ignored or bypassed as Alberta contemplates its future whether that is as part of Canada or not.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith appealed a May court ruling that also went against her government. Days later, she called the referendum, wording the independence question in a way that sidestepped the court ruling. Albertans were asked whether the province should remain a part of Canada or begin the process for a binding referendum on independence.

Ahead of last month’s vote, a number of First Nations raised concerns that their members were not given the opportunity to vote in advance polls because of staff shortages. Some First Nations, including Kainai Nation, also known as the Blood Tribe, took part in get-out-the-vote campaigns, along with the Blackfoot Confederacy, which also includes Siksika Nation and Piikani Nation.
Kainai held an information rally the week before the referendum, including a vehicle parade from Cardston to Moses Lake, to show support for treaty rights.
“That’s what really boosted the interest in the referendum, and at the end of the day, influenced the vote too,” Mr. Plaited Hair said.
Kainai saw the number of ballots cast at its polling stations increase about 554 per cent, in comparison with the 2023 provincial election.
Siksika Nation, located about an hour east of Calgary, saw a ballot increase of about 715 per cent on referendum day.
“We know that in the past, some of our nation’s leaders and even our elders would actually discourage voting in provincial elections,” said Siksika Chief Samuel Crowfoot.
“A lot of them were told this, do not vote because it validates a system, a colonial system that we don’t necessarily have full faith and credit in.”

Matthew Wildcat, director of Indigenous Governance and Partnership at the University of Alberta, said strong opposition by First Nations to Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party was the “number one explanation” for such high Indigenous turnout.
“The far-right political circles are very hostile to the rights and distinctiveness of Indigenous peoples,” Mr. Wildcat said.
“People came out because it was an opportunity to vote against, or to show, a political demonstration against this government and the things that they stand for.”
Mr. Wildcat is a member of Ermineskin Cree Nation, which as one of the four nations of Maskwacis saw a voter increase of about 293 per cent.
On the first half of the referendum questions, regarding immigration, 75 to 85 per cent of Indigenous people voted No compared with 42 to 48 per cent in the rest of the province.
Both Blackfoot chiefs said they believe that their members voted according to strong traditional values, adding that their nations and families extend “beyond the Canada-U.S. border.”
“Anything that has to do with immigration has the ability to affect the treaty rights,” Mr. Crowfoot said.
For question five, ON proof of Canadian citizenship being needed to vote in future elections, about 79 per cent of Indigenous voters rejected the idea, versus 42 per cent in the province overall.
Mr. Wildcat said that while the idea wouldn’t necessarily hurt Indigenous people specifically, it would affect marginalized and vulnerable communities.
“Whenever a government puts additional obstacles, and they are obstacles, in the name of secure voting or whatever, it disenfranchises our people,” Mr. Crowfoot said.
Mr. Plaited Hair said not every member “has a passport, and not everyone has a provincial ID or government ID,” adding that many members carry band membership or Indian status cards.

In a statement from the Ministry of Indigenous Relations, the province said the government “will carefully consider how we work to implement the results of the referendum, including proof of citizenship.”
The government did not respond to any of The Globe’s other referendum-related questions for this story.
Mr. Crowfoot and Mr. Plaited Hair see the referendum turnout as setting the table for the next provincial election, scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027.
“I told our nation’s voters the referendum’s a warm-up,” Mr. Crowfoot said.
“They’re going to respect us, and they’re going to give us more attention now.”
Mr. Plaited Hair said not only has membership “woken up to the idea that their voice really does matter,” so has the province.
Mr. Crowfoot said he is proud that his peoples’ voices were heard and remains hopeful his members will continue to be more politically engaged.

“150 years ago, when the treaties were signed, and helped form Alberta, they were instrumental in the building of Canada, and 150 years later, our people fought on behalf of Canada to keep it united.”

Election results don’t show whether a ballot was cast by an Indigenous voter. The Globe looked at results from polling stations on First Nations reserves and Métis settlements. These stations mostly serve people who live in those communities, but some of their voters May not be Indigenous, and they don’t capture the many Indigenous voters who live off reserve.

To identify the stations, The Globe overlaid Elections Alberta’s 2026 voting-area boundaries on the province’s map of First Nations reserves and Métis communities. A station was included if at least 75 per cent of its voting area lies within the Indigenous land. The analysis covers 61 stations and counts only election-day ballots, because Elections Alberta does not report advance votes by station.

stories.summary: The budget's $30-billion commitment is being praised but experts and advocates say Ottawa will have to think creatively.
stories.author: Omar Mosleh
stories.content:
Dr. Stephen Hwang, a Canada Research Chair in Homelessness, Housing and Health, called the plan an “enormously important deal.”

Richard Lautens/Toronto Star file photo

ByOmar Mosleh Staff Reporter

The Carney government’s ambitious plan to end homelessness within 10 years has been met with cautious optimism, with experts and advocates saying the feds will need to think outside the box to avoid the fate of previous governments that failed to achieve that goal.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government announced Friday it would invest nearly $30 billion to address the country’s homelessness crisis, which includes $10 billion through Crown corporation Build Canada Homes to build 25,000 supportive and transitional homes nationwide, but also billions for mental health supports and benefits for Canadians on the verge of losing their housing.

At a press conference Friday alongside Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, Carney outlined the three-pronged approach of focusing on “help, housing and health.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Meta’s methods of moderation

Image 13Image 14Image 15

“We understand both how difficult this will be, but equally how imperative it is,” Carney said. In Canada, “we do things because they’re right, not because they’re easy.”

Federal Politics

The budget also includes another boost to the GST rebate and other tax credits to help those struggling to make ends meet.

Carney said previous efforts to eliminate homelessness in Canada were “inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated (and) not sustained.” In 2019, the Trudeau government pledged to reduce chronic homelessness by 50 per cent by 2028, which did not pan out; homelessness has increased exponentially in cities from coast to coast, although the pandemic played a large role.

On Friday, Mayor Olivia Chow said she was “very encouraged” to hear of the government’s plan, but noted the importance of delivering health care and wraparound services in conjunction with new housing units.

“I hope that this provincial government in Ontario would step up and do the agreement with the federal government so that we can provide and build, very quickly, many more supportive housing (projects) and end homelessness,” Chow said.

Ontario’s Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing did not respond to a request for comment.

A report by the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives analyzed Canada’s 10-year National Housing Strategy, launched in 2017, and said while the federal government was investing more in housing than it had in decades, “the emphasis has been to incentivize private for-profit developers, which is mostly creating housing that is not affordable.”

“The issue is most of that money went to private developers, which wasn’t creating rent-geared-to-income or affordable housing,” said Greg Cook, outreach team lead at Sanctuary Toronto.

He said this commitment is “more hopeful than the direction we’ve been going,” but added the government needs to move faster.

“A lot of this funding doesn’t look like it’s going to start flowing until 2027-2028,” Cook said. “It’s a crisis now … people are dying. This isn’t going to help them.”

Dr. Stephen Hwang, a clinician-scientist at St. Michael’s Hospital and Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Homelessness, Housing and Health, called the plan an “enormously important deal” and said the government’s stated approach of combining housing, supports and health care is one that has been proven to work.

“I think that the challenge is going to be how to actually implement that,” Hwang said.

He said making a meaningful dent in the number of homeless Canadians is not just about “building one building and filling it up,” but creating a system that has linkages between helping people get off the street and supporting them with multidisciplinary teams that includes case managers, peer support workers, psychiatrists and social workers.

Hwang said congregate living facilities are effective for many who are transitioning out of chronic homelessness, but added we also need to look at other models, such as more affordable stand-alone homes and apartment units integrated into existing communities.

Kinew said they would be looking at innovative models such as modular units and tiny homes to create a diversity of housing options.

Hwang said that too often, plans of this scope are announced with “very little accountability and deliverables,” adding it will be crucial for the government to track progress and for the public to be informed where and when units are being built.

According to researchers, adding 20,000 more homes and renewing existing housing stock would

“We do need to track outcomes rigorously … you have to have continuous monitoring and measurement,” he said.

Cook said he’d like to see some kind of commitment to make affordable and supportive housing more accessible, which is currently a major shortcoming, he said.

“Even if you can afford housing as a disabled person, if it’s not accessible, you’re homeless,” Cook said.

He also highlighted the general affordability crisis that needs to be addressed, as well as issues such as youth unemployment, which has played a major role in the rates of youth homelessness in Toronto.

He said while it’s noteworthy that the plan includes mental health and addiction supports, the government also needs to ensure they’re making housing accessible to every Canadian that needs it.

“I think the underlying issue is that people just can’t afford housing. And no matter what your mental health is or what your addiction situation is, you should have housing.”

With files from David Rider

Omar Mosleh is a Toronto-based reporter covering social issues for the Star. Reach him here:omarmosleh@thestar.ca.

ByAlyshah Hasham City Hall Bureau

Caledon’s night sky will be filled with dancing multicoloured lights on Saturday evening to celebrate Diwali— not fireworks, but drones.

The town, which held its first Diwali drone show in 2023, has been at the forefront of a growing wave of municipalities and organizations eschewing the blaze of fireworks for a swarm of drones, with reasons ranging from public safety to fear of sparking wildfires to a preference for the futuristic technology that can tell a story in 3D images.

Brampton’s annual Diwali Mela now incorporates a drone show along with fireworks, as did a Diwali festival in Ajax last month (they were not permitted to also have fireworks due to the event being outside the three days where Diwali fireworks are permitted by the Town of Ajax, according to a town spokesperson).

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

For Caledon, a drone show was a way to honour the festival’s message of the triumph of light over darkness and the local South Asian community, while also taking a more eco-friendly, safer and less noisy approach, said Hunar Kahlon, chair of the Caledon South Asian Association. Caledon imposed a personal-use fireworks ban in 2022. Brampton did the same in the wake of raucous and dangerous displays of fireworks going off all night on residential streets. Chaos at Victoria Day and Canada Day fireworks events have also prompted municipalities to consider switching to drone shows or cancelling outright.

The association between Diwali and fireworks is tough to break, Kahlon said.

“I think people are divided over it. Some definitely want fireworks; others are like, we are happy that the fireworks ban came in. But at the same time, the celebration must be there. So they’re thankful that the void has been filled,” he said.

The quality of drone shows has also improved year after year, with advances in technology, and Kahlon said he’s seen people be won over. Last year, they had 4,000 people attend. This year, they expect even more, with the addition of cultural performances and food vendors.

The town’s Nov. 7 drone show is being performed by Frankford, Ont., based North Star Entertainment, who also did last year’s performance. General manager Dustin Hadley says the custom storytelling is where drones are “really able to shine,” and the ability to creatively showcase company logos within the show opens up sponsorship or advertising opportunities to help cover costs and highlight local businesses.

Kahlon loves that the show introduces the story of Diwali both to younger generations and new audiences.

“It is all about learning each other’s cultures and living in harmony,” he said.

“I’m a fireworks guy, believe me, I love fireworks,” says Jeff Clarmo, chief operating officer of Pixel Sky Animations. “If there’s still a situation where we can work fireworks into a Diwali scenario, we should. But it’s just so many cities outlawing fireworks.”

He’s found drone shows bring people together in other ways. He had goosebumps as a crowd of hundreds of thousands in Vancouver did a Freddie Mercury call-and-response during a show in the summer of 2025.

Pixel Sky Animations' Vancouver drone show from 2025.

“For 10 minutes, if it’s done right, you forget everything,” Clarmo said.“You forget about your worries, your bank account, your sickness, your health.”

Clarmo’s company did the Diwali show in Ajax on Oct. 24 and has done similar shows for temples. He and other drone show operators say they’ve been getting an increasing number of inquiries for Diwali and other holidays.

The challenge is that drone shows are still more expensive than fireworks, though costs are rapidly coming down with the takeoff of the commercial and defence-related drone industry.

Shows are also getting longer and more dazzling, with battery-life improvements allowing shows to go beyond the typical 10 minutes, and the introduction of pyrotechnics where drones can blast out a trail of sparks. They need roughly the same weather conditions as fireworks, but drone shows require more setup time.

“Most operators are doing a Diwali show this year,” said Anugrah Patel of Drone Light Show Canada.He’s found that seeing familiar religious symbols hovering in the sky can be a moving spiritual moment that you don’t get from a fireworks show.

A Diwali drone show from Caledon in 2025.

Drone shows are a “great idea” and offer a more inclusive way to continue cultural traditions, said Baljit Singh Ghuman, the Brampton-based founder of Sikhs For Autism, and long-time advocate to end the use of fireworks in Diwali and other celebrations, including Canada Day.

There are other ways to bring people together to celebrate, have food, dance and mingle, he said — “I think that is more important.”

The real future of drone shows might not be in civic, sports and holiday events, some drone operators say. It’s in advertising.

But as Patel found out earlier this year, it’s not so simple. He was the pilot for a 1,000-drone ad for a Loblaws health services app in the downtown Toronto sky. That eventprompted so many complaintsthat Transport Canada is reviewing drone show regulations and may ban similar efforts going forward, he said.

“We did not expect that, to be honest with you,” Patel said. He was thinking about it as a cooler sci-fi version of a digital billboard or a plane pulling a banner, but it was received by many as intrusive and dystopian.

“I think it is the future,” he said, though the approach might need to be adjusted.

stories.title: A time change that sets back Canadians
stories.summary: Staying permanently on summer time tends to be popular until people experience it
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
A curious thing happened this week with the national atomic clocks, the most accurate timepieces in Canada: They no longer reflected reality west of Ontario.

To be fair, the problem was not actually the clocks but the webpage that disseminates their time. This service tells people – to two decimal places – how close their computer clock is to the real time. Starting last weekend, that information was a full hour out of whack for all of the Western provinces.

The reason, of course, is that those provinces don’t change the clocks. So when most Canadians “fell back” last weekend, enjoying an extra hour of sleep, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia stuck with summer time.

This was the first year for those provinces. While the atomic clocks’ confusion will prove fleeting, the confusing effect on visitors, business and people elsewhere trying to set up online meetings with those in the region can be expected to endure. It’s a decision the provinces will likely come to regret.

Staying on permanent summer time comes at the cost of more darkness in the morning. And that means more bleary-eyed starts to the day, more traffic collisions and more risk to children walking or cycling to school.

In the depths of winter this year, the sun won’t rise until close to 10 a.m. in Edmonton, a stiff price to pay for a bit more light in the evening.

Saskatchewan, meanwhile, also didn’t change its clocks. But that’s because it stays on standard time all year round. This is the logical approach and one the rest of the west should have emulated instead of doubling down on daylight time.

The research shows that changing the clocks is associated with a host of negative health issues, particularly with the spring change, including rises in strokes and heart attacks.

But staying on summer time year round is worse than staying on winter time. And choosing either without co-ordinating with nearby jurisdictions makes it harder for cross-border businesses.

Most of British Columbia is now out of whack with the Western United States for nearly half the year. However, in a geographic perversion, it will share a time zone during those months with residents in the southwestern part of North Dakota – people who live more than 1,500 kilometres east of Victoria.

B.C. had originally pledged not to stop changing the clocks unless neighbouring U.S. jurisdictions did the same, an alignment that would stave off obvious problems. The need for co-operation was the key reason Canada and the United States acted in concert in 2007 to change the dates for the clock shift.

However, former premier David Eby decided earlier this year – based on a survey that didn’t offer permanent winter time as an option – to go it alone and keep his province on summer time. Alberta decided to ignore a slim referendum vote against staying on summer time, arguing the need to co-ordinate with B.C. And then Manitoba made the same policy change, based on a survey that found widespread support for staying on summer time.

Attempts to jigger with time date back millennia. The Egyptians, and later the Romans, divided each day into 12 hours of darkness and 12 hours of light. This has the odd effect of making summer hours up to 30 minutes longer than winter hours.

More recently, daylight saving time began in 1908 in what is now Thunder Bay, and spread during the First World War as a way to save electricity by adding sunlight in the evening. It was not, as popularly believed, done to benefit farmers.

In the end, though, we can’t fool our bodies. The rising and setting of the sun controls our circadian rhythms and is the ultimate unit of measurement for time, not the arbitrary numbers on a clock.

In fact, previous attempts in both the United States and Russia to make daylight saving time permanent ended because people didn’t like being so out of sync with the sun.

There’s a part of the movie One Battle After Another in which a drug-addled former revolutionary is unable to establish to old colleagues that he is who he says he is. To verify his identity he must provide the correct response to the question “What time is it?” What he needs to say, but can’t remember, is that “Time doesn’t exist, yet it controls us anyway.”

There’s a deeper lesson there. The Western provinces are attempting to control time. Instead, they are likely to find that they, too, are controlled by it.

content_blocks.text: More recently, daylight saving time began in 1908 in what is now Thunder Bay, and spread during the First World War as a way to save electricity by adding sunlight in the evening. It was not, as popularly believed, done to benefit farmers.

stories.title: Does anybody really know what time it is?
stories.summary: The mess around daylight saving shows how disjointed and disconnected we can be
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
The current shemozzle over Canadian time zones says a lot about the state of the federation, none of it good.

British Columbia has switched to permanent daylight time. So have Alberta, the Northwest Territories and now Manitoba. Sensible Saskatchewan decided back in 1966 to put the province on Central Standard Time all year.

Parts of northwestern Ontario are adopting year-round daylight time to keep in step with neighbouring Manitoba, but the rest of Ontario is still turning its clocks forward for only half the year. Quebec is leaning toward scrapping the twice-a-year clock change, but has yet to act.

Got that? The changes have come about willy-nilly, with little co-ordination among the provinces, much less with Ottawa. Many Canadians are understandably confused.

Wait, British Columbia is only two hours behind Ontario and Quebec? And you enter a new time zone when you travel to Seattle from Vancouver?

Yes, Western Canada is now on a different time than neighbouring parts of the United States, which remains our biggest trading partner despite Donald Trump and all his tariff nonsense. The East Kootenay region of southeast British Columbia, which voted in August to go with the new “Alberta Time” year-round, now finds itself on the same time as part of the Florida panhandle. Alaska is two hours behind British Columbia, although the two share a lengthy border.

Is this any way to run a railroad? Or a country?

China, nearly as broad as Canada, has just one time zone. So does India.

Parts of the United States have been talking about getting rid of “spring forward, fall back” for years – and most of Arizona actually did in 1968 – but the idea that the states would all just sort of make up their own minds and pull the trigger when they felt like it is inconceivable, even though the American federal system, like ours, gives wide powers to its constituent parts. The three times the United States went temporarily to year-round daylight time – during the world wars and the oil crisis of the 1970s – it was Congress that made the call for the whole country.

We in Canada are so used to living in a disjointed, fractious cage match of a country that we scarcely notice it any more. The time-change mess is only one tiny example among many.

We put up with interprovincial trade barriers that penalize consumers and trim billions from our economic output. We tolerate the absurdity of a referendum on the possible future separation of the richest, most favoured province while in the midst of a perilous confrontation with our powerful neighbour. We see the separatist leader of Quebec spurn the Constitution and exclude the Lieutenant-Governor from his swearing-in ceremony with barely a murmur of protest from elsewhere.

The usual explanation for our disunity is that Canada is a big country cobbled together from disparate peoples and parts. But that could be said of almost any nation. The United States started as a quarrelsome collection of 13 British colonies. France has so many distinct regions that Charles de Gaulle lamented: “How can you govern a country that has 246 varieties of cheese?” India has hundreds of languages, thousands of ethnic groups and countless sects and castes.

Canada is a uniform, easily governed country by comparison. You can fly from Victoria to Halifax and find little difference in the way people speak, eat or live. Yes, we have lots of ethnic diversity and a big language minority, the French-Canadians, but Nigeria has three major language groups and many smaller ones.

Our variety is not unique. What stands out is the way we fetishize it. Freud called this the narcissism of small differences. Wikipedia helpfully describes it as “the idea that when people in a relationship or community have a lot in common, they can actually be more likely to fight with each other and mock each other, because they become overly sensitive to small differences they notice in one another and treat those differences as bigger than they are.”

We Canadians have become masters at it. We often act more like a pack of feuding principalities than a country with 159 years of success. It won’t do. Today we face the biggest threat to our independence in memory, coming from right next door. The moment demands unity, not narcissism.

Now would be a good time to get over ourselves and accept that we have far more in common than keeps us apart and far more to gain by working together than by squabbling over who gets how much.

We could start by agreeing on what time of day it is.

In 1980, Gazette cartoonist Terry Mosher, a.k.a. Aislin, was holding an exhibition of his work at a popular Bishop St. bar when none other than Leonard Cohen walked through the door.

A mutual friend, photographer Hazel Field, took this photo of the pair as they struck up a conversation about sketchbooks and pens, Cohen having expressed an interest in drawing:

Gazette cartoonist Terry Mosher (right) encounters Leonard Cohen (left) at an exhibition of Mosher's work at Darwin's bar in Montreal in 1980. Hazel Field via Terry Mosher

"Indeed, several years later, when Apple released its first computer, Cohen began creating bitmap drawings on his computer that he began publishing with some of his songs and poems," Mosher recalls.

"Somewhere in a drawer, I still have some of those early drawings that he sent along."

Being the Montreal icon he was, Cohen appeared in Mosher's work on multiple occasions over the decades. To mark 10 years since Cohen's death on Nov. 7, 2016, here's a compilation of some of those drawings.

Created for the Montreal Star to accompany a piece by Juan Rodriguez on Leonard Cohen's world tour performance at Place des Arts.

Aislin / Montreal Star

Published in the Montreal Star's entertainment section following the release of Leonard Cohen's second studio album, Songs from a Room.

Leonard Cohen was faced with money troubles following the discovery that his former manager, Kelley Lynch, had stolen millions from him. To rebuild his finances, Cohen returned to touring in his 70s. The move would ultimately revitalize his career and introduce his music to a new generation. Aislin / Montreal Gazette

In the years following Leonard Cohen's death in 2016, there was some discussion about naming a Montreal street after him in addition to the murals created in his honour. Aislin / Montreal Gazette

The COVID-19 pandemic continues to grip Quebec and the rest of the world, alluded to here with Aislin's update to the iconic Leonard Cohen mural in downtown Montreal. Aislin / Montreal Gazette

stories.title: Tale of two outbreaks: Canada stamps out measles while cases grow in the U.S.
stories.summary: Two infants among three deaths linked to the disease in the United States this week
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
A string of measles deaths in the United States this week – two in states that haven’t reported deaths of this kind in more than three decades – is underscoring the divergent responses to the highly contagious virus in the U.S. and Canada and the resulting outcomes.

Both countries have faced widespread and deadly measles cases that have sickened thousands, fuelled by growing pockets of unvaccinated individuals, particularly in Mennonite communities. But Canada has managed to do what the U.S. hasn’t: Put an end to the outbreak.

Down south the situation is growing worse, with three deaths announced this week. On Thursday, health officials in Wisconsin reported an infant death, the first measles-related fatality in the state since 1990. It followed the deaths of a seven-month-old in New York – another first in 30 years – and a Pennsylvania resident.

Immunologist Dawn Bowdish, a professor of medicine at McMaster University in Hamilton, said it will take time and greater analysis to compare the response of the two countries, but Canada’s strong commitment to public health and emphasis on vaccination likely set it on a different path.

“In Canada, that’s been a very clear part of our control in these outbreaks, whereas in the U.S. we hear every day more and more misinformation about measles coming from the highest officials of the land.”

Dr. Bowdish said Canadian officials, regardless of their political stripe or the province they represent, have not questioned measles deaths or engaged in sustained vaccine misinformation efforts, unlike U.S. Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“People do make their decisions based on what they hear in the news and what they hear from public health officials,” she said. “There’s no doctor, public health official or chief medical officer who I can think of in Canada who’s ever criticized the value of vaccination in reducing the measles epidemic.”

Canada declared the years-long measles outbreak over in October, after more than two months without a new, linked case being reported. The outbreak began in October 2024 in New Brunswick before spreading across the country, infecting more than 6,400 people and killing two premature babies .

Cases in Canada greatly eclipsed the total count in the United States in 2025, even though the U.S. population is more than eight times larger.

The U.S. outbreak began in Texas that January and has resulted in around 7,000 confirmed cases, with the majority identified this year. The number of infections is likely much higher because of under-reporting. At least 10 deaths – a combination of children and adults – have been confirmed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments.

Many U.S. public health officials have blamed Mr. Kennedy for worsening the crisis. He has led a significant overhaul of federal health agencies – constraining the government’s ability to track and manage cases – advanced vaccine skepticism and disputed measles-related deaths.

The measles outbreak emerged as a prominent issue ahead of the recent midterms, which saw the Democrats take control of the House and Senate in a stunning rebuke to U.S. President Donald Trump . Roughly a dozen doctors and nurses, many of whom made their opposition to Mr. Kennedy’s agenda a feature of their campaign, flipped Republican-held congressional seats.

There is now buzz that Democrats will work to strengthen public health and address a range of health issues, such as the price of prescription drugs and vaccine policies. This shift could help clamp down on the spread of measles, a once forgotten disease.

Annie Andrews, who became the first pediatrician to be elected to the U.S. Senate after she defeated Republican Darline Graham in South Carolina on Tuesday, has vowed to hold her “arch nemesis” Mr. Kennedy accountable for public health damage, also blaming him for the measles surge in her home state last spring.

Cross-border travel and shared religious and cultural communities mean the U.S. and Canada are intrinsically connected when it comes to measles transmission. While Canada was stripped of its measles elimination status last year, it is working hard to earn it back. Continued spread in the U.S. and elsewhere, however, pose a risk to these efforts.

Joss Reimer, Chief Public Health Officer, said last month that Canada had reached an “encouraging milestone” by ending its outbreak. But she warned that measles continues to circulate globally and said to expect travel-related cases to pop-up here.

“Vaccination remains our best defence against measles, and keeping routine vaccinations up-to-date is essential to preventing future outbreaks and protecting our communities,” Dr. Reimer said in a statement.

Achieving blanket immunity against measles requires 95 per cent of the population to be fully immunized with two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine or have had a previous infection. Both the U.S. and Canada are shy of the 95 per cent national threshold and, in certain regions, have rates far below.

Dr. Bowdish stressed that Canada cannot take its eye off the ball, considering measles is one of the world’s most contagious diseases.

“You can’t be lax with the rules we have in place. You can’t underfund public health and we have to work on trust,” she said. “You don’t get to relax with these sorts of things. You have to keep working on it, otherwise we’ll be in the same place again.”
