stories.title: Being obsessed with Angine de Poitrine is my microtonal math-rock midlife crisis
stories.summary: The Quebecois duo – now trio? – has a certain appeal to middle aged dads like myself
stories.author: J. Kelly Nestruck
stories.content:
The sold-out crowd at History gasped and pulled out their phones: There’s a third one now!

Angine de Poitrine, the intergalactic microtonal math-rock duo based in Saguenay, Que., introduced a new band member on stage in Toronto on Thursday night.

She – he? they? – was smaller than Khn, the two-piece’s guitar-bassist with the polka-dotted pope hat and priapic proboscis, and Klek, the flaccid-nosed bucket-headed drummer. The shy box-headed musician with antennae for ears played, fittingly, the triangle – which, shape-wise, is the symbol of the band.

I thought Khn and Klek were alone among their kind on our planet – and was unexpectedly moved to learn that they have started a family together. Or maybe they have a little sister who has joined the band? (“Unfortunately, we will not be providing any clarification on the subject!” a publicist for the band said by e-mail, in French.)

But a big part of the pleasure of being a fan of Angine de Poitrine is learning that we are not alone – in the universe, or on our planet. Indeed, there more and more of us stanning the ridiculous, virtuosic duo out every day.

I joined the band’s fanbase in April on the day I turned 45.

My initial conversion came, counterintuitively as their songs are unsingable, in a karaoke room I had rented for my birthday.

My oldest friend showed up first and as we were waiting for others, he popped on the famous video of Angine de Poitrine that was uploaded to YouTube by Seattle’s Kexp in February and made them go viral. I was entranced – but a little skeptical.

Then my fellow middle-aged friends arrived and we all sang the old familiar songs from the 1990s and 2000s; there was, naturally, a sing-along of Cornershop’s Brimful of Asha (On the 45) .

But the next morning, all I could hear in my head was Angine de Poitrine. I played the Kexp video a couple more times, then downloaded the band’s two albums Vol I and Vol II .

I’d fallen out practice of searching for new music and the algorithms kept feeding me the tried and true. But these angular, looping tunes became the soundtrack to the summer and I slowly discovered how many of my male friends had become similarly snapped out of old listening ways.

During a summer camping trip with fellow dads, there was a day where we floated down a lazy river in canoes and communicated primarily by trying to imitating the first squawky, herky-jerky notes of the band’s unlikely hit single Fabienk .

Watching Angine de Poitrine on stage for the first time on Thursday was the first time I’d been to a concert that wasn’t a reunion tour or anniversary revisit of a classic album since the pandemic.

Seeing the band in person, I realized exactly what their alien costuming does – and how it’s not a gimmick at all. It’s part and parcel of what helps the band appeal to many demographics, perhaps particularly mine.

For one thing, the alien conceit – the band speaks in their own squeak-grunt language – creates the conditions for the band to not have to make political statements on stage. And also, crucially, for them not have to make statements about not making political statements.

I’m all for artists who want to say something to the crowd – but it changes the energy of a room and, to someone of my generation, can come across as branding or second-hand clicktivism at best.

Even more annoying, however, are musical artists who come on stage to lecture you about how they’re not lecturing you. Metallica frontman James Hetfield went viral last month in that manner, saying he wasn’t playing a concert “like some other entertainers, to influence you.” Great, man, then just play Enter Sandman , already.

Angine de Poitrine’s body-covering costumes conjure a listening space where we can forget about all kinds of hang-ups and divides, including old Canadian ones around language or nationalism.

There’s definitely something quintessentially Quebecois about Angine de Poitrine, from its unapologetic embrace of prog to its polka-dot painted toes.

Folks usually reference Cirque du Soleil, which is fair, but the shape-oriented costumes also summon old memories of the hosts on the old children’s show Passe-Partout for me. I’m reminded too of the funny aliens in Le facteur de l’espac e, a popular series of Quebec graphic novels about an intergalactic postman that my son reads.

As a francophile ex-Montrealer, however, I didn’t realize how fun it was to engage with a group of artists from my home province without having to think about my own complicated relationship to Quebec culture – or that dated old idea of the two solitudes.

Instead, I could just immerse myself in a room full of solid dudes who know to dim their phone screen if they’re going to take a picture and to keep videos short. (There were lots of women at History, too; please forgive the pun.)

I enjoyed my night among them, combatting the male loneliness epidemic and worshipping a triangle symbol without having to join the Freemasons.

I ran into an old pal at History who told me he doesn’t go to gigs as much as he used to – but was seeing Angine de Poitrine for the second time. He, in turn, ran into another friend who was on his third Angine concert.

The music is addictive. There’s something obsessive about it – the repetition in the music itself, the rhythms that keep you off balance – that appeals to brains that might otherwise go down wormholes online wondering what the purpose of life exactly was again.

As far as male midlife crises go, you could do worse than to be become obsessed with Khn and Klek. △

stories.title: Nearly 3,000 Parks Canada employees face potential job cuts
stories.summary: Work force adjustment expected to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Thousands of Parks Canada employees have received notice that their jobs May be cut as the federal agency moves to shrink its work force and reduce services in line with the government’s cost-cutting measures.

Parks Canada has sent letters to 2,917 employees across the country to inform them their jobs are “impacted by workforce adjustment,” spokesperson Meaghan Bradley said in an e-mail. Not every one of those employees will lose their job, but decisions will be made in the coming weeks, she said.

The cuts are expected to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments and scale back visitor program, outreach and camping services. As well, the search-and-rescue dog program at Banff National Park – the only such program in Canada – has been discontinued.

“Over the coming months, Parks Canada will implement organizational changes to align with available funding, modernize operations, strengthen field-based decision-making and ensure it remains well positioned to deliver on our mandate into the future,” Ms. Bradley said.

The Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society, an environmental charity, said it is “deeply concerned” by the planned reductions, which it said could put ecosystems, visitor safety and local economies at risk. It also argued the move makes little economic sense: Parks Canada had a budget of about $1.3-billion in 2025-26, while visitors spent $6.5-billion in or near its sites, according to the federal agency.

Kecia Kerr, executive director of the society’s northern Alberta chapter, said the province’s national parks are already struggling to manage tourism and its effects on wildlife and visitor safety.

In Elk Island National Park, which is slated to lose its park-warden detachment, Ms. Kerr said speeding drivers have resulted in at least 11 bison deaths that she is aware of. There have also been issues with poaching at both Elk Island and Jasper National Park.

“Human-wildlife conflict, and a need for additional education for visitors on how to behave around wildlife, are already issues and these cuts will make those issues much worse,” she said.

She added that the federal cuts compound provincial decisions that have reduced protections for ecological reserves and removed portions of provincial parks for resort development, putting more pressure on Alberta’s protected areas.

A recent employment equity annual report stated that as of March 2025, Parks Canada had a total work force of about 6,000 employees, of which 48.5 per cent were seasonal. The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat, meanwhile, recorded 4,773 active Parks Canada employees this year.

The Public Service Alliance of Canada said 2,671 of its members at Parks Canada received the notices. To date, the employer has not explained which specific programs or services will be affected, the union said.

Jamey Mills, Psac regional executive vice-president for B.C., said 217 Parks Canada staff across seven sites in the province received the letters, including “entire workforces” at some sites. The park-warden detachment in B.C.’s Gulf Islands National Park Reserve will also close.

He said the cuts are particularly concerning in a province with geographically diverse parks that require workers with specialized training.

“It is important that there are on-the-ground staff with the ability to respond to potential emergencies, maintain critical infrastructure, meet visitor needs, and protect sensitive ecosystems,” Mr. Mills said in a statement.

Jean-Michel Lavergne, president of the Union of National Employees, a component of Psac, said in an e-mail that ending the search-and-rescue dog program in Banff raises concerns about avalanche searches, missing-person rescues and replacement response capacity. He added that park-warden detachment closures could mean longer response times and less backup for officers.

Other detachments set to close include those in Kluane National Park and Reserve in Yukon, Point Pelee National Park in Ontario, Kejimkujik National Park in Nova Scotia, Fundy National Park in New Brunswick and Nahanni National Park Reserve in the Northwest Territories.

Ms. Bradley said Parks Canada will maintain law-enforcement coverage through a regionalized model, with wardens redistributed according to need and risk.

Janet Sumner, executive director of the conservation organization Wildlands League, said the cuts undermine a plan announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney to protect 30 per cent of the country’s land and waters by the end of the decade.

“How do you do that while at the same time cutting the very agency that’s going to be responsible for managing some of that?” she said.

Reducing the agency’s work force could also have implications for national urban parks, which are particularly important because of the biodiversity they contain, she said.

The agency reductions are part of the Carney government’s comprehensive expenditure review. The review is expected to cut federal spending by $9-billion in 2026-27, $10-billion in 2027-28 and $13-billion in 2028-29, according to the government.

Parks Canada’s share of those cuts totals about $145-million: $24.6-million in 2026-27, $45.3-million in 2027-28 and $75-million in 2028-29.

The 2026 federal budget , released Thursday, commits $3.6-billion over 10 years to Parks Canada to maintain capital assets, as well as $282.7-million over 11 years, and $18-million annually, to establish and operate two new national marine conservation areas. The funding is separate from the planned spending reductions, which target the agency’s operating costs, staffing and existing services.

The budget also allocates $76-million to renewing the popular Canada Strong Pass program, which was first introduced in summer 2025 and offered free or discounted admission to Parks Canada sites, participating museums and galleries, as well as discounted rail travel. Visits to Parks Canada sites increased by 13 per cent because of the pass, the budget document said.

However, Psac said in its October statement on the work force cuts that there was no additional staffing to handle the increased tourism.

“This announcement is an insult after our members did more with less all summer long,” the union said.

stories.title: Dangerous bacteria found in tests of 11K vials of seized peptides: Health Canada
stories.summary: Health Canada says it found dangerous bacteria in tests done on more than 11,000 vials of unauthorized peptides seized from online retailers.
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
Health Canada says it found dangerous bacteria in tests done on more than 11,000 vials of unauthorized peptides seized from online retailers.

The federal health agency says injectable peptides from Shanghai ERP Peptide Biotechnology Co. Ltd. – a Chinese-based wholesaler of peptide products – were sold by two Canadian retailers, truenorthbiolabs.CA and bcaxiompeptide.com. Tests conducted on more than 11,400 vials seized found bacteria capable of causing serious infections.

“While unauthorized peptides are often promoted for weight loss, muscle growth, anti-aging, or wellness, they May expose you to significant and unpredictable health risks,” Health Canada said in a statement.

“Injecting contaminated products can cause serious infections, hospitalization, and in severe cases, life-threatening sepsis. The risk of infection is higher in people with a compromised immune system.”

Health Canada says if you have used an unauthorized injectable peptide drug and develop symptoms such as redness, swelling, pain at the injection site, fever, chills or you feel unwell, seek medical attention immediately, as these May be signs of a serious infection.

Health Canada says as a result of compliance and enforcement action, the two websites have been shut down. They have requested ERP Peptide to immediately stop selling illegal peptides into Canada while directing the Canada Border Services Agency to stop unauthorized shipments from entering the country.

Authorized prescription drugs in Canada have an eight-digit Drug Identification Number (DIN) on the label. You can also check whether a drug has been authorized for sale by searching Health Canada’s Drug Product Database .

Health Canada says if you have used an unauthorized injectable peptide drug and develop symptoms such as redness, swelling, pain at the injection site, fever, chills or you feel unwell, seek medical attention immediately, as these May be signs of a serious infection.

Health Canada says as a result of compliance and enforcement action, the two websites have been shut down. They have requested ERP Peptide to immediately stop selling illegal peptides into Canada while directing the Canada Border Services Agency to stop unauthorized shipments from entering the country.

Authorized prescription drugs in Canada have an eight-digit Drug Identification Number (DIN) on the label. You can also check whether a drug has been authorized for sale by searching Health Canada’s Drug Product Database .

stories.title: U.S. sanctions eight Canadian financial services firms over alleged Iran ties
stories.summary: Treasury Department says the Canadian companies helped the Irgc and its affiliates exchange Iranian rials and other currencies for crypto assets
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
U.S. authorities on Friday announced sanctions on eight Canadian companies that they alleged had offered financial services to the Iranian regime and its associate entities, thereby helping the country’s leadership evade sanctions and fund terrorism networks.

In a statement, the U.S. Treasury Department said the Canadian companies have helped facilitate transactions on behalf of sanctioned digital asset exchanges or accounts associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (Irgc). The Canadian financial services companies have helped those entities exchange Iranian rials for digital cryptocurrencies that the country then used to sidestep international economic sanctions, the department said.

“Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the statement.

stories.title: Budget 2026: Ottawa to introduce legislation on private airport investments, high-speed rail
stories.summary: Opposition parties criticize use of omnibus budget bill for loosely related projects and amendments
stories.author: Bill Curry
stories.content:
The federal government is planning to introduce budget-related legislation covering a wide range of issues, including attracting private investment for Canada’s four largest airports and new expropriation powers tied to high-speed rail, reviving concerns about Ottawa’s use of omnibus budget bills.

Thursday’s budget includes 54 entries in an annex called legislative measures, which historically is a precursor for including the items in a budget bill.

Each item in the annex offers only a brief summary of the planned change.

For instance, the list says the government will bring in legislation related to private investments in airports. It also says the government will move to “support accelerating the construction of Alto High-Speed Rail,” in reference to the proposed high-speed rail line running to Quebec City from Toronto with stops in between. It says this will include streamlining expropriation activities and enabling preconstruction work.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced plans in September to attract private investment to Canada’s four largest airports through an operating concession model. Thursday’s budget includes $37.6-million over three years for due diligence, legal advice and completing a competitive process to select an operator by 2029.

The number of entries in the legislative section is lower than the 75 in last year’s federal budget . Before that, the 2024 budget mentioned 62 changes, up from 49 in the 2023 budget.

Last year’s initial budget bill , C-15, was more than 600 pages and included the new High-Speed Rail Network Act, which listed steps that would accelerate expropriations and regulatory approvals related to impact assessments. It is not clear what additional powers Ottawa is proposing. A follow-up budget bill, C-31, is more than 300 pages and still before Parliament.

Critics have long challenged the use of omnibus budget bills to pass legislation that is only loosely connected to a budget, saying it limits Parliament’s ability to study and vote on individual items.

Because of the wide-ranging nature of budget bills, MPs and Senators tend to focus on only a few elements, leaving other aspects to be approved with little to no witness testimony in committees about their potential impact.

The Senate’s national finance committee released a report in March criticizing the government’s increasing use of budget bills to pass changes that are not strictly financial. Titled Omnibus Budget Bills: A Growing Problem, the report said the size of such bills has expanded significantly since the 1990s.

NDP MP Heather McPherson said the issue of attracting private investment in Canadian airports deserves a stand-alone study in Parliament.

“Privatization of airports is a real problem, and we should have an opportunity to meaningfully debate that within the House,” she said in an interview.

She added: “There needs to be a lot more consultation, a lot more discussion that needs to happen, and these omnibus budget bills don’t allow us to do that as parliamentarians.”

Conservative MP and transport critic Dan Albas said in an e-mail that his party views the high-speed rail project as a boondoggle that should be scrapped.

“Unfortunately, the Liberals are still committed to giving themselves more power to seize properties and cut off communities,” he said. “If the Liberals believe in Alto, they should be clear with residents, property owners and Canadians about these changes rather than trying to bury them in another omnibus bill for a budget that makes little reference to the project.”

Barry Tchir, national president of the Union of Canadian Transportation Employees, said his members have many questions about Ottawa’s airport plan and what it means for safety and job security. He’s concerned they won’t have the opportunity to raise these issues if changes are pushed through a budget bill.

“We’d like to have some input as to how that’s framed and mapped out,” he said.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne brushed off criticism of his government’s approach on Friday.

“It’s the same thing they say at every budget,” he said at an event in Montreal in response to a question from The Globe and Mail. “There’s no big news there. They always say that. What we need to do is to be very conscious of the parliamentary process, but also to act at the speed of the world.”

Lawyer and community advocate Erin Durant, who lives in an area that could be affected by the planned high-speed rail line between Ottawa and Montreal, says the public deserves full hearings on matters such as expropriating private property.

“They are taking what I would call a bulldozer approach to communities and not spending time in them and communicating with them,” said Ms. Durant, who opposes the project. “And I fear that this signal in the budget that they want to even have more powers to operate quickly will only worsen the already tense situation that exists in these communities.”

Other legislative measures referenced in the budget’s annex range from amendments to the Patent Act to the creation of the Canada Strong sovereign wealth fund. Among them are a crackdown on predatory lenders; new rules related to Crown corporation borrowing; an extension of the prohibition on foreign home buyers; and amendments to the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act.

The list also includes a new law creating a federal department called Digital Transformation Canada, which will replace Shared Services Canada and take on other duties, and amendments to the Bank Act related to stablecoins and new powers for the finance minister to address national security risks “with a supporting information-gathering authority.”

With a report from Nicolas Van Praet in Montreal

stories.title: Hanover man charged with sexual exploitation by Sudbury police
stories.summary: A 52-year-old from Hanover has been charged with luring a person under the age of 16 following an investigation by the Sudbury Police.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A 52-year-old from Hanover has been charged with luring a person under the age of 16 following an investigation by the Sudbury Police.

In March 2026, Sudbury Police launched an undercover investigation into individuals targeting young people attempting to lure children for a sexual purpose.

As a result of that investigation, they have charged a 66-year-old from Waterloo and a 52-year-old from Hanover.

Sudbury Police are warning the public that the suspect from Hanover was using the online social media name of @Hiltonhaven, while communicating with and allegedly attempting to lure young people online.

stories.title: Health Canada warns of bacteria found in unauthorized peptides sold online
stories.summary: In Canada, injectable peptides are generally regulated as prescription drugs, which are advised to be used under the case of a licensed healthcare professional.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Health Canada is warning consumers not to use unauthorized peptides after lab testing found bacteria in products sold online.

In Canada, injectable peptides are generally regulated as prescription drugs , which are advised to be used under the care of a licensed healthcare professional.

The health agency said it seized more than 11,400 vials of the drugs from Shanghai ERP Peptide Biotechnology Co. Ltd. (ERP Peptide) as well as two online retailers that sold ERP Peptide products.

During testing of the product, Health Canada said it found three different bacteria that could be harmful to humans.

Unauthorized products sold by ERP Peptide include Human Chorionic Gonadotropin, Mots-C, NAD+, Retatrutide, Tesamorelin and Tirzepatide.

“Selling unauthorized drug products is illegal. Unauthorized products have not been assessed for safety, efficacy, and quality by Health Canada. They have not been demonstrated, through scientific trials, to provide the health benefits that they claim,” Health Canada said.

“While unauthorized peptides are often promoted for weight loss, muscle growth, anti-aging, or wellness, they May expose you to significant and unpredictable health risks.”

Those risks can include hormonal imbalance, mood swings, blood sugar imbalance, liver or kidney damage, blood clots, and growth of cancerous tumours, the health agency said.

Unauthorized drugs are also not tested for safety, quality, or sterility, it added. As a result, products May contain too little or too much of the active ingredient, use dangerous or unknown ingredients, lead to allergic reactions or medical interactions, or contain solvents, heavy metals, particles of glass and plastic, or microbials.

Health Canada said it has requested ERP Peptide to immediately stop selling illegal products into Canada and is working with the Canada Border Services Agency to stop unauthorized shipments from entering the country.

The agency is encouraging consumers to stop buying these products. If you have used them and develop a fever or pain and swelling at the injection site, Health Canada said to seek immediate medical attention.
paragraphs: Health Canada is warning consumers not to use unauthorized peptides after lab testing found bacteria in products sold online.
In Canada, injectable peptides are generally regulated as prescription drugs , which are advised to be used under the care of a licensed healthcare professional.
The health agency said it seized more than 11,400 vials of the drugs from Shanghai ERP Peptide Biotechnology Co. Ltd. (ERP Peptide) as well as two online retailers that sold ERP Peptide products.
During testing of the product, Health Canada said it found three different bacteria that could be harmful to humans.
Unauthorized products sold by ERP Peptide include Human Chorionic Gonadotropin, Mots-C, NAD+, Retatrutide, Tesamorelin and Tirzepatide.

“Selling unauthorized drug products is illegal. Unauthorized products have not been assessed for safety, efficacy, and quality by Health Canada. They have not been demonstrated, through scientific trials, to provide the health benefits that they claim,” Health Canada said.
“While unauthorized peptides are often promoted for weight loss, muscle growth, anti-aging, or wellness, they May expose you to significant and unpredictable health risks.”
Those risks can include hormonal imbalance, mood swings, blood sugar imbalance, liver or kidney damage, blood clots, and growth of cancerous tumours, the health agency said.

Unauthorized drugs are also not tested for safety, quality, or sterility, it added. As a result, products May contain too little or too much of the active ingredient, use dangerous or unknown ingredients, lead to allergic reactions or medical interactions, or contain solvents, heavy metals, particles of glass and plastic, or microbials.

Health Canada said it has requested ERP Peptide to immediately stop selling illegal products into Canada and is working with the Canada Border Services Agency to stop unauthorized shipments from entering the country.

The agency is encouraging consumers to stop buying these products. If you have used them and develop a fever or pain and swelling at the injection site, Health Canada said to seek immediate medical attention.

stories.title: Why Halifax’s ‘Hockey Helps the Homeless’ tournament is now the fastest-growing event of its kind in Canada
stories.summary: Several hundred hockey players of all ages and skill levels took to the ice in large numbers for Hockey Helps the Homeless, a one-day tournament raising money to combat a growing homelessness problem in Nova Scotia and across Canada.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Dartmouth, N.S. - Several hundred hockey players of all ages and skill levels took to the ice in large numbers for Hockey Helps the Homeless, a one-day tournament raising money to combat a growing homelessness problem in Nova Scotia and across Canada.

“The homeless issue is a big deal for us in Nova Scotia, and I think it is necessary that people rally behind it and support it and try to help this cause.”

“I think hockey in Canada brings everyone together,” said Brandon Prust, who played 486 games in the NHL over nine seasons. “This is my fourth straight year playing in this event and I love coming to it.”

The charity tournament raised more than $350,000. Proceeds will directly support Vets Canada, Adsum for Women & Children, a Halifax-based emergency shelter and Souls Harbour Rescue Mission, which operates 14 locations providing meals and housing across Nova Scotia.

“It will feed thousands and it will shelter hundreds in overnight shelters for women, for children and men in our recovery program,” said Cherry Laxton, CEO of Souls Harbour Rescue Mission.

“The lives it will touch in the end, are countless.”

According to Murray, there are 23 Hockey Helps the Homeless tournaments held across Canada each year. The Nova Scotia event began in 2018 and has since generated more than a $1 million.

“We as a committee want to compete and match other efforts across the country and raise the bar for everyone,” Murray said. “We think we can grow this and raise more than a million dollars in one day.”

Prust said the ex-professional players enjoy the opportunity to play, meet fans and leverage their talents for a good cause.

“I think hockey in Canada brings everyone together,” Prust said. “We are raising money for a great cause and hockey is our sport,” “It’s a great way to get everyone together, have fun and raise money.”

stories.title: U.S. Treasury sanctions Canadian firms connected to Ryan Wedding and Iran
stories.summary: The department says it sanctioned money services businesses in British Columbia and Ontario in co-ordination with Fintrac, Canada's anti-money laundering watchdog.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The United States Treasury Department has slapped sanctions on eight Canadian businesses for allegedly helping to evade sanctions on Iran’s government.

The department says it sanctioned money services businesses in British Columbia and Ontario in co-ordination with Fintrac, Canada’s anti-money laundering watchdog.

The U.S. Treasury said several of the entities being sanctioned also worked with Ryan Wedding, the alleged drug kingpin and former Canadian Olympic snowboarder.

The department names several companies based in Ontario and British Columbia, including the Million Exchange, NIA Nations Currency, Farah Exchange, Darvish Exchange and several numbered companies.

The department alleges that Wedding used several of these services to launder millions of dollars in drug money through the transfer of digital assets before he was arrested in January.

“Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions-evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a news release.

“Treasury will pursue and disrupt the Iranian regime’s financial channels anywhere in the world.”

The sanctions are the latest in a series of moves by the United States to clamp down on financial transactions evading sanctions as it continues its war with Iran.

Wedding was arrested in Mexico in January this year and taken to the United States to face drug trafficking, murder and attempted murder charges.

He remains in federal custody awaiting two trials in March and October of next year.

A Mexican judge was arrested this week on allegations that he accepted a $2-million bribe in exchange for granting bail to a man accused of acting as second-in-command to Wedding.

The U.S. Department of Justice said Luis Benitez Alcantara is accused of unlawfully securing the release of Andrew Clark, a Canadian man alleged to have played a key role in a violent international drug trafficking ring.

Wedding is alleged to have ordered the murders of several people, including a witness who could testify against him in a 2024 narcotics case. U.S. authorities have said Wedding had been on the run for years.

Wedding represented Canada in a snowboarding slalom during the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City.

Canadian and American law enforcement officials allege that after competing in the Olympics, he became deeply involved in drug trafficking.

He was convicted in the United States of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and was sentenced to prison in 2010. U.S. authorities have alleged that after Wedding’s release from prison, he resumed drug trafficking under the protection of the Sinaloa Cartel in Mexico.

U.S. court documents said Wedding’s drug trafficking enterprise brought cocaine from Colombia into Mexico, then used semi-trailers to distribute the drug in the United States and Canada.

Eight people were also arrested in Canada a year ago as part of the U.S. investigation of Wedding.

— With files from Paola Loriggio in Toronto

stories.title: Wingham man charged for allegedly defrauding Milton church
stories.summary: A 40-year-old from Wingham has been charged with allegedly defrauding a GTA church out of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A 40-year-old from Wingham has been charged with allegedly defrauding a GTA church out of hundreds of thousands of dollars.

The Halton Regional Police allege the man, who was the former secretary of the Serbian Orthodox Diocese of Canada submitted fraudulent expense claims, and improperly redirected church fund into his personal accounts.

Police believe more than $200,000 was improperly diverted from the church.

The investigation began in August 2026. The Serbian Orthodox Diocese of Canada is based in Milton.

Anyone with information regarding this investigation is asked to contact the Financial Crimes Unit of the Halton Regional Police at 905-825-4777 ext. 8746.

November 6, 2026 at 6:12 p.m.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe says the recently released federal budget is “generally positive” for his province.

The budget addresses "a number of the priorities that Canadians have from coast to coast to coast, including those here in the province of Saskatchewan," Moe said during a Friday news conference at Saskatoon's Prairieland Park, one day after the document was released.

Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Phillipe Champagne tabled Budget 2026: Masters of our Destiny in the House of Commons on Thursday.

In a news release, Champage said the 2026 federal budget is about "unlocking investment, building more at home, strengthening our energy and natural resource advantage, and helping Canadian businesses grow and compete on the world stage."

Further investment in resource development will include Saskatchewan's potash industry, the world's No. 1 producer of fertilizer minerals.

Key changes in the federal budget include tax incentives such as the Productivity Mega Deduction, designed to jump start construction projects and investments into Canada. That incentive can reduce the financial pressure of making many capital investments, by allowing businesses to "fully write off the cost of an investment in the year that it becomes available for use," according to a government backgrounder.

The measure is expected to cost $36 billion over five years.

Moe said these incentives will be positive for Saskatchewan's industries, both medium and large. He said current projects will benefit, and added there will be more underway, "like some of the uranium mines, for example."

Montreal - A lawyer representing a man who was convicted of murder and attempted murder for attacks committed in 1984 says McGill University’s decision to revoke his admission was rushed and lacking in due process.

Lawyer Nora Demnati says the school decided to unenrol Jeffrey Ewert from its law faculty without offering him an in-person meeting or giving him a chance to fully address concerns.

Ewert, now in his 60s, was sentenced to two life sentences after he sexually assaulted and strangled two women in British Columbia in separate 1984 incidents that left one victim dead and the other severely disabled.

McGill’s provost announced earlier this week that he was no longer a student, after news he was attending law classes while on day parole sparked concern about student safety and debate over whether or not he should be allowed to attend.

Demnati says Ewart disclosed his criminal history to McGill when he applied and was accepted.

Demnati also said McGill told him its decision to rescind Ewert’s admission was based on his failure to disclose aspects of a post-release parole board decision in his admissions application.

She said that’s a retroactive and unreasonable expectation, and is urging McGill to reconsider its decision until Ewert can present his case to stay at the school.

“In a context where criminalized people turn to higher education to positively transform themselves and expand the post-release opportunities available to them, the stakes are high, and the precedent set by McGill University has important ramifications well beyond the institution,” Demnati said in a statement released Friday.

“McGill would do well to take the time to better understand the implications of their actions and to approach both process and outcome more thoughtfully.”

McGill did not immediately respond for a request for comment.

Demnati says no concerns were raised to Ewert about his presence or behaviour until he was removed from campus on Oct. 6. She said he had returned each night to the halfway house where he was staying and followed the rules of his release, including reporting friendships with women to his parole officer and disclosing his past to them. She said concerns about his behaviour were only raised after his attendance made headlines.

“Mr. Ewert’s behaviour as a McGill student, which did not raise concern when it occurred, was scrutinized after the fact through the lens of his past convictions,” she said. “As a result, he faced unconfirmed accusations and — due to their anonymous, ambiguous and delayed nature — is not in a position to either defend himself against or engage in community accountability processes to address them.”

She said both Ewert and his supporters have received death threats.

Amid the firestorm, Correctional Service Canada issued a warrant to suspend Ewert’s conditional release and confirmed he had returned to custody while the situation is being reviewed. Demnati said his arrest on Oct. 30 prevented him from making “substantive representations” to the school.

She also said McGill’s decision was not “formally” based on any student concerns.

“Rather, it is based on Mr. Ewert’s supposed failure to disclose in his admissions application — not his criminal history, which he did voluntarily despite there being no requirement to — but select aspects of a decision rendered by the Parole Board of Canada after his release in 2025,” she wrote. “This imposed an unreasonable, retroactive obligation that Mr. Ewert could not have reasonably known. Nowhere does McGill admissions guidance indicate that this kind of information is necessary or even welcome.”

She said an obligation to include parole decisions in a university application would be “dangerous” because it seems to assign the school a law enforcement and risk assessment role that it lacks the expertise to fulfil.

The lawyer also said the school failed to consider the merits of Ewert’s admission, which include “strong academic promise, decades of prisoners’ rights advocacy, an active role in developing the law through successful court challenges, peer-reviewed publications, strong reference letters and community volunteering experience.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

stories.title: From a PoW camp to the concert hall: How a heartbreaking wartime diary was set to music
stories.summary: A London-area man is delighted that a detailed diary from his father’s time in a Second World War prisoner of war camp will be presented through music this weekend.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A London-area man is delighted that a detailed diary from his father’s time in a Second World War prisoner of war camp will be presented through music this weekend.

Ken Irwin spent nearly 10 months in captivity detailing every struggle he encountered.

The pages written over 80 years ago reveal a Canadian flyer doing everything he can to survive.

On many pages, Ken wrote how he and other soldiers were just hanging on.

“And you can see the difference in the boys now. The lack of food, damp clothes, it is drafty. It is taking a toll on the size of our sick friends,” he wrote in late 1944.

Ken’s son, Barry, now holds the diary. The London-area resident and his brothers knew little of their father’s war record until he called upon them just weeks before dying from cancer in 1976.

He told them to cherish it, Barry recalled.

“He wanted to see to it that we would honour him, and see the experiences that he went through, which were just horrendous.”

Ken was a bombing aimer on a Lancaster in the late spring of 1944, when the aircraft was hit by flak returning from Frankfurt. Seven crew members were onboard.

“Only two, my dad and another chap, got out which was sad because the rest of the crew were lost,” said Barry.

Parachuting into Germany uninjured, Ken writes that he moved through the night hoping to make it back to allied lines.

On the fourth night, he was caught and sent to a prisoner of war camp in what is today southern Poland.

There he logged each day in captivity through a diary entry or a hand-drawn cartoon.

As the Soviet Army advanced in early 1945, Ken and other soldiers were forced to March nearly 1,000 kilometres towards another camp near Berlin.

Along the way, he managed to hide his diary from guards. On the trip, he wrote about seeing friends falling beside him, only to be left to die.

He also wrote about his own illness towards the end of the March.

“He thought this would be his last day because he felt so bad,” said Barry.

Ken wrote he stayed alive by dreaming of roast beef dinners at home in Canada, something he couldn’t even fathom by the time freedom came in late April 1945.

Starved and malnourished, he walked out of the camp into the arms of American soldiers.

He soon returned home and shelved his diary until that day in 1976.

Later, in the hands of his granddaughter, the diary became a family project.

In this decade, it has attracted the Amabile Choir.

They put Ken’s words of survival and sacrifice to music in a presentation that warms his son’s heart.

“It is absolutely phenomenal!”

The performance of ‘A London PoW’s Story’ takes place this Sunday at St. Peter’s Cathedral Basilica at 3 p.m.

stories.title: Mayor of Montreal suburb expresses regret over anti-Palestine comments
stories.summary: Montreal - The mayor of a Montreal suburb is expressing regret about his online comments about Palestine.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The mayor of a Montreal-area suburb posted online comments about Palestine that were “violent in nature” and have no place in society, said the disciplinary committee of the Quebec order of professional accountants in a new ruling.

The disciplinary committee said it was ordering Hampstead Mayor Jeremy Levi to pay a $30,000 fine and undergo mandatory training, noting that his comments posted on social media in 2024 and 2025 undermined the reputation of the accounting profession.

stories.title: Justin Trudeau accepts fellowship at Oxford University
stories.summary: The former prime minister will join the school's World Leaders Circle on a roster that includes Jacinda Ardern of New Zealand and the United Kingdom's Rishi Sunak.
stories.author: Adshayah Sathiaseelan
stories.content:
The former prime minister will join the school’s World Leaders Circle on a roster that includes Jacinda Ardern of New Zealand and the United Kingdom’s Rishi Sunak.

ByAdshayah Sathiaseelan Staff Reporter

Justin Trudeau’s latest move since leaving politics is taking him across the Atlantic, where the former prime minister has landed a fellowship at Oxford University.

The university announced Friday that Trudeau has joined its Blavatnik School of Government as a distinguished fellow and member of the World Leaders Circle.

The World Leaders Circle is an “international network of former heads of government, whose experience and insight shape the Blavatnik School’s work to improve governance around the world,” the university said in a release.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

Trudeau, who served as Canada’s prime minister for a decade before resigning in January 2025, joins a roster of former world leaders that includes Jacinda Ardern of New Zealand and the United Kingdom’s Rishi Sunak.

“In the decade that I was prime minister, the world went through profound change both geopolitically and technologically, which fundamentally reshaped our world,” Trudeau said in a statement released by Oxford.

He said he looks forward to sharing his experiences, as well as engaging with the next generation of government and policy leaders.

The Blavatnik School’s dean said Trudeau is expected to visit Oxford later this month.

The university said fellows will mentor students and alumni, while exploring new approaches to government.

The appointment is the latest venture for Trudeau. In September, he announced the launch of a production company, Hope & Hard Work, with his former chief of staff Katie Telford at the Toronto International Film Festival. The pair unveiled plans for film and television projects focused on Canadian stories.

Since leaving Parliament Hill, the 54-year-old has also offered glimpses into his personal life on social media, including travels with his girlfriend, pop star Katy Perry, and support for his son Xavier’s budding music career.

Adshayah Sathiaseelan is a staff reporter with the Star. She can be reached at asathiaseelan@thestar.ca.

stories.title: Minister says tax credits will spur investment to expand electricity grid
stories.summary: Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says she’s confident billions of dollars in tax credits in the new federal budget will encourage private investment to build out Canada’s electricity grid.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says she’s confident billions of dollars in tax credits in the new federal budget will encourage private investment to build out Canada’s electricity grid.

Thursday’s federal budget committed $50 billion to help implement Ottawa’s electricity strategy, which looks to double the size of the grid by 2050. More than $38 billion was committed to tax credits the government says will stay in place until 2042.

Speaking to The Canadian Press on Thursday, Dabrusin said the measures came from government consultations on the electricity strategy.

“These are the things that people have set out for us when we have done consultations,” she said.

“We put out our electricity strategy earlier this year. This is what was told to us is what was needed, and I think that this is a huge step forward for how we build up clean energy for our country.”

Thursday’s budget included measures to extend the existing Clean Technology and Clean Electricity Investment tax credits to the end of 2040 — the former was supposed to be phased out in 2034. The budget also proposed to expand eligibility for the latter tax credit “for the highest-voltage intra-provincial electricity transmission lines in each province” for property acquired.

The budget also signalled Ottawa’s intent to update the Clean Electricity Regulations. The government said the goal is to introduce flexibility into the current system.

That includes allowing power plants to operate for longer and laying the groundwork for the government’s planned LNG buildout, as Ottawa indicated in its electricity strategy.

The strategy, released in May, placed a heavy emphasis on expanding the role of natural gas in powering the grid.

“Under some interpretations of the current electricity regulations, it would be difficult to build some additional natural gas that would complement much bigger builds,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said at the time.

“We have some of the cheapest gas in the world in Canada,” he said, citing natural gas as an affordability play in the strategy. Carney said at the time the strategy had a goal of lowering energy costs for 70 per cent of Canadian households.

The budget also promised $4 billion over 10 years for electricity infrastructure, including new funding for a Natural Resources program to expand renewable energy.

That program has paid out more than $1.3 billion for more than 100 projects dating back to 2021.

In a media statement, Clean Energy Canada, a think tank out of Simon Fraser University, welcomed the focus on building clean electricity supply but said the government must set clear goals.

“Today’s federal budget provides significant investments in electrifying Canada’s economy and households, but further work will be required to establish the concrete goals needed to fully realize a generational opportunity,” executive director Rachel Doran said.

“While moving from plans to action is critical, without concrete goals, Canada risks trading a climate plan with an accountability metric to one that is a list of actions without a final destination.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

stories.title: U.S. Treasury sanctions Canadian firms connected to Ryan Wedding
stories.summary: Ottawa - The United States Treasury Department has slapped sanctions on eight Canadian businesses for allegedly helping to evade sanctions on Iran's government.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The United States Treasury Department has slapped sanctions on eight Canadian businesses for allegedly helping to evade sanctions on Iran’s government.

The department says it sanctioned money services businesses in British Columbia and Ontario in co-ordination with Fintrac, Canada’s anti-money laundering watchdog.

The U.S. Treasury said several of the entities being sanctioned also worked with Ryan Wedding, the alleged drug kingpin and former Canadian Olympic snowboarder.

The department names several companies based in Ontario and British Columbia, including the Million Exchange, NIA Nations Currency, Farah Exchange, Darvish Exchange and several numbered companies.

The department alleges that Wedding used several of these services to launder millions of dollars in drug money through the transfer of digital assets before he was arrested in January.

“Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions-evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a news release.

“Treasury will pursue and disrupt the Iranian regime’s financial channels anywhere in the world.”

The sanctions are the latest in a series of moves by the United States to clamp down on financial transactions evading sanctions as it continues its war with Iran.

Wedding was arrested in Mexico in January this year and taken to the United States to face drug trafficking, murder and attempted murder charges.

He remains in federal custody awaiting two trials in March and October of next year.

A Mexican judge was arrested this week on allegations that he accepted a $2-million bribe in exchange for granting bail to a man accused of acting as second-in-command to Wedding.

The U.S. Department of Justice said Luis Benitez Alcantara is accused of unlawfully securing the release of Andrew Clark, a Canadian man alleged to have played a key role in a violent international drug trafficking ring.

Wedding is alleged to have ordered the murders of several people, including a witness who could testify against him in a 2024 narcotics case.

U.S. authorities have said Wedding had been on the run for years.

Wedding represented Canada in a snowboarding slalom during the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City.

Canadian and American law enforcement officials allege that after competing in the Olympics, he became deeply involved in drug trafficking.

He was convicted in the United States of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and was sentenced to prison in 2010. U.S. authorities have alleged that after Wedding’s release from prison, he resumed drug trafficking under the protection of the Sinaloa Cartel in Mexico.

U.S. court documents said Wedding’s drug trafficking enterprise brought cocaine from Colombia into Mexico, then used semi-trailers to distribute the drug in the United States and Canada.

Eight people were also arrested in Canada a year ago as part of the U.S. investigation of Wedding.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

— With files from Paola Loriggio in Toronto

stories.title: Alek Minassian, convicted in deadly 2018 Toronto van attack, drops appeal
stories.summary: Ontario's top court says Alek Minassian has abandoned the appeal of his convictions on 10 counts of first-degree murder and 16 of attempted murder.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The man who carried out a deadly van attack in Toronto eight years ago is no longer challenging his more than two dozen convictions.

Ontario’s top court says Alek Minassian has abandoned the appeal of his convictions on 10 counts of first-degree murder and 16 of attempted murder.

Minassian had filed a notice of appeal in July 2022, about a month after he was sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for 25 years.

He was also sentenced to 20 years for 15 counts of attempted murder, to be served concurrently.

Eight women and two men died on April 23, 2018, when Minassian — enraged that women wouldn’t sleep with him and radicalized online — deliberately drove a rented van down a crowded sidewalk in his quest for infamy.

He admitted at trial that he planned and executed the attack, but argued that he should be found not criminally responsible due to his autism spectrum disorder.

Prosecutors, meanwhile, argued Minassian is a mass killer who knew right from wrong and happens to also have autism.

The presiding judge, Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy, rejected the defence’s argument that Minassian never developed empathy as a result of his autism and was unable to make rational decisions.

The 10 people killed in the rampage were Ji Hun Kim, 22; So He Chung, 22; Anne Marie D’Amico, 30; Andrea Bradden, 33; Chul Min “Eddie” Kang, 45; Renuka Amarasingha, 45; Dorothy Sewell, 80; Geraldine Brady, 83; Munir Najjar, 85; and Mary Elizabeth “Betty” Forsyth, 94.

Another victim, Amaresh Tesfamariam, died in 2021 from injuries sustained in the attack.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Canada’s $6B Csis boost fuels speculation over foreign intelligence plans
stories.summary: Experts say that the Canadian government is “absolutely” considering a new branch to collect foreign human intelligence, akin to Britain’s MI6.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is revealing few details about the plans for a massive $6 billion budget boost to Canada’s domestic spy agency.

The new funding for the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis), to be doled out over the next decade, came as a surprise to national security watchers in Thursday’s federal budget.

The budget documents devoted a few short sentences to how the biggest cash injection in the agency’s history will be used, other than it will allow Csis to better “engage” Canadians and protect against threats like terrorism, foreign interference and espionage.

Both Csis and Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree deferred questions about the budget plans to Finance Canada. In response to Global News questions, Finance Canada spokesperson David Barnabe sent an email restating the language from Thursday’s budget documents.

The size of budget boost, coupled with the sparse details provided by the government, fueled speculation among national security researchers about whether the money could be used to create a foreign intelligence gathering branch within Csis, a longstanding topic of debate among Canada’s intelligence community.

Stephanie Carvin, a professor at the Norman Paterson School for International Affairs at Carleton University and a former Csis analyst, said that both the National Security Strategy and the significant boost to the agency’s resources suggest the government is planning some foreign intelligence “capability.”

Carvin also pointed to comments Friday from Dominic Rochon, a top national security official in the Privy Council, who suggested the government was planning legislative changes to the Csis Act.

“All of this suggests, at the very least, the creation of a foreign human intelligence capability, probably within an existing agency like Csis,” Carvin said.

Currently, the agency is limited in what intelligence it can gather abroad and instead focuses more narrowly on Canada. Csis largely cannot recruit human sources abroad to gain insight into foreign governments’ plans, and Canada does not have a dedicated foreign intelligence agency like most close allies do — think MI6 in the U.K., or the CIA in the U.S.

That needs to change, according to longtime intelligence researcher Wesley Wark, who said he believed serious discussions are taking place within government about creating a foreign human intelligence capability.

“It May strike some people as odd in this world of high tech that you would go back to this kind of classic model of intelligence collection, but the reality is that almost all of our allies that run such agencies continue to say that it is an important methodology,” Wark said in an interview Friday.

“I think … undoubtedly it’s being given serious consideration. I think the chances of the decision being taken that would be favourable to some kind of startup are certainly greater than 50 per cent, now, and that’s a higher proportion than its ever been certainly in my lifetime.”

Wark agreed that many of the senior intelligence officials who would be advising Carney on the idea would likely be warm to the idea of Canada having its own foreign intelligence capabilities.

David Morrison, the deputy secretary to cabinet for national security and intelligence, is the former deputy minister of Global Affairs Canada. Csis Director Daniel Rogers also has a background in foreign intelligence, having served as a senior official at the Communications Security Establishment (CSE) responsible for signals intelligence collection.

One line within the budget does suggest Carney’s government wants to reduce the reliance on foreign intelligence provided by allies like the U.S.

Canada is a member of the Five Eyes security alliance, which includes the U.S., U.K., Australia and New Zealand. Among allied nations, Canada is a net importer of intelligence — meaning it receives more intelligence from partners than it collects and shares.

In the government’s recently released National Security Strategy, Carney repeatedly stressed the need for “sovereign” capabilities to reduce Canada’s reliance on intelligence garnered from allies.

The “rupture” represented by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration to the Canada-U.S. relationship is not explicitly mentioned, but can be read between the prime minister’s lines.

“The long-held belief that the combination of our geography, interconnectedness, and a rules-based international order could substitute for Canadian sovereign capacity to protect ourselves is no longer tenable,” Carney’s introduction to the strategy reads.

“Once distant threats are now proximate and immediate. The global order that long protected our sovereignty has ruptured. We are prepared to protect Canada’s sovereignty, and when it is threatened, we will act.”

stories.title: London leaders praise federal budget support for municipalities
stories.summary: Local leaders are buzzing over Thursday’s federal budget they say did not disappoint.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Local leaders are buzzing over Thursday’s federal budget they say did not disappoint.

It includes everything from financial support for a new rec centre to solving homelessness within 10 years.

Municipalities across Canada had been united in their call for the homelessness issue to be a nation building project.

Now the federal government has committed $11.2 billion dollars over four years starting in 2027-2028, plus $17.8 billion in future years toward ending homelessness within 10 years.

London Mayor Josh Morgan says it will need all hands on deck.

“To meet and put these federal dollars to work we’re going to need more operating dollars for the facilities that can be built across the country. Mental health and addiction facilities. More supportive housing. These types of things that actually get people off the street and into the care they need,” Morgan said.

London Chamber of Commerce CEO Graham Henderson says addressing homelessness is directly tied to the health of downtown.

“This is a concern that people constantly raise when they’re being asked, ‘do you want to go downtown, do you want to come downtown, do you want to work downtown. No I don’t because, dot dot dot.’ That doesn’t mean we don’t care. We do care. It has to be treated compassionately. The two go together,” Henderson said.

Much of the government’s support during the trade war with the Trump administration has been targeted toward big industry, such as steel and auto. But in this federal budget, there is also support for small business.

It comes on the heels of a London idea to create a tariff response service to help small businesses navigate tariff rules.

“The budget recognizes the importance of that. It specifically talks about the need to assist local chambers in assisting smaller businesses with this issue,” said Henderson.

Civic leaders also point to support for housing and infrastructure, including funding they hope will help London complete its transit network.

The budget also specifically pledges support for a rec centre in Northwest London.

“I want to commend our local MPs for the advocacy work they have done to get that in there. Huge need in the northwest. We expect when we build this facility it will have over 300,000 visits a year to meet the growing need in a growing part of the city,” said Morgan.

stories.title: Unifor believes Stellantis has finalized sale of Brampton assembly plant to Roshel
stories.summary: Sale of facility that shuttered in 2023 is expected to be announced next week, source says
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
The Unifor union says it believes automaker Stellantis NV Stla-N has finalized the sale of its idled assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., to defence contractor Roshel Inc.

A source familiar with the matter said the sale of the plant is expected to be announced early next week. The source, whom The Globe and Mail is not identifying because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter, said the plan is for Stellantis to sell the plant to Brampton-based Roshel and lease it back for production purposes. The source declined to elaborate. It is not clear what Stellantis would do with the plant.

Unifor, which represents about 3,000 workers who were laid off almost three years ago at the factory near Toronto, said it met with the automaker Friday and the company would not confirm or deny the sale was final.

“Unifor is interpreting this refusal as confirmation that the Brampton Assembly Plant has been sold,” Lana Payne, Unifor’s national president, said in a statement to The Globe.

Stellantis spokesperson LouAnn Gosselin said the automaker had “nothing to announce” on Friday afternoon.

Roshel declined to comment.

As part of the arrangement to sell the plant, Stellantis would also pay back money to the federal government it received to retool the facility after it closed in 2023, the source said.

Stellantis, which makes Dodge, Chrysler and several other brands, said in the summer it had a preliminary agreement to sell to Roshel . Stellantis repeated this in a statement to The Globe on Thursday.

The automaker planned to make the Jeep Compass at the factory but last year shifted this plan to its plant in Illinois. That angered the union and the federal government, which said Stellantis was violating the terms of its funding arrangement.

Unifor walked away from collective bargaining with Stellantis in September over the planned sale.

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada and the office of Industry Minister Mélanie Joly did not respond to The Globe’s e-mails.

Fraser Johnson, a professor at Western University’s Ivey School of Business, said the sale is apparently part of Stellantis’s efforts to solve its company-wide challenges. “Stellantis globally has huge problems with poor profits, low vehicle sales and too much capacity.”

The U.S. tariffs made the business case for operating the plant even more doubtful, Prof. Johnson said.

For Roshel, the sale is an attractive opportunity to purchase a world-class facility that rarely presents itself, he said.

But a plant operated by Roshel, which makes relatively small production runs of armoured vehicles, will not provide the same employment, supply chain purchases or other economic benefits as an auto assembly operation, Prof. Johnson said. “There’s a significant number of people affected by this.”

stories.title: Pitching in: Bringing fitness to young mental-health patients at Sunnybrook Hospital
stories.summary: After his daughter was diagnosed with bipolar II, John Bain teamed up with Evan Wallman, a fitness trainer, to help patients get active
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizers: John Bain and Evan Wallman

The pitch: Raising $93,000 and climbing

The cause: A fitness program for young mental-health patients

When John Bain’s daughter took up competitive swimming in high school she experienced so much anxiety that she eventually had to be admitted to Toronto’s Sunnybrook Hospital.

“It was Grade 11 when she basically had what we used to call a breakdown,” Mr. Bain, 60, recalled from his home in Toronto where he works as a tax partner at Kpmg. His daughter was diagnosed with bipolar II, a less intense form of bipolar I which involves recurring mood swings. It’s treatable, Mr. Bain added, and his daughter is now thriving.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Mr. Bain was working out with a personal trainer, Evan Wallman, when they began talking about the importance of exercise to mental health. Mr. Bain’s daughter had mentioned that she’d found exercising helpful at the hospital but there was no structured program.

Mr. Wallman had already reached out to some psychiatrists to see if their patients might benefit from physical activity. “And then John said, “They’re not doing anything on the ward at Sunnybrook. How about I start a fund, a program there, and you go and try to get them moving?” Mr. Wallman recalled.

Mr. Bain started raising money and they came up with a concept in 2023. They took it to the hospital and after months of hashing out the details, Mr. Wallman started a fitness program on the 10-bed youth mental-health ward in 2024. He spends a couple of hours twice a week on the ward, working with patients on activities as varied as boxing, yoga, weight training and incline hiking.

They’ve raised $93,000 to cover equipment costs and Mr. Wallman’s training sessions, which have become an integral part of the hospital’s treatment along with art therapy and music. They hope the hospital will takeover the funding one day, but for now they’re committed to raising as much as possible.

Mr. Bain still marvels at the role fitness played in his daughter’s recovery. “I can’t say enough about how she’s been able to leverage physical activity and set herself goals. It’s been amazing,” he said.

Mr. Wallman said he was skeptical about the program at first, but now finds it fulfilling. “When you see them smiling and having fun, singing and laughing, and when they say how this is impactful for them, I’m like, ‘Okay, I can keep doing this’.”

St-Pierre Plamondon was travelling to Toronto for personal and family reasons and took the opportunity to reach out to Ford for a meeting.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford speaks at the Grand Cru Culinary Wine Festival at Toronto's Enercare Centre on Oct. 29, 2026.

Catherine Lévesque

November 6, 2026 at 4:29 p.m.

Ottawa — While Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon would not travel to Ottawa or Montreal to hold a first in-person meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney, he has agreed to meet with Ontario Premier Doug Ford in Toronto.

St-Pierre Plamondon and Ford were expected to meet at a luxurious Toronto hotel on Friday at 5 p.m. for a private meeting. There was initially speculation from Quebec officials about the premiers meeting at Queen’s Park, but that changed hours prior.

The Quebec premier’s spokesman, Alex Boissonneault, told Montreal radio station 98,5 FM that St-Pierre Plamondon was already travelling to Toronto for personal and family reasons this weekend and he took the opportunity to reach out to Ford for a meeting.

Both men had spoken on the phone after St-Pierre Plamondon’s victory last month.

Boissonneault said it was always the intention for both premiers to rapidly convene a meeting, since Quebec and Ontario have close economic ties. He also said it is fortunate that this encounter is happening the day after the federal budget.

The Quebec government has been grumbling about the lack of increase in federal health transfers and Ottawa’s unilateral decision to create a “productivity mega deduction” that would deprive Quebec of $1 billion per year.

St-Pierre Plamondon will probably hope to find an ally in Ford to push Ottawa for more funds, but Ford has generally been in agreement with many of Carney’s decisions.

There is no expectation of a photo opportunity or media availability after the meeting.

Ford had developed a close relationship with former Quebec premier François Legault during his tenure. They were photographed sipping beers — Ford’s was a non-alcoholic one — on the margins of an economic recovery summit in Toronto in 2020.

The photo had sparked controversy because Legault and Ford, even though they were outside, were not respecting the social distancing rules during the pandemic.

“Our mouths remained more than two meters apart,” justified Legault at the time.

Even though St-Pierre Plamondon and Ford will probably remain cordial in public, it remains unlikely that they will become as good friends since both are on opposite sides about whether Canada should remain a united country or Quebec should separate from it.

Back in January, Ford said “it would be a disaster for our countryif the separatists got elected,” referring to St-Pierre Plamondon’s Parti Québécois leading in the polls.

The PQ leader shot back, saying Ford was putting on a “bad show” and that it was “a bit of a caricature” for the premier of Ontario to suddenly tell Quebecers how to vote.

Ford changed his tune after St-Pierre Plamondon formed government in October.

Speaking to reporters after a meeting with Carney in Ottawa, Ford said he was looking forward to paying St-Pierre Plamondon a visit to discuss how Quebec and Ontario could grow their economies together.

“I love Quebecers,” he said. “There’s some connection there. I have come to the conclusion they’re passionate. They’re fighters. I’m passionate. I’m a fighter, and I just connect with them. So, we look forward to working with the premier.”

“What’s more important than anything to Quebecers and Ontarians is certainty and stability and jobs. And that’s what we’re going to work together on,” he added.

Things have not gone as smoothly with Carney, who will be meeting with St-Pierre Plamondon during the Francophonie Summit in Cambodia later in November.

Carney had offered for them to meet in the Ottawa-Gatineau area or in Montreal, but St-Pierre Plamondon insisted Carney travel to the capital of his province because of a provincial law that claims important meetings should take place in Quebec City.

Carney might pay a visit to the premier in Quebec City later this year.

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

stories.title: Carney says Canada welcomes ‘any moves’ to restore free trade after U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government welcomes "any moves" to restore free trade between Canada and the United States as officials south of the border push to end the trade war.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government welcomes “any moves” to restore free trade between Canada and the United States as officials south of the border push to end the trade war.

In the days since the U.S. midterm elections gave the Democrats firm control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, several party officials have indicated repealing President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian products is a priority.

They include Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon who is expected to chair the Senate finance committee when the new Congress is seated in January. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Wyden was already talking to colleagues about legislation to combat Trump’s tariffs, including those on Canada.

Even if a bill is introduced, Trump retains the power to block it by issuing a veto. The president’s veto can only be overridden by a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress.

The Democrats likely will need more than 20 Republicans in the House, and 10 to 12 Republicans in the Senate, to vote with them to override a Trump veto. Some Republicans have said they know the tariffs are among the reasons their party lost.

“Tariffs have made everything too expensive,” longtime Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz said in his post-midterms statement.

Ahead of the elections, some Republican candidates also broke with Trump over his trade war with Canada, including failed Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers. Rogers loudly backed the tariffs in the summer but changed his tune in October.

Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rogers, has said ending what he called the “stupid tariffs on Canada” is among his priorities.

Speaking to reporters Friday, Carney said he hasn’t spoken with Democrats about plans to introduce legislation to end the tariffs.

He said a free-trade agreement is in the interests of both Canadians and Americans and his government will continue to work with Washington to get a deal that serves Canada.

“We welcome any moves to restore a free trading arrangement between Canada and the United States, which is in the interests of American families struggling with affordability. It’s in the interest of American workers looking for good, high-paying jobs and it’s fundamentally in the interest of Canadians,” said Carney.

Before the midterm results were known on Tuesday, Carney said more formal talks with the U.S. were restarting following a call with Trump. The prime minister indicated the Trump administration had softened its position and said the Americans were “asking less” and “offering more.”

Conservative MP Jamil Jivani, who has visited Washington in an attempt to move forward Canada-U.S. trade negotiations, said Ottawa still needs to find ways to work with Trump.

“I would love nothing more than for us to be able to get this done and move on because we got a lot of problems in our own country we need to solve,” said Jivani. “This whole U.S. thing has become a massive distraction from a lot of our own domestic issues.”

After trade talks between Canada and the U.S. collapsed in August, Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs on specific American imports.

Trump again escalated trade tensions the following month by banning imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some liquor and whey products.

Last month, Trump lifted some tariffs on Canadian exports while adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.

A U.S. food importer also filed a legal challenge of Trump’s use of a Depression-era trade statute — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — to hit Canada with the heavy duties and trade embargoes.

Politicians on both sides of the border are looking at the midterm elections results as an opportunity to rebuild the Canada-U.S. relationship.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Wednesday the Liberal government’s push to diversify trade won’t change direction in the midterms’ wake. He also said recent talks with Trump’s administration have been productive and he looks forward to speaking more with his American counterparts in the coming days.

Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller would become White House chief of staff. Miller currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.

After Carney met with Trump in Washington in May 2025, Miller told Fox News that it was like “watching a grandmaster in chess perform.”

“President Trump has opened up a completely new relationship with Canada because of his strength and because of his diplomacy,” he said.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Friday there is a need to address the sectoral tariffs that have been hitting Canadians “extremely hard,” including those on steel and aluminum.

Anand added that Canada has to “keep going with asserting Canadian interests.”

“We are standing for Canadian sovereignty, Canadian domestic economic resilience and our strategic autonomy,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

— With files from Kyle Duggan, Kelly Geraldine Malone and The Associated Press

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press
