content_blocks.text: Truro, N.S. – Eli MacKinnon was just 13 when he was sexually assaulted while in P.E.I.’s care. Nearly seven years later, he’s still dealing with the ripple effects of what happened and, even more so, how the province handled it.

Now 20 and living in Nova Scotia, MacKinnon is coming forward about his experience while he was living at a provincial group home for teens during an eight-month period stemming from tensions with his mother. According to documents related to his case, another minor, also in the province’s care, sexually touched him without his consent during an outing at a Charlottetown pool on Dec. 30, 2019. But MacKinnon says there were multiple instances spanning several days, including in rooms that were supposed to be supervised by staff.
“It’s been hard to have friends and have relationships too, with family,” he said. “I just became a very angry person for a long time. Depressed.”

MacKinnon disclosed what happened to a youth worker, triggering procedures and a safety plan was implemented. But he says that plan didn’t do enough to protect him – and more than five years after the assault, Child Protection Services agreed.

In a letter dated July 3, 2025, P.E.I.’s child protection director, Mike Henthorn, and children’s services manager, Cheryl Jamieson, recognized shortcomings in their division’s handling of the incident, and that they contributed to emotional distress that might still be taking a toll.
“We again offer our deep regret and our apologies for not doing more to support you in these areas,” the pair wrote.
Later that year, in November 2025, P.E.I.’s Office of the Ombudsperson also agreed the division’s response had been unfair.

“I am very sorry for what you experienced,” wrote deputy ombudsperson Matthew Chapman. “I hope that you can take some small comfort in knowing that you have helped improve an important service for Island children.”
Steps taken and not taken

According to the Child Protection Services letter, MacKinnon’s mother was informed following the incident, along with a counsellor to offer support. A child protection social worker conducted interviews and consulted with police. The division encouraged discussions about deciding if and when to report the incident to officers. It also ensured extra staff were present at the group home to supervise his contact with the other youth.

But MacKinnon says his mother was informed what happened too late, a couple days after the incident. He says his calls for the other youth to be moved to another group home were dismissed, even though taunting and inappropriate comments persisted.
“I didn’t want him near me,” he said.
His main complaint, however, is that police weren’t contacted for a proper investigation, while more evidence could have potentially been collected.
It wasn’t until spring 2022 that MacKinnon made a formal complaint to police. He says the experience was “eating (him) up inside.”

The other youth was charged with sexual assault, and on the Crown’s recommendation completed extrajudicial sanctions, according to the provincial letter. Those are measures outside the traditional court process for those aged 12-17 to take responsibility for an offence.

Child protection law expert Rollie Thompson said the most important thing about these investigations is that they’re done quickly, using careful, non-leading questions and interviewing the young people separately.

“Before others can pollute what they have to say or influence it, before details start getting lost,” said Thompson, an emeritus professor who co-teaches a child protection law course at Dalhousie University’s Schulich School of Law.
In their letter, leaders at P.E.I.’s Child Protection Services recognized that MacKinnon had expressed feeling unsafe, writing that “more could have been done” to support his emotional well-being.
That included setting up an immediate interview with police and moving the other youth while the allegations were formally investigated.
Today, Child Protection Services’ approach to addressing similar reports has evolved, operating under a different legal framework.
OmbudsPEI’s letter says the division has since adopted practices requiring police interviews and promptly separating children when one alleges a sexual assault by another.

Asked about those procedures, the province said it separates the youths involved while a report is assessed and investigated. It said interview timelines depend on the circumstances of each case and the child’s needs and safety.

In September 2024, the Child, Youth and Family Services Act came into effect. Consistent with United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, it gives children’s views about decisions affecting them due weight in accordance with their age and maturity. It also empowers them to raise concerns or recommendations.

“Care plans are developed in collaboration with children and youth, their social workers and, where appropriate, their families and support networks,” a spokesperson for P.E.I.’s Department of Social Development and Seniors told CTV News in a statement. She added that staff receive specialized training that aligns with the Act, with social work procedures being revised to embed a rights-based approach throughout.
The province’s child and youth advocate, Marvin Bernstein, has called it “historic, groundbreaking and aspirational,” leading the way for this kind of legislation in Canada.
Thompson agrees there’s been progress – but says previous rules set a low bar.

“It was such a flawed statute it wouldn’t take much to improve it,” he said. “The fact of the matter is those are just good principles. The older the child the more they should have a say. That’s not rocket science.”
Thompson says the real test of any measures is whether they’re consistently put into practice. High caseloads, staff turnover and a shrinking supply of foster homes make that harder, he says.

This summer, MacKinnon filed complaints against two social workers with the P.E.I. Social Work Registration Board related to how his case was handled. In September, the registrar referred them to an investigation committee. And next week, MacKinnon says he’s meeting with that committee.
Both social workers deny any wrongdoing, unprofessional conduct or unethical behaviour.
“I think if somebody does something wrong, especially if they have authority over children or anybody who doesn’t have a say, they should be held accountable as far as it can go,” MacKinnon said.
His hope is that if another child goes through what he did, they’ll be heard and taken seriously when they ask for help.

stories.title: How U.S mid-terms are shaping the stock market
stories.summary: Now that the results of the U.S mid-terms are in, attention has shifted to how those results are influencing s...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
Now that the results of the U.S mid-terms are in , attention has shifted to how those results are influencing stock markets on both sides of the border.

The Democrats’ strong showing in the 2026 U.S midterms could impact the direction of key policies, including U.S tariffs and trade measures. The transfer of power is leading to new opportunities for investments and businesses.

With Canada’s economy closely tied to the United States, the mid-term results are already affecting the stock market. The S&P/TSX Composite Index soared by 809.12 points (2.28%), to close at 36,341.40 on Nov. 4th.

Other notable stock gains include:

Photo Credit: Matt Johnson / CC

Air Canada (AC.TO) is up 6.54%

Colliers International Group Inc: up 8.01%

WSP Global Inc: 5.37%

FirstService Corp: 4.96%

Agnico Eagle Mines Ltd: 3.30%

Sharmistha Nag, from the Lawrence Kinlin School of Business is cautious when asked about the changes in the market .

She notes the importance of the Democrats now having control of both chambers of U.S. Congress – the House and Senate – for the rest of Republican President Donald Trump’s term.

One area of concern for Nag is investments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and technology. Following the Democrats’ win, the party shared plans to push for strict rules, enforcing safety standards and building stronger data center security.

Nag worries that “We May not see that AI boom given the restrictions that May be put in place.” Nag notes the potential restrictions will have impacts on Canadian investors, specifically those invested in technology.

The U.S midterms have created renewed hope and also uncertainty for investors.

stories.title: Western grads receive 2026 Governor General’s Gold Medal
stories.summary: Three Western University grads earn 2026 Governor General’s gold medal for academic excellence in their research fields.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Three Western graduates are among the recipients of this year’s Governor General’s Academic Medals. Since 1873, the awards have recognized outstanding students across Canada.

Western PhD graduates Deanne Wah, Gezheng Xu and Julia Yates have received the Gold Medal, awarded for academic excellence at the graduate level.

In a series of experiments, they examined the foundational cognitive processes involved in reading. This research included the use of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to link brain activity to computational models of reading in both healthy adult readers and children learning to read.

Their studies demonstrated key differences in how children with dyslexia represent the spelling and sound of written words and how these representations align with the predictions of a computational model of reading. Their findings significantly enhance our understanding of the neuropsychological foundations that support the uniquely human capacity for reading. The research also informs critical developments in educational practices related to the identification and treatment of dyslexia.

Wah is currently a psychologist at the Thames Valley District School Board.

Gezheng Xu completed her PhD in the department of computer science at Western, supervised by professors Boyu Wang and Charles Ling.

Throughout her doctoral studies, Xu has published 25 peer-reviewed articles in leading international conferences and journals. Her research received spotlight distinctions at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (2022), the International Conference on Learning Representations (2023) and the International Conference on Machine Learning (2026), highlighting the significance of her contributions. Her excellence in research and teaching has also been recognized through Western’s Robert and Ruth Lumsden Graduate Award, the Fields Postdoctoral Fellowship Award and the Graduate Student Teaching Award. Xu was also named a Rising Star in Foundations of AI Research by the University of Warwick and the Oxford Ellis Unit, the only researcher from Canada to receive this recognition.

Xu currently continues to advance trustworthy AI at Western and will soon join the University of Oxford as a postdoctoral researcher, where she will expand its applications to scientific discovery.

Yates’ work was supposed by a Sshrc Canada Graduate Scholarship, and she was recognized with internal, external and tri-council awards to support the dissemination of this important work.

During her graduate studies, Yates published 41 articles in peer-reviewed journals, authored three encyclopedia chapters, delivered over 50 presentations at local, national and international meetings or conferences and provided 23 integrated knowledge translation presentations for various organizations across Canada.

Yates is currently a Killam Postdoctoral Fellow in the department of community health and epidemiology at Dalhousie University.

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: What does it take to satisfy Gta’s sweet tooth during Diwali?
stories.summary: We went inside a massive sweets fair to find out
stories.author: Zahra Khozema, Photography by Laura Proctor
stories.content:
The mithai mela – or sweets market – wasn’t the original destination for Balwinder Sandhu and her 20-year-old daughter, Saaj. The two had stopped by the Indian restaurant Punjabi by Nature for pakoras but couldn’t resist exploring the colourful tent in the middle of a Brampton parking lot.

A soaring cherry blossom tree anchored the arches under swathes of bright fabrics and fairy lights. Punjabi music drowned out all else.

The mela at Brampton's Punjabi by Nature's Gore Road location is set up in a parking lot.

Inside, gloves on and boxes in hand, shoppers made their way down rows of yellow ladoos and perfectly squared milk cakes. Some carefully picked their favourite mithai.

Others piled boxes high. Brampton resident Ms. Sandhu, who has lived in Canada for 33 years, says celebrating traditions remains important to her, as is bringing all three of her adult children to the gurdwara and cultural events such as this.

This mela, which sits on Gore Road near several places of worship including the Hindu Sabha Mandir and a gurdwara, is expected to have around 150,000 visitors during the week-long festival going until Nov. 8.

Many shoppers stop in to buy mithai before heading to prayers, then return for more sweets and gift boxes to share with family and friends, says Nisarg Barot, marketing manager at Punjabi by Nature.

The setup is just one part of a bigger Diwali operation spanning 10 locations across the GTA and Kitchener, Ont., up from eight last year. But it all began as a small tent outside the restaurant nearly 15 years ago.

To prepare for the Diwali rush, Punjabi by Nature has stocked over a million empty boxes across its locations. At this time of year, more than 200 varieties of sweets are on offer compared to the roughly 120 throughout the year.

And milk cakes – a dense, fudge-like mithai with a grainy texture – take the cake as the best seller. Mr. Barot estimates the company makes 10 to 15 times as much of it as any other sweet, with trays sometimes emptying within 15 minutes.

Keeping them full is a job in itself. More than 100 workers are involved in making mithai during the festive season. Production runs in shifts and refrigerated trucks deliver fresh stock from their local factory several times a day.

Chef Ajab Sandhu, who has been with Punjabi by Nature's Gore Road location for more than 15 years, makes the very popular jalebi.

Outside, oil sizzles as chefs squeeze ribbons of batter made from flour, water and baking powder onto a giant pan, twisting them into bright spirals. A quick dip in sugar syrup and the jalebis are ready.

“It’s such a famous dish, kids like it, adults like it, everyone likes it,” said Charanjit Singh, one of the two chefs making the popular sweet here. He’s been doing it for five years and by the end of his 9-to-9 shift, his wrists often ache.

This weekend, he expects to go through about 200 kilograms of batter as lines stretch around the plaza.

For Shristi Sharma, the mela is a reminder of Diwali celebrations back home in India. She drove in from North York with her husband Himanshu and their nine-year-old son Yuvaan after spotting the event on social media.

The family moved to Canada about four years ago and spent their first few years focused on work and settling in, leaving little time to celebrate festivals. Now, she wants Yuvan, who was four and a half when they arrived, to experience more of the traditions she grew up with.

“Here, you have all those vibes that you miss,” she said.

stories.title: Health Canada approves Moderna’s combined COVID, flu shot for some
stories.summary: Both of the vaccines are only approved for Canadians aged 50 and older, and it's not clear yet when they might be available to get at your pharmacy.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Health Canada has approved Moderna’s combined influenza and COVID-19 vaccine as well its mRNA shot for seasonal influenza.

Canada’s top health agency says mFLUSIVA, an mRNA flu vaccine, as well as mCOFLU, a combination influenza and COVID-19 shot, can both now be used for adults 50 years of age and older.

In August, the mRNA flu shot was approved for use in the United States and in April, the combination jab was approved for use in Europe, but Canada is the first country to approve both, Moderna said in a statement.

“Health Canada’s authorizations of mFLUSIVA and mCOFLU today mark another important step in bringing the benefits of mRNA technology to seasonal respiratory vaccination. It’s not every day that a company gets two product approvals on the same day,” Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in a statement.

It is unclear when the shots will be available for Canadians over 50 to get, but Moderna said it “will engage with Canadian health authorities and immunization partners as it advances plans for the future availability of mFLUSIVA and mCOFLU in Canada.”

Global News has reached out to Moderna for more information on when the vaccines will be available in the market.

According to experts , mRNA-based vaccines have the potential to be more effective than traditional vaccines.

Traditional flu vaccines use microbial protein or dead microbes to build protection against a disease. In contrast, mRNA vaccines give your cells a recipe they can use to produce proteins needed to fight the disease. They are typically considered fast-acting.

“After injection, the cells in your arm muscles pick up the mRNA, make the protein, and display it on the cell’s surface,” the Vanderbilt University Medical Center website says.

The National Advisory Committee on Immunization recommends that everyone six months of age and older get the non-mRNA flu shot that is available this year.

A higher-dose version of the flu vaccine is recommended for adults aged 65 and older because aging immune systems often need a bigger boost.

The committee also strongly advises COVID-19 vaccination for anyone 65 years of age and older and residents of long-term care, retirement homes or assisted living.

–with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Bail for former Alberta junior hockey exec charged with sex offences against players
stories.summary: Okotoks - A former Alberta junior hockey executive accused of sexually exploiting three players has been released on bail.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Okotoks - A former Alberta junior hockey executive accused of sexually exploiting three players was granted bail Friday.

Tyler King, 39, appeared in court in Okotoks, Alta., after being arrested last week at a U.S. border crossing in Ontario.

He is charged with luring, sexual exploitation and making child pornography.

Details of the bail hearing are under a publication ban. But conditions of King’s release prohibit him from contacting the complainants and from being with anyone under 18.

He must also follow restrictions on using social media.

RCMP began investigating King in 2024, around the time he left as assistant general manager with the Okotoks Oilers, a team that plays in the British Columbia Hockey League.

Mounties said the Oilers reported in June 2024 that a former employee had allegedly solicited and compensated players for intimate images and sexual videos.

The complainants, all under 18 at the time of the allegations, were junior A players from Saskatchewan and Alberta.

RCMP said King had worked with various teams across Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia.

After Okotoks, King went to work for the Bchl’s Nanaimo team, then wound up teaching sports journalism at a university in New York state.

King, wearing handcuffs, was escorted into court by two officers. He said little during his appearance other than to confirm his identity and date of birth.

Two hours later, he left carrying a duffel bag and police were to drive him to Calgary.

He’s scheduled to be back in court Dec. 18.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Scattered showers throughout the weekend
stories.summary: An area of low pressure has stalled across southwestern Ontario and will cause scattered showers throughout the weekend.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
An area of low pressure has stalled across southwestern Ontario and will cause scattered showers throughout the weekend.

CTV weather specialist Reta Ismail said the scattered showers will continue until Sunday morning.

“We’re in and out of that activity as this system continues to turn,” she said.

“So, low pressure system going to swing on through this evening and with that, we could be in some heavier rainfall embedded non-severe thunderstorms possible as well, but not everybody’s getting that.”

Heading into Saturday, mostly cloudy conditions, overcast skies, and light drizzle.

Here’s a full look at your forecast:

Friday night: Showers. Amount 10 to 20 millimetres. Wind west 20 km/h becoming light after midnight. Low 4 C.

Saturday: A few showers ending late in the afternoon then cloudy. Wind becoming northwest 20 km/h in the morning. High 9 C.

Sunday: A mix of sun and cloud. Windy. High 10 C.

Monday: A mix of sun and cloud. High 11 C.

stories.title: Budget 2026 is proposing an ‘Rrsp-for-life.’ Here’s what it means for you
stories.summary: Budget 2026 proposes an 'Rrsp-for-life,' which could even carry over until after a person’s death. Here’s how it differs from the way your Rrsp currently works.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Finance Minister Francois-Phillipe Champagne tabled the federal budget in Parliament on Thursday, proposing a major change to how your Registered Retirement Savings Plan, or Rrsp , is managed in the years after you stop working.

Budget 2026 proposes an “Rrsp-for-life,” which could even carry over until after a person’s death.

Here’s how it differs from the way your Rrsp currently works.

Currently, retirement planning in Canada is split into two stages – the accumulation stage and the decumulation stage.

“You have the accumulation stage, which is the Rrsp, where we contribute and we get a tax deduction against our income for the amount we contribute,” said Jamie Golombek, managing director of tax and estate planning with Cibc Private Wealth.

At age 71, Canadians with an Rrsp face a choice.

They can either cash out of their Rrsp before they turn 71, buy an annuity that guarantees them a fixed income or convert their Rrsp into a Registered Retirement Income Fund, or Rrif.

They are then required to make minimum withdrawals from their Rrif.

In Budget 2026, the federal government proposed merging the core features of the Rrsp and Rrif into one single “Rrsp-for-life.”

“This would eliminate the need for individuals to convert their Rrsp to a Rrif at age 71,” budget document said.

The proposal is “more of an administrative issue” than a tax change, Golombek said.

“The concept is basically you could just have one retirement vehicle that you have until the day you die or you’ll also May be allowed to name a successor,” he said.

Currently, Canadians cannot name a successor for an Rrsp like they can for a Tfsa. The budget proposes allowing Canadians to include a “successor holder” who can be a spouse or a common law partner.

“This could permit a Rrsp to remain open until the death of the successor holder (i.e., the original holder’s surviving spouse or partner) and avoid the value of Rrsp property being included in the income of the deceased,” the budget said.

Changing the system would save retirees a lot of paperwork and save banks the time the spend reaching out to their clients with RRSPs who are about to turn 71, Golombek said.

“Under the new system called ‘Rrsp-for-life’, they’ll actually get rid of the entire Rrif concept,” he said.

He said, however, it is unclear whether existing RRIFs would be converted back to Rrsp or if the change would apply to people turning 71 after the changes go into effect.

The group Conference for Advanced Life Underwriting (Calu), which has been calling on the federal government to make this change, said it was “pleased to see” the changes to the Rrsp system, which they say will begin “modernizing the retirement income system.”

“However, this does not change the current requirement to make minimum withdrawals once the holder attains the age of 71,” the group, which represents professionals in the life insurance and financial advisory industries, said in a statement.

This would mean that while the Rrif wouldn’t exist, anyone over the age of 71 would have to make mandatory minimum withdrawals from their accounts.

The proposal also makes no changes to the age of contribution.

“(There are) no changes for how long you can contribute. You can only contribute to the end of the year you turn 71,” Golombek said.

For now, however, nothing changes since the budget only announces the government’s “intention” to bring in this change — the budget implementation bill will still need to be passed in the House of Commons then in the Senate, and specific regulations and technical details could change pending consultations that are taking place on the proposed changes.

If the changes go through as proposed, Canadians will still have three options on how to decumulate their savings.

“You could cash in your Rrsp at 71 and pay tax, which almost nobody does,” Golombek said.

For most people, the choice will come down to choosing the Rrsp-for-life or buying a registered annuity.

“If you want a regular, predictable, guaranteed amount of income every single year, you could choose the registered annuity route,” he said.

However, having the Rrsp-for-life would mean your money stays invested, often in a combination of ETFs, mutual funds, stocks or bonds.

It would also give you more flexibility on how and when to withdraw your money.

“Most people want the flexibility to be able to (withdraw), if they need a large sum of money for healthcare or medical or travel or whatever,” he said.

They can either cash out of their Rrsp before they turn 71, buy an annuity that guarantees them a fixed income or convert their Rrsp into a Registered Retirement Income Fund, or Rrif.
They are then required to make minimum withdrawals from their Rrif.
In Budget 2026, the federal government proposed merging the core features of the Rrsp and Rrif into one single “Rrsp-for-life.”
“This would eliminate the need for individuals to convert their Rrsp to a Rrif at age 71,” budget document said.
The proposal is “more of an administrative issue” than a tax change, Golombek said.
“The concept is basically you could just have one retirement vehicle that you have until the day you die or you’ll also May be allowed to name a successor,” he said.
Currently, Canadians cannot name a successor for an Rrsp like they can for a Tfsa. The budget proposes allowing Canadians to include a “successor holder” who can be a spouse or a common law partner.

“This could permit a Rrsp to remain open until the death of the successor holder (i.e., the original holder’s surviving spouse or partner) and avoid the value of Rrsp property being included in the income of the deceased,” the budget said.
Changing the system would save retirees a lot of paperwork and save banks the time the spend reaching out to their clients with RRSPs who are about to turn 71, Golombek said.
“Under the new system called ‘Rrsp-for-life’, they’ll actually get rid of the entire Rrif concept,” he said.
He said, however, it is unclear whether existing RRIFs would be converted back to Rrsp or if the change would apply to people turning 71 after the changes go into effect.

The group Conference for Advanced Life Underwriting (Calu), which has been calling on the federal government to make this change, said it was “pleased to see” the changes to the Rrsp system, which they say will begin “modernizing the retirement income system.”

“However, this does not change the current requirement to make minimum withdrawals once the holder attains the age of 71,” the group, which represents professionals in the life insurance and financial advisory industries, said in a statement.
This would mean that while the Rrif wouldn’t exist, anyone over the age of 71 would have to make mandatory minimum withdrawals from their accounts.
The proposal also makes no changes to the age of contribution.
“(There are) no changes for how long you can contribute. You can only contribute to the end of the year you turn 71,” Golombek said.

For now, however, nothing changes since the budget only announces the government’s “intention” to bring in this change — the budget implementation bill will still need to be passed in the House of Commons then in the Senate, and specific regulations and technical details could change pending consultations that are taking place on the proposed changes.
If the changes go through as proposed, Canadians will still have three options on how to decumulate their savings.
“You could cash in your Rrsp at 71 and pay tax, which almost nobody does,” Golombek said.
For most people, the choice will come down to choosing the Rrsp-for-life or buying a registered annuity.
“If you want a regular, predictable, guaranteed amount of income every single year, you could choose the registered annuity route,” he said.
However, having the Rrsp-for-life would mean your money stays invested, often in a combination of ETFs, mutual funds, stocks or bonds.
It would also give you more flexibility on how and when to withdraw your money.
“Most people want the flexibility to be able to (withdraw), if they need a large sum of money for healthcare or medical or travel or whatever,” he said.

stories.title: Young Canadians are struggling to find work: ‘I thought that by now I’d have some sort of job’
stories.summary: Statistics Canada data shows unemployment among young Canadians has increased over the past five years
stories.author: Addison Fallis
stories.content:
For Abby Daniel, graduating from university was supposed to mark the beginning of her career. Instead, more than a year after completing her degree, she’s still trying to find a job in her field.

Daniel, who graduated from Carleton University in 2025 with a degree in health sciences, expected to land work in public health, government or a health-care organization.

“When I graduated, I thought that … by now I’d have some sort of job that is linked to my actual undergrad degree,” she told National Post.

She began looking for work a couple of months after graduating, using LinkedIn and Indeed, while also reaching out to her former Carleton professors. But finding employment has proven more difficult than she anticipated.

Canada’s struggling youth job market leaves young graduates facing an uncertain future.

Statistics Canada’s September 2026 Labour Force Survey recorded 68,000 fewer jobs nationally, including 48,000 among Canadians aged 15 to 24.

Data visualization chart showing the percentage of unemployment among non-students over the span of the last five years, ages 15-24 and 20-24. Chart created on Excel, by Addison Fallis.

Statistics Canada Labour Force Survey data shows that unemployment among young Canadians has increased over the past five years. Between April 2022 and April 2026, the unemployment rate among Canadians aged 15 to 24 rose from 11.5 per cent to 13.5 per cent. For those aged 20 to 24 the rate increased from 10.5 per cent to 11.2 per cent.

The data, collected through Statistics Canada’s monthly Labour Force Survey, provides an indication of the growing challenges young Canadians face when entering the workforce. An increasingly competitive entry-level job market is creating uncertainty about their career prospects, financial independence and future plans.

Daniel said that since graduating, the job market appears to have declined. She also noticed changes in hiring practices, including the growing use of artificial intelligence. During a recent job interview, Daniel recalled, she was told the interview would be recorded and processed through AI software to transcribe or summarize the conversation.

“It kind of feels a little bit less authentic,” she said.

Abby Daniel is a recent graduate of Carleton University. Handout

When asked whether her university education had adequately prepared her for the realities of finding employment, she affirmed, “Definitely not. After I completed my degree, I would have hoped for (my professors) to give me resources, or have built connections so I had something to lean towards.”

She even mentioned that experience gained while she was a student did not prove to be useful post-grad. “I did my placement at the Queensway Carleton Hospital and my supervisor wasn’t even a connection for me at that point.”

Carleton University Health Sciences professor and department chair Martin Holcik said the university takes students’ transition into the workforce seriously. He shared a statement on behalf of the university in response to Abby’s concern: “We are sorry to hear when a graduate feels disappointed by their employment experience after graduation. While I cannot speak to the circumstances of any individual student, supporting students’ transition from university to careers is something we take very seriously.

“Throughout their studies, Health Sciences students have access to a range of supports, including faculty mentorship, career development resources, networking opportunities, and experiential learning,” the statement said.

The university also noted that “career outcomes are influenced by many factors, including labour market conditions, individual career goals, and how students engage with available opportunities.”

Tim Lang, president and chief executive officer of Youth Employment Services (YES), a charity that helps young people find employment, said the organization has noticed growing distress among young job seekers.

“Although the numbers have been fairly consistent, we have seen more desperation in the last couple years that we haven’t seen in over a decade,” Lang told National Post.

He noted that previously, immigration into Canada caused more young people to compete for the same number of jobs. While that has subsided, he said trade and tariff complications have created new challenges, causing businesses to slow down or become more cautious.

“The problem now is, (young people) eventually do get jobs. The timeframe to get them is just longer,” Lang said.

He empathized with young people and acknowledged how the market has gotten increasingly difficult. “Even three or four or five months can seem excruciating when you’re in that situation.”

The consequences of prolonged unemployment can extend beyond the immediate difficulty of finding a job.

Lang pointed to what is known as the “scarring effect” or “wage scarring” referring to a research paper by Deloitte Canada that found people who experience long periods of unemployment can face lower earnings throughout the rest of their lives, which inherently has a negative GDP effect on the economy.

He said this is why governments and businesses should be less hesitant to hire young workers when opportunities arise.

“That’s why we urge governments and businesses to not be so cautious to hire people if they think they can need them because it’s a net benefit, not only to that person but to the overall economy,” Lang said.

While Canada has experienced difficult economic periods in the past, Lang said the current job market presents a different challenge, particularly because of the growing role of artificial intelligence.

“On one hand, you could argue that over the last 50 years we’ve seen worse recessions and more difficult times, like the early 90s was a tough time,” he said.

However, he said AI could have a permanent effect on certain entry-level positions as organizations increasingly look to use the technology to cut costs and replace aspects of human work. Not only is it used to supplant the workforce but, “AI is now being used by employers to sift through thousands of resumes looking for keywords,” Lang said.

He added that some young people seeking assistance through YES report sending out hundreds of applications without receiving a single response. He honed in on the importance in young job seekers understanding how to navigate hiring processes increasingly influenced by AI, including learning how to customize resumes and cover letters.

Despite the challenges, Lang said there are reasons to remain optimistic about Canada’s job market. He pointed to potential business growth through provincial tax reductions, including in Ontario, which he said could help stimulate economic growth.

“There’s still reason for optimism,” Lang said.

He regularly encourages the tens of thousands of young people he works with to remain positive throughout their job search: “It is so important to stay optimistic, because even in the face of adversity when you find that potential opportunity, if you’re a bit negative, they might not hire you.”

stories.title: Canadian dollar hits nearly three-week low on surprise jobs loss
stories.summary: The loonie was trading ⁠0.7 per cent lower
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar fell to a nearly three-week ​low against its US counterpart on ‌Friday after domestic data showed the economy shed jobs for a third straight month, cooling expectations for Bank of Canada interest rate hikes.

The loonie was trading ⁠0.7 per cent lower ​at 1.4110 per U.S. dollar, or 70.87 US cents, after touching its weakest intraday level since October 19 at 1.4125.

For the week, the currency was on track to lose nearly 1 per cent, after ​three straight weeks of gains, as equity ‌markets globally were buffeted by a selloff in AI stocks.

“The CAD has failed to deliver on the potential for its recent rebound to extend this week,” Shaun Osborne and Eric Theoret, FX strategists at Scotiabank, said in a ‌note.

“Elevated equity-market ​volatility has overshadowed pretty much ‌everything else, although the combination of weak Canadian and strong U.S. ​jobs data has given the CAD an ⁠added nudge lower into the weekend,” the strategists said.

Canadian ⁠employment fell 4,700 in October and the jobless rate rose to a six-month ​high of 6.7 per cent. Analysts had expected a 13,600 jobs gain.

Chances the Bank of Canada would tighten in December dipped to 35 per cent from 40 per cent, swap market data showed.

The Canadian central bank unveiled on Thursday a new five-year monetary policy framework ⁠with the federal finance ministry, keeping its inflation target unchanged at 2 per cent.

Also on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s budget showed that he plans to use windfall oil revenue to boost Canada’s productivity and build infrastructure while keeping his previous fiscal goals intact.

US nonfarm ⁠payrolls increased more than expected in October, boosting ​the US dollar against a basket of major currencies.

U.S. crude futures ⁠added to their steep weekly decline, trading 0.1 per cent lower at US$90.40 a barrel, after the election losses ‌of US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party raised hopes of a de-escalation in the ​US-Israeli war on Iran. Oil is one of Canada’s major exports.

The Canadian 2-year yield was down 3.3 basis points at 3.123 per cent, while it fell 6.8 basis points further below the ​equivalent US rate to a gap of about 139 basis points.

stories.title: Poilievre accuses government of cooking books on immigration
stories.summary: Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says the government is hiding the facts on the number of newcomers it's bringing to Canada, despite the focus in the new immigration levels plan on people who are already here.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre on Friday accused the government of hiding the facts on the number of newcomers it’s bringing to Canada, despite the focus in the new immigration levels plan on people who are already here.

In Winnipeg on Friday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the one-time permanent residency measures in the levels plan are about making longtime temporary residents permanent.

But Poilievre said at a news conference in Brampton, Ont., the current government is blowing past the Trudeau government’s immigration numbers with plans to grant permanent residency to 200,000 temporary residents this year, in addition to the broad target of 380,000 permanent residents.

“It will bring the total number of new permanent residents to 650,000, by far a record and much bigger than any of the years when Justin Trudeau was prime minister,” Poilievre said.

“We love immigration for people in numbers that we can absorb, where there are jobs, health care and housing, but not when the numbers exceed our capacity to absorb people. It is not fair to immigrants. It is not fair to people already here.”

Carney said the workers expected to receive permanent residency under the new levels plan are people who have been in Canada for years and whose workplaces apply annually to renew their permits.

“They are members of the community, as I say, and they are in many respects — in all respect — permanent residents of the country and we’re formalizing it,” Carney said Friday.

Immigration Minister Lena Diab’s office declined a request to interview her about the newly tabled immigration levels plan. She also did not take questions after the plan was tabled on Thursday.

Diab did not face any questions on the levels plan from the opposition during Friday’s question period, despite being in the chamber on a day when many MPs are on their way back to their home constituencies.

Immigration department officials said during a not-for-attribution technical briefing Friday that the vast majority of those eligible for the one-time plan to shift 200,000 people to permanent residency are already in Canada.

That one-year program will select, in collaboration with the provinces and territories, 100,000 people here on work visas who already have applied for permanent residency.

The other 100,000 applicants will be chosen from humanitarian permanent residency streams. Government officials say this is meant to clear a decade-long backlog of applications.

Those applicants include about 32,000 former Hong Kong residents who came to Canada through a special program to flee persecution from the Chinese government, and nearly 19,000 Ukrainians who came here through a program for those fleeing Russia’s invasion.

“So these are people who are not permanent in terms of the classification, but are effectively permanent residents and we’re recognizing that,” Carney said.

“It’s the right thing to do and we are absolutely clear about that, and it’s within the context of a sustainable immigration system.”

Andy Wong, president of the Canada-Hong Kong Link, said this is welcome news for those who came to Canada on the Hong Kong pathway.

“It’s even better than we expected because we thought, like, maybe they would try to have a one-time measure gradually for three years to take care of backlog,” Wong said. “So that is a very pleasant surprise and we absolutely are delighted.”

He extended thanks to the Liberal, New Democrat and Conservative MPs who called for expedited permanent residency for those who came on the Hong Kong pathway.

Roy Lee, a former Hong Kong resident with a permanent residency application, said those using the pathway program aren’t technically refugees, but rather people who came to Canada after the Chinese government cracked down on pro-democracy demonstrators in Hong Kong.

“We May return to Hong Kong without any sentences,” Lee said, adding that those who fled the Chinese city fear someday crossing “the red line of the Hong Kong government.”

“So what we are afraid of is the hidden, invisible bottom line that we May somehow reach it in the future and maybe we will suddenly get sentenced,” he said.

Department officials say this humanitarian permanent residency program will include about 45,000 family admissions for spouses, common law partners and children, plus about 12,600 people who have been approved for permanent residency on humanitarian grounds but whose applications have not been finalized.

The stated goal of this program is to reduce application wait times to the 12-month target.

The government says the broad pool of 380,000 permanent residents will be chosen mostly from people already in Canada on work and study visas, with some successful applicants coming from outside the country.

Poilievre also said the Temporary Foreign Worker Program should not be open to communities with unemployment rates higher than 5.5 per cent.

The government signalled in the budget it intends to reform that program in collaboration with the provinces, but the plan is light on details at this point.

There are restrictions in place on low-wage temporary worker applications in census metropolitan areas where unemployment is above six per cent.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

University says Dr. Anil Kishen 'did not intend to promote antisemitism, and he had limited knowledge about antisemitic imagery'

The U of T's Faculty of Dentistry building is seen on Edward Street in Toronto. (Google Maps)

November 6, 2026 at 12:34 p.m.

The University of Toronto has announced that Dr. Anil Kishen is stepping down as the dean of the institution’s faculty of dentistry, effective immediately.

In a letter released by the office of the vice-president and provost and shared on social media, Provost Trevor Young wrote that an external investigator found that Kishen used two antisemitic images in his lecture material earlier this year.

One of the images showed a figure with its face painted in the colours of the Palestinian flag, bound by ropes and an Israeli flag, although the Star of David has been removed from the flag.

The second showed a hook-nosed man relaxing in a swimming pool full of money and labelled with the word “Immunity,” surrounded by several figures who are looking up.

“This latter image is a well-known antisemitic trope that has historically been used to dehumanize Jewish people,” the group Canadian Women Against Antisemitism pointed out pointed out in February, when the images were used.

Young wrote: “To provide clarity to our community, the findings of this process confirm that: Dr. Kishen did not intend to promote antisemitism, and he had limited knowledge about antisemitic imagery and tropes associated with Jewish people when he included the images in his lecture materials.”

However, Young added: “He knows his usage of them has been very painful to many members of the community. He recognizes that many community members have lost confidence in his ability to continue to lead the Faculty of Dentistry. His voluntary resignation as Dean reflects his acceptance of the University’s sanction.”

It is good to see that antisemitism has consequences I hope this example at the faculty of dentistry at the University of Toronto sets a strong precedent in the academic world In short, the dean who included antisemitic content in his lecture has been relieved of his duties pic.twitter.com/hW89bxzBsn — Image 13: 🏳️‍🌈Dr. Hershl Berman Image 14: 🏳️‍🌈(@BermanPCMD) November 5, 2026

Kishen is said to have undergone training to better understand antisemitism, and he will remain a tenured faculty member at the university. “He will return to the full scope of faculty duties during the 2027-28 academic year,” Young added.

Laura Tam, who has been in the role of acting dean since February, will now be named Interim Dean while a search for a new dean is undertaken. Kishen became dean of the school of dentistry on July 1, 2025, for a five-year term.

Kishen has been on leave since Feb. 26, when he wrote in an email to the dentistry faculty: “Last night I became aware that two cartoon images that I included in a recent lecture contained discriminatory imagery. I selected these images as visual analogies for two concepts. I was not trying to make any political statements with these images. I say this not as an excuse for this mistake.”

He added: “I condemn antisemitism and discrimination in all their forms.”

Antisemitism and antizionism have permeated into all corners of academia in this country. We are living in a Canada where a senior academic, the dean of a dental faculty, feels emboldened enough to sabotage a lecture on strangulation theory and dental pulp with vitriolic and… pic.twitter.com/JTbMU1L1xf — B'nai Brith Canada (@bnaibrithcanada) February 26, 2026

B’nai Brith Canada, the local chapter of a Jewish human rights organization, shared the images in a post on X last year, and was among the many to express outrage and concern over their use.

Young wrote that the investigation “revealed deep divisions at the Faculty of Dentistry; some community members accepted Dr. Kishen’s immediate apology, while others were deeply hurt by the use of the images.”

National Post has reached out to the Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario to ask if Kishen’s status has changed there. The organization’s website currently lists him as a member who is currently entitled to practice.

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: Joly asks Competition Bureau to probe comments from Cliffs CEO
stories.summary: Lourenco Goncalves has said his company bought Stelco to stop it from flooding the U.S. market; it’s unclear what steps the regulator can take
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has asked the Competition Bureau to investigate whether recent comments made by Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N CEO Lourenco Goncalves on his motives for buying Canadian steelmaker Stelco Inc. warrant enforcement action.

In a CBC interview on Oct. 27, Mr. Goncalves said he bought Stelco because he couldn’t afford to have it “flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company.”

In her Friday complaint letter, which was obtained by The Globe and Mail, Ms. Joly asked interim competition commissioner Jeanne Pratt to investigate the matter.

“This type of conduct is highly questionable and may be reviewable under the Competition Act,” she said.

The letter is the latest move by the federal government to ratchet up pressure on Cliffs to recall laid-off steel workers in Hamilton.

In late September, Stelco announced that it was cutting up to 500 jobs in Canada because of its inability to make money in its galvanized-steel business.

Ms. Joly has repeatedly alleged that Cliffs is in violation of legally binding commitments it made at the time of the 2024 Stelco acquisition concerning specific employment levels. In multiple letters and public appearances, she has warned the company that the government could sue Cliffs, which could force it to pay financial penalties or divest Stelco.

It is unclear what steps the Competition Bureau could take. Ms. Joly’s letter said the bureau reviewed the Stelco acquisition in 2024 and issued a “no action” letter.

The Competition Bureau is an independent law enforcement agency that enforces the Competition Act. Its mandates include ensuring a healthy and competitive domestic marketplace and preventing individual companies from becoming too powerful in order to protect consumers.

“At minimum, Mr. Goncalves’ statements indicate his company’s disregard for the importance of fair competition in the marketplace, and the important role that competition policy plays in delivering greater choice and affordability for consumers,” Ms. Joly said in her letter.

Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

Sarah Brown, a spokesperson for the Competition Bureau, confirmed in an e-mail to The Globe that it has received Ms. Joly’s letter. But she declined to provide additional information, or confirm whether it is investigating the matter, citing confidentiality constraints.

Subrata Bhattacharjee, national chair of the competition and foreign investment review group with Borden Ladner Gervais LLP, said the lack of specifics in Ms. Joly’s letter around what the commissioner should focus on weakens its impact.

“The letter seems to fall short of a direction to the commissioner to look at this conduct under a particular provision of the act,” he said.

Mr. Bhattacharjee added that if the bureau decides an investigation is merited, the timeframe for an outcome could be months or even years.

The fracas between Cliffs and Ottawa has been dragging on for more than a month. After the layoffs were announced, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Cliffs had “betrayed” its work force.

Cliffs is adamant that it is complying with the promises it made as a condition for acquiring the Canadian steelmaker. The company said it expects to report to Ottawa that Stelco’s annual employment numbers for both its unionized and non-unionized work force will be well above the minimum required.

The Official Opposition says that Ms. Joly isn’t doing enough to hold Cliffs’s feet to the fire and believes her tactics aren’t working.

In an e-mail to The Globe, MP Michael Guglielmin, chair of the Conservative steel caucus, said that despite multiple warning letters sent by Ms. Joly to Cliffs, the layoffs haven’t been reversed.

“Now she’s sending a fourth letter, shifting accountability to the competition commissioner,” he said. ”Conservatives called on the minister to sue weeks ago. File the lawsuit, save Canadian jobs.”

Cliffs has classified the layoffs as “temporary.” Mr. Goncalves said last week that 175 people have been laid off so far in Canada, and no more cuts are planned. He said workers could be back on the job by Christmas, depending on sufficient domestic procurements of steel.

stories.title: St. Thomas police warning of new phone scam circulating city
stories.summary: The St. Thomas Police Service is warning the community of a new phone scam that’s circulating.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The St. Thomas Police Service is warning the community of a new phone scam that’s circulating.

Police posted on social media, outlining the scam.

They said it starts with a phone call from someone claiming to represent your cell phone provider. They offer you a better plan and phone.

After a phone is shipped to your house, another call comes and they say the wrong phone was shipped. They will arrange someone to get the phone or give a shipping address, which is the scam.

“The St. Thomas Police Service has received multiple reports involving people posing as various cell phone company representatives, scamming local residents here in St. Thomas,” said Samantha Wakefield, corporate communications coordinator for the Stps.

“If this happens to you, stop. Before shipping the phone or handing it to anyone, contact your local provider directly using the number on your bill or on their official website.”

Stps can be contacted at 519-631-1224.

The St. Thomas Police Service has received multiple reports of fraudsters posing as cell phone company representatives to scam local residents. stories.title: Canada added no private sector jobs from 2019 to 2024 — U.S. did the exact opposite
stories.summary: Study by Fraser Institute found Alberta was the only province where government employment didn’t outpace private sector employment
stories.author: Emily Renae Kapralik
stories.content:
The United States outperformed Canada in adding private sector jobs from 2019 to 2024, according to a new study.

The data comes following news of turmoil in Canada’s economy, such as the Bank of Canada raising its policy rate last month, the unemployment rate jumping to 6.7 per cent in October from 6.5 per cent in September, and losing 4,700 jobs in October per Statistics Canada — all while ongoing trade tensions with the U.S. linger in the background.

According to the Fraser Institute, a Canadian non-partisan think tank, the U.S. added 7.6 private sector jobs per 1,000 working-age people, whereas Canada added none.

Additionally, Canadian provinces performed much worse in private sector job creation than U.S. states.

Handout /Fraser Institue

The study examined whether Canada’s private sector employment growth was keeping up with population growth by comparing Canada’s performance to its closest neighbour.

The strength of private sector employment acts as an indicator of an economy’s capacity to generate sustainable economic growth.

Ben Eisen, the co-author of the study, told National Post that what’s happening to the private sector (in terms of job creation and overall employment growth) can end up getting overlooked when people only see aggregate numbers.

“If you only look at the broad numbers, which includes robust government job growth, you can miss out on a very important story,” Eisen said. “Private sector job creation in most of the country has not been adequate to keep pace with the working age population.”

The study found that within the 2019 and 2024 timeframe, Alberta was the only province where government employment didn’t outpace private sector employment.

B.C. was the province with the largest gap between government and private sector growth, at 26.7 percentage points.

The study also observed how Canadian provinces are faring compared to jurisdictions in the United States that share comparable geography, economic trends and industries.

Ontario had the worst private sector job growth in the Great Lakes region.

The number of private sector jobs in Ontario per 1,000 people fell by approximately 17.8 over the five-year period. Quebec also lost an average of 5.5 private sector jobs during that same period.

B.C. had the worst record throughout the Pacific Northwest, with an average of 35.7 private sector jobs lost.

Alberta performed the worst compared to other energy-producing states, with 8.8 jobs lost per 1,000 people.

Most Atlantic and Maritime provinces lagged behind their U.S. counterparts, except for Newfoundland and Labrador, which added 20.6 private sector jobs per 1,000 working people.

The period of 2019 to 2024 was chosen in order to compare developments over a significant period of time, according to Eisen.

The year 2019 was chosen as a starting point in order to properly analyze data throughout the COVID recession and recovery, and the authors ended the study at the “most recent year of available data.”

Eisen hopes that this study will encourage analysts and the government to make sure they’re paying attention to private sector job growth in the future, and adjust their plans when there is weakness.

“We can’t simply look at headline numbers,” Eisen said, adding that people should pay more attention to the private sector in order to gauge how well the economy is doing.

In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the federal government wrote that it created a total of 330,000 jobs over the previous year, which “exceeded expectations of private sector economists.”

Employment increased by 7.4 per cent from 2019 to 2024, which they called the “strongest increase in the G7.”

If private sector job creation in Canada had kept up with the United States since 2019, there would have been 554,000 more private sector jobs in 2024, according to the study.

The study used data acquired from Statistics Canada, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the U.S. Census Bureau to determine its findings.

Ben Eisen, the co-author of the study, told National Post that what’s happening to the private sector (in terms of job creation and overall employment growth) can end up getting overlooked when people only see aggregate numbers.

“If you only look at the broad numbers, which includes robust government job growth, you can miss out on a very important story,” Eisen said. “Private sector job creation in most of the country has not been adequate to keep pace with the working age population.”
The study found that within the 2019 and 2024 timeframe, Alberta was the only province where government employment didn’t outpace private sector employment.
B.C. was the province with the largest gap between government and private sector growth, at 26.7 percentage points.
The study also observed how Canadian provinces are faring compared to jurisdictions in the United States that share comparable geography, economic trends and industries.
Ontario had the worst private sector job growth in the Great Lakes region.
The number of private sector jobs in Ontario per 1,000 people fell by approximately 17.8 over the five-year period. Quebec also lost an average of 5.5 private sector jobs during that same period.
B.C. had the worst record throughout the Pacific Northwest, with an average of 35.7 private sector jobs lost.
Alberta performed the worst compared to other energy-producing states, with 8.8 jobs lost per 1,000 people.
Most Atlantic and Maritime provinces lagged behind their U.S. counterparts, except for Newfoundland and Labrador, which added 20.6 private sector jobs per 1,000 working people.
The period of 2019 to 2024 was chosen in order to compare developments over a significant period of time, according to Eisen.

The year 2019 was chosen as a starting point in order to properly analyze data throughout the COVID recession and recovery, and the authors ended the study at the “most recent year of available data.”
Eisen hopes that this study will encourage analysts and the government to make sure they’re paying attention to private sector job growth in the future, and adjust their plans when there is weakness.
“We can’t simply look at headline numbers,” Eisen said, adding that people should pay more attention to the private sector in order to gauge how well the economy is doing.
In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the federal government wrote that it created a total of 330,000 jobs over the previous year, which “exceeded expectations of private sector economists.”
Employment increased by 7.4 per cent from 2019 to 2024, which they called the “strongest increase in the G7.”
If private sector job creation in Canada had kept up with the United States since 2019, there would have been 554,000 more private sector jobs in 2024, according to the study.
The study used data acquired from Statistics Canada, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the U.S. Census Bureau to determine its findings.

stories.title: Nova Scotia selects this year’s Christmas tree to say ‘thank you’ to Boston
stories.summary: Nova Scotia sends the U.S. city a large Christmas tree every year to thank it for sending medical personnel and supplies after the Halifax Explosion in 1917.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A 14-metre white spruce from Nova Scotia will soon be shipping out to Boston.

Nova Scotia sends the U.S. city a large Christmas tree every year to thank it for sending medical personnel and supplies after the Halifax Explosion in 1917.

Boston sent a relief train within 24 hours of the disaster that killed almost 2,000 people and left many more injured and homeless.

This year’s tree will be cut on the property of Henry and Pat Knol in East Amherst, N.S., who say it’s a great honour to be chosen.

The public is invited to a tree-cutting ceremony on their property on Nov. 18.

It will be shipped to the United States by truck, and lit up on the Boston Common on Dec. 3.

“Some years ago our cousin transported the tree to Boston while working for the Department of Transportation,” the Knols said in a joint statement. “Although he is no longer with us, it is very special to know that our family has this connection to such a special tradition.”

stories.title: Manitoba Métis Federation 'appalled' at lack of Métis funding in federal budget
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Manitoba Métis Federation says it's appalled by the lack of Métis-specific funding in Prime Minister Mark Carney's new budget.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The Manitoba Métis Federation is “appalled” by the lack of Métis-specific funding in Prime Minister Mark Carney’s new budget.

While First Nations and Inuit have targeted funding measures in the budget, Métis do not, despite having pressed the government for supports in areas like housing and health care.

The only mention of Métis in the budget, released Thursday, is in association with $806 million set aside over five years to implement a Trudeau-era Indigenous child welfare law.

Manitoba Métis Federation president David Chartrand said there is “no doubt” Red River Métis citizens will be angered by the fact that their needs were dismissed, despite the MMF holding meetings with the prime minister and ministers to outline their priorities ahead of the budget.

“The hugely successful distinctions-based approach has vanished, and government is reverting to phrases like ‘Indigenous’ when, in reality, they mean First Nations and Inuit,” Chartrand said.

“We are never looking for a handout. Rather, we are looking for our tax dollars to be reinvested in the Red River Métis so we can put a shovel in our hands and continue addressing the critical needs of our Nation and strengthen Canada.”

Victoria Pruden, president of the Métis National Council, said in a media statement Thursday that Métis governments are being treated as an afterthought rather than partners in Canada’s future.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty said she can sympathize with Chartrand. She said when she served as a grand chief, she was sometimes disappointed at being passed over for federal funding.

She pointed to what she called “historic” new funding for First Nations in the budget, including $32 billion over 10 years to repair, replace and build First Nations infrastructure. The Assembly of First Nations has said that work will require more than $32 billion.

The budget is largely framed around building up the Canadian economy. The government says the First Nations infrastructure funding will make essential services more reliable and help communities retain skilled workers.

There is a deep infrastructure gap between First Nations communities and the rest of Canada. The Assembly of First Nations and the Conference Board of Canada estimate it would take about $375 billion to close it.

Many First Nations communities suffer from a lack of modern roads, schools and housing, poor internet connectivity and defective water treatment plants.

The federal budget earmarks $11 billion over 10 years to maintain, renovate and build First Nations homes, and $18.5 billion to build roads, bridges and schools. The budget also commits $5.8 billion over five years for First Nations elementary and secondary education.

Prior to the budget, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak repeatedly said the gap between First Nations and the rest of the country will only continue to grow without targeted investments.

After the budget, Woodhouse Nepinak said the 10-year funding cycle will help communities plan better and allow them to turn their advocacy efforts elsewhere, since they won’t have to lobby the federal government for that funding each year.

“A budget titled ‘Masters of our Destiny’ should also better support First Nations right to self-determination and we will increase advocacy on these over the year ahead,” Woodhouse Nepinak told The Canadian Press on Friday.

She also praised the new federal homelessness strategy and called for First Nations leaders to be included in it at the start to tailor services toward their community members.

The budget earmarks $6 billion for Jordan’s Principle over six years — to ensure First Nations children receive the health and social supports they need — and $575 million over five years for a similar program for Inuit called Pirutsiagutiit.

The federal government is also setting aside $610 million over four years for the Nutrition North subsidy to help offset high grocery prices in the North.

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, the organization that represents Inuit in Canada, has said the program has failed to improve food security and reduce prices in the region. In a media statement Thursday, the organization said investing in the program will not address the structural changes needed to eliminate food insecurity in the Inuit homelands.

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami says it’s also concerned about the lack of Inuit-specific housing and infrastructure funding in the budget.

“Inuit uphold Canada’s sovereignty. Investments in Inuit communities are investments in Canada. Aside from the welcome funding for Pirutsiagutiit, the broader sustainability of our communities is not reflected in this budget,” ITK president Natan Obed said.

“It makes significant investments in projects but building projects is not enough. The lack of investment in building healthy Inuit communities is a risk to this country.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

The move is part of the federal government’s plan to 'modernize' the Crown corporation, the Federal Budget says

The cost of a stamp will jump to $2 in 2027, according to the federal budget. (File photo)

November 6, 2026 at 11:21 a.m.

Mailing a letter will cost more in the new year, according to the federal budget.

The present cost of $1.44 for a stamp will jump to $2 in 2027. It’s part of the federal government’s plan to “modernize” the Crown corporation.

Ottawa notes in the budget that the move will “help bring Canada Post’s stamp pricing more closely in line with Oecd peers by raising stamp rates.”

After 2027, the price of a stamp will continue to increase every year by 7 per cent.

“This measure will have a relatively limited impact on consumers and small businesses, with an estimate of only approximately $6 per year for consumers and $9 per year for small businesses. This increase will further offset costs while ensuring continuous affordability,” states the budget.

Even though Ottawa sees Canada Post Corporation as “a longstanding national institution,” it admits in the budget that “the use of traditional letter mail for communication and commerce continues to decline.”

Moreover, it states that “Canada Post’s existing model no longer works for 21st-century Canada’s needs. This is why we are taking steps to improve the corporation’s efficiency, accountability, and long-term financial sustainability.”

The federal government intends to provide additional funds to Canada Post, $1.4 billion over two years, while already providing $1.2 billion over seven years to enable the shift from door-to-door urban delivery to community mailboxes.

The latter move, announced in September 2025, “is expected to generate approximately $2.2 billion in savings over 10 years, helping put Canada Post back on the path toward financial sustainability.”

As previously reported by National Post, the shift came about after Canada Post admitted delivery to Canadians’ doors costs “significantly more.”

And citing its “deteriorating financial situation,” a substantial loss in 2025 continuing into the first quarter of 2026, the present state of affairs “underscores the urgency of this transformation,” said the corporation in a statement in June.

Conversions to community mailboxes, it noted, is a key element of its plan to transform the postal service and stop it from becoming “a recurring burden on taxpayers.”

The budget states that Ottawa will be increasing Canada Post Corporation’s “Annual Reference Levels” (funding allocation) by $101.4 million from 2026-27 to 2030-31.

This presumes the corporation won’t continue to be hit by labour strife. The union representing Canada Post workers went on strike twice in 2025.

How much of the federal funding will go to executive bonuses is unclear. Earlier this year, the Canadian Taxpayers Federation called Canada Post to task for giving out $30.8 million in bonuses to its management employees in 2025, National Post reported.

The Crown corporation’s president and CEO, Doug Ettinger, conceded in an appearance before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Government Operations and Estimates on June 18 that it lost $1.57 billion in 2025, but insisted it was a bad year due to “labour disruptions” of 220 days. He suggested the “real deficit” was “closer to a billion.” (The $1.57 billion was admitted to in Canada Post’s 2025 annual report.)

Ettinger didn’t mention the $1.03 billion federal government bailout in early 2025, or another $1.01 billion given to Canada Post by Ottawa in February 2026 as a “short-term financial bridge.”

“If Canada Post is taking taxpayer-funded bailouts, then there’s no way its managers and executives should be showering themselves with bonuses,” said Franco Terrazzano, the Ctf’s federal director, in a July 14 statement.

Ottawa says in the federal budget that it will also subsidize the special postage rate for library materials and for expanded postal inspections, particularly in Indigenous, northern, and remote communities with another “$28 million in future years.”

stories.title: 'He's made it clear': Gretzky backs Carney's call to bar Russia from world juniors
stories.summary: Toronto - Wayne Gretzky says he backs Canada's decision to bar Russia from the upcoming world junior hockey championship in Alberta.
stories.author: Joshua Clipperton The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Wayne Gretzky played a big part in one of his country’s crowning moments on the international sporting stage.

The Great One fed fellow superstar Mario Lemieux for the decisive goal that secured the 1987 Canada Cup final against the Soviet Union in the waning stages of the Cold War.

Almost 40 years later, he’s on board with a political move that has big ramifications on and off the ice.

Wayne Gretzky says he backs Canada’s decision to bar Russia from the upcoming world junior hockey championship in Alberta. Prime Minister Mark Carney announced earlier this week Russian and Belarusian athletes will not be permitted to represent their countries on Canadian soil while the war in Ukraine continues. (Nov. 6, 2026)

Gretzky said Friday he backs Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to bar Russia from the upcoming world junior hockey championship in Alberta because of Moscow’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and a war that is approaching its fifth year.

“Nobody likes war, right?” said the NHL’s all-time points leader, whose Eastern European heritage includes roots in present-day Ukraine, Belarus and Poland. “We definitely don’t want to see this. We hope it ends. We wish it didn’t start. I understand the stance the prime minister is taking, and good for him.”

Carney announced earlier this week that Russian and Belarusian athletes will not be permitted to represent their countries on Canadian soil while the war continues. Teams from Russia and Belarus have been banned since shortly after the invasion.

“While Russia and (Belarus) are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as long as that’s going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” Carney told reporters Tuesday in Antigua at the Commonwealth Summit when asked if Russian players would be denied visas.

“So if you’re asking specifically about the world juniors, the Russians will not be there.”

The decision came after the Court of Arbitration for Sport in Switzerland ruled Russia must be reinstated to international hockey competition, starting with the world juniors, which are scheduled to run from Dec. 26 through Jan. 5 in Edmonton and Red Deer.

Speaking at a ceremony hosted by Upper Deck to unveil the newly renamed Walter Gretzky Upper Deck Hockey Resource Centre in honour of his late father, in conjunction with the Hockey Hall of Fame, Gretzky said he supports Carney’s position.

“He’s made that stance, and he’s made it clear,” said the Brantford, Ont., product. “I think a lot of the players and the people of Canada feel the same way.”

The federal government has said it would use its immigration powers to prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete under their national symbols.

“This measure is not directed at the Russian and Belarusian people,” the government said in a statement. “Rather, it is intended to prevent the governments of Russia and Belarus from using international sporting events hosted in Canada as platforms for state representation, political legitimacy and propaganda.”

Entry would be assessed individually, the government added, while athletes competing as neutrals could still participate at international events hosted by Canada.

Russian sports minister Mikhail Degtyarev said in an Oct. 30 statement the CAS ruling was final.

He added his country would work with the International Ice Hockey Federation to secure its return to competition, starting with the world juniors.

Meanwhile, a number of European hockey federations, including Sweden, Finland, Czechia and Latvia, have said their teams will not play Russia.

Gretzky and Upper Deck — a trading card and memorabilia company — also announced a series of partnerships Friday.

The 65-year-old was asked what he thinks those might do to help his reputation among Canadians, which has taken a hit in recent years because of his close association with U.S. President Donald Trump.

“I can’t do anything about that,” Gretzky said with a laugh. “Your friends are your friends, right? People can have their own opinions. That’s what life is all about, and you just take it with a grain of salt. People are entitled to what they believe in and what their opinions are … as simple as that.

“My dad always told me, ‘You treat people how they treat you.’ And that’s how I live life.”

The only NHL player to ever reach 200 points in a season — he did it four times — Gretzky was also queried about Connor McDavid’s start to the current season.

The Edmonton Oilers captain has 44 points in 17 games and is on pace to reach 217 in 2026-27. That would top Gretzky’s record of 215 points set in 1985-86.

“Remarkable,” said Gretzky, who won the Stanley Cup four times as Oilers captain. “What he’s doing for his hockey team, and for the game, and for the city of Edmonton, it’s unmatched right now. I think he’s on a mission to win a Stanley Cup. He wants it desperately, and that’s what you need out of your best player and out of your captain.

“You need that leadership that you want to get to the next level, and he has that.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

stories.summary: Merritt, British Columbia, Canada - A hunter missing in the backcountry of British Columbia's southern Interior for several days has been found dead.

RCMP in Vernon, B.C., say the 57-year-old man was reported missing Monday morning after he failed to return from a hunting trip in the Douglas Lake area near Merritt.

Central Okanagan Search and Rescue said Wednesday that six teams were deployed, including Nicola Valley Search and Rescue.
