stories.title: Mustangs looking forward to Semi-finals match up
stories.summary: It was a rainy practice Wednesday, but the Western Mustangs are confident ahead of their semi-final game again...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
It was a rainy practice Wednesday, but the Western Mustangs are confident ahead of their semi-final game against the Windsor Lancers.

Western Head coach Michael Faulds (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM news)

“This is an energetic and motivated group of guys that are improving every day,” said Western Mustangs Head Coach Michael Faulds.

The Mustangs are coming off a bounce back win against the Laurier Golden Hawks 58-41, after dropping the season finale to the Golden Hawks 55-39.

“We got to limit our turnovers, create our team turnovers on defense and spread the ball around offensive,” Faulds said. “Windsor has one of the best defensive lines in the country and a physical quarter back so we need to execute in all three phases.”

Faulds is in his first season as head coach after Greg Marshall being head coach for almost 20 years.

Western QB Ben Casselman (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM news)

Ben Casselman is one of the QB for Western and Faulds said he’s come out of his shell sharing the ball.

“We’re taking it week by week and Faulds stated we’re four quarters away and it’s a new game,” Casselman said. “Windsor is a physical team and are good offensively.”

Casselman shares his spot with Jerome Rancourt both in the top 10 passing touchdowns in the OUA. Casselman is also one of the top passing completion percentage at 71.4 per cent.

“Winning the Yates cup is the dream of every kid doing this and I’ve been to some games having my parents being Western Alumni,” Casselman said. The Mustangs have the most Yates cups in OUA history but haven’t won since 2023 and haven’t won the Vanier cup since 2021.

The last time the two teams meant was early in the season with Western winning 44-37.

“Both teams have grown a lot and both teams have changed quite a bit,” Faulds said. “Some of our guys were playing in their second game and we have to be ready.”

Western practice (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM news)

Kick off for the semi-final game is set for 1:00 p.m. at Western Alumni Stadium.

Heavy offensive teams

Western practice in the rain (Credit: Daniel Thuss

The Mustangs and Lancers are two of the countries top scoring teams with Windsor in 3rd at 312 points scored and Western a top with 370 points scored. However Western is 15th for points scored against while Windsor is 8th. Faulds said playoff football does involve heavy rushing games and both team sit in the top 3 for rushing yards.

stories.title: Gas and groceries: Budget measures on the table for middle-class Canadian families
stories.summary: Some families who had hoped the new budget would provide some relief say there are few items that will directly put money back into their pockets.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Montreal — Some Canadian families who had hoped the new budget would provide some relief say there are few items that will directly put money back into their pockets.

Jamillah Jean hoped for help with groceries and gas. She is a mother of two children from the West Island of Montreal.

“We might be a two-income household, but activities cost a lot, groceries cost a lot, gas costs a lot,” says Jean. “There is a definite pinch in my pocket when it comes to groceries.”

Ottawa extended a top-up to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit that will see a couple with two children receive up to $2,570 for the year. But her family income is above the threshold established for the base year 2025 at $73,592 for a couple with two children.

“I absolutely understand we come from a place of privilege in that regard,” says Jean. “You want to be able to make sure that the benefits help people that have a lower income. And at the same time, groceries are hitting us hard. What would have cost us $800 a month just a couple of years ago, now we are over $1,000. “

She sees a disconnect between what is considered a middle-class income today and the reality of rising costs for families, and her salary has not kept pace.

Her 15-year-old daughter, Nahyma, is budget-savvy and she finds coupons to help lower the price of her lunches. But she is finding fewer deals. She and her nine-year-old, Jayha, are very active in volleyball, track and soccer. The cost of gas has driven up the price of pick-ups and drop-offs.

“We have to figure out what we are leaving the house to do,” says Jean. “We have to be really strategic in our movements in terms of how to stretch a tank of gas.”

A federal gas tax suspension that saves drivers roughly 10 cents per litre has been in place since April 20, and Jean would have liked that to continue. But the budget calls for the tax to be phased back in.

Shilpa Matade hoped there would be even more help for families coping with higher gas prices. The mother of two young girls says she often keeps the car parked to save money.

“I take it as little as possible,” she says. “Or we carpool. My friend and I, we share a car to go out for groceries.”

For a weekly fill-up for a minivan with a 70-litre tank, families saved roughly $364 a year with the tax suspension, but by April 1 it will be fully back in place.

Other measures that could impact families’ pocketbooks include a $1.5-billion investment over nine years to build, expand and renovate community recreational facilities and ice rinks across Canada. The budget also pledges free entry to Canada’s national museums for people under the age of 25.

stories.title: Discovery of rare baby right whale off Canada gives scientists cause for celebration
stories.summary: It puts the number of baby right whales discovered from the most recent birthing season at 24, the most productive year for the whales since 2009
stories.author: Patrick Whittle
stories.content:
It would seem difficult to miss a 6,804-kilogram baby, but for months scientists who study rare whales did just that, and now they couldn’t be happier.

Researchers in Canada captured images of an unidentified baby North Atlantic right whale, one of the rarest sea mammals in the world, off Anticosti Island in Quebec in September. Scientists with the New England Aquarium in Boston said this week that after analyzing photos and data about right whales, they have determined it was a calf likely born months ago that went unseen during winter surveys for the giant animals.

The discovery puts the number of baby right whales discovered from the most recent birthing season at 24, the most productive year for the whales since 2009 and the fourth-highest count on record, the aquarium said. The whales number only about 380 in the world, and their population has fallen since 2010.

The whale was seen with its mother, a 38-year-old whale known to researchers as Silt, scientists said. Right whales give birth off the southeastern U.S. in winter before venturing north to New England and Canada to feed.

The whales are extensively catalogued with photography by researchers because they are so rare. It’s also rare for the researchers who study the whales to miss a baby, but the discovery was a welcome surprise, said Amy Warren, a scientist at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center.

“Silt was briefly seen in the southeastern U.S. calving grounds in February 2026, so it’s possible she had the calf there but snuck away before they were documented together. This is an exciting discovery for us so late in the year,” Warren said.

Baby right whale births are closely tracked by scientists because the tiny population needs successful calving years to remain viable. There are only about 70 reproductive-age females left in the population, and scientists have said the whales have reached 20 calves in a season only a few times since 2010.

That was when their numbers started falling, as they lost about 25 per cent between 2010 and 2020. The whales are vulnerable to collisions with large ships and entanglement in commercial fishing gear, and the warming of the ocean has heightened those threats because they have strayed from protected areas, scientists have said. They also suffered a disastrous year in 2018 when no babies were born.

Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, as the whales have gained back some of their population since 2020. But conservationists have decried recent moves by the U.S. government to delay new protections for the whales for a decade in favour of commercial fishing interests.

The baby whale sighted off Quebec was spotted by researchers with Mingan Island Cetacean Study, a non-profit research organization in the province’s coastal Côte-Nord region. The whale wasn’t seen by researchers despite boat-based and aerial surveys along the U.S. East Coast all spring and summer, the New England Aquarium said.

Scientists are celebrating the animal’s addition to a successful breeding season for the rare whales, said Richard Sears, founder and director of Mingan Island Cetacean Study.

“It just goes to show you how big the ocean is, and how those animals can get lost out there,” he said.

stories.title: Expert insight: School psychologists could improve learning for entire classrooms
stories.summary: Western University researchers believe school psychologists' expertise can be applied across multiple levels of influence.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Across Canada, students and families face longwait times forschool-based psychological assessments.

These waits reflect broader national shortages in school psychology services. The school psychology profession has faced longstanding staffing shortages, and demand continues to rise.

The federal government currently projects a high risk of a national shortage of school psychologists through 2033.

In Ontario, the consequences have been visible for years. In 2023-24, only 26 per cent of elementary schools reported regularly scheduled access to a psychologist. Twenty-four per cent reported having no access at all.

The lack of access to this professional knowledge is significant as school psychologists can do much more than assess individual students struggling with their learning, behaviour and mental health.

Their expertise can be applied across multiple levels of influence: They can consult with teachers, develop school-based prevention and intervention programs and contribute to policies across school systems.

Psychological assessment reports can be enormously valuable in identifying barriers to student success and recommending supports.

School teams May recommend a student for a psychological assessment following a period of targeted intervention when questions remain about how to best support a student’s continued learning and development.

During the assessment process, a psychologist May examine a student’s learning, attention, memory, executive functioning, behaviour and social-emotional functioning to better understand why they’re struggling at school.

They integrate a range of data – for example, from interviews or questionnaires with parents and teachers, observations of the student and assessments related to the above areas – to then develop a specific case formulation. This integrates the psychologist’s best understanding of the student’s strengths and needs. This May or May not include a specific diagnosis.

The psychologist generates a written report that provides recommendations. These are intended to translate what was learned about the student into action – particularly in classrooms.

This could include recommending changes to teaching practice related to:

How information is presented;

Breaking complex tasks into manageable steps;

Providing organizational supports;

Offering different ways to access and demonstrate learning;

Reducing other barriers in the learning process.

A psychological assessment’s recommended strategies May also represent evidence-informed, accessible teaching practices that could benefit an entire classroom.

Some strategies that originated in “special education” or for students with identified differences are now understood to have benefits across a larger student population. For example, instructional approaches for writing, assessing the growth of students in basic skills and positive behaviour support interventions and supports are now considered effective universal teaching practices.

Universal design for learning (UDL) is an educational framework to strengthen inclusion. It supports educators in anticipating learner variability and reducing barriers to learning for all students.

The UDL framework stresses the intentional design of learning environments to support student agency. It offers corresponding guidelines and checkpoints that focus on designing options for students to engage, access information and demonstrate their understanding.

UDL can become a shared framework for collaborative conversations between psychologists and educators. This can help them connect what is learned through the assessment with decisions about instruction and classroom design.

Many assessment report recommendations – for example, teaching explicit skills and reducing unnecessary cognitive demands – overlap in meaningful ways with evidence-based instructional practices and principles emerging from the science of learning.

The effectiveness of extending recommendations beyond the individual student depends partly upon how they’re communicated to educators, caregivers and other school staff.

Our research team in the Improving Accessibility and Application in School Psychology lab at Western University, led by Colin King, the first author of this story, used the UDL framework to conduct pilot work. This examined how common areas of student need identified through psychological assessment aligned with UDL concepts.

In this pilot work, we found that in a sample of 50 psychological profiles, there were many areas of overlap between student need and UDL concepts. Common areas included options to support access to language and symbols and ways to support executive functioning and self-regulation skills.

Rachel Krahn, the second author of this story, is drawing on her earlier master’s research in the lab to explore in her PhD how school psychologists can support collaborative and inclusive practice and how UDL May be applied in this work.

Continued research will highlight educators’ beliefs on UDL and how their perspectives can inform impactful psychological recommendations and consultation.

Ontario’s Right to Read inquiry Report, released in 2022, noted that psychologists are limited in their ability to support professional development for teachers due to the demand for individualized assessments.

Providing earlier, evidence-based instruction and intervention for reading challenges could provide greater flexibility to support students and teachers through consultation and professional development.

Maximizing the knowledge and expertise from school psychologists to improve learning environments at large will require more than writing different recommendations or assessing more students.

Our preliminary research, as well as past research related to actualizing assessment reports, suggests that a shift is needed in psychologists’ and broader educational systems practices. The shift involves focusing more on building relationships with teachers, strengthening consultation and using psychological knowledge to build capacity across school systems.

Past scholarship has highlighted the need for a larger framework for school psychology that also includes the important role of rich teacher education training to support inclusive practice.

When psychological services are scarce, questions remain about how to use the knowledge generated through assessment more effectively and how to translate it from individual learners into stronger learning environments for everyone.

This would help systems leverage a key principle from UDL: “What is necessary for some is beneficial for all.”Image 1: The Conversation

Colin King, Director, Mary J. Wright Child and Youth Development Clinic, Western University and Rachel Krahn, PhD student, School and Applied Child Psychology, Western University.

stories.title: Cartel boss accused of being Ryan Wedding's protector is shot dead in gunfight with Mexican police
stories.summary: Edgar Aarón Vazquez, identified as the leader and founder of the New Empire Cartel, was shot dead Thursday evening while Mexican federal officers were executing a warrant for his arrest.
stories.author: Calvi Leon
stories.content:
A man identified as the cartel boss who protected ex-Olympian and alleged drug kingpin Ryan Wedding while he was a fugitive in Mexico has been killed in a gunfight with federal authorities there, the country’s top security official says.

Edgar Aarón Vazquez, known as “the General” and identified as the leader and founder of the New Empire Cartel, was shot dead Thursday evening while Mexican federal officers were executing a warrant for his arrest in Naucalpan, State of Mexico, the Secretariat of Security and Citizen Protection Omar García Harfuch announced .

Vazquez was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department last year over his links to Wedding’s alleged cocaine empire. At the time, the department said Vazquez provided protection for the then-fugitive and used his police contacts to help locate murder targets for the drug ring.

Wedding is accused of running a billion-dollar criminal enterprise that worked with Mexican cartels and ordered multiple murders around the globe — including the mistaken identity killings of an innocent Indian couple in Caledon, Ont., and the assassination of a U.S. federal witness who helped dismantle part of the network.

Despite the allegations, Vazquez, 42, was not facing U.S. charges in either of the two indictments against Wedding and dozens of his alleged associates.

The New Empire Cartel is described as a violent criminal group largely based in Mexico City. According to Harfuch’s statement, he was being investigated for offences ranging from kidnapping and murder to money laundering and trafficking drugs to the United States and Canada.

It wasn’t immediately clear whether the pending charges against Vazquez were directly tied to the sprawling prosecution in the Wedding case.

Mexican federal judge Luis Benítez Alcántara, 49, of Mexico City, was arrested on Sunday in Colombia.

The raid came the same day that U.S. authorities announced the arrest of a Mexican judge for allegedly accepting a $2-million bribe to release Wedding’s Canadian right-hand man from Mexican custody.

The judge, Luis Benítez Alcántara, 49, of Mexico City, was arrested Sunday in Colombia.

Mexican officials described Vazquez as the mastermind behind the high-profile murder of police commissioner Milton Morales Figueroa in July 2024.

At the time, Figueroa was head of the Mexico City police’s Tactical Strategy and Special Operations Unit. He and Harfuch worked closely together at a time when Harfuch was gearing up to take on his current post.

“Honouring his memory means continuing the investigations until all those responsible for this crime are brought to justice,” Harfuch wrote on Thursday in his statement announcing Vazquez’s death.

The operation targeting Vazquez involved agents from the security ministry, navy, federal criminal investigations unit and national intelligence agency.

The Secretariat of Security and Citizen Protection said in a news release that the officers were conducting field work when the occupants of a vehicle identified them as law enforcement and started shooting.

Vazquez and a second unidentified man died in the exchange.

Wedding is accused of leading one of the largest cocaine pipelines into Canada, via the U.S., Mexico and Colombia, while orchestrating murders against enemies or rivals of the organization.

Before his arrest earlier this year, U.S. authorities say Wedding was hiding out in Mexico as one of the FBI’s top 10 most wanted fugitives.

Wedding is scheduled for two trials in March and October 2027, although it’s possible the dates change due to the complexity of the case.

stories.title: Unemployment ticked up to 6.7% in October, says StatCan
stories.summary: Canada's unemployment rate increased 0.2 percentage points to 6.7 per cent last month as more people looked for work — especially younger Canadians.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canada’s unemployment rate increased 0.2 percentage points to 6.7 per cent last month as more people looked for work — especially younger Canadians .

A Reuters poll of economists had expected the economy would bounce back with a gain of 13,600 jobs in October.

Statistics Canada said Friday that Canada’s workforce shed 4,700 jobs in October, with the unemployment rate for youth aged 15-24 rising 0.7 percentage points from September to 13.7 per cent.

Young students found it especially challenging to find work with the unemployment rate at 13.5 per cent compared to 12.3 per cent of young Canadians who were not attending school. Statistics Canada also notes the proportion of youth attending school in October was 63.3 per cent, up from 62.2 per cent a year earlier.

Meanwhile, unemployment was unchanged last month for core-aged working Canadians (25 to 54 years old), Statistics Canada says, at 5.8 per cent for men and 5.3 per cent for women.

Most of the job losses last month were concentrated in retail and wholesale trade, where 29,000 jobs were shed. At the same time, there were increases for construction and educational sectors with 16,000 and 15,000 jobs added each respectively.

Private sector employment fell by 53,000 positions last month, marking the first decline in the segment since February. Employment in the public sector, meanwhile, was up 50,000 positions.

StatCan noted that, ON a year-over-year basis, private sector jobs are still up while the public sector is down.

Statistics Canada says nearly a quarter, or 23.7 per cent of Canadians who are able and willing to work were considered on long-term unemployment last month, meaning they had been continuously searching for work for 27 weeks or more. That’s up from 21.5 per cent a year earlier.

The job market overall has been struggling amid the trade war with the U.S., and especially in recent months as U.S. tariffs continue to impact Canadian businesses and leave many feeling uncertain about the future and hesitant to hire new workers.

From August through October, Canada’s job market has shed nearly 115,000 jobs, and the unemployment rate has increased from 6.4 in August.

“For anyone hoping that October would bring a recovery in the Canadian job market after back-to-back negative surprises, today’s release is a disappointment,” says economist Sneha Puri at Indeed in a statement.

“There are visible cracks in the labour market, especially for young jobseekers, and if this optimism isn’t then translated into a strong jobs report in the months ahead, the surprising weakness in headline employment will start to look less temporary and more like the beginning of a renewed cooling in the labour market.”

At the same time, the layoff rate — the share of workers who were laid off between September and October — was little changed last month at 0.7 per cent compared to 0.6 per cent in September.

One economist believes the latest round of U.S. tariffs have not yet led to widespread layoffs.

“New U.S. tariffs implemented since Aug. 22 have not, and are not expected to lead to widespread layoffs in Canada. They are severe but of a narrow scope,” said senior economist Claire Fan at Royal Bank of Canada in a statement.

“Manufacturing jobs changed little in August and September. Sectors disproportionately affected by U.S. tariffs including auto and steel manufacturers can continue to look to increasing government support to transition out of a period of reduced U.S. demand.”

The Bank of Canada increased its benchmark interest rate last month for the first time in three years, and mainly to get ahead of what’s expected to be higher inflation in the coming months.

But if the Canadian job market continues to show signs of stress, that could influence the central bank to hold its key policy rate next month at the last meeting of the year.

“The temporary factors that we expected to flatter today’s data showed up less than we had envisioned, but that doesn’t account entirely for the downside surprise, with underlying labour market dynamics appearing to have weakened again in recent months,” says senior economist Andrew Grantham at Cibc in a statement.

– with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Former Manitoba law dean accused of fraud to be extradited from France
stories.summary: Jonathan Black-Branch was arrested in France on allegations he mismanaged hundreds of thousands of dollars in Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A court in France has ruled in favour of extraditing a former law dean of the University of Manitoba, who was arrested in the country on allegations he mismanaged hundreds of thousands of dollars in Canada.

A document from the Versailles Court of Appeal says the Indictment Division has granted Canada’s request to extradite Jonathan Black-Branch.

No date was given for when he is to be transferred back to Canada.

Black-Branch was arrested in April in Neuilly-sur-Seine, near Paris, after a Canada-wide arrest warrant was issued for fraud over $5,000.

He was in court last month opposing his extradition.

An internal investigation by the University of Manitoba says Black-Branch misused and mismanaged more than $600,000 of the school’s funds for personal bills, pricey meals at a members-only club and personal education at Ivy League schools.

Black-Branch was disbarred by the Law Society of Manitoba in 2024 following the investigation.

The university asked police in Winnipeg to investigate after the law society’s decision. It also sued Black-Branch for breaching terms of his employment agreement.

In May 2025, Manitoba Court of King’s Bench ordered Black-Branch to repay the school more than $682,000 plus interest. The university has said it’s pursuing all available collection options to recoup the money.

Black-Branch was hired as the Winnipeg university’s law dean in 2016 but suddenly left the post in 2020 and moved to Europe. Court documents relating to the lawsuit said he was believed to be living in Switzerland.

stories.title: Scientists discovered an unknown baby right whale off Canada. They say it’s a cause for joy
stories.summary: Portland, Maine (AP) — It would seem difficult to miss a 15,000-pound (6,804-kilogram) baby, but for months scientists who study rare whales did just that, and now they couldn't be happier.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Portland, Maine (AP) — It would seem difficult to miss a 15,000-pound (6,804-kilogram) baby, but for months scientists who study rare whales did just that, and now they couldn’t be happier.

Researchers in Canada captured images of an unidentified baby North Atlantic right whale, one of the rarest sea mammals in the world, off Anticosti Island in Quebec in September. Scientists with the New England Aquarium in Boston said this week that after analyzing photos and data about right whales, they have determined it was a calf likely born months ago that went unseen during winter surveys for the giant animals.

The discovery puts the number of baby right whales discovered from the most recent birthing season at 24, the most productive year for the whales since 2009 and the fourth-highest count on record, the aquarium said. The whales number only about 380 in the world, and their population has fallen since 2010.

The whale was seen with its mother, a 38-year-old whale known to researchers as Silt, scientists said. Right whales give birth off the southeastern U.S. in winter before venturing north to New England and Canada to feed.

The whales are extensively cataloged with photography by researchers because they are so rare. It’s also rare for the researchers who study the whales to miss a baby, but the discovery was a welcome surprise, said Amy Warren, a scientist at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center.

“Silt was briefly seen in the southeastern U.S. calving grounds in February 2026, so it’s possible she had the calf there but snuck away before they were documented together. This is an exciting discovery for us so late in the year,” Warren said.

Baby right whale births are closely tracked by scientists because the tiny population needs successful calving years to remain viable. There are only about 70 reproductive-age females left in the population, and scientists have said the whales have reached 20 calves in a season only a few times since 2010.

That was when their numbers started falling, as they lost about 25% between 2010 and 2020. The whales are vulnerable to collisions with large ships and entanglement in commercial fishing gear, and the warming of the ocean has heightened those threats because they have strayed from protected areas, scientists have said. They also suffered a disastrous year in 2018 when no babies were born.

Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, as the whales have gained back some of their population since 2020. But conservationists have decried recent moves by the U.S. government to delay new protections for the whales for a decade in favor of commercial fishing interests.

The baby whale sighted off Quebec was spotted by researchers with Mingan Island Cetacean Study, a nonprofit research organization in the province’s coastal Côte-Nord region. The whale wasn’t seen by researchers despite boat-based and aerial surveys along the U.S. East Coast all spring and summer, the New England Aquarium said.

Scientists are celebrating the animal’s addition to a successful breeding season for the rare whales, said Richard Sears, founder and director of Mingan Island Cetacean Study.

“It just goes to show you how big the ocean is, and how those animals can get lost out there,” he said.

Patrick Whittle, The Associated Press

stories.title: Disbarred former Manitoba law dean loses extradition fight in French Appeal Court
stories.summary: A document from the Versailles Court of Appeal says the Indictment Division has granted Canada's request to extradite the man. No transfer date was given.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A court in France has ruled in favour of extraditing a former law dean of the University of Manitoba, who was arrested in the country on allegations he mismanaged hundreds of thousands of dollars in Canada.

A document from the Versailles Court of Appeal says the Indictment Division has granted Canada’s request to extradite Jonathan Black-Branch.

No date was given for when he is to be transferred back to Canada.

Black-Branch was arrested in April in Neuilly-sur-Seine, near Paris, after a Canada-wide arrest warrant was issued for fraud over $5,000.

He was in court last month opposing his extradition .

An internal investigation by the University of Manitoba says Black-Branch misused and mismanaged more than $600,000 of the school’s funds for personal bills, pricey meals at a members-only club and personal education at Ivy League schools.

Black-Branch was disbarred by the Law Society of Manitoba in 2024 following the investigation.

The university asked police in Winnipeg to investigate after the law society’s decision. It also sued Black-Branch for breaching terms of his employment agreement.

In May 2025, Manitoba Court of King’s Bench ordered Black-Branch to repay the school more than $682,000 plus interest. The university has said it’s pursuing all available collection options to recoup the money.

Black-Branch was hired as the Winnipeg university’s law dean in 2016 but suddenly left the post in 2020 and moved to Europe. Court documents relating to the lawsuit said he was believed to be living in Switzerland.

stories.title: ‘A mission rehearsal’ for Canadian troops training near the border of Russia
stories.summary: Nato’s largest-ever exercise along the border of Russia and Belarus is being called “a mission rehearsal” by the Canadian commander at the helm of Nato operations in Latvia.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Adazi, Latvia -- Nato’s largest-ever exercise along the border of Russia and Belarus is being called “a mission rehearsal” by the Canadian commander at the helm of Nato operations in Latvia.

Col. David Brassard commands Nato’s Canadian-led multinational brigade in Latvia. This week, he has deployed 3,000 soldiers from 14 Nato nations to multiple locations along Nato’s eastern flank, where all roads lead to Russia and Belarus.

“What we’re doing is sending a message: we have a defence plan, we have equipment, we have the personnel,” Brassard said.

Latvia, along with Estonia to the north and Lithuania to the south, makes up Nato’s eastern flank. The threat from Russia toward the Baltic region has only grown since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“The situation has deteriorated in the east,” Brassard said during a one-on-one interview with CTV National News at the Adazi Military Base in Latvia.

Asked how he views the threat Russia currently poses to eastern Europe, Brassard says the situation is fragile, but stable for the time being.

However, he lists drone incursions, incidents of “espionage and even sabotage through acts of arson” as a form of hybrid warfare he believes Russia is carrying out against multiple European countries including Latvia.

“Is going to the east 100 per cent safe right now? No, it isn’t. We must take precautions when we get close to the border,” Brassard said.

That’s exactly what Brassard’s brigade has executed this week, moving roughly 600 vehicles and thousands of personnel toward a training ground on Russia’s doorstep.

Pointing to a map of Latvia in his office, Brassard shares that he had a platoon within five to seven kilometres of the Baltic defence line and Russia in recent days.

CTV News has embedded with multiple battalions and squadrons along Nato’s eastern flank this week for the historic exercise, dubbed “Resolute Reforger.”

On Thursday, while embedded with a squadron of military engineers, CTV News toured a newly constructed underground bunker and trench system just 30 kilometres from Russia’s border.

The fully covered bunker was constructed to train soldiers how to protect themselves while remaining on the offensive during modern warfare.

From deep inside the dark bunker, drone operators can stay covered and concealed while remotely flying a drone into enemy territory.

“Tactics on the battlefield are evolving very fast,” said a captain of the Multinational Engineer Squadron, whose name CTV News agreed to withhold to protect his identity.

“Things have changed, we’ve learned and we’re adapting with our partners to be able to adapt our training for the next-generation war environment.”

Brassard says he’s waiting on a $4-million order of drones to arrive in Latvia as he works to provide Nato troops with a cutting edge, modern-day arsenal.

“Do I have all the capability that I want (at my disposal) no I don’t,” Brassard said. “However, one thing for sure is I do have the capabilities that I need to be able to address any crisis in the east.”

Brassard says that military spending is no longer just an empty promise; he says Canada is beginning to deliver on its pledge to increase military spending while making a meaningful contribution to Nato.

The colonel has confirmed that an even larger exercise is planned for this coming April. Dubbed “Resolute Warrior,” 900 military vehicles, and 3,600 personnel are expected to take part across Nato’s eastern flank.

“This is only the beginning,” the commander said.

stories.title: Fantasy league teams draft a new player: AI
stories.summary: Chatbots and custom agents are suggesting top picks and more. But are they taking away the fun?
stories.author: Danielle Groen
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence is muscling into fantasy sports leagues. It’s making draft selections. It’s setting starting lineups and grabbing guys off waivers. And its value to a fantasy general manager reflects a broader divide between AI superusers and traditionalists.

That divide could not have been clearer last month at the draft for one long-running league. A dozen members of Fun Time Fantasy Basketball – they picked the name back in high school, 26 years ago – sat around a boardroom table in a midtown Toronto office, beer and Halloween candy spread out between them.

At one end, Mitchell Forster had his laptop open to the custom command centre he’d spent weeks finessing in ChatGPT, which provided a dizzying array of projections and game plans that adjusted in real time as the draft went on. At the opposite end, Harley Hayman rifled through three sheets of paper. He had printed out last season’s stats for the available NBA players. Once they were taken, he used a highlighter to cross off their names.

The algorithm-versus-analogue showdown at Fun Time Fantasy Basketball has been brewing for the better part of a decade.

“I’d always built sophisticated Excel spreadsheets to prepare for the draft,” Mr. Forster said.

Meanwhile, Mr. Hayman declared, “I’ve been getting dissed for eight to 10 years for not even bringing a laptop.”

This is the first time, however, that Mr. Forster is relying on agentic AI to manage his team. It was a natural evolution. “With the AI boom we’re now in,” he said, “I can tell ChatGPT, ‘Create me a tool as if you were the best fantasy basketball expert on Earth.’”

ChatGPT whipped up a strategy for his season, assembling a roster that prioritized meaningful assists and successful free throws while supporting field goal percentage and blocks. It also assigned each player a value for those categories, then piped in with advice throughout the draft. “[Milwaukee Bucks centre Myles] Turner supplies blocks and threes, but his projected FG% does not balance Trae,” it cautioned. (Like most NBA announcers, ChatGPT is on a first-name basis with Washington Wizards guard Trae Young.)

That’s a very small sample of what it’s come back with. “This is definitely overkill,” Mr. Forster acknowledged, adding that he’ll probably dial down the model next year.

AI isn’t calling all of the shots. “I’m still in the loop,” he said. “I still watch games and look for stars in the making. I don’t think AI can do that yet.”

But by off-loading much of his league’s time-consuming labour – poring over endless fantasy stats; staying on top of what’s happened in the NBA – he frees himself up to focus on other aspects of his life.

“As we get older, time is ever more precious,” Mr. Forster said. “We all have kids and families and jobs. So if I can save myself some hours by using AI, hey, why not?”

It makes sense he’d see it that way: Mr. Forster works in tech software sales and turns to AI often. Mr. Hayman, ON the other hand, isn’t a habitual user of agentic AI. He’s not against it – don’t be fooled by the highlighter and printouts – he just has an inverse take on the free-time issue.

“I’ve got a wife, two young kids at home and a job with a lot of moving pieces,” said Mr. Hayman, the director of an overnight summer camp. “I do not have time to go down the road of learning these AI programs and having them train me.”

He appreciates that there are benefits to the technology. But it’s more efficient for him to lean on the basketball knowledge he’s acquired over the past quarter century.

“Winning takes shrewd pickups and sharp trades that require working the other GMs in the league,” Mr. Hayman says. “I’m going to use my brain for that.”

It was inevitable that fantasy sports leagues would find themselves weighing the usefulness of AI. Roughly one in 10 Canadians played fantasy sports last year, but nearly 80 per cent of us now use AI tools, according to Leger, up from 47 per cent a year and a half ago. Although Pew Research found the most common application remains basic information searches, through chatbots and Google’s AI Overviews, AI personal agents surged in popularity in the past two months. Meta’s Muse has been the most downloaded app in Canada since its September debut.

Renee Miller, a professor of neuroscience at the University of Rochester and chief executive officer of Franchise League Football, has clocked a rise in the reliance on AI across fantasy sports. Most of the few thousand members of her league are holdouts, she said, preferring to steer the decision-making themselves. But that doesn’t mean they’re wholly opposed to the advantages of these tools.

“My league is actually looking into building an AI bot that would step in for absentee managers,” Prof. Miller says. The agent could set fantasy lineups, make adjustments and even add a few waiver pickups. “It would keep the league competitive, because no one wants to play against a team that only has three active players in their starting lineup.”

So how big a presence should AI have in a recreational hobby? That’s been the subject of much debate at another Toronto fantasy basketball league, where more than half of the 10 members began using AI for their teams this season. Arguments volleyed between Nick Poissant, a pen-and-paper traditionalist, and the league’s Claude Code power users.

One AI-savvy member built an exhaustive program that analyzes multiple fantasy-stats providers, every relevant news source and the league’s own history to determine the best strategy for a winning team. He just volunteered to share the tool with his fellow managers, positioning it as a way to level the playing field.

Mr. Poissant is unmoved by that offer. “I like trying to figure it out on my own,” he said. The challenge is worth the investment of his time. He’s willing to stick with the league this season, but maybe not much longer. “If it becomes guys just punching buttons on their laptop, I’ll probably move on.”

Over at Fun Time Fantasy Basketball, Mr. Hayman is happy to be an AI resister among the GMs in his league. “It’s honestly a badge of honour for me. I’m going to keep competing. I’m going to keep winning.”

And though it’s early in the season, he’s quick to point out that he’s second in the standings – one spot ahead of Mr. Forster.

That’s been the subject of much debate at another Toronto fantasy basketball league, where more than half of the 10 members began using AI for their teams this season. Arguments volleyed between Nick Poissant, a pen-and-paper traditionalist, and the league’s Claude Code power users.

One AI-savvy member built an exhaustive program that analyzes multiple fantasy-stats providers, every relevant news source and the league’s own history to determine the best strategy for a winning team. He just volunteered to share the tool with his fellow managers, positioning it as a way to level the playing field.

Mr. Poissant is unmoved by that offer. “I like trying to figure it out on my own,” he said. The challenge is worth the investment of his time. He’s willing to stick with the league this season, but maybe not much longer. “If it becomes guys just punching buttons on their laptop, I’ll probably move on.”

Over at Fun Time Fantasy Basketball, Mr. Hayman is happy to be an AI resister among the GMs in his league. “It’s honestly a badge of honour for me. I’m going to keep competing. I’m going to keep winning.”
And though it’s early in the season, he’s quick to point out that he’s second in the standings – one spot ahead of Mr. Forster.

stories.title: London teen facing charges in connection with break-and-enter
stories.summary: A London teen is facing charges in connection with an attempted break-and-enter.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A London teen is facing charges in connection with an attempted break-and-enter.

On Wednesday around 7 p.m., London police responded to a home near Highbury Avenue North and Huron Street. They said the suspect fled before arrival.

Through an investigation, officers said they learned the suspect uttered threats before the break-and-enter.

The suspect was found near Belmont Drive and Wharncliffe Road South. Police said the suspect tried to run from officers but was arrested with the help of a police service dog.

The suspect was taken to hospital with minor injuries.

A 17-year-old boy is charged with two counts of failing to comply with a release order, mischief $5,000, uttering threats, and resisting arrest.

stories.title: Cineplex posts record revenue as Spider-Man, Odyssey drove moviegoers
stories.summary: Revenue for the quarter totalled $440.2 million, up from $348.9 million in the same quarter last year, as theatre attendance rose to 14.8 million people, up from 12.1 million.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Cinema giant Cineplex Inc. reported a third-quarter profit of $23.8 million as it saw record revenue for the period, boosted by “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey.”

The movie theatre company says the profit amounted to 34 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

The result compared with a profit of $1.2 million or two cents per diluted share a year ago.

Revenue for the quarter totalled $440.2 million, up from $348.9 million in the same quarter last year, as theatre attendance rose to 14.8 million people, up from 12.1 million.

Box office revenue per patron totalled $14.54 for the quarter, up from $13.23 a year ago, while concession revenue per patron amounted to $9.99, up from $9.65.

In September, Cineplex named former Landmark Cinemas CEO Bill Walker as its new chief executive and announced plans for a review of strategic alternatives, including, but not limited to, a potential sale.

stories.title: Report alleges China linked to at least 18 overseas police stations in Canada
stories.summary: China has exponentially expanded its network of illegal overseas police stations, to “extend its tentacles” across a web of new community associations, according to a report by international human rights group Safeguard Defenders.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
Ottawa - China has exponentially expanded its network of illegal overseas police stations, to “extend its tentacles” across a web of new community associations, according to a report by international human rights group Safeguard Defenders.

In its latest report, the Spanish non-governmental organization (NGO) identifies nearly 1,250 overseas Chinese associations which they say are fronts for suspected police centres in 91 countries.

“That network is being used to watch the diaspora. To watch what they do, what they say and to essentially police them,” says Laura Harth, Safeguard Defender’s China director in an interview with CTV News.

The new figures are also a 12-fold increase from the Ngo’s findings four years earlier.

In 2022, the NGO identified 100 illegal Chinese police stations operating in more than 50 countries, including Canada.

The report, A Formula for Repression , asserts that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is exporting “its domestic system of surveillance and control to Chinese diaspora communities around the world.”

China has more than 60 million citizens living abroad.

Michael Kovrig, senior advisor for the International Crisis Group, says the report reveals “an early stage” of the Ccp’s efforts to expand its ability to influence the political choices of sovereign nations across the globe.

Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat who was arbitrarily detained by China in 2018 says the “stunning” apparatus revealed by Safeguard Defenders could lead to the “slow erosion of the rights of Canadian citizens to express their own views and vote as they wish.”

The ‘magic weapon’

Safeguard Defenders says the associations are run by overseas party operatives under the direction of Beijing’s United Front Workers Department (Ufwd).

President Xi Jinping calls the Ufwd a “magic weapon” for monitoring and controlling its citizens, no matter where they live.

Safeguard was able to identify 1,247 community hubs that had acknowledged they were “liaison points” to Chinese police and prosecutor websites and in publications.

The NGO says any association connected to the Ufwd can be mobilized to participate in its mass surveillance program.

China says it has “tens of thousands” of Ufwd affiliated organizations around the world.

Instead of being chastened by the past exposure of its illegal activities, Harth, the report’s lead researcher, says China has gotten better at covering its tracks.

“They’ve learned their lesson. The public security bureaus were maybe a bit too enthusiastic. They (previously) put their own logos on walls and doors. Now post 2022, they’re more careful about (not) naming the exact associations they’re working with.”

How the network grows

A Formula for Repression details how China’s global grid for community control works.

Researchers say that more than 10 police forces from five provinces in China are working through a vast network of Chinese Federation hubs on foreign soil.

The hubs are marketed as a place for the diaspora to connect culturally and foster business and tourism ties with various provinces and cities in China.

Safeguard Defenders lists the names of 80 regional associations linked to Chinese law enforcement. In 2022, it only found four associations that had set up police stations.

The NGO warns that the Ccp’s tentacles extend “into every part of ordinary life.”

The Canadian picture

Safeguard’s report reveals 18 alleged Chinese police monitoring stations in Canada, compared to the five that it found in 2022.

However, additional research by Jamestown, an American think tank cited in the report, uncovered 575 organizations linked to the Ufwd in Canada.

New Democratic Party MP, Jenny Kwan calls the allegations troubling.

“If true, it suggests that existing government responses have not been sufficient to deter these illegal activities,” Kwan wrote in an open letter addressed to Canada’s public safety minister.

“Canada must close the legal gaps, investigate these operations and ensure that people in our communities can speak, organize and exercise their democratic rights without coercion, intimidation or fear.”

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree represents a riding in Scarborough, Ont., with a high population of ethnic Chinese constituents. He’s cautioning against jumping to conclusions.

“I can say that foreign interference of any sort is unacceptable. It’s something that we will not tolerate. With respect to these specific allegations – they are allegations and have not been investigated,” Anandasangaree said.

In 2023, the RCMP closed its investigation into two Chinese service centres in Montreal alleged to be police stations. No charges were laid. The organizations are now suing the federal government.

Anandasangaree says law enforcement will do their due diligence and follow up on the information in the report but says investigations must be conducted with “nuance.”

He says some of the associations are sports or book clubs, that on a day-to-day basis “just go about providing civic life to members of the Chinese diaspora.”

Will the foreign influence registry make a difference?

CTV News asked Anandasangaree if he had spoken to the Chinese Embassy about registering the co-ordinators of overseas Chinese organizations as foreign agents.

Canada’s foreign-influence registry started operating in August . Under the act, failure to register foreign organizations could result in fines of $250,000 to $1 million.

Anandasangaree said the onus of education is with the individual embassies and that it’s up to Canada’s first Foreign Influence Transparency Commissioner, Anton Boegman to ensure compliance.

The minister also said he’s concerned the “unsubstantiated” numbers of reported organizations will cause difficulties for the Chinese community.

“Of course (foreign interference) is a concern. The other side is mislabelling and putting people and communities in fear unnecessarily.”

The organizations May promote recreation and culture, but Harth points out some also actively repress other communities who take part in celebrations the CPP doesn’t like, such as Tibetan or Uyghur culture.

“We can’t give legitimacy to a system that does not deserve it … We need to start sending clear signals that this kind of thing isn’t going to pass and put the United Front on notice.”

The Chinese Embassy has not responded to a request for comment from CTV News.

Fear in ethnic communities

The highest profile example of an illegal police station comes from New York City. In May 2026, Lu Jianwang, a U.S. citizen was convicted of operating a clandestine police station, to gather information on Chinese dissidents for Beijing.

In Canada, the RCMP says it has investigated five alleged Chinese police stations in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver. However, no charges were laid.

Uyghur-Canadian Rukiye Turdush, the executive director for Center for East Turkistan National Interest, calls the massive spike in China’s overseas police stations “shocking and scary,” but not a surprise.

She has organized protests against China’s violation of human rights in Xinjiang and says she has seen firsthand how the Ufwd is suppressing dissent.

Turdush, says fellow Uyghur activists who received visas to visit relatives in China were pressured to sign documents stating support for Chinese national law.

“They come back and they’re scared …They hide and can no longer come to my organization.”

The activist is also concerned that her organization has been infiltrated by CCP operatives to launch attacks on the leadership and spy on members.

“That’s how China is dividing the community. We don’t trust each other and we don’t feel safe,” Turdush said.

Canada-China police co-operation agreement

Safeguard Defender’s new data comes 11 months after Prime Minister Mark Carney signed a new police co-operation agreement with President Xi.

In January, the two leaders committed the RCMP and China’s Ministry of Public Security (MPS) to increased co-operation in combating corruption and transnational crimes such as telecommunications fraud, cyberfraud and the trafficking of illegal synthetic drugs.

The prime minister has refused to release the text of the agreement despite calls from the Conservatives and the NDP to do so .

I’m calling on @MarkJCarney govt to stop hiding RCMP–MPS MOU signed in Beijing. Reports that RCMP needs Beijing’s “permission” to show this MOU to Canadians are a threat to our sovereignty. Our diaspora communities deserve to know how their safety and rights are being protected. pic.twitter.com/JnZAFAghEC — Jenny Kwan (@JennyKwanBC) May 12, 2026

Kovrig says Canada should not have signed the agreement because of the “political signal” it sends.

The former diplomat points out that China has a record of arbitrary detention, executions and psychological and physical torture. Kovrig himself was detained by China for more than 1,000 days.

Canada does not have an extradition treaty with China, but Kovrig says the agreement implies that the RCMP and the MPS are co-equal policing organizations that follow similar norms and behaviours.

“That’s simply not the case. The RCMP is not setting up fake police stations to influence Canadians abroad. It’s not involved in subversive activities in foreign countries. We should be calling for the agreement to be released. We need transparency and accountability.”

The NGO says any association connected to the Ufwd can be mobilized to participate in its mass surveillance program.
China says it has “tens of thousands” of Ufwd affiliated organizations around the world.
Instead of being chastened by the past exposure of its illegal activities, Harth, the report’s lead researcher, says China has gotten better at covering its tracks.

“They’ve learned their lesson. The public security bureaus were maybe a bit too enthusiastic. They (previously) put their own logos on walls and doors. Now post 2022, they’re more careful about (not) naming the exact associations they’re working with.”
How the network grows
A Formula for Repression details how China’s global grid for community control works.
Researchers say that more than 10 police forces from five provinces in China are working through a vast network of Chinese Federation hubs on foreign soil.
The hubs are marketed as a place for the diaspora to connect culturally and foster business and tourism ties with various provinces and cities in China.
Safeguard Defenders lists the names of 80 regional associations linked to Chinese law enforcement. In 2022, it only found four associations that had set up police stations.
The NGO warns that the Ccp’s tentacles extend “into every part of ordinary life.”
The Canadian picture
Safeguard’s report reveals 18 alleged Chinese police monitoring stations in Canada, compared to the five that it found in 2022.
However, additional research by Jamestown, an American think tank cited in the report, uncovered 575 organizations linked to the Ufwd in Canada.
New Democratic Party MP, Jenny Kwan calls the allegations troubling.
“If true, it suggests that existing government responses have not been sufficient to deter these illegal activities,” Kwan wrote in an open letter addressed to Canada’s public safety minister.

“Canada must close the legal gaps, investigate these operations and ensure that people in our communities can speak, organize and exercise their democratic rights without coercion, intimidation or fear.”
Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree represents a riding in Scarborough, Ont., with a high population of ethnic Chinese constituents. He’s cautioning against jumping to conclusions.

“I can say that foreign interference of any sort is unacceptable. It’s something that we will not tolerate. With respect to these specific allegations – they are allegations and have not been investigated,” Anandasangaree said.
In 2023, the RCMP closed its investigation into two Chinese service centres in Montreal alleged to be police stations. No charges were laid. The organizations are now suing the federal government.
Anandasangaree says law enforcement will do their due diligence and follow up on the information in the report but says investigations must be conducted with “nuance.”
He says some of the associations are sports or book clubs, that on a day-to-day basis “just go about providing civic life to members of the Chinese diaspora.”
Will the foreign influence registry make a difference?
CTV News asked Anandasangaree if he had spoken to the Chinese Embassy about registering the co-ordinators of overseas Chinese organizations as foreign agents.
Canada’s foreign-influence registry started operating in August . Under the act, failure to register foreign organizations could result in fines of $250,000 to $1 million.
Anandasangaree said the onus of education is with the individual embassies and that it’s up to Canada’s first Foreign Influence Transparency Commissioner, Anton Boegman to ensure compliance.
The minister also said he’s concerned the “unsubstantiated” numbers of reported organizations will cause difficulties for the Chinese community.
“Of course (foreign interference) is a concern. The other side is mislabelling and putting people and communities in fear unnecessarily.”

The organizations May promote recreation and culture, but Harth points out some also actively repress other communities who take part in celebrations the CPP doesn’t like, such as Tibetan or Uyghur culture.
“We can’t give legitimacy to a system that does not deserve it … We need to start sending clear signals that this kind of thing isn’t going to pass and put the United Front on notice.”
The Chinese Embassy has not responded to a request for comment from CTV News.
Fear in ethnic communities

The highest profile example of an illegal police station comes from New York City. In May 2026, Lu Jianwang, a U.S. citizen was convicted of operating a clandestine police station, to gather information on Chinese dissidents for Beijing.
In Canada, the RCMP says it has investigated five alleged Chinese police stations in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver. However, no charges were laid.

Uyghur-Canadian Rukiye Turdush, the executive director for Center for East Turkistan National Interest, calls the massive spike in China’s overseas police stations “shocking and scary,” but not a surprise.
She has organized protests against China’s violation of human rights in Xinjiang and says she has seen firsthand how the Ufwd is suppressing dissent.
Turdush, says fellow Uyghur activists who received visas to visit relatives in China were pressured to sign documents stating support for Chinese national law.
“They come back and they’re scared …They hide and can no longer come to my organization.”
The activist is also concerned that her organization has been infiltrated by CCP operatives to launch attacks on the leadership and spy on members.
“That’s how China is dividing the community. We don’t trust each other and we don’t feel safe,” Turdush said.
Canada-China police co-operation agreement
Safeguard Defender’s new data comes 11 months after Prime Minister Mark Carney signed a new police co-operation agreement with President Xi.

In January, the two leaders committed the RCMP and China’s Ministry of Public Security (MPS) to increased co-operation in combating corruption and transnational crimes such as telecommunications fraud, cyberfraud and the trafficking of illegal synthetic drugs.
The prime minister has refused to release the text of the agreement despite calls from the Conservatives and the NDP to do so .

I’m calling on @MarkJCarney govt to stop hiding RCMP–MPS MOU signed in Beijing. Reports that RCMP needs Beijing’s “permission” to show this MOU to Canadians are a threat to our sovereignty. Our diaspora communities deserve to know how their safety and rights are being protected. pic.twitter.com/JnZAFAghEC — Jenny Kwan (@JennyKwanBC) May 12, 2026
Kovrig says Canada should not have signed the agreement because of the “political signal” it sends.
The former diplomat points out that China has a record of arbitrary detention, executions and psychological and physical torture. Kovrig himself was detained by China for more than 1,000 days.
Canada does not have an extradition treaty with China, but Kovrig says the agreement implies that the RCMP and the MPS are co-equal policing organizations that follow similar norms and behaviours.

“That’s simply not the case. The RCMP is not setting up fake police stations to influence Canadians abroad. It’s not involved in subversive activities in foreign countries. We should be calling for the agreement to be released. We need transparency and accountability.”

stories.title: U.S. midterms and rate hikes leading to buyer uncertainty and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Nov. 6
stories.summary: Plus, one Red Deer couple searches for the perfect home
stories.author: Jacob Dubé
stories.content:
This week: The Liberal government has released their latest budget, putting billions towards building new homes. Plus, the housing market adjusts after the Bank of Canada’s rate hike, and experts weigh in on the practicality of home-built saunas.

On Nov. 5, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal government tabled its second federal budget . Over the five-year horizon, net new spending will amount to $151.5-billion, spread across a variety of initiatives, including boosting Canada’s housing supply.

Ottawa said it would add $13-billion in new capital over ten years on a cash basis to Build Canada Homes, an agency it launched in September 2025 to accelerate home construction. That would bring its total capital to $45-billion, and the government said the new investment would set the agency “on a path” to build 200,000 new homes across Canada over the next decade.

Ottawa said it would also spend $1.5-billion over four years, starting in 2027-2028, and $387.4-million in subsequent years to ready federal land for new housing projects.

At the same time, the government said it would introduce legislation to extend a ban on foreign residential property purchases to January 1, 2029. The restrictions had been set to expire this coming January.

From business investment to increasing the debt, read the highlights from the budget .

Variable-rate mortgages were having a moment – until the Bank of Canada raised its trendsetting interest rate last week, citing concerns about high oil prices.

Canadians had been flocking to variable rates over the past few months as turmoil in the bond market pushed up fixed mortgage rates. Nearly half of consumers taking out or renewing a mortgage in 2026 signed up for a variable one, as of September, compared to less than 10 per cent who did so in 2024, according to data from National Bank of Canada.

But, as Mariya Postelnyak writes, the BoC’s rate hike had variable rates inching up a notch last week. The potential of a few more hikes in the coming months has left mortgage shoppers wondering whether a variable rate is still worth it .

The answer hinges on a number of variables, including risk tolerance, the availability of financial buffer room, and whether the borrowers are first-time homebuyers or more experienced homeowners. But experts say going variable might still turn out to be the cheaper option for many mortgage shoppers , especially for those choosing longer terms.

Derek and Jordanna Gibeault first met in 2017, but it wasn’t until 2023 that they reconnected and began dating. By May, 2023, Jordanna, a realtor, purchased a five-bedroom, three-bathroom semi-detached home in Red Deer, Alta., for $330,000.

While the home had a spacious interior, the couple thought about buying a detached home together one day, with more storage and better exterior spaces, including a bigger backyard and a larger garage. They began to consider what they could afford and what they wanted out of their new home, given a budget of around $550,000.

The couple wanted at least four bedrooms so that they could have personal office spaces, host visiting family, and convert one bedroom into a gym. A larger private backyard space was also a must-have, not only for their two large dogs – a mixed breed named Crue and a black lab named Tikka – but also for themselves.

From a home in Southeast Red Deer with a loft space above the garage, a five-bedroom bungalow with a spacious yard and a split-level home in Deer Park, find out which property the couple decided to buy .

Rates shown are the lowest available for each term/type and category (insured vs. uninsured) as of market close on Thursday, Nov. 5 .

Market watchers in many tranches of Toronto real estate are detecting a palpable fear of commitment this fall: Buyers are reluctant to submit a bid and sellers are balking at making a counter-offer.

As Carolyn Ireland writes, steady activity in the first half of October became quieter in the second half as consumers watched the lead-up to U.S. midterm elections and waited for more clarity on tariffs, interest rates and Canada’s economy.

The Bank of Canada’s rate hike has many consumers fretting about their own budgets and economists predicting a slow grind towards the end of the year in the Greater Toronto Area.

As for potential buyers, they are trying to gauge how much farther home prices have to fall and whether the potential for a lower price offsets the risk of higher rates. Realtors share how buyers and sellers might come to a deal in these times .

Studies show saunas can reduce stress, soothe sore muscles, relieve pain and improve heart health. Some research suggests they could also lower the risk of dementia. But, Matthew Hague writes, are those benefits worth the sweat and headache of a home installation?

Building a home sauna can be tricky. For starters, there are several different kinds to consider: wood burning, electric and infrared. Placement is up for debate, too. Common options include basements, backyards, bathrooms or even bedrooms.

According to Alan Jalasjaa, who hosts a sauna podcast and serves as Canada’s Sauna Ambassador, at-home saunas tend to have lower ceilings compared to commercial ones, which help keep the heat on you.

One sauna designer said the best place to install a home sauna is the backyard. Basements and ensuites can also work, but it’s vital to ensure proper insulation and drainage to avoid mould.

7 Colchester Court, Toronto – Full gallery here

Elena Stavreska was mother to a toddler, with another baby on the way, when she and her husband decided to move from their King Street West penthouse to the Edenbridge area in suburban Etobicoke – full of winding streets, expansive lots and plenty of parkland along the Humber River.

When thinking about renovations to the modern two-storey dwelling, the couple aimed to create a more calming interior and a tranquil backyard retreat.

On the main level, the foyer opens to a double-height living area with a ceiling height of 28 feet. Stairs lead to a raised dining area with temperature-controlled wine storage. The kitchen has custom cabinetry, integrated appliances, a geometric island and a breakfast bar.

Upstairs, the primary suite has floor-to-ceiling windows in the sleeping area, a bathroom with a double vanity and stand-alone tub, and a large walk-in closet. Four additional bedrooms on that floor each have ensuite bathrooms and built-in cabinets.

Outside, the couple built an in-ground pool and integrated hot tub, surrounded by 5,500 square feet of heated patios and walkways. The pool is heated year-round, in an effort to prolong the short Canadian summers.

What do you think is the asking price for the property?

a. $5,999,000 b. $6,745,000 c. $8,299,000 d. $10,449,000 b. The asking price is $6,745,000.

stories.title: $56-million penalty hasn’t stopped alleged cult leader’s attacks on Canadians
stories.summary: You might think that a $56-million penalty would be an effective deterrent for pretty much anything, but it has done little to stop an alleged cult leader from publicly attacking three Canadians.
stories.author: Derek Miller, Avery Haines
stories.content:
Warning: This article contains harsh language.

You might think that a $56-million penalty would be an effective deterrent for pretty much anything, but it has done little to stop an alleged cult leader from publicly attacking three Canadians.

In August, a Honolulu jury awarded the Canadians C$56 million after finding that the self-described spiritual teacher, Liana Shanti, defamed them. The trio from Saskatchewan was not a part of the Liana Shanti community, but were targeted because they were in disputes with estranged family members who were Shanti students.

Liana Shanti believed the Canadians were behind a social media account and online posts that called her a cult leader and a fraudster. She filed a defamation suit against them. The Canadians filed a counter-suit because of her online posts that called them, among other things, “pedo supporters,” “Satanists” and child abusers.

If you have tips on this, or any other story, reach out confidentially to avery.haines@bellmedia.CA .

At a civil trial in Honolulu in August, the jury sided with the Canadians and handed out one of the largest awards in Hawaii history.

The attacks continue

Since that August verdict, Liana Shanti has continued to post online content about the three - by name - 207 times. Some of that content is similar to what was found to be defamatory by the jury.

One of the Canadians who successfully counter-sued Liana Shanti, Byron Horvath has been mentioned in 142 posts on Instagram. Many include vile accusations, which were rejected by the jury, involving abuse of his young daughter.

For example, ON Oct. 27, 2026 Shanti posted an Instagram story that said, in part, “...her dad locks her in her room and won’t let her out to pee so she has been peeing on her bedroom floor.”

At trial, one of the statements that the eight-person jury found to be untrue and defamatory included the similar phrase, “Byron Horvath…Locked her in a room for hours where she had to pee on the floor.”

On Oct. 26, 2026, she posted that Horvath “sexually and physically abused their child,” and attributed it to his ex-wife, Haley, who used to be a Liana Shanti student.

Shanti has repeatedly posted old messages from Haley to lend credence to her new online attacks.

But it’s clear that Haley is no longer a supporter of Liana Shanti or what she posts online.

In a statement to W5, Byron’s ex-wife, Haley writes, “Byron, his wife Stefanie, our daughter, our families, others and myself have walked through hell and back because of my involvement in [Shanti’s] programs.”

“[We] lovingly co-parent our daughter, who is thriving…I choose to focus on love and repairing all that was broken after my time spent in a cult.”

Haley’s statement is included, in full, at the bottom of this article.

On Oct. 7, 2026, Liana Shanti posted on Instagram about Byron’s wife, Stefanie, with the caption, “IS [sic] Stefanie covering up abuse?” She posted another version of that story the following day.

During the trial, similar statements were deemed to be untrue and defamatory including: “[e]vil dark satanic people like Byron Horvath, Stefanie Vogt, manipulate and use corrupt systems to gag and silence mothers speaking out about abuse.”

Liana Shanti has also put out a call to her followers to feed her content about Byron’s wife, Stefanie, posting, “Do you have any information regarding Stefanie Horvath?”

Shanti has made similar posts on X, formerly Twitter, naming all three Canadians repeatedly in the past few days.

Her promise to the court

All of this comes despite the fact that after the verdict, Shanti signed a declaration to the court that read, “I will not post in the future any statement about the defendants that I know to be false…”

In an email, W5 asked Shanti about the new posts and their similarity to statements found to be defamatory. She defended her actions, writing, “I have no intention of sharing anything I know to be false.” Her defence is that what she writes was told to her by other people and she believes it to be true.

She writes in one online post, “Truth is a defense to defamation. But I wasn’t alllwed [sic] to Speak on the truth I was given.”

And then Shanti turned her attention to W5, suggesting that we have been bribed. She writes, “Shortly after I finished my recent stories, a Canadian news reporter who has been obsessed with this case emailed me about my intentions… I have no doubt they are being paid by [the father of one of the defendants].”

She followed that up with a post on Wednesday of this week that says, “Imagine the fool who considers themself a ‘journalist’ and doesn’t actually seek out facts. Those with a cognition level beyond a second grader see right through it.”

W5 has repeatedly offered Liana Shanti the opportunity to sit down and tell her side of the story. We also offered to hear from her current students. She refused both requests and has now blocked W5 from her Instagram account.

Secrets are weapons

Amanda Brady, who was a Liana Shanti student for more than eight years, says that her former teacher collects and then weaponizes information that she gleans from her followers.

“Especially if it’s somebody who has knowledge of Liana’s inner workings and her life, the online attacks start,” she says in an interview from her home in Regina. “She goes after that person on her social media as an attempt to shut them up.”

Amanda says that when she was kicked out of the community, Shanti shared - and continues to share - hundreds of posts about personal and private information.

“Now you have to worry about the fear and the fallout of what’s going to happen if all of my deepest, darkest things that I’ve ever shared with my teacher who I trusted are blasted on the internet for everyone to see,” says Amanda. “Of course no one’s going to want to leave on their own accord, right?”

On Thursday, Liana Shanti wrote on Instagram, “I Will speak until ALL OF THE Evidence Proof Facts Documents Timeline are for all the world to see…I don’t give a Fuck what anyone says about me because Jesus knows me by name.”

Full statement from Haley Winter, Byron Horvath’s ex-wife:

I have not seen internet posts from Liane Wilson for over three years. Others have shared that Liane Wilson [aka Liana Shanti] has consistently continued to speak and post on the internet about myself and others involved in recent legal judgements.

I do not consent to anyone using a public platform in any way to control, slander and publicly humiliate myself, family or anyone else connected to me. I experienced first-hand the cost of trusting Liane Wilson, taking her advice and believing her to be an authority over my life.

My family is one of many targeted. Byron, his wife Stefanie, our daughter, our families, others and myself have walked through hell and back because of my involvement in her programs. I have taken accountability for my choices and the consequences of them.

We have moved on. I have rebuilt my life. Byron, his wife Stefanie and I lovingly co-parent our daughter who is thriving. I wish for anyone reading this to choose peace and love over chaos, gossip and illusion. For myself, I choose to focus on love and repairing all that was broken after my time spent in a cult.

“Now you have to worry about the fear and the fallout of what’s going to happen if all of my deepest, darkest things that I’ve ever shared with my teacher who I trusted are blasted on the internet for everyone to see,” says Amanda. “Of course no one’s going to want to leave on their own accord, right?”

On Thursday, Liana Shanti wrote on Instagram, “I Will speak until ALL OF THE Evidence Proof Facts Documents Timeline are for all the world to see…I don’t give a Fuck what anyone says about me because Jesus knows me by name.”

I have not seen internet posts from Liane Wilson for over three years. Others have shared that Liane Wilson [aka Liana Shanti] has consistently continued to speak and post on the internet about myself and others involved in recent legal judgements.

I do not consent to anyone using a public platform in any way to control, slander and publicly humiliate myself, family or anyone else connected to me. I experienced first-hand the cost of trusting Liane Wilson, taking her advice and believing her to be an authority over my life.

My family is one of many targeted. Byron, his wife Stefanie, our daughter, our families, others and myself have walked through hell and back because of my involvement in her programs. I have taken accountability for my choices and the consequences of them.
