stories.title: Carney heads to Winnipeg to tout budget plan to end homelessness in 10 years
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is expected in Winnipeg today to highlight new measures in the federal budget aimed at eliminating homelessness within 10 years.
stories.author: Ashley Joannou The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Winnipeg - Prime Minister Mark Carney says the federal government has learned from past mistakes as it sets out its ambitious aim of eliminating homelessness within 10 years.

“For decades, governments and communities have tried to address this crisis. Too often, these efforts have been inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated and not sustained,” he said at a press conference Friday in Winnipeg.

Carney said he chose to make Manitoba his first stop after releasing the budget Thursday, because there’s already a plan in place.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says the federal government has learned from past mistakes as it sets out the ambitious aim of eliminating homelessness within 10 years. He says he chose to make Manitoba the first stop after releasing the budget on Thursday because all levels of government and the private sector have already come together to develop a comprehensive plan to tackle the problem. (Nov. 6, 2026)

“The government of Canada, the province of Manitoba, the City of Winnipeg and private philanthropy in recent months have all been coming together to develop a comprehensive plan that works.”

The budget estimated about 65,000 Canadians are homeless but critics say the figure could be much higher.

The federal government said its approach includes not only building enough affordable housing but also helping the vulnerable and providing health supports to help people escape homelessness long-term.

To fund the efforts countrywide, the federal budget offers $11.2 billion to tackle homelessness over four years, starting next year, and $17.8 billion over 10 years.

The partnerships with other levels of government would see the federal government fund construction costs, while provinces and other partners cover operations.

Winnipeg gets some of that money first, with at least $1 billion in new money going toward 2,000 new housing units and construction of a Centre for Mental Health and Addictions.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said the federal money is a “huge, humungous deal” for the province.

“Some people were saying this is a generational investment. I don’t know if every generation gets an investment like this.”

As part of the deal, Manitoba is committing $84 million a year to support what Ottawa has committed to build.

Kinew said while the province hasn’t chosen a location yet for the health-care campus, he’ll be pushing to have it done within the three years Carney has set as a goal.

“We’re going to get it done right, we’re going to get it done quick,” said Kinew.

The aim to move quickly comes as the provincial NDP works toward its shorter-term timeline of ending chronic homelessness by 2031.

Faster progress is possible because of unprecedented co-ordination among all levels of government, including Indigenous leaders along with other partners, he said.

“It’s the first time in our country’s history where every level of government has come together to tackle homelessness, including First Nations and Métis governments,” said Kinew.

“This is a fundamental step to succeed.”

The event Friday was held under the latticework of rafters at Wehwehneh Bahgahkinahgohn, the former Hudson Bay store in the city being transformed into an Indigenous hub of housing and other services by the Southern Chiefs’ Organization.

Jerry Daniels, the organization’s grand chief, said he’s not sure what new housing funding will come their way, but that the announcement was welcome.

“I think it’s good for the people of Winnipeg,” Daniels said.

“We’re very hopeful for the people who are living on the street, and who are experiencing homelessness, going through addictions and experiencing mental health challenges.”

Jennifer Moore Rattray, CEO of End Homelessness Winnipeg, said she was excited by the investments.

“We have a real opportunity in Winnipeg, in Manitoba and in Canada to actually end homelessness.”

She said there’s already tremendous co-ordination between Indigenous and non-Indigenous organizations in the city and the province to reduce homelessness. What they haven’t had before was enough funding.

“We know what works in community. We have been doing it for years,” said Rattray.

“Now we actually have the investment.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

stories.title: For a fascinating farm-to-table foodie trip, head to Salt Spring Island, B.C.’s boho haven
stories.summary: Here, the heartfelt food scene is rooted in passionate farmers and small-scale makers.
stories.author: Lisa Kadane Special to the Star
stories.content:
At Lost Field Farm on Salt Spring Island, B.C., tall rows of Glass Gem corn cast long shadows in the evening light. Farmer Zack Hemstreet feels each ear for firmness, then peels back the husk to reveal small red, orange and purple kernels. Hemstreet uses the rainbow-hued cobs to teach kids about pollination during summer camps and farm school Fridays.

“The farm has been through many iterations and grown many things, but the main goal is education,” says Hemstreet, who hopes hands-on activities like hand dusting pollen onto corn silks will foster a connection to the land. He points out rows of Swiss chard, radishes and carrots, honey hives lined up along a fence, and a greenhouse growing cherry tomatoes that taste like tart liquid sunshine.

The Glass Gem corn at Lost Field Farm.

Back at the barn, we eat fresh-picked apples and figs, roast organic chicken, and risotto with butternut squash prepared by chef Haidee Hart, who owns the Woodshed , a farm stand and catering company just down the road. Everything is sourced locally, including a delicious Pinot Noir from nearby Kutatás Wines .

It’s my first full day on Salt Spring Island and I have a serious case of farmer envy. On this food-themed trip with Tour Salt Spring , every stop at a farm, vineyard or restaurant is met with just-harvested veggies, crisp wine or cider, fresh-baked desserts, and folks who bring their love of honest food and drink to the table.

Produce at the Woodshed.

“Our makers, bakers and growers are passionate about what they do,” says Jason Griffin, co-owner of the tour company. “No one moves to Salt Spring to get rich. It’s about the lifestyle.” Griffin leads travellers around the island in a van that runs entirely on waste vegetable oil, and in spring 2027, he’ll officially launch culinary tours like the one we’re on. (While you can certainly visit the island over winter, many farms/farm stands operate seasonally; plan to come from April to October for the fullest experience.)

Located in the Salish Sea, a short float plane or ferry ride from Vancouver, Salt Spring Island has a reputation as an artists’ haven. Galleries and boutiques line the streets of Ganges, the main town, selling landscape paintings, handmade jewelry, live edge tables and even wearable art. Bright murals on buildings depict marine life and coastal ecology.

That bohemian ethos extends to the hyper-local food scene, which dates back to the late 1800s when early settlers planted apple orchards, farmed the land and raised livestock. Those traditions continued into the 1960s and ’70s when a new wave of “back to the landers,” including hippies and draft dodgers, arrived because property was inexpensive.

“They stayed because it’s a nice place to live,” says Griffin. “Everyone is very focused on sustainability.”

Stowel Lake Farm grows vegetables and flowers in its regenerative market gardens, selling them directly to locals at its seasonal farm stand.

At communal enterprises like Stowel Lake Farm , that means growing cover crops to maintain soil health and selling produce directly to customers at its on-site market. At the Garden , another farm, it means catching rain water for irrigation, and turning organic waste into fertilizer for plants and energy to heat the greenhouse in winter.

The island seems to operate on a kind of symbiosis; someone is usually growing or making what somebody else needs. If not, just stop by one of the approximately 220 honour-system farm stands selling fresh eggs or wrinkly shishito peppers, or visit the seasonal Salt Spring Saturday Market , which draws customers all the way from Vancouver.

It feels like an agrarian Shangri-La, with lifestyle perks. Stow your hoe and there are rainforest trails for hiking, miles of rugged shoreline for sea kayaking, and wineries for socializing.

In the vineyard at Garry Oaks Winery. Only grapes grown on this estate are used for its wines.

“Everyone’s got their little niche here,” says Lara Truscott, pouring samples of Pinot Grigio and rosé from a horse trailer that’s been converted into a wine bar at Garry Oaks Winery .

Like most island properties, the winery has wild apple trees along the vineyard’s edges. In the late 1800s, Salt Spring was B.C.’s primary apple basket, before growing shifted to the Okanagan Valley . When demand collapsed, many orchards were left untended, but the trees survived and propagated around the island, now outnumbering people. Some of them are used to make hard cider at Salt Spring Wild , which collects excess heirloom apples from local farms.

Lara Truscott offering samples at Garry Oaks Winery.

During our tour, we try the island’s original fruit in numerous ways: a slice of apple butter cheesecake, a mug of hot chai apple cider, and during a tasting at Salt Spring Sea Salt , where we sprinkle orange zest- and lavender-flavoured sea salt (the island’s “merroir”) onto apple wedges for a briny kick.

We save the best apple for last, though. At Foxglove Farm , located on one of the island’s original homesteads, Michael Ableman slices into a Pink Pearl apple. Its insides are rosy, its flesh firm, its taste a perfect balance between sweet and tart. I’m as smitten by the apple as I am with Ableman’s story.

After falling in love with Salt Spring Island on a family cycling trip, he came for a one-year farming sabbatical and never left. In addition to growing everything from French melons to baby ginger on his land, Ableman uses it as a springboard to educate and inspire farming-curious people like me.

“Salt Spring Island, it’s one of those places,” says Ableman, who’s written numerous books about farming and sustainable food systems. “The land chooses us more than we choose it. It kept pulling us back.”

As my float plane takes off from Ganges Harbour for the 20-minute flight to Vancouver, I look down at the forests, farms and rugged coastline I’m leaving behind. I can already feel Salt Spring Island calling me back.

Lisa Kadane travelled as a guest of Destination BC, Southern Gulf Islands Tourism and Tourism Vancouver Island, which did not review or approve this article.

content_blocks.text: Located in the Salish Sea, a short float plane or ferry ride from Vancouver, Salt Spring Island has a reputation as an artists’ haven. Galleries and boutiques line the streets of Ganges, the main town, selling landscape paintings, handmade jewelry, live edge tables and even wearable art. Bright murals on buildings depict marine life and coastal ecology.

content_blocks.text: That bohemian ethos extends to the hyper-local food scene, which dates back to the late 1800s when early settlers planted apple orchards, farmed the land and raised livestock. content_blocks.text: Like most island properties, the winery has wild apple trees along the vineyard’s edges. When demand collapsed, many orchards were left untended, but the trees survived and propagated around the island, now outnumbering people. stories.title: Champagne, Carney travelling across country to sell federal budget to Canadians
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canada's leaders are fanning out today to sell communities on this year's federal budget.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney and his cabinet ministers fanned out across the country Friday to sell Canadians on their latest federal budget — while the Conservatives sought to portray the document as a costly spending binge.

Speaking at a news conference in Winnipeg alongside Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, Carney highlighted his government’s pledge to end homelessness in Canada within a decade.

“For decades, governments and communities have tried to address this crisis. Too often, these efforts have been inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated and not sustained,” Carney said.

“We are investing an unprecedented $30 billion in a co-ordinated national plan. We understand both how difficult this will be, but equally how imperative it is that we succeed.”

The budget sets aside $11.2 billion over four years and $17.8 billion over 10 years for the effort. The federal government says some 65,000 Canadians are currently homeless.

Carney and Kinew unveiled a new partnership tied to the budget to build about 2,000 units of transitional housing and to fund a new mental health and addictions centre in Winnipeg.

Kinew said Carney has put nation-building at the centre of his government and there is no greater nation-building project than “building up the people of Canada” by tackling homelessness.

“Full credit belongs to the prime minister for saying we want to build the housing to end homelessness in Canada,” Kinew said. “No one in a country as rich as Canada should ever be homeless.”

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne went to Montreal on Friday for an event hosted by the Montreal Council on Foreign Relations to promote the federal spending plan, which sets aside billions of dollars to stoke investment.

In his speech, Champagne said the homelessness initiative and the productivity “mega deduction” that lets businesses deduct new investments are the two budget measures that will have the greatest impact in ten years’ time.

Champagne has presented the budget, titled “Masters of our Destiny,” as an ambitious plan to help Canada gain a solid economic footing in an increasingly volatile world.

“It’s about being more resilient, more independent, stronger,” the finance minister told reporters Friday.

“When you’re stronger, whatever happens south of the border, whatever happens in the Middle East or elsewhere in the world, you’re just more resilient. That’s really what I wanted to [have] Canadians understand when we say ‘masters of our destiny.’ There’s something profound about that.”

Opposition leaders have argued the budget falls short, particularly when it comes to helping people struggling with the high cost of living.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre described it on Friday as a “costly credit-card budget” full of “wasteful spending” that will drive up national debt.

“When you put more money on the credit card, you pay more interest to the financial institutions,” Poilievre said. “The Liberals should have called their budget ‘Mastered by Debt.'”

Poilievre made the comments while speaking at a news conference at a local food bank that is facing supply shortages and a spike in demand.

Food banks across the country are under pressure as households grapple with the high cost of living.

“We’ve gone beyond a food crisis to a food emergency,” the Conservative leader said. “People cannot afford to eat. This is the inflation hell that people are living in after 11 years of Liberal government and it’s getting worse.”

The budget includes a pledge to renew a local food infrastructure fund. The fund would provide money to food banks and other aid organizations to both buy food and upgrade facilities, such as greenhouses, kitchens, and transportation equipment. It’s a $124 million investment over three years, starting in 2027.

The Conservatives and Liberals already have sent out fundraising notes to supporters with competing narratives about the new fiscal plan.

The Liberals said the budget will facilitate economic growth and make life more affordable for Canadians, while the Conservatives said the “out of control” spending will lead to higher taxes.

In question period in the House of Commons on Friday, Conservative finance critic Michael Chong accused the government of allowing interest costs on the national debt to “skyrocket.”

“It is the fastest growing expense in the government’s budget,” Chong said. “What is the government going to do if we face another crisis like we did in 2008 and 2020?”

Parliamentary Secretary Ryan Turnbull replied that the government has charted a course that remains within its fiscal guardrails.

“We’re balancing the operating budget one year ahead of schedule and sticking to our debt-to-GDP ratio declining path,” he said.

Unlike Carney’s first budget, which was tabled under a minority government, the Liberals now have a majority and can get their agenda passed without the support of other parties.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

— with files from Maan Alhmidi in Brampton, Ont. and Morgan Lowrie in Montreal

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Statistics Canada to release October labour force survey numbers today
stories.summary: Ottawa — Statistics Canada will release its latest snapshot of the country's job market today.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Some economists are getting worried that a string of job losses in recent months is revealing cracks in the labour market.

Statistics Canada said Friday that the unemployment rate rose two tenths of a point to 6.7 per cent in October. The labour market shed 4,700 jobs last month, the agency said, and more people were also looking for work.

October’s modest decline followed a cumulative loss of 110,000 jobs across September and August. A Reuters poll of economists had expected the economy would bounce back with a gain of 13,600 jobs in October.

“For anyone hoping that October would bring a recovery in the Canadian job market after back-to-back negative surprises, today’s release is a disappointment,” said Sneha Puri, economist with jobs search site Indeed, in a media statement.

Private sector employment fell by 53,000 positions last month, marking the first decline in the segment since February. Employment in the public sector, meanwhile, was up 50,000 positions.

StatCan noted that, ON a year-over-year basis, private sector jobs are still up while the public sector is down.

Employment in the wholesale and retail trade industry has trended down over the past year and the sector led losses in October, shedding 29,000 roles. Transportation and warehousing and food and accommodation also posted losses last month, offset by some gains in construction and education.

Cibc senior economist Andrew Grantham said in an interview that he had expected more of a lift in the October labour market from one-time factors like the Alberta referendum.

While he had been anticipating the jobless rate would tick up in the fourth quarter in the face of tariff-related headwinds, Friday’s employment figures suggest there’s more underlying softness in the jobs market.

“It does look as if we’re seeing some weakness in the labour market outside of those trade-sensitive areas. So that’s a concern for us right now,” Grantham said.

That could dampen expectations for a rebound in job growth in 2027, he added.

The unemployment rate for young workers aged 15 to 24 jumped to 13.7 per cent in October, up 0.7 percentage points from September, as employment edged down and more youth looked for work.

StatCan said the unemployment rate was higher for students compared with youth not attending school.

The agency said the layoff rate – the proportion of people employed in September who were laid off by October – was “virtually unchanged” compared with a year earlier at 0.7 per cent.

Average hourly wages rose 2.2 per cent annually in October, edging down from 2.3 per cent in September.

Puri said Indeed’s Canadian job postings ticked up at the end of last month, which could be an indication of future hiring.

If Canada can gain clarity on U.S. trade policy in the wake of the midterm elections this week, she said that could give employers the confidence to hire again.

“If this optimism isn’t then translated into a strong jobs report in the months ahead, the surprising weakness in headline employment will start to look less temporary and more like the beginning of a renewed cooling in the labour market,” Puri warned.

The October job figures come a little over a week after the Bank of Canada delivered its first interest rate hike in more than three years, raising its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent.

Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients that the uptick in the unemployment rate and muted wage growth should tell the Bank of Canada that there’s still slack in the job market right now.

The October jobs data should therefore push back on calls for much more tightening of monetary policy, he argued.

“Ultimately, this adds to our conviction that the bank will hike rates no more than twice more as a precaution against upside inflation risks, before calling it a day,” Ryan said.

Financial market odds of another quarter-point hike at the Bank of Canada’s final rate decision of the year on Dec. 9 stood at 35 per cent as of Friday afternoon, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.

Bank of Canada officials made clear after the October rate hike that their focus is on getting ahead of inflationary pressures spreading from the global energy shock, Grantham noted.

Soft labour market data and recent declines in the benchmark price of oil take pressure of the central bank to deliver another rate hike next month, he said.

“We have a lot of days for oil prices to do something volatile between now and December. But if those two forces stay in effect, we do forecast that they will hold interest rates at the December meeting,” Grantham said.

stories.title: Former Quebec diplomat sees opportunity to rebuild energy ties after U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Montreal - A former Quebec delegate general in New York says the U.S. midterm results have created an opportunity for Canada to rebuild ties with Americans in the energy industry.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec is eager to safeguard its trade relationship with the United States following midterm elections that handed Democrats control of Congress, according to a senior government official.

Marie-Claude Francoeur, Quebec assistant deputy minister for the Americas and the Indo-Pacific region, said she has already delivered this message to new ministers in the Parti Québécois government as the province hopes to maintain its hydroelectric exports to the U.S. Eastern Seaboard.

stories.title: New Ontario law a ‘stealth privatization’ of Toronto Hydro, other local power utilities, critics warn
stories.summary: A proposed new law would bar municipal representatives from serving on the boards of Ontario's local power utilities — including Toronto Hydro, Alectra and Elixicon in the GTA.
stories.author: Marco Chown Oved; Mahdis Habibinia
stories.content:
The province is pushing ahead with legislation that opens the door to the privatization of municipal hydro utilities across the province, including Toronto Hydro.

Before councillors have had a chance to be sworn in following the municipal election, dozens of local public utilities could be forced to kick city staff and elected officials off their boards and replace them with private-sector directors, according to the proposed law being considered at Queen’s Park.

These reforms, critics say, are the first steps on a roadmap to allow institutional investors to take stakes — or even take over — Ontario’s local power companies.

The province says the changes are meant to strengthen and modernize local utilities, based on the recommendations in a new report by a provincial advisory panel. Among other things, the new law would force Ontario’s local distribution companies — including Toronto Hydro, Alectra and Elixicon in the GTA — to change the composition of their boards of directors so they’re entirely made up of independent, “skills-based” directors, who would then have to submit reports to the province identifying future funding shortfalls.

Those directors cannot be elected officials, municipal employees, or members of any local board, reads the proposed law , which was introduced the day after the municipal election and passed second reading at the legislature on Monday.

While the proposal stops there, the new report prepared by the Panel on Utility Leadership and Service Excellence (Pulse) lays out how the funding shortfalls could be addressed with private-sector investment ranging from minority shareholding to majority stakes to outright buy-outs.

The Ministry of Energy stresses that the report is simply a recommendation and that the current reforms do not enable private-sector takeovers of public utilities. But for critics, the legislation amounts to a push toward “stealth” privatization.

“It’s very clearly intended to open the doors to privatization,” said outgoing Coun. Dianne Saxe, who was Ontario’s independent environmental commissioner and a former board member of Toronto Hydro. Saxe said the province starved municipalities of funds and is now using that to justify private investment.

The Ministry of Energy said the reforms will “future-proof” the economy by strengthening the local distribution companies (LDCs) that deliver electricity service to homes, businesses and public buildings.

“Ontario’s utilities were designed for a different era — well before soaring electricity demand and President Trump’s tariffs,” said Energy Minister Stephen Lecce in a news release . “Ontario’s utilities are facing real pressure to expand capacity, replace aging infrastructure and deliver the power needed to grow.”

In background discussions with the Star, ministry officials emphasized that the governance reforms now being proposed have already been implemented voluntarily by some publicly-owned utilities, like London Hydro.

“This reform is about strengthening good governance by separating the role of municipal shareholders from independent board oversight, while preserving a municipal voice,” a spokesperson for Lecce said in a statement.

Privatizing hydro has been politically fraught in Ontario, and former premier Kathleen Wynne suffered a crushing defeat at the polls in 2018 amid controversy over the decision to sell off 53 per cent of the provincial transmission utility, Hydro One.

The politics of privatization

In announcing the legislative reforms for hydro, Lecce credited the Pulse report, which recommends private investment in LDCs to help them meet increasing electricity demand.

“With input from the sector (we’re) taking a phased approach and introducing changes based on several of the recommendations —virtually, almost all of them — from the Pulse panel,” he said .

“Access to external investment, particularly from Canadian institutional investors, is likely to be a critical determinant of whether electricity distribution utilities can deliver required infrastructure on time and at reasonable cost,” the Pulse report states.

The panel recommended a funding strategy that includes “equity investments, debt financing, expectation of dividends and other funding tools.”

In order to “incentivize” these investments, the panel recommended tax reforms that would eliminate tax on investments that take ownership of up to half of any LDC, and charge tax only on any stake that goes past 50 per cent. It also suggested using public funds — in particular, the provincial Building Ontario Fund (BOF) — to spur private investment.

The province’s reforms, which were announced only hours after polls closed in municipal elections across the province, caught city staff and elected officials off guard. Council’s new term doesn’t begin until Nov. 15, and the first council meeting won’t be until December. Meanwhile, councillors are struggling to get a briefing from city bureaucrats.

“The recent election demonstrated clearly that Torontonians will not support privatizing public utilities,” said Shirven Rezvany, spokesperson for Mayor Olivia Chow, referencing the controversy over rival candidate Brad Bradford’s proposal to incorporate Toronto’s water division .

“Mayor Chow will not support any move to open Toronto Hydro to private investment or ownership.”

This past June, council passed a Chow motion affirming that the city would remain sole owner of Toronto Hydro.

Rezvany said the legislation appears to be aimed at addressing governance and finance challenges at smaller LDCs — “issues that Toronto Hydro does not face.”

Newly-elected councillor Mike Layton questioned the timing of the reforms, “when we don’t even have the ability to respond as a council.”

Ontario’s hydro distribution system

Ontario currently has 58 LDCs, 44 of which are municipally-owned, three are owned by First Nations, three are private, and the rest are co-owned by public and private entities. Collectively, they’re facing $120 billion in upcoming infrastructure costs, according to the province.

Industry has long been ringing the alarm bells about inadequate investment in the electricity grid, says Benjamin Dachis, vice president of research and outreach at Clean Prosperity, a free-market-oriented climate think tank.

“The province has been investing heavily in generation, and we need investment at the local level to get that electricity to consumers,” said Dachis, who previously worked in Premier Doug Ford’s office.

“It’s going to come from one of two sources: debt or equity. Right now, a lot of them are at their debt limits. If they’re going to find equity investment, it’s either going to come from taxpayers or they need to find it somewhere else.”

Other members of civil society warn that private-sector investment comes with strings attached.

“The only thing being future-proofed with this kind of stealth privatization are billionaires’ profits, while the public gets stuck paying the costs through worse service and higher costs,” said Keith Stewart, senior energy strategist with Greenpeace Canada and the co-author of a book on former premier Mike Harris’ attempt to privatize electricity.

The provincial reforms will require LDCs to appoint new boards of directors and remove any existing municipal directors.

A municipality will be able to designate a sole “board participant” who can be an elected councillor or municipal employee, but that participant will not have voting rights, the law says.

During the legislation’s announcement, Lecce quoted an Ivey Business School report that stated: “municipal governments — who are the main shareholders of local distribution utilities — often do not have sufficient industry expertise or professional capacity to effectively monitor LDCs.”

Toronto Hydro’s board is made up of three city councillors and 10 people drawn from the private, non-profit and public sectors.

The new boards will then be required to submit 10-year plans with a funding strategy for additional assets, “ensuring LDCs are financing system investments appropriately,” according to the ministry briefing.

The reforms also include several measures addressing customer protection and streamlining procurement.

The current legislation seems “partially done,” said A.J. Goulding, President of London Economics International and a professor of energy economics at Columbia University.

“This is a beginning and not an ending,” he said. “The authors of the Pulse report put together a package. While you can implement one or two (recommendations) individually, that package works best if they’re all implemented. So far, we don’t know whether there will be additional provisions that will address the other elements of the report.”

Correction - Nov. 6, 2026

This article was updated from a previous version that incorrectly said former premier Kathleen Wynne sold off 60 percent of the provincial transmission utility, Hydro One. In fact, it was 53 percent.

Ontario currently has 58 LDCs, 44 of which are municipally-owned, three are owned by First Nations, three are private, and the rest are co-owned by public and private entities. Collectively, they’re facing $120 billion in upcoming infrastructure costs, according to the province.

Industry has long been ringing the alarm bells about inadequate investment in the electricity grid, says Benjamin Dachis, vice president of research and outreach at Clean Prosperity, a free-market-oriented climate think tank.

“The province has been investing heavily in generation, and we need investment at the local level to get that electricity to consumers,” said Dachis, who previously worked in Premier Doug Ford’s office.

“It’s going to come from one of two sources: debt or equity. Right now, a lot of them are at their debt limits. If they’re going to find equity investment, it’s either going to come from taxpayers or they need to find it somewhere else.”
Other members of civil society warn that private-sector investment comes with strings attached.

“The only thing being future-proofed with this kind of stealth privatization are billionaires’ profits, while the public gets stuck paying the costs through worse service and higher costs,” said Keith Stewart, senior energy strategist with Greenpeace Canada and the co-author of a book on former premier Mike Harris’ attempt to privatize electricity.
The provincial reforms will require LDCs to appoint new boards of directors and remove any existing municipal directors.
A municipality will be able to designate a sole “board participant” who can be an elected councillor or municipal employee, but that participant will not have voting rights, the law says.

During the legislation’s announcement, Lecce quoted an Ivey Business School report that stated: “municipal governments — who are the main shareholders of local distribution utilities — often do not have sufficient industry expertise or professional capacity to effectively monitor LDCs.”
Toronto Hydro’s board is made up of three city councillors and 10 people drawn from the private, non-profit and public sectors.

The new boards will then be required to submit 10-year plans with a funding strategy for additional assets, “ensuring LDCs are financing system investments appropriately,” according to the ministry briefing.
The reforms also include several measures addressing customer protection and streamlining procurement.
The current legislation seems “partially done,” said A.J. Goulding, President of London Economics International and a professor of energy economics at Columbia University.

“This is a beginning and not an ending,” he said. “The authors of the Pulse report put together a package. While you can implement one or two (recommendations) individually, that package works best if they’re all implemented. So far, we don’t know whether there will be additional provisions that will address the other elements of the report.”
Correction - Nov. 6, 2026
This article was updated from a previous version that incorrectly said former premier Kathleen Wynne sold off 60 percent of the provincial transmission utility, Hydro One. In fact, it was 53 percent.

stories.title: Multiple charges laid
stories.summary: London, ON (November 6, 2026) – A London youth is facing multiple charges after an attempted break and enter in the north end of the city.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 6, 2026) – A London youth is facing multiple charges after an attempted break and enter in the north end of the city.

On Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, at approximately 7 p.m., members of the London Police Service (LPS) Frontline Division, with the assistance of the LPS Canine Unit, responded to a residence near Highbury Avenue North and Huron Street in relation to an attempted break in at a residence.

The suspect fled prior to police arrival. Through the investigation, it was determined that the suspect had uttered threats prior to the attempted break and enter.

The suspect was located in the area of Belmont Drive and Wharncliffe Road South. He attempted to flee from officers but was taken into custody with the assistance of an LPS police service dog.

The suspect was transported to hospital by paramedic services with minor injuries.

As a result of the investigation, a 17-year-old male, who cannot be named under provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act, has been charged with the following offences:

Two counts of failing to comply with a release order;

Mischief under $5,000;

Uttering threats; and

Resisting arrest.

The accused was also arrested on additional outstanding warrants.

The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

Friday, November 6, 2026

Temporary closure of Highbury Avenue over Highway 401

Highbury Avenue over Highway 401 will be closed for approximately 24 hours starting Saturday morning, November 7, while crews pour concrete for the bridge.

During the closure, motorists will not be able to cross Highway 401 using Highbury Avenue. A signed detour will be in place for the northbound and southbound traffic that will require drivers to use Pond Mills Road via Bradley Avenue and Wilton Grove Road.

Motorists are encouraged to plan ahead, follow posted detour signs and allow additional time when travelling through the area.

What is MTO doing?

The overnight closure is part of theMinistry of Transportation’s (MTO) Highbury Avenue South underpass bridge replacement and interchange rehabilitation project.

The MTO project includes replacing the Highbury Avenue bridge over Highway 401 and making improvements to the Highway 401 interchange.

What is the City doing?

At the same time, the City of London is completing a separate rehabilitation project onHighbury Avenue South.

The City is reconstructing Highbury Avenue South and making improvements to the stormwater system. The project also includes repairs to the Commissioners Road and Bradley Avenue underpasses and the signalized intersection on Commissioners Road, west of Highbury Avenue South.

While the two projects are separate, they are taking place in the same area and may affect travel through Highbury Avenue South and the Highway 401 interchange.

Stay informed

For information about the City of London’sHighbury Avenue South rehabilitation project, including construction updates, project timelines, visit the City’s Get Involved webpage.

For information about the MTO project, including construction updates, project details and traffic impacts, visit theMTO project website.

stories.title: Missing Person – Jadyn Russell
stories.summary: London, ON (November 6, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 28-year-old Jadyn Russell, of London Ontario.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 6, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 28-year-old Jadyn Russell, of London Ontario.

The missing person is described as female, White, 28-years-old, approximately 5’8”, medium build, long brown hair with the right side of her head shaved. She was last seen wearing a tan coloured shirt, light blue pants, white and black checkerboard shoes, and a pair of black glasses.

The missing person was last seen today at approximately 12 p.m. in the area of Commissioners Road East and Wellington Road, and was reported missing to police.

Family and police are concerned for the missing person’s welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Minister denies new law amounts to ‘stealth’ privatization for Toronto Hydro
stories.summary: 'There's no change to the ownership model of utilities,' Energy Minister Stephen Lecce said of new legislation affecting Ontario's local hydro utilities.
stories.author: Marco Chown Oved; Mahdis Habibinia
stories.content:
Energy Minister Stephen Lecce has denied criticism that Ontario’s plan to reform local hydro utilities is a step toward privatization.

“That is not what we’re contemplating today,” Lecce said Friday in Scarborough, responding to questions about the Star’s reporting on the province’s proposed Bill 140 , the Building Ontario Faster Act.

“There’s no change to the ownership model of utilities,” Lecce said. “We’re changing the people who sit on the boards.”

The province has argued that new legislation introduced at Queen’s Park last week is needed to strengthen and modernize Ontario’s local hydro utilities — including Toronto Hydro, Alectra and Elexicon in the GTA — based on the recommendations in a recent report by a provincial advisory panel.

Among other things, the new law would require the local distribution companies (LDCs) to appoint boards of directors entirely made up of independent “skills-based” directors, while banning elected officials, municipal employees, or members of any local board from serving as a director.

A municipality will be able to designate a sole “board participant” who can be an elected councillor or municipal employee, but that participant will not have voting rights, the bill says.

Ontario currently has 58 LDCs, 44 of which are municipally-owned, three are owned by First Nations, three are private, and the rest are co-owned by public and private entities. If it passes, the new law would not force municipally-owned LDCs to accept private shareholders.

Toronto Hydro, Alectra and Elexicon, the major publicly-owned LDCs in the GTA, have between three and five elected politicians on their 13-person boards, all of whom would be removed under the proposed reforms.

“Look no further than some of the utility appointments today,” said Lecce. “You tell me, does the current political representation on some of these boards, does it make sense to you as a citizen, as a ratepayer? No experience in electricity, in energy, in the private economy, no experience in the build out.”

At an unrelated news conference Friday, Mayor Olivia Chow said Toronto Hydro belongs to the residents of Toronto and the city should have some governance power to manage it.

A proposed new law would bar municipal representatives from serving on the boards of Ontario’s local power utilities — including Toronto Hydro,

“We should have a right to put our elected representative as a voting member onto the hydro board that governs it,” Chow said. “The city has been very clear.”

The province says Ontario’s local utilities are facing $120 billion in upcoming infrastructure costs to bring growing generation to houses, businesses and industry. The government projects that electricity demand will grow by 75 per cent by 2050.

The proposed law was introduced the day after the municipal election and passed second reading at the legislature on Monday.

Critics have said the law amounts to “stealth” privatization: the first steps on a road map to allow institutional investors to take stakes — or even take over — Ontario’s local power distributors. And it came at a time soon after local elections, when local councils are unable to muster a collective response.

The Toronto Hydro building at 14 Carlton St.

They point to the new report prepared by the Panel on Utility Leadership and Service Excellence (Pulse), which recommends the board reforms and then goes a step further to call for bringing in private-sector investors.

Lecce said the proposed law is drawn from the Pulse report, but his office has stressed that it has taken no action on the tax reforms and public subsidies the panel recommends in order to incentivize private investments.

He cited the local utilities owned by the cities of Oshawa, Oakville and London, which have voluntarily taken politicians and city staff off their boards.

“We need experts. We need engineers. We need finance leaders,” Lecce said Friday.

Outgoing Coun. Dianne Saxe, a former board member of Toronto Hydro, called the bill the first step to privatization in practice — if not by name. Being a board member is a key role in running the corporation and controlling its money, she added.

The province is “bulldozing obstacles right now,” she said.

Lecce also listed a number of groups who have called for reforms, including the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).

The AMO published a statement two days after the legislation was tabled saying that while it reflects some of their recommendations, “The proposal does not reflect a key AMO recommendation: local flexibility to choose the right governance and financial models.”

“Critically, it would limit municipalities to only one non-voting LDC Board member who would be barred from certain discussions. This would significantly impact municipal voice on a wide variety of issues, even if a municipality retains majority ownership.”

The AMO confirmed to the Star Friday that it has not changed its position.

The proposed law was introduced the day after the municipal election and passed second reading at the legislature on Monday.

Critics have said the law amounts to “stealth” privatization: the first steps on a road map to allow institutional investors to take stakes — or even take over — Ontario’s local power distributors. And it came at a time soon after local elections, when local councils are unable to muster a collective response.
The Toronto Hydro building at 14 Carlton St.

They point to the new report prepared by the Panel on Utility Leadership and Service Excellence (Pulse), which recommends the board reforms and then goes a step further to call for bringing in private-sector investors.

Lecce said the proposed law is drawn from the Pulse report, but his office has stressed that it has taken no action on the tax reforms and public subsidies the panel recommends in order to incentivize private investments.
He cited the local utilities owned by the cities of Oshawa, Oakville and London, which have voluntarily taken politicians and city staff off their boards.
“We need experts. We need engineers. We need finance leaders,” Lecce said Friday.

Outgoing Coun. Dianne Saxe, a former board member of Toronto Hydro, called the bill the first step to privatization in practice — if not by name. Being a board member is a key role in running the corporation and controlling its money, she added.
The province is “bulldozing obstacles right now,” she said.
Lecce also listed a number of groups who have called for reforms, including the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO).

The AMO published a statement two days after the legislation was tabled saying that while it reflects some of their recommendations, “The proposal does not reflect a key AMO recommendation: local flexibility to choose the right governance and financial models.”

“Critically, it would limit municipalities to only one non-voting LDC Board member who would be barred from certain discussions. This would significantly impact municipal voice on a wide variety of issues, even if a municipality retains majority ownership.”
The AMO confirmed to the Star Friday that it has not changed its position.

stories.title: Canada is adding 200,000 permanent resident spots. Here’s how it will work
stories.summary: Ottawa will work with provinces to decide how to divvy up the extra 100,000 permanent resident spots set aside in 2027 for temporary foreign workers already working in Canada and
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
Ottawa will work with provinces to decide how to divvy up the extra 100,000 permanent resident spots set aside in 2027 for temporary foreign workers already working in Canada and contributing to the economy.

In a technical briefing Friday, senior immigration officials said the one-time measure is meant to help retain workers whose skills and experience are already supporting local employers and communities, particularly in regions facing labour market challenges.

“We have a very large population of temporary residents in Canada with a right to work, many of whom have already applied for permanent residence,” said the officials, who spoke on background about the federal government’s 2027-29 immigration levels plan released this week.

“They are located throughout the country, across provinces and territories. So our goal here with the provinces and our conversation with them will be to determine which of those populations they wish to bring forward to respond to their specific labour market needs.”

Last year, the Immigration Department rolled out a similar time-limited initiative to transition current work permit holders to permanent residence, but was criticized for the lack of communication on the criteria, timing and workings of the program . It fuelled confusion and misinformation as unscrupulous agents tried to take advantage of desperate migrants.

Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Lena Metlege Diab is pictured in the House of Commons on Thursday.

While details for the 100,000 spots allocated for workers in 2027 have yet to be determined, officials noted: “Clients who have already applied for permanent residence don’t need to take any action to be considered under the time-limited measure.”

On Thursday, Ottawa unveiled its immigration levels plan for the next three years , keeping the yearly intakes of new permanent residents at 380,000, the same as 2026.

However, the conversion of the 100,000 current foreign workers to permanent residence is on top of that annual target. So are the additional 100,000 spots set aside to grant permanent status to temporary residents for family reunification and humanitarian purposes.

The opposition Conservatives have accused the government of “cooking the books” by excluding these 200,000 extra permanent residents from the 380,000 headline count.

On Friday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the temporary residents qualifying for the one-time initiative have been working for the same employers and living in the same communities for years, and “in all respects,” permanent residents of Canada.

“We’re formalizing that,” Carney told reporters. “We’re recognizing that it’s the right thing to do, and we’re absolutely clear about that, and it’s within the context of a sustainable immigration system.”

Immigration officials said the humanitarian stream will include 45,000 spouses and children as well as 32,000 Hong Kongers and 18,800 Ukrainians awaiting permanent residence under special pathways. The rest are allocated to people approved in principle for permanent residence on humanitarian grounds. They have been kept waiting for permanent status due to the limited admission quotas each year.

“This will reduce inventories with unreasonable wait times and support more predictable processing times,” immigration officials said at the technical briefing.

“Many of the people covered by this measure are already living in Canada or will be joining family members who are established here. These admissions are expected to have a limited impact on housing, infrastructure and public services.”

The officials said the government is still committed to reducing the share of temporary residents in Canada to five per cent of the country’s population by the end of 2027. As of July, that rate still stood at 6.7 per cent.

In addition to transitioning select people in Canada to permanent residence, the immigration levels plan will cap the arrivals of new international students at 150,000 and temporary foreign workers at 220,000 in each of the next three years.

stories.title: Kelowna woman calls for action on public safety in wake of frightening attack
stories.summary: Robertson says she fought back, kicking at her attacker before the two fell to the ground.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
A Kelowna woman says she’s still shaken after being violently attacked in broad daylight in the city’s downtown core, leaving her with bruises, a sore scalp and a large clump of missing hair.

“I was fighting with everything I had,” Robertson told Global News.

Robertson was waiting for a friend on the sidewalk in the 400-block of Lawrence Avenue shortly after 1 p.m. Sunday when a woman she didn’t know approached her.

Without warning, Robertson says the woman grabbed a handful of her hair, pulled hard and began punching her.

“She was about here from me, and she said, “I’m really sorry about this,” and she grabbed a mitt full of my hair and pulled it so hard and started pummeling me with her other hand,” Robertson said.

Robertson says she fought back, kicking at her attacker before the two fell to the ground.

“She twirled me around with my hair, and we fell to the ground. And then I started screaming for help,” Robertson said.

Robertson says she believes her screams scared the woman off.

The attacker fled with Robertson’s phone, but it was later recovered after Robertson connected with members of the Downtown Kelowna Association (DKA) red-shirt on-call team.

The DKA team managed to get a photo of the suspect, who was still in the area, and called police.

Robertson says the experience has left her feeling shaken and less safe in an area she’s visited many times.

“I have never felt this unsafe here before,” she said.

She says the realization of how much worse the attack could have been only hit her afterward.

“Oh My God, what is she had a knife?, Like, it really shook me then how close we came,” Robertson said. “She could have bashed my head into the ground or whatever.”

Robertson’s daughter, Nina Harder, posted a photo of the suspect on social media.

Harder said she had several people reach out since, sharing stories of encounters with the same woman.

“There was a lot of people who had said that they had recognized her and had seen her around town and also shared stories of similar attacks that had happened to them,” Harder said.

RCMP say they located a suspect the day after the Nov.1 attack adding that one person was taken into custody but has since been released.

Police say no charges have yet been laid but the investigation is ongoing.

“I was really upset and shocked how fast this you know, catch and release, really is,” Harder said. “I thought for sure that they would hold her longer.”

Robertson says she believes more needs to be done to address growing concerns around public safety.

“Like involuntary holding medical rooms, medical beds. They’ve talked about it, but it’s not happening,” Robertson said. “It’s time to push the boundaries a little more and try and demand some kind of action.”

Robertson added that she feels grateful she did not sustain more serious injuries.

“I have a couple of bruises and sore scalp and missing hair but other than that, I feel so grateful,” she said.

“Oh My God, what is she had a knife?, Like, it really shook me then how close we came,” Robertson said. “She could have bashed my head into the ground or whatever.”
Robertson’s daughter, Nina Harder, posted a photo of the suspect on social media.
Harder said she had several people reach out since, sharing stories of encounters with the same woman.
“There was a lot of people who had said that they had recognized her and had seen her around town and also shared stories of similar attacks that had happened to them,” Harder said.
RCMP say they located a suspect the day after the Nov.1 attack adding that one person was taken into custody but has since been released.
Police say no charges have yet been laid but the investigation is ongoing.
“I was really upset and shocked how fast this you know, catch and release, really is,” Harder said. “I thought for sure that they would hold her longer.”
Robertson says she believes more needs to be done to address growing concerns around public safety.

“Like involuntary holding medical rooms, medical beds. They’ve talked about it, but it’s not happening,” Robertson said. “It’s time to push the boundaries a little more and try and demand some kind of action.”
Robertson added that she feels grateful she did not sustain more serious injuries.
“I have a couple of bruises and sore scalp and missing hair but other than that, I feel so grateful,” she said.

“I was fighting with everything I had,” Robertson told Global News.
Robertson was waiting for a friend on the sidewalk in the 400-block of Lawrence Avenue shortly after 1 p.m. Sunday when a woman she didn’t know approached her.
Without warning, Robertson says the woman grabbed a handful of her hair, pulled hard and began punching her.
“She was about here from me, and she said, “I’m really sorry about this,” and she grabbed a mitt full of my hair and pulled it so hard and started pummeling me with her other hand,” Robertson said.
Robertson says she fought back, kicking at her attacker before the two fell to the ground.
“She twirled me around with my hair, and we fell to the ground. And then I started screaming for help,” Robertson said.
Robertson says she believes her screams scared the woman off.
The attacker fled with Robertson’s phone, but it was later recovered after Robertson connected with members of the Downtown Kelowna Association (DKA) red-shirt on-call team.
The DKA team managed to get a photo of the suspect, who was still in the area, and called police.
Robertson says the experience has left her feeling shaken and less safe in an area she’s visited many times.
“I have never felt this unsafe here before,” she said.

stories.title: Public relations expert tells court Galloway bungled response to sexual assault scandal
stories.summary: Defence witness says author had reputational advantages, such as support from high-profile literary figures, but failed to carry on his career
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Bestselling author Steven Galloway had all the tools needed to rehabilitate his public image and career after the University of British Columbia fired him a decade ago, a public relations expert testified Thursday.

Norman Stowe, managing partner of the public relations firm Pace Group Communications, told B.C. Supreme Court that despite being accused of sexual assault by a former creative writing student, Mr. Galloway could have leveraged several strengths if he had a coherent crisis communications plan in place.

Mr. Stowe was testifying as a defence witness at the trial for the defamation case Mr. Galloway first launched in 2018, which alleges that his lucrative literary career cratered after he faced public accusations of sexual harassment and sexual assault in 2015. He is suing the former student with whom he had an affair from 2011 to 2013, whose complaint sparked the firestorm, and three others who repeated her allegations online in the years that followed.

Mr. Galloway was suspended and then, seven months later, fired in June 2016 as head of Ubc’s creative-writing program without severance because of breach of trust.

Mr. Stowe testified Mr. Galloway’s advantages included having enduring public support from prominent members of Canada’s literary community; media coverage that was, by and large, positive; a UBC-commissioned report from a retired judge exonerating him of the sexual assault allegations; and two settlements from his alma mater.

“He had a lot going for him that never seemed to come together in a way that he could move on from this,” Mr. Stowe testified.

Mr. Stowe wrote a report this summer for the defence team of the woman who levelled the allegations. She can only be referred to as A.B. because of a trial publication ban.

Mr. Stowe’s expert report is expected to be used by the defence in closing arguments to argue that Mr. Galloway’s reputation was affected by his own response to this scandal.

Mr. Galloway initially sued two dozen defendants in his lawsuit alleging that his career was effectively ended by the allegations. Ubc’s independent investigator found he had committed sexual harassment by entering into an affair with A.B. but he was never charged with a crime and has always denied the allegations of sexual assault.

A.B. is not testifying and, at the start of the trial last month, her lead lawyer Arden Beddoes told the court that he was withdrawing her defences of truth and fair comment. Mr. Beddoes said A.B. was amending her defence to say she reported sexual assaults and is no longer saying she had been sexually assaulted, but she is still not admitting that she spread lies about Mr. Galloway. Mr. Beddoes has said that A.B. had tried to kill herself twice this year because of the stress of the case.

During cross-examination from Mr. Galloway’s lead lawyer Daniel Burnett, Mr. Stowe agreed that he had incorrectly found in his report that the author took “no steps” to rehabilitate his career after the scandal.

Mr. Stowe maintained that high-profile people have had “reputational challenges” as bad or worse than Mr. Galloway’s, and had moved on and been successful, citing Bill Clinton, Martha Stewart and Tiger Woods.

Mr. Burnett interjected to ask if these people had been accused of misconduct “as bad as rape?” to which Mr. Stowe agreed that sexual assault allegations are “powerful.”

But, Mr. Stowe testified that regardless of the allegations, the plan for rehabilitating one’s public image “from scratch” is very similar and, in his opinion, Mr. Galloway’s actions stalled.

“He had all of these opportunities and tools and assets and support,” Mr. Stowe said.

Last month, the court heard Mr. Galloway testify he did not seek out professional public relations help after he was suspended from UBC, but did talk to friends about his strategy to push back against allegations of sexual assault he has always denied.

Mr. Burnett explained how his client had followed the three public-facing steps of Mr. Stowe’s six ironclad rules for managing a crisis, as detailed in the expert report: “build a narrative and stick to it” (by always maintaining his innocence), “enlist facts and voices of others” (by having literary stars such as Margaret Atwood sign an open letter in 2016 supporting him), and “don’t be a recluse” (by doing an interview with The Globe and Mail’s Gary Mason and, later, writing an op-ed for the National Post).

Later Thursday, defendant Mandi Gray, who is on medical leave from her position as an assistant professor of criminology at Trent University due to the proceedings, also began her testimony. She and two other women are accused of defaming Mr. Galloway online by repeating A.B.’s claims he sexually assaulted her.

Vanshika Dhawan, Dr. Gray’s lawyer, told the court that her client was also withdrawing the defences of qualified privilege and responsible communication for five social media posts she made in 2016 and 2018. She is not defending three of these alleged instances of defamation but will argue fair comment for the remaining two, Ms. Dhawan said.

“If I had the opportunity to go back in time, I would have said this using different language,” she said of her three defamatory posts on the platform X, formerly Twitter, which she added was not “really a platform known for nuanced thought.”

Ms. Dhawan said her client recognizes the “profound personal consequences” Mr. Galloway has faced, but disputes that any damages awarded should be substantial if defamation is proven.

stories.title: B.C. woman sentenced to 13 years for assault, kidnapping and sex trafficking
stories.summary: NEW Westminster - A woman who pleaded guilty to multiple charges in a child sex trafficking case in British Columbia has been sentenced to 13 years in prison.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
NEW Westminster - A woman who pleaded guilty to multiple charges in a child sex trafficking case in British Columbia has been sentenced to 13 years in prison.

The B.C. Prosecution Service says Jennifer Stephens has also been ordered to provide a DNA sample and report to the National Sex Offender Registry for 20 years, and she has been handed a 10-year firearms ban.

The B.C. Prosecution Service says Jennifer Stephens has also been ordered to provide a DNA sample and report to the National Sex Offender Registry for 20 years, and she has been handed a 10-year firearms ban.

stories.title: East of Adelaide gets its own board game
stories.summary: A new board game designed in London celebrates all things “East of Adelaide”.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A new board game designed in London celebrates all things “East of Adelaide”.

Called London-opoly: East of Adelaide Edition, the game turns the tables on the once negative EOA nickname for east London by celebrating its unique businesses and community touchpoints.

6 years after moving to 100 Kellogg Lane, L.A. Mood Comics and Games spent months designing the game to mark its anniversary.

The classic Monopoly board has been transformed with street names, schools, and businesses from east London.

“It was tough to pick all the street names and businesses that we were going to put on the board. It was very difficult and we apologize if your favourites didn’t make it on the board,” said Jamie Dean, Supervisor at L.A. Mood. “Maybe next year we’ll do another one and try to include some more places!”

The game is a partnership with the London Children’s Museum, Anderson Craft Ales, Forked River Brewing Co., and Old East Village Business Improvement Area (BIA).

The traditional Community Chest and Chance cards now contain a distinctly local flare.

“You ate too much cheese from the Western Fair Market! Lose 1 turn to recover,” said Dean.

The board also acknowledges recent decisions impacting the east end, including a square labelled “traffic jam”, and the Free Parking spot represented by the Old East Village BIA.

“We wanted to give something back to our neighbourhood, and this is our little love letter,” Dean explained.

Copies of London-opoly East of Adelaide Edition will be available to purchase at L.A. Mood’s store and website, as well as Anderson Craft Ales, Forked River Brewing Co., and the London Children’s Museum.

stories.title: Ottawa reviewing circumstances of Indigenous woman’s death after she missed postsurgery appointments
stories.summary: Family of Miranda Mamakwa asked Ontario Provincial Police Commissioner to investigate federal officials for criminal negligence
stories.author: Willow Fiddler
stories.content:
The federal government says it is improving access to medical care for Indigenous patients in the remote North and reviewing the circumstances surrounding the death of a 31-year-old woman who missed follow-up appointments after open-heart surgery.

Miranda Mamakwa, from Fort Severn First Nation, a remote community along the Hudson Bay, underwent open-heart surgery in April and died in September. She was a recipient of Non-Insured Health Benefits, a federal program run by Indigenous Services Canada. Among its responsibilities is providing transportation and accommodations for First Nations patients who must travel to a different community to receive medical services.

Ms. Mamakwa’s family alleges she missed four scheduled postsurgery appointments because the Nihb failed to make such arrangements.

“ISC is in full agreement that it is important to have an understanding of Ms. Mamakwa’s interactions with the health care system, included programs and services directly delivered by ISC, and the circumstances surrounding her death,” Carolane Gratton, a spokesperson for Indigenous Services Canada, said in an e-mailed statement to The Globe and Mail.

The statement said the department is working at improving service efficiency, including a newly implemented “simplified travel submission process” organized and supported by on-site community medical transportation co-ordinators.

Ms. Gratton said that ISC recognizes the service gaps in the Nihb program and the “very serious impacts” on patients. “ISC acknowledges that medical transportation is a critical service for remote and fly-in communities.”

Sol Mamakwa, the MPP for Kiiwetinoong, which includes Fort Severn First Nation, said more is needed.

“The actions that Indigenous Services Canada has taken are not enough to bring accountability for their repeated failure to arrange Miranda Mamakwa’s medical travel,” Mr. Mamakwa told The Globe. (He is not related to Ms. Mamakwa.)

“It’s time for ISC to make real change so no one else dies a preventable death because their medical travel was not arranged.”

Indigenous patients in the remote North, particularly where there is no road access to urban health care, rely heavily on the Non-Insured Health Benefits program – part of the federal government’s treaty obligations – because of the complicated and expensive logistics involved with travel.

To get to her follow-up appointment in Thunder Bay, about 850 kilometres south, Ms. Mamakwa would have faced a 2.5-hour flight to Sioux Lookout – longer if a direct flight wasn’t available – a four-hour layover and then an hour-long flight to Thunder Bay. Airfare for a one-way trip on a Dash 8 runs between $1,700 and $2,400, according to the Wasaya Airways website.

Flights in and out of the North are also unreliable, often cancelled or postponed because of weather, mechanical issues and other reasons.

Federal staff in Sioux Lookout are responsible for approving and processing travel arrangements for regional patients in the Nihb program after receiving referrals from a patient’s local nursing station staff or other health care providers.

The federal program has long been sharply criticized by some Indigenous leaders, who call it a systemic failure bound by red-tape bureaucracy that has cost lives.

A news release issued by the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority and Nishnawbe Aski Nation after Ms. Mamakwa’s death demanded accountability from the feds. It said Ms. Mamakwa’s death was a result of failures of the federal program responsible for getting her to appointments.

The family of Ms. Mamakwa has asked the Ontario Provincial Police Commissioner to investigate federal officials for criminal negligence. Her parents, Eva Mamakwa and Mike Bluecoat, said in a press release last week that their daughter’s death was preventable.

“This should never have happened to Miranda. She should be alive today. We deserve to know how something like this happened, and we want the individual or individuals responsible for failing to respond to these urgent requests for transportation to be held accountable. They cost Miranda her life. They cost her children a future without their mother.”

The statement, put out by Falconers LLP, which is representing the family, says after Ms. Mamakwa had her open-heart surgery in April in Ottawa, she recovered in Thunder Bay before going home to Fort Severn in May.

A total of four follow-up appointments were scheduled to take place in Thunder Bay over the summer, said the statement, and the local nursing station had faxed the required paperwork to the Nihb office in Sioux Lookout requesting arrangements be made. But the Nihb failed to respond, never making any travel arrangements for Ms. Mamakwa despite follow-up calls and requests, the law firm said.

In September, Ms. Mamakwa went to the Fort Severn nursing station in medical distress and was medevaced to Thunder Bay. She died on Sept. 8 after being removed from life support.

In the weeks before her death, Ms. Mamakwa wrote a Facebook post telling people to “go after” the Nihb program if she were to die.

The statement from Falconers said that the disregard shown for Ms. Mamakwa’s life must be investigated and that public officials should be held accountable.

The Ontario Provincial Police said in an e-mailed statement to The Globe that it is reviewing the letter from the Mamakwa family and will not comment further at this time.

stories.title: Health Canada approves Moderna's mRNA flu and flu-COVID combo vaccines
stories.summary: Toronto - Health Canada has authorized Moderna's mRNA vaccine for influenza, as well as its combination mRNA vaccine for flu and COVID-19.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Health Canada has authorized Moderna’s mRNA vaccine for influenza, as well as its combination mRNA vaccine for flu and COVID-19.

Both are approved for adults 50 years of age and older.

But Moderna told The Canadian Press they will not hit pharmacies in time for this respiratory virus season.

The National Advisory Committee on Immunization recommends that everyone six months of age and older get the non-mRNA flu shot that is available this year.

Health Canada has authorized Moderna’s mRNA vaccine for influenza, as well as its combination mRNA vaccine for flu and COVID-19. (Nov. 6, 2026)

A higher-dose version of the flu vaccine is recommended for adults aged 65 and older because aging immune systems often need a bigger boost.

The committee also strongly advises COVID-19 vaccination for anyone 65 years of age and older and residents of long-term care, retirement homes or assisted living.

Moderna and Pfizer both have mRNA COVID-19 vaccines available in Canada this year.

A spokesperson for Moderna said Health Canada notified the company that its flu vaccine — called mFLUSIVA — and its combination flu and COVID-19 shot — called mCOFLU — were approved on Thursday.

In a news release, the company said its mRNA flu shot was approved in the United States in August and its combination vaccine was approved in Europe last April.

It said Canada is the first country to authorize both of the vaccines.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Pillar Nonprofit Network marking 25 years of helping organizations
stories.summary: Pillar Nonprofit Network has always given a helping hand to those organizations that offer a helping hand in the London community.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Pillar Nonprofit Network has always given a helping hand to those organizations that offer a helping hand in the London community.

CEO Maureen Cassidy says it provides learning and development programs along with leadership and peer support to many grassroot organizations.

“It’s all the things that help strengthen a non-profit organization fundamentally at its roots,” said Cassidy.

She says now more than ever non-profit organizations find themselves in a tight spot when it comes to an increase in community needs along with a squeeze on funding.

“It’s tough economic times and people are struggling,” said Cassidy. “There is greater need for the services that are provided in the non-profit sector and at the same time the funding is dwindling.”

Pillar is marking its 25 th anniversary with a new program and fundraiser. It’s all coming together with a breakfast at its King Street location on Wednesday, Nov. 25 at 8 a.m.

“We would like to raise $25,000 and we would like to increase our monthly donors by 25,” said Cassidy.

Looking ahead to the next quarter century, Cassidy knows they will be around to play an important roll in the community, “We know the reason that Pillar exists is because we are all stronger together and Pillar will always be here to help.”
