stories.title: Elections Alberta says referendum cost $84-million, exceeding agency’s annual budget
stories.summary: Elections Alberta says it needs the government to cover nearly $50-million through additional funding
stories.author: Lisa Johnson and Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta ’s elections agency says last month’s historic separation vote came with a price tag of $84-million.

The cost, which is more than double the roughly $37-million spent on the 2023 general election, was revealed Thursday when officials from Elections Alberta appeared before a legislature committee.

The 10-question referendum saw about 75 per cent of voters say they want Alberta to stay in Canada instead of holding a second, binding vote on separating.

Albertans also approved, by slim margins, five questions related to the province taking more control over immigration. Four proposals for changing the Constitution were rejected.

Gordon McClure, the province’s chief electoral officer, told the committee the referendum cost nearly $50-million more than what the agency’s annual budget could pay for. He asked the bipartisan committee for $59-million in additional funding, which was unanimously approved.

McClure said $26-million is needed just to pay staff who hand-counted the more than 22 million ballots that were cast.

Renting voting and counting spaces came out to about $7-million, he added, while nearly $11 million was spent on security, IT equipment, and shipping and postage for ballots.

McClure and other officials also said the referendum was “crushing” for staff, with many working long hours.

One staff member, McClure said, even developed appendicitis and put off getting treatment.

“People went above and beyond,” he told the committee.

Steve Kaye, the agency’s chief administrative officer, said his longest shift was 22 hours and that the executive team worked multiple 16- to 20-hour days.

“But that comes with the territory,” he said. “We’re not here complaining.

“We have had our foot on the gas for a long time,” he added.

“People are tired, and we have some concerns going forward about being able to hire some of the people that have worked for us in the past.”

NDP committee member David Shepherd thanked Elections Alberta for their work, calling it a heroic effort.

He said it’s no surprise Elections Alberta was forced to push their staff to the limit, and noted that it was a decision of Premier Danielle Smith and her government to hold the referendum.

“We will leave that to Albertans, I guess, to determine what the return on investment is,” said Shepherd.

Smith’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As part of its funding request Thursday, the agency is also receiving about $9 million to aid preparations for next year’s general election, which is scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027.

The committee also granted Elections Alberta about $1-million in extra funding to hire additional full-time staff.

Kaye said that compared to other electoral agencies in Canada, Elections Alberta has one of the leanest workforces and that the referendum proved it was unsustainable.

“If we lost a person for medical reasons or whatever, the gap that created was exponential, and the staff we had to pick up the ball and run with it.”

He said if the agency had the same staffing level on a Per-capita basis as Quebec’s elections body, than Elections Alberta would have more than quadruple its current 54 full-time employees.

Kaye also said the committee should be prepared for further staffing requests next month when the agency makes its submissions for next year’s budget.

The committee also heard Thursday that Elections Alberta will be able to deliver the next general election on time, despite raising concerns last week about the government planning to put controversial new electoral maps into law before the end of the year.

McClure had said the agency needed more time to properly implement and adjust to new voting districts, but the government denied his request to delay the election or hold it under the current boundaries.

Officials told the committee that some processes that normally take months to adjust to new electoral boundaries are being foregone while others, like updating elector information, are being expedited with the help of temporary staff.

McClure said having time to be fully prepared makes the agency more efficient with its spending. He said rushing Elections Alberta to adjust to the maps could see the agency “paying a lot more” to run the 2027 vote.

Justice Minister Mickey Amery said earlier this week that the new electoral boundaries will be put into law before Christmas.

stories.title: Tenants upset with squalid conditions at central Edmonton apartment building
stories.summary: The apartment building in the McCauley neighbourhood, where the water and heat hasn't worked in a week, shows signs of disrepair on the outside and evidence of drug use inside.
stories.author: Joel Gotlib
stories.content:
Some residents of a central Edmonton apartment building say they’re frustrated with deteriorating conditions, after going about a week without heat or running water following a fire in a vacant basement suite.

Tenants also say copper piping and wiring have been stripped and stolen from the Parkside Village Square building, which on Thursday showed signs of vandalism and dilapidation: spray-painted doors and windows and holes in the roof.

“It’s gotten really bad in the last year with the homeless coming in, the gangs coming in,” said Shawne Edel, 67, who lives in the building with her roommate, Darlene Lent, also 67.

The building in the McCauley neighbourhood, near 91 Street and 106A Avenue, shows signs of disrepair on the outside and evidence of drug use inside.

Residents say strangers have been squatting.

“We’re intimidated,” Lent said. “There’s people always in the halls. We see only junk. They’re sitting there charging their phones. They have more rights than we do living here.”

With no baseboard heaters working, some residents are using space heaters to stay warm.

Through tears, Edel said she doesn’t know where to turn.

“We’re seniors, (we) don’t know what to do,” she said.

Another tenant, Dafala Makki, said conditions have deteriorated since the fire in the basement.

The floor of the trashed suite was littered with garbage, drug paraphernalia and a Naloxone overdose reversal kit.

“This fire, since it happened, the heat is cut, plus electricity is being cut, so we’ve been with no running water, no toilet to use — nothing,” Makki told Global News.

While at the property on Thursday, the owner of Parkside Village Square arrived and spoke with Global News.

Like his tenants, Ersen Lika also blamed many of the problems on strangers he said are entering and staying in the building without permission.

“These are not tenants of the building. They are all homeless from the street, coming and destroying, and they ask the owners to bear all the bills,” Lika said.

“We are under attack every day, as you see.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We are under attack every day, as you see."

Lika said police have removed transpassers from the building, only for them to return.

“Police came, two hours, they kick them out, they come back. But look at the damages,” he said.

As if on cue, officers arrived at the apartment building while Global News was there speaking with the owner and residents.

Police wouldn’t say what brought them to Parkside Village Square on Thursday, but they appeared to want to speak with Lika — who insists he is working with EPCOR to restore power and heat to the building.

Utility workers were seen near the property on Thursday.

For tenants, repairs can’t come soon enough.

“They should really help us in this situation so we can live a better life, ’cause this is hard on all of us,” Makki said.

With files from Karen Bartko, Global News

stories.title: Separatism referendum cost $84 million, exceeded Elections Alberta’s budget
stories.summary: Elections Alberta said the price tag is nearly $50 million more than its annual budget could pay for and needs the province to cover the rest through additional funding.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson and Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta’s elections agency says last month’s historic separation vote came with a price tag of $84 million.

Officials from Elections Alberta shared the total when they appeared at a legislature committee on Thursday.

Chief electoral officer Gordon McClure says the Alberta referendum price tag is nearly $50 million more than the agency’s annual budget could pay for and that it needs the government to cover the rest through additional funding.

He says roughly $26 million is needed just to pay staff who counted more than 22 million ballots that were cast in the 10-question vote.

McClure and other officials added that the referendum was crushing, with staff working long hours; one staffer developed appendicitis and put off getting treatment.

“I myself worked a 22-hour shift; that was my longest shift,” Steve Kaye, the agency’s chief administrative officer, told the committee.

“Everybody here at this table worked probably at least 16 to 20-hour days. But that comes with the territory. We’re not here complaining.”

He said that compared with other provinces their agency is one of the leanest.

“We have had our foot on the gas for a long time. People are tired, and we have some concerns going forward about being able to hire some of the people that have worked for us in the past,” Kaye said.

Elections Alberta also asked for an additional $9 million in funding to start preparing for next year’s general election, which it says it will be able to deliver on time despite the government planning to bring new electoral maps into law in the coming weeks.

— More to come…

stories.title: From forestry to food banks, what's in Budget 2026 for British Columbia?
stories.summary: The federal budget handed down on Thursday includes funding pledges that are expected to benefit British Columbia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The federal budget handed down on Thursday includes funding pledges that are expected to benefit British Columbia.

Here’s a look at some of them.

FORESTRY BOOST

The budget is proposing $6.5 billion in funding to support the forestry sector nationally over six years.

It doesn’t provide a province-by-province breakdown, although it points out that B.C. accounts for 29 per cent of the national forest sector’s GDP, representing the biggest share in Canada.

There’s $4 billion for a new “forestry sector accelerator” to make investments in large facilities and major transformations of existing facilities, “including biorefineries, biofuel facilities, and other facilities producing higher-value and innovative forest products.”

A further $2 billion is to help businesses in the forest sector modernize and expand, while $500 million goes towards strengthening fibre supply chains and supporting forest management.

EARTHQUAKE INSURANCE

The budget notes the significant earthquake risk in southwest B.C. and elsewhere.

It announces planned legislation to establish the Canadian Earthquake Insurance Facility.

The facility would be funded by levies on insurers and provide emergency funding of up to $50 billion to the insurance sector after an “extreme” earthquake.

INDIGENOUS LOAN GUARANTEE

Budget 2026 announces a $64-million loan guarantee to support the Tla’amin Nation acquiring 100 per cent ownership of Western Forest Products’ Stillwater Forest Operation, which the budget says will provide stable revenues and creating economic opportunities.

SALMON PLEDGE

The budget’s $3.7-billion nature strategy includes a pledge to protect, conserve and restore wild Pacific salmon in B.C. and the Yukon.

COMMUNITY PROJECTS

The budget lists a series of B.C. projects being targeted for funding by the Build Communities Strong Fund. They include the revitalization of a rooftop garden at Vancouver’s Chinese Canadian Museum, playing field facilities at the Mackie and Hawthorne Park in Delta, the implementation of a master plan for Hume Park in New Westminster and funding for the Cowichan Valley Basket Society, a food bank in Duncan.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Four people struck by vehicle in Richmond Hill, Ont., police say
stories.summary: York regional police say four pedestrians were struck by a vehicle in Richmond Hill, north of Toronto, ON Thursday afternoon.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
York regional police say four pedestrians, including two children, were struck by a vehicle in Richmond Hill, north of Toronto, ON Thursday afternoon.

They say two women and the children, ages seven and one, were struck by an SUV at the intersection of Major Mackenzie Drive and Newkirk Road at around 3:18 p.m.

stories.title: Feds promise at least $1 billion for Winnipeg mental health and addictions centre
stories.summary: Winnipeg - The federal government has promised more than $1 billion in funding for a Centre for Mental Health and Addictions in Winnipeg.
stories.author: Ian Bickis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The government says the funding is part of a partnership with Manitoba to “create the conditions to end homelessness” in the city.

It says the centre combines patient care with permanent supportive and transitional housing.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

Image 9Image 10

The federal government says the commitment includes up to $800 million in capital to build 2,000 of the housing units, while Manitoba will fund operations.

Winnipeg Mayor Scott Gillingham says in a statement that it is a once-in-a-generation investment in the city that is a big step toward addressing some of the city’s biggest challenges.

The federal government says the Winnipeg centre will follow the model already being used at the Dunn House supportive housing initiative in Toronto.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Canada’s new immigration level plan revealed in Budget 2026
stories.summary: Ottawa plans to hold immigration levels mostly steady over the next three years, according to Budget 2026.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Ottawa plans to hold immigration levels mostly steady over the next three years, according to Budget 2026 .

The new federal immigration targets were revealed Thursday and will maintain the number of temporary resident arrivals at 370,000 per year in each of 2027, 2028 and 2029, while the target for the number of permanent resident admissions would stay at the current level of 380,000 in each of those years.

The budget says it will provide $56.9 million over four years, starting next year, for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada to help implement this plan.

Up to 200,000 temporary residents will be given the opportunity to become permanent residents by the end of 2027, and half of them will be considered for the Express Entry or the Provincial Nominee Program. This, the budget says, will allow for more flexibility for provinces and territories and respond to regional labour market needs.

Another $302.3 million will be provided to help make this happen.

The budget, released Thursday afternoon, says the updated immigration plan aims to strike “a balance” that favours the needs of both the economy, as well as housing, health care and social services.

“The 2027-2029 Immigration Levels Plan will continue to seek a balance between the needs of Canada’s employers, industries, and communities and our ability to meet the needs of newcomers, while avoiding undue pressures on housing, health care, and social services,” the budget said.

“The Plan will also support pathways for people already living and working in Canada to continue contributing to our shared economic future.”

There will also be reforms to Canada’s Temporary Foreign Worker Program (Tfwp), with an injection of $151.5 million over five years, starting this year, and funnelled through Employment and Social Development Canada.

Budget 2026 does not mention specifics about reforms to the Tfwp, but the federal government says it will aim to “better align with regional labour market needs, in collaboration with provinces and territories, while improving processing time and strengthening employer compliance.”

stories.title: Liberals budget $12 million to create Justin Trudeau archives
stories.summary: Library and Archives Canada holds records of prime ministers dating back to Sir John A. MacDonald, including personal correspondence
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
The 2026 federal budget sets aside $12 million over four years to acquire, preserve and make public the archives of the country’s 23rd prime minister, Justin Trudeau.

Library and Archives Canada (LAC) holds records of prime ministers dating back to Sir John A. MacDonald, including personal correspondence, artworks, photos and speeches. “A Prime Minister’s time in office is documented through multiple sets of records acquired by LAC,” the library said in an emailed statement to the Ottawa Citizen in 2015, after it started the process to collect material from former prime minister Stephen Harper.

“These include official records such as Cabinet documents and the records of the government of Canada institutions, as well as websites. The records of parliamentarians are also acquired by LAC.”

stories.title: LHSC attracts world renowned clinician to head Children’s Health Research Institute
stories.summary: London Health Sciences Centre has attracted a world-renowned clinician to head its Children’s Health Research Institute (Chri).
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
London Health Sciences Centre has attracted a world-renowned clinician to head its Children’s Health Research Institute (Chri).

Dr. Susa Benseler comes with a highly respected pedigree, and a philosophy of bringing research and care together.

“I think this is where the opportunity lies because literally all diseases have their origins in childhood,” said Dr. Benseler.

LHSC has named her as the new Scientific Director of the Chri.

With a background as a paediatrician caring for children with rare inflammatory diseases, she became a researcher from questions arising through patient care.

“So, all of us clinical researchers I think are grounding our work in caring for children and families. That’s where we put all our strengths. That’s where we pull our inspiration. I’m just like everybody else. You know I see children in clinics, and I see children in emergency departments, and I learn what matters to them and how we can make their lives better,” she explained.

In an environment where every research dollar matters, she understands the need for relationships.

“If you establish effective partnerships, partnerships that really can move the needle, you will get the funding,” she said.

Dr. Benseler has held roles with SickKids, Alberta Children’s Hospital Research Institute, and, most recently, with Children’s Health Ireland.

She has nothing but praise for the Canadian health care system.

“It’s an approach where we can all thrive, and most importantly where we rally around children and families. I don’t think I’ve worked in a better place than the Canadian health care system.”

stories.title: Halifax councillors question how infrastructure will be funded after extended fee freeze
stories.summary: Nova Scotia has extended its freeze on increasing development fees in Halifax and some councillors say they're concerned about where to find money for infrastructure upgrades.
stories.author: Angela Capobianco, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Nova Scotia has extended its development fee freeze in Halifax Regional Municipality , and some councillors say they’re concerned about where to find money for infrastructure upgrades.

The province made the announcement Thursday morning and said it was to ensure affordability.

“It’s not a full freeze, it’s not an unlock either, but this is going to allow developers to plan and know what it’s going to (be),” said the province’s Municipal Affairs Minister John A. MacDonald.

“Which means people who are buying those houses, renting those apartments, actually have an idea of what the rents are going to be like,”

The extension lasts until 2029 and includes all development-related fees for the municipality and Halifax Water.

The freeze has been in place since 2023 and MacDonald said it’s being extended to meet federal funding requirements.

“I’m not going to give up $366 million of federal money. And the federal government has made it clear this has to be (part of the deal),” he said.

But regional councillors say the move impedes Hrm’s ability to properly fund infrastructure and growth, especially given the fact the municipality has some of the lowest fees in the country already, according to a staff report.

Councillors told Global News they anticipate making tough decisions in the upcoming budget deliberations.

“It puts us between a rock and a hard place,” said District 10 Coun. Kathryn Morse.

“You have to get revenue from somewhere. It comes from taxes or fees. So if fees aren’t going up, taxes will probably have to go up instead.”

Deputy Mayor Patty Cuttell points out that “we need housing, we need the transit.”

“We are already at a breaking point. I can feel the pressure of growth and … I’m seeing the cracks now. So this isn’t a future state that we need to address, it’s today,” she said.

Jillian Ramsay, the sustainable cities program manager with the Ecology Action Centre, says she believes the freeze will only help developers and ultimately hurt taxpayers.

“So things like fire stations, community centres, parks, and more are all built using the development charges,” said Ramsay. “If the developers aren’t paying for it, the taxpayers will.”

But Mayor Andy Fillmore says he sees the freeze benefiting affordability and doesn’t anticipate it will impact Hrm’s ability to get projects off the ground.

“As always, I will continue to … push our municipality to supplement our infrastructure funding through other sources, whether it’s another order of government or even if it’s in coordination and partnership with the private sector,” he told Global News.

stories.title: Stamp prices are going up for Canadians under Budget 2026
stories.summary: The 40 per cent increase will have a 'relatively limited impact' on consumers and small businesses, the government said in the federal budget.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Canada Post will raise the price of stamps starting in 2027 to offset some of the losses incurred by a decline in letter-sending.

Stamp prices will rise to $2 per stamp, according to the federal budget tabled Thursday , up from the current $1.44 per stamp.

The 40 per cent increase will have a “relatively limited impact” on consumers and small businesses, the government said. The budget estimates the change will amount to approximately $6 per year more for individual consumers and $9 per year for small businesses.

“This increase will further offset costs while ensuring continuous affordability,” the budget states.

The price will continue to rise seven per cent per year continuously.

The last time the cost of a stamp increased was in 2025 when it rose 25 per cent to $1.44. Less than 10 years ago, a single stamp cost $1.

The budget says the increase will bring Canada Post’s stamp pricing “more closely in line with Oecd peers.”

The cost of a single stamp in the United Kingdom cost £1.80 (equivalent to approximately $1.89 CAD), whereas in New Zealand a single stamp cost $3.60 NZD (equivalent to approximately $2.82 CAD).

The United States is believed to have the lowest price stamps out of all Oecd countries when adjusted for purchasing power parity with one stamp costing $0.82 USD (equivalent to approximately $1.15 CAD).

The budget does not state exactly when the increase will occur just that it will come sometime in 2027.

stories.title: Bruce Power nuclear facing federal charges for massive 2025 fish kill
stories.summary: Ontario’s largest nuclear plant is facing two charges under the Federal Fisheries Act following a February 2025 fish kill that saw as many as five million fish caught and killed in the company’s underwater infrastructure.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Ontario’s largest nuclear plant is facing two charges under the Federal Fisheries Act following a February 2025 fish kill that saw as many as five million fish caught and killed in the company’s underwater infrastructure.

“Just a couple of years ago, in 2023, there was another fish kill. Not to the same magnitude as what was experienced in 2025, but certainly it was a large enough kill that we hoped it would serve as a kind of a wake-up call,” said Ryan Lauzon, Fisheries Management Biologist with the Chippewas of Nawash Unceded First Nation.

One of the byproducts of that process is warm water, which is ultimately discharged back into Lake Huron. That warm water attracts fish, specifically Gizzard Shad. During the 2025 incident, nearly eight million fish were hovering near this warm water exchange pipe, and entered a recirculation duct through a gate that is only open in the winter, to keep frazil ice from forming, and clogging up Bruce Power’s pumps.

Frazil ice is a collection of loose, sub-millimeter to millimeter-sized ice crystals that form in turbulent, supercooled open water and is notorious for blocking water intakes for hydropower plants and nuclear facilities.

“When that happens, and they open up that that passageway, they opened a clear route for these fish to get sucked from the discharge, which is directly connected to the lake. All these fish are getting attracted. Then they get sucked into the intake side of the system.

And like we saw, we had potentially as many as, five million fish killed within that event according to Bruce Powers own numbers,” said Lauzon. Bruce Power says the 2025 fish kill, which actually forced them to take their Unit 2 nuclear reactor offline for 1.5 weeks, occurred during very unique circumstances they hadn’t seen in decades.

“The 2025 event occurred during a rare convergence of environmental conditions, including prolonged cold weather, and an unusually large presence of Gizzard Shad following several warm years. The last time this convergence of factors occurred was in the late 1970s.” said Bruce Power officials.

Bruce Power says they have since invested millions of dollars in fish deterrents for their connection to Lake Huron, including nets, sound barriers, and enhanced monitoring. “Immediately following the event, Bruce Power invested millions of dollars in additional protective measures, including physical barriers (nets), acoustic and strobe light deterrents, enhanced monitoring using sonar and camera-based systems, and expanded lake monitoring and research to better understand fish movement and ecosystem responses.

This was all implemented for the winter of 2026. The lessons learned and mitigation strategies developed through this work have been shared across the global nuclear industry,” said Bruce Power. Lauzon who works with Bruce Power, amongst other companies, ON fish management practices for local indigenous groups says the mitigation measures have had mixed results.

He says one of the nets installed has already had to be removed. “We do know that it had to be removed because it became so clogged with algae and dead fish. So, it’s really hard to get those nets perfectly aligned. You end up having gaps and fish can still enter.

So, you know, I think it is an important step, but you know, it’s not necessarily a solution,” said Lauzon. Lauzon says putting warm water back into a cold lake creates an artificial ecosystem that attracts some species of fish.

He calls it “a giant fish trap”, that can be mitigated, but not ever entirely stopped, as long as the nuclear plants continue to operate. “I don’t think we’re going to stop all the environmental effects. It’ll be very, very difficult.

But I do think that we can reduce a lot of these major events like this one, and really reduce our impact on the lake,” said Lauzon. Bruce Power could face up to a $200,000 fine for the February 2025 fish kill, and exceeding their annual allowable fish kill limits.

Their first court appearance will be Nov. 24 in Walkerton. Below is the entirely of Bruce Power’s statement on the Department of Fisheries charges. “Bruce Power has been formally notified that it will face two charges under the federal Fisheries Act related to the Gizzard Shad event that took place early 2025.

The company takes its environmental responsibilities seriously and is committed to protecting the environment and the biodiversity of Lake Huron. We will respond to the charges through the appropriate process. The 2025 event occurred during a rare convergence of environmental conditions, including prolonged cold weather and an unusually large presence of Gizzard Shad following several warm years.

The last time this convergence of factors occurred was in the late 1970s. As these factors unfolded, Bruce Power took proactive and conservative operational action, including removing Unit 2 from service while mitigation measures were implemented.

Throughout the event and in the months that followed, Bruce Power was transparent with regulators, Indigenous Nations and local municipalities and the public regarding the circumstances of the event and our response actions.

This includes ongoing engagement with Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission. Immediately following the event, Bruce Power invested millions of dollars in additional protective measures, including physical barriers (nets), acoustic and strobe light deterrents, enhanced monitoring using sonar and camera-based systems, and expanded lake monitoring and research to better understand fish movement and ecosystem responses.

This was all implemented for the winter of 2026. The lessons learned and mitigation strategies developed through this work have been shared across the global nuclear industry. Protecting the environment remains a core responsibility, and Bruce Power will continue to work with regulators, Indigenous Nations, local communities and scientific experts to better understand the factors that contributed to this rare event and help prevent a similar occurrence in the future.”

stories.title: NDP renews call for emergency debate on $10B Cape Breton AI data centre project
stories.summary: The Official Opposition in Nova Scotia is renewing its call for emergency debate in the legislature following last month's announcement of a $10-billion AI data centre project.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Skye Bryden-Blom
stories.content:
The official Opposition in Nova Scotia is renewing its call for emergency debate in the legislature following last month’s announcement of a $10-billion AI data centre project in Cape Breton.

NDP Leader Claudia Chender told reporters Thursday her party has heard concerns from thousands of Nova Scotians.

“Is there going to be a tax levy? Will there be additional income? Will our environment be protected? Show us the regulations that prove that. Will ratepayers be protected? Put it in law,” she said.

EverWind Fuels is planning on building an 18,600-square-metre facility in Point Tupper, N.S., ON Cape Breton Island.

American tech company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for the centre, which would draw 95 megawatts of electricity in its first phase. A 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028.

The plan has drawn criticism among residents in the area and across the province. Two lengthy information sessions were held this week by EverWind in the community where residents were able to ask company officials about the project.

During Thursday’s NDP news conference, two parents shared their concerns when it comes to power rates and the impact on the environment.

“I don’t believe building a data centre for an American AI company is putting our province first,” said Bethany Isaksen.

“Proposing a project that could drastically increase our power bill is not what we’re asking for, and a project that could potentially lead to lasting effects on our environment that our children are left to deal with is not what we’re asking for.”

Sam Walerickton said the rising cost of living and the risks posed by AI are things decisionmakers need to consider.

“A data centre in our beautiful province scares me for many reasons. From the risks posed by the AI it might support, to the environmental impacts, and the simple fear of our day-to-day life becoming untenably expensive with rising power bills,” she said.

“It makes me deeply sad to think our family May not grow and know the joy of another child simply because our power bill is too high and our water supply is too low.”

In a statement to Global News, Nova Scotia’s Energy Department said all three levels of government and EverWind have committed to not negatively affecting power rates.

EverWind has echoed that sentiment, saying it will also use a closed-loop watering system.

— with a file from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Calgary water system had ‘systemic’ issues before pipe failure: Report
stories.summary: The report found the 2024 and 2025 failures exposed systemic governance, asset-management, financial-management and accountability weaknesses — rather than simply a failed pipe.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
A report into Calgary’s beleaguered water system says the city wasn’t properly aware of the extent of its infrastructure problems and issues over the years were systemic rather than the fault of city councillors.

The findings came from an inspection the Ministry of Municipal Affairs ordered to be carried out back in March, looking into the City of Calgary’s management of the Bearspaw South Feeder Main.

The water main carries 60 per cent of the city’s drinking water and has experienced two major ruptures since 2024.

The third-party report, dated Oct. 8, 2026 and released to the public on Thursday, examined the city’s management of its overall water system dating back to 2004.

The report was authored by independent inspector David Goldie, who previously served as Alberta Energy Regulator board chair from 2020 to 2024.

Goldie’s report found the failures of the Bearspaw South Feeder Main identified weaknesses in how the city managed infrastructure risks.

The underlying problem was systemic rather than narrowly technical, the report said.

“No city can guarantee that a pipe will never fail, but Calgarians can expect that critical risks would be understood, acted upon and clearly reported,” David Goldie said to reporters when releasing his report on Thursday.

The investigation involved 50 interviews and review of 58,260 documents and records. ( The full report can be found at the bottom of this story .)

The report found multiple recommendations from a decade ago were never presented to council and that a gap between planned and completed capital projects likely contributed to the feeder main’s deterioration.

In January 2015, the City of Calgary hired utility advisory firm Raftelis to review the water system’s governance, finances and management.

Goldie’s probe found the mayor’s office received an advance briefing on the final draft, but the full Raftelis report and a majority of the recommendations were not passed on to city council.

“I think a case could be made that if those recommendations had been considered and potentially implemented, that the utility could’ve gone on a different course,” Goldie said.

Goldie’s report said senior city administration, led by city manager Jeffrey Fielding, debated the recommendations, while then-mayor Naheed Nenshi and his chief of staff were included in an advance briefing stream and were sent the draft version of the final report but there is no evidence it was provided to other councillors.

The inspector said five of nine priority recommendations were “consciously excluded” from material presented to councillors, including Raftelis’ first two priorities: clearer financial accountability and independent expert governance.

“The handling of the review was irregular, improper and improvident: administration was entitled to disagree with Raftelis, but not to prevent council from considering major governance choices,” the report said.

It added, “Although the evidence does not establish that the mayor directed or knowingly approved the omissions, the mayor’s office was part of a pre-council briefing and consultation process in which it was informed while council collectively was not.”

Nenshi, who is now leader of the provincial Opposition NDP, says he doesn’t recall the recommendations.

“Why would you need to put in that line (in the report)? Because I didn’t. It’s because the government put out a personal vendetta to try and find a smoking gun on me,” he said to reporters at the Alberta legislature on Thursday.

Nenshi denied any wrongdoing.

“That report was one report 10 years ago, that had nothing whatsoever to do with anything that would’ve changed a thing on the Bearspaw water main.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That report was one report 10 years ago, that had nothing whatsoever to do with anything that would've changed a thing on the Bearspaw water main."

Another issue identified: some approved funds earmarked for infrastructure work went unspent.

Between 2006 and 2024, actual utility capital expenditure averaged about 35 per cent below their approved budgets, as the city persistently delivered less work than council had approved.

“Capital investment also compared unfavourably with national infrastructure benchmarks and did not keep pace with inflation and population growth,” the report said.

The report says the main constraint was not an absence of funds, but rather persistent inability to execute the capital programs.

The inspector noted that does not mean spending every approved dollar would have prevented the feeder-main failures, but said the sustained delivery gap increased the long-term risk and “likely contributed” to infrastructure deterioration.

The report makes 20 recommendations, including the creation of an arm’s-length, municipally controlled water utility corporation — similar to the City of Edmonton-owned utility provider Epcor.

The Goldie report said integration with electricity and natural gas-provider Enmax — which is already owned by the City of Calgary — is the preferred long-term option, subject to an assessment proving Enmax is up to the task.

The 125-page report’s conclusion is that the 2024 and 2025 failures exposed systemic governance, asset-management, financial-management and accountability weaknesses, rather than simply a failed pipe.

“The report is being released publicly today so all Calgarians and Albertans can review the independent inspector’s findings and his recommendations to the minister,” Municipal Affairs Minister Dan Williams said.

In his report, Goldie suggests action on the recommendations within the next 24 months. Williams said he will review the findings before deciding any next steps.

“Its release doesn’t represent a decision from me on what future actions, if any, May be appropriate. The report is now public for Calgarians to review and consider as well.”

The Alberta government covered the cost of the inspection and report, but the amount spent on it has not yet been made public.

The report comes as Calgarians and residents in surrounding communities are being asked to once again comply with water restrictions due to ongoing construction on the Bearspaw South Feeder Main.

Work to replace the existing feeder main, which Mayor Jeromy Farkas has called “terminally ill,” began in late January.

An August update said it was on schedule and on budget, expected to be done before the end of 2026.

As the end of October, the six-kilometre replacement was 95 per cent complete.

The city said a project of that magnitude would normally take four years but construction was fast-tracked following the two catastrophic breaks .

Goldie’s report said it’s too early to assess whether the city’s recent reforms have materially reduced future failure risk.

The main has ruptured twice in the last two years — on June 5, 2024 and then again on the evening of Dec. 30, 2025 — leading to intermittent water restrictions while the pipe is overhauled and replaced.

That independent report released this past January was commissioned after the June 2024 rupture forced the city to spend millions of dollars on emergency repairs and implement weeks of strict water conservation measures.

The findings of the six-member independent panel were supposed to be released later in 2026, but the release was expedited after the Bearspaw feeder main ruptured for the second time in December 2025.

Although the report was written prior to the pipe’s second failure, it noted the recommendations remained relevant.

That report found the line will “continue to be unreliable” no matter how many repairs are conducted; the report noted it must be replaced.

stories.title: Federal budget outlines plan to end homelessness within 10 years
stories.summary: The Carney government is promising to end homelessness in Canada within a decade.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
The Carney government is promising to end homelessness in Canada within a decade.

The 2026 budget, released Thursday, offers $11.2 billion to tackle homelessness over four years, starting next year, and $17.8 billion over 10 years.

The federal government says it would “create the conditions to end homelessness” by setting up a new fund to support projects addressing health, addictions and social supports. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne called it one of the government’s “flagship” policies.

“We are committed to changing how Canada addresses homelessness and supports those who are unhoused, because every Canadian should have the security of a warm home,” the budget document says.

“This is a call to action for every level of government, Indigenous partners, the private sector, and the not-for-profit sector to come together to reach this goal.”

The budget document says it will help build new supportive and transitional housing across the country. It proposes that Ottawa take on capital costs while provincial and territorial governments foot the bill for ongoing operations and services like training, income and health supports.

The government says it will work to sign agreements with provinces and territories ahead of next year’s spring economic update.

The federal spending plan also commits to expanding non-market housing and building 200,000 new homes across Canada in the next decade.

The strategy proposes building new community mental health and addictions facilities with a $2 billion commitment, along with continued support for the Veterans Homelessness Program.

An estimated 65,000 people across the country were reported as experiencing homelessness in a 2025 count by the federal government.

A 2022 Statistics Canada study found nearly one in eight households reported experiencing some form of homelessness at some point. For Indigenous people, that rate jumps to more than one in four.

stories.title: Meta pauses change to terms of service after publishers voice concerns
stories.summary: The U.S. tech giant behind Facebook and Instagram is pausing the implementation of a policy that concerned Canadian news publishers.
stories.author: The Canadian Press

Jeff Chiu/The Associated Press[](https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/meta-pauses-change-to-terms-of-service-after-publishers-voice-concerns/article_9c9d4c9b-64f4-5b34-9b23-ec02ac044f5f.html)

By The Canadian Press

Media companies feared the changes to Meta’s terms of services would allow websites associated with a business account to be scraped for artificial intelligence purposes.

Meta spokesperson Julia Perreira says in an email that the company is pausing the changes.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

Image 9Image 10Image 11

She says the pause will help the company engage with stakeholders and “take the time to get this right.”

Several Canadian journalism organizations, whose content Meta has blocked from its platforms in response to the Online News Act, were worried about how their work would be impacted by the once-incoming policy.

European and British publishers has similar concerns and had asked governments and regulators to step in.

Some Canadian news publishers already use robots.txt to block bots from AI companies like OpenAI.

A number of news outlets, including The Canadian Press, have launched lawsuits against OpenAI and Anthropic over the use of copyrighted content for training AI systems.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Budget raises questions about defence spending targets after 2030
stories.summary: Ottawa — The Liberal government's new budget leaves unanswered a major accounting question about Ottawa's plans to meet its 2035 Nato defence spending commitments.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Liberal government’s new budget leaves unanswered a major accounting question about Ottawa’s plans to meet its 2035 Nato defence spending commitments.

The budget charts a path to meet alliance defence spending targets from now through to 2030 — but the math stops there.

Reaching the goal of spending five per cent of national GDP on defence by 2035 would heap mounds of new spending pressure on future budgets.

Former parliamentary budget officer Kevin Page has warned Ottawa is not being transparent by ending its projections at 2030.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne argued that Ottawa is offering more transparency on its defence spending plans than other alliance members facing the same difficult task.

“In terms of spending on defence … you’ll see more transparency than most G7 countries,” he said at a Thursday news conference.

“You’ll see the spending on a cash basis for every year until 2030.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said that if Ottawa put out a full plan, it would be outdated quickly because of how rapidly modern warfare is changing.

When Nato nations met in The Hague last year, they agreed to massively increase alliance members’ defence spending targets to the equivalent of 5 per cent of annual GDP by 2035.

The federal budget says Canada will reach 4 per cent by 2030.

But core defence spending — a key figure that includes things like bullets, bombs and soldiers’ salaries — is expected to reach 3.5 per cent by 2035.

The budget says core defence spending will reach 2.6 per cent of GDP by 2030, about $99 billion.

That’s already a big leap. In 2024, core defence spending was just $43.9 billion.

But parliamentary budget officer Annette Ryan estimates that to reach the 3.5 per cent target, core defence spending would have to hit $163.6 billion in 2035.

The difference between two per cent and 3.5 per cent amounts to an extra $70 billion per year, according to her office’s calculations.

The alliance has come under sustained pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump to hike spending to the new targets. Nato plans to review its 2035 targets by 2030 — after Trump leaves office.

The federal government is currently in negotiations to purchase a fleet of up to 12 submarines from German defence firm Tkms, a massive purchase expected to cost tens of billions of dollars.

It’s also in talks for advanced radar planes for the air force from the Swedish firm Saab — a procurement worth billions of dollars — and is looking at whether to pursue a mixed fighter jet fleet.

No funding has been set out for any of these purchases.

The budget also commits new funding for the families of victims of the tragedy at CFB Wainwright. A sudden fire at the base last month overtook a training exercise, claiming the lives of four soldiers and injuring dozens more.

The fiscal plan sets aside $25 million for support for Canadian Armed Forces members, their families and local communities affected by the fire.

The government has not provided a further breakdown of the funding envelope. Another $3 million will be put toward the Wainwright Military Family Resource Centre.

While Ottawa has rolled out major defence spending initiatives since Carney took office, the 2026 budget only pencils in $755 million in new defence funding over the next five years.

It touts plans to spend billions more — but much of that money was either already on the books under pre-existing programming or, according to the budget document, will be “sourced from existing departmental resources.”

The budget sets out $7.6 billion to support Canada’s overseas military deployment in Latvia.

Canada has some 2,000 troops stationed there and announced plans at this year’s Nato summit in Turkey to increase that figure to 2,600 and extend the mission to 2031.

The document earmarks $2.3 billion for the Defence Drone Initiative, a program meant to help develop drones domestically and allow the military to acquire them faster.

The budget suggests Canada could spend $61.9 million over the next four years to participate in the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan program.

Participation would allow Canadian firms to compete for about 60 billion euros in Ukraine defence contracts, the budget document said.

stories.title: Defence spending will soon outstrip health transfers — and other things we learned from Federal Budget 2026
stories.summary: This budget continues to pour billions of dollars into national defence spending as Canada seeks to make good on its Nato commitments
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Ottawa — Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne has titled his second budget Masters of Our Destiny, and it includes plenty of buzzwords like investment supercycle and productivity mega deduction. It also includes more funding for arts and culture, tweaks to the tax system and a goal of ending homelessness.

Here are five things in the government’s latest spending plan.

The Canada Health Transfer – the largest single transfer of money from federal coffers to the provinces and territories – is estimated to grow to $67.7 billion by 2030-31, up from $54.7 billion this fiscal year.

This budget continues to pour billions of dollars into national defence spending as Canada seeks to make good on its Nato commitments. Allies have agreed to spend at least the equivalent of two per cent of GDP per year on their national defence, rising to five per cent by 2035. That five per cent commitment is something Nato pledged to do in response to threats from U.S. President Donald Trump, who has long complained that European and Canadian allies are not pulling their weight.

The budget lays out a plan to push defence spending above 4.1 per cent of GDP by 2030-31, including $99.2 billion in core defence spending and another $58.3 billion in defence-related and security funding.

That outstrips the growth of overall major transfers to municipalities, provinces and territories – including funds for health, social programs, equalization payments and child care – which are projected to reach $131.2 billion in 2030-31.

Premiers and their health ministers across the country have been raising the alarm about the amount coming to them through the federal health transfer since last year’s budget.

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, the previous federal government cut temporary deals with provinces and territories to add billions of dollars on top of the Canada Health Transfer to reduce wait times and fund mental health and addictions programs. It also boosted the annual increase to the transfer to a minimum of five per cent per year, ending in 2027-28. The end of these funding agreements is a “fiscal cliff” for their own budgets, the premiers said after a recent Council of the Federation meeting in July.

This year’s federal budget holds firm to the plan to return to a minimum growth rate of three per cent per year after the next fiscal year, although Health Minister Marjorie Michel has said talks with her provincial and territorial counterparts are ongoing.

The income tax filing deadline is moving to May 15 next year, a measure the government says will save Canadians about $230 million over five years in interest and penalties.

That’s part of a section of this budget aimed at simplifying the tax system to “reduce the time spent by citizens unnecessarily interacting with the government.”

The changes come after the auditor general reported last fall the Canada Revenue Agency was not only failing most of the time to answer calls within its own standards, it was also giving inaccurate information in response to general questions more than 80 per cent of the time.

The budget “sets Canada on a path to end homelessness over the next decade,” and estimates that some 65,000 Canadians do not have a roof over their heads.

The plan sets aside $11.2 billion over four years, including $1.8 billion of that which is meant to create a fund for projects that include housing, health care, mental health, addictions and social support. Another $3.6 billion over four years will go toward building supportive and transitional housing. The federal government will provide capital funding for these projects, and expects the provinces and territories to fund the services that go along with it.

The first practical step in the budget is building a new Centre for Mental Health and Addictions in Winnipeg and setting aside $800 million in capital funding to create 2,000 transitional and supportive homes in that city.

Jacob Tierney, the creator of the breakout show Heated Rivalry, gets a mention in the budget document alongside cultural icons Celine Dion, Margaret Atwood and Edward Burtynsky.

The Liberals announced a slate of CanCon measures to build “a country where Canadian culture thrives, where Canadians see themselves in their stories, music, songs and movies.”

There’s funding to celebrate Canada’s 160th anniversary in 2027 and host the Francophonie in 2028.

The cultural funding also includes a pledge to make more of the iconic Heritage Minutes, extend the Canada Strong Pass (so that everyone under age 25 gets free entry to national museums, permanently), and create a tax credit to exclude up to $45,000 of business income derived from “original and creative artistic works.”

It also includes $32.2 million over four years to create a digital collection of books by Canadian authors that Canadians can borrow and read for free. The plan is to start with 200 titles next year, and grow to up to two million loans per year by 2031.

The budget sets aside $12 million over four years to acquire, preserve and make public the archives of the country’s 23rd prime minister, Justin Trudeau.

Library and Archives Canada holds records of prime ministers dating back to Sir John A. MacDonald, including personal correspondence, artworks, photos and speeches.

Former prime minister Stephen Harper’s archives were formally launched last February, 20 years after his Conservative party was elected government.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

The budget “sets Canada on a path to end homelessness over the next decade,” and estimates that some 65,000 Canadians do not have a roof over their heads.

The plan sets aside $11.2 billion over four years, including $1.8 billion of that which is meant to create a fund for projects that include housing, health care, mental health, addictions and social support. Another $3.6 billion over four years will go toward building supportive and transitional housing. The federal government will provide capital funding for these projects, and expects the provinces and territories to fund the services that go along with it.

The first practical step in the budget is building a new Centre for Mental Health and Addictions in Winnipeg and setting aside $800 million in capital funding to create 2,000 transitional and supportive homes in that city.
A Heated Rivalry shoutout
Jacob Tierney, the creator of the breakout show Heated Rivalry, gets a mention in the budget document alongside cultural icons Celine Dion, Margaret Atwood and Edward Burtynsky.
The Liberals announced a slate of CanCon measures to build “a country where Canadian culture thrives, where Canadians see themselves in their stories, music, songs and movies.”
There’s funding to celebrate Canada’s 160th anniversary in 2027 and host the Francophonie in 2028.

The cultural funding also includes a pledge to make more of the iconic Heritage Minutes, extend the Canada Strong Pass (so that everyone under age 25 gets free entry to national museums, permanently), and create a tax credit to exclude up to $45,000 of business income derived from “original and creative artistic works.”

It also includes $32.2 million over four years to create a digital collection of books by Canadian authors that Canadians can borrow and read for free. The plan is to start with 200 titles next year, and grow to up to two million loans per year by 2031.
Creating the Justin Trudeau archive
The budget sets aside $12 million over four years to acquire, preserve and make public the archives of the country’s 23rd prime minister, Justin Trudeau.
Library and Archives Canada holds records of prime ministers dating back to Sir John A. MacDonald, including personal correspondence, artworks, photos and speeches.
Former prime minister Stephen Harper’s archives were formally launched last February, 20 years after his Conservative party was elected government.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

stories.title: Five things: What the federal budget means for your cost of living
stories.summary: The federal budget contains a lot of government jargon like "supercycles" and "mega deductions" that might mean little to people struggling with the high cost of living.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
By Meredith Bond

Posted November 5, 2026 4:16 pm.

The federal budget contains a lot of government jargon like “supercycles” and “mega deductions” that might mean little to people struggling with the high cost of living.

Finance Minister Francois Philippe Champagne said Thursday the budget’s overarching goal is to strengthen both Canada’s sovereignty and the economy by boosting productivity rates that have sagged for decades.

The idea is that a stronger economy will help many Canadians with day-to-day affordability challenges, but there are some targeted affordability policies in the 511 page budget document.

The Groceries and Essential Benefit, a rebranded version of the GST credit, is one of the government’s key affordability measures. The budget proposes a one-time 50 per cent top-up to the benefit for the 2026-27 fiscal year, that will be sent to families early next year.

A similar payment was issued in June.

The budget document says this money will increase the average benefit to $339 for a qualifying single person and $679 for a couple with two children, and will increase the total annual benefit for a family to about $2,570.

The budget document says this expanded program will cost about $4.1 billion.

Food affordability is one of the biggest challenges facing many households. Food banks across the country reported more than 2.3 million monthly visits in March — a grim record for a wealthy country like Canada.

The budget proposes adding $124 million over three years to the Local Food Infrastructure Fund, which helps food banks and similar organizations buy food and invest in infrastructure.

That funding is set to start in the 2027-28 fiscal year, which begins on April 1.

The budget lays out an ambitious housing agenda that includes building more homes on federally owned land and ending homelessness within the next 10 years.

It includes a pitch to establish an Integrated Supports Fund to set up transitional housing with mental health, addictions and social supports for homeless people. The government plans to put $1.8 billion over four years into this fund, with the goal of supplementing it with private, public and philanthropic cash.

The budget also pitches a $2 billion, two-year fund to build more crisis mental health and addictions facilities across Canada.

Plans include putting billions of dollars into the Canada Housing Benefit over the next decade to help low-income Canadians cover rent.

The budget says the plan to end homelessness will require close collaboration with provinces, territories and municipalities.

The budget says the government plans to draft regulations that would require banks to provide customers with annual, clear statements of the fees paid on their chequing and savings accounts.

The stated goal of this change is to give Canadians all the information they need to pick the banking option that’s best for them and avoid unnecessary fees.

The government also says it will launch consultations on legislative changes aimed at focusing credit card payments at the portion of a balance with the highest interest rate. The document says this practice is already in place in Quebec.

The goal of this proposed change is to ensure payments go first to loans with the highest interest rates to help customers pay down credit card debt faster.

The taxman comes for everyone eventually — starting in 2028, he’ll be checking in with most Canadians about two weeks later.

The budget proposes setting a single tax deadline of May 15 for filing 2027 returns. This would move the deadline from April 30 for most people, and from June 15 for self-employed people.

stories.title: Federal budget extends foreign buyer ban on existing residential properties until 2029
stories.summary: Ban that was set to expire in January of next year will now exempt new properties
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – The federal budget announced the extension of the foreign buyer ban on existing residential properties until Jan. 1, 2029, but will now exempt new construction properties.

The foreign buyer ban first enacted on Jan. 1, 2023, by former finance minister Chrystia Freeland, prohibits non-Canadians from purchasing residential properties such as houses or condos with three or fewer units.

It was extended in 2024 and was on track to expire in January of next year. Originally, the ban was put in place to tackle the run-up in housing prices in 2022.

“This would help protect housing affordability by keeping the vast majority of the market available for Canadians, while unlocking additional investment in new housing supply,” the budget document said.

“We will continue to support a range of policy measures, such as those levied by other levels of government, which address housing market pressures, including speculation,” it added.

The change to exempt new builds from the ban is in line with what some policymakers were asking for, given how much the housing market has changed since peak prices in 2021-2022. The exemption is also in line with the policy in Australia, which limited its ban to established dwellings.

“The reason why we did that is that we look at other jurisdiction(s), including Australia, but mainly in Canada, is that we realize that yes, we have federal rules, but in many respects, municipalities and provinces have been acting already,” said Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, during a press conference on Thursday.

“We just said, you know, we’ll amend our part of the equation to allow foreign buyers to buy new homes, and we’ll let you (municipalities and provinces) regulate the rest of the market,” he added. “And I think we’ve seen that’s what they did in Australia, and it seems to be a better way to do it.”

The budget references the Bank of Canada’s housing affordability index, which showed the share of household income needed to cover housing costs has fallen by roughly one quarter since the pandemic.

Despite improvement in housing market conditions, new home construction is expected to not keep pace with demand. New housing starts have fallen from 271,198 units in 2021 to 259,028 units in 2025.

A recent report by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (Cmhc) estimates an annual supply gap of 187,000 to 238,000 homes to restore pre-pandemic affordability levels by 2026.

“Canada still needs roughly twice as much housing construction as is currently projected to improve affordability over the next decade,” the report said.

Build Canada Homes, the federal government’s new crown corporation in charge of increasing the non-market housing stock, has faced criticism from the opposition for barely putting a dent in that gap.

One budget measure is to provide $100 million over three years in partnership with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities to speed up housing permitting processes, by supporting municipal e-permitting and the adoption of artificial intelligence.

So far, Build Canada Homes has committed to supporting the construction of 19,000 affordable units, but only about 2,000 have begun construction.

Starting in 2027-2028, Budget 2026 pledges $13 billion in additional funding to Build Canada Homes over 10 years, to build affordable housing.

Other housing measures in the budget include a pledge to end homelessness in 10 years, by promising $11.2 billion starting in 2027-2028 over four years on several measures, in partnership with the provinces and municipalities. The budget pledges this annual funding will go up to $17.8 billion in future years.

These measures include $1.8 billion over four years to establish a new “Integrated Supports Fund” that would support projects that bring housing, health, mental health and social support together.

An additional $3.6 billion over four years will go towards funding supportive and transitional housing, with federal funding providing the capital costs and provincial and territorial governments expected to provide health, job and training services. Build Canada Homes will administer the annual federal funding, which is supposed to increase in future years.

The budget also promises to renew the Canada Housing Benefit for 10 years, providing $1.7 billion over three years starting in 2028-2029 and $3.9 billion in future years.

In total, the new investments announced in this year’s federal budget will bring the total capitalization of Build Canada Homes to $45 billion, which includes the initial $13 billion in capitalization the housing agency was allocated in Budget 2025. The federal government said this will put the crown corporation on track to build 200,000 homes in the next 10 years, which equates to 20,000 units per year

Jordan Gowling joined National Post's parliamentary bureau in 2026 after two years as Financial Post's economics reporter on Parliament Hill. She previously worked as a producer at CTV News in Ottawa.

stories.title: Ottawa boosts journalism tax credit by $501M, extends eligibility to broadcasters
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million over five years, with $85 million in ongoing annual funding.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa first said in its spring fiscal update that it would consult Canadians and stakeholders about extending the Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit to broadcasters.

The federal budget tabled today says that measure, as well a move to renew a higher credit rate that was set to expire, will cost $501 million.

It says keeping the 35-per-cent rate in place will provide “greater stability as the sector adapts to a changing media landscape.”

The initiative provides qualifying journalism organizations with a refundable 35-per-cent tax credit on wages for eligible newsroom employees, up to $29,750 per employee.

The government will extend the credit, which previously applied only to original written news content, to the production of audio and audiovisual news.

stories.title: Canada’s military and spy agency are getting spending boosts in Budget 2026
stories.summary: The budget documents said the increased funding would help Csis 'better protect Canadians from terrorism, foreign interference, espionage and other evolving threats.'
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The Liberals have laid out a plan to dramatically boost defence and security spending over the next five years, including committing $451 billion to core defence spending alone while giving the domestic spy agency more money in a bid to help to rely less “on foreign partners.”

While the 2026 budget does not provide a complete breakdown of planned defence spending, it does break out a few details — such as $2.3 billion for the Defence Drone Initiative, a program aimed at acquiring and developing new unmanned aerial systems (UAS) for both the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and the Canadian Coast Guard.

Prime Minister Mark Carney committed to boosting defence spending part of his election platform. For years, Canada lagged behind Nato’s target of spending two per cent of GDP on defence.

The Liberal government announced they had hit that target in 2025, and pledged to reach Nato’s new benchmark of five per cent of GDP by 2035. While Carney’s first budget maintained that promise, it did not break down planned spending.

The budget document also committed $7.6 billion over five years to extend Operation Reassurance, Canada’s largest foreign deployment, which has thousands of CAF personnel stationed on Nato’s eastern flank in Latvia. The budget notes that money will come from existing National Defence resources.

The Nato commitment includes both core defence spending and a category of “security and defence-related funding” — investments on critical infrastructure like highways, civil preparedness, public safety and research.

Taken together, core defence spending and security-related funding are projected to reach 4.1 per cent of GDP in 2030-2031, according to the budget documents, or roughly $700 billion over the five-year planning horizon.

The budget also includes a significant boost for Canada’s domestic spy agency, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis).

The agency will receive $6 billion over 10 years, starting in 2027, and $579.5 million in ongoing funding to “expand its presence and capabilities.”

It’s a significant increase in Csis budget, which came in at roughly $700 million in 2024-25.

The budget documents said the increased funding would help Csis “better protect Canadians from terrorism, foreign interference, espionage and other evolving threats.”

Canada — and Csis — rely on international partners, particularly the U.S., to share vital intelligence about threats to the country. While that’s unlikely to change, the budget document also suggests the bigger budget would also reduce Csis’s “reliance on foreign partners” to do its job.

stories.title: No charges for Winnipeg police officers who handcuffed overdosing suspect
stories.summary: Manitoba's police watchdog opted not to authorize charges against officers after Winnipeg police handcuffed an overdosing suspect who later died in hospital.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Manitoba’s police watchdog did not authorize charges against the Winnipeg police officers who handcuffed an unconscious suspect believed to be overdosing and who later died.

Placing the man in handcuffs was an appropriate action that allowed the officers to administer naloxone, an overdose-reversing drug, according to the final report from the head of the Independent Investigation Unit (IIU) of Manitoba.

“The civilian director declined to designate a subject officer,” said the report, which was authored by IIU civilian director, Bruce M. Sychuk, meaning a specific officer who could not be identified as being responsible for any alleged misconduct.

The five officers who responded to the call were deemed witnesses, along with nine civilians who were at the scene or provided medical care. The IIU also viewed a video that was captured inside a home during the incident, it said

Winnipeg Police Service (WPS) officers received a call about a reported break-and-enter at a home in the 100 block of Burrin Avenue , ON the morning of Apr. 1. Both people inside the home identified the man as the suspect to police, the report said.

A woman who was inside the home told the watchdog that the man entered uninvited through the home’s back door. In response, the other occupant put him in a bear hug, grabbed a knife and called the police, according to the Iiu’s recounting of her story.

During that time, the witness reported that the suspect was “talking gibberish and speaking to dogs and people who were not there. She also noted that (he) was foaming at the mouth area and his eyes were completely dilated,” the report said.

Both of the witnesses who were inside the home attested that police did not apply force to the suspect.

“(One of the witnesses) confirmed that (the suspect) was breathing after he was handcuffed, although his lips were blue,” according to the report.

People who provided medical care to him confirmed to the IIU that no obvious injuries or trauma were sustained, it added.

The man was rushed to St. Boniface Hospital, where he died. A toxicology report shared in the Iiu’s document said that he tested positive for drugs, including cocaine and a benzodiazepine derivative known as nordiazepam.

His autopsy found his cause of death to be acute cocaine toxicity.

stories.summary: Ottawa — The Liberal government says it is providing "unprecedented" support in the new federal budget for culture and recreation through $4 billion in funding over five years.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Liberal government says it is providing “unprecedented” support in the new federal budget for culture and recreation through $4 billion in funding over five years.

“Culture is foundational to a strong, proud and sovereign Canada,” says the budget document tabled Thursday.

The measures include a total of $783.1 million on a cash basis over five years for Canadian museums.

The budget says the money will go to support Canada’s national museums, the National Battlefields Commission, the National Arts Centre and Library and Archives Canada. It is to “help repair and renew aging facilities, protect national collections, and sustain the exhibitions, performances, and services that connect Canadians to our history and culture.”

The budget is also making admission to Canada’s national museums free for those under 25. It will provide $46.3 million over five years, and $11.5 million ongoing, to national museums and the National Battlefields Commission.

The National Gallery of Canada will get $60 million over four years on a cash basis for travelling exhibitions and improving digital access to its collections. The budget said this will help “Canadians across the country, including those in rural, northern, and remote communities, engage with Canadian and Indigenous art.”

The document also outlines $1.5 billion over nine years to construct and rehabilitate community recreational facilities and ice rinks across the country. The budget says the money “will help extend the life of aging facilities.”

The budget promises $300 million in new funding for CBC/Radio-Canada, which it says will allow the public broadcaster “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”

The funding effectively extends a $150 million increase included in last year’s federal budget.

The government is also renewing the Canada Strong Pass, which offers discounts on Via Rail travel and admission to museums and national parks, for another summer.

Other measures include $32.2 million over four years for a free national digital collection of books by Canadian authors.

“Launching with at least 200 titles in 2027-28, the collection will grow to more than 2,000 titles, with capacity for up to 2 million loans annually by 2031-32,” the budget document says.

The government also plans to consult on a new tax credit for artists. It says the tax credit, combined with the basic personal amount, will “provide tax recognition on up to $45,000 of annual qualifying net business income derived from original and creative artistic works.”

But the budget only includes one year of a promised $600 million in annual funding for Canadian content. The money was meant to replace financial contributions from streamers previously mandated by the Crtc.

The Canadian Media Producers Association said the funding would “serve as an essential bridge while the government works to deliver new policy directions for the Online Streaming Act.”

In June, the government said it would direct the Crtc to review its decision to require streamers to pay 15 per cent of their annual Canadian revenues to funds devoted to producing Canadian content. The government said it would instead provide funding directly to Canadian content producers and give the Crtc a new policy direction on how to implement the Online Streaming Act.

“In particular, we welcome the expedited timeline that will see these funds distributed within the current fiscal year. This will enable a number of ‘shovel-ready projects’ to go to camera in the coming months and for great Canadian stories to reach audiences across the country and around the world,” Reynolds Mastin, president of the media producers association, said in a statement.

The Association québécoise de la production médiatique said in a press release that it was happy the government followed through on its commitment, but that it had concerns about the lack of details about how the money would be distributed.

The budget will also provide $225 million in new funding next year for Canada’s 160 th anniversary, with the money going to a variety of uses, including Heritage Minutes.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press
