November 5, 2026 at 4:08 p.m.

Ottawa – Liberals are proposing to transition up to 200,000 temporary residents to permanent residency by the end of next year as the government ends its immigration level cuts.

On Thursday, the Liberals released a broad overview of the immigration levels for 2027 to 2029 in the 2026 budget.

Liberal Immigration Minister Lena Diab is expected to table the full annual immigration levels plan in Parliament soon, though she is already days behind the legally mandated Nov. 1 tabling date.

Despite some signals from the Liberals that immigration levels could increase after two years of cuts, the brief summary of their plan in the budget shows expected intake levels will plateau for the next three years.

In the budget, the government says it aims to let in 370,000 new temporary residents and 380,000 new permanent residents annually until 2029. Those are the same numbers announced in last year’s budget for 2026.

“Since assuming office 20 months ago, we have taken back control of immigration,” reads the Liberals’ budget, which says that the new levels are meant to “stabilize” the intake of newcomers to “sustainable levels.”

New Canadians take part in a Canada Day citizenship ceremony in Calgary on July 1, 2026. Gavin Young / Postmedia

But it also promises to allow up to 200,000 existing “longstanding” temporary residents to apply for permanent residency by the end of next year. Those new permanent residents would not count against the annual immigration levels.

The budget is sparse on details as to how that will happen and which stream of temporary residents will be allowed to apply for permanent residency. It only notes that 100,000 temporary foreign workers will be able to make the switch through certain provincial-nomination programs.

The aim is to recognize “the important role of temporary foreign workers in supporting growth, especially in rural and remote communities, offering a fast track to permanent residency for many temporary workers who are already working in Canada and contributing to their communities,” reads the budget.

The plan in the budget contains a significant omission: it does not detail how many of the temporary residents will be international student visas versus temporary foreign workers.

The budget promises to reform the Temporary Foreign Worker Program “to better align with regional labour market needs,” but does not explain how.

Immigration has been a hot button issue for years in Canada after intake rates reached record-high levels under former prime minister Justin Trudeau. The Liberals have aimed to cut levels for two successive years.

In an interview with the New York Times in September, Prime Minister Mark Carney signalled that he’s thinking about when to begin a “controlled increase” in immigration levels.

Numbers had reached historic highs under Trudeau, who began slashing the levels in his last year in office due to high inflation and serious pressures on the housing market.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne meet before tabling the federal budget on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Nov. 5, 2026. Blair Gable / Postmedia

Carney’s comments sparked significant controversy in Canada, with Conservatives as well as various provincial premiers denouncing a potential uptick in immigrants just as the system was stabilizing.

“Let me be perfectly clear — the Conservative Party of Canada will vigorously oppose any efforts by Prime Minister Carney and his Liberal government to increase immigration,” Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel-Garner said in a statement in response to the New York Times article.

“We will also continue to press for major decreases of immigration levels. We expect immigration levels to be set much, much lower in the upcoming immigration levels report.”

stories.title: Budget 2026 highlights: Tax support for artists, entrepreneurs and billions for new housing
stories.summary: Fiscal plan also includes significant infrastructure funding for Indigenous communities
stories.author: Jason Kirby, Dexter McMillan
stories.content:
The federal government has plenty of additional cash rolling in. Over the next five fiscal years, including the current 2026-27 period, government revenues will be on average $23.9-billion higher annually than projected in the spring.

Ottawa has loads of extra headroom to increase spending – which it is, according to proposals in Thursday’s budget.

Over the five-year horizon, net new spending will amount to $151.5-billion, spread across a variety of initiatives, from boosting housing supply to bulking up cultural sovereignty . With that in mind, here are 10 key takeaways from the budget .

A big question ahead of the budget was how the Carney government would balance its ambitious investment agenda against fiscal constraints. The answer is a deficit that looks better than it did in the spring, but declines more slowly than many fiscal hawks would like.

The deficit for the 2026-27 fiscal year amounts to $62.3-billion, roughly in line with private-sector expectations. The government said the deficit will shrink slightly in the coming years, reaching $52.9-billion by 2030-31.

The Liberal government is arguing that tax changes, cultural supports and billions of dollars aimed at stoking investment in Budget 2026 will give Canada the freedom to shape its own…

The government said this would allow it to meet its fiscal anchors of balancing day-to-day operating spending with revenue a year ahead of its earlier 2027-28 target, while continuing to reduce the deficit as a share of the economy in the coming years.

However, last month Canada’s budget watchdog, Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan, said she was skeptical Ottawa can meet that second target, and forecast annual deficits that are cumulatively $44.7-billion larger than Ottawa’s over the next five years.

To meet its budget shortfalls, the Carney government will continue to pile on debt in the coming years, though it insists it is doing so responsibly.

The federal debt is slated to hit $1.36-trillion in the 2026-27 fiscal year, which amounts to 39.9 per cent of gross domestic product, down slightly from 40.2 per cent last fiscal year. By 2030-31, the debt load is projected to grow by $227-billion, though as a share of the economy it is expected to remain at around 40.1 per cent.

There’s still much that could go wrong with that outlook, depending on Canada’s growth trajectory and borrowing costs, which have been on the rise this year. Yet under what the budget describes as the “global supply disruptions scenario” – in other words, more war, more political tensions – the government still projects debt-to-GDP will be only a notch higher by 2030-2031, at 40.5 per cent.

With a sunnier outlook for the economy baked into the budget’s fiscal assumptions, the federal government has in turn boosted new spending by $150-billion since the spring economic update. Several buckets of new money stand out.

Long-term funding for infrastructure in Indigenous communities is a headline here. Thursday’s budget announced $18.5-billion over 10 years in new funding for on-reserve infrastructure: everything from roads and bridges to health care facilities, plus further funding for water and wastewater infrastructure. It also earmarks $11-billion over 10 years to maintain nearly 120,000 existing housing units and build 6,900 new homes.

Housing, more broadly, is a focus of Thursday’s budget as well. Toward a goal of ending homelessness in the next 10 years, the government is earmarking $11.2-billion over the next four years, and $17.8-billion in years after that. This funding will support housing that integrates health care and mental health supports, and the construction of new transitional housing. It also bolsters rental assistance for vulnerable people and mental health support for homeless veterans.

The federal government has also announced a host of new measures under its Powering Canada Strong action plan, which amounts to $8.7-billion over four years starting in fiscal 2027-28. That includes extending the clean technology and clean energy investment tax credits to 2040, while expanding eligibility to high-voltage intraprovincial transmission lines. The budget said the government would also provide $4-billion over 10 years to support electricity infrastructure expansion and renewable energy projects.

In a budget document leaning heavily on themes of destiny and self-determination, page one carries a declaration about Ottawa’s view of how housing fits into those goals: “Sovereignty begins chez vous, in your home.”

On the dollar side of that equation, Ottawa said it would add $13-billion in new capital over ten years on a cash basis to Build Canada Homes, an agency it launched in September 2025 to accelerate home construction. That would bring its total capital to $45-billion, and the government said the new investment would set the agency “on a path” to build 200,000 new homes across Canada over the next decade.

Ottawa said it would also spend $1.5-billion over four years, starting in 2027-2028, and $387.4-million in subsequent years to ready federal land for new housing projects.

At the same time, the government said it would introduce legislation to extend a ban on foreign residential property purchases to January 1, 2029. The restrictions had been set to expire this coming January.

Earlier this week, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne had touted the budget as being “about entrepreneurs.” Whether business innovators will feel the same way is unclear.

They’ll certainly welcome some measures. The budget announced a new exemption from capital gains of up to $15-million from investments in eligible Canadian companies that have assets of $100-million or less at the time of investment and are Canadian-controlled private corporations.

At the same time, the budget will enhance the small-business rollover, which allows investors in successful companies to defer taxes on capital gains when the proceeds are reinvested in another small or medium-sized Canadian business.

The federal government said it would also further expand the Scientific Research and Experimental Development program, a tax incentive that encourages businesses to conduct R&D within Canada. For instance, the expansion would cover spending on tests and studies needed to meet regulatory requirements as well as costs related to intellectual property protection, measures the budget said would provide $930-million in support over five years, and $235-million a year afterward.

All that said, those hoping for broad-based corporate tax reductions will be disappointed.

While the budget doesn’t include any broad-based personal tax cuts, there are changes that will benefit some families.

Against a backdrop of rising fuel and food costs, the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which replaced the GST/HST tax credit last July, is set to get a boost with a one-time payment in early 2027 to more than 12 million low- and medium-income households. That will be equivalent to a 50-per-cent increase and will provide up to $2,570 for a family of four within one year.

The budget also addresses a long-standing frustration among retirees who have saved for retirement in registered retirement savings plans. Currently, Rrsp holders who turn 71 are required to convert their investments into a registered retirement income fund, or Rrif. The government intends to do away with RRIFs and introduce an “Rrsp-for-life.” The new vehicle will still come with the minimum withdrawal requirements that exist now, but will do away with paperwork.

Ottawa said it will allow surviving spouses or partners to become successor holders of an Rrsp, and make it easier to transfer savings tax free to survivors when an account holder dies.

Meanwhile, the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation will finally ramp up the amount of deposits it insures at banks and in guaranteed investment certificates to $250,000. The insurance limit has been set at $100,000 since 2005 despite years of inflation.

And for chronic late filers, there is some breathing room: the new tax-filing deadline is May 15.

The budget continues a theme from last year with a number of announcements streamlining federal institutions.

Chief among these is a plan to combine Export Development Canada and the Business Development Bank of Canada, citing cost savings and the fact that both Crown corporations have similar goals.

But there are few details on how much the merging of the agencies will cost or what annual savings are expected.

The budget largely maintains progress on the government’s stated goal of bringing public-service employment in line with Canadian population growth, after employment peaked in 2023-24. Federal public service employment has fallen by 10 per cent since an early retirement incentive program was introduced in the 2025 budget.

The budget also intends to roll the Indigenous Loan Guarantee program, which gives Indigenous groups financing to invest in major infrastructure projects in Canada, under the Canadian Investment Bank umbrella.

Whereas immigration has been a hot issue for previous governments, the subject is largely absent from this budget.

The government’s stated priority remains to use immigration to address critical labour shortages and to use temporary foreign workers to support rural and remote growth in particular. It is holding immigration targets stable through 2027-29.

The budget proposes about $150-million over five years to implement reforms to the Temporary Foreign Worker program. These include better aligning the program with regional labour market needs, improving processing time and strengthening employer compliance.

Also announced is a push to transition up to 200,000 temporary residents to permanent resident status by the end of 2027. That represents a sizable increase over last year’s efforts, which converted 160,000 temporary residents.

Last month, the PBO criticized the government for providing few details of how it would reach the new defence spending target of 5 per cent of GDP by 2035, set in June 2025.

Thursday’s budget provides only small answers on some of those concerns.

The Defence Drone Initiative, a drone marketplace launched in July and built to sell Canadian drones, will receive $2.3-billion over five years, starting in 2027-28, to accelerate its efforts.

Currently, Canada is the only country in the G7 without the ability to launch its own rockets, but this budget aims to address that.

Ottawa has earmarked up to $2.7-billion in other defence funding to go toward multiple priority measures, which include jumpstarting Canada’s medium-lift rocket launch capabilities, building off earlier efforts to expand small-lift launch capabilities.

In the wake of the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, the government is also allocating a surprise $25-million over two years to boost support for members of the Canadian Armed Forces and their families .

The budget includes a smattering of other pockets of funding.

The government will renew the Canada Strong Pass for another year, providing free or discounted access to national parks, museums, galleries and rail travel. It cited a 13-per-cent increase in visits to Parks Canada sites, and a 15-per-cent increase at national museums.

It’s early, but the government has announced its intentions to consult on a Canada Creative Credit, which will offer a tax break for creative output. More details are expected in the spring economic update in 2027.

Electric-vehicle infrastructure is getting a shot in the arm, with new funding of $587-million over five years to install more than 55,000 more charging stations on top of the approximately 50,000 stations that already exist across Canada.

And if you’re sending mail any time soon, you May want to stock up on stamps: Thursday’s budget announced the price of a standard stamp will jump to $2 in 2027 (from the current $1.44), then increase continually by 7 per cent a year, bringing it in line with Oecd peers.

Coming right on the heels of wildfire season, the government has earmarked up to $2.5-billion in financing to increase water bomber production in Alberta.

And for book lovers, the budget includes $32.2-million over four years, plus $9.5-million annually after that, to establish a free national digital collection of books. The collection will launch with at least 200 titles and expand in future years.

stories.title: Carney’s ‘ambitious’ but ‘risky’ budget eyes investment in uncertain world
stories.summary: The budget comes just two days after the U.S. midterm elections that saw voters deliver a stark rebuke to the administration south of the border over the soaring cost of living.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The Liberal government is significantly boosting federal spending in an attempt to draw in business investment and address the affordability struggles of Canadians just days after Prime Minister Mark Carney said that the world is becoming “more dangerous and divided.”

It’s a document experts say is both “ambitious” and “risky” amid significant global unknowns and volatility that has left consumers struggling with the soaring cost of just about everything.

Carney’s sophomore budget commits an additional $151 billion over five years in “supports” for Canadian households, businesses and other levels of government.

That money is entirely taken from better-than-expected government fiscal projections, both higher than expected revenues and tightened government operational spending, which gave Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne $158 billion to play with the planning horizon.

The decision to use the windfall for spending gave the government room to take some big fiscal swings while keeping the deficits relatively stable at $62.3 billion in 2026-27 and declining over the five-year spending plan.

“With solid revenue growth, and (a) shift towards capital investment and clear strategies, we are in a position to transform our economy towards stronger growth and productivity,” Champagne said in his budget speech Thursday.

“Economic growth gives us the means. Our plan is to turn that growth into greater opportunity, greater security, and a better life for all.”

Champagne is selling the budget as built around three broad pillars: boosting business investment, addressing the affordability crunch, and defending Canadian sovereignty while celebrating shared heritage.

To attract private sector investment, the government is strategy is centered on a productivity “mega deduction,” which allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of new investments, the Canada Growth Incentive to encourage entrepreneurs to reinvest capital gains into new businesses, and billions toward research and development.

Taken together, the government is calling these an “investment supercycle.” The hope is to both boost Canadian business investment while attracting $1 trillion in foreign direct investment over the coming years.

Jimmy Jean, the chief economist with the Desjardins Group, characterized the budget as “risky” but said it’s clear that the government is leaning heavily into the push to drum up investment and grow the economy.

“Really they’re going all in on this. So very ambitious,” said Jean.

“But if they don’t execute, then, it means that our debt metrics will have considerably deteriorated and it will be up to a workforce that is aging to support all of that into the future … There’s a lot at stake in terms of the execution part of it.”

Taken together, the government is spending $67 billion on various initiatives aimed at enticing investment and strengthening the economy.

The budget comes just two days after the U.S. midterm elections that saw voters deliver a stark rebuke to the administration south of the border over the soaring cost of living caused by the war in Iran and the trade war, as well as growing global unrest in India, France, Italy, and multiple European countries over deteriorating public services and prospects for youth.

The budget includes multiple consumer and affordability measures including changes to simplify the tax system for individuals and businesses, multiple new tax credits, raising the limit on consumer savings covered by Cdic insurance from $100,000 to $250,000, making the Canada Strong Pass permanent, making museum admission free for those under 25, allowing the intergenerational farm transfer to be used for nieces and nephews, and enhancing the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, which would boost the benefit by $339 for a single person and up to $679 for a couple with two children.

The government is also boosting the Nutrition North program by $610 million over five years to address astronomical food costs for northern Canadian communities, and making the federal caregiver credit fully refundable.

Still, the amount allocated on affordability measures is comparatively small, Jean says.

“It seems like, affordability is more treated from the lens of what they are provided for: for groceries or for rebates. Certainly, they extend some of that, but they’re not going much further in terms of, addressing some of the still-acute cost of living issues many Canadians are dealing with,” Jean said.

By far the biggest change in this year’s budget is that the government is providing hard figures on their plans to dramatically increase defence spending. After years of lagging behind, Canada hit the Nato target of spending two per cent of GDP on defence this year. Carney has committed to upping that to five per cent of GDP by 2035.

Based on government’s plan Thursday, core defence spending will increase from $75.1 billion in 2026-27 to $99.2 billion in 2030-31 — making defence, along with Old Age Security and debt service charges, among the most significant line items in the federal budget.

While it’s mentioned throughout the document, trade tensions with the U.S. — the single largest political issue of Carney’s prime ministership so far —is not a central focus of the budget document. In fact, the document opens by noting that the economic headwinds created by Donald Trump’s trade war have been largely offset by stronger-than-expected economic performance to start 2026.

But Kevin Page with the Institute for Fiscal Studies and Democracy said the government’s highlighting of its fiscal position does not take tell the full story.

While deficit numbers remain relatively stable over the budget’s planning horizon, Page noted, the federal government’s financial requirements — including loans and investments — is significantly higher. The cost of servicing the federal debt is likewise increasing over the budget’s planning horizon.

That’s going to reduce the federal government’s room to maneuver in future years, Page warned.

“We know finance ministers and cabinet ministers that are looking to fund new initiatives going forward, they’re going to have less and less fiscal room because the fastest (growing) spending component is interest on the public debt,” Page said in an interview.

In his budget speech, Champagne noted that Canada has seen “what happens around the world when governments lose their fiscal room to manoeuvre.”

“Choices become harder,” Champagne’s speech read.

Speaking to reporters Thursday afternoon, Champagne downplayed concerns over debt servicing costs — noting that things aren’t as bad as in the late 1980s, when the Canadian government was in a fiscal crisis that led to massive cuts to public spending in the early 1990s.

stories.title: Budget 2026: Ottawa bets spending boost will deliver future economic gains
stories.summary: Government reveals major revenue windfall driven by high global oil prices, outlines more than $150-billion in new expenditures
stories.author: Bill Curry, Mark Rendell
stories.content:
The Liberal government is using a federal balance sheet bolstered by stronger-than-expected revenues to pursue a long-term investment agenda, betting that increased borrowing will deliver future economic gains.

Through tax cuts and other business supports, the budget aims to boost private-sector investment and major nation-building projects, including doubling the capacity of Canada’s energy grid.

It also announces tens of billions of dollars for housing, First Nations infrastructure and other social supports, including a one-time top-up to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (Cgeb).

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne’s 2026 budget reveals a major revenue windfall since Ottawa’s spring update, driven largely by soaring global oil prices. The government plans to spend nearly all of it, leaving its bottom line largely unchanged with a deficit of $62.3-billion in 2026-27 and projected annual deficits in the $50-billion to $60-billion range over the next five years.

All told, the federal budget outlines $151.5-billion in new spending over five years compared with the spring economic update. That is more than offset by a $158.3-billion improvement in the government’s revenue and expense forecasts.

The budget is the second delivered since Mark Carney became Prime Minister. It adds details to his major policy priorities, including plans to use Crown corporations and federal investment funds to “catalyze an investment supercycle.”

The government says economic growth could improve if its investment plans deliver as hoped. But the annual cost of servicing a growing debt load is projected to climb to $85.5-billion by 2030-31 from $60.2-billion this year, a trend that the Parliamentary Budget Officer has flagged as a concern.

In his speech to the House of Commons, Mr. Champagne portrayed the budget as a comprehensive response to global uncertainty driven by international conflicts and trade tensions with the United States.

“In the face of adversity, we’re seizing opportunities and working together to rebuild stronger,” he said in French. “I sincerely believe that in a few years, Canadians will see this moment as another turning point in our history.”

The Liberal government is arguing that tax changes, cultural supports and billions of dollars aimed at stoking investment in Budget 2026 will give Canada the freedom to shape its own…

Ottawa benefited from a stronger economic starting point than projected in the spring economic update, as well as a slightly improved growth outlook.

This time last year, economic growth was flatlining, and many economists expected Canada’s tariff-battered economy to fall into recession. Growth picked up through the middle of this year, while a surge in global oil prices, driven by the war in the Middle East, boosted Canada’s nominal GDP – the largest measure of the country’s tax base.

With that stronger baseline, the budget projects $23.9-billion more in annual revenues on average over the next five years than the spring update, with more money coming into federal coffers from corporate and personal income taxes as well as goods and services taxes.

It also trimmed its outlook for direct program expenses by an average of $12.4-billion per year over the forecast horizon, as a result of ongoing efforts to shrink the size of the civil service and find other efficiencies.

The projected federal debt-to-GDP ratio was revised down by almost about 1.5 percentage points over the forecast horizon compared with the spring update. It remains essentially flat at around 40 per cent over the next five years.

The deficit-to-GDP ratio rises to 1.8 per cent this year from 1.2 per cent last year, which is at odds with the government’s pledge to maintain a declining ratio. It then falls gradually to 1.3 per cent over the following five years.

Ottawa says it has met its other fiscal anchor – balancing the operating budget so that all borrowing is for capital spending – one year ahead of schedule. The government says the plan “keeps us on track to meet both fiscal anchors.”

Desjardins chief economist Jimmy Jean and deputy chief economist Randall Bartlett cautioned that a sustainable debt position can’t be taken for granted.

“With little fiscal room left, a continued climb in long-term interest rates, re-escalation in the trade war or some other negative external shock could put the federal debt-to-GDP ratio on an unsustainable path,” they wrote in a note to clients.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre dismissed the government’s plan as a “credit card budget,” saying it will worsen inflation and the cost of living.

“The minister would have more aptly named this budget ‘Mastered by Debt,’ ” Mr. Poilievre said, a reference to the budget’s title, Masters of Our Destiny.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet said the budget was designed to put Quebec’s new Parti Québécois government in a tough spot by completely ignoring the province’s priorities on housing, health and seniors. NDP Leader Avi Lewis described it as a “Christmas came early for the billionaires” budget, saying the focus on corporate incentives does not help with the cost of living.

The budget also briefly references more than 50 legislative changes tied to the budget, which will likely be introduced through one or more omnibus budget bills.

The budget continues the Carney government’s push to boost business investment, expand infrastructure and attract foreign capital.

The biggest-ticket item is the $36-billion “Productivity Mega Deduction,” announced in September, which allows companies to write off the cost of capital investments upfront.

Ottawa also announced what it called the “Canada Growth Incentive,” aimed at encouraging successful entrepreneurs to reinvest in new businesses. The two-part measure lets entrepreneurs avoid paying taxes on up to $15-million in capital gains when they sell an eligible business, and to defer capital-gains taxes if the proceeds are reinvested in another small or medium-sized Canadian business.

There were changes to the Scientific Research and Experimental Development tax credit aimed at supporting the commercialization of Canadian intellectual property. And there were a number of simplification measures aimed at making the business tax system less cumbersome.

“Some of the changes are more important or less important than others, but as a package, I think it’s constructive and productive,” said Brian Ernewein, senior tax adviser at Kpmg Canada. “It’s not tax reform, and there’s been a number in the business and tax community who have been looking for that…But it’s still good news.”

Ottawa plans to merge Export Development Canada and the Business Development Bank of Canada, two Crown corporations that support businesses and invest alongside the private sector. It will also create a standalone Crown corporation to house its new sovereign wealth fund, the Canada Strong Fund.

The budget commits $8.7-billion over five years to measures aimed at expanding Canada’s electrical grid, and $3.1-billion for the construction of the Mackenzie Valley Highway in the Northwest Territories.

It also books $11.5-billion over five years to support industries and workers affected by the trade war, though most of these measures had been announced ahead of the budget. And it announced $2.2-billion worth of additional supports for the forestry sector over five years and extended mining exploration tax credits.

“Building a stronger, more independent economy will deliver lasting benefits to all Canadians, but these structural gains will take time to be fully realized,” Mr. Carney and Mr. Champagne wrote in a joint budget cover letter. “That’s why we are helping families facing affordability pressures with a boost today and bridge to tomorrow.”

The heart of the affordability package is another one-time top-up to the Cgeb, previously known as the GST/HST credit, as well as funding for housing and First Nations infrastructure.

Policy analysts widely view the Cgeb as an efficient way to deliver income support because it is based on reported income and paid directly to recipients.

In January, Ottawa announced a 25-per-cent increase to the benefit for five years and approved a one-time payment issued in June. The budget adds a top-up, to be issued in early 2027.

The budget also commits $45-billion over 10 years to housing programs, including a pledge to end homelessness within a decade. The government estimates that 65,000 Canadians are homeless. Federal efforts will begin by focusing on permanent housing for the more than 2,000 people who are homeless in Winnipeg.

Ottawa will work with other levels of government and private partners to support mental health and addictions programs, as well as add transitional and supportive homes.

New spending on First Nations issues includes $32-billion over 10 years for housing and infrastructure.

The budget also announces enhancements to the Canada Caregiver Credit and the Build Canada Workers Benefit, both of which provide income support.

The budget pledges $4-billion over five years to support Canadian culture, describing “cultural sovereignty” as a pillar of national sovereignty.

The funding includes money to repair aging infrastructure and improve collections at national museums and galleries, with the aim of expanding access.

The budget makes admission to national museums permanently free for people under 25 and proposes a national digital library.

The budget’s update to the Immigration Levels Plan leaves Ottawa’s targets essentially unchanged: 370,000 new temporary resident arrivals and 380,000 permanent resident admissions in each of 2027, 2028 and 2029.

Scotiabank economist Rebekah Young said one risk for the government is that if its investment plans take off, it could create bottlenecks and labour shortages.

“We could have an economy that is, if not overheating, that’s at maximum capacity,” she said in an interview.

On defence, the budget sets out year-by-year plans to meet Canada’s Nato commitments through 2030-31.

“At a time when the world is more dangerous and divided, Canada is rebuilding its Armed Forces,” Mr. Champagne told the House of Commons, according to his prepared remarks.

The budget offers little new funding or policy for artificial intelligence. It accounts for the $2.0-billion Ottawa has already pledged to its updated national AI strategy, released in June, which includes financing, technology literacy and safety programs.

Ottawa does, however, promise financial guarantees to developers of AI infrastructure, using its balance sheet to expand the domestic supply of processing power needed to train and run AI models and applications.

Although Mr. Champagne promoted the budget earlier this week as one that would benefit small business, it leaves some of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business’s main requests unaddressed.

Cfib president Dan Kelly had urged the government to introduce an across-the-board tax cut for small business.

“There’s lots of talk of mega projects, but right now I feel mega disappointed,” he said in an interview.

He said the vast majority of his members won’t benefit from the investment credits announced in the budget. “This May provide some incentives for new investments in businesses, and that’s good for the long term. But in terms of short-term relief or a light at the end of the tunnel, I don’t see it.”

With reports from Stephanie Levitz, Murad Hemmadi and Aya Dufour

stories.title: Final vote count set to begin in B.C. provincial elections
stories.summary: Mail-in, absentee and assisted phone ballots could determine a handful of tight races
stories.author: Chuck Chiang
stories.content:
It May be almost two weeks since British Columbia ’s election resulted in a landslide win for the B.C. Conservatives, but it’s still a tense time for a handful of candidates.

New Democrat legislator Stephanie Higginson will be among those watching closely as the final count of mail-in and other ballots begins Friday.

“I feel like a bag of nerves,” Higginson said from her riding of Ladysmith-Oceanside, where the preliminary tally gave her a 13-vote lead over Conservative candidate Kris McNichol.

Elections BC said there are about 150,000 mail-in ballots to tally, in addition to absentee and assisted phone ballots that will be included in the final count.

It did not provide a breakdown of how many of those ballots are in each of B.C.’s 93 ridings.

But four ridings had leading margins of fewer than 200 votes.

Elections BC said Thursday that the uncounted ballots are contained in certification envelopes.

It said final results will be posted no later than Tuesday.

“Before being counted, certification envelopes are checked against the voters’ list to make sure the voter is eligible and that they only voted once. This process is important for election integrity,” it said.

Elections BC will conduct separate recounts in Ladysmith-Oceanside and Burnaby-South Metrotown because the current margin is fewer than 100 votes.

Burnaby-South Metrotown incumbent Paul Choi leads Conservative David Xie by 66 votes.

In Cowichan Valley and Kelowna Centre, Conservative candidates Bert Chen and Kristina Loewen hold leads of 151 votes and 132 votes, respectively.

The final count won’t change the fact that the B.C. Conservatives, led by Lorne Doerkson, will take power with a huge majority, having won about two-thirds of the seats.

But the fate of candidates such as Higginson still hangs in the balance.

“I feel like at the end of this process, no matter what happens, for me personally I will have my family and my home and my health, and that’s a lot more than most people right now,” she said. “So I remain grateful for that.

“Having said that, I’m also not a very patient person, so this has been a personal growth opportunity, I’m calling it,” Higginson added with a laugh.

“It’s completely out of my control.”

Chen in Cowichan Valley took part in “MLA School” in Victoria this week, described by the B.C. Legislative Assembly as a way to prepare new legislators for their new responsibilities.

Chen said he will join his scrutineers in witnessing the final count in Duncan, B.C., but isn’t particularly nervous about the results.

“It really is just business as usual,” he said.

He said that attending MLA school and “just soaking up all the information” is “good general information to have, whether I do win a final count or not.”

Chen said he and his party trust the process.

“Elections BC is very confident in all of this,” he said.

“Of course, we understand that they had very compressed timelines (leading up to the election), so that’s why on the tail end, if you’re waiting for a (candidate) certification, it takes a bit longer. But we fully trust the process.”

Higginson said more seats for her Opposition party would allow it to better defend the Ndp’s record in government.

“Democracy is messy, and this is one of those parts of it,” she said. “Elections are tough, and I have a deep understanding and respect for the work that Elections BC does, that our local elections officers are doing.”

“There isn’t really anything that can prepare you for this, but I am trying very hard to keep it all in perspective and remain grounded.”

stories.title: ‘Downtown is the heart of London!’: Businesses sign off on BIA plan to keep the core safe, clean and promoted
stories.summary: A four-year path forward has been unveiled to members of the Downtown London Business Association (BIA).
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A four-year path forward has been unveiled to members of the Downtown London Business Association (BIA). The document acknowledges the societal and economic challenges facing the core, but also touts new businesses, new residents, and changing attitudes. “Downtown is the heart of London!” said Brahm Wiseman, the operator of Heroes Comics, to applause.

“Let’s keep it that way!” That proclamation came just moments after the BIA outlined its vision of a welcoming, thriving, compelling and collaborative downtown. The document points to successes, including more people living downtown and a rising number of events. BIA interim executive director, Vicki Smith told CTV News that small businesses in the city are noticing.

“We’ve had more businesses come in (the downtown) than close, so that’s positive.” But while many Londoners have embraced downtown, the BIA acknowledges some still shy away. “There’s lots of people who do love being down here. We just have to show everyone else all the great things that are available,” said Smith The BIA continues to commit a large portion of members’ fees towards keeping the downtown beautiful and to assist in repairs caused by vandalism.

Mayor Josh Morgan acknowledged the struggle with homelessness, housing and addiction in the core, but in the same breath contended affordable housing partnerships are making a difference. “We know how to move people off the streets, out of doorways, out of municipal parks into different types of housing.

The problem is we cannot keep up with the number of people falling into homelessness,” the mayor said to attendees gathered at Museum London. Still the owner of several restaurants in the core, including Joe Kool’s, stated the economy is a bigger concern. Mike Smith states taxes at all levels of government along with the downturn are combining to hurt the core.

“These are lean times economically for everybody. I’ve talked to all kinds of different businesses. That’s why it is more important than ever to support each other.” Smith, who was awarded by his peers at the event, later called on Londoners to keep their money at home. “I think it’s important to support local businesses.

Yes, obviously, the greatest concentration is downtown, but local businesses around the city as well.” Vicki Smith stated that kind of support would lead to fewer vacancies. “So, if we could fill those buildings with either residents or businesses, or a mix of both, as both are important, that would be great.”

stories.title: Western wins grant to co-create Canada’s first university Indigenous Community Research Circle
stories.summary: Western proposal for Canada's first university Indigenous Community Research Circle wins Robbins-Ollivier Award for Excellence in Equity
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
A Western University team has received the Robbins-Ollivier Award for Excellence in Equity, a $100,000 federal grant to improve equity and break down systemic barriers in postsecondary research. The project proposes to create Canada’s first university Indigenous Community Research Circle (the Circle), a new framework guiding how Western engages with the priorities of Indigenous communities.

Canada’s three federal research funding agencies jointly offer the award to help faculty members lead “bold and potentially game-changing initiatives.” The Circle, co-created by four Indigenous faculty and staff, and one allied faculty member, aims to empower Indigenous communities to set their own research priorities and help the university build reconciliation through research.

The team includes Katie Big-Canoe, Indigenous research specialist (Western Research); Desmond Moser, Earth sciences professor and assistant dean (decolonization); Chantelle Richmond, Canada Research Chair in Indigenous Health and the Environment, and professor in the department of geography and environment and in the Indigenous studies program; Christy R. Bressette, vice-provost and associate vice-president (Indigenous Initiatives); and Clinton Jacobs, the Faculty of Science’s Indigenous senior advisor on science objectives, and instructor in Indigenous studies and Earth sciences.

“This initiative is transformative because it will fundamentally change the way Western, as an institution, supports Indigenous research engagement and how it is operationalized within our research ecosystem,” said Big-Canoe.

This new project addresses two significant concerns: the increasing volume of fragmented requests to communities for consultation or partnership and the lack of pathways for researchers to respectfully engage with Indigenous communities and organizations. These result in “unsustainable burdens” on Indigenous communities, Big-Canoe said.

The Circle, which will include representatives from local First Nations, Métis and other Indigenous organizations, would give researchers a single platform for engagement and let Indigenous members identify areas of potential partnership that centre Indigenous priorities.

“With the award, we can now start contacting communities to co-develop the best path and process by which they can identify research priorities and receive proposals from researchers,” Big-Canoe said.

### “This will bring together academic Indigenous and allied leaders, scholars and staff to elevate Indigenous community research priorities.” – Katie Big-Canoe, Indigenous research specialist, Western Research

The project team plans to consult and co-create the Circle with local Indigenous communities over the next year before they begin shaping the Circle’s work together.

“The Circle will create a sustainable, ethical process for Indigenous communities to share their priorities with Western and to choose their partnerships,” said Penny Pexman, Western’s vice-president (research). “It will result in more relevant research that fosters long-term reciprocal relationships.”

The Robbins-Ollivier Award, granted to just three projects nationally each year, makes the future implementation of this project possible. The Circle is the second Robbins-Ollivier Award that Western has received in the last three years. It recognizes faculty members who invest their time, expertise and experiences into improving equity within their universities and broader research communities.

In 2023, Godwin Arku, now associate dean, graduate studies, in the Faculty of Social Science and a professor in the department of geography and environment, was awarded the grant for his project aimed at creating more belonging and opportunities for Black students and youth. It was inspired by a public forum where parents voiced concerns ranging from discrimination in workplaces to mental health challenges and interactions with police. Arku’s project shares a goal with Moser’s – to build new bridges between Western and communities.

These projects advance Western’s strategic plan for equity, diversity, inclusion, decolonization and accessibility (Edida), launched in 2024, to guide that work across campus. The university’s commitment to reconciliation is outlined in its strategic plan, Towards Western at 150. The Circle is expected to put those commitments into practice and improve the process for future engagement with Indigenous communities.

“We’re excited about the new connections that will be forged between Western and the Indigenous community, and the future research informed through the Circle,” Moser said. “It’s also important to our team to share what we’ve learned with other communities and institutions. We want to support reconciliation through research, both locally and across the country.”

Learn more about how Western is navigating new realities.

stories.title: Police escort B.C. students to school after bear attack
stories.summary: Nuxalk Nation held a drum circle to honour Jenny Balcarras and Selah Reed, whose bodies were found earlier this week
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois
stories.content:
The Nuxalk Nation in Bella Coola, B.C., said additional Mounties have been brought into the region to escort students to school after a fatal bear attack killed a mother and daughter in the community.

It said in a social media post that police would also be conducting more night patrols in the area and offering rides home for youth who are out at night.

The nation held a drum circle on Wednesday to honour school art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her adult daughter, Selah Reed, whose bodies were found near a set of trails earlier this week.

“We are in a time of layered tragedy,” elected chief Samuel Schooner said in the post, encouraging members to check in on each other.

“The recent attack has brought up many difficult emotions, including painful memories of experiences that some of us are still trying to come to terms with.”

Bella Coola, about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver, was also the site of an attack by a grizzly on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers last November, leaving an adult and three children badly injured.

The animal involved in that attack was never captured, and the BC Conservation Officer Service has said bear DNA from last year’s attack site would be compared with samples gathered in the wake of the latest attack.

In an update posted to social media on Thursday, the service said conservation officers were working with provincial wildlife biologists, but no animal had been caught.

“Various trapping techniques are being implemented as these efforts continue, with officers being rotated into the community,” it said.

The post said public safety remained a priority and it urged the public to continue to avoid the Snooka West Trail area where the victims were found.

A post to a fundraiser page set up by Mary Melissa Smith, a relative of Balcarras’s, thanked the nation for setting up the drum circle tribute.

She highlighted the work of the RCMP and conservation officers, as well as others in the community who have rallied around the family, providing accommodations, food and a floral tribute to the victims.

“The compassion shown by this community has been extraordinary, and we are forever grateful,” Smith said.

Jenny Balcarras’s brother, Matthew Balcarras, said Wednesday that his older sister had built a new career in mid-life as an art therapist and moved to Bella Coola only a few months ago, working at a local school.

The Central Coast Teachers’ Association said on social media that Balcarras had joined their school community as a counsellor in August, and had devoted “countless hours to connecting with the students she served and worked closely with teachers and other staff supporting their well-being.”

Authorities have imposed a voluntary 8 p.m. curfew in the community, as the search for the animal or animals behind the attack continues.

stories.title: Cadet leader assaulted during poppy campaign faces 'long recovery': Hamilton mayor
stories.summary: Hamilton - The mayor of Hamilton says a cadet leader faces a "long recovery" after a violent attack that police say stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young Remembrance Day poppy sellers.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hamilton - The mayor of Hamilton says a cadet leader faces a “long recovery” after a violent attack that police say stemmed from a confrontation over the harassment of young Remembrance Day poppy sellers.

Outgoing mayor Andrea Horwath says Capt. Kenneth Kunkel was helping young air cadets on Sunday and the community is struggling with the “shocking and violent” attack that left him hospitalized.

The Oct. 17 fire on a military base took four lives and injured 39, with 25 still in hospital as of Nov. 4

A bouquet of flowers is visible at the main entrance to CFB Wainwright on Sunday, Oct. 18, after a mass casualty event occurred at the base on Saturday. (David Bloom/Postmedia Network)

November 5, 2026 at 3:43 p.m.

Almost three weeks have passed since a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta took the lives of four members of the Canadian military and wounded 39 others, 19 of them critically. As investigations into the disaster and convalescence of the wounded continue, so too do efforts to raise money in support of the victims and their famililes.

Support Our Troops (SOT), the official charitable cause of the Canadian Armed Forces since 2007, has a page dedicated to the disaster.

“The CFB Wainwright Support Fund is a dedicated charitable assistance program created to provide immediate financial support to CAF families affected by the recent incident at CFB Wainwright,” it says. “The fund focuses on helping families address unexpected expenses and challenges resulting from injury or loss. “

The program is a collaborative effort involving SOT, the similarly focused organization True Patriot Love, the Canadian Forces Morale and Welfare Services and the Edmonton Military Family Resource Centre, as well as CFB leadership and support personnel.

“Eligible families May receive up to a maximum $10,000 per family during the initial phase of the program,” it notes, adding: “In exceptional circumstances, additional support May be considered on a case-by-case basis.”

Four members of the Third Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were killed in the Oct. 17 disaster. They have been identified as Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark and Sgt. Morgan Wong.

This week, the Department of National Defence released an update on the injured personnel.

“Following careful medical assessment and recommendations from medical professionals, four hospitalized members have been transferred to healthcare facilities closer to their home communities in British Columbia and Ontario, where they can continue receiving the medical care they need while being closer to family and loved ones,” it said in a statement.

It also noted that, “as of November 4, 2026, 14 of the personnel injured in the incident have been released from hospital.” A further 25 remain hospitalized.

“All members and their families will continue to be provided with the full range of CAF supports available, including assigned Designated Assistants who serve as a vital direct liaison for members and their families,” it added.

In the days after the tragedy, scam websites popped up to take advantage of people’s sympathy. They included one discovered by Patricia Farrell, the mother of Shaun Farrell, who said her deceased son’s name and photo were being used in an fake donation page on spotfund.com.

Since then, the real GoFundMe page for Farrell has collected more than $14,000 for the family of the Saskatchewan-born soldier.

“Behind the uniform was a deeply loved son, brother, grandson and friend,” the page says. “Shaun served his country with devotion and lived with integrity, loyalty and care for those around him. His warmth and strength touched the lives of those who knew him. His loss leaves a space that no words can fill.”

Another GoFundMe campaign has been started for Liam Ramage, who suffered third and fourth-degree burns to approximately 40 per cent of his body and needed critical medical care.

“Liam’s dedication, strength, and service are evident to everyone who knows him, but he now faces an extraordinarily long and challenging road to recovery,” the page says.

A GoFundMe page for Trevor Flegel, started by his friend Kyle Germuth, says he was critically injured and suffered severe burns covering approximately 50 per cent of his body. “Trevor is currently receiving medical care in Edmonton (and) has already undergone his first extensive surgery,” it notes.

A donation page for Daniel Thrasher calls him “a kind, courageous and hard working young man who decided to selflessly serve his country.” It has already raised more than its goal of $100,000, and was at $114,000 as of Nov. 5. Other pages include donation efforts for Cpl. Liam Keen and Cpl. Matthew Nystrom.

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

content_blocks.text: The Oct. 17 fire on a military base took four lives and injured 39, with 25 still in hospital as of Nov. 4
A bouquet of flowers is visible at the main entrance to CFB Wainwright on Sunday, Oct. 18, after a mass casualty event occurred at the base on Saturday. (David Bloom/Postmedia Network)
November 5, 2026 at 3:43 p.m.

Almost three weeks have passed since a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta took the lives of four members of the Canadian military and wounded 39 others, 19 of them critically. As investigations into the disaster and convalescence of the wounded continue, so too do efforts to raise money in support of the victims and their famililes.
Support Our Troops (SOT), the official charitable cause of the Canadian Armed Forces since 2007, has a page dedicated to the disaster.

“The CFB Wainwright Support Fund is a dedicated charitable assistance program created to provide immediate financial support to CAF families affected by the recent incident at CFB Wainwright,” it says. “The fund focuses on helping families address unexpected expenses and challenges resulting from injury or loss. “

The program is a collaborative effort involving SOT, the similarly focused organization True Patriot Love, the Canadian Forces Morale and Welfare Services and the Edmonton Military Family Resource Centre, as well as CFB leadership and support personnel.

“Eligible families May receive up to a maximum $10,000 per family during the initial phase of the program,” it notes, adding: “In exceptional circumstances, additional support May be considered on a case-by-case basis.”
Editor’s Picks

Four members of the Third Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were killed in the Oct. 17 disaster. They have been identified as Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark and Sgt. Morgan Wong.
This week, the Department of National Defence released an update on the injured personnel.

“Following careful medical assessment and recommendations from medical professionals, four hospitalized members have been transferred to healthcare facilities closer to their home communities in British Columbia and Ontario, where they can continue receiving the medical care they need while being closer to family and loved ones,” it said in a statement.
It also noted that, “as of November 4, 2026, 14 of the personnel injured in the incident have been released from hospital.” A further 25 remain hospitalized.

“All members and their families will continue to be provided with the full range of CAF supports available, including assigned Designated Assistants who serve as a vital direct liaison for members and their families,” it added.

A donation page for Daniel Thrasher calls him “a kind, courageous and hard working young man who decided to selflessly serve his country.” It has already raised more than its goal of $100,000, and was at $114,000 as of Nov. 5. stories.title: Post-secondary students protest Ford government Osap changes, tuition hikes
stories.summary: Thousands of students brandishing signs that state “Hands Off Our Education!” marched across a swath of campuses to draw attention to an “attack on education."
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Students across 15 post-secondary campuses in Ontario walked out Thursday to protest the Ford government’s revoking of students’ Ontario Student Assistance Program (Osap) funding, hikes to tuition fees and allegations of government interference in university and college affairs.

Thousands of students brandishing signs that state “Hands Off Our Education!” and “Hands Off Our Osap!” marched across a swath of campuses, including the University of Toronto and the University of Ottawa, to draw attention to what the Canadian Federation of Students (CFS) is calling an “attack on education” by Premier Doug Ford and his government.

“Education is a right and students are prepared to fight for it,” said Leah St. Germain, an Ocad University student with the CFS Ontario at Queen’s Park Thursday.

“We are the ones consistently bearing the brunt of your failure. And we are going to continue to use every tactic in our playbook to apply pressure,” she said. “We are not stopping until we see a publicly-funded system that leaves no one behind.”

Cyrielle Ngeleka, CFS Ontario chairperson, said in a news release that the Ford government continues to “evade accountability” while schools go underfunded and students are plunged into debt due to the gutting of Osap.

In February, the Ford government announced it would significantly cut student assistance grants due to “unsustainable” costs. Beginning Aug. 1, the proportion of non-repayable grants a student can receive from Osap was reduced from 85 per cent to a 25 per cent maximum, with the rest in loans.

A seven-year freeze on tuition was also lifted, allowing colleges and universities to raise tuition by up to two per cent per year for the next three years.

Many students are reporting they are now deeply burdened by debt due to the massive cuts to Osap grants as economic uncertainty buoyed by tariffs and an unstable geopolitical environment has resulted in rising costs.

The CFS said students are demanding Osap comes in grants, not loans, that interest is removed, that tuition costs are curbed and that the government ends any involvement in admissions, student fees and research security plans.

The protests have sprung up at a moment when the Ford government is facing mounting questions around the province’s freeze of Osap for students attending private career colleges, as the government is investigating some schools for alleged fraudulent activity.

Data obtained by the Canadian Press in June found that between the 2023-24 and 2024-25 academic years, the province spent $465 million more on Osap grants, and 95 per cent of that went to private career college students.

The Ford government has said the Osap freeze was necessary as it investigates the alleged fraud. Critics have accused the province of destroying the futures of the private career college students who have a clean record and have had their studies upended without their expected Osap payments.

Changing Osap over to mostly loans was necessary, as the program was “unsustainable,” reaching $4.1 billion per year, Ford told Global News in February.

The Ford government has invested $6.4 billion into the province’s college and universities, said Bianca Giacoboni, a spokesperson for the office of Nolan Quinn, the Minister of Colleges and Universities.

“Students receive top tier education at less cost than comparable post-secondary institutions in the United States,” she said. The previous Osap framework was “no longer sustainable,” and qualified low-income Ontario students are being supported, they said. The government’s “tuition framework,” she said, is “one of the lowest increase rates in the country.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles was quick to stand with students Thursday, stating in a press release that Ford “has spent this year attacking students.”

She said the NDP called on Ford to provide immediate relief to students who need financial help. “He and his government refused,” she said. “Now, the Premier has no choice but to hear their voices.”

stories.title: Children’s Hospital hosts pain awareness carnival to help children living with chronic pain
stories.summary: Carnival games, prizes and activities brought a little fun to Children’s Hospital in London on Thursday, but the event had a much more serious purpose: raising awareness about chronic pain in children.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Carnival games, prizes and activities brought a little fun to Children’s Hospital in London on Thursday, but the event had a much more serious purpose: raising awareness about chronic pain in children.

The Pain Awareness Carnival, held as part of Canadian National Pain Awareness Week, brought together patients, families and hospital staff to highlight the challenges faced by children living with ongoing pain.

London Health Sciences Center says chronic pain affects an estimated one in five children and adolescents. Because pain is not always visible, young patients can struggle to have their experiences understood while dealing with impacts on their sleep, education, activities and family life.

The carnival featured games, prizes and opportunities for children and families to learn more about pain management in an interactive setting.

Di Valentin said families often arrive at the hospital exhausted after trying numerous ways to manage their child’s pain.

The goal is to help children develop tools to manage their pain and return to the activities they enjoy.

“We provide help. We provide hope. We assist them in learning new ways of addressing the pain, providing new strategies, new treatments, both pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies that parents themselves can initiate right away in their home,” Di Valentin said.

Foundation CEO Scott Fortnum said the issue is also personal for him, having experienced the challenges of chronic pain through his son’s journey.

“I’ve lived it with my son. He experiences chronic pain or has and it’s a very difficult thing because it affects them so, so much,” Fortnum said.

He said donor support helps make resources available to children and families who need them.

For patient Logan Pennings, the carnival offered an opportunity to enjoy some activities while connecting with others facing similar challenges.

“It’s fun to have a Carnival to just help patients who are going through lots of pain. It helps cheer us up,” Pennings said.

Organizers say the message extends beyond the carnival: children’s pain should be taken seriously, even when it cannot be seen.

stories.title: Iconic Maple Leaf missing from Iihf-mandated Canada women’s hockey jerseys
stories.summary: Canadian hockey players often speak of their pride in representing the Maple Leaf, but that iconic national symbol will be missing from this year’s world women’s hockey championship. Both Canada and the United States have been mandated by the International Ice Hockey Federation to wear generic jerseys designed by the Iihf and its jersey supplier, […]
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canadian hockey players often speak of their pride in representing the Maple Leaf, but that iconic national symbol will be missing from this year’s world women’s hockey championship.

Both Canada and the United States have been mandated by the International Ice Hockey Federation to wear generic jerseys designed by the Iihf and its jersey supplier, True Hockey, at the tournament, which starts Friday in Denmark.

A photo taken at Thursday’s media day and posted on the Iihf’s Facebook page shows Canada goaltender Kayle Osborne wearing a red jersey with few adornments.

“Canada” appears in white block letters across the chest. The jersey otherwise features a white collar with a red map of Canada in the middle, along with red and black horizontal stripes between two white stripes near the bottom of the sleeves and torso.

The Iihf announced an agreement with True Hockey in a press release last October that stated the company would be the “exclusive supplier of team uniforms and apparel for all Iihf member national associations for all international events” beginning in 2026-27.

Hockey Canada and USA Hockey, meanwhile, have apparel and jersey contracts of their own in place with Bauer and CCM, respectively, and have challenged the Iihf arrangement in a Swiss court.

The absence of the Maple Leaf wasn’t entirely unexpected. A Zurich court rejected Hockey Canada’s bid to temporarily block the Iihf’s deal with True Hockey on Sept. 16.

The court noted the proposed generic jersey did not use any of Hockey Canada’s protected marks. The Maple Leaf appears in 11 of the 12 trademarks cited in the court case and in eight of the organization’s official marks.

The court also noted the Iihf had promised not to use those marks without permission and said Hockey Canada could take part in the design process. The ruling dealt with interim measures and left the broader dispute over commercial rights unresolved.

Iihf bylaws state that it has final approval on jersey designs.

The recently released Hockey Canada jersey designed by Bauer features the national body’s logo — a silhouette of a hockey player skating in front of a red and black Maple Leaf.

Canada starts its tournament Friday against Sweden.

stories.title: Adam Cohen’s tribute concerts to his father are a ‘powerful panacea’ against estate litigation ugliness
stories.summary: Exactly 10 years after Leonard Cohen’s death, his son and grandson will honour the Canadian artist at Toronto’s Meridian Hall
stories.author: Brad Wheeler

A son inherits and wears his dad’s jacket, but it will never truly be his. The same might apply to houses, depending on the father.

Adam Cohen, son of Leonard, is on the phone from Montreal. He says he’s on his first coffee of the day, sitting in the kitchen of the family home. “Your father’s old house?” I ask, meaning the well-known triplex at 28 Rue de Vallières.

Cohen pauses before replying, “It’s in my name now. But it’s always going to be my father’s house.”

He’s in town rehearsing for a short tour of Everybody Knows Leonard Cohen, a tribute concert that arrives at Toronto’s Meridian Hall on Saturday, 10 years to the day after the Hallelujah singer’s death. Performers include Leslie Feist, Rufus Wainwright and Adam’s son, Cassius. “Three generations of Cohens,” he says.

The 54-year-old’s mother is Suzanne Elrod (who is not the subject of the 1967 song Suzanne ). He splits his time between Los Angeles and the Greek island of Hydra, with pitstops in Montreal. It’s familiar circuit in the Cohen family.

There’s a giant mural of Leonard nearby called Tower of Song . It stands some 20 storeys tall and casts one heck of a shadow.

Adam, a singer-songwriter, has four albums to his name, including 2011’s Like a Man , which went gold in Canada. But his last LP was We Go Home , released a dozen years ago. He produced his father’s final two albums: 2016’s You Want It Darker and the posthumous Thanks for the Dance , from 2019.

“I’ve had at best a very modest, unnoteworthy career,” he says. “It was truly an honour to be part of my father’s legacy. Producing You Want It Darker was a pinnacle for me, and the stewardship of my father’s work since then is also the most important stuff that I’ve done.”

The stewardship has been plagued by a legal fight between the family and his father’s music lawyer and manager, Robert Kory. Adam and sister Lorca disputed Kory’s accounting related to the sale of Cohen’s music publishing catalogue in 2012.

This spring, an L.A. judge found Kory did nothing wrong . Kory testified that Adam wanted to diminish his father’s legacy to “create space to get out from under the shadow.”

Cohen’s public actions since his father’s death would seem to contradict Kory’s characterization. He organized a star-studded memorial tribute concert at Montreal’s Bell Centre in 2017. More recently, he put on a free open-air concert in Athens on his father’s birthday. The current tribute tour, which he describes as a “powerful panacea against the backdrop of litigation,” heads to Europe and Australia next year.

Cohen says because the matter is still ongoing, there are things he can’t discuss. “It doesn’t need any more attention,” he says, before quoting from one of his father’s poems: “I will place my paper hat on my concussion and dance.”

When I suggest we switch the line of questioning from the courtroom to the music, Cohen is all for it. “Amen,” he exhales. (Not hallelujah?) He describes his father’s songbook as “jaw-droppingly good music,” and says the concert set list unavoidably includes the expected chestnuts: Suzanne , Bird on the Wire , So Long, Marianne , Dance Me to the End of Love and Hey, That’s No Way to Say Goodbye .

“If you didn’t play them, it would be a travesty. I have my own favourites as well, but those will be a surprise.”

There have been several tribute events surrounding the 10th anniversary of his father’s death. Ballets Jazz Montréal, for one, stages Dance Me – Music by Leonard Cohen in Montreal and Kitchener, Ont., later this month. The piece choreographed by Andonis Foniadakis, Annabelle Lopez Ochoa and Ihsan Rustem was approved by Leonard before he died. Not all Cohen tributes are sanctioned.

“There are elements of jankiness and opportunism,” says the son.

The poster for his own tribute makes it crystal clear the concerts are legitimately presented by the Cohen family. It is an “official licensed event,” stamped with an Estate of Leonard Cohen copyright. It might be the most lawyered concert poster since Pink Floyd toured without co-founder Roger Waters.

“Despite the ugliness and the years and years of litigation around the estate, this is really a moment to celebrate my father and keep his songbook alive,” Cohen says. “And with three generations of Cohens represented, it’s the ultimate act of rebellion.”

stories.title: Outgoing president says he is proud of college of physicians' role as a social actor
stories.summary: Montreal - Mauril Gaudreault is proud of the Quebec college of physicians' shift toward becoming a social actor over his eight-year tenure as president.
stories.author: Katrine Desautels The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Mauril Gaudreault is proud of the Quebec college of physicians’ shift toward becoming a social actor over his eight-year tenure as president.

The outgoing president said the professional association has become much more vocal on certain social issues, which has at times generated a great deal of media coverage.

Gaudreault, 78, made the comments in an interview after completing his second term at the helm of the association.

Over coffee in Montreal, Gaudreault said his key achievements included bringing the association closer to the public, helping to expand the scope of professional practice, and becoming a social advocate.

He was also the first president to undertake an extensive tour of Quebec’s regions to meet with health-care professionals and the public.

His most controversial stance was calling on doctors to stop their pressure tactics while the medical federations were in the midst of negotiations with the government over their compensation.

Many doctors perceived this as political interference by the college in an already heated standoff with Quebec. Some called for his removal, which ultimately did not occur.

Gaudreault did, however, receive a motion of censure passed at an extraordinary general assembly — a first in the history of the association.

“Psychologically, it was a difficult experience for me. It was the hardest period of my presidency,” he said.

Although it caused a stir, he said he has no regrets.

“A professional association exists to protect the public by ensuring high-quality medical care … and in my view — and this is the opinion of many — when the association witnesses actions that could compromise public safety, we have a duty to act, to respond, and to take a clear stand,” he said.

He also believes that this has helped raise awareness of the college’s purpose, one of his key priorities.

In recent years, the college has, among other things, spoken out in favour of phasing out polluting anesthetic gases in health-care facilities and opposed the environmental exemptions granted to the Horne Smelter.

“I’m pretty proud of that. We’ve done the same for other societal issues,” said Gaudreault.

Gaudreault’s presidency was also marked by the COVID-19 pandemic. He said this period accelerated collaboration with other professional associations.

The expansion of professional roles continues to gain momentum today. Specialized nurse practitioners can see patients on their own and pharmacists have greater autonomy in treating various conditions.

Gaudreault said those changes faced some resistance from the medical community, mainly around whether other professionals had the necessary skills to administer this kind of care.

“Once competence has been demonstrated, it is well received,” said Gaudreault.

Nathalie Saad, a pulmonologist, has succeeded Gaudreault, becoming the first female president of the Quebec college.

During her term, she said she plans to focus her efforts on issues surrounding the aging population, primary care and access to health care.

stories.title: First Nation criticizes Holt government for not consulting about lifting fracking ban
stories.summary: Premier Susan Holt's Liberal government is reviewing a long-standing ban on fracking and development of shale gas in the Maritime province.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
A First Nation in New Brunswick says the province should keep its moratorium on shale gas fracking.

Premier Susan Holt’s Liberal government is reviewing a long-standing ban on fracking and development of shale gas in the Maritime province.

But a chief from Wolastoqey Nation in New Brunswick says Holt’s government is failing to honour its commitment to carry out meaningful consultation in partnership with Indigenous communities.

Chief Ross Perley of Neqotkuk, one of the Wolastoqey communities, says the province is prioritizing timelines over genuine Wolastoqey involvement.

Wolastoqey Nation says its negotiators remain dissatisfied with the government’s engagement process.

Perley says that if the province lifts the fracking ban without Indigenous community support, it would not be good for any future partnership.

“Our communities must be consulted on the scope of the review, environmental impacts and potential economic benefits,” Perley said in a statement.

“Proper community consultation includes (taking) the time to ensure that consultation can be meaningful.”

A spokesperson for the provincial government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
