stories.title: Belleville multifaith prayer walk shows solidarity after synagogue attack
stories.summary: After the Sept. 20 shooting at Sons of Jacob Synagogue, many congregations wanted to show solidarity with the Jewish congregation and with police
stories.author: Scott Maniquet
stories.content:
Belleville religious groups, police and citizens on Thursday joined in an interfaith prayer walk to promote peace and unity after September’s attack on the local synagogue.

Belleville police estimated about 150 to 200 people walked from St. Thomas’ Anglican Church, east of downtown, to Robin Jeffrey Park in the east end.

Rev. Brad Beale is St. Thomas’ priest and the Belleville Police Service’s chaplain. He was a lead organizer of the walk, which he said was intended to show gratitude and prayers for police and emergency services, and for harmony, unity, and safety in the community.

“An attack on any community of faith is an attack on us all, and an attack on the very foundations of our community,” Beale told listeners in the park.

Suspect dies after gunfire exchange at Belleville Synagogue: SIU

Rise in antisemitic violence in Canada has police on guard

Injured police officer hailed a hero for actions in synagogue shootout

Belleville police officer, suspect hospitalized after synagogue shooting

After the Sept. 20 shooting at Sons of Jacob Synagogue, he said, many local congregations wanted to hold an event in solidarity with the Jewish congregation and with police, who had defended the Jewish congregation during the attack.

Consts. Jeff Smith and Michael McCurdy exchanged gunfire with the attacker, who later died of his injuries. Smith suffered critical gunshot wounds and is now recovering at home. He and McCurdy have to date not returned to work.

Contrary to some reports, Beale and Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said, there was never a plan to involve Consts. Smith and McCurdy in the walk.

“People are respecting their privacy, which we appreciate,” Rodd said.

Rodd told the crowd “the world became a very small place” after the shooting because of the outpouring of support for police which came “from literally around the world.”

Rodd said police “are convinced … there was divine intervention” during the Yom Kippur shooting, because the right officers were at the right place at the right time.

“Our message to all assembled is that we will be with our Jewish community – or any community that needs us – now, at the moment of need, and after.”

There was an increased police presence in and around the park.

People gathered at St. Thomas’ before walking one kilometre to the park. Beale said support came from several Christian congregations, along with those of the Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, and Buddhist faiths.

Sandra Amaral of Brighton and Pastor Andrew King of Toronto carried a banner created for the event by a local artist. It depicted four hands cradling a dove and olive branch.

“We’re doing this not only because of what happened but also because our son is in the police here in Belleville, so we have to keep praying,” said Amaral. She and King are members of Belleville Seventh-day Adventist Church.

“More prayer, more power,” King said.

“The statement that we need to make, for one and for all, is that we are one Belleville,” said Pastor Gareth Geddes of the Adventist church. Mayor-elect Paul Fleming echoed the statement and thanked first responders and the public for attending.

Pastor Mansfield Edwards, chaplain of York Regional Police, said a diverse group had gathered “to show that in Belleville there are no differences between us.

“Differences can be seen from a negative perspective, but diversity can be beautiful,” Edwards said.

Pentecostals of Quinte Lead Pastor Shawn Stickler added: “It was acts of violence that tried to create division and fear in our community, but today, as neighbours … we are doing the opposite.”

Belleville synagogue congregation now stronger after shooting

Belleville police lay hate charges in new antisemitism case

Evidence confirms Sons of Jacob Synagogue shooting was 'hate motivated'

Synagogue president Norm Weddum read a prayer in Hebrew. He said afterward his congregation “absolutely” feels supported by the public.

“I think it was fantastic,” he said of the walk.

“The Belleville community is being excellent toward us,” he said. “We’re feeling very appreciative.”

The synagogue attack was one of three antisemitic incidents in September and October. Flyers with antisemitic messages were distributed near the synagogue soon after the shooting, and police in October announced charges against a city man in a third, separate case.

In a Wednesday telephone interview, walk co-organizer Beale said he believes in open debate and conversation.

“I just worry that we've become so polarized as a society,” he said, and people with different views “can’t even talk to each other, let alone hear each other or discuss” issues.

He said there is “too much drama and emotionally-driven” behaviour instead of people basing ideas on facts and data, not what they’ve heard from others.

Beale said he is shocked when he reads online comments suggesting “violence is somehow justified.

“How have we forgotten our history? … We’ve been down this road before, and it never leads to good ends.”

The Oct. 17 fire on a military base took four lives and injured 39, with 25 still in hospital as of Nov. 4

Luis Benítez was taken into custody in Colombia on Sunday and faces nine charges in the US, including assisting the accused drug trafficker

Nikolay Sapov, 48, is accused of interstate and electronic stalking of his former pro tennis tournament coworker

The victim in the attack was Ken Kunkel, a husband, father of two, grandfather and dedicated community volunteer

stories.title: A list of fatal bear attacks in B.C., after mother and daughter killed in Bella Coola
stories.summary: Deadly bear attacks in British Columbia are rare, but there have been at least 10 fatalities since the 1990s, including this week's attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in Bella Coola.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Deadly bear attacks in British Columbia are rare, but there have been at least 10 fatalities since the 1990s, including this week’s attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in Bella Coola.

Four-year-old Ian Dunbar is killed in a bear attack near 70 Mile House. It was among a spate of bear maulings reported in B.C. that season. Thirty bears were shot in Whistler and Prince George alone.

Two hunters are killed by a sow grizzly with two cubs on Oct. 9, 1995, near Radium Hot Springs, while the hunters were hauling out the carcass of a bull elk. All three bears were later killed.

Patti McConnell, 37, of Paris, Texas, and Raymond Kitchen, 56, of Fort Nelson, B.C., are killed in an attack by a black bear in Liard River Hotsprings Provincial Park on Aug. 14, 1997. The attack happened as four campers moved through brush between two hot springs in the park. The bear was shot and killed by a tourist and an examination later showed the bear was gaunt and malnourished.

Arthur Louie, 60, is killed by a grizzly while walking along a road near Invermere, B.C., in late September 2005.

Bernice Evelyn Adolph, 72, a member of the Xaxli’p First Nation, is killed by a black bear near her remote cabin near Lillooet, B.C. Her body is found June 30, 2011, a couple hundred metres down the hill from the cabin.

Hunter Joe Pendry is attacked by a grizzly in the East Kootenay region on Oct. 2, 2025. He shot the bear and fought it off, but died in hospital more than three weeks later. The bear was found dead.

Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, 20, are killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack in Bella Coola, B.C. They were reported missing on Sunday, before their remains were found about 150 metres apart on Monday and Tuesday in the west trail area of the Snooka trail system. Insp. Jeff Tyre of the B.C. Conservation Officer Service said it was not yet clear whether more than one bear was involved.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto’s first electric ferry will soon begin journey to Canada
stories.summary: The first of two new electric ferries commissioned by the City of Toronto will soon begin its journey across the Atlantic Ocean before its expected December arrival.
stories.author: Matthew Bingley
stories.content:
The first of two new electric ferries commissioned by the City of Toronto will soon begin its journey across the Atlantic Ocean before its expected December arrival.

A video showing the launch of the Lady of Quays ferry was posted by the city in late May, but there have been few updates on sea trials for the vessel since then. The city confirmed that the ferry, which has capacity for up to 650 passengers and 14 vehicles, was towed via tug boat from a Romanian shipyard to Istanbul.

General Manager of Fleet Services Abi Thomas said in an emailed statement the completed ferry will be loaded onto a ship and transported across the ocean. Thomas said once it begins its journey, residents will be able to track the journey online.

The city’s strategic communications division declined multiple interview requests to provide more details. No details were provided on the status of construction of the second vessel commissioned by the city, named Toronto Islander, which is due for delivery sometime in early 2027.

Once each vessel arrives in the city, lake trials and crew training will need to be completed before passengers will be able to hop aboard. It’s unclear how long the testing period will take.

About 1.4 million passengers are carried across the city’s inner harbour by the current fleet of ferries, but all four are between 61 to 90 years old.

Although the procurement process to acquire new ferries began more than a decade ago, there have been several delays due to council changing its mind over the design. In 2018, council voted in favour of swapping the ferries to a hybrid diesel-electric propulsion system, but in 2022 it changed course again to fully electric models.

More than a year after a contract was signed with Dutch shipbuilding company Damen, councillors learned city staff hadn’t accounted for charging infrastructure at the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal. The discovery ended up seeing oversight of the city’s ferries shift to its fleet management division from parks and recreation.

When the vessels arrive, they will replace two of its current ferries, including the William Inglis, which struck a wharf in 2023 after it lost propulsion, injuring a crew member.

In 2022, the Sam McBride also crashed, injuring several passengers and lead to the Transportation Safety Board ruling the City of Toronto’s safety protocols had been lacking at the time of the incident.

stories.title: Russian-Canadian man used ‘full rubber mask’ in U.S. stalking incident: officials
stories.summary: Nikolay Sapov, 48, is accused of interstate and electronic stalking of his former pro tennis tournament coworker
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
A Russian-born Canadian national charged with physically and digitally stalking a former coworker in the U.S. once showed up at his alleged victim’s doorstep unannounced in a rubber mask, officials say.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Northern District of Texas indicted Nikolay Sapov, 48, ON charges of stalking through interstate travel and stalking through electronic communications this week. The accused’s precise residence in Canada is not provided, but an FBI affidavit indicates he travelled to the U.S. through Toronto earlier this year.

In 2021, the alleged victim, identified only as L.M., started working in player services for Spanish-speaking athletes at the Miami Open, a three-week top-tier professional tennis tournament held annually in March.

At the time, Sapov, a Russian speaker, had done the same job at the event for “at least five years,” and the two have been coworkers for the three-week tournament every year since.

While colleagues, L.M. believed him to be “nice and polite,” but his unusual behaviour over time made her “feel uncomfortable on numerous occasions.”

When she shared her concerns with her father, a clinical psychotherapist, he advised her to “be nice” to Sapov, whom he suspected to be on the autism spectrum, and not to make him “mad or upset him,” according to the affidavit.

L.M.’s parents had met Sapov at her first Miami Open and again in 2022, when he gifted her mother a traditional Argentine dessert. That same year, L.M. and her father accepted Sapov’s invitation to join him for a day at the U.S. Open in New York that September.

He had also started to learn Spanish and “had become obsessed with Argentina,” the affidavit reads.

L.M. was wary of his behaviour, but she and the family continued to act kindly towards him due to the father’s advice, “despite him continuing to make them feel uncomfortable.”

“During the first few days of the tournament, Sapov was ‘normal’ and would banter with the player services team, but after the tournament, he sent text messages to L.M. for the next eight months,” the investigating FBI agent wrote, noting she later muted them outside the tournament window.

“I told others we are together, which is a lie. Yet through it, I get a glimpse of that what if,” he wrote in a July 2023 text message.

She responded in March 2024, after that year’s tournament, that the lie was disrespectful and asked that he no longer communicate outside the tournament.

But Sapov was unavoidable in Miami, and L.M. told investigators she felt “powerless” to do anything about it because she viewed him as “untouchable” after he was spared consequences for once allowing a third party to use his tournament credentials.

Outside the tennis world, L.M. allowed Sapov to partially follow her on Instagram — choosing to prohibit him from seeing the stories she predominantly shares — but he also started following her relatives located around the world who didn’t share her surname, something she found strange.

While living in Plantation, Fla. in 2023, L.M. received a package at her residence containing a certificate that a star had been named in her honour, which she believed came from Sapov because the handwriting on the back appeared to match writing on items he’d given her in the past.

“The brightest star in my sky is you,” the author wrote on the back, also reaffirming a previous profession of love and asking forgiveness for “every second of pain and disappointment.”

The star registration certificate and handwritten note L.M. received. U.S. Department of Justice

L.M. remains uncertain how he obtained her address, as she never shared it with him or in his presence.

At some point, Sapov also opened a limited liability company (LLC) in L.M.’s name, prompting her father to contact him and clarify she “was not financially responsible for anything in relation to the business,” which they later confirmed with the U.S. Internal Revenue Service.

The affidavit alleged the “conduct escalated” this June 23, when L.M., now living in Dallas with her partner of five years, arrived at their gated apartment complex to find Sapov walking nearby — she had never given him her address and her name was not on the lease.

L.M. contacted security, and police were called to complete “a harassment offence report.” Later that same night, L.M. and her partner heard someone coming up the stairwell to the apartment and looked through their peephole to see Sapov wearing an Argentinian national soccer team jersey.

Dallas police were called back, “completed a stalking offence report and Sapov was criminally trespassed from the property and released.”

Nikolay Sapov in Dallas on June 23. U.S. Department of Justice

When the couple was on their way home the following day, their neighbour called to warn them to stay away “because someone matching Sapov’s description with a full rubber mask on his face” was outside their place “looking at a package and doing something in the area of the door handle.”

The masked person immediately fled when confronted by the neighbour through a doorbell camera.

Fear led the couple to move into a hotel, acquire additional surveillance cameras and buy a gun for protection. Dallas police issued a warrant for Sapov’s arrest on June 25, but he continued sending L.M. text messages until Aug. 20, according to the affidavit.

In August of this year, Sapov sent L.M. three text messages — one about the sale of the LLC, another inviting her to the U.S. Open and a third that included an AI-generated photo of her embracing him from behind, a wedding band visible on her left hand.

L.M. vowed to have never posed with Sapov in this way and finds it “very disturbing.”

“To many good moments and to building a successful path forward,” Sapov’s accompanying message reads.

L.M. told police she believes this image is AI because she never posed for a photo with Sapov in this manner. U.S. Department of Justice

He was taken into custody by U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers on Aug. 22 while taking an Amtrak train into the U.S. from Canada. He had a Flipper Zero — “an electronic device that reads, copies, and mimics analog and digital radio signals.”

He also had two iPhones containing “numerous pictures of women, pictures of L.M., a screenshot of a note containing two streets that surround L.M.’s neighbourhood, (a) photograph of women’s shoes exhibited in an apparent sexual way, and screenshots of key copying/locksmith companies.

“There were also explicit AI-generated photographs and videos of a woman who resembled L.M.”

Waiving his Miranda Rights and speaking without counsel, Sapov told FBI agents he was seeking her out because he believed she owed him money for their LLC. He also admitted to wearing the mask because of the earlier interaction with police.

When the FBI became involved, agents discovered and told L.M. that the Orlando Police Department detained Sapov near her parents’ home, where she was staying, ON May 15, 2025 — the day before the 2025 Miami Open tournament began. L.M. had walked roughly eight kilometres around a lake behind her parents’ house earlier that day.

On Sapov, they found a Flipper Zero.

Nikolay Sapov speaks with Orlando police officers, one of whom is holding a Flipper Zero device. U.S. Department of Justice

L.M. then told the FBI about an attempted break-in at her Plantation apartment in 2023, which, according to a local police report, notes that she used her peephole to see a male suspect appearing to pick her lock.

“When the door opened, L.M. said, ‘what the f—‘ and the unknown male immediately turned around and exited the residence.”

L.M. also fled, but returned to retrieve belongings, finding a Papa John’s Pizza box with a key taped to it that Plantation PD determined unlocked her door. Sapov’s subpoenaed financial records show he had purchased from a Papa John’s less than 500 metres away that same day.

Sapov’s current charges do not relate to either of those incidents.

“No individual has the right to terrorize another human being or shatter their sense of safety inside their own home,” U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould said in a news release. “From relentless digital harassment to an international stalking campaign that spanned across the globe, this defendant went to chilling lengths to hunt down, disguise himself, and intimidate this victim.”

If convicted of new charges, Sapov faces a maximum of five years in federal prison for each count of felony stalking, followed by a supervised release and potential financial penalties.

He could request to serve his time in Canada through a transfer of offender treaty with the U.S., but it would require the approval of both countries.

In 2021, the alleged victim, identified only as L.M., started working in player services for Spanish-speaking athletes at the Miami Open, a three-week top-tier professional tennis tournament held annually in March.
At the time, Sapov, a Russian speaker, had done the same job at the event for “at least five years,” and the two have been coworkers for the three-week tournament every year since.
While colleagues, L.M. believed him to be “nice and polite,” but his unusual behaviour over time made her “feel uncomfortable on numerous occasions.”
Editor’s Picks

When she shared her concerns with her father, a clinical psychotherapist, he advised her to “be nice” to Sapov, whom he suspected to be on the autism spectrum, and not to make him “mad or upset him,” according to the affidavit.

L.M.’s parents had met Sapov at her first Miami Open and again in 2022, when he gifted her mother a traditional Argentine dessert. That same year, L.M. and her father accepted Sapov’s invitation to join him for a day at the U.S. Open in New York that September.
He had also started to learn Spanish and “had become obsessed with Argentina,” the affidavit reads.
L.M. was wary of his behaviour, but she and the family continued to act kindly towards him due to the father’s advice, “despite him continuing to make them feel uncomfortable.”

“During the first few days of the tournament, Sapov was ‘normal’ and would banter with the player services team, but after the tournament, he sent text messages to L.M. for the next eight months,” the investigating FBI agent wrote, noting she later muted them outside the tournament window.
“I told others we are together, which is a lie. Yet through it, I get a glimpse of that what if,” he wrote in a July 2023 text message.
She responded in March 2024, after that year’s tournament, that the lie was disrespectful and asked that he no longer communicate outside the tournament.

But Sapov was unavoidable in Miami, and L.M. told investigators she felt “powerless” to do anything about it because she viewed him as “untouchable” after he was spared consequences for once allowing a third party to use his tournament credentials.

Outside the tennis world, L.M. allowed Sapov to partially follow her on Instagram — choosing to prohibit him from seeing the stories she predominantly shares — but he also started following her relatives located around the world who didn’t share her surname, something she found strange.

While living in Plantation, Fla. in 2023, L.M. received a package at her residence containing a certificate that a star had been named in her honour, which she believed came from Sapov because the handwriting on the back appeared to match writing on items he’d given her in the past.
“The brightest star in my sky is you,” the author wrote on the back, also reaffirming a previous profession of love and asking forgiveness for “every second of pain and disappointment.”
The star registration certificate and handwritten note L.M. received. U.S. Department of Justice
L.M. remains uncertain how he obtained her address, as she never shared it with him or in his presence.

At some point, Sapov also opened a limited liability company (LLC) in L.M.’s name, prompting her father to contact him and clarify she “was not financially responsible for anything in relation to the business,” which they later confirmed with the U.S. Internal Revenue Service.

The affidavit alleged the “conduct escalated” this June 23, when L.M., now living in Dallas with her partner of five years, arrived at their gated apartment complex to find Sapov walking nearby — she had never given him her address and her name was not on the lease.

L.M. contacted security, and police were called to complete “a harassment offence report.” Later that same night, L.M. and her partner heard someone coming up the stairwell to the apartment and looked through their peephole to see Sapov wearing an Argentinian national soccer team jersey.
Dallas police were called back, “completed a stalking offence report and Sapov was criminally trespassed from the property and released.”
Nikolay Sapov in Dallas on June 23. U.S. Department of Justice

When the couple was on their way home the following day, their neighbour called to warn them to stay away “because someone matching Sapov’s description with a full rubber mask on his face” was outside their place “looking at a package and doing something in the area of the door handle.”
The masked person immediately fled when confronted by the neighbour through a doorbell camera.

Fear led the couple to move into a hotel, acquire additional surveillance cameras and buy a gun for protection. Dallas police issued a warrant for Sapov’s arrest on June 25, but he continued sending L.M. text messages until Aug. 20, according to the affidavit.

In August of this year, Sapov sent L.M. three text messages — one about the sale of the LLC, another inviting her to the U.S. Open and a third that included an AI-generated photo of her embracing him from behind, a wedding band visible on her left hand.
L.M. vowed to have never posed with Sapov in this way and finds it “very disturbing.”
“To many good moments and to building a successful path forward,” Sapov’s accompanying message reads.
L.M. told police she believes this image is AI because she never posed for a photo with Sapov in this manner. U.S. Department of Justice

He was taken into custody by U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers on Aug. 22 while taking an Amtrak train into the U.S. from Canada. He had a Flipper Zero — “an electronic device that reads, copies, and mimics analog and digital radio signals.”

He also had two iPhones containing “numerous pictures of women, pictures of L.M., a screenshot of a note containing two streets that surround L.M.’s neighbourhood, (a) photograph of women’s shoes exhibited in an apparent sexual way, and screenshots of key copying/locksmith companies.
“There were also explicit AI-generated photographs and videos of a woman who resembled L.M.”

Waiving his Miranda Rights and speaking without counsel, Sapov told FBI agents he was seeking her out because he believed she owed him money for their LLC. He also admitted to wearing the mask because of the earlier interaction with police.

When the FBI became involved, agents discovered and told L.M. that the Orlando Police Department detained Sapov near her parents’ home, where she was staying, ON May 15, 2025 — the day before the 2025 Miami Open tournament began. L.M. had walked roughly eight kilometres around a lake behind her parents’ house earlier that day.
On Sapov, they found a Flipper Zero.
Nikolay Sapov speaks with Orlando police officers, one of whom is holding a Flipper Zero device. U.S. Department of Justice

L.M. then told the FBI about an attempted break-in at her Plantation apartment in 2023, which, according to a local police report, notes that she used her peephole to see a male suspect appearing to pick her lock.
“When the door opened, L.M. said, ‘what the f—‘ and the unknown male immediately turned around and exited the residence.”

L.M. also fled, but returned to retrieve belongings, finding a Papa John’s Pizza box with a key taped to it that Plantation PD determined unlocked her door. Sapov’s subpoenaed financial records show he had purchased from a Papa John’s less than 500 metres away that same day.
Sapov’s current charges do not relate to either of those incidents.

“No individual has the right to terrorize another human being or shatter their sense of safety inside their own home,” U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould said in a news release. “From relentless digital harassment to an international stalking campaign that spanned across the globe, this defendant went to chilling lengths to hunt down, disguise himself, and intimidate this victim.”
If convicted of new charges, Sapov faces a maximum of five years in federal prison for each count of felony stalking, followed by a supervised release and potential financial penalties.
He could request to serve his time in Canada through a transfer of offender treaty with the U.S., but it would require the approval of both countries.

stories.title: Two people flee explosion, fire at house south of Calgary
stories.summary: The Foothills Fire Department said it began receiving calls around 7 a.m. for an explosion on North Coulee Trail, northeast of Okotoks, Alta.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Two people were able to flee a house just south of Calgary Thursday following a fire and explosion.

The Foothills Fire Department said it began receiving calls around 7 a.m. for an explosion on North Coulee Trail, northeast of Okotoks, Alta.

Crews found the home engulfed in flames, and the fire department said two people who were inside were able to make it out safely.

People who live in the area told Global News they were awoken by multiple explosions so strong their homes were damaged as well.

Dave Simms, deputy chief of the Foothills Fire Department, said the two people who were inside the house were taken to hospital as a precaution.

Officials have not confirmed the cause of the fire or the blast.

An investigation is ongoing.

stories.title: Stellantis extends shutdown of Windsor, Ont., plant as it weighs ‘evolving market conditions’
stories.summary: Continued layoffs underline impact of Trump’s tariff war
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Stellantis NV Stla-N has extended the shutdown of its assembly plant in Windsor, Ont., for the sixth week since mid-September, citing sales and tariffs.

The plant, which employs about 6,000 unionized workers and makes Chrysler minivans and Dodge Charger muscle cars, will be closed for production next week, said LouAnn Gosselin, a spokesperson for Stellantis.

“Stellantis continues to evaluate and adjust its manufacturing operations in response to evolving market conditions, including consumer demand and the impact of tariffs,” Ms. Gosselin said.

The temporary layoffs underline the impact of the trade war launched by U.S. President Donald Trump in 2025. He imposed 25-per-cent tariffs on non-U.S. content in Canadian-made cars, disregarding the decades-old free trade agreement between the two countries.

He has also said Canada’s auto-tariff rate will rise to 50 per cent and include auto parts on Jan. 1. Mr. Trump last year threatened 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian auto parts, but reversed course under pressure from the industry, which warned such levies would quickly halt assembly plants across North America.

Formal trade talks between Ottawa and Washington are expected to resume shortly.

Flavio Volpe, head of Canada’s Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association, called Mr. Trump’s threat to tariffs auto parts in January hollow.

“We all know that’s going to shut down the industry, including him,” Mr. Volpe said. “That’s why he backed off last year.”

Still, the tariffs have caused automotive layoffs in Ontario and reduced car shipments between the two countries.

Since the tariffs were announced in early 2025, General Motors idled its electric van plant in Ingersoll, Ont., laying off more than 1,000 workers, and eliminated one of three shifts at its Oshawa pickup-truck plant.

Stellantis, meanwhile, moved planned production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois from its Brampton, Ont., plant that once employed about 3,000 people.

The factory northwest of Toronto remains idle and is at the heart of a dispute involving the company, the Unifor union and the federal government.

Stellantis said it has a preliminary agreement to sell the plant to Roshel, a maker of armoured vehicles, ending 30 years of carmaking at the site.

“Stellantis believes that Roshel represents a strong path to restoring sustainable operations at Brampton Assembly, preserving the site’s strategic role in Canada’s advanced manufacturing sector and helping to avoid a prolonged period of inactivity,” Ms. Gosselin said.

Unifor walked away from collective bargaining with Stellantis in September over the planned sale, which it opposes. Employees recently voted in favour of strike if no deal can be reached, but are not in a legal work stoppage position.

Lana Payne, Unifor’s national president, ON Wednesday called for an “urgent” meeting with Stellantis and officials from the Ontario and federal governments over the plant’s future. “The economic and job security implications of a closure and sale for Unifor members, and Canada’s auto industry, are severe,” Ms. Payne said in an open letter to federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Vic Fedeli, Ontario’s Minister of Economic Development.

The federal government has said idling the plant and moving production puts Stellantis in violation of a funding agreement that saw the company receive millions of taxpayer dollars to retool the plant. Ottawa has said it intends to get its money back. Stellantis said on Thursday talks with Ottawa are ongoing.

stories.title: More community questions raised about Nova Scotia's first proposed AI data centre
stories.summary: Lower River Inhabitants, N.S. - Some Nova Scotians said they were left with outstanding questions after two lengthy information sessions on a planned artificial intelligence data centre in southern Cape Breton.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Lower River Inhabitants, N.S. - Some Nova Scotians said they were left with outstanding questions after two lengthy information sessions on a planned artificial intelligence data centre in southern Cape Breton.

EverWind Fuels hosted the second session Wednesday night at a community centre in the rural town of Lower River Inhabitants, N.S. The company also held a session Tuesday in D’Escousse, N.S.

Both sessions ran late as residents lined up to ask company officials about plans for a $10-billion, 18,600-square-metre data centre in nearby Point Tupper, N.S., a project expected to come online by the end of 2027.

American tech company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for the centre, which would draw 95 megawatts of electricity in its first phase. A 325-megawatt expansion is scheduled for mid-2028.

Julissa Stewart, a resident of Richmond County who lives about 20 minutes from the construction site, attended both sessions and asked several questions.

“Between last night and tonight, I think a lot of great questions were posed, and we still didn’t get answers,” she said after Wednesday’s meeting.

Stewart asked officials about the project’s lack of an environmental assessment and how the firm would be held accountable. She said it felt as if the officials were not giving direct or complete answers.

“I’m in the same position I was in prior to the information sessions … We need to put this (project) on pause until we have all the information, until we can write regulations,” she said.

Stewart said she’s worried about the unknown, long-term impacts that a massive data centre could have on the environment and people’s health. She’s also concerned that assurances provided by the company and the provincial government have not been written into legally binding agreements.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston has said he doesn’t know whether any new legislation is needed to regulate what would be the province’s first AI data centre.

He’s repeatedly said the existing approval processes come with guidelines that would be followed.

During the two sessions, community members asked about pollution potential, and what environmental protections would be in place. Many also said they were concerned about the American AI giant that plans to lease the centre.

As the meeting on Wednesday started, the event’s moderator said EverWind officials were prepared to stay until everyone got a chance to ask their questions.

Mark Stewart, the firm’s engagement director, told the crowd that EverWind was aware of their concerns and would take in feedback. He said additional community consultations would be arranged as the project progresses.

Cassie Kiftle from Bible Hill, N.S., a two-hour drive west of Lower River Inhabitants, said she had concerns about Anthropic and the security of Canadian data. She asked whether EverWind would be held accountable if Anthropic leaked Canadians’ data.

“It would be their data, their obligations and their responsibility,” said Brendan Chard, EverWind’s vice-president of power. “We’re providing the infrastructure, we’re building the data centre … The company would be responsible.”

Kiftle said she appreciated the efforts of EverWind officials to share what information they could, but she said she left the session believing the data centre proposal was a bad idea.

“I don’t want an AI data centre here. Not because I don’t want economic growth for the province, but because of the company that will be leasing it,” she said.

Teresa MacNeil attended Tuesday’s session and asked EverWind to share details of the investors behind the $10-billion project. EverWind officials said they could not speak about private investors.

MacNeil said that without details about who would pay for the project, it was unlikely the community would get on board.

“I am not for or against the data centre, but I need more information,” she said in an interview Wednesday. “I did not get that information last night.”

Brandon Kroetsch also attended Tuesday’s session. He said he felt “slightly more informed” afterwards, but he said much of the information provided lacked detail.

“There’s a lot of information that’s been pumped out that’s very boilerplate, scripted and just not useful,” he said.

Earlier Wednesday, the premier said he was happy with how public consultations had progressed. Houston said he heard that Tuesday’s information session was calm and respectful.

“There were lots of answers and (we) certainly know that there are no answers that would satisfy some people on this file,” Houston told an unrelated news conference in Dartmouth, N.S. “But we’re just trying to make sure we follow the science, we follow facts and we just move forward in an appropriate way .... But the data centres … It’s happening.”

On Wednesday, NDP Opposition Leader Claudia Chender held a news conference to highlight the concerns of two mothers who expressed their concerns over the potential impact on power bills and the environment.

Chender said Nova Scotians have many unanswered questions about the project, and need to see written agreements with more details on promised community benefits, jobs, environmental protections and a guarantee power rates will not increase.

“The premier wants Nova Scotians to take the companies involved, Everwind and Anthropic, at their word. But promises from American billionaires... and giant AI companies’ assurances are not enough for Nova Scotians,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

— With files from Devin Stevens in Halifax

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston has said he doesn’t know whether any new legislation is needed to regulate what would be the province’s first AI data centre.
He’s repeatedly said the existing approval processes come with guidelines that would be followed.

During the two sessions, community members asked about pollution potential, and what environmental protections would be in place. Many also said they were concerned about the American AI giant that plans to lease the centre.
As the meeting on Wednesday started, the event’s moderator said EverWind officials were prepared to stay until everyone got a chance to ask their questions.

Mark Stewart, the firm’s engagement director, told the crowd that EverWind was aware of their concerns and would take in feedback. He said additional community consultations would be arranged as the project progresses.

Cassie Kiftle from Bible Hill, N.S., a two-hour drive west of Lower River Inhabitants, said she had concerns about Anthropic and the security of Canadian data. She asked whether EverWind would be held accountable if Anthropic leaked Canadians’ data.

“It would be their data, their obligations and their responsibility,” said Brendan Chard, EverWind’s vice-president of power. “We’re providing the infrastructure, we’re building the data centre … The company would be responsible.”
Kiftle said she appreciated the efforts of EverWind officials to share what information they could, but she said she left the session believing the data centre proposal was a bad idea.
“I don’t want an AI data centre here. Not because I don’t want economic growth for the province, but because of the company that will be leasing it,” she said.
Teresa MacNeil attended Tuesday’s session and asked EverWind to share details of the investors behind the $10-billion project. EverWind officials said they could not speak about private investors.
MacNeil said that without details about who would pay for the project, it was unlikely the community would get on board.
“I am not for or against the data centre, but I need more information,” she said in an interview Wednesday. “I did not get that information last night.”
Brandon Kroetsch also attended Tuesday’s session. He said he felt “slightly more informed” afterwards, but he said much of the information provided lacked detail.
“There’s a lot of information that’s been pumped out that’s very boilerplate, scripted and just not useful,” he said.
Earlier Wednesday, the premier said he was happy with how public consultations had progressed. Houston said he heard that Tuesday’s information session was calm and respectful.

“There were lots of answers and (we) certainly know that there are no answers that would satisfy some people on this file,” Houston told an unrelated news conference in Dartmouth, N.S. “But we’re just trying to make sure we follow the science, we follow facts and we just move forward in an appropriate way .... But the data centres … It’s happening.”

On Wednesday, NDP Opposition Leader Claudia Chender held a news conference to highlight the concerns of two mothers who expressed their concerns over the potential impact on power bills and the environment.

Chender said Nova Scotians have many unanswered questions about the project, and need to see written agreements with more details on promised community benefits, jobs, environmental protections and a guarantee power rates will not increase.

“The premier wants Nova Scotians to take the companies involved, Everwind and Anthropic, at their word. But promises from American billionaires... and giant AI companies’ assurances are not enough for Nova Scotians,” she said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.
— With files from Devin Stevens in Halifax

stories.title: B.C. bus crash response hindered by lack of cell service
stories.summary: Twenty injured when shuttle bus went off highway along Highway 39
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Communications problems along Highway 39, which May have complicated the emergency response to a bus crash that injured 20 on Wednesday, are a familiar issue for northern residents, the provincial legislator for Mackenzie, B.C., said.

Kiel Giddens, the member of the legislature for Prince George-Mackenzie, said poor or non-existent cellphone coverage is part of life in northern British Columbia.

“It’s something that northerners deal with on a regular basis and something that I’m certainly familiar with,” he said Thursday.

A shuttle bus chartered by a contractor for a data centre company went off the highway near Mackenzie on Wednesday in a remote area known for spotty cellphone coverage, prompting a response involving 12 ambulances and the declaration of Code Orange mass casualty events at two hospitals.

Northern Health issued an update on Thursday saying 15 of the 20 people assessed and treated in its facilities after the crash have since been discharged.

One person was taken by air ambulance to another facility, while four were admitted to hospital, the health authority said, adding it would not provide any further updates on the status of patients in order to protect their privacy.

Giddens said cell coverage quickly drops off when people leave Mackenzie, located about 180 kilometres north of Prince George, and head south on Highway 39.

Cpl. Jennifer Cooper with North District RCMP has said the crash happened in an area with no cellphone reception and poor satellite coverage.

She said first responders had difficulty with radio communications and information from the area was slow to come out during the initial emergency response.

But Sgt. Michael McLaughlin, a media relations officer with the BC Highway Patrol, said he had no information to suggest radio issues were a problem in the investigation of the crash.

“Any mass casualty event is going to be chaotic in the first instance – and that’s especially true in a small or remote community where resources are less plentiful,” he said in an e-mail Thursday.

“In spite of that, all casualties have received timely medical treatment and the investigation is proceeding satisfactorily and making good progress.”

Giddens praised the emergency response to the crash and said that while the local hospital had limited resources to treat patients, their care and co-ordination in sending people to other hospitals as needed was “phenomenal.”

He said the crash highlights the hardships northern and remote communities face.

“We need to work together to support those living in the north and encourage both economic opportunity and safe transportation,” Giddens said.

Ian Tait with Ambulance Paramedics of BC, a union representing about 6,000 ambulance paramedics and dispatchers, said issues with radio and cellphone reception in rural areas are a common complaint among members.

“We struggle with communications like a lot of first responders,” he said of service in rural and remote areas, where some paramedics May still use analogue radio systems and experience problems with radio and cellphone towers.

BC Emergency Health Services did not immediately respond to a question Thursday about whether the 12 ambulances, six ground and six air, dispatched to the bus crash near Mackenzie had experienced any communications issues.

An earlier statement from the service said an air ambulance took one person to hospital in serious condition, while six others were transported by ground ambulance to hospital, then airlifted to another facility. Of those six patients, two were in serious condition and four were in serious but stable condition.

Another 13 patients in stable condition were transported by bus to hospital accompanied by advanced-care paramedics, the service said.

The province has said about 38 per cent of B.C.’s highways lack cell service, with limited access to reliable power cited as a key barrier to expanding coverage.

In 2023, the NDP government said it would provide $75 million through a program administered by the Northern Development Initiative Trust to fund projects expanding cellular service to another 550 kilometres of highway by 2027.

stories.title: Carney says Canada is ‘confident,’ focus not changing after U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said his priority remains on putting Canadians first as trade talks resume with the United States.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is a “confident country” and is focused on the same issues as before the U.S. midterms, when asked by reporters about how the results impact his approach to dealing with the U.S.

“We’re focused on affordability, and we’re focused on opportunity. We’re focused on sovereignty for Canada, more independence so we can live our lives as we choose and make our own decisions,” Carney told reporters.

“So yes, it’s important what happens in the U.S. and things will evolve, but we’re focused here. We’re focused on the same issues as we were at the start of the week, as we will focus on next week. It’s a confident country moving forward, and I think that’s the core message. Yes, we’re a great partner for many countries around the world, including the United States.”

Canadian politicians were quick to speak following the Democrats sweeping win of both the House of Representatives and the Senate earlier this week.

Tensions have simmered between Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump after trade talks came to a crashing halt in August. Since, the two countries have been deadlocked in a trade war launched by Trump that is hurting businesses and consumers on both sides of the border.

Carney had said Tuesday that “more intense” trade negotiations with the U.S. were resuming following a phone call with Trump over the weekend.

stories.title: Canadians ‘disgusted’ over vicious attack on Canadian Armed Forces member selling poppies with cadets
stories.summary: The victim in the attack was Ken Kunkel, a husband, father of two, grandfather and dedicated community volunteer
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
The public continues to express outrage over the vicious attack on an air cadet commander in Hamilton, Ont.,that has reportedly left 59-year-old Capt. Ken Kunkel unable to walk.

According to a statement by the family obtained by Global News, Kunkel suffered life-altering injuries, underwent spinal surgery and won’t be able to walk for the unforeseeable future.

A GoFundMe page was set up this week by a friend of the family, Selina P. As of Thursday afternoon, more than $60,000 of the $70,000 goal has been donated.

The GoFundMe page states that Kunkel is a Commanding Officer of 826 Griffin Squadron Royal Canadian Air Cadets and has been involved with the organization “for the last 20 years. Both of his children were also in cadets and now his wife, Shelly, is also involved in growing the cadet core.”

Kunkel, a husband, father of two, grandfather and dedicated community volunteer was supporting two air cadets selling poppies on Sunday in advance of Remembrance Day. According to Hamilton Police the attack began midday Sunday when two youths approached the young Air Cadets in front of a restaurant and blew an air horn into their ears.

Kunkel followed the youth suspects into the restaurant to speak to them about what they did, say police. But a struggle followed, with an adult female, not initially involved in the altercation, jumping in and assaulting Kunkel.

He fell to the ground and one of the male youths struck him several times before leaving the restaurant.

Police later arrested the youth and adult female suspects, charging them with causing Kunkel’s “life-altering”injuries.

The Youth Criminal Justice Act ensures that the identity of the youth cannot be published. National Post has reached out to the police service to confirm the identify of the woman.

Federal Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre has expressed disgust over the attack on Kunkel.

In a social media post earlier this week, he wrote: “I am disgusted by the brutal attack on a Canadian Armed Forces member supervising young cadets selling poppies in Hamilton. He stepped in after the cadets were assaulted. … No child should fear violence while selling a poppy. No Canadian should be brutalized for standing up for them.”

Referencing the upcoming Remembrance Day, he urged people to wear their poppies proudly, adding, “Support our veterans. And stand with the Canadians who serve and protect us.”

I am disgusted by the brutal attack on a Canadian Armed Forces member supervising young cadets selling poppies in Hamilton. He stepped in after the cadets were assaulted. He was left with injuries police describe as life-altering. He was helping young Canadians honour those who… — Pierre Poilievre (@PierrePoilievre) November 3, 2026

Hamilton East-Stoney Creek MP, Ned Kuruc, also shared his disgust on social media platform X. He wrote on Wednesday: “Those who dedicate their time to honouring our veterans should never have to fear for their safety.”

I am absolutely disgusted by the violent attack on a Canadian Armed Forces member while supervising young cadets at a poppy drive in Hamilton. Those who dedicate their time to honouring our veterans should never have to fear for their safety.#Hamiltonpic.twitter.com/ORZMigJRz0 — Ned Kuruc (@NedKurucMP) November 4, 2026

Ontario MPP for Brampton North, Graham McGregor, wrote on X this week that he was “appalled to learn of the assault on Kunkel and that people like him “who volunteer their time to serve our youth and honour our veterans deserve our utmost respect, not violence.”

I am appalled to learn of the assault on a Royal Canadian Air Cadets leader in Hamilton while participating in the annual poppy campaign. This is especially disturbing as we approach Remembrance Day, a time to honour the courage, service and sacrifices of our veterans and fallen… — Graham McGregor (@BramptonGraham) November 3, 2026

The Commissionaires, which is the country’s largest employer of Canadian veterans, posted on X that the organization is “deeply saddened by the senseless assault.”

We are deeply saddened by the senseless assault of a @CanadianForces member who was supervising air cadets selling poppies in Hamilton. Our thoughts are with the injured member and his family, and with the young cadets affected by this incident. — Commissionaires (@Commissionaires) November 3, 2026

Pointing to the horrific attack, the GoFundMe page organizer says that “in a matter of moments, this family’s entire world changed. (Kunkel) is now facing a long and uncertain road ahead, including spinal surgery, an extended hospital stay and what will undoubtedly be an incredibly challenging recovery.

“Behind the headlines is a real family. A wife, two children and four young grandchildren who are suddenly navigating fear, uncertainty and the overwhelming reality of having someone they love so deeply fighting through something no family should ever have to experience.

She says the fundraiser has been started to help the family with the financial burden of costs of: travel, parking, meals, time off from work for Kunkel as well as his wife and family members as they support him, and medication and equipment that May be needed due to his injuries.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Lack of cell service complicated B.C. bus crash response
stories.summary: Mackenzie - The provincial legislator for Mackenzie, B.C., says communications problems along Highway 39 that complicated the emergency response to a bus crash on Wednesday is a familiar issue for northern residents.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Mackenzie - Communications problems along Highway 39, which May have complicated the emergency response to a bus crash that injured 20 on Wednesday, are a familiar issue for northern residents, the provincial legislator for Mackenzie, B.C., said.

Kiel Giddens, the member of the legislature for Prince George-Mackenzie, said poor or non-existent cellphone coverage is part of life in northern British Columbia.

“It’s something that northerners deal with on a regular basis and something that I’m certainly familiar with,” he said Thursday.

A shuttle bus chartered by a contractor for a data centre company went off the highway near Mackenzie on Wednesday in a remote area known for spotty cellphone coverage, prompting a response involving 12 ambulances and the declaration of Code Orange mass casualty events at two hospitals.

Northern Health issued an update on Thursday saying 15 of the 20 people assessed and treated in its facilities after the crash have since been discharged.

One person was taken by air ambulance to another facility, while four were admitted to hospital, the health authority said, adding it would not provide any further updates on the status of patients in order to protect their privacy.

Giddens said cell coverage quickly drops off when people leave Mackenzie, located about 180 kilometres north of Prince George, and head south on Highway 39.

Cpl. Jennifer Cooper with North District RCMP has said the crash happened in an area with no cellphone reception and poor satellite coverage.

She said first responders had difficulty with radio communications and information from the area was slow to come out during the initial emergency response.

But Sgt. Michael McLaughlin, a media relations officer with the BC Highway Patrol, said he had no information to suggest radio issues were a problem in the investigation of the crash.

“Any mass casualty event is going to be chaotic in the first instance — and that’s especially true in a small or remote community where resources are less plentiful,” he said in an email Thursday.

“In spite of that, all casualties have received timely medical treatment and the investigation is proceeding satisfactorily and making good progress.”

Giddens praised the emergency response to the crash and said that while the local hospital had limited resources to treat patients, their care and co-ordination in sending people to other hospitals as needed was “phenomenal.”

He said the crash highlights the hardships northern and remote communities face.

“We need to work together to support those living in the north and encourage both economic opportunity and safe transportation,” Giddens said.

Ian Tait with Ambulance Paramedics of BC, a union representing about 6,000 ambulance paramedics and dispatchers, said issues with radio and cellphone reception in rural areas are a common complaint among members.

“We struggle with communications like a lot of first responders,” he said of service in rural and remote areas, where some paramedics May still use analog radio systems and experience problems with radio and cellphone towers.

BC Emergency Health Services did not immediately respond to a question Thursday about whether the 12 ambulances, six ground and six air, dispatched to the bus crash near Mackenzie had experienced any communications issues.

An earlier statement from the service said an air ambulance took one person to hospital in serious condition, while six others were transported by ground ambulance to hospital, then airlifted to another facility. Of those six patients, two were in serious condition and four were in serious but stable condition.

Another 13 patients in stable condition were transported by bus to hospital accompanied by advanced-care paramedics, the service said.

The province has said about 38 per cent of B.C.‘s highways lack cell service, with limited access to reliable power cited as a key barrier to expanding coverage.

In 2023, the NDP government said it would provide $75 million through a program administered by the Northern Development Initiative Trust to fund projects expanding cellular service to another 550 kilometres of highway by 2027.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

— With files from Ckpg

stories.title: Alexander Graham Bell descendants upset after Parks Canada calls inventor a eugenicist
stories.summary: Review says Bell 'discouraged the use of sign language' and held 'eugenics beliefs'
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
The family of Alexander Graham Bell, the Scottish-born Canadian inventor of the telephone, is upset over a planned redesign of a commemorative plaque that could add that he was a proponent of eugenics and held controversial views about deaf people.

Bell was designated as a national historic person in 1977 by Parks Canada, which installed a commemorate plaque in Baddeck, N.S., near his summer home where he died in 1922.

The plaque says he “devoted his life, with unusual success, to the benefit of mankind,” and that he “produced important inventions and discoveries in medicine, aeronautics, marine engineering, genetics and electrical science, and greatly advanced the methods and practices of teaching the deaf.”

However, a Parks Canada website notes that, last year, “this designation was reviewed to understand Bell’s connection to the eugenics movement.”

It adds: “As a teacher of Deaf people, he developed oralist methods of instruction and discouraged the use of sign language among the Deaf community. Due to his eugenics beliefs, Bell argued against the intermarriage of congenitally Deaf people.”

That’s poppycock, says Ed Grosvenor. He’s a great-grandson of Bell, editor-in-chief of American Heritage magazine and the author of several books including Alexander Graham Bell: The Life and Times of the Man Who Invented the Telephone.

Bell did in fact discourage the use of sign language, Grosvenor told National Post.

“But what people today don’t understand is that what he opposed was the sign language of 140 years ago. That’s not modern sign language. Modern sign language was developed in the 1950s, and I am certain that he would have thought it was brilliant.”

He added that Bell’s last communication was in sign language.

“I discovered this when I was researching my book,” he said. “His last word was signed to his wife because she was completely deaf. He’s lying on his bed, dying. And she says, ‘Alec, don’t leave me.’ And he just signs ‘No’ into her hands, and then goes.”

Grosvenor added: “It’s not fair to say somebody in the 1880s opposed something from the year 2026. It’s a classic fallacy.”

From left, Helen Keller, her teacher Annie Sullivan and Alexander Graham Bell. Handout

The eugenics label, he said, comes from a similar misunderstanding. The science of genetics was still new in Bell’s lifetime, and his primary connection with it was through sheep farming, not human-centred eugenics.

“He developed a herd of sheep that delivered twins, because sheep only deliver a single lamb at a time, and then it takes them a couple years, and that’s a long time for the farmers to develop a herd of sheep. If you could do it two at a time instead, twins instead of single ones, that would be geometrically much more efficient, and so he was part of this. He was one of the founders of the American Breeders Association.”

Bell, a polymath, was also interested in genetic factors connected to longevity. That was “when he was in his 70s and hoping to last a little longer,” Grosvenor noted.

Bell also pointed out that if deaf people had children together, there might be a risk of those children also being deaf. But he went no further.

Alexander Graham Bell, seated, worked to develop sheep that would consistently give birth to twins. Handout

In an 1891 speech in Washington titled Marriage, An Address To The Deaf, Bell said: “I know that an idea has gone forth, and is very generally believed in by the deaf in this country, that I want to prevent you from marrying as you choose, and that I have tried to pass a law to interfere with your marriages. But, my friends, it is not true. I have never done such a thing, nor do I intend to.”

He continued: “You can marry whom you choose, and I hope you will be happy. It is not for me to blame you for marrying to suit yourselves, for you all know that I myself, the son of a deaf mother, have married a deaf wife.”

Parks Canada says designations are reviewed for several reasons, including “colonial assumptions … that were written from an overly European perspective,” “outdated or offensive terms or word choices,” “controversial beliefs and behaviours,” and “to reflect new information, new sources, or recent scholarship.”

But Sara Grosvenor, Ed’s sister and president of the Alexander and Mabel Bell Legacy Foundation, told National Post: “The Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada never contacted the Foundation or the family and did not cite their sources.”

Ed Grosvenor added he was “totally surprised” by the news from Parks Canada, and is opposed to the thinking behind it.

“It’s called presentism,” he said. “It’s making judgments about people using present points of view.”

He pointed out that Bell was a humanitarian, organized protests against segregation in Canada, and advocated for women’s suffrage.

“And most of the money that he gave away — and he died not a wealthy man — most of it was given away to the deaf, to help the hearing impaired. And it just seems to me like it’s kind of mean to focus on one aspect that you don’t agree with, that you take out of context.”

National Post has reached out to Parks Canada for more information.

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: ‘Where’s the door?’: Accessibility advocate says Saskatoon BRT stations need more work
stories.summary: As Saskatoon moves forward with building out its bus rapid transit system, an accessibility advocate and bus rider is raising concerns about some of the new platforms.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
When Robin East waits for a bus, he makes several considerations before it arrives.

“So if I’m standing here and then I hear the bus coming, I’m going to have to figure out when it’s going to stop, but where’s the door?” he said.

East, who is blind, has to consider everything from where he can stand safely on a platform to where he should board.

Sometimes, the obstacles are literal. During an interview with Global News, East demonstrated how he would navigate Saskatoon’s new bus rapid transit (BRT) stops along Broadway Avenue, but walked into the branches of a tree located on the bus platform.

“So that’s always a problem,” East said. Without echoes or other audio cues, he said, there’s often nothing to tell him a shelter or other physical barriers are in the way.

East helped bring voice announcements to Saskatoon buses more than a decade ago. Now, he is concerned the city is not listening on its latest BRT designs.

“I think the city has done some good work in communications and some good work with regards to that meaningful engagement, but it hasn’t gone far enough,” he said.

“It seems to have a plan and it doesn’t want to move too far from that plan and that means that that engagement is not meaningful.”

East says he considers meaningful engagement an ongoing process between people with disabilities and those designing the system, with good design aligning with accessibility codes.

“We have the Accessible Canada Act and we have a number of pieces from Accessible Standards Canada which allow us to have wayfinding to and from these transportation pieces,” he said. “So there’s no reason why, as they build this system, that it’s not fully accessible.” City councillors approved a plan in late September for BRT lanes on a stretch of First Avenue, with stations in the centre of the road.

East wonders how those stations will be made accessible, given his concerns about new platforms built in other parts of the city, such as on Broadway Avenue.

The BRT stations built so far are on the side of the road, while those planned for First Avenue and College Drive will be configured differently, with platforms in the centre of the road.

“I’m really frustrated that at this point in time with the building of the platforms, there’s a lot of accessibility pieces that are missing,” he said.

Jay Magus, Saskatoon’s director of transportation, said the city has consulted on accessibility extensively since the BRT project began about a decade ago.

He said the city built a pilot bus station at Saskatoon’s Civic Operations Centre where accessibility advocates were invited to provide feedback and that designers follow the Transportation Association of Canada accessibility standards, which inform factors such as sidewalk width and minimum grades.

When there are no published standards on certain design elements, Magus says the city uses best practices or looks to what has been done in other cities. This method was what informed the yellow tactile strips along the edge of stations, said Magus.

“We saw other cities doing that and so we did some research and we invited accessibility folks into our office to help us pick which one they thought was best for us.”

As work continues on the stations along College Drive, which are expected to be complete in 2027, Magus says accessibility committee members will get a chance to see the stations before they open.

“So they can see the infrastructure, see how it’s going to work, get a feel for it, and then take that back to their memberships.”

Magus adds that a third party will conduct safety audits during multiple stages of the design process for the lanes on 1st Avenue, including during construction and post-opening, that will consider accessibility alongside traffic operations.

Accessibility consultants say designing a BRT system is complicated and that standards alone don’t guarantee a system works for everyone.

“When we think about accessibility and we think of the diversity of disability and lived experience, those types of guidelines don’t always match up with what will actually be accessible for people,” said Pia Dimayuga, accessibility specialist and transit innovator at accessibility and transit consulting firm Left Turn Right Turn.

Dimayuga said it is important that codes are followed to make sure there is consistency in design across cities, but how people interact with design is unique to each city and people with different kinds of disabilities, emphasizing the importance of getting hands-on feedback.

Getting accessibility advocates to test out a system before it is operational is also a good idea, said Dimayuga, adding that it is not typical for cities to do it.

“I think more places should do this to basically show people either an implementation or a prototype of what the system will actually look like,” she said. “The devil is really in the details when it comes to accessibility and someone with a disability May not know that there’s an issue until they actually see it.”

The Canadian National Institute for the Blind (Cnib) says the city has consulted with it on the BRT stations, but it is awaiting further updates.

“There hasn’t been too much recent consultation, but we hope to change that as the project continues on,” said Muhammed Ali, advocacy lead for Cnib Saskatchewan.

Muhammed says the Cnib gave feedback to Saskatoon’s Accessibility Advisory Committee on bus stop locations and other design considerations such as lighting contrast and wayfinding, adding that the group hopes to complete its own accessibility audit on the system.

Magus said that while station designs are complete, adjustments are possible if needed.

However, some items, such as trees located at bus stops, are fixed and cannot be removed.

“So hopefully folks that are partially sighted or blind, they’ll learn where those things are so when they approach that area next time hopefully they can have some sense of where to go,” he said, adding that designers are looking to make sure there is enough clearance for these items.

The city now anticipates the entire BRT system will be fully operational in the summer of 2029, according to a news release on Thursday, citing the recently approved corridor on 1st Avenue as the “biggest obstacle” to an earlier full-service launch date.

The city says it will begin service improvements in January, marking the start of a “gradual phase-in” of the system.

Previously, the city targeted a 2028 launch of service.

“With a 2029 full launch, additional time would support testing and further refinement of transit signal priority, queue-jump lanes, staff training and the operational transition to the redesigned network,” the news release says.

The city expects the transit corridor on 1st Avenue, along with other hubs connecting local routes, to be the last portion completed in 2029.

In a report from city administrators to the governance and priorities committee, July is identified as the preferred launch month because ridership dips in summer, leaving time to adjust before schools resume in the fall.

City councillors approved the designs along 1st Avenue in September after administration spent months consulting with stakeholders . The city is still designing this corridor, with construction expected to run into late 2028 and possibly spill over into 2029, according to the report. Running the new Link network will cost about $13.5 million a year, up from an earlier estimate of $11 million. About $4.3 million is already in the 2026 and 2027 budgets, leaving roughly $9.2 million for council to consider in the 2028-29 budget, according to the report.

The city expects BRT lanes along College Drive to be complete by fall of 2027. Meanwhile, construction on the transit hub will begin in 2028 with a targeted launch in July of 2029.

A 2029 launch would also mean the remaining estimated $9.2 million in operating phase-in costs will be spread over two budget cycles — in 2028 and 2029 — rather than primarily in 2028, the city said.

The BRT system is designed to support rapid transit service across three lines and includes 94 transit station platforms and signal priority, according to the city.

Dimayuga said it is important that codes are followed to make sure there is consistency in design across cities, but how people interact with design is unique to each city and people with different kinds of disabilities, emphasizing the importance of getting hands-on feedback.
Getting accessibility advocates to test out a system before it is operational is also a good idea, said Dimayuga, adding that it is not typical for cities to do it.

“I think more places should do this to basically show people either an implementation or a prototype of what the system will actually look like,” she said. “The devil is really in the details when it comes to accessibility and someone with a disability May not know that there’s an issue until they actually see it.”
The Canadian National Institute for the Blind (Cnib) says the city has consulted with it on the BRT stations, but it is awaiting further updates.
“There hasn’t been too much recent consultation, but we hope to change that as the project continues on,” said Muhammed Ali, advocacy lead for Cnib Saskatchewan.

Muhammed says the Cnib gave feedback to Saskatoon’s Accessibility Advisory Committee on bus stop locations and other design considerations such as lighting contrast and wayfinding, adding that the group hopes to complete its own accessibility audit on the system.
Magus said that while station designs are complete, adjustments are possible if needed.
However, some items, such as trees located at bus stops, are fixed and cannot be removed.

“So hopefully folks that are partially sighted or blind, they’ll learn where those things are so when they approach that area next time hopefully they can have some sense of where to go,” he said, adding that designers are looking to make sure there is enough clearance for these items.

The city now anticipates the entire BRT system will be fully operational in the summer of 2029, according to a news release on Thursday, citing the recently approved corridor on 1st Avenue as the “biggest obstacle” to an earlier full-service launch date.
The city says it will begin service improvements in January, marking the start of a “gradual phase-in” of the system.
Previously, the city targeted a 2028 launch of service.

“With a 2029 full launch, additional time would support testing and further refinement of transit signal priority, queue-jump lanes, staff training and the operational transition to the redesigned network,” the news release says.
The city expects the transit corridor on 1st Avenue, along with other hubs connecting local routes, to be the last portion completed in 2029.

In a report from city administrators to the governance and priorities committee, July is identified as the preferred launch month because ridership dips in summer, leaving time to adjust before schools resume in the fall.

City councillors approved the designs along 1st Avenue in September after administration spent months consulting with stakeholders . The city is still designing this corridor, with construction expected to run into late 2028 and possibly spill over into 2029, according to the report. Running the new Link network will cost about $13.5 million a year, up from an earlier estimate of $11 million. About $4.3 million is already in the 2026 and 2027 budgets, leaving roughly $9.2 million for council to consider in the 2028-29 budget, according to the report.
The city expects BRT lanes along College Drive to be complete by fall of 2027. Meanwhile, construction on the transit hub will begin in 2028 with a targeted launch in July of 2029.
A 2029 launch would also mean the remaining estimated $9.2 million in operating phase-in costs will be spread over two budget cycles — in 2028 and 2029 — rather than primarily in 2028, the city said.
The BRT system is designed to support rapid transit service across three lines and includes 94 transit station platforms and signal priority, according to the city.

content_blocks.text: When Robin East waits for a bus, he makes several considerations before it arrives.
“So if I’m standing here and then I hear the bus coming, I’m going to have to figure out when it’s going to stop, but where’s the door?” he said.
East, who is blind, has to consider everything from where he can stand safely on a platform to where he should board.

Sometimes, the obstacles are literal. During an interview with Global News, East demonstrated how he would navigate Saskatoon’s new bus rapid transit (BRT) stops along Broadway Avenue, but walked into the branches of a tree located on the bus platform.
“So that’s always a problem,” East said. Without echoes or other audio cues, he said, there’s often nothing to tell him a shelter or other physical barriers are in the way.
East helped bring voice announcements to Saskatoon buses more than a decade ago. Now, he is concerned the city is not listening on its latest BRT designs.
“I think the city has done some good work in communications and some good work with regards to that meaningful engagement, but it hasn’t gone far enough,” he said.
“It seems to have a plan and it doesn’t want to move too far from that plan and that means that that engagement is not meaningful.”
East says he considers meaningful engagement an ongoing process between people with disabilities and those designing the system, with good design aligning with accessibility codes.

“We have the Accessible Canada Act and we have a number of pieces from Accessible Standards Canada which allow us to have wayfinding to and from these transportation pieces,” he said. “So there’s no reason why, as they build this system, that it’s not fully accessible.” City councillors approved a plan in late September for BRT lanes on a stretch of First Avenue, with stations in the centre of the road.

“I’m really frustrated that at this point in time with the building of the platforms, there’s a lot of accessibility pieces that are missing,” he said.
