stories.title: Balloon blowing kits sold by Walmart.CA recalled over chemical hazard
stories.summary: The agency said the kits, distributed by the Chinese companies Tojiyi and PawBabyBloom, were previously available on the Walmart.CA Marketplace.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Health Canada is advising the public to stop using balloon blowing kits immediately due to a chemical hazard.

The agency said the kits, distributed by the Chinese companies Tojiyi and PawBabyBloom, were previously available on the Walmart.CA Marketplace.

Balloon blowing kits containing solvents are banned in Canada under the Toys Regulations of the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act, Health Canada said.

The solvent mixture comes in a tube that is squeezed on the end of a plastic straw. Children can then blow through the straw to create a bubble.

“The safety concern is that blowing the balloons exposes a child to inhaling the vapours of any solvents present,” the Health Canada recall states. “If children blow this type of solvent containing balloon for extended periods they May experience early symptoms of central nervous system depression or dysfunction, including euphoria, hallucinations, dizziness, and difficulties with coordination of voluntary movements.”

Walmart.CA Marketplace reported that six units of the affected products were sold in Canada, according to the health agency. The products have since been removed from sale online.

Health Canada said it has contacted the foreign third-party sellers and is advising consumers to stop using the products immediately.

To date, no incidents or injuries related to these products have been reported, the agency said.

stories.title: Cadet captain unable to walk after ‘senseless attack’ during Hamilton poppy sale
stories.summary: A man who suffered life-altering injuries during an incident involving cadets selling poppies underwent same-day spinal surgery and is now in rehabilitation, his son says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A man who suffered life-altering injuries during an incident involving air cadets selling poppies underwent same-day spinal surgery and is now in rehabilitation, his son says.

Capt. Kenneth Kunkel cannot walk for the “foreseeable future,” according to a statement from his son, Christopher Kunkel, who said the family has been “decimated” by the “senseless attack.”

The 59-year-old was supervising the cadets outside a restaurant in Hamilton, Ont., ON Nov. 1 when two youths allegedly approached and blew an air horn directly into their ears, Hamilton police said.

Police said Kunkel followed the youths into the restaurant and confronted them. During the ensuing struggle, an adult woman intervened and allegedly assaulted him, causing him to fall, before one youth allegedly struck him several times.

Christopher said his father’s legs buckled and he lost movement during the confrontation after the woman allegedly became involved. He said Kenneth told bystanders that he needed help and could not move his legs.

“After an unforgettable Halloween evening where Captain Kenneth Kunkel walked his four grandchildren around the neighbourhood to visit friends and neighbours, we are decimated by the senseless attack that May have forever robbed four kids of their grandfather’s playful, loving tendencies,” Christopher said.

His father has been helping cadets for almost 20 years, he said, adding Kenneth was instrumental in his own journey through the cadet program and into service with the Canadian Armed Forces.

Christopher said his father’s work also influenced former cadets who later joined municipal police services, the RCMP and the military, or became more involved in their communities.

“Even as he got older, Captain Kenneth Kunkel would physically prepare for weeks in advance so he could train with cadets and be a role model as they underwent fitness evaluations as part of the cadet program,” he said.

A crowdfunding campaign has been established to help financially support Kunkel’s recovery.

A 12-year-old boy was arrested Sunday and was charged with assault level one as well as aggravated assault. A 48-year-old woman was arrested Tuesday and charged with aggravated assault.

Police did not announce charges against the second youth.

The investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Two more soldiers injured in CFB Wainwright fire out of hospital
stories.summary: The Department of National Defence also says four of the 25 soldiers who remain hospitalized have been relocated to centres in British Columbia and Ontario.
stories.author: Fakiha Baig
stories.content:
Two more soldiers injured in a deadly fire at an Alberta military base have been discharged from hospital.

The Department of National Defence also says four of the 25 soldiers who remain hospitalized have been relocated to centres in British Columbia and Ontario, so they can receive treatment closer to their families.

The update comes a little more than two weeks after a fierce wind whipped a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright onto troops in a training exercise.

The Oct. 17 blaze killed four and left 39 wounded, many with serious burns.

Officials previously said 13 were in critical condition.

A total of 14 have now been released from hospital.

“Recovery will look different for each injured person and their family. Some may face a long journey ahead, but they will not face it alone,” said a news release.

“Ongoing support and services remain available to injured personnel, their families, and all CAF members as they continue to navigate the effects of this tragedy.”

Three separate investigations are looking into the fire.

stories.title: Southwestern Public Health approves move to centralized Woodstock facility by 2027
stories.summary: The health unit’s board of health has approved a move to 712 Peel St., bringing services currently spread across three Woodstock locations under one roof.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Southwestern Public Health says it plans to consolidate its Woodstock operations into a single location by 2027.

The health unit’s board of health has approved a move to 712 Peel St., bringing services currently spread across three Woodstock locations under one roof.

Southwestern Public Health currently operates from offices at 410 Buller St. and 93 Graham St., as well as leased dental space at the Oxford County Community Health Centre.

The move is expected to take place in late summer 2027. As a tenant, the health unit said it will occupy about half of the building, while the remainder will continue to be used independently by the property owner.

The board struck a special building committee in 2023 to explore options for consolidating operations, including new construction, leased space and other development opportunities.

The committee selected the Peel Street site, citing its location, functionality and value.

“This central site offers an efficient use of existing public sector space that is currently underused,” Bernia Martin, chair of the Southwestern Public Health Board of Health, said in a statement.

“It keeps public health services local, with a more practical approach to delivering those services to our clients.”

Renovations are scheduled to begin this fall, with completion anticipated in late summer 2027.

The health unit says it will provide updates to the community as planning for the move progresses.

stories.title: 1 in 3 teens face dating violence, and doctors should be on alert: pediatric society
stories.summary: The Canadian Paediatric Society is urging doctors to talk to teen patients about healthy relationships and dating violence. In new guidance issued Thursday, the society said one-third of teens in Canada experience physical, psychological, sexual or technology-related abuse — including stalking — in relationships. Dating violence among teens is not new, but…
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
The Canadian Paediatric Society is urging doctors to talk to teen patients about healthy relationships and dating violence.

In new guidance issued Thursday, the society said one-third of teens in Canada experience physical, psychological, sexual or technology-related abuse — including stalking — in relationships.

Dating violence among teens is not new, but technology like texting or social media can facilitate abusive behaviour, such as teens tracking their partners or forbidding them from communicating with friends, said Dr. Megan Harrison, chair of the society’s adolescent health committee, in an interview.

“Those types of behaviours happen to adults as well. So not just teens, but the difference is an adolescent is still, you know, forming their own identity,” she said.

“So it’s a more vulnerable time for things like that to be occurring.”

The guidance says health-care providers can normalize talking about healthy and unhealthy relationships by routinely bringing up the topic during adolescent patient visits.

“The more places where teens can feel comfortable to ask questions about relationships and to know that it’s something that they can bring up in a safe place … the better we’ll be able to prevent these unhealthy situations,” said Harrison, who is a pediatrician in the division of adolescent medicine at the Children’s Hospital of Eastern Ontario in Ottawa.

Harrison emphasized that doctors don’t need to have answers if a teen patient discloses a problematic relationship, but are providing a safe, non-judgmental space and then connecting them to other resources in the community as needed.

“You can really do a whole lot of good in actually what ends up being a really short period of time,” she said.

The guidance recommends doctors talk to teen patients alone during part of their visits and assure them that their conversation is confidential, unless the physician is immediately worried for their safety or the safety of someone else.

It also says doctors should share educational resources about healthy relationships and teen dating violence that their patient can keep or share with friends. The guidance provides an example for health-care providers on how to start that conversation.

“A lot of dating relationships are great experiences. But some patients have shared that they have experienced situations in their relationships that made them feel uncomfortable or even scared,” the sample script says.

“We now talk to all our patients about their relationships because they can impact health. We also provide education on this topic because it is likely you or someone you know could use it.”

If the teen discloses problematic behaviour in a relationship, the health-care provider should support them by thanking them for their trust and connecting them with other resources in the community that can help.

In some cases, that can include taking the first step with the patient, Harrison said.

“If the youth feels comfortable at that time, maybe I make a phone call with the youth in the office. Maybe I help them make an appointment if that’s what they’d like, or I sit there with them while they make the phone call, or we open up the web page together.”

If the patient is going to access resources later on their own, the guidance advises discussing the possibility that an abusive partner May track the teen’s online activity and asking if printed materials would be a safer option.

Some teens are at increased risk for dating violence, including those who are homeless or living in poverty, gender-diverse youth, Black and Indigenous female teens, and young people living in care systems, the guidance says.

stories.title: Merlot from the Okanagan deserves some spotlight. Here are three bottles to try
stories.summary: The underrated red wine is consistently one of the best categories from the region, say winemakers
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Although merlot has played an important role in the evolution of British Columbia’s wine industry, it’s less celebrated among winemakers than more expressive red varieties, such as pinot noir, cabernet franc or syrah.

In the 1990s and early 2000s, merlot gained favour among B.C. wineries because it ripens earlier than cabernet franc and cabernet sauvignon, making it a more reliable choice for the Okanagan’s relatively short growing season. Despite its role in producing some of British Columbia’s best bottles, merlot remains an underrated variety, according to Evan Saunders, winemaker at Blasted Church since 2017.

“I don’t think it gets the respect that it should,” he says. “Merlot is one of the most consistent reds that we produce in the valley.”

Saunders uses merlot to produce red blends with playful names, such as Big Bang Theory and Nectar of the Gods, as well as single variety examples. “Who doesn’t like its plummy, jammy character, with chocolate and coffee and everything else you get vintage in and vintage out,” he wonders.

Nevertheless, merlot has yet to find its place in the spotlight. Saunders wonders if it’s too successful to be taken seriously.

Before back-to-back cold events in 2022 and 2025 caused widespread crop and vine losses, it was British Columbia’s most widely planted grape, covering nearly 753 hectares, or more than 14.5 per cent of the province’s total vineyard acreage. In the aftermath, grape growers have been replanting damaged vineyards with varieties, such as pinot noir, chardonnay and gamay, which they hope will reduce the threat of frigid temperatures. (Winegrowers of British Columbia plans to release an up-to-date vine census next year that will reflect the changing face of its vineyards.)

Saunders says exploring alternative grapes helps determine what will be successful in vineyards in the Okanagan and other parts of the province. Blasted Church planted nebbiolo near the winery in 2023 and has purchased other Italian grape varieties, including refosco, teroldego, and lagrein, from a grower in the Similkameen.

Italian grapes are well-suited to the increasing temperatures experienced in the southern Okanagan, he explains. (Saunders also produces a tart and refreshing rosé from blaufränkisch, a Slovenian grape variety planted in 1996 on what is now the winery’s estate vineyard in Okanagan Falls.)

“Just because the Bordeaux varieties were planted first doesn’t mean we have to stick with them entirely,” he says. “But merlot is always going to have a place.”

Tony Holler, owner of Poplar Grove in Penticton, believes merlot is enjoying renewed interest among consumers. “Our merlot sells out before our cabernet franc,” he says.

In addition to producing a merlot under its own label, Poplar Grove uses the variety in its flagship red blend, Legacy, alongside cabernet sauvignon, petit verdot, cabernet franc and malbec. The proportions of each grape vary depending on the vintage.

Merlot is also a regular component of Poplar Grove’s annual rosé blend.

Here are three Okanagan wines that display merlot’s star power.

Blasted Church Merlot 2022 (Canada), $34

Produced with merlot grapes grown in Blasted Church’s estate vineyard on the Skaka Bench appellation, this smooth and concentrated red wine offers a charming mix of savoury, spicy and dark fruit flavours. The full-bodied style gains complexity from chocolate and tobacco notes. This has 14.9-per-cent alcohol by volume and 0.4 grams a litre residual sugar. Drink now to 2030. Available at the above price direct, blastedchurch.com , various prices in Alberta, $34 in Manitoba.

Painted Rock Merlot 2022 (Canada), $49.99

Painted Rock Merlot has consistently stood out among the labels produced by the Skinner family at its estate overlooking Skaha Lake. The 2022 vintage is the result of an exceptional growing season, which contributes to the satisfying mix of juicy berry and cherry flavours and savoury oak-derived notes. Like all of Painted Rock’s red wine portfolio, this full-bodied merlot has excellent aging potential because of its serious structure and impressive length. This has 14.6-per-cent ABV and 2.7 g/litre r.s. Drink now to 2032. Available at the above price direct, paintedrock.CA , $54.99 in British Columbia, various prices in Alberta.

Poplar Grove Merlot 2022 (Canada), $32.99

A small percentage of malbec is blended into this flavourful merlot, made from grapes grown in south-central Okanagan. The wine showcases dark fruit flavours that are enhanced by chocolate and spice notes. Its concentrated character and supple texture are balanced by a polished structure and lingering finish. Ripe and age-worthy, the winery has held back inventory to release as a 10-year-old wine to showcase its aging potential. This has 14.9-per-cent ABV and 0.39 r.s. Drink now to 2035. Available at the above price direct, poplargrove.CA , $35.99 in British Columbia, various prices in Alberta, $34.99 in Manitoba.

stories.title: Restoration plans for historic Emslie Field grandstand to be determined by 2027 budget
stories.summary: St. Thomas city council has decided it can wait a little longer after deferring restoration options to the incoming council and the 2027 budget.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The fate of the historic grandstand at Emslie Field in St. Thomas, Ont., has been a contentious issue over the past 12 months.

St. Thomas city council has decided it can wait a little longer after deferring restoration options to the incoming council and the 2027 budget.

“The decision to defer this to the budget is good news for us,” said Derek Brooks, director of the St. Thomas Minor Baseball Association (Stmba).

Since the city closed the grandstand for safety reasons in November 2025, there have been concerns the city would tear down the structure, which was built in 1938.

Council was presented with three options:

A full rehabilitation lasting 40 to 50 years for $1,172,000.

A minimum rehabilitation for $785,950 (with $600,000 previously earmarked in the capital budget and $100,000 committed by St. Thomas Minor Baseball) lasting 15 years.

Demolition and modern replacement with bleachers for $971,000.

After a structural condition assessment was completed , city staff recommended council choose the second option . However, council was divided at the meeting.

“If we go to a full restoration of the current building for about $472,000 more, we get 45 to 50 years,” said Coun. Gary Clarke.

“I just think that with the high cost of doing a part way renewal, that 15 years from now, we’re back where we were, and it’s kind of a waste of money.”

Coun. Steve Wookey supported either of the two rehabilitation options.

“I’m okay with refurbishing it and us putting in our 600,000 and other people coming with the rest, as long as that’s revenue neutral,” said Wookey.

“I’m also okay with it being the fuller rebuild, because I talk all the time about cost-benefit analysis. If we can do something that’s going to last 50 years instead of 15 years, then we are reducing our costs later on.”

Outgoing councillor Jim Herbert was supportive of the minimum rehabilitation, while outgoing councillor Joan Rymal wondered if a new structure was a better idea.

“All I want is for it to be safe and usable,” Wookey told CTV News.

“If the baseball community wants it to be redone as opposed to something new built, I have respect for that. I’m pleased to do that as long as it’s revenue neutral for the taxpayers of the city of Saint Thomas. If we put $600,000 into it, and they want to put the other $185,000 into it, then I’m great with that and we keep something that people really want.”

With members of the Stmba in the gallery, council ultimately decided to include the options in the 2027 budget and let the incoming council decide the grandstand’s fate.

“Ultimately the restoration of the existing structure is what we wanted whether that was the first option or the second option,” said Brooks.

“We’re committed to support financially what we were willing to put forward initially, and that hasn’t changed. So, we’ll continue to work with city council and the new city council for sure when they’re sworn in.”

Brooks and many members of the community have expressed their desire to keep the historic structure, which provides shade for those attending games throughout the summer and gives a classic look to the ballpark, which opened in 1898 at Pinafore Park.

“There’s a ton of history there,” said Brooks.

“You look at Bob Emslie (former MLB pitcher and umpire) and you look at Jack Graney (former MLB pitcher and broadcaster). All of those historical baseball figures have roots here in Saint Thomas. That grandstand, with the recent dedication of the press box to Graney and obviously the name of the park after Emslie. It’s important to maintain that park as close to the way it is now for the future.”

The views of the community and the Stmba are not lost on members of city council.

“I was a history teacher for 30 years,” said Wookey outside the meeting.

“I care a lot about history, and so I’d love to see it maintained and saved as long as it makes financial sense for all the parties involved. Baseball (Stmba), as always, put their money where their mouth is and I have a great deal of respect for that. They’re doing the same thing again this time, so I’d be pleased to support them in that.”

stories.title: U.S. midterm results spark joy among Canadians but trust in America remains shaky
stories.summary: Many Canadians welcome the Democratic sweep of U.S. Congress, but have mixed views on whether voters’ strong rebuke of President Donald Trump’s administration will change their attitude toward America amid the ongoing trade war.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — Many Canadians welcome the Democratic sweep of U.S. Congress, but have mixed views on whether voters’ strong rebuke of President Donald Trump’s administration will change their attitude toward America amid the ongoing trade war.

Trump’s punishing tariffs on Canadian goods, repeated musings about making Canada the 51st state and escalating tensions that include changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America have had a profound impact on the relationship between the two countries.

The response from Canadians has been strong, with many avoiding cross-border travel and U.S.-made products, and reconsidering the long-standing cultural and economic ties with their American neighbours.

Juli Taylor said even though she’s happy with the midterm results, she isn’t planning to visit the United States any time soon.

“I’m Canadian, we are very proud of our country and we have been picked on a lot and we are done — and we’re absolutely overjoyed with the outcome in the States,” she said in an interview in Toronto the morning after the midterms.

Taylor said she would probably consider vacationing across the border if the tariff dispute is resolved, “but it’s not my first choice, anyways.”

“We live in a beautiful country and the best country in the world, so we need to put our money back in our own economy,” she said.

Blair Coyle, who also said he stopped visiting the United States, hopes Democratic control of the House of Representatives and the Senate will help ease tensions between the two nations.

“It means that maybe I can go to the U.S. again on a vacation,” he said, adding that he instead travelled to Europe three times this year.

Uwe Richter said while he strongly favours any political change in the United States that puts a check on Trump’s power, he still plans to boycott American products “as much as it’s possible.”

“And that will not change easily,” he said, “because what Trump has done is he has damaged the situation between our two countries and the rest of the world very, very much.”

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Wednesday that Ottawa’s push to diversify trade won’t change as Democrats take control of Congress, and that recent talks with Trump’s administration have been productive.

Richter said it will take a lot of work to rebuild trust and the Canada-U.S. relationship nearly two years into Trump’s second term.

“I think there would have to be quite a lot of change in the situation between our two countries before I would put any money over there, by travelling over there,” he said at a downtown Toronto park.

For some Canadians, the Republicans’ defeat in these elections doesn’t necessarily signal a change in course.

Gerry Carlin noted that Trump has stated he would use “tremendous” veto powers if his party loses in the midterms.

“I don’t trust him, first of all, and I don’t trust the policies he’s got. I don’t know that they’re going to disappear,” he said.

“I would hope that the Democrats having power in both houses now will ease those ... but we don’t know, there’s no guarantee of anything at this point,” Carlin added.

“You still got two years to go.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Sharif Hassan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: CBC to broaden personal finance programming with launch of CBC Money
stories.summary: Public broadcaster hiring 16 journalists for the unit, which will feature new and existing content dedicated to money matters
stories.author: Nicole Thompson
stories.content:
Canada’s public broadcaster is launching a slate of new personal finance programming under the umbrella CBC Money.

CBC says the content dedicated to “money matters” will launch next year, with programming “across entertainment and news” on TV, radio and online.

It will include a new video series from CBC Radio’s Cost of Living hosted by business journalist Paul Haavardsrud, offering practical tips.

CBC Money will also feature new personal finance entertainment shows.

The broadcaster says existing programming, such as Dragon’s Den , will also fall under the CBC Money umbrella.

It says it’s hiring 16 new journalists to support the initiative, including nine who will work out of a new studio in downtown Calgary.

CBC says it will also hire five new business reporters in Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg and Halifax to support the programming, plus two producers in Toronto.

“With CBC Money, we will move beyond market updates and boardroom chatter, delivering essential stories of money-planning strategies and financial resilience to help Canadians make more informed decisions,” said Brodie Fenlon, editor-in-chief of CBC News, in a statement.

stories.title: A Toronto home of both function and whimsy
stories.summary: The two-storey addition engages with the older building, but nothing about it is ordinary
stories.author: Alex Bozikovic
stories.content:
The building on Jones Avenue was trying to disappear. A 1950s doctor’s office, it had been converted to apartments, carelessly clad with siding and vinyl windows. But the building found people who could see its inherent beauty, and add to it. Architect Anne-Marie Armstrong of AAmp Studio and her husband, graphic designer Todd Temporale, noticed handsome limestone window surrounds and a wall of glazed yellow brick. These things signalled a gem worth polishing.

And Ms. Armstrong revels in such a task. “There’s a belief that Toronto can feel a bit beige,” she says. “And yet there are these wonderful moments hiding in some of these buildings. Finding those excites me.”

Attentiveness to history, to detail and to the potential of an existing building: these are characteristics of any good architect, and AAmp has them in abundance. Ms. Armstrong founded the office with colleague Andrew Ashey in 2017 after meeting as architects in Los Angeles. Together, their work has emphasized hospitality projects and adaptive reuse of existing buildings, or both, as at a hotel in Georgia carved out of a mid-century bank building.

At the Jones building, the work came in two stages. A 2020 renovation reworked the building as an office and two apartments. Last year, the couple completed a 2,500-square-foot addition as a home for their family.

The two-storey addition engages with the older building, nearly – but not quite – matching its brick and adding blue glazed masonry to complement the original’s lemon yellow. But nothing about the addition is ordinary: it is an extraordinarily deft composition, the work of architects whose spatial intelligence is matched by their sensitivity. The interlocking levels and carefully orchestrated views evoke the spatial drama of Richard Neutra’s California houses. A second-floor kitchen and dining room look south across Toronto while a double-height void, framed by a wall of oak cabinetry, connects them with the bedroom above. The vertical volume is set against the horizontal sweep of the city.

The interior reflects the owners’ highly refined taste. There are Chandigarh chairs, bought second-hand, and a Carlo Scarpa table that belonged to Mr. Temporale’s father. Red marble and moss-green laminate punctuate a palette of white walls and pale wood.

But the addition is just as compelling where it intersects with the old medical building – as in the stairwell, where old pale-brown brick meets crisp new masonry and carefully crafted terrazzo. A red-painted railing provides a hit of spice.

An architect’s home is usually a manifesto, and Ms. Armstrong is explicit about her principles here. “This place is robust, it is functional, but there are these moments of whimsy that are selective. There’s a certain attitude that a building can have these moments at the scale of the person.”

Its brickwork uses stack bond, as does part of the original façade – a pattern in which the bricks are laid out in a regular grid with their long sides out – and some new windows relate to the openings below. But those alignments are selective, extending the composition of the original façade in asymmetric fashion. This is a conversation between the generations. Ms. Armstrong devoted effort even to restoring the original building: when the old yellow glazed brick couldn’t be matched in contemporary production, she convinced an Italian manufacturer, SantAnselmo, to make a small custom order.

That’s a big lift for a building with no heritage protection and no pedigree. (Its original designers are identified on the 1956 drawings as Design Incorporated, a firm that has receded into history.) But the building’s former use as a doctor’s office is well known. People have stopped to tell Mr. Temporale and Ms. Armstrong that they once came here to see Dr. Baggs and Dr. Coulter. “I really want to care for this building,” Ms. Armstrong says, “because I think the neighbourhood cares for the building too. And that means bringing new life to it.”

While architects often pay lip service to that idea, AAMp’s work builds on it. Mr. Ashey, who runs a second office for AAmp in Portland, Maine, described the studio’s design approach as open-minded. “We really consider design a democratic process,” he said. “We don’t come to the table with any preconceived ideas about how a project will evolve. The result is a product of the clients and the context where we are working – the city and the buildings.”

Not just great buildings, but ordinary ones. That specific ethos goes back to the famously jumbled streetscape of Los Angeles, where Ms. Armstrong worked for Frank Gehry and Marmol Radziner. There Mr. Ashey and Ms. Armstrong created a publication, Annotated Journal , as a way of recording aspects of the city that caught their attention: often peculiar details that might not be considered architecture at all.

Such a democratic eye is a gift in Toronto, where the buildings that define its old main streets are products of a humble industrial town. Toronto city planning has in recent years used heritage policy to lock down thousands of older buildings, good ones and bad ones alike. That censorious attitude doesn’t come with a route for the old city to change and evolve. On Jones Avenue, AAmp have defined a different attitude to the city fabric: to work with old buildings out of love and not duty, with creativity and the odd jot of colour. That is how a city can evolve and stay alive, ever changing.

stories.title: Price cut, finishing touches help find a buyer for lakefront cottage
stories.summary: Three-bedroom bungalow sells for more than $2.6-million
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
383 Snug Harbour Rd., Lindsay, Ont.

Asking price: $2.85-million (August, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $3.35-million (March, 2025); $3,449,000 (January, 2025); $3,449,000 (December, 2024)

Selling price: $2,625,000 (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: Not applicable

Taxes: $13,814 (2025)

Days on the market: 33

Property days on market: 332

Listing agents: Jason Challenger, John Ireland and Bryce Boyce, Affinity Group Pinnacle Realty Ltd.

This three-bedroom bungalow, newly built on a 1.04-acre lot on Sturgeon Lake northeast of Toronto, was listed around $3.4-million for about 10 months in 2025. Buyers were astonished by its custom design, but disappointed by unfinished elements, like the driveway to the attached, triple garage.

“There were only a handful of places sold over $2-million in the last two years,” said agent John Ireland. “It’s very rare for properties to go over that price point in this area.

“A lot of people in the country have gravel driveways, but if someone’s going to spend $2.5-million to $3-million, they want an asphalt driveway.”

The property, taken off the market for one year, reappeared with a new driveway and boathouse, and a reduced price tag this summer. It had visitors every week, including repeat guests who took a swim along the 32-foot shoreline before negotiating a $2,625,000 deal this fall.

“At one point, I had 22 listings, and this one had more activity than almost all of them combined,” Mr. Ireland said.

“If this house was up in Muskoka, depending on what lake it’s on and other variables, it could be worth probably double. People find value here in the Kawarthas, and you’re only an hour and a half [drive] from the city.”

This bungalow has 2,897 square feet of living space, including a kitchen, three bathrooms and a laundry room connected to well water and septic systems.

The main floor has three bedrooms and a living room with vaulted ceilings and access to a deck.

The basement has three bedrooms and a recreation area with an exit to the patio.

“It was an exceptional home,” Mr. Ireland said.

“For example, they put in under 90 tons of limestone on the exterior, and you never see that.”

stories.title: Court certifies class action alleging negligence at LTC home led to COVID-19 deaths
stories.summary: A lawsuit alleging that gross negligence at a Toronto long-term care home led to hundreds of deaths from COVID-19 has been certified as a class action.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A lawsuit alleging that gross negligence at a Toronto long-term care home led to hundreds of deaths from COVID-19 has been certified as a class action.

An Ontario Superior Court judge granted the certification last week with the consent of the defendants, the Downsview Long-Term Care Centre Limited and the company that owns it, Gem Healthcare Group Limited.

The lawsuit alleges Downsview and Gem were grossly negligent in their response to the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in multiple outbreaks at the home between late January 2020 and early May 2023.

It alleges those outbreaks caused at least 1,966 residents to get COVID-19 and at least 244 to die from it.

The plaintiffs include residents, people receiving care and visitors who contracted COVID-19 at the home during that period or their estates, as well as their family members.

The allegations have not been tested at trial. Downsview and Gem have said they intend to defend themselves against the allegations.

Billy Powell, whose mother Zellora Graham lived at Downsview until she died from COVID-19 in May 2020, is named as a representative plaintiff in a statement of claim filed a year ago.

Graham moved to Downsview in September 2017, a few months after suffering a hip fracture, the document said. She had arthritis and used a walker to get around. She had no other chronic conditions, it said.

By the time the pandemic hit the province, Graham was living in a private room but ate and watched TV in communal areas, the statement of claim said.

Powell last visited his mother in early March 2020, about a week before the Ontario government imposed restrictions on visits to long-term care homes, the document said. After that, he received “little to no information” about his mother or her health, it said.

He only learned of the possible risk to his mother after his wife saw a news article in late April about a COVID-19 outbreak at Downsview, the statement of claim said. Staff asked if he wanted Graham to stay at Downsview or get transferred to hospital, and Powell and his siblings agreed she should go to a hospital, it said.

Once she arrived, Graham tested positive for COVID-19, the statement of claim said. The lawsuit further alleges the outbreaks were preventable had Downsview and Gem not breached their common law obligations.

In his ruling, Justice Edward Morgan said there is some factual basis to support those allegations for the purpose of certification.

“Given the number of class members and the economics of pursuing a claim of this nature requiring expert evidence, a class proceeding is the preferable procedure for ensuring their just and expeditious determination, promoting judicial economy, and seeking behaviour modification,” he wrote.

stories.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk to perform second spacewalk
stories.summary: Before Kutryk, the last Canadian to perform a spacewalk was David Saint-Jacques in 2019
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk completed his second spacewalk on Thursday, spending nearly seven hours in the vacuum of space as he worked to upgrade the International Space Station’s power system.

Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon stepped back into the space station at the end of a six-hour, 59 minute spacewalk that ended at 3:35 p.m. ET.

NASA astronaut Nichole Stilwell, who served as spacewalk communicator from Houston, congratulated the crew, which also included NASA’s Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins inside the station.

“You all showed us what the best of humanity looks like, executing one of the most difficult and dangerous things humans do, and making it look easy,” she said in a message that could be heard in NASA’s live broadcast.

Kutryk, in his first message upon returning to the space station, praised and thanked the teamwork that made the spacewalk possible.

“It really shows out here when you’re in the seat, hanging over the Earth, so thank you for that,” he said.

Kutryk became the fifth Canadian to perform a spacewalk on Oct. 29 when he and Menon worked together to install new solar arrays needed to upgrade the station’s power capacity.

Thursday was a fifth spacewalk for Menon, NASA said.

The astronauts installed the eighth and final solar array on the starboard side of the truss, which serves as the station’s structural backbone.

The spacewalk got under way just after 8:30 a.m., when the astronauts switched their suits to battery power. Kutryk was first to emerge from the Quest airlock, with a red stripe on the legs of his space suit setting him apart from his colleague.

Video broadcast by NASA showed the two working step by step with tools while tethered to the space station, sometimes with a view of Earth in the background.

The campaign to upgrade the solar arrays began in 2021 and is expected to increase the station’s power generation capacity by up to 30 per cent, according to the agency.

As the spacewalk ended, Menon paid tribute to over 15 years of development effort that went into the solar arrays, which he said will “provide power that will continue to allow the station to be a staircase for the moon, and eventually Mars.”

The Canadian Space Agency says spacewalks are among the most difficult and dangerous tasks for astronauts, but are needed to repair or install equipment or carry out manual work.

Before Kutryk, the last Canadian to perform a spacewalk was David Saint-Jacques in 2019.

Kutryk and his fellow crew members took off for the International Space Station on Oct. 1 for a mission expected to last six months.

The Canadian Space Agency says there were several Canadians playing key roles in Thursday’s spacewalk. Those include CSA astronaut Jenni Gibbons, who spoke with the crew as capsule communicator, or capcom, from Houston.

The Canadarm 2 robotic arm was used to move the solar array, while CSA teams in Longueuil, Que., helped to support operations, the agency said.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly identified Jenni Gibbons as capsule commander. She is the capsule communicator.

stories.title: Ghana praises Canada for advocating against a ‘rigged global system’ for African countries
stories.summary: Canada has for years called for reforms to financing rules for developing countries, many of which face high interest rates and crushing debtloads
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Ghana’s head of state praised Canada this week for advocating against what he called a “rigged global system” that keeps African countries trapped by debt and mired in climate chaos.

His comments come as Canadian officials confirm Ottawa will appoint a new Africa envoy, months after leaving the post vacant.

“Canada has a favourable disposition towards the Global South,” Ghana’s President John Mahama said Tuesday as he met with Prime Minister Mark Carney at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda.

“With what is going on in the world, I think that this is a time for us to come closer together.”

Developing countries advocated for financial reforms at the Commonwealth summit.

Canada has for years called for reforms to financing rules for developing countries, many of which face high interest rates and crushing debtloads.

Many of those countries – particularly smaller island countries in the Caribbean and South Pacific – are also being hit hard and more often by natural disasters.

Carney’s predecessor Justin Trudeau co-led a United Nations project that advocated for reforms to how the World Bank and others extend financing to countries. The project’s goal was to free up capital that countries could invest in climate-resilient hospitals and schools.

Carney has called for reforms to multilateral development banks and used the G7 summit in Alberta last year to announce funding for those institutions to bring in private capital to meet goals in education and climate adaptation.

Ghana now faces its worst economic crisis in a generation, due in part to its debt structure and the effects of climate change on major crops like cocoa. These trends have contributed to coups and instability in other parts of West Africa.

“You are a fresh, new voice in terms of global advocacy,” Mahama told Carney.

“Africa has been talking about the rigged global system, where Africa borrows more expensively. Africa contributed the least to climate crisis – four per cent contribution to climate crises – yet faces some of the worst crises caused by the climate events, and have to borrow at a higher rate to be able to deal with those climate fallouts.”

Mahama also noted Carney’s advocacy for rules-based trade as the U.S. trade war continues.

“You are quite vocal on issues to do with the breakdown in multilateralism and the rise of unilateral actions by some nations,” he said, adding Canada has borne “the brunt of some of the strongest tariffs.”

Carney made a widely publicized speech to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January. In it, he urged smaller countries to band together to limit coercion by superpowers.

Ghana is among many African states calling for a more equitable multilateral system. They’ve called for the United Nations to be restructured so rich, Western countries share more power with other nations.

Global Affairs says Ottawa will ultimately appoint a special envoy for Africa, after leaving the post vacant since June.

The new role was part of the Trudeau government’s Africa Strategy, which called for Canada to shift its policy for the continent away from a focus on foreign aid, and to pursue more economic engagement and trade with the continent’s young population.

The Trudeau government delayed the Africa strategy for years, issued it without a news conference days before an election call, and provided no new funding for the strategy. In 2022 the Indo-Pacific strategy came with a $2.3-billion pledge.

Last December, as experts warned Canada was losing influence on a continent where it used to have stronger ties, the Senate foreign affairs committee urged the Carney government to clarify its stance on Africa.

Officials testified last week to the committee in response to that report. Cheryl Urban, who leads the Africa branch of Global Affairs Canada, confirmed a continental envoy will be appointed, though she wasn’t sure when.

“We are currently reviewing it but we will have an appointment,” she testified in French, adding that the government is looking for someone with a background in business and trade.

Mahama said Canada should work to restore the reputation it built on the continent decades ago through the work of former aid agency Cida and as a major lender to African countries.

“Canada has had a very favourable ... opinion in Ghana. I think that there are things we can do to build back up,” he said.

stories.title: COVID class action certified over alleged negligence at Toronto long-term care home
stories.summary: Lawsuit alleges Downsview and Gem were grossly negligent in their response to the pandemic, resulting in multiple outbreaks at the home
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A lawsuit alleging that gross negligence at a Toronto long-term care home led to hundreds of deaths from COVID-19 has been certified as a class action.

An Ontario Superior Court judge granted the certification last week with the consent of the defendants, the Downsview Long-Term Care Centre Limited and the company that owns it, Gem Healthcare Group Limited.

The lawsuit alleges Downsview and Gem were grossly negligent in their response to the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in multiple outbreaks at the home between late January, 2020 and early May, 2023.

It alleges those outbreaks caused at least 191 residents to get COVID-19 and at least 65 to die from it.

The plaintiffs include residents, people receiving care and visitors who contracted COVID-19 at the home during that period or their estates, as well as their family members.

The allegations have not been tested at trial. Downsview and Gem have said they intend to defend themselves against the allegations.

Billy Powell, whose mother Zellora Graham lived at Downsview until she died from COVID-19 in May, 2020, is named as a representative plaintiff in a statement of claim filed a year ago.

Ms. Graham moved to Downsview in September, 2017, a few months after suffering a hip fracture, the document said. She had arthritis and used a walker to get around. She had no other chronic conditions, it said.

By the time the pandemic hit the province, Ms. Graham was living in a private room but ate and watched TV in communal areas, the statement of claim said.

Mr. Powell last visited his mother in early March, 2020, about a week before the Ontario government-imposed restrictions on visits to long-term care homes, the document said. After that, he received “little to no information” about his mother or her health, it said.

He only learned of the possible risk to his mother after his wife saw a news article in late April about a COVID-19 outbreak at Downsview, the statement of claim said. When he called the home, a nurse told him Ms. Graham was doing well and the virus had not spread to her section, the statement of claim said.

He asked to speak with his mother but was told she had gone to bed, and received the same answer when he called again in the following days, it said.

On May 1, 2020, Mr. Powell returned a missed call from the home and was told his mother was not doing well and was suspected to have COVID-19, the document said. Staff asked if he wanted Ms. Graham to stay at Downsview or get transferred to hospital, and Mr. Powell and his siblings agreed she should go to a hospital, it said.

Once she arrived, Ms. Graham tested positive for COVID-19, the statement of claim said. A doctor called Mr. Powell that evening, saying his mother was severely dehydrated and struggling to breathe, and that she had a 20-per-cent chance of survival, it said. A call the next day confirmed she was not improving, it said.

Ms. Graham died two days later.

The lawsuit alleges that long-standing deficiencies – including overcrowding, inadequate infection prevention and control practices, systemic failures to ensure compliance with regulatory, legal and industry standards, as well as understaffing – made the facility vulnerable to outbreaks.

It also alleges Downsview and Gem didn’t act quickly or proactively to impose infection prevention and control measures, and those they did implement did not reflect the state of knowledge on the virus and the risk it posed for elderly people.

The lawsuit further alleges the outbreaks were preventable had Downsview and Gem not breached their common law obligations.

In his ruling, Justice Edward Morgan said there is some factual basis to support those allegations for the purpose of certification.

“Given the number of class members and the economics of pursuing a claim of this nature requiring expert evidence, a class proceeding is the preferable procedure for ensuring their just and expeditious determination, promoting judicial economy, and seeking behaviour modification,” he wrote.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that the lawsuit alleged outbreaks caused at least 1,966 residents to get COVID-19 and at least 244 to die from it. This version has been corrected according to the amended court document, which states the lawsuit alleges that virus outbreaks caused at least 191 residents to get COVID-19 and at least 65 to die from COVID-19.

stories.title: The truth behind aquaculture and fish farming
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses the fishmeal industry and what consumers should know before choosing tonight's dinner.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Aquaculture was designed to relieve pressure off of the world’s fish supply. Instead, it’s compromised it.

Small fish are farmed, cooked, and grounded into fishmeal at the more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across the world – nine of which are located in Canada. The conditions inside and around these factories and boats threaten communities, local economies and dozens of lives.

Host Maria Kestane speaks to Maya Martin and Susan Ryan from the Outlaw Ocean Project to discuss their investigation into the fishmeal industry, and what consumers should know before choosing tonight’s dinner.

stories.title: Short film created by London brothers recognized internationally
stories.summary: London, Ont. brothers Andrey and Dmitriy Sarumyan scored two major titles at the Forest City Youth Film Festival.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
London, Ont. brothers Andrey and Dmitriy Sarumyan made history by becoming the first students from Saint André Bessette Catholic Secondary School to sweep two major titles at the Forest City Youth Film Festival.

“We always wanted to do a short film about action,” said Andrey. “Suspense and adventure.”

The short film, 1440 Minutes , won best overall film and most enterprising film.

“It has a small budget,” said Dmitriy. “You can compare it to Hollywood movies because we used our creativity.”

The film follows an agent who has exactly 1440 minutes, or 24 hours, to complete a mysterious mission, racing against time.

“The message we have for the audience is that we can’t really take back time,” said Andrey. “Every minute matters, every minute matters to us.”

The film is now receiving international recognition, winning awards in Amsterdam and Romania.

“We also got screeners at the American Film Festival and also the Niagara Film Festival,” said Dmitriy. “Those are important festivals, it’s not just for students, it’s also for high level filmmakers.”

The Grade 12 students hope their story encourages other young creators.

“For now, it’s a hobby,” said Andrey. “In the future we want to pursue this one and keep doing these great films like we did.”

stories.title: Cppib invests $50-million in fast-rising Toronto AI star Beacon Software
stories.summary: It’s a rare Canadian investment for the pension giant’s growth equity unit, which has also backed Cohere and Wealthsimple
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
Canada Pension Plan Investment Board has made a rare investment in a Canadian technology startup, buying a US$50-million stake in Toronto’s Beacon Software, which is putting an AI spin on the software consolidation playbook pioneered by Constellation Software CSU-T .

Beacon announced in June it had raised US$225-million in a financing led by U.S. private capital giants General Catalyst and HarbourVest Partners. It has since increased the round size to US$425-million, including Cppib’s investment, which it will announce Thursday.

The upsized deal values the company, legally named Beacon Acquisition Corp., at US$1.75-billion, including cash received. Beacon has now raised $750-million-plus since its 2024 founding, an unprecedented haul for such a young Canadian company.

That has fuelled equally head-spinning growth. The profitable company, following in the footsteps of fellow software giant Constellation, has bought 45 businesses in the sector. (Company leaders ring gongs in Beacon’s Toronto, New York and San Francisco offices on a Google Meet videocast every time it announces a new acquisition internally.)

Consolidated annual revenue at Beacon now tops US$200-million. Other investors include U.S. heavyweights Lightspeed Venture Partners, D1 Capital Partners and Canada’s Intrepid Growth Partners.

The growth hasn’t just come from acquisitions. Beacon buys software companies serving small conventional businesses such as campgrounds, concrete makers, dance studios, wealth managers, unions and private schools. It then adds AI agents built to address hundreds of workflows common across software businesses, such as incident response management and invoicing, said chief executive officer and co-founder Nilam Ganenthiran. Deploying those autonomous tools saves its acquired companies an average of 9.6 employee hours a week each, he said, freeing them for other business-building tasks.

Beacon’s strategy has paid off: Revenue growth at acquired companies has expanded by 10 percentage points after a year, increasing to a 20-percentage-point gain after two years, without any change to their employee head count, he said. That improves their operating profits. Intrepid co-founder Mark Shulgan called Mr. Ganenthiran “an execution machine” who has “far exceeded the base case that we underwrote.”

Mr. Ganenthiran said, “On the surface it looks like we’re building another Constellation, but that isn’t my goal.” He calls Beacon a “centralized AI holding company.”

Beacon CEO Mr. Ganenthiran, 42, grew up in the Toronto suburb of Scarborough after emigrating with his parents to Canada from Malaysia when he was a child. He was a young entrepreneur with an interest in grocery and consumer product businesses. He went to Harvard Business School and worked as an assistant brand manager on the IAMs pet food line for Procter & Gamble. He joined Instacart in 2013, later becoming president of the grocery delivery giant. He left in 2022, briefly serving as an investor with D1.

Mr. Ganenthiran was inspired to start Beacon as the first generation of AI agents came to market. His early goal was to bring the advances of AI to companies serving customers. He tried to build an AI incubator to create AI software for small companies, but customers were content with their existing vendors. So he decided to buy the vendors instead. He targeted self-financed, entrepreneur-led subscription software vendors with between US$1-million and US$25-million in annual revenues that provided essential software used by specific subsectors to run their businesses, but were limited in their ability to deploy AI.

Beacon has integrated acquired companies into a shared operating platform, deployed its own engineers to improve their code, provided sales leaders and embedded fintech for payment processing, banking and payroll – and added AI agents to their operations.

The company now has the capacity to go after larger deals, said Mr. Ganenthiran, and has also started making “acquihires,” buying small AI companies primarily for their talent, to beef up its engineering capacity.

Cppib, Canada’s largest institutional investor, backed Beacon through its growth equity unit, which has $13-billion under management. It buys US$50-million-plus stakes in tech companies globally except in Asia, often co-investing with venture capital firms it backs. It also has stakes in Canadian companies Cohere Inc. and Wealthsimple Financial Corp.

The Cppib group has leaned into AI, backing U.S. companies Anthropic, OpenAI and Databricks. Max Miller, Cppib’s head of growth equity, said he was impressed by Beacon’s combination of “an exceptional founder with a great market opportunity. That made a ton of sense to us. A lot of software companies realize they need to AI-ify themselves. Beacon can help with that.” Other companies including Bending Spoons and Banyan Software are following similar strategies, he noted.

Mr. Ganenthiran said “it’s a tremendous point of pride” to have Cppib invest. “It’s great validation for a team that is Canadian to be able to tell their parents ‘Hey, the work I’m doing will help pay for your retirement.’”

stories.title: MDA Space reports $30.9-million in third-quarter profit, raises guidance
stories.summary: Expects annual revenue between $1.9-billion and $1.95-billion
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MDA Space Ltd. MDA-T reported $30.9-million in net income for its third quarter, up from $27-million in the same quarter last year and raised its guidance for the year.

The company says the profit amounted to 19 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30 compared with a profit of 21 cents per diluted share a year ago when it had fewer shares outstanding.

On an adjusted basis, MDA says it earned 37 cents per diluted share in its latest quarter, the same as the same quarter last year.

Revenue for the quarter totalled $498.1-million, up from $409.8-million in the third quarter of 2025. The increase came as satellite systems revenue rose to $358.3-million, up from $283.5-million a year ago, while robotics and space operations revenue notched $79.9-million, up from $78.3-million. Geointelligence revenue was $59.9-million, up from $48-million.

In its outlook, MDA says it now expects revenue for 2026 to total between $1.9-billion and $1.95-billion, up from earlier expectations for $1.8-billion to $1.9-billion.

Mda’s order backlog stood at $3.95-billion at Sept. 30, compared with $4.39-billion a year earlier.

Companies in this story: (TSX:MDA)

stories.title: Alleged cult leader who defamed Canadians has history of falsely confirming sexual abuse memories
stories.summary: When Riley Lawson saw the Instagram message, she sat on the floor and cried. She knew her life would never be the same.
stories.author: Derek Miller
stories.content:
In part three of this five-part W5 investigation: “ Fake Filtered Cult Leader ,” CTV News’ investigative unit examines a self-described spiritual teacher whose online presence helped attract followers around the world. Drawing on interviews and extensive reporting, W5 explores concerns raised by former members and the questions surrounding the organization behind the carefully curated public image.

When Riley Lawson saw the Instagram message, she sat on the floor and cried. She knew her life would never be the same.

Riley is from Saskatchewan and was an online “student” of a Hawaii-based self-styled spiritual teacher who went by the name of Liana Shanti. She had just completed an online meditation guided by Shanti’s recorded voice with a hypnotic drone-like soundtrack. The meditation was titled, Journey to the Chamber of Wounds .

“It was meant to be a meditation that allows you to uncover wounds that you’ve experienced in your life. Anything -- from somebody just making fun of you on the playground, to abuse,” she says to W5 in an interview at her home in Saskatchewan. “We were encouraged to [listen] several times a week.”

In a trance-like state, Riley says a horrifying thought occurred to her. Could her father have sexually assaulted her when she was a little girl? It was not something that she had ever thought of before.

She immediately messaged Liana Shanti on Instagram.

“I think I saw my dad molest me as a kid. Is that what I saw?” she recalls.

W5 has seen the screenshot of the exchange with Shanti.

Liana Shanti wrote, “Yes, I’m so sorry. He did.”

The ‘psychic’ confirmations of abuse

The reason Riley Lawson believed that Liana Shanti could confirm such a thing is because Shanti claimed to have a supernatural power that many of her students passionately believed.

“She claimed to be psychic,” says Riley. “She spoke about her spiritual abilities and how she was privy to information that not every normal person has.”

The fallout was catastrophic. Riley told her mother, who believed her, and it led to her parents divorcing. Both she and her mother temporarily cut him out of their lives. Riley says “he was broken” and was forced to move into a basement apartment.

Riley now says she knows that memory was false. Her father did not abuse her as a child.

Riley says she and many students felt pressure to find and publicly reveal traumatic events of abuse and when they did, they were celebrated.

“If I get there and uncover this, then this magic will happen in my life. And I wanted the magic so bad that I created the memory to get there. I think that’s what happened,” she says.

A ‘sick and twisted’ agenda

Riley Lawson was not the only follower for whom Shanti falsely-confirmed sexual abuse. Amanda Brady, also from Saskatchewan, was a committed Liana Shanti follower for eight years and says she witnessed Shanti confirm sexual abuse many times.

“The amount of screenshots that we have of her telling people that they were abused is astounding,” she says.

W5 has reviewed several screenshots of those false confirmations of abuse. One follower told Shanti she had a “gut feeling” that she was sexually abused and asked if it was her grandfather or her father.

Shanti responded, “I see your father.”

Another follower asked Shanti if a cousin who used to babysit her sexually abused her. Shanti wrote, “Yes, a molestation that occurred that you can now clear.”

Amanda Brady says Shanti offered to “clear” or free followers from past traumas or negative energy. She would charge a fee for those sessions.

“She told me once that my grandfather on my mom’s side sexually abused me when I was young and I didn’t believe her,” she says. “I knew in my heart that that was not true.”

Amanda says she believes Shanti did it for a purpose.

“I believe that she has her own very sick and twisted agenda and it’s part of her isolation tactics. Because you need to cut off contact with those people,” she says.

A disturbing pattern emerges

Cult expert and host of the podcast The Cult Vault Kacey Baker says a vast number of former followers tell similar stories of Shanti confirming sexual abuse. Baker has interviewed more than 30 former Shanti followers, their families and other cult experts.

“What former members have described is a pattern that feels unbelievable,” she says from her home studio in Liverpool, England. “Multiple reports…of women experiencing the same type of abuse at the same point in their childhood and all of these repressed memories seem to be coming up after sessions…or affirmations from Liana Shanti.”

But Kacey Baker says that psychic reputation held power and Shanti herself didn’t need to do anything to reinforce it.

“If you are a new member within the community, you might have a whole host of people come to you and say, ‘She is psychic, I’ve seen it, I’ve seen her do things, I’ve seen her predict things,’” she says. “That social proofing along with confirmation bias is almost like a perfect storm for people to believe everything that she says.”

Even fabricated allegations confirmed

Baker says some claim to have baited Shanti to see if she would confirm something they know didn’t happen.

“Former followers have gone to Liana Shanti saying, ‘Did my uncle do this to me?’ knowing that that’s not true because they didn’t live in proximity to that uncle. And she has come back and said, ‘Yes, it happened at this age in this way.’”

Kacey Baker has produced an 11-part podcast on Liana Shanti, called The Instascammer .

Liana Shanti refused requests from W5 for an interview. In emails, she wrote that she is on a campaign to advocate for people who have been abused and to publicly reveal the alleged abusers.

“The actual story is how violent abusers and pedophiles weaponize the family court system, coercive control, and the extreme lengths they go to silence a woman with the courage to expose them because I couldn’t be gagged,” she wrote in an email to W5.

In August, Liana Shanti, whose real name is Liane Wilson, sued three Canadians for defamation in a Honolulu court. She alleged they called her a cult leader and a “fake, con artist master manipulator.” The Canadian defendants counter-sued, saying Shanti called them child abusers, pedophile supporters and Satanists. A jury rejected Shanti’s claim and awarded the Canadians C$56 million.

W5 has verified numerous Instagram and Facebook posts where Shanti claims to be psychic.

When questioned in court, she testified: “I don’t use the word ‘psychic.’”

Riley Lawson, who falsely accused her father of sexual abuse, is trying to repair the damage done. When she asked for his forgiveness, he gave it immediately.

“I said there’s nothing to forgive – you’re my daughter. I knew that she was in trouble,” he says outside his Regina basement apartment. “I can tell from the look in her eyes that she is back on track. So that makes me very happy.”

Watch the one-hour special presentation of W5’s Avery Haines Investigates Saturday at 7 p.m. ET live on W5’s official YouTube channel and on CTV and Crave

“She claimed to be psychic,” says Riley. “She spoke about her spiritual abilities and how she was privy to information that not every normal person has.”

The fallout was catastrophic. Riley told her mother, who believed her, and it led to her parents divorcing. Both she and her mother temporarily cut him out of their lives. Riley says “he was broken” and was forced to move into a basement apartment.
Riley now says she knows that memory was false. Her father did not abuse her as a child.
Riley says she and many students felt pressure to find and publicly reveal traumatic events of abuse and when they did, they were celebrated.
“If I get there and uncover this, then this magic will happen in my life. And I wanted the magic so bad that I created the memory to get there. I think that’s what happened,” she says.
A ‘sick and twisted’ agenda

Riley Lawson was not the only follower for whom Shanti falsely-confirmed sexual abuse. Amanda Brady, also from Saskatchewan, was a committed Liana Shanti follower for eight years and says she witnessed Shanti confirm sexual abuse many times.
“The amount of screenshots that we have of her telling people that they were abused is astounding,” she says.

W5 has reviewed several screenshots of those false confirmations of abuse. One follower told Shanti she had a “gut feeling” that she was sexually abused and asked if it was her grandfather or her father.
Shanti responded, “I see your father.”
Another follower asked Shanti if a cousin who used to babysit her sexually abused her. Shanti wrote, “Yes, a molestation that occurred that you can now clear.”
Amanda Brady says Shanti offered to “clear” or free followers from past traumas or negative energy. She would charge a fee for those sessions.
“She told me once that my grandfather on my mom’s side sexually abused me when I was young and I didn’t believe her,” she says. “I knew in my heart that that was not true.”
Amanda says she believes Shanti did it for a purpose.
“I believe that she has her own very sick and twisted agenda and it’s part of her isolation tactics. Because you need to cut off contact with those people,” she says.
A disturbing pattern emerges

Cult expert and host of the podcast The Cult Vault Kacey Baker says a vast number of former followers tell similar stories of Shanti confirming sexual abuse. Baker has interviewed more than 30 former Shanti followers, their families and other cult experts.

“What former members have described is a pattern that feels unbelievable,” she says from her home studio in Liverpool, England. “Multiple reports…of women experiencing the same type of abuse at the same point in their childhood and all of these repressed memories seem to be coming up after sessions…or affirmations from Liana Shanti.”
But Kacey Baker says that psychic reputation held power and Shanti herself didn’t need to do anything to reinforce it.

“If you are a new member within the community, you might have a whole host of people come to you and say, ‘She is psychic, I’ve seen it, I’ve seen her do things, I’ve seen her predict things,’” she says. “That social proofing along with confirmation bias is almost like a perfect storm for people to believe everything that she says.”
Even fabricated allegations confirmed
Baker says some claim to have baited Shanti to see if she would confirm something they know didn’t happen.

“Former followers have gone to Liana Shanti saying, ‘Did my uncle do this to me?’ knowing that that’s not true because they didn’t live in proximity to that uncle. And she has come back and said, ‘Yes, it happened at this age in this way.’”
Kacey Baker has produced an 11-part podcast on Liana Shanti, called The Instascammer .
Liana Shanti refused requests from W5 for an interview. In emails, she wrote that she is on a campaign to advocate for people who have been abused and to publicly reveal the alleged abusers.

“The actual story is how violent abusers and pedophiles weaponize the family court system, coercive control, and the extreme lengths they go to silence a woman with the courage to expose them because I couldn’t be gagged,” she wrote in an email to W5.

In August, Liana Shanti, whose real name is Liane Wilson, sued three Canadians for defamation in a Honolulu court. She alleged they called her a cult leader and a “fake, con artist master manipulator.” The Canadian defendants counter-sued, saying Shanti called them child abusers, pedophile supporters and Satanists. A jury rejected Shanti’s claim and awarded the Canadians C$56 million.
W5 has verified numerous Instagram and Facebook posts where Shanti claims to be psychic.
When questioned in court, she testified: “I don’t use the word ‘psychic.’”
Riley Lawson, who falsely accused her father of sexual abuse, is trying to repair the damage done. When she asked for his forgiveness, he gave it immediately.

“I said there’s nothing to forgive – you’re my daughter. I knew that she was in trouble,” he says outside his Regina basement apartment. “I can tell from the look in her eyes that she is back on track. So that makes me very happy.”

stories.title: Majority of Canadians want fewer immigrants in 2027: Nanos
stories.summary: A majority of Canadians want the country to accept fewer immigrants and temporary residents next year, according to a new Nanos Research survey commissioned by CTV News.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
A majority of Canadians want the country to accept fewer immigrants and temporary residents next year, according to a new Nanos Research survey commissioned by CTV News, as the country continues to grapple with immigration levels and their impact on housing, services and the economy.

The survey found that 52.3 per cent of respondents believe Canada should accept fewer immigrants and temporary residents in 2027, compared with 33.5 per cent who want the numbers to remain about the same.

Just 8.4 per cent said Canada should accept more, while 5.9 per cent were unsure.

The findings come as Canada’s immigration targets include 380,000 new permanent residents and an additional 385,000 workers and students as temporary residents in 2026.

Similar results found in March survey

The survey, conducted between Oct. 31 and Nov. 2, asked respondents: “As you May know, in 2026 Canada aims to accept 380,000 new immigrants as permanent residents, and an additional 385,000 workers and students as temporary residents. Should Canada accept more, about the same or fewer immigrants and temporary residents in 2027?”

The results suggest Canadians are largely in favour of reducing immigration and temporary resident levels, with more than half of respondents selecting fewer.

The October findings are consistent with those recorded in March, when 52 per cent of Canadians said they wanted fewer immigrants and temporary residents in the following year.

In March, 35 per cent favoured maintaining the same levels, compared with almost 34 per cent in October. Support for accepting more declined slightly, from nine per cent in March to eight per cent in October.

The proportion of respondents who were unsure increased from four and a half per cent to almost six per cent over the same period.

Regional and age differences emerge

The survey also found differences in opinions across the country.

Respondents in the Prairies were the most likely to favour fewer immigrants and temporary residents, with 58.3 per cent selecting that option.

Ontario and Quebec followed at 53.5 per cent and 53.1 per cent, respectively. In Atlantic Canada, 44.2 per cent wanted fewer, while 43.7 per cent of respondents in British Columbia said the same.

British Columbia had the highest proportion of respondents who wanted immigration and temporary resident levels to remain about the same, at 41.2 per cent.

Findings show differences across age groups

Canadians aged 35 to 54 were the most likely to favour fewer immigrants and temporary residents at 56.4 per cent, closely followed by those aged 18 to 34 at 56 per cent.

Among respondents aged 55 and older, 46.6 per cent wanted fewer, while 38.9 per cent favoured maintaining current levels — the highest proportion among the three age groups.

The Nanos Research survey was conducted using a dual-frame hybrid telephone and online random survey between Oct. 31 and Nov. 2, 2026.

A total of 1,058 Canadians were surveyed. The results are weighted to the true population proportion.

The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
