stories.title: Spy watchdog flags privacy risk from military’s online intelligence activities
stories.summary: The review agency says information publicly available online can still raise privacy concerns when it's collected and analyzed by government organizations.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
A national spy watchdog report says the military’s policy on the collection of information about Canadians doesn’t sufficiently address the privacy risks posed by online searches.

The National Security and Intelligence Review Agency found the Defence Department and the Canadian Armed Forces have the legal authority to collect publicly available information from the internet for intelligence purposes, but the watchdog noted shortcomings on privacy protection and oversight.

The review agency says information publicly available online can still raise privacy concerns when it’s collected and analyzed by government organizations.

It says Canadians should be able to trust that intelligence collection has a clear, lawful purpose and that their privacy rights are respected.

The watchdog found the military does not systematically record the link between open-source collection activities on the internet and the approved operation or defence activity.

It also says policies and record-keeping do not adequately address all privacy risks or demonstrate that collection involving Canadians is necessary.

stories.title: Bombers expected to wait before naming starter
stories.summary: Head coach Mike O'Shea knows the Winnipeg Blue Bombers will be in Montreal on Saturday playing in the East Division final.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
Head coach Mike O’Shea knows the Winnipeg Blue Bombers will be in Montreal on Saturday playing in the East Division final.

Who will be his starting quarterback, though, is an entirely different matter.

Dru Brown orchestrated last weekend’s 25-22 East semifinal win over the Toronto Argonauts. Brown hit Nic Demski on a 23-yard TD pass with 44 seconds remaining, then found Demski for the two-point conversion.

Zach Collaros didn’t suit up due to a rib injury suffered in Winnipeg’s playoff-clinching 34-10 win over B.C. on Oct. 23. Brown replaced Collaros and went 11 of- 1 passing for 185 yards and two TDs as the Bombers outscored the Lions 24-10 in the fourth quarter.

Winnipeg didn’t confirm Brown would start the East semifinal until releasing its depth chart the day before the game. The expectation is the same will happen this week.

Winnipeg will face a rested Montreal squad that hasn’t played since a 33-16 road win over Toronto on Oct. 23. Quarterback Davis Alexander’s last start was a 44-24 win over Saskatchewan on Oct. 12, a game where he threw for 403 yards with five TDs and an interception while rushing three times for 40 yards.

Dustin Crum started both of Montreal’s final regular-season games, with Caleb Evans playing the second half of the regular-season finale in Toronto.

The win over Saskatchewan was also the last time Canadian Tyson Philpot and Tyler Snead — who finished 1-2 among CFL receivers — both started. Montreal and Winnipeg split their season series 1-1, with each winning at home.

The Alouettes were 9-0 during the regular season at Molson Stadium.

Alexander threw for 697 yards with five TDs versus Winnipeg while completing 70.4 per cent of his passes.

Philpot and Snead were both key figures versus the Bombers. Philpot registered 18 catches for 294 yards and a TD while Snead had 14 receptions for 224 yards and three touchdowns.

Alexander and Philpot are finalists for the CFL’s outstanding player award, along with Edmonton quarterback Cody Fajardo. Philpot is also up for the top Canadian honour.

Winnipeg’s Brady Oliveira rushed for 95 yards on 20 carries last week versus Toronto. The CFL rushing leader (1,493 yards, 6.3-yard average) ran for 150 yards on 25 carries (six-yard average) and a TD versus Montreal.

Ontaria Wilson was Winnipeg’s leading receiver against Montreal with 14 catches for 223 yards and three TDs. The Bombers were 5-3 versus East Division teams and 4-4 during the regular season on the road.

Pick: Montreal.

B.C. Lions versus Edmonton Elks (Saturday afternoon)

At Edmonton, the Elks are in the playoffs for the first time since 2019 and host their first post-season contest in 11 years. They split their season series with B.C. 1-1, with each team winning at home.

Edmonton was 8-1 at Commonwealth Stadium this season while B.C. was 4-5 on the road.

Nathan Rourke threw for 320 yards with a TD and two interceptions in B.C.’s 36-24 win over Edmonton on July 4. But he was injured in the Elks’ 19-17 win on July 17 as Chase Brice finished 20 of 34 passing for 226 yards with a TD and four interceptions.

Last week, Rourke had 366 passing yards and three TDs in the Lions’ 33-26 victory over the defending-champion Saskatchewan Roughriders.

Keon Hatcher Sr. registered nine receptions for 175 yards and a TD versus Edmonton, while defensive back Jackson Findlay had 13 tackles and an interception.

Edmonton’s defence should provide a stout test. The Elks led the CFL in fewest offensive points allowed (23.6 per game), offensive yards (338.6), most interceptions (27) and fumble recoveries (15) and were second against the pass (272.7 yards) and run (81.4).

B.C.’s unit was the stingiest against the run (71.3 yards per game) and second in fewest net offensive yards allowed (355.2).

Veteran Cody Fajardo has been a key figure for the resurgent Elks, having amassed a career-high 4,788 passing yards and 25 touchdowns. He also ran for 517 yards and eight touchdowns.

Fajardo completed 69.3 per cent of his passes versus B.C. for 677 yards and four TDs. Austin Mack was Fajardo’s favourite receiver against the Lions with 12 catches for 180 yards (15-yard average) and a touchdown.

Justin Rankin was the CFL’s second-leading rusher this season (1,170 yards, 5.7-yard average). But he ran for just 28 yards on 14 carries in the two games versus B.C.

Rankin added 16 catches for 146 yards, giving him 174 scrimmage yards from 30 touches.

The ground game is important for both offences. Edmonton was tops in the CFL (127.6 rushing yards per game), with B.C. (118.7) second overall.

Last week: 1-1.

Overall: 54-29.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Police watchdog investigating death of armed man found in burned Fredericton home
stories.summary: The police watchdog says crisis negotiators tried to communicate with the man for a couple of hours before the home started burning.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
New Brunswick’s police oversight agency is investigating the death of an armed man inside a Fredericton home.

The Serious Incident Response Team says the man had recently barricaded himself inside the home, which caught fire.

The man’s body was later found inside the burned residence, but the agency did not say how he died.

When officers from the Fredericton Police Force were dispatched to the home on Murray Avenue on Sunday night, they learned the man had a weapon.

The police watchdog says crisis negotiators tried to communicate with the man for a couple of hours before the home started burning.

After the man’s body was found inside, the municipal police force immediately referred the case to the agency.

stories.title: Canada’s focus ‘hasn’t changed’ despite U.S. midterm blue wave, minister says
stories.summary: Canadian leaders say it would be “dangerous” to assume relations with the U.S. will change immediately following a major sweep of the House and the Senate by the Democrats Tuesday.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Canada’s focus on trade talks with the United States “hasn’t changed” following a major sweep of the House of Representatives and the Senate by the Democrats Tuesday, says Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc.

LeBlanc cautioned that the current Congress remains in place until January and Canada must continue to collaborate with the representatives who are currently in office.

“Our focus hasn’t changed. Yesterday we went to work on issues of affordability for Canadians, ON building major projects, ON strengthening the Canadian economy, ON diversifying our trade relationships,” he said. “That is actually our focus today and will be the focus tomorrow in the budget.”

LeBlanc said it would not be “constructive” to interpret what drove the results, where the war in Iran and the cost of living — which has soared due to both the conflict and the U.S. administration’s trade war on Canada and other countries — played a significant role, according to polling.

“Our job is to focus on what we can control, and that’s to work with the people that Americans have elected,” he said.

The Democrats swept both the House and the Senate Tuesday night in a blow to the Republican Party.

Some experts have said the results south of the border show how fed up Americans were with the ongoing trade war. Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington blew up in August igniting a fire that led to even broader tariffs on Canadian goods.

Canada retaliated by implementing counter-tariffs ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on approximately $27.6 billion worth of U.S. imports.

But Canada has also looked to diversify its trade portfolio, with recent trips to China and India, and signing on as an associate member with the European Union.

“I think it’s dangerous to make assumptions about what might take place before you actually have the opportunity to sit down with partners,” Minister of Justice and Attorney General Sean Fraser told reporters Wednesday.

“The strategy for Canada going forward remains the same: to defend our economic interests by diversifying trade partners, seeing if we can work through the challenges that we continue to have vis-a-vis the United States.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that “more intense” trade negotiations with the U.S. had already begun following a phone call with President Trump over the weekend.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Carney needs to take advantage of the “immense leverage” of the midterms to get a good deal with the U.S.

“The results yesterday demonstrate that Americans hate tariffs,” he said. “A tariff on Canada is a tax on Americans.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said that while he was elated with the midterm results , the strained relationship between the U.S. and Canada would remain.

Ford, who has been heavily critical of tariffs in the past, said he will be directing his ministers to head down to Washington to connect with senators, congresspeople and governors about their trade relationship as soon as the newly elected officials are sworn in at the end of January.

“We’re going to be down there, communicating, building those relationships,” he said. “We have to continue making sure that we move faster, quicker, immediate on everything across the board.”

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said his government is planning a “diplomatic offensive” to launch south of the border.

“I think we’re in a better position to possibly find a solution because Americans have spoken, the situation has changed,” he told reporters in Quebec City. “So what we’re going to do is prepare a diplomatic offensive of discussion with the Americans to see if there isn’t a solution.”

Quebec has been one of the provinces hardest hit by U.S. tariffs which target softwood lumber, aluminum and various manufactured foods.

But St-Pierre Plamondon said he doesn’t plan for Quebec to carry out direct trade notifications just yet.

“I think before positioning ourselves on that, we’ll open up the channels of discussions,” he said.

In a statement on social media, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said he looks forward to working together to lower costs on both sides of the border “by ending the war in Iran (gas & diesel prices) and the Trump tariffs (the price of everything else).”

He also gave a special nod to Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, the first Native woman elected to the Senate; Deb Haaland, who will lead New Mexico as the first Native woman to serve as a U.S. governor; and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who is the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said the Democrat win is an opportunity for Canada to “reset our relationship” with the U.S. and to “restore free and fair trade between our two countries.”

“I know Canada is ready to do this,” he said in a statement on social media. “Hopefully the U.S. is as well.”

paragraphs: Canada’s focus on trade talks with the United States “hasn’t changed” following a major sweep of the House of Representatives and the Senate by the Democrats Tuesday, says Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc.
LeBlanc cautioned that the current Congress remains in place until January and Canada must continue to collaborate with the representatives who are currently in office.

“Our focus hasn’t changed. Yesterday we went to work on issues of affordability for Canadians, ON building major projects, ON strengthening the Canadian economy, ON diversifying our trade relationships,” he said. “That is actually our focus today and will be the focus tomorrow in the budget.”

LeBlanc said it would not be “constructive” to interpret what drove the results, where the war in Iran and the cost of living — which has soared due to both the conflict and the U.S. administration’s trade war on Canada and other countries — played a significant role, according to polling.
“Our job is to focus on what we can control, and that’s to work with the people that Americans have elected,” he said.
The Democrats swept both the House and the Senate Tuesday night in a blow to the Republican Party.

Some experts have said the results south of the border show how fed up Americans were with the ongoing trade war. Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington blew up in August igniting a fire that led to even broader tariffs on Canadian goods.
Canada retaliated by implementing counter-tariffs ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on approximately $27.6 billion worth of U.S. imports.
But Canada has also looked to diversify its trade portfolio, with recent trips to China and India, and signing on as an associate member with the European Union.

“I think it’s dangerous to make assumptions about what might take place before you actually have the opportunity to sit down with partners,” Minister of Justice and Attorney General Sean Fraser told reporters Wednesday.

“The strategy for Canada going forward remains the same: to defend our economic interests by diversifying trade partners, seeing if we can work through the challenges that we continue to have vis-a-vis the United States.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that “more intense” trade negotiations with the U.S. had already begun following a phone call with President Trump over the weekend.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Carney needs to take advantage of the “immense leverage” of the midterms to get a good deal with the U.S.
“The results yesterday demonstrate that Americans hate tariffs,” he said. “A tariff on Canada is a tax on Americans.”
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said that while he was elated with the midterm results , the strained relationship between the U.S. and Canada would remain.

Ford, who has been heavily critical of tariffs in the past, said he will be directing his ministers to head down to Washington to connect with senators, congresspeople and governors about their trade relationship as soon as the newly elected officials are sworn in at the end of January.
“We’re going to be down there, communicating, building those relationships,” he said. “We have to continue making sure that we move faster, quicker, immediate on everything across the board.”
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said his government is planning a “diplomatic offensive” to launch south of the border.

“I think we’re in a better position to possibly find a solution because Americans have spoken, the situation has changed,” he told reporters in Quebec City. “So what we’re going to do is prepare a diplomatic offensive of discussion with the Americans to see if there isn’t a solution.”
Quebec has been one of the provinces hardest hit by U.S. tariffs which target softwood lumber, aluminum and various manufactured foods.
But St-Pierre Plamondon said he doesn’t plan for Quebec to carry out direct trade notifications just yet.
“I think before positioning ourselves on that, we’ll open up the channels of discussions,” he said.

In a statement on social media, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said he looks forward to working together to lower costs on both sides of the border “by ending the war in Iran (gas & diesel prices) and the Trump tariffs (the price of everything else).”

He also gave a special nod to Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, the first Native woman elected to the Senate; Deb Haaland, who will lead New Mexico as the first Native woman to serve as a U.S. governor; and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who is the first Muslim elected to the Senate.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said the Democrat win is an opportunity for Canada to “reset our relationship” with the U.S. and to “restore free and fair trade between our two countries.”
“I know Canada is ready to do this,” he said in a statement on social media. “Hopefully the U.S. is as well.”

stories.title: Canada, China agree to extend deal on canola and steel access to late 2028
stories.summary: On Wednesday, Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said the deal on canola and access for Chinese steel is being extended by two years, to the end of 2028.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson and Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Beijing and Ottawa are extending a January agreement to provide Chinese market access to Canadian imports in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.

In March, after Prime Minister Mark Carney’s January visit to Beijing, China dropped tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab.

Canada agreed in return to allow in certain Chinese steel and aluminum products. The deal was set to expire at the end of this year.

On Wednesday, Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said the deal is being extended by two years, to the end of 2028.

“This extension gives Canadian farmers, producers and harvesters stable access to China and supports billions in export opportunities,” Sidhu said in a media statement.

He said the credit goes to a trade body Canada and China relaunched in January as Ottawa moved to increase exports to China by 50 per cent by 2030.

Sidhu was in Beijing for meetings with officials ahead of Carney’s planned visit to China’s tech city Shenzhen later this month for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit.

“The timing of the announcement is significant,” said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, in an emailed statement.

She said the clearing of “an immediate trade irritant” allows Carney to focus on boosting Chinese investment during his visit to Shenzhen. It also locks in Chinese steel and aluminum access, which she said will be a factor in Ottawa’s trade talks with Washington.

“Ottawa is increasingly having to navigate its economic relationships with Beijing and Washington simultaneously, and decisions made in one relationship inevitably have implications for the other,” she wrote.

In June 2025, Sidhu said he and Wang Wentao, China’s minister of commerce, agreed to restart a joint economic and trade commission to address trade issues. In January, he said Ottawa secured a preliminary joint arrangement in Beijing which opened up more than $7 billion in market space for Canadian workers and businesses.

Sidhu said since the arrangement took effect in March, canola seed exports to China have increased by 84 per cent, from $1.04 billion to $1.91 billion, compared to the same period last year.

He said canola meal exports more than doubled, from $146 million to $390 million, while pea exports grew from $107 million to $345 million. Sidhu also said lobster exports increased by 57 per cent, from $128 million to $200 million.

Canadian beef also returned to the Chinese market in January for the first time since 2021, said Sidhu. From January to August, he said, Canada sent $363.2 million in beef exports to China, nearly double what it sold there in all of 2021.

“Over the past year, I’ve met with industry representatives, including the Canola Council of Canada, Pulse Canada, the Fisheries Council of Canada, the Canadian Cattle Association and the Canadian Meat Council,” he said.

“They told me an extension would give them the predictable, long-term access to the Chinese market and the certainty they need. We listened, and we delivered.”

Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said on social media the extension provides “immediate certainty” for lobster and crab harvesters and exporters. She said discussions are continuing on other seafood products.

“Last week in China, I met with government officials and industry leaders to make the case for Canada as a trusted supplier,” she said. “Canada’s fish and seafood harvesters catch the best seafood in the world and their work drives rural and coastal communities across the country.”

In Beijing earlier this year, Carney outlined steps to build a new strategic partnership with China, including more cultural exchanges and “people-to-people” ties.

Carney said during his visit that Ottawa hoped the renewal would become an “example to the world of co-operation amidst a time globally of division and disorder.”

Culture Minister Marc Miller made a five-day trip to China last month with dozens of representatives from Canadian creative industries. His office said seven new commercial agreements worth more than $4.2 million were signed during the trip.

The Carney government is seeking to double non-U.S. exports in the next decade in response to the unstable geopolitical and trading environment ushered in by the re-election of U.S. President Donald Trump.

China is Canada’s second largest single-country merchandise trading partner, accounting for $125.7 billion in two-way merchandise trade in 2025.

stories.title: ‘I was scared’: needles found in Halloween candy in Huron County
stories.summary: A Huron County mom is warning others about a ‘shocking’ find in her daughter’s Halloween candy.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A Huron County mom is warning others about a ‘shocking’ find in her daughter’s Halloween candy.

A needle sticks out of a mini Aero chocolate bar, ON Jaime Hoy’s kitchen countertop. Her 10-year-old daughter found it, after trick or treating in Seaforth, Saturday night.

“So Sunday afternoon, Brooklyn and her dad were going through her candy, and she was about to eat the Aero bar. When she opened it up, and broke it in half, she saw the needle sticking out. She came in running, saying what she’d found,” says the Kippen area mother.

Hoy says she was shocked. She’d heard of needles found in Halloween candy, but not in Huron County.

“I was scared. I automatically got to the other parents of the two other children that came with us trick or treating, and called them. Then I called the OPP,” says Hoy.

After posting a warning about what she’d found in her daughter’s candy on Facebook, she found she wasn’t alone. Parents reported finding needles in candy in Goderich, Vanastra, and Mitchell.

“I’ve heard of at least 4 or 5 in our area. My inbox is overflowing with needles and candies right now,” says Hoy.

Similar warnings about tampered Halloween Candy were issued in St.Thomas, LaSalle, and Hamilton. Hoy doesn’t believe the candy was tampered with by those handing it out.

“Somebody definitely put it in, but I don’t think it was from our community. I think that it was put in either during packaging or some other way. We know the places that we went and they’re all familiar. And, from all the other places being involved, I just don’t think that that you can say that it’s a community problem,” she says.

Along with contacting the OPP, Hoy says she’s contacted the candy maker, who has asked for information including pictures, and package barcodes. Hoy says it’s certainly troubling, and has her daughter reconsidering whether this was her last Halloween collecting candy.

stories.title: It would be a mistake to repeal B.C. housing legislation, says UBC expert
stories.summary: Victoria - A housing expert says the current glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the housing market is working, and she warns against repealing key parts of the out-going NDP government's housing legislation.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - A glut of empty condos in British Columbia should not be seen as evidence that the market is working, said a housing expert who warned against winding back policies of the outgoing NDP government designed to tame prices and rent.

Alexandra Flynn, who teaches housing policy at the University of B.C., said the province still needs a lot of homes for low-to very-low-income residents, despite the thousands of empty units.

“We do have a number of empty condos, but market housing for above-average income earners is not the housing we need,” she said. Left alone, the market cannot supply affordable and deeply affordable housing, she added.

“If you asked any developer, they would tell you, absent some kind of government intervention and granting and funding, they are not going to be able to do it.”

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has promised to repeal key aspects of the provincial housing legislation introduced by the outgoing government of Premier David Eby.

“We will return housing decisions to the people and the communities, who know their neighbourhoods so much better than Victoria,” Doerkson said during the inaugural meeting of the Conservative caucus.

Doerkson was referring to the proposed repeal of Bill 44, which New Democrats consider their signature piece of housing legislation.

The legislation legalized higher densities on single-lot properties in municipalities with populations above 5,000 people, but also came with housing targets, which have been heavily criticized by local governments.

Sarrah Storey, president of the Union of the British Columbia Municipalities, said Bill 44 was “highly problematic” and municipalities pushed back because the government imposed it as a “one-size-fits-all model” without getting input.

Storey said Ubcm agrees with the idea that housing policy for Williams Lake should not be made in Victoria, but if government wants to make changes to Bill 44, it should give municipalities choice.

“There are some local governments that will want to remain with the policies that are in place, allowing multiple homes on single family lots, for example, and they should be able to do so,” she said.

Storey, who is the mayor for Fraser Lake, said any housing plan must also consider infrastructure needs.

“I say the best way to support developers is to ensure that the local governments can direct development to areas that are ready to support growth,” she said.

Flynn disagrees with the plan to repeal, saying the law can be a “powerful tool,” and while some of it needs to be fixed, it would be a mistake to just throw it away.

“If I was the new government, I would not be making any knee-jerk reactions right now,” she said.

Flynn said she understands criticism from municipalities, saying there was “no question” that the dialogue between municipalities and Victoria must be improved.

“The province should not be dictating what municipalities do without actually engaging and having the bilateral relationships that are appropriate,” Flynn said.

She said housing in British Columbia is in a better place now than it was in 2017 for lots of reasons.

They include the work of the non-profit housing sector, municipalities, the federal government, and the provincial government, she said.

“So, the NDP government introduced some of the most transformative housing reforms in Canada,” she said.

Changing circumstances over time do not negate the fact that municipalities need to ensure affordable housing can be built in their communities, she said.

“This is not the time to be thinking about what to repeal,” she said. “It’s a time to set the course for a new agenda moving forward.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario ‘all in’ on ending seasonal time changes if Quebec, eastern U.S. agree, Ford says
stories.summary: Premier Doug Ford says he’s open to discussions if Quebec, New York and the ‘eastern corridor of the U.S.’ agree
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he’s “very open” to discussions with the new Quebec premier on whether to keep up seasonal time changes.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said last month that his government intends to abolish the twice-annual switch, but hasn’t yet decided whether to keep daylight time or standard time year-round and will consult with experts before making a final decision.

British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories all chose this year to stick with daylight time.

Asked whether the rest of Ontario would follow suit, Ford says he’s “easy going.”

Ford says he’s “all in” if not only Quebec, but also New York and the “eastern corridor of the U.S.” agreed.

Permanent daylight time would push Toronto’s winter solstice sunrise to around 8:45 a.m. and sunset to around 5:45 p.m.

A move to darker winter mornings has drawn criticism from some sleep experts, with a recent analysis from the Canadian Medical Association Journal favouring permanent standard time instead.

stories.title: Pearson gold heist mastermind spent 11 months in prison. He is already up for parole
stories.summary: He pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was sentenced in April to four years’ imprisonment, minus time spent in custody
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
After serving 296 days in custody for orchestrating Canada’s largest gold heist — making off with $22.5 million in gold bullion and cash — Arsalan Chaudhary on Wednesday asked to be release from prison on parole.

Chaudhary, 44, of Mississauga, said he and an Air Canada insider jointly organized the audacious 2023 heist of a high-value shipment that had just arrived at Toronto’s Pearson international airport on a flight from Switzerland. He then fled to Dubai when he learned he was a suspect.

He has been in custody since Jan. 12, 2026, when he returned from Dubai and was arrested at the same airport where he pulled off the gold heist. He pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was sentenced in April to four years’ imprisonment, minus time spent in custody prior to sentencing.

At his first parole hearing, Wednesday morning, Chaudhary sat placidly, wearing a heavy plaid button-up shirt over a blue T-shirt. His salt-and-pepper hair was brushed back. He told the parole board he was feeling “nervous, anxious.”

He was asked by parole board member Sean O’Connor what led him to commit the airport gold heist.

“I was unemployed, recently divorced, and I was just financially in a bad state,” he said.

“I was in a money crisis. And one of my friends introduced me to one of the guys (planning a heist). He goes, ‘there’s a money opportunity for you.’ And I went and met up with those people, and they talked to me about the crime. And from there on, we just had more meetings and more meetings until it led up to it happening,” he told the board.

“My thoughts were basically, I was in a financial crisis, and this could take me out of my financial crisis and lead me to a better life. At that point, I wasn’t thinking of the consequences.

“I was an idiot for what I did.”

Chaudhary asked to be released on day parole to the home of a relative, where he would have access to a vehicle to get to work at a job he had arranged at a pizza joint. If that was a step too far, he said release to a halfway house would work, but feared it would be awkward because of media attention and the public’s interest in him and his case.

“They’re calling me golden boy and stuff,” he said. “Wherever I go, they talk about me: ‘There’s the gold guy, there’s the gold guy.’ It does make me very nervous in situations.”

What makes it harder, he said, is despite successfully pulling off the heist, he lost all his loot and people think he still has millions.

“It was me and the guy that worked inside the airport who got the money. I got 30 per cent and the guy who worked at the airport got 70 per cent of the money. Then I was supposed to distribute it to the driver,” and others who helped him, he said.

He then lost his loot when he went to Pakistan for help liquidate and launder his assets. There he was betrayed by an associate and kidnapped and tortured into giving up millions in gold and cash, he said. “I told the kidnappers where it was and they went there and they took everything.” He said the ordeal left him traumatized and mentally fragile.

Chaudhary said he now knows what he has to do to protect himself in the future from such criminal influences: stay away from his old crowd, earn legitimate money, stay close to family, reinvigorate his religious faith, and remember the shame of his experience.

“My family has been really ashamed because of my actions, and everyone else who I put through this. It was the stupidest thing I could have done, especially sitting here with nothing coming out of it.”

Chaudhary said he is now working to complete his high school diploma, wants to get a license allowing him to drive trucks to start paying back the restitution order his trial judge issued.

He wants to “get back to normal living.”

“Find a nice girl that I could marry and have some kids and live a happy life, the way my brother and sister are being married and working nine to five.

“I never want to come to prison again.”

The Correction Service of Canada (CSC) recommended the Parole Board of Canada approve a day parole plan to a halfway house. A prison parole officer said that while the financial value of the theft was enormous there was no evidence of physical harm or individual victim trauma, meaning the heist did not meet Csc’s criteria of causing “serious harm.”

Inside the minimum-security wing of Collins Bay prison, Chaudhary has been a model prisoner, working in the prison kitchen without any evidence of engaging in inmate subculture, the board was told.

The board also heard that Chaudhary had prior convictions, including counterfeiting, credit card data theft and possession of property obtained by crime.

After a two-hour hearing, the two-member board deliberated for half an hour before returning with a decision.

Chaudhary was denied any day parole release.

“You appear to be in the early stages of demonstrating insight into your risks and what’s needed to mitigate those risks. But the board believes based on your file and the hearing that there’s still significant work to do,” O’Connor told him.

Chaudhary sat scowling as he listened.

O’Connor said that in both the interest of public safety and Chaudhary’s rehabilitation day parole was not yet acceptable.

The new proposed powers are contained in Bill S-8, which the Liberals tabled in the Senate on Tuesday afternoon.

Chaudhary asked to be released on day parole to the home of a relative, where he would have access to a vehicle to get to work at a job he had arranged at a pizza joint. If that was a step too far, he said release to a halfway house would work, but feared it would be awkward because of media attention and the public’s interest in him and his case.
“They’re calling me golden boy and stuff,” he said. “Wherever I go, they talk about me: ‘There’s the gold guy, there’s the gold guy.’ It does make me very nervous in situations.”
What makes it harder, he said, is despite successfully pulling off the heist, he lost all his loot and people think he still has millions.

“It was me and the guy that worked inside the airport who got the money. I got 30 per cent and the guy who worked at the airport got 70 per cent of the money. Then I was supposed to distribute it to the driver,” and others who helped him, he said.

He then lost his loot when he went to Pakistan for help liquidate and launder his assets. There he was betrayed by an associate and kidnapped and tortured into giving up millions in gold and cash, he said. “I told the kidnappers where it was and they went there and they took everything.” He said the ordeal left him traumatized and mentally fragile.
Editor’s Picks

Chaudhary said he now knows what he has to do to protect himself in the future from such criminal influences: stay away from his old crowd, earn legitimate money, stay close to family, reinvigorate his religious faith, and remember the shame of his experience.

“My family has been really ashamed because of my actions, and everyone else who I put through this. It was the stupidest thing I could have done, especially sitting here with nothing coming out of it.”
Chaudhary said he is now working to complete his high school diploma, wants to get a license allowing him to drive trucks to start paying back the restitution order his trial judge issued.
He wants to “get back to normal living.”
“Find a nice girl that I could marry and have some kids and live a happy life, the way my brother and sister are being married and working nine to five.
“I never want to come to prison again.”

The Correction Service of Canada (CSC) recommended the Parole Board of Canada approve a day parole plan to a halfway house. A prison parole officer said that while the financial value of the theft was enormous there was no evidence of physical harm or individual victim trauma, meaning the heist did not meet Csc’s criteria of causing “serious harm.”

content_blocks.text: Inside the minimum-security wing of Collins Bay prison, Chaudhary has been a model prisoner, working in the prison kitchen without any evidence of engaging in inmate subculture, the board was told.
The board also heard that Chaudhary had prior convictions, including counterfeiting, credit card data theft and possession of property obtained by crime.
After a two-hour hearing, the two-member board deliberated for half an hour before returning with a decision.
Chaudhary was denied any day parole release.

“You appear to be in the early stages of demonstrating insight into your risks and what’s needed to mitigate those risks. But the board believes based on your file and the hearing that there’s still significant work to do,” O’Connor told him.
Chaudhary sat scowling as he listened.
O’Connor said that in both the interest of public safety and Chaudhary’s rehabilitation day parole was not yet acceptable.
The new proposed powers are contained in Bill S-8, which the Liberals tabled in the Senate on Tuesday afternoon.

stories.title: Boxing legend Roy Jones Jr. coming to London, Ont. in partnership with Boomerz Boxing Club
stories.summary: A man widely considered as one of the most dominant boxers in history is coming to London, Ont. in a co-promotion with Boomerz Boxing Club.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
A man widely considered as one of the most dominant boxers in history is coming to London, Ont. in a co-promotion with Boomerz Boxing Club. Roy Jones Jr. is partnering with Jouda Promotions for the Nightmare on York Street on May 15, 2027, at RBC Place.

“We’re going to be hosting a pro show in London, Ontario with boxing legend Roy Jones Junior,” said Matt Boom of Boomerz Boxing Club. “Headlining will be our pro fighter Natasha ‘The Nightmare’ Spence. The night will be called the Nightmare on York Street.” Matt Boom and Abdul Jouda first met Jones Jr. when Spence was fighting for his promotion in the U.S.

“Roy was my dad’s favorite fighter, and we were in Washington where Natasha was fighting for a title,” said Boom. “We’re hanging out with Roy Jones right there, and I just mentioned it to him and said, ‘Hey, Natasha’s been flying all over the world coming in on the B side.

We’d love to have a local fight with her being the hometown hero and have you come out with us.’ He told us to put it together and let him know, so we did.” Spence is the WBA International Middleweight Champ. She has won four fights in a row and is the number two contender in the world behind Claressa Shields.Even after nearly two years of knowing Jones, she can’t believe he’s coming to her hometown.

“I’m grateful, but it still feels like a dream,” said Spence. “From the moment I met him, to having phone calls with him and texting him, and seeing his name pop up on my phone, it still doesn’t even feel real to me.” Spence is still waiting for that crack at Shields who has a professional record of 19–0 with four knockouts.

“We’re looking to match with Claressa,” said Spence. “The calls went out; emails have gone out to Salita promotions. I’m ranked number two by the WBA, right in the running to be next in line for her. When she gets back to the gym and starts focusing on boxing again, maybe she’ll check her emails and maybe they’ll answer the call?

“Roy Jones Jr. is a legend, and I’ve got my own legend in Natasha Spence. London is a fight city, and we are we’re going to continue to pour gas on the fire and continue to feel that right here in London, Ont.” The venue at RBC Place will seat about 1,500 people and main sponsors will get a chance to meet Jones Jr. prior to the show.

“It’s going to be our biggest show ever,” said Jouda. “We’re investing so much time and energy reaching out to people to fight Natasha. She’s going to be hard to match, and we’ve asked 100-plus fighters already and nobody’s answered the phone call yet, and that’s why we call her ‘The Nightmare’.” Jouda says the card will be full of up-and-coming fighters from around the world and a few that have names for themselves from the Toronto area.

“They’re going to come down and fight in front of Roy Jones Jr. in the Forest City,” said Jouda with a smile.

stories.title: Code Orange mass casualty event declared by B.C. hospital after bus crash
stories.summary: Mackenzie and District Hospital say they can’t yet provide details about number of victims or their conditions
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police say 20 people were hurt when a shuttle bus chartered by a contractor for a data centre company went off a highway near Mackenzie, B.C., resulting in two hospitals declaring Code Orange events as patients were transported in a fleet of air and ground ambulances.

A statement from the RCMP said it was a “chaotic scene,” and injuries ranged from minor to serious.

Police said they were called to the remote site on Wednesday around 9:10 a.m. about a single-vehicle crash on Highway 39.

The bus was found down an embankment about four kilometres south of Mackenzie, which is about 900 kilometres north of Vancouver.

The complete shutdown of the highway was required and the Northern Health Authority said the Mackenzie and District Hospital and the University Hospital of Northern BC in Prince George both declared a Code Orange, which is typically used to designate a mass casualty event.

“This was a chaotic scene, and police will need time to sort out many of the details,” Sgt. Michael McLaughlin with BC Highway Patrol said in the statement.

“We need to speak with anyone who has dash camera video of the bus, or any witnesses who saw what was happening prior to the crash.”

The Northern Health authority said the Code Orange was lifted at the Mackenzie hospital at 3:30 p.m. Wednesday, while it was taken down an hour later at the university hospital.

A statement from BC Emergency Health Services said one patient was transported from the scene by air ambulance in serious condition.

Six others were transported by ground ambulance to a hospital then transferred by air ambulance to another facility. Two were in serious condition and four were in serious but stable condition.

Another 13 patients in stable condition were transported by bus to hospital accompanied by advanced-care paramedics.

A spokesperson for the multinational data centre company Iren, which has a 4.5-hectare data centre site in Mackenzie, confirmed that the bus was chartered by one of its contractors.

“We are in close contact with the contractor, emergency responders and the RCMP as they work to establish what happened,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Iren, which operates three data centres in B.C., said its immediate concern was for those on the bus and their families and the company is supporting the response.

The company also has data centres in the United States, with projects planned in Spain and Australia.

Kiel Giddens, the legislature member for Prince George-Mackenzie, said he was thinking about the small community of about 3,300 people, calling the crash a “scary situation.”

Giddens said the data centre is an “important employer in the community.”

“When it’s a small town, a place like Mackenzie, these are friends, neighbours, family members impacted. That’s why these situations can be scary and that’s why my heart goes out to anyone impacted,” he said.

Police said the cause of the crash is still uncertain and “nothing has been ruled out.”

stories.title: Additional charges laid against man charged in exploitation probe
stories.summary: A London man in custody is facing 11 more charges after police said they seized identity documents that belong to nine people, in connection with an exploitation probe.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A London man in custody is facing 11 more charges after police said they seized identity documents that belong to nine people, in connection with an exploitation probe .

On Oct. 27, the London Police Service arrested a man in connection to an investigation being carried out by the LPS Criminal Investigation Division and Human Trafficking Unit.

Police said they seized a bag containing identification that belonged to the accused, and identification belonging to nine other people.

Officers seized driver’s licenses, health cards, social insurance number documents, and birth certificates. The LPS said at least two of the documents were previously reported stolen.

Police are working to contact those who have been affected.

34-year-old Abdulla Walid Kaddoura of London has been charged with nine counts of possession of an identity document belonging to another person and two counts of possession of property obtained by crime under $5,000.

This is on top of previous charges .

stories.title: Doug Ford ‘all in’ on ending seasonal time changes if Quebec, eastern U.S. agree
stories.summary: The discussion about ending seasonal time changes has been revived for Ontario as several provinces and territories all opted to keep daylight time this year.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he will be “all in” on ending seasonal time changes only if Quebec and parts of the United States are fully on board.

“I’m easy going. This argument has been going on for decades,” he said. “If Quebec and New York and the eastern corridor of the U.S. wants to do it, I’m all in,” he said.

Quebec Premier Paul St- Pierre Plamondon announced last month that the province is planning to scrap the twice-annual time switch, but the government hasn’t decided yet if it will keep daylight time or standard time for the entire year.

“(Plamondon) was going to do it, then he pulled back,” said Ford. He said he’s ready to get on the same page once Plamandon is ready.

“At the end of the day, it’s pitch black out there. So I am very open to discussions with the premier of Quebec.”

Ontario has made regulatory changes to the Time Act and allowed regions west of the 90th meridian to align with Manitoba and keep daylight time. Manitoba decided in September to make daylight time permanent.

The discussion about ending seasonal time changes has been revived for Ontario as Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories and British Columbia all opted this year to keep daylight time in perpetuity. Saskatchewan does not adjust its clocks.

“At the end of the day, it’s pitch black out there. So I am very open to discussions with the premier of Quebec.”

stories.title: CBC article on Israel ‘falls short’ of journalistic standards: Ombud
stories.summary: 'CBC reporting lies about Israel fuels the already rampant antisemitism in Canada,' says reader who made complaint
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
A CBC News article critiquing Israel “falls short” of the publication’s journalistic standards, according to a review by the CBC Ombud.

The admission was made after a reader complained about anti-Israel bias — and it’s not the first time CBC has come under fire for this reason.

In August 2024, CBC published an article written by journalist Chris Brown. It focuses on an Israeli military operation in the West Bank and the effects of the settler movement.

Reader Susan Glickman filed a complaint. “CBC reporting lies about Israel fuels the already rampant antisemitism in Canada,” she wrote.

In particular, she pointed out a sentence in the article that she said blamed Israel for failing to achieve peace in the region, it says in the review. She asked for a retraction as well as an apology.

A correction was made, but CBC Ombud Maxime Bertrand wrote that the modification was “highly questionable.”

Colby Cosh: Even the CBC doesn’t give a hoot about Eurovision

Jesse Kline: CBC shows anti-Jewish bias with suspension of Neil Herland

“To the general reader — CBC’s primary audience — the passage could still be read as singling out Israel for blame in the failure to find peace,” she said.

Glickman, who was joined by another reader, Aaron Eisen, both expressed their disappointment after the sentence was rephrased.

“Somehow, even after Oct. 7 your reporter is blaming Israel for demanding the right to exist,” they wrote.

Bertrand said that CBC was “acting within journalistic norms in publishing a critique” of Israel and “was under no obligation to include extensive backgrounding.” She also noted that the story was part of its “dedicated coverage” of the developing situation in the Middle East.

“Having said all this,” she wrote in the review, “there is one important point I’d like to address: journalistic neutrality.”

She concluded: “Therefore, I find the modified text falls short of meeting the CBC’s Journalistic Standards and Practices requirements for accuracy and impartiality.”

It was not clear what next steps would be taken, if any.

Bertrand did not immediately respond to National Post’s request for comment.

The CBC has faced similar scrutiny in the past.

A study published in January by HonestReporting, which monitors Canadian news for bias, found that CBC “humanizes Palestinian suffering through individualized, emotionally rich portrayals and direct quotation, while Israelis —including hostages — are rendered largely invisible as people.”

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, called for “an independent commission of inquiry to investigate” its coverage and “hold the broadcaster accountable.”

A January report by Jewish advocacy group B’nai Brith Canada that analyzed nearly 300 CBC articles about the Israel-Hamas war found only 37 per cent were balanced or neutral.

Nonprofit pro-Israel organization StandWithUs condemned CBC after one of its Jewish reporters, Neil Herland, was suspended for posting on X about his personal experience while walking to a Yom Kippur service in downtown Toronto, where anti-Israel protesters were stationed.

stories.title: Police arrest 12 in connection to unsanctioned Guelph homecoming party
stories.summary: Accused are between ages of 17 and 21 and face charges of assault with a weapon, causing a disturbance and two counts of mischief
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police in Guelph, Ont., say 12 people have been arrested in connection to September’s large unsanctioned university homecoming party.

All the accused are between the ages of 17 and 21.

Police say they each face charges of assault with a weapon, causing a disturbance and two counts of mischief.

One man faces an additional charge of assaulting a police officer with a weapon.

Videos from an off-campus homecoming party on Sept. 26 showed massive crowds of young people in the streets, with police accusing some of shoplifting and vandalizing local businesses.

The gathering prompted police, the University of Guelph and the local hospital to form a “homecoming working group” intended to support community safety and accountability.

stories.title: Amazon breaks ground on 200,000-square metre fulfilment warehouse in the Halifax area
stories.summary: The online retailer says the warehouse in Dartmouth, N.S., will cover more than 200,000-square metres in the Burnside industrial park.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
American e-commerce giant Amazon held a ground-breaking ceremony in the Halifax area today for a massive new warehouse that will use robots and more than 1,000 full-time employees to fulfil orders.

The online retailer says the warehouse in Dartmouth, N.S., will cover more than 200,000-square metres in the Burnside industrial park.

Amazon issued a statement saying employees will work alongside the robots, which the company says will make for a safer and more productive workplace.

The company says the goal is to improve delivery speed and expand product selection for customers across the region.

The Seattle-based company says that since 2010, it has invested more than $65 billion in its Canadian operations, and its workforce has grown to more than 46,000 people at more than 60 sites.

In January 2026, Amazon Canada announced it would close all seven of its Quebec warehouses within two months, eliminating 1,700 permanent jobs and 250 temporary ones.

At the time, the company said the move was aimed at cutting costs and improving service, and it insisted the closures had nothing to do with a successful unionization drive in the province.

stories.title: AMD to pay $2.9-billion for AI chip firm Taalas in one of the largest Canadian tech takeovers
stories.summary: California-based chip company discloses price of deal first announced in August
stories.author: Murad Hemmadi
stories.content:
Advanced Micro Devices Inc. AMD-Q said Wednesday that it will pay about US$2.9-billion for Toronto-based semiconductor startup Taalas Inc., making it one of the largest takeovers of a Canadian technology company.

Santa Clara, Calif.-based AMD announced the deal in August, and in a securities filing Wednesday it disclosed the price of the cash-and-stock acquisition. It said US$1.4-billion of the purchase amount is dependent on unspecified conditions.

The deal has yet to close and is subject to regulatory approval and other conditions.

Amd’s acquisition of Taalas is the largest known transaction involving a Canadian technology company since Ecolab Inc. of St. Paul, Minn., agreed to acquire Calgary-based CoolIT Systems, which makes data-centre cooling equipment, for US$4.75-billion in March. Amd’s Taalas takeover also tops the US$2.75-billion that Nasdaq Inc. paid in November 2020 for Verafin Inc., a St. John’s-based cybersecurity startup – then a landmark exit of a venture-backed, private Canadian technology company.

Former long-time AMD executives Ljubisa Bajic and Lejla Bajic and Drago Ignjatovic co-founded Taalas in August 2023. The startup set out to meet the growing demand for chips to run large language models (LLMs) and the generative tools they power. Rather than building general-purpose processors, Taalas bet that it could develop faster and more energy-efficient semiconductors by designing its hardware for specific AI systems. Its first chip was tailored to Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama family of LLMs, which have been widely used and modified because they are freely available.

Taalas had raised over US$225-million in venture financing, including a US$169-million funding round in February that included Fidelity Management & Research Co. and San Francisco-based Quiet Capital. At the time, CEO Ljubisa Bajic said the startup had 24 employees and had spent just US$30-million of its cash.

The deal represents a big markup in the company’s valuation, based on an analysis of corporate filings. Taalas issued new equity as part of its Series B funding round in November 2025 at a price of US$94.51 per share. That would have given the company an implied valuation of over US$750-million, based on the number of shares it was authorized to issue at the time.

AMD said in August that it would integrate Taalas’s technology into future chips designed for so-called inference – the process of running AI models to produce outputs like text, images or the actions of AI agents.

At the time, AMD chief software officer Andrej Zdravkovic, who is based in Toronto, said in a social media post that the Taalas team would be joining Amd’s Canadian work force.

The U.S. semiconductor company has made a series of acquisitions recently as it tries to catch up to Nvidia Corp. Nvda-Q , which dominates the market for the chips used to train and run AI models.

In September, AMD announced it was buying World Labs, a San Francisco-based AI company, for US$8.2-billion. AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li co-founded the startup, which developed world models, a new type of system that more accurately reflects the real world. World Labs was backed by Radical Ventures, a Toronto-headquartered tech investor where Ms. Li is a scientific partner. And in June 2025, AMD agreed a deal to hire the engineering employees of Toronto-based Untether, a chip startup that subsequently shut down.

AMD has over 3,800 employees in Canada, including many engineering and other technical staff. The firm has maintained a major office in Markham, Ont., since acquiring ATI Technologies – at the time Canada’s second-largest technology company – in October 2006.

The market for AI inference chips is heating up as cloud services and businesses seek cheaper alternatives to Nvidia’s processors to run generative tools and AI agents.

Last month, Tenstorrent Holdings Inc. raised US$1.5-billion in a financing that valued the company at US$6.2-billion. Backers included Fidelity, Morgan Stanley, Sandisk Corp. and T. Rowe Price.

Taalas CEO Mr. Bajic founded Tenstorrent in Toronto in March 2016 after leaving AMD. But he gave up the CEO role to early investor Jim Keller, a prominent chip designer, in October 2022 and left the firm a few months later. Tenstorrent relocated to the United States in November 2023.

stories.title: Saskatchewan soldier killed in CFB Wainwright fire remembered as close friend, loving son
stories.summary: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, was one of four soldiers killed when a grass fire at the base overtook troops in a training exercise
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Pte. Shaun Farrell was remembered Wednesday as a hard-headed soldier, branded with a tattoo reading “Comfort Kills Dreams” and with a love for the hard guitar-riffing Ram Jam rock anthem Black Betty .

Hundreds of Canadian military personnel stood at attention and saluted as a flag-draped casket carrying Farrell’s body was escorted into the armoury in Prince Albert, Sask., for an hour-long funeral witnessed by family, friends and Premier Scott Moe.

The 23-year-old was one of four soldiers killed last month, when a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta overtook troops in a training exercise. Thirty-nine others were injured, and many remain in hospital.

“Shaun was a fighter,” Lt.-Col. James Cressall, commanding officer of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, told the service.

Cressall said he never had a chance to meet Farrell but learned about him from friends and those who trained him.

“His instructors described him as a good, hard-headed, stubborn, determined dog. One simply said there was no breaking him,” Cressall said.

“Shaun had three words tattooed on his side: ‘Comfort Kills Dreams,’” he added.

“I think those words tell us a great deal about Shaun.”

A Canadian flag, paired with a regimental flag, was placed at the front of the armoury. Farrell’s military headdress and a wreath were laid on his casket next to large photo of him in uniform.

Farrell’s family, who moved to Prince Albert from South Africa when he was a teen, has said he had dyslexia and Asperger’s syndrome and was once told he’d never graduate high school. They said he refused to let labels or low expectations define him.

He enlisted in the military last year.

Pte. Luke Jessiman described Farrell as a fellow recruit who became a brother.

“We arrived as strangers, not knowing exactly what we had gotten ourselves into or what the months and years ahead would bring,” he said.

“When one of us was struggling, the other found a way to keep them going, and eventually we continued our training together.”

Matthew Meachem, a longtime friend, said he and Farrell would always try and put each other on the spot. “I would give anything for that one more day. You will never be forgotten. You left a mark on my life that nobody could ever replace.”

Heloise Vermeulen, a family friend, read a final letter from Farrell’s mother. Patricia Farrell said she never imagined she would have to say goodbye to a child. And the day the military knocked on her door, she knew her life would never be the same.

“My heart aches that I will never get the last hug I asked for,” she wrote.

“I would give anything for one more naughty smile, one more cupcake, one more sassy comment, one more, ‘Yes Mommy,’ and one more, ‘I love you, Mommy.’”

Moe said the Canadian flag, which was flown at half-mast at the Saskatchewan legislature when Farrell was killed, was put into a shadow box and given to the family.

“We, as your Saskatchewan family, our hearts hurt for you and our hearts are with you each and every day,” Moe said.

The other soldiers killed in the fire were: Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

The remains of Pte. Aidan Goulding, killed in the grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta on Oct. 17, have returned to British Columbia. The Canadian Press

A motorcade escorted the hearse carrying Goulding’s remains from the Vancouver airport to a funeral home in New Westminster on Wednesday.

Police and firefighters stood at attention and saluted as the hearse passed beneath a large Canadian flag strung over the road using fire truck ladders.

Sgt. Maj. Ray Gardner from the Vancouver Police Department was among those who lined the route to honour the 23-year-old soldier from North Vancouver.

Gardner, a veteran of the Canadian Armed Forces, shared his deepest condolences for Goulding’s family and said the young soldier “mattered to the country.”

“It’s so important that they can at least take that with them, that we all feel deeply, deeply affected,” he said.

“I know that all of Canada is feeling heartbroken about what happened,” Gardner said.

Fire Chief Jim Wishlove from Richmond Fire-Rescue said first responders had come from across Metro Vancouver to pay their respects to Goulding and the other soldiers who died, while showing support for their families.

“We’re hurting with them today,” he said.

“It brings it to light for us how incredibly dangerous all of these jobs are, and particularly the Armed Forces.

“These people are serving their communities, serving Canada.”

Brennan MacLachlan, a reservist with the Canadian Armed Forces and the emergency programs manager for the City of Richmond, said no words could assuage the grief the families of the soldiers who died are feeling.

“But we stand with them,” he said, after the motorcade carrying Goulding’s remains passed by.

“It’s a weight that we all carry.”

stories.title: Ford says Osap auditors will clear low-risk career colleges first; no timeline given
stories.summary: Career college students say they don't know how they will pay their rent and living expenses, let alone tuition, without their Osap funding that had been previously approved.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says an audit firm that is investigating student financial aid usage at career colleges is making it a priority to clear lower-risk schools first so their funding can be unfrozen, but he was not clear on a timeline.

Ford’s government paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all career colleges and private post-secondary institutions while Kpmg is conducting an audit looking at serious concerns with the integrity of the system.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has said that pause will last until the government puts a new and strengthened approval process in place for career colleges looking for Osap eligibility, and he expects that to be done in the new year.

In the meantime, career college students say they don’t know how they will pay their rent and living expenses, let alone tuition, without their Osap funding that had been previously approved.

Career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions have been calling on the government to take more targeted action against schools they refer to as “bad actors,” while not making innocent students pay the price.

Ford says his government has asked Kpmg to prioritize low-risk colleges to get money flowing again as soon as possible, but he did not give a specific idea of timing.

‘We’re in tough times’: Doug Ford shuts the door on new funding deal for Toronto
paragraphs: Ontario Premier Doug Ford says an audit firm that is investigating student financial aid usage at career colleges is making it a priority to clear lower-risk schools first so their funding can be unfrozen, but he was not clear on a timeline.

Ford’s government paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all career colleges and private post-secondary institutions while Kpmg is conducting an audit looking at serious concerns with the integrity of the system.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has said that pause will last until the government puts a new and strengthened approval process in place for career colleges looking for Osap eligibility, and he expects that to be done in the new year.
In the meantime, career college students say they don’t know how they will pay their rent and living expenses, let alone tuition, without their Osap funding that had been previously approved.

Career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions have been calling on the government to take more targeted action against schools they refer to as “bad actors,” while not making innocent students pay the price.
Ford says his government has asked Kpmg to prioritize low-risk colleges to get money flowing again as soon as possible, but he did not give a specific idea of timing.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Hospital declares Code Orange mass casualty event after northern B.C. bus crash
stories.summary: RCMP in Mackenzie say the crash happened early Wednesday on Highway 39 south of the community that's about 180 kilometres north of Prince George.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police say 20 people were hurt when a shuttle bus chartered by a contractor for a data centre company went off a highway near Mackenzie, B.C., resulting in two hospitals declaring Code Orange events as patients were transported in a fleet of air and ground ambulances.

A statement from the RCMP said it was a “chaotic scene,” and injuries ranged from minor to serious.

Police said they were called to the remote site on Wednesday around 9:10 a.m. about a single-vehicle crash on Highway 39.

The bus was found down an embankment about four kilometres south of Mackenzie, which is about 900 kilometres north of Vancouver.

The complete shutdown of the highway was required and the Northern Health Authority said the Mackenzie and District Hospital and the University Hospital of Northern BC in Prince George both declared a Code Orange, which is typically used to designate a mass casualty event.

“This was a chaotic scene, and police will need time to sort out many of the details,” Sgt. Michael McLaughlin with BC Highway Patrol said in the statement.

“We need to speak with anyone who has dash camera video of the bus, or any witnesses who saw what was happening prior to the crash.”

The Northern Health authority said the Code Orange was lifted at the Mackenzie hospital at 3:30 p.m. Wednesday, while it was taken down an hour later at the university hospital.

A statement from BC Emergency Health Services said one patient was transported from the scene by air ambulance in serious condition.

Six others were transported by ground ambulance to a hospital then transferred by air ambulance to another facility. Two were in serious condition and four were in serious but stable condition.

Another 13 patients in stable condition were transported by bus to hospital accompanied by advanced-care paramedics.

A spokesperson for the multinational data centre company Iren, which has a 4.5-hectare data centre site in Mackenzie, confirmed that the bus was chartered by one of its contractors.

“We are in close contact with the contractor, emergency responders and the RCMP as they work to establish what happened,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Iren, which operates three data centres in B.C., said its immediate concern was for those on the bus and their families and the company is supporting the response.

The company also has data centres in the United States, with projects planned in Spain and Australia.

Kiel Giddens, the legislature member for Prince George-Mackenzie, said he was thinking about the small community of about 3,300 people, calling the crash a “scary situation.”

Giddens said the data centre is an “important employer in the community.”

“When it’s a small town, a place like Mackenzie, these are friends, neighbours, family members impacted. That’s why these situations can be scary and that’s why my heart goes out to anyone impacted,” he said.

Police said the cause of the crash is still uncertain and “nothing has been ruled out.”

With files from Wolfgang Depner in Victoria

stories.title: Saskatchewan soldier killed in CFB Wainwright fire remembered at funeral
stories.summary: Prince Albert - Hundreds of Canadian military personnel stood at attention and saluted as a flag-draped casket carrying Pte. Shaun Farrell was escorted into the armoury in Prince Albert, Sask.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
PRINCE ALBERT - Pte. Shaun Farrell was remembered Wednesday as a hard-headed soldier, branded with a tattoo reading “Comfort Kills Dreams” and with a love for the hard guitar-riffing Ram Jam rock anthem “Black Betty.”

Hundreds of Canadian military personnel stood at attention and saluted as a flag-draped casket carrying Farrell’s body was escorted into the armoury in Prince Albert, Sask., for an hour-long funeral witnessed by family, friends and Premier Scott Moe.

The 23-year-old was one of four soldiers killed last month, when a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta overtook troops in a training exercise. Thirty-nine others were injured, and many remain in hospital.

“Shaun was a fighter,” Lt.-Col. James Cressall, commanding officer of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, told the service.

Cressall said he never had a chance to meet Farrell but learned about him from friends and those who trained him.

“His instructors described him as a good, hard-headed, stubborn, determined dog. One simply said there was no breaking him,” Cressall said.

“Shaun had three words tattooed on his side: ‘Comfort Kills Dreams,’” he added.

“I think those words tell us a great deal about Shaun.”

A Canadian flag, paired with a regimental flag, was placed at the front of the armoury. Farrell’s military headdress and a wreath were laid on his casket next to large photo of him in uniform.

Farrell’s family, who moved to Prince Albert from South Africa when he was a teen, has said he had dyslexia and Asperger’s syndrome and was once told he’d never graduate high school. They said he refused to let labels or low expectations define him.

He enlisted in the military last year.

Pte. Luke Jessiman described Farrell as a fellow recruit who became a brother.

“We arrived as strangers, not knowing exactly what we had gotten ourselves into or what the months and years ahead would bring,” he said.

“When one of us was struggling, the other found a way to keep them going, and eventually we continued our training together.”

Matthew Meachem, a longtime friend, said he and Farrell would always try and put each other on the spot. “I would give anything for that one more day. You will never be forgotten. You left a mark on my life that nobody could ever replace.”

Heloise Vermeulen, a family friend, read a final letter from Farrell’s mother. Patricia Farrell said she never imagined she would have to say goodbye to a child. And the day the military knocked on her door, she knew her life would never be the same.

“My heart aches that I will never get the last hug I asked for,” she wrote.

“I would give anything for one more naughty smile, one more cupcake, one more sassy comment, one more, ‘Yes Mommy,’ and one more, ‘I love you, Mommy.’”

Moe said the Canadian flag, which was flown at half-mast at the Saskatchewan legislature when Farrell was killed, was put into a shadow box and given to the family.

“We, as your Saskatchewan family, our hearts hurt for you and our hearts are with you each and every day,” Moe said.

The other soldiers killed in the fire were: Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

On Thursday, a motorcade escorted Goulding’s body from the Vancouver airport to a funeral home in New Westminster, B.C., as emergency workers and members of the public lined sides of the highway in tribute.

At Farrell’s service, members of his unit were encouraged to place their Remembrance Day poppies on his photo as they walked out.

As Farrell’s body was carried from the armoury, “Black Betty” was played, the lyrics resonating for him one final time with its trademark refrain.

“Bam-ba-lam.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

— By Bill Graveland in Calgary
