stories.title: Canadian aluminum industry sees hope for tariff relief after U.S. midterm elections
stories.summary: The head of Canada's aluminum industry says the U.S. midterm election results could mark a turning point in the trade dispute between Canada and the United States.
stories.author: Brett Bundale The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canadian manufacturers battered by tariffs are optimistic the U.S. midterm election results could mark a turning point in the trade dispute between Canada and the United States.

Business leaders hope the Democratic sweep of Congress will help end trade tensions that have disrupted exports, raised prices and forced companies to overhaul supply chains.

But they warn that tariffs and uncertainty will continue to hurt Canadian businesses until a deal is reached.

“I’m certainly far more optimistic than I’ve ever been, because the signal is overwhelmingly clearer than I thought it would be,” Jean Simard, president and chief executive of the Aluminum Association of Canada, said Wednesday.

He said the election results could increase pressure on Washington to roll back tariffs and reach a trade deal sooner.

“I’m not sure it’s going to work, but it certainly adds momentum,” Simard said.

Canada produces roughly 3.3 million tonnes of aluminum annually, exporting about 90 per cent of its output, Simard said.

The vast majority of those exports historically went to the United States, but U.S. tariffs have prompted Canadian producers to redirect shipments to Europe, he said.

Canada’s steel industry is also facing U.S. tariffs of up to 50 per cent.

Blair Dickerson, president and chief executive of the Canadian Steel Producers Association, said a change in the political landscape in Washington doesn’t guarantee an immediate change in U.S. trade policy.

Still, she said the steel industry is encouraged by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s recent comments that Canada-U.S. trade talks are progressing, and that the government remains focused on getting a good deal for all Canadians.

“Our priority remains clear,” Dickerson said. “We need a fair and predictable trading relationship so that the Canadian steel sector can compete and grow.”

The lack of predictability for the manufacturing sector remains a major concern for business owners as it makes it difficult to plan investments and manage costs.

“It keeps everybody on edge because the rules seem to be changing day to day,” said Marc Lecours, owner of Preferred CNC and Michmar Engineering in Windsor, Ont.

“It’s hard to make decisions moving forward when you don’t know what your profit margin could be, if any.”

He said tariffs have forced his companies, which manufacture components and design plastic injection molds for the automotive industry, to buy American steel and aluminum, driving up costs.

Lecours said his companies have experienced some layoffs, while trade uncertainty has made it difficult to plan new investments.

He said the election results could help mend Canada-U.S. relations.

“It’s an opportunity for both countries to take a look at how we can establish a better trade relationship and maybe repair some of the damage that’s been done,” Lecours said.

For other Canadian manufacturers, the trade war has already taken a toll on exports and competitiveness, adding urgency to calls for a deal.

Darrin Noble, president and chief operating officer of Surrey, B.C.-based Cloverdale Paint, said the election results offer hope for Canadian manufacturers struggling with U.S. tariffs.

“It is certainly a step in the right direction,” he said. “It signals a shift of U.S. voters and their level of satisfaction with their president.”

Noble said U.S. tariffs have made the company’s paint less competitive south of the border, threatening its export business.

He said stockpiled inventory in the United States initially helped cushion the impact, but the company is now beginning to feel the effects.

Noble said Ottawa granted the company tariff relief on steel paint cans, but other imported supplies continue to face duties that ultimately increase costs for Canadian consumers.

For example, Canadian retaliatory tariffs are driving up the cost of paint brushes, rollers and other supplies imported from the United States, he said.

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Canadian Federation of Independent Business president Dan Kelly said he hopes the election results will push Washington toward a lasting trade deal with Canada.

He said the results show the trade dispute has worsened affordability concerns in border states and the Midwest. Kelly added that 87 per cent of Canadian small businesses want an agreement reached as quickly as possible.

But Andreas Schotter, a professor of international business at Western University’s Ivey Business School, said Canadian companies should not expect a dramatic shift in U.S. trade policy.

“Even on the Democratic side, there’s a strong ‘America First’ notion,” he said. “For businesses, there’s no immediate change … I don’t see us all of a sudden going back to full Cusma.”

The Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement replaced Nafta in 2020.

Meanwhile, Canada was largely exempt from the 10 per cent U.S. aluminum tariffs imposed during Trump’s first term, until his second administration raised them to 25 per cent in March 2025 and 50 per cent in June.

Simard said Canada’s three major primary aluminum producers — Rio Tinto, Alcoa and Aluminerie Alouette — initially continued fulfilling orders to American customers despite the tariffs before redirecting shipments to Europe.

He said Canadian producers have exported roughly 800,000 tonnes of aluminum to Europe since March 2025, compared with about 100,000 tonnes over a comparable period under normal market conditions.

Simard said the strategy has allowed the industry to maintain production without layoffs or production cuts.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: New Liberal bill to allow police to search mail, reverse promised ban on crypto ATMs
stories.summary: The new proposed powers are contained in Bill S-8, which the Liberals tabled in the Senate on Tuesday afternoon.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Liberals tabled an unexpected new law enforcement bill on Tuesday which would allow police to search and retain mail and secretly provide individuals’ personal information to financial institutions to prevent money laundering or terrorism financing.

The new proposed powers are contained in Bill S-8, which the Liberals tabled in the Senate on Tuesday afternoon. The bulk of the changes in the bill aim to beef up the federal anti-money laundering and terrorism financing act.

The legislation would allow law enforcement and intelligence agencies to secretly share information linked to money laundering to regulated businesses, ban cash payments or donations of $10,000 or more and give the finance minister veto power over which money services businesses get approved by watchdog agency Fintrac.

Bill S-8 largely resuscitates a contentious failed proposal from the Liberals in 2025 to allow police to search Canadians’ mail. It also confirms the Liberals are backtracking on an earlier commitment to ban cryptocurrency ATMs in Canada, instead proposing to subject them to Fintrac oversight and reporting.

“Fraud and money laundering are serious crimes that harm Canadians, undermine confidence in our financial system and help fund organized crime,” Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said in a news release.

“This bill will make it harder for criminal networks to operate and will better protect Canadians.”

A key aim of S-8 is to allow both Fintrac and the federal government to further crack down on criminal abuses committed by money service businesses (MSB), such as currency exchanges, digital payment companies or virtual currency dealers.

The federal government said last year that criminals are increasingly using money service businesses to “launder money, finance terrorism, evade sanctions, and defraud Canadians.”

In S-8, Ottawa proposes to allow the finance minister to direct Fintrac to deny or revoke an Msb’s registration or even temporarily pause the registration of all or certain types of MSBs for national security reasons.

The legislation would also make it harder for an individual with a criminal record to own an MSB and would expand Fintrac’s ability to refuse or revoke such a business’s registration.

Other proposals in Bill S-8 are certain to give civil liberty and privacy advocates pause.

For example, the legislation offers law enforcement, intelligence agencies and unidentified government departments the ability to secretly share an individual’s personal information with regulated businesses.

That can be done if the discloser “considers” that the shared information will help combat money laundering, terrorist activity financing or sanctions evasion.

The legislation does not appear to set a legal threshold for the secret sharing of personal information or require court approval.

“It’s fair to say that there should be a little bit easier information sharing between law enforcement, prescribed government departments, agencies and reporting entities,” said Jessica Davis, president of Insight Threat Intelligence and a specialist on terrorism and illicit financing.

“There should be pretty good limits on that, though,” she added. “As the bill is written right now, I’m not confident that there are the right restrictions on that.”

The revived proposal to allow police broader power to seize and search mail transiting through Canadians will also likely prove to be controversial. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals first attempted a similar reform in their first ever legislation last spring, Bill C-2.

Currently, police can only obtain a warrant to seize and search parcels and mail envelopes weighing over 500 grams.

But under the new proposed regime, police could search and seize “anything in the course of post” if they have “lawful authority” do to so under the Criminal Code, the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act or the Cannabis Act.

The bill does not define “lawful authority,” nor does it specify that police would require a warrant to search the mail under the new legislation.

“Right now, law enforcement are limited in their ability to search and seize mail in transit, even when they have sufficient evidence to obtain a warrant,” reads a government release on the bill.

Unlike Bill C-2, this legislation does not extend the mail search and seizure power to postal inspectors.

In the bill, the Liberals also backtrack on a promise made in the 2025 budget to ban cryptocurrency ATMs. That’s despite the government’s own analysis that the machines are a “primary method for scammers to extract cash from victims and for criminals.”

Seniors in particular are vulnerable to scammers and extortioners pushing them to use a crypto ATM to send them money that becomes virtually untraceable for police.

Instead, the bill proposes that crypto ATM operators be compelled to register with Fintrac (the federal financial crimes watchdog) and track and report every transaction completed by the machine to the agency.

Furthermore, it would cap the maximum value of crypto transactions within 24 hours at an ATM by a single individual at $1,000.

The government’s decision to backtrack on the crypto ATM ban is an unwelcome change to Davis, who says the new proposed system is a more complicated way to hopefully achieve the same outcome.

“They’re trying to put all of these additional measures onto cryptocurrency ATMs… to achieve the same thing that a ban would achieve, but then also increasing the costs to Fintrac and maintaining the compliance burden for Fintrac,” Davis said.

That can be done if the discloser “considers” that the shared information will help combat money laundering, terrorist activity financing or sanctions evasion.
The legislation does not appear to set a legal threshold for the secret sharing of personal information or require court approval.

stories.title: Bloc leader blasts Liberals’ use of ‘masters in our own home’ slogan on budget cover
stories.summary: Yves-François Blanchet urged Mark Carney to ‘show some respect’ in appropriating an iconic phrase of the Quiet Revolution.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — On the eve of the budget, Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet is taking issue with its cover.

The title of the document in French, “Maîtres chez nous,” is a direct reference to an flagship slogan during Quebec’s “Quiet Revolution” in the 1960s.

“You are entitled to the benefit of the doubt, but perhaps you have already exhausted it by displaying an implausible ignorance of the reality and history of Quebec,” he wrote, referring to Carney’s Plains of Abraham speech that resonated poorly in the province.

“Please show some respect: what is ‘home’ to you is not necessarily ‘home’ to me.”

Carney has been loosely using the iconic phrase since he ran for the federal Liberal leadership in early 2025. Even at the time, it irked Blanchet and other Quebecers who believed Carney was appropriating the phrase of a critical time in Quebec history.

In 1960, the Quebec Liberals led by Jean Lesage put an end to the reign of the Union Nationale, a party which had been in power since 1944, was committed to outdated traditional values and kept Quebec under the thumb of the Catholic Church.

The “Quiet Revolution” refers to the rapid succession of social and political changes that marked that period. Those included the secularization of Quebec society and a series of economic reforms to improve the living conditions of French Canadians.

In 1962, Lesage called a snap election to secure a clear mandate to proceed with the nationalization of hydroelectricity. The campaign slogan, “Maîtres chez nous,” quickly became a rallying cry for Quebecers to take back control of their economic destiny.

The man at the heart of the nationalization was Liberal Resources Minister René Lévesque, who would eventually create the separatist Parti Québécois.

Hydro-Québec, for its part, would become a symbol of economic nationalism and is now one of the largest hydroelectric power producers in the world.

Carney said last week he is well aware of the historical context surrounding the Quiet Revolution and said he agrees Quebec forms a nation with its own heritage.

But he noted that the world has changed since the Quiet Revolution.

“In a dangerous and divided world — and in a world where we must be masters in our own home — we need to find reliable partners to strengthen our sovereignty, so that Canadians and Quebecers can live their lives as they choose,” he said in French.

Carney has taken a keen interest in economic nationalism, often bringing up the fact that his government intervened to broker a deal between Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador to expand the power grid in Churchill Falls and Gull Island.

He has touted this project as the “largest clean energy investment in North American history.”

Bloc finance critic Jean-Denis Garon said on Tuesday that he was concerned about the government leaking a preview of an official budget document to the public before it was tabled in the House of Commons and MPs had an opportunity to see its contents.

“I believe that parliamentarians should be the first ones to see the budget — from the very first page to the last,” he said. “This is a lapse that should not be repeated.”

Garon shrugged when asked if he was annoyed by the federal Liberals’ use of “Maîtres chez nous” for its upcoming budget.

“Regardless of whether or not one adopts slogans from Quebec’s past that are deeply rooted in identity, it is clearly an attempt to woo the people of Quebec,” he said. “We shall see who is truly master in their own home come Thursday.”

stories.title: Sherritt to temporarily lay off 280 employees, almost half of Canadian staff
stories.summary: Company will work to restore operations at Alberta refinery after feed inventory from Moa mine in Cuba ran out
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Sherritt International Corp. S-T says it will temporarily lay off nearly half of its Canadian staff as it works to restore operations at its refinery in Alberta.

The company shut down refining operations at its mill in Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., earlier this year when feed inventory from its Moa mine in Cuba ran out.

Sherritt says it’s temporarily laying off about 280 employees, representing 47 per cent of its Canadian work force. The layoffs are expected to last about 90 days.

The company says some work will continue during the layoff period, including production and sales of ammonia fertilizer and sulphuric acid as well as maintenance and continuing environmental protection and safety work.

Operations at the Moa joint venture were paused as Cuba faced fuel shortages after the U.S. cut off access to oil from Venezuela in January.

Last month, Sherritt said it received a licence from the U.S. government authorizing the purchase and delivery of fuel to its Moa mine and processing operations in Cuba. It said the licence is the first of a series of emergency licences that will be necessary for it to be able to restart operations.

stories.title: ‘We’re in tough times’: Doug Ford shuts the door on new funding deal for Toronto
stories.summary: The initial three-year, $1.2 billion new deal was ironed out in November 2023 after Olivia Chow was first elected mayor.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford is shutting down any talk of a new funding deal for the City of Toronto, suggesting Ontario’s $16.9 billion deficit has left the province facing “tough times” with less room to support municipal budgets.

The initial three-year, $1.2 billion new deal was ironed out in November 2023 after Olivia Chow was first elected mayor.

As part of the agreement, the province agreed to fund new transit vehicles, upload both the Gardiner Expressway and the Don Valley Parkway, and gave the city $353 million for operation and maintenance until the upload is complete.

As the city crafts its latest budget, hopes for a revised funding deal remained high.

Under repeated questioning from Global News, however, the finance minister, municipal affairs minister and premier said the government doesn’t have plans for a new deal 2.0.

“There’s no 2.0, to answer your question directly,” Ford said during a news conference at Queen’s Park on Wednesday.

“Keep in mind with collaboration with the federal and the provincial government, we’ve given Toronto $9 billion — with a ‘B’. They have to be responsible for their own budget.”

While the premier said he was willing to look at “certain priorities” such as crime reduction and public safety on subways, he also suggested the province might be tapped out of cash to help municipal governments.

“You can’t always rely on the province. We’re in tough times right now, really tough times. So we’re going to be prudent fiscal managers, respecting the taxpayer,” Ford said.

The comments come after the Ford government tabled the fall economic statement, which included $36 billion in deficits over the next three years and once again delayed the province’s path to balancing the budget.

Critics say the government overleveraged on capital construction during its early years, leaving the province with little capacity to help.

“You know, we have cost overruns at the Ottawa Hospital, the Ontario Line, the Eglinton Crosstown, the Scarborough subway. We’re spending billions of dollars on things that we build, but the stuff that happens inside, it’s not working,” said interim Liberal leader John Fraser.

“What’s the point in building a hospital or a school if the stuff happens inside isn’t working for people? And this government needs to start to focus on that.”

“If the municipalities don’t get a new fiscal deal, we’re likely going to see double-digit property tax increases. I’ve been telling mayors they should call it the Doug Ford property tax increase,” Schreiner said.

“Homelessness is also only going to get worse. Municipalities cannot solve this crisis. They don’t have the fiscal resources to do it. We need the province to step up.”

content_blocks.text: As part of the agreement, the province agreed to fund new transit vehicles, upload both the Gardiner Expressway and the Don Valley Parkway, and gave the city $353 million for operation and maintenance until the upload is complete.
As the city crafts its latest budget, hopes for a revised funding deal remained high.
Under repeated questioning from Global News, however, the finance minister, municipal affairs minister and premier said the government doesn’t have plans for a new deal 2.0.
“There’s no 2.0, to answer your question directly,” Ford said during a news conference at Queen’s Park on Wednesday.
“Keep in mind with collaboration with the federal and the provincial government, we’ve given Toronto $9 billion — with a ‘B’. They have to be responsible for their own budget.”

While the premier said he was willing to look at “certain priorities” such as crime reduction and public safety on subways, he also suggested the province might be tapped out of cash to help municipal governments.
“You can’t always rely on the province. We’re in tough times right now, really tough times. So we’re going to be prudent fiscal managers, respecting the taxpayer,” Ford said.

The comments come after the Ford government tabled the fall economic statement, which included $36 billion in deficits over the next three years and once again delayed the province’s path to balancing the budget.
Critics say the government overleveraged on capital construction during its early years, leaving the province with little capacity to help.

“You know, we have cost overruns at the Ottawa Hospital, the Ontario Line, the Eglinton Crosstown, the Scarborough subway. We’re spending billions of dollars on things that we build, but the stuff that happens inside, it’s not working,” said interim Liberal leader John Fraser.
“What’s the point in building a hospital or a school if the stuff happens inside isn’t working for people? And this government needs to start to focus on that.”

“If the municipalities don’t get a new fiscal deal, we’re likely going to see double-digit property tax increases. I’ve been telling mayors they should call it the Doug Ford property tax increase,” Schreiner said.
“Homelessness is also only going to get worse. Municipalities cannot solve this crisis. They don’t have the fiscal resources to do it. We need the province to step up.”

stories.author: The Canadian Press

stories.title: Could this Canadian hybrid-electric aircraft reduce northern Ontario medevac times?
stories.summary: Horizon is building a hybrid-electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, one of the first in the world, which could change how remote communities across Canada access critical and lifesaving care.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Lindsay, Ont. -- An aircraft sits in the Lindsay, Ont., airport that could change how remote communities across Canada access critical and lifesaving care.

“We’re developing an aircraft that can take off and land just like a helicopter,” said Horizon Aircraft co-founder Brandon Robinson. “So, you don’t need a runway, but enroute it has some special technology whereby it can fly just like a normal aircraft on wing-borne flight.”

Horizon is building a hybrid-electric vertical takeoff and landing (Vtol) aircraft, one of the first in the world. Robinson says the plane could allow better access to remote communities and help with search-and-rescue missions where space for landings is limited.

“It’s about twice as fast as a helicopter, much cheaper to own and operate and much safer,” Robinson said. “It’s the agility of a helicopter with the speed and range of an airplane, which, in a country like Canada, can have huge implications for small communities.”

Horizon currently has a half-scale version of its Cavorite X7, which has been through a full test program. The company is now building the full-size version which will be able to carry six passengers and a pilot, travel at speeds of up to 450 kilometres per hour and have a range of up to 800 kilometres.

The plane uses fans hidden inside its wings to lift straight up. Once airborne, the fans are covered and the aircraft flies forward like a conventional airplane. Take-off and landing are both electric, and the batteries recharge while the aircraft is in flight.

Built for the North

Remote medevac is central to Horizon’s business plan. The company aims to better connect hard-to-reach Indigenous communities in the North.

It carries its own generator on board and doesn’t need infrastructure on the ground to recharge.

“It can land in the middle of nowhere in a flat space,” Robinson said. “We can drop off those critical medical supplies or a surgeon or extract a critically injured patient from those northern communities in a much more efficient fashion.”

The aircraft is being designed specifically to operate in a variety of elements including forest fires, the cold, snow and low-visibility conditions which would allow it to serve remote communities year-round.

The aircraft’s potential caught the attention of Constance Lake First Nation, which is about 500 km northeast of Thunder Bay, Ont. Constance Lake has just signed a memorandum of understanding with Horizon to advance the potential purchase of a Cavorite X7.

“It could land right on the spot. Doesn’t need a runway. It’s just like a helicopter or an aircraft built in one,” said Constance Lake First Nation Chief Richard Allen. “That new innovation and technology that brings the best sort of aircraft and saving people that May need that.”

Allen said he hopes his community will be at the front of the line when the first aircraft becomes available, allowing better access for his community but also for neighbouring first nations. While his community is accessible by road many northern First Nations are not, creating challenges in emergencies.

“Our main mission is to save lives,” he said.

The Cavorite X7 isn’t only being built for Canadian conditions, it’s being built in Canada, a choice Robinson says was intentional.

“There are so many exciting things about doing this right here in Canada. Canada is one of the only countries that has full clean sheet design, build, test and certify,” he said. “We have a proud history of manufacturing aircraft and certifying commercial aircraft and military machines as well.”

Horizon plans to have the full-size aircraft finished and in testing by late spring or early summer. Certification would be the next step and could come as early as 2030.

stories.title: Timeline: How Russia’s hockey comeback bid collided with Canada
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney's refusal to allow Russian players to compete at the 2027 world junior hockey championship in Alberta is the latest twist in a years-long battle over Russia's place in international hockey.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press

Posted November 4, 2026 12:52 pm.

Last Updated November 4, 2026 1:29 pm.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s refusal to allow Russian players to compete at the 2027 world junior hockey championship in Alberta is the latest twist in a years-long battle over Russia’s place in international hockey.

What began with a ban following Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine has turned into a legal and diplomatic dispute, with a court ruling ordering Russia’s reinstatement, European hockey powers threatening boycotts and Canada standing firm against its return.

Here’s how the dispute unfolded:

Feb. 28, 2022: The International Ice Hockey Federation (Iihf) barred Russia and Belarus from international tournaments following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and Belarusian support for it. The federation later stripped Russia of hosting rights for the 2023 world junior championship.

July 5, 2022: The Iihf disciplinary board rejected appeals by Russia and Belarus, ruling their exclusions were a safety measure rather than a sanction. Iihf president Luc Tardif said allowing the teams to compete would have posed an unacceptable safety risk.

Aug. 20, 2022: At the rescheduled world juniors in Edmonton, Tardif acknowledged Russia’s absence had eliminated marquee matchups. He said the federation would assess Russia’s possible return year by year.

Jan. 5, 2023: At the world juniors in Halifax, Tardif defended the decision to move the tournament from Russia to Halifax and Moncton, N.B. He also said Russia’s exclusion had delayed the NHL’s hopes of reviving the World Cup of Hockey.

April 16, 2023: Tardif said Russia and Belarus would remain excluded while the war continued. He expressed hope they could return as soon as possible, saying that would mean the war was over.

Feb. 24, 2024: Hockey Canada announced Alberta would host the 2027 world juniors. The province committed $11 million to several hockey events.

Feb. 4, 2025: The Iihf extended the exclusion of Russia and Belarus through the 2025-26 season, covering all world championships and the 2026 Winter Olympics unless the International Olympic Committee decided otherwise.

Nov. 18, 2025: Hockey Canada, the Canadian Hockey League and the Iihf named Edmonton and Red Deer as hosts of the 2027 world juniors, scheduled from Dec. 26, 2026, to Jan. 5, 2027.

Jan. 22, 2026: The Iihf said Russian and Belarusian youth teams would remain excluded for another season but opened the door to Russia’s possible return to under-18 competition in 2027-28. The federation again cited security concerns.

May 29, 2026: The Iihf said it would determine Russia’s eligibility for the 2026-27 season on an event-by-event basis. The announcement followed an appeal that overturned a January decision to exclude Russian teams. The Iihf maintained the ruling did not automatically reinstate Russia.

June 8, 2026: The Iihf unveiled the groups for the 2027 men’s world championship without Russia, setting the stage for a sixth straight absence from the tournament since the invasion.

July 30, 2026: The Iihf barred Russia from four tournaments in 2027 following a council review, citing safety, security and sporting-integrity concerns. The decision covered the world juniors, men’s worlds and under-18 men’s and women’s championships. The women’s world championship would be reviewed separately.

Oct. 30, 2026: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ordered Russia’s immediate reinstatement to Iihf championships, affecting five tournaments in 2027, including the world juniors in Alberta and the women’s world championship in Quebec City. Hockey Canada expressed disappointment and sought clarity on the ruling’s implications.

Nov. 2, 2026: Finland’s hockey federation said its national teams would refuse to face Russia in international tournaments while the war continued. Sweden, Czechia and Latvia announced similar positions the following day.

Nov. 3, 2026: Carney said Russian players would not be permitted to compete at the world juniors in Alberta. Ottawa said it would assess Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials individually and prevent them from entering Canada to compete under their national symbols. Hockey Canada supported the government’s position.

Nov. 4, 2026: The Iihf reaffirmed its opposition to the CAS ruling but did not directly address Canada’s decision. Sport secretary Adam van Koeverden dismissed concerns about international blowback, while veteran sport lawyer Dick Pound said CAS could not force Canada to admit Russian players.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

The Canadian Press

The premier says Canadians are ready to rebuild the relationship and strengthen the economies of both countries.

Formal trade talks stalled when Canada walked away from negotiations in August, but Prime Minister Mark Carney said there have been official trade discussions in recent days.

Kinew also specifically congratulated: Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, who is the first Indigenous woman elected to the Senate; Deb Haaland, who will lead New Mexico as the first Indigenous woman to serve as a U.S. governor; and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who is the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

stories.title: ‘A victory across the world,’ Ontario Premier Doug Ford says after U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Ford said the trade war is not over, but he is buoyed by the rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump by the American electorate.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he was “doing cartwheels” after the Democrats took control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in the U.S. midterm elections.

Ford said the trade war is not over, but he is buoyed by the rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump by the American electorate.

“You ever seen a big guy like me doing cartwheels? I was jumping up and down when the results were coming in,” Premier Ford told reporters on Wednesday. “It’s very simple: the American people spoke.”

He says he has directed his cabinet to head to the United States once the new members are sworn in to build relationships to de-escalate the trade war with Trump.

“The governors have big say in the U.S., and President Trump has to start listening,” said Premier Ford. “He lost a big election last night. He lost a lot of seats… He has to start listening to the people.”

Trump has begun backpedalling following the losses, shifting blame elsewhere but also pledging to work with the Democrats.

Ford said this is a victory for Canadians and the rest of the world.

“We’re going to be down there communicating, building those relationships,” the premier said. “I can’t wait.”

Trump recently placed tariffs on Canadian garbage headed to the United States and has said he’ll lay heavy tariffs on the auto sector on Jan. 1 in addition to previously announced tariffs against the country.

“I want to emphasize, the war is not over,” Premier Ford continued. “President Trump wants to blame everyone else but himself. He says, ‘Just pretend that my name is on the ballot.’ Well, the American people listened to that, and they showed what they thought about President Trump.”

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Wednesday that while the election results were interesting, he refused to interpret them and said the new Congress won’t change the federal government’s trade agenda.

“What the new Congress might decide to do when they’re seated two months from now is an interesting discussion at a faculty club luncheon at Mount Allison University today,” LeBlanc said.

“That’s not going to change the work that we have to do in the next two weeks. The American Congress will act in the interests of the American Congress. Our work will be focused on what we can do here at home.”

With files from Lucas Casaletto of CityNews

stories.title: QuickQuotes: Canadian leaders react to Democratic majority win in U.S. Congress
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Democrats will take control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate in January, following decisive victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
stories.author: Alyssa Wheeler The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The Democrats will take control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate in January after decisive victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The Republicans previously held a majority of seats in both houses of Congress.

Here is what some Canadian leaders are saying.

“We congratulate those who were elected but our focus hasn’t changed. Yesterday we went to work on issues of affordability for Canadians, ON building major projects, ON strengthening the Canadian economy and diversifying our trading relationships. That was our focus yesterday, that is actually our focus today and will be the focus tomorrow in the budget.”

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc

“What the midterms did do is reconfirm what I said all along, which is we have massive leverage in the form of the goodwill of the American people. I mean Americans hate these tariffs. Everywhere I went in the States, and it didn’t matter if it was Texas or Detroit or New York, Democrat, Republican, worker or business union or management, everybody hates the tariffs. We’ve got to use that goodwill to pressure for tariff-free trade.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre

“Obviously we watch them with interest, but I think the strategy for Canada going forward remains the same — to defend our economic interests by diversifying trade partners, seeing if we can work through the challenges that we continue to have vis-a-vis the United States. Congratulations to everyone who has put their name forward on the ballot, including specifically those who have been elected, but the work remains the same for Canada today and tomorrow.”

Justice Minister Sean Fraser

“I think we’ve always made it a point of our diplomacy to engage at all levels with the U.S. government. Last night is just another example of the American people speaking … I think we’ve always fought for the best deal possible. The Americans have their reasons for what they did yesterday, and I think that’s their choice, and I obviously respect it.”

Canadian Heritage Minister Marc Miller

“Last night’s U.S. election results were due at least in part to the impact of those harmful tariff policies. We now have an opportunity to reset our relationship with the U.S. and restore free and fair trade between our two countries. I know Canada is ready to do this. Hopefully, the U.S. is as well.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe

“The American people have delivered a resounding rejection of the president’s actions over the past two years. Canadians are ready to rebuild the relationship and strengthen our economies.”

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew

“Our focus continues to be fighting for the best possible trade deal and delivering good paying jobs for New Brunswickers. We are looking forward to building relationships with the newly elected Governors, Senators and Congresspeople and expect that their leadership will result in improved trade conditions for N.B. entrepreneurs and workers.”

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt

“I’m directing our ministers as soon as everyone gets sworn in, go down to Washington, connect with the senators, the congresspeople, and of course, I’ll be talking to the governors and seeing how we can move forward. But let’s be under no illusion that this trade war is done. It’s not done. It’s not even close to being done because the president still has the power.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford

“It is a vindication of our approach when it comes to tariffs. We always have objected to tariffs. We know it hurts us. It hurts the Americans. It is also is a vindication of our approach when it comes to reaching across the aisle.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith

“Our relationship with the U.S. is grounded in shared interests, longstanding partnerships, and enduring connections. We remain committed to working together on priorities such as trade, economic growth, and regional development.”

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Fact File: No evidence for Trump claim Canada will 'pay for all' of Keystone pipeline
stories.summary: United States President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Canada would pay for the entirety of a revived Keystone XL pipeline. Experts on Canada’s natural resource sector say such funding seems unlikely.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
United States President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Canada would pay for the entirety of a revived Keystone XL pipeline. While the project has yet to be revived, the Prairie Connector pipeline that would reuse Keystone XL infrastructure is jointly owned by two independent companies, one Canadian and one American, with no federal funding commitments as of yet.

Experts on Canada’s natural resource sector say such funding seems unlikely. The claim During a media scrum in Dubuque, Iowa, Trump said trade negotiations with Canada would include the Keystone pipeline. “They’re going to build the Keystone pipeline.

They’re going to pay for it. They’re going to pay for all of it,” he said, adding that the U.S. would provide the route and Canada the financing. Both Trump and the reporter appeared to be referring to the Keystone XL pipeline project, not the Keystone pipeline, which began operating in 2010.

Keystone XL would have seen crude oil sent from Western Canada to American refineries. But TC Energy cancelled Keystone XL in 2021, after then-U.S. president Joe Biden revoked its cross-border permit. “They build it, they pay for ALL of it, and we give them the route,” reads an X post from an account that echoed Trump’s claim.

The pipeline claim was shared multiple times on X, as well as on Facebook. The facts While the Keystone XL pipeline project remains dormant, Canadian critical energy infrastructure company South Bow aims to partner with American crude oil transportation company Bridger Pipeline on a pipeline that reuses some Keystone XL infrastructure on the Canadian side of the border.

This Prairie Connector pipeline would extend from Hardisty, Alta., to the U.S. border, where it would connect to the Bridger Pipeline Expansion system planned to reach as far as Oklahoma. Before the Keystone XL termination, the Alberta government said it had provided $1.5 billion in equity investment in 2020 and a $6-billion loan guarantee in 2021 to support the project, while the federal government did not provide funding.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has not responded to Trump’s claim about Keystone XL, though he said Sunday that overall trade negotiations have been constructive. Carney had previously raised the prospect of reviving the pipeline with Trump about a year ago, with the aim of linking energy co-operation and supporting Canada’s steel and aluminum sectors.

Jean-Thomas Bernard, an economics professor at the University of Ottawa who specializes in natural resources economics, said he would be surprised if Trump were able to renew Keystone XL with only two years left in his term.

“Mr. Trump approved this project in his first time around, and nothing got off the ground,” Bernard said in an interview Tuesday. He said opposition from some states and First Nations, competition with cheaper oil producers in the Middle East, and Canada’s interest in building oil pipelines to the West Coast to access the Pacific market are some of the obstacles a revived Keystone XL could face.

Bernard said Canada’s agreement to share with the United States toll revenues from the Gordie Howe Bridge, outside of a previously established agreement, was an example of a joint infrastructure project that became a “burden” to Canada.

Trump, who had called the toll terms unfair for the United States, made multiple false claims about Canada’s role in the project. He said Canada owned the entire bridge, built it with almost no American materials and that the United States would “get nothing” from the bridge.

“I hope that Canada learned a lesson out of this experiment and that we don’t put any money south of the border,” Bernard said. Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said it’s unclear how the Prairie Connector pipeline will be funded since South Bow says it will not reach a final investment decision until next year.

“But there’s never been an indication it would need government money,” she said in an email Monday. “The fact they had a successful open season is strong indication of commercial viability and therefore ability to access private equity and debt.” South Bow said its open season, which allowed shippers to bid on contracts, was successful and resulted in 20-year binding commitments.

According to a September report from the Globe and Mail, South Bow told investors it was looking into several ways to pay for the pipeline, including selling a stake to private equity fund managers, and executives said a federal tax break on investments in assets “strengthened the case” for the pipeline.

Exner-Poirot said that it would be hard to believe the Canadian federal government would finance an American company and its American infrastructure. Bill Salvin, a spokesman for Bridger Pipeline, said Canadian government funding does not apply to the American side of the pipeline expansion because it is a U.S.-based project.

He said the private company does not release the financial details of its projects. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026. Marissa Birnie, The Canadian Press With files from Timon Johnson

stories.title: Doug Ford says he did ‘cartwheels’ after seeing U.S. midterm election results
stories.summary: As soon as the newly elected U.S. officials are sworn in at the end of January, Ford said he’s directing his ministers to head down to Washington, D.C.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford said he was doing “cartwheels” and was “as happy as possible” when he saw the results of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections , which saw the Democratic Party flip the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, in a clear rebuke of Donald Trump’s presidency.

“Trump wants to blame everyone but himself,” said Ford. “The cheese has slipped off the cracker with this guy.”

But Ford cautioned that Ontario is “under no illusions that the trade war is done.” “It’s not even close to being done because (Trump) still has the power…the January tariffs are still on the table,” he said.

As soon as the newly elected U.S. officials are sworn in at the end of January, Ford said he’s directing his ministers to head down to Washington, D.C. and connect with senators, congresspeople and governors about the importance of Ontario as a trading partner and the damage done by the trade war with the U.S.

“We’re going to be down there, communicating, building those relationships,” he said. “We have to continue making sure that we move faster, quicker, immediate on everything across the board.”

As the midterm results flowed in Tuesday night, the sheer scale of the Democrat’s win quickly became apparent. Democrats flipped long-held Republican Senate seats in Texas, Maine and South Carolina. Seven seats were flipped in total.

Democrats also triumphed in the House of Representatives, clearing the number of seats needed to take control of the chamber. Historic wins were seen in several governor races, with Keisha Lance Bottoms being elected as Georgia’s first Black female governor.

It was a clear indication of Americans’ disapproval of Trump’s policies, which have led to higher prices at the pump and grocery stores.

New officials in office is a huge opportunity for Ontario, said Ford, particularly as the trade war with Canada became ballot box issues in Michigan and Maine, where the province is a key trading partner.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive senator-elect who won the Michigan race, is someone Ford said he’s willing to work with.

“He wants jobs, he wants prosperity. He wants economic growth in Michigan….we’re going to continue building that great relationship,” he said.

But Ontario Liberal Leader John Fraser said Ford needs to temper his excitement as “the reality is we’re not out of the woods.”

“Trump is still the president. The representatives that were elected last night won’t take office until January. What we need is a plan,” he said.

Fraser urged Ford to take a more “disciplined” approach and follow the tone set by Prime Minister Mark Carney. “I would not get excited and say ‘Trump lost’, how’s that going to do any good?” said Fraser. “You’re getting out of the gate.”

When it comes to ironing out a trade deal with the president, Ford said it’s ultimately up to Prime Minister Mark Carney and shook his head when asked if Trump can be relied upon in negotiations.

“I can’t trust [Trump] as far as I could throw him…maybe the Prime Minister feels differently, but he has shown, over and over again, that he can’t be trusted,” said Ford.

On Tuesday, Carney said “more intense” trade negotiations with the U.S. had begun following his call with Trump last weekend. He said both sides have made progress on the issue of restricting Canada’s ability to negotiate deals with other countries.

In August, Carney called off formal trade talks with the U.S., after rejecting what he described as a “bad deal.” Canada launched retaliatory counter-tariffs in September that ranged from 15 to 50 per cent on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. goods.

Three Canadians are among 63 people facing charges related to alleged election offences across the United States, including illegally voting and falsely claiming American citizenship.

The U.S. Department of Justice announced the new charges Monday , the day before Americans headed to the polls for the midterm elections , outlining cases involving voter registration fraud, illegal voting and false statements about citizenship.

stories.title: Canadian woman accused of joining Isis was ‘brainwashed,’ former friend testifies
stories.summary: At Canada's first trial of a woman accused of living under Isis in Syria, a witness described Ammara Amjad's descent into extremism.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
A witness testifying at the trial of a Canadian woman accused of joining Isis in Syria has described watching her close friend become “brainwashed.”

Naveed Deol said she and Ammara Amjad were once like sisters. But Amjad’s extremist rhetoric eventually became so preachy that they parted ways.

“It just wasn’t the same person,” Deol testified.

Captured in Syria during the 2019 defeat of Isis , Amjad is currently on trial in Brampton, Ont., for participating in the activities of a terrorist group.

She is the first Canadian woman to face criminal prosecution for allegedly living under the Islamic State in Syria as the terror group committed atrocities.

The Crown wrapped up its case against the Pakistan-born 32-year-old mother of two on Wednesday, following testimony from the RCMP officer who extracted Amjad’s messages from her mother’s phone.

Appearing as a Crown witness on Tuesday, Deol described her former friend’s sudden transformation — a change she blamed on Amjad’s first husband, Canadian extremist Bilal Khan .

Deol said she first met Amjad when their families lived in Montreal. She later moved in with the Amjads in Brampton while she completed her studies.

Far from an extremist in her teens, Amjad came from a happy Pakistani-Canadian family, would drink alcohol and remove her hijab once she had left home, Deol said.

But in 2015, when the two met at a Boston Pizza, Amjad said Khan had been sending her reading materials, people were suffering and she wanted to help.

Then Amjad asked Deol to take her to the airport. She said she was flying to Turkey to meet Khan, who was already in the Middle East, she explained.

Deol said she felt Amjad, then a 19-year old Walmart worker who had never showed any interest in politics or current affairs, was having an “existential crisis.”

Although Amjad was vague about specifics, Deol suspected she was heading for Syria to join an extremist group and refused to take her friend to the airport.

“I was concerned for her safety,” Deol said, adding she feared Khan was misleading a naive teenager. “I felt that he had brainwashed her.”

On March 17, 2015, Amjad applied to renew her Canadian passport, writing that she was travelling on March 19. She allegedly crossed from Turkey into Isis controlled Syria.

Although she never gave away her location, she messaged Deol upon arriving to say that she had married Khan, a suspected Isis fighter, and “was happy.”

“Bilal left today,” according to a message Amjad sent to Deol on WhatsApp. “I don’t know when he’s going to be back or even if he will be back.”

When Khan was killed in November 2015, Amjad took it in stride, Deol said. “She always knew that he was going to die and she was prepared for it.”

Amjad later gave birth to their child, but the baby only lived a day. Again, she was fatalistic. “I’m happy. Whatever happens, happens for a reason,” she said.

Amjad then allegedly married British Isis member Hamza Parvez. But she did not tell Deol anything about her new husband, except that they had two kids.

Deol, who said she was not religious, said Amjad would accuse her of being “blinded” and not knowing anything, and that she needed to think about the afterlife

Over time, they lost touch. Deol said she was busy with her own life and had grown tired of the way Amjad spoke to her about religion.

By the time they reconnected, Amjad had been taken prisoner by U.S.-backed Kurdish fighters and was being held at a camp for Isis families in northeast Syria.

“I guess whatever group she was in, it ended,” Deol testified.

Deol said Amjad asked her to send money but she refused. She didn’t want to be associated with someone with extremist beliefs, she explained.

“I just don’t know you anymore,” she told Amjad.

She said she felt guilty that she hadn’t warned Amjad’s parents that their daughter was talking about going to Turkey. But she decided to let her friend go.

She tried to message her once more, when the RCMP visited her in 2020 and said they were trying to bring her home from Syria, but Amjad never responded.

Amjad spent four years in detention camps for Isis suspects until the Canadian government brought her home from Syria in April 2023. She was charged with terrorism in October 2023.

Dozens of Canadian extremists left B.C., Alberta, Ontario and Quebec to join Isis after the terror group emerged from Al Qaeda and seized parts of Syria and Iraq.

While many died, several were captured during the 2019 rout of Isis. Canada has repatriated nine women from Syria, at significant expense . Two have pleaded guilty, but a half-dozen others have not been charged .

The Crown’s case hinges largely on Amjad’s own messages, which are mostly in Urdu, while the defence has challenged the accuracy of the RCMP’s translations.

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.CA

stories.title: From home kitchens to store shelves, Diwali finds a wider audience in Canada
stories.summary: Families preparing for Diwali can find sweets, clay lamps known as diyas, decorations and specialty ingredients at major retailers.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
By Loveen Gill, OMNI News

Posted November 4, 2026 12:09 pm.

On her first Diwali in Canada, Harminder Grewal made kheer, said a prayer and thought about her family in India. She had arrived as a new bride in August 1975. When the Festival of Lights came around, she and her husband marked it quietly at home.

“On Diwali day we would sit here and miss family. There was nothing to do,” she recalled. “We would make kheer [Indian rice pudding], pray and that was it.”

A phone call home lifted her spirits, even if her husband, Surinder Grewal, had one eye on the clock.

“When she called home, I was happy to see her happy, but my heart would sink knowing it was five dollars per minute,” he said.

More than five decades later, families preparing for Diwali can find sweets, clay lamps known as diyas, decorations and specialty ingredients at major retailers. Schools and community groups mark the occasion through classroom activities, dance performances and public celebrations. The festival the Grewals once observed quietly at home now has a place on Canadian postage stamps, in toy aisles and in bank catalogues.

“Diwali means everything to us”

For Harminder, that change happened gradually. As the couple got to know more families, Diwali grew from a quiet evening into a gathering. Pulling out an old photo album, she remembered how everyone pitched in to make about 100 samosas and plenty of sweets, all from scratch.

Sortur said the gatherings were a chance to learn from one another. As the women cooked together, they taught each other how to make dishes from their home states.

Years later, the two friends were shopping for Diwali supplies together when Sortur sent a video from the store to a friend. The reply captured how much had changed.

“Yesterday when I went to store to buy Diwali things with Harminder, I sent video to my friend,” Sortur said. “She said, ‘Wow, you live in India or Canada?'”

Harminder, a former Punjabi teacher, remembers bringing a diya from India to show her students how it was traditionally lit. At home one Diwali, Surinder asked her to put out an incense stick because he worried the neighbours might object to the smell.

“But now you get everything at stores. It’s amazing,” she said. “The times have changed now. The new generations have brought Diwali here.”

Diwali holds particular significance for Hindus. Around the same time, Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas and Jains observe Mahavira Nirvana Diwas, distinct religious occasions that also have traditions involving light. Statistics Canada noted in an October 2025 article that the 2021 census counted about 828,000 Hindus, 772,000 Sikhs and 8,300 Jains in Canada.

Retailers see a market, too. Walmart Canada said more than half of its stores stocked Diwali products in 2025, including food, décor, clothing and gifts. “Diwali means everything to us,” he said.

stories.title: Multiple bears May be linked to B.C. attack that killed mother and daughter
stories.summary: The Conservation Officer Service says it’s ‘not yet clear if more than one bear was involved,’ and any bears captured in the area will be assessed
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The brother of a woman who was killed along with her daughter in a suspected grizzly bear attack in Bella Coola, B.C., says she was “remarkable” and an inspiration to her siblings.

Matthew Balcarras said on Wednesday that Jenny Balcarras was “incredibly strong” and had lived in many difficult, remote places, including Alaska, before moving to Bella Coola on B.C.’s central coast a few months ago.

Conservation officers said the remains of two people were found near a set of trails this week, after Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, 20, were reported missing by relatives over the weekend.

Authorities have imposed a curfew on the community, about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver, as the search for the animal or animals behind the attack continues.

“She was a beautiful artist and was an inspiration for me and my brothers,” said Matthew Balcarras said of his sister, adding that they came from a family of six.

He said he asked police to perform a wellness check at his sister’s Bella Coola home on the weekend and there was no sign of her or her vehicle, which police later located at a trailhead.

Balcarras said he later met with police and conservation officers at the local RCMP detachment and was told what had likely happened.

“You hear somebody say words that you don’t normally hear and a lot of vivid pictures come to mind. So, what comes to mind is incoherent noise, like being overwhelmed,” said Balcarras.

The deaths come nearly a year after a grizzly attack on a group of 20 elementary school students and teachers near the same set of trails, which left one adult and three children badly hurt.

The animal involved in that attack last November was never captured.

Insp. Jeff Tyre with the B.C. Conservation Officer Service said on Wednesday that bear DNA from last year’s attack site would be compared with samples gathered in the wake of the latest attack.

“As we collect bear (DNA), capture bears, we will send that DNA off to the lab and hopefully get a match,” said Tyre in a virtual news conference.

But he added that there was a “very large” bear population in the area, and it was too early to speculate if both attacks involved the same animal.

Tyre said no bears were captured in traps set overnight, and it wasn’t yet clear if more than one bear was involved in the most recent attack.

“There are numerous grizzly bears that live in the Bella Coola Valley, and we have received reports of sightings in the area. Any bears that we capture will be assessed,” said Tyre.

If the “offending bear” is captured it will be killed to protect public safety, added Tyre.

Tyre said the remains of the mother and daughter were found about 150 metres apart on Monday and Tuesday, but declined to provide details about how the tragedy might have unfolded “out of respect for the family.”

Terry Webber, chief administrative officer of the Nuxalk Nation, said the community was still healing from last year’s attack and the new tragedy made the wounds more difficult to heal.

“Our community members are retriggered, and our priority is to continue to ensure they’re safe,” said Webber.

Webber said an 8 p.m. curfew was in place and residents were being provided transport to ensure safety.

Balcarras said his older sister had built a new career in mid-life as an art therapist and moved to Bella Coola only a few months ago. She worked at the local school.

“She had previously done similar work in Bella Bella, and she cares deeply about working with kids in art therapy,” said Balcarras.

The Central Coast Teachers’ Association said on social media that Balcarras had joined their school community as a counsellor in August, and she devoted “countless hours to connecting with the students she served and worked closely with teachers and other staff supporting their well-being.”

“Her time among us was far too brief, but her kindness, dedication, and care have left a lasting impression on our school community. She will be deeply missed,” said the release.

A fundraiser set up by relative Mary Melissa Smith said Reed had “her whole life ahead of her,” while Jenny Belcarras left behind three young adult children, as well as a grandchild.

Smith said in the post that Balcarras had moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career and start a new chapter in her life. No one could have anticipated “such an unimaginable loss,” she said.

Kim Titchener, founder of Bear Safety in education based in Calgary, said she was concerned when she saw reports about the missing women on Facebook hiking groups.

“When I saw that they were missing, and in the area that they were missing, my heart just dropped because I just kind of knew this could be a bear attack,” said Titchener.

“This community and area have suffered so much last year,” she said.

Titchener said she had several daycares and school groups calling her for bear safety training following last year’s attack.

Bella Coola is well-known for its large population of grizzly and black bears, and Titchener said it was common for people in Bella Coola to see bears walking near their homes.

Titchener said there have “concerning pressures” on bear populations in B.C. due to the loss of habitat, food stress caused by drought and climate change, setting off more conflicts with people.

“I don’t know if Bella Coola suffered from any drought issues, but certainly other parts of the province of B.C. did.”

The conservation service has asked residents to stay away from the west trail area of the Snooka trail system where the attack happened.

“We understand a fatal grizzly bear attack can generate many questions and concerns in the communities and beyond. I can assure you, a thorough investigation is being conducted to try and find answers as to what May have led to the attack,” said Tyre.

stories.title: 23 arrested, 90 charges laid after York Regional Police seize $7.5M in drugs
stories.summary: Investigators allege a group involved in the production, trafficking and exportation of illicit cannabis sourced illicit marijuana from across Ontario.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Twenty-three people are facing a total of 90 charges after York Regional Police seized more than $7.5 million in drugs.

Police said Wednesday the seizure is tied to its probe dubbed Project North Star, which began in February 2026.

Investigators allege a group involved in the production, trafficking and exportation of illicit cannabis sourced illicit marijuana from across Ontario, including a large-scale illicit cannabis grow operation in London, Ont.

Police allege the cannabis was produced outside Ontario’s cannabis regulation framework before being distributed through the underground market, including through an online illicit dispensary.

Investigators also claim the group allegedly exported cannabis throughout North America and parts of Europe using commercial parcel delivery services.

Search warrants were executed this July through to September in Markham, Scarborough, Vaughan, Burlington, Milton, London and the rural village of Ailsa Craig.

The searches resulted in the seizure of more than 1,550 pounds of cannabis, more than 8.5 pounds of hashish and more than 4.4 pounds of cannabis derivatives, among other contraband.

Officers also shut down the grow operation in London. The cannabis seized there is worth roughly $4.8 million, police said.

One person remains wanted.

Markham resident Zongyu Zhu, 26, is wanted for conspiracy to commit an indictable offence and possession for the purpose of distributing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Beijing, Ottawa agree to extend deal on canola, Chinese steel access to late 2028
stories.summary: Ottawa - Beijing and Ottawa are extending a January agreement to provide Chinese market access to Canadian imports in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Beijing and Ottawa are extending a January agreement to provide Chinese market access to Canadian imports in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.

The news comes as one of China’s most important officials prepares to visit Vancouver and Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to return to China later this month.

In March, China dropped tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab. Canada agreed in return to allow in certain Chinese steel and aluminum products.

The deal was negotiated by Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping during a visit to China. It was set to expire at the end of this year.

On Wednesday, Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said the deal is being extended by two years, to the end of 2028.

“This extension gives Canadian farmers, producers and harvesters stable access to China and supports billions in export opportunities,” Sidhu said in a news release.

He said the credit goes to a trade body Canada and China relaunched in January as Ottawa moved to increase exports to China by 50 per cent by 2030.

Sidhu was in Beijing for meetings with officials ahead of Carney’s planned visit to China’s tech city Shenzhen later this month for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit.

“The timing of the announcement is significant,” said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, in an emailed statement.

She said the clearing of “an immediate trade irritant” allows Carney to focus on boosting Chinese investment during his visit to Shenzhen. It also locks in Chinese steel and aluminum access, which she said will be a factor in Ottawa’s trade talks with Washington.

“Ottawa is increasingly having to navigate its economic relationships with Beijing and Washington simultaneously, and decisions made in one relationship inevitably have implications for the other,” she wrote.

On Wednesday, Ottawa announced that Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng will visit Vancouver on Sunday and Monday.

Though he is not China’s trade or finance minister, Lifeng plays a major role in crafting Beijing’s trade and economic polices.

Sidhu and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will welcome He and events are also planned with Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem and financial regulators.

Sidhu’s office said Wednesday the canola news stems from months of efforts to improve trade relations with China.

In June 2025, Sidhu said he and Wang Wentao, China’s minister of commerce, agreed to restart a joint economic and trade commission to address trade issues. In January, he said Ottawa secured a preliminary joint arrangement in Beijing which opened up more than $7 billion in market space for Canadian workers and businesses.

Sidhu said that since the arrangement took effect in March, canola seed exports to China have increased by 84 per cent, from $1.04 billion to $1.91 billion, compared to the same period last year.

He said canola meal exports more than doubled, from $146 million to $390 million, while pea exports grew from $107 million to $345 million. Sidhu also said lobster exports increased by 57 per cent, from $128 million to $200 million.

Warren Kaeding, Saskatchewan’s trade minister, told reporters in Regina that farmers are pleased with the deal.

“That helps so much in them being able to plan their cropping rotations into next year,” he said. “(They’re) going into the spring with a bit of confidence that they at least have a two-year extension on tariff reductions on canola and peas.”

Canadian beef also returned to the Chinese market in January for the first time since 2021, said Sidhu. From January to August, he said, Canada sent $363.2 million in beef exports to China, nearly double what it sold there in all of 2021.

“Over the past year, I’ve met with industry representatives, including the Canola Council of Canada, Pulse Canada, the Fisheries Council of Canada, the Canadian Cattle Association and the Canadian Meat Council,” says a media statement from Sidhu’s office.

“They told me an extension would give them the predictable, long-term access to the Chinese market and the certainty they need. We listened, and we delivered.”

Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said on social media the extension provides “immediate certainty” for lobster and crab harvesters and exporters. She said discussions are continuing on other seafood products.

“Last week in China, I met with government officials and industry leaders to make the case for Canada as a trusted supplier,” she said. “Canada’s fish and seafood harvesters catch the best seafood in the world and their work drives rural and coastal communities across the country.”

In Beijing earlier this year, Carney outlined steps to build a new strategic partnership with China, including more cultural exchanges and “people-to-people” ties.

Carney said during his visit that Ottawa hoped the renewal would become an “example to the world of co-operation amidst a time globally of division and disorder.”

Culture Minister Marc Miller made a five-day trip to China last month with dozens of representatives from Canadian creative industries. His office said seven new commercial agreements worth more than $4.2 million were signed during the trip.

The Carney government is seeking to double non-U.S. exports in the next decade in response to the unstable geopolitical and trading environment ushered in by the re-election of U.S. President Donald Trump.

China is Canada’s second largest single-country merchandise trading partner, accounting for $125.7 billion in two-way merchandise trade in 2025.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

— With files from Kyle Duggan and Jeremy Simes

stories.title: Quebec to launch diplomatic offensive in U.S. after midterms, premier says
stories.summary: Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says his government will launch a diplomatic offensive south of the border following the U.S. midterm elections.
stories.author: Patrice Bergeron
stories.content:
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says his government will launch a “diplomatic offensive” south of the border following the U.S. midterm elections that saw the Democrats gain control of both houses of Congress.

St-Pierre Plamondon believes Canada and Quebec will have an easier time finding allies to ease tensions after a result that’s widely viewed as a rejection of U.S. President Donald Trump’s policies.

“I think we’re in a better position to possibly find a solution because Americans have spoken, the situation has changed,” he told reporters in Quebec City. “So what we’re going to do is prepare a diplomatic offensive of discussion with the Americans to see if there isn’t a solution.”

Democrats flipped long-held Republican Senate seats in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, while holding on to battleground seats in Georgia and Michigan.

The trade war with Canada became a ballot box issue in close contests in Maine and Michigan, where Democrats defeated their Republican rivals.

Quebec is one of the provinces most affected by U.S. tariffs, which target softwood lumber, aluminum, and various manufactured goods.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he didn’t plan for Quebec to carry out trade negotiations directly with the Americans — at least for now.

“I think that before positioning ourselves on that, we’ll open up the channels of discussion,” he said.

The Quebec premier was also asked when he would meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney, after recent tension between the two leaders.

St-Pierre Plamondon did not attend the Canada-European Union Summit in Montreal last week after Ottawa refused to grant him official speaking rights.

The premier has accepted an invitation to meet with Carney, but doubled down on Wednesday on insisting that the meeting take place in Quebec City.

“We’ll take the first date in Quebec,” the premier said, while acknowledging that he might end up speaking with Carney at the upcoming Francophonie summit in Cambodia later this month, which they are both attending.

Carney and St-Pierre Plamondon have not formally met in person since the Oct. 5 provincial election, but they have spoken on the phone.

stories.title: Fire, smoke shutters SkyTrain service at Burnaby, B.C., stations
stories.summary: Burnaby - SkyTrain service in Metro Vancouver has been disrupted after a fire near a station in Burnaby, B.C.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TransLink says in a release that the fire happened near the Gilmore station, resulting in the shutdown of the station as well as the nearby Rupert and Brentwood stations.

Bus bridge services have been set up in both directions while the Millennium Line route has been closed, although the Canada and Expo lines are not affected.

Article continues below

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

TransLink says it is investigating the SkyTrain infrastructure affected by the fire to make sure Gilmore station and the tracks are in safe operating condition before services are restored.

Videos on social media show a large fire under the station’s elevated platform that generated heavy smoke inside the station.

stories.title: Canfor reports smaller third-quarter loss than a year earlier, sales edged up
stories.summary: Company anticipates market conditions will remain challenging through rest of the year, CEO says
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canfor Corp. CFP-T reported a third-quarter loss of $88.2-million compared with a loss of $172.4-million in the same quarter last year.

The forestry company says the loss amounted to 75 cents per diluted share for the quarter compared with a loss of $1.48 per diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.

Sales for the quarter totalled $1.28-billion, up from $1.26-billion a year earlier.

On an adjusted basis, Canfor says it saw an operating loss of $43.8-million in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted operating loss of $188.5-million a year ago.

Canfor CEO Susan Yurkovich said the company anticipates market conditions will remain challenging through the balance of the year, with softer seasonal demand for lumber and continued pressure in global pulp markets.

During the quarter, the company announced the permanent closure of its sawmill in Fox Creek, Alta., and the Northwood pulp mill in Prince George, B.C.
