stories.title: ‘They’re not going to be the same’: Top burn surgeon on the painful road ahead for Wainwright victims
stories.summary: Two Ontario soldiers severely burned in the fire on the Alberta military base are now under the care of the country's largest burn centre
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Soon after operating on one member of the Armed Forces and before he was due to operate on a second, Dr. Alan Rogers described how the lives of his patients, both “young, healthy guys” severely burned in the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright, have been forever altered.

“For me, it’s devastating to see young boys getting injured like this, honestly,” said Rogers, a plastic and reconstructive surgeon at the Ross Tilley Burn Centre at Toronto’s Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, the country’s largest burn unit.

“On the other hand, I appreciate that I have some of the skills and knowledge, and I’m part of an excellent team, and we can help these guys.

“But what we can do doesn’t bring back how they looked before, how they functioned before.

unfortunately,” he said.

“We’ll do our very best.”

The two men were transferred by air ambulance Friday to Sunnybrook from a specialized Edmonton burn unit. “We’ve essentially repatriated our own patients,” Rogers said of the two service members who are from Ontario.

He could not divulge personal details because of patient confidentiality. He didn’t want to get into specifics, for fear of crossing a boundary.

“But I can say that they both have very extensive burns.”

A third service member from Ontario was discharged from hospital and is being followed as an outpatient at Sunnybrook.

All three were among those injured when a grass fire broke out during training exercises at CFB Wainwright in Alberta on the afternoon of Oct. 17. According to military officials, the fire ignited in the area where soldiers were using live munitions and spread rapidly because of high winds. The inferno claimed the lives of four soldiers and left 39 others injured, 19 critically.

As of last Wednesday, 27 remained in hospital, 13 in critical condition.

Ten specialized burn nurses and a burn surgeon from the Sunnybrook burn centre arrived in Alberta days after the fire.

“I think this has been one of the most traumatic experiences for them,” Rogers said of his colleagues, some of whom are close friends

“Many of them have been doing burn nursing for 30 years or more. Some of our most experienced nurses. For them to say that this is one of the most traumatic experiences that they’ve observed says a lot.”

The burn injuries in otherwise fit and healthy young people are extensive. That’s traumatic enough on an individual level, but the sheer scale of the tragedy makes it even more devastating, Rogers said.

A major burn goes beyond the skin; it affects the whole person, he said. “Fluid requirements are higher, nutritional requirements are higher” and people are at dramatically heightened risk for infection because they’ve lost the barrier to the environment, their skin.

People can get pneumonia, urinary infections, or bloodstream infections. “And of course most of the bacteria come from the wounds, because the wounds are not yet closed; they’re open.”

The advantage of young people is that they tend to heal well. “Assuming we do all the right things, they should heal,” Rogers said.

But with severe burns, the greatest surgical challenge is that there often isn’t enough unburned skin left to use for traditional skin grafts.

With deep, extensive burns, skin is no longer viable, Rogers said. It undergoes cell death, or necrosis. The dead tissue needs to be removed and replaced with the person’s own healthy skin, because the skin is the body’s primary protection against infection.

Burned skin is often temporarily replaced with cadaver skin, “and then we change it for their own (skin) by way of skin graft surgery,” said Rogers, who is also an associate professor of plastic, reconstructive and aesthetic surgery at the University of Toronto.

With conventional skin grafting, thin layers of skin are taken from unburned areas and moved to burned ones. But sometimes there isn’t enough skin to go around, and unburned skin needs to be reused more than once, which means waiting for the donor site to heal before moving to the next section.

Donor skin can be expanded and stretched to cover larger areas. More revolutionary treatments might also be used on the soldiers, including a product developed by Laval University researchers that involves using a skin substitute grown from the patient’s own cells.

Later, people need reconstruction, scar treatment, rehabilitation, and help returning to family life and jobs, Rogers said.

But the psychological toll begins with what happened at the time of the burn, he said. People can experience a form of post-traumatic stress, re-living the fire in recurring nightmares. Some might experience feelings of guilt for those who didn’t survive. Some witnessed people dying.

Some of the patients will be disabled. Some will be completely dependent on their families. Some will never go back to work. It has a massive socioeconomic and psychological effect

At the hospital, care involves balancing the patient’s level of awareness.

“We can’t keep them completely sedated the entire time. That has ill effects too,” Rogers said.

But being awake not only means having to deal with the physical pain of dressing changes; being awake also means having to confront the harsh realities of their injuries.

“These are young patients, many of whom have been disfigured by the burn injury,” Rogers said.

“They’re never going to look the same. However good the surgery we do, their skin is not going to be normal. They’re going to have a number of contractures. They’re going to have some disability. Range of motion is going to be affected. Strength is going to be affected,” Rogers said.

“Some of them will lose fingers. Some will have amputations. Each and every part of that is traumatic.”

While the psychological burden is tied to the physical injuries, “it can be so much greater, and so much more enduring, well after all the wounds have healed.”

Families can feel relatively powerless at first, Rogers said.

Many of the injured have young families — partners, wives, young children. “Many are in their mid-20s,” Rogers said.

“The impact is enormous.”

The goal while in hospital is “to do as good as a job as we can (so that) they survive. They survive with reasonably well-healed wounds, and they rehabilitate as best they can,” he said.

Some who survive severe burns ultimately become supporters to others experiencing similar trauma, “because they have that to offer, and it’s very rewarding for them,” Rogers said.

“Some really struggle.”

The Wainwright tragedy is especially heartbreaking “because it sounds as if there were circumstances that were preventable,” Rogers said.

Military police are investigating, and a separate independent board of inquiry will be conducted, officials have said.

stories.title: Canadians can’t keep up with their debt: Benchmark Canada
stories.summary: One insolvency firm says its clients carried average unsecured debts of more than $67,000 last year, up 37 per cent over three years
stories.author: David George-Cosh, Special to National Post
stories.content:
Countries don’t typically get report cards, but there are hard facts that can be collated, assessed and compared. Enter Benchmark Canada , a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings together more than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance. This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

Canadians are falling further behind on car loans, credit cards and personal loans, with arrears in all three categories hitting their highest levels in the decade-long period tracked by Benchmark Canada.

Canada’s debt strain is greatest in instalment loans, which include unsecured personal loans and point-of-sale financing. The share of those loans that are at least 90 days overdue reached 2.95 per cent, more than triple the 0.95 per cent recorded in late 2015, the Macdonald-Laurier Institute project showed.

Meanwhile, auto-loan arrears stood at 0.87 per cent, up from a pandemic low of 0.39 per cent in 2021. Credit-card arrears reached 0.80 per cent, nearly double from their 2021 low of 0.44 per cent.

Doug Hoyes, co-founder of insolvency firm Hoyes, Michalos & Associates Inc., said borrowers often tap a line of credit to make up for lost income. When that runs out, they turn to credit cards, then higher-cost instalment loans and payday lenders.

“You cannot keep layering borrowing on top of borrowing,” he said.

Hoyes said many of his clients use those loans to cover bills after exhausting cheaper sources of credit, hoping their income will recover before the payments become unmanageable.

His firm’s clients carried average unsecured debts of more than $67,000 last year, up 11 per cent from a year earlier and 37 per cent over three years, and owed money to an average of 10 creditors.

Matt Fabian, TransUnion Canada’s senior director of financial services research and consulting, said that while Canadians are having trouble paying back their loans, they’re still relatively managing their debtload. Payment deferrals, government support and reduced spending during the pandemic helped pushed overall arrears to unusually low levels from the recession of 2008-2009 before bouncing higher in the past year, he noted.

“For some products, in some segments, it’s higher than it was pre-COVID. For some, it’s just returning,” he said.

Your governments are to blame for high gas prices: Benchmark Canada

Canadians quickly falling behind on their mortgages: Benchmark Canada

Instalment loans performed worse partly because of the type of borrower who takes them out, Fabian said. Borrowers seeking debt-consolidation loans likely already have financial problems, while alternative lenders serve higher-risk customers who May not qualify for traditional bank loans.

Those borrowers pay higher interest rates and have less room to absorb increases in living costs or a loss of income. Fabian described subprime consumers as “constantly living in their own personal recession.”

TransUnion’s latest quarterly credit report found average non-mortgage debt in Canada reached $28,118 per customer in the second quarter, up 7.6 per cent from a year earlier. Total consumer debt, including mortgages, hit a whopping $2.64 trillion.

The TransUnion data showed the share of borrowers who were at least 30 days overdue on their payments fell to 4.27 per cent from 4.34 per cent a year earlier. But the share of those at least 90 days overdue rose to 1.81 per cent from 1.77 per cent. Benchmark Canada’s figures, drawn from Bank of Canada calculations using TransUnion data, measure the share of loans at least 90 days overdue.

The share of debt balances falling into arrears is also rising faster than the share of income coming into one’s accounts, Fabian said. That suggests borrowers with larger debts are having more difficulty keeping up their payments, and face increased pressure with higher minimum payments, he said.

A C.D. Howe Institute report published this month found that national debt figures are masking growing strain among younger and lower-income Canadians.

The share of household disposable income used to pay debt fell to 14.5 per cent in the second quarter, from a 2023 peak of 15.2 per cent, the C.D. Howe analysis found. But younger Canadians carry unsecured debts without the cushion of home equity older Canadians can enjoy thanks to Canada’s frothy real estate market.

More borrowers are also seeking formal debt relief. Consumer debt proposals accounted for nearly 80 per cent of insolvency filings in the second quarter, up from about 60 per cent before the pandemic, TransUnion reported. Banks often have established programs to help restructure payments and have an incentive to preserve relationships with customers who hold chequing and savings accounts with them, Fabian said.

Saul Schwartz, professor at the School of Public Policy and Administration at Carleton University, cautioned against reading the rise in consumer proposals as a sign of worsening borrower behaviour. Instead, Canada’s banking system is inducing more borrowers to pay more of what they owe, he said.

Proposals can help borrowers protect assets and spread payments over time, but most pay more than they would in bankruptcy, Schwartz said. Governments can help, he noted. “Establishing publicly funded debt advice services, either nationally, provincially or even municipally, would be a big step forward.”

He also pointed to the Breathing Space program in England and Wales (Scotland runs its own separate debt program), which freezes most interest and charges on qualifying debts for up to 60 days while borrowers seek advice on how to make their repayments.

Hoyes said he expects rising arrears to lead to more insolvencies as borrowers exhaust their remaining credit.

“Nobody files bankruptcy at the first missed payment,” he said. “They file when they’ve run out of ways to keep going.”

Hoyes said many of his clients use those loans to cover bills after exhausting cheaper sources of credit, hoping their income will recover before the payments become unmanageable.
His firm’s clients carried average unsecured debts of more than $67,000 last year, up 11 per cent from a year earlier and 37 per cent over three years, and owed money to an average of 10 creditors.

Matt Fabian, TransUnion Canada’s senior director of financial services research and consulting, said that while Canadians are having trouble paying back their loans, they’re still relatively managing their debtload. Payment deferrals, government support and reduced spending during the pandemic helped pushed overall arrears to unusually low levels from the recession of 2008-2009 before bouncing higher in the past year, he noted.
“For some products, in some segments, it’s higher than it was pre-COVID. For some, it’s just returning,” he said.
Your governments are to blame for high gas prices: Benchmark Canada
Canadians quickly falling behind on their mortgages: Benchmark Canada

Instalment loans performed worse partly because of the type of borrower who takes them out, Fabian said. Borrowers seeking debt-consolidation loans likely already have financial problems, while alternative lenders serve higher-risk customers who May not qualify for traditional bank loans.

Those borrowers pay higher interest rates and have less room to absorb increases in living costs or a loss of income. Fabian described subprime consumers as “constantly living in their own personal recession.”

TransUnion’s latest quarterly credit report found average non-mortgage debt in Canada reached $28,118 per customer in the second quarter, up 7.6 per cent from a year earlier. Total consumer debt, including mortgages, hit a whopping $2.64 trillion.

The TransUnion data showed the share of borrowers who were at least 30 days overdue on their payments fell to 4.27 per cent from 4.34 per cent a year earlier. But the share of those at least 90 days overdue rose to 1.81 per cent from 1.77 per cent. Benchmark Canada’s figures, drawn from Bank of Canada calculations using TransUnion data, measure the share of loans at least 90 days overdue.

The share of debt balances falling into arrears is also rising faster than the share of income coming into one’s accounts, Fabian said. That suggests borrowers with larger debts are having more difficulty keeping up their payments, and face increased pressure with higher minimum payments, he said.
A C.D. Howe Institute report published this month found that national debt figures are masking growing strain among younger and lower-income Canadians.

The share of household disposable income used to pay debt fell to 14.5 per cent in the second quarter, from a 2023 peak of 15.2 per cent, the C.D. Howe analysis found. But younger Canadians carry unsecured debts without the cushion of home equity older Canadians can enjoy thanks to Canada’s frothy real estate market.

More borrowers are also seeking formal debt relief. Consumer debt proposals accounted for nearly 80 per cent of insolvency filings in the second quarter, up from about 60 per cent before the pandemic, TransUnion reported. Banks often have established programs to help restructure payments and have an incentive to preserve relationships with customers who hold chequing and savings accounts with them, Fabian said.

Saul Schwartz, professor at the School of Public Policy and Administration at Carleton University, cautioned against reading the rise in consumer proposals as a sign of worsening borrower behaviour. Instead, Canada’s banking system is inducing more borrowers to pay more of what they owe, he said.

Proposals can help borrowers protect assets and spread payments over time, but most pay more than they would in bankruptcy, Schwartz said. Governments can help, he noted. “Establishing publicly funded debt advice services, either nationally, provincially or even municipally, would be a big step forward.”

He also pointed to the Breathing Space program in England and Wales (Scotland runs its own separate debt program), which freezes most interest and charges on qualifying debts for up to 60 days while borrowers seek advice on how to make their repayments.
Hoyes said he expects rising arrears to lead to more insolvencies as borrowers exhaust their remaining credit.
“Nobody files bankruptcy at the first missed payment,” he said. “They file when they’ve run out of ways to keep going.”
The need for armed deterrence was evident on Sept. 20, when armed police officers protected a Belleville Jewish congregation from an armed attacker, says Tafsik

stories.title: W5 investigation finds alleged cult leader pushed followers to leave Canada for Florida home
stories.summary: A Hawaii-based alleged cult leader persuaded more than two dozen Canadians to move to Florida, with accusations that Canada was a danger zone.
stories.author: Derek Miller
stories.content:
In part two of this five-part W5 investigation: “ Fake Filtered Cult Leader ,” CTV News’ investigative unit examines a self-described spiritual teacher whose online presence helped attract followers around the world. Drawing on interviews and extensive reporting, W5 explores concerns raised by former members and the questions surrounding the organization behind the carefully curated public image.

A Hawaii-based alleged cult leader persuaded more than two dozen Canadians to move to Florida, with accusations that Canada was a danger zone.

The Canadians were students of an online self-described spiritual teacher named Liana Shanti, whose real name is Liane Wilson.

At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, in December 2022, 16 Canadians from in and around Regina, Sask. moved to Jacksonville, Florida. They say their spiritual instructor had repeatedly told them that Canada, with its vaccine rules and public gathering restrictions, was becoming an oppressive state. She also shared conspiracy theories that suggested the vaccine was dangerous.

“She’d speak of Canada literally turning into the depths of hell,” says former Shanti student, Amanda Brady. “And at one point we had a chat where she was likening it to The Handmaid’s Tale and we fully believed that if we stayed here our lives were in danger and our children’s lives were in danger.”

The Handmaid’s Tale is a dystopian television series and book about a totalitarian Christian theocracy that is especially oppressive for women.

Amanda and her husband bought a large property in Jacksonville so the Canadian followers could all live together. They nicknamed it Destiny Manor.

Was the run for the border a kidnapping?

Several of Liana Shanti’s followers took their children over the American border without the consent of the children’s fathers. Some considered it an outright kidnapping. Amanda Brady’s ex-husband, Wade Martin is one of them.

When Amanda fled with their two daughters to Florida, he did not see for much of the next four years.

“They left little girls and they came back - still my little girls - but not really, you know?” says an emotional Martin. “And it’s four years that I feel were stolen from me that no amount of money can ever get back.”

But he does not completely blame his ex-wife.

“I do feel that there was somebody in Amanda’s ear telling her what to do,” he says. “I don’t think this was all Amanda’s decision.”

Amanda Brady agrees.

“Do I understand Wade’s feelings? Absolutely, and that is something that I don’t know that I will ever be able to apologize enough for,” she says.

Amanda says that Liana Shanti had an overwhelming influence over everything she did. She has left the Shanti community and now believes that she was part of a cult.

Students start to question their teacher

Riley Lawson was one of the women who moved from Saskatchewan to Destiny Manor in Florida. She says the group eventually became disillusioned with the advice and perceived restrictions that Liana Shanti put on them. She says Shanti discouraged them from talking outside online platforms that she controlled.

“You just start constantly feeling like you’re being evaluated for what you do and don’t do,” she tells W5. “It was exhausting. … That was my life for that whole time.”

Riley says during their time in Florida, people began to share frustrations and dissent about Liana Shanti and her teachings. Eventually, all but one of them left the Shanti community and returned to Canada.

“There were 10 or 15 of us that actually had been questioning things for quite some time but never brought it up to anybody because we were afraid that somebody would turn on us even if they were our closest friend,” she says.

And she says when she decided to leave, Liana Shanti targeted her and others.

“She found out where I moved to in Canada, found out the town … she told her whole community that the reason I left the United States was because ICE was at my door,” she says, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “And since we left, we have been bullied online….and lied about.”

She and Amanda both say that Liana Shanti has a long history of vindictive behaviour, which includes doxxing people and sharing deeply personal information from what they thought were private conversations with their trusted teacher.

“I know there’s going to be repercussions from my sitting here with you today and talking about this,” says Riley.

The Canadians who fought back and won

In August, a civil jury in Honolulu found that Liana Shanti defamed three Canadians who were connected to ex-wives in the Shanti community. The spiritual guru carried out a relentless online hate campaign against the trio, calling them child abusers, pedophile supporters and Satanists, among other things. The jury awarded damages of more than C$55 million.

Despite the verdict, Liana Shanti has continued to post similar Instagram stories about the three and former followers. She says she is simply repeating information that other people have told her and that she believes to be true.

W5 repeatedly asked Liana Shanti for an interview. She declined, but says she intends to appeal the verdict.

Watch the one-hour special presentation of W5’s Avery Haines Investigates Saturday at 7 p.m. ET live on W5’s official YouTube channel and on CTV and Crave

stories.title: VIA Rail partnership expands free travel for London children’s hospital patients
stories.summary: Families travelling to London for specialized children’s health care will have access to complimentary train trips through an expanded partnership between VIA Rail Canada and Canada’s Children’s Hospital Foundations.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Families travelling to London for specialized children’s health care will have access to complimentary train trips through an expanded partnership between VIA Rail Canada and Canada’s Children’s Hospital Foundations.

The three-year partnership, announced Tuesday, will provide free rail travel to patients and families accessing care at 13 children’s hospitals across Canada, including Children’s Hospital at London Health Sciences Centre.

The initiative builds on an existing partnership between VIA Rail and Children’s Health Foundation in London, which was announced in April 2026. Since then, the program has helped families book more than 250 complimentary train journeys to and from specialized medical care.

The expanded program will also support families travelling to children’s hospitals in Toronto, Hamilton, Ottawa, Montreal and Quebec City, among other locations along the Quebec City-Windsor corridor.

For families whose children require specialized or ongoing treatment, travelling long distances can add financial, logistical and emotional pressures to an already difficult experience.

VIA Rail says the partnership is intended to reduce some of those barriers by helping families reach the care their children need.

“Connecting people and communities across Canada is at the heart of VIA Rail’s mandate,” said Mathieu Paquette, VIA Rail president and CEO.

He said accessible passenger rail can be an important transportation option for families seeking specialized medical care, as well as people with disabilities or limited transportation options.

Adam Starkman, president and CEO of Canada’s Children’s Hospital Foundations, said the partnership will give hospitals more ways to support families who need to travel outside their home communities.

In 2025, children and families across Canada accessed care at children’s hospitals 3.9 million times, according to the organizations.

The partnership also includes support for children’s hospital foundations in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador.

The initiative builds on an existing partnership between VIA Rail and Children’s Health Foundation in London, which was announced in April 2026. Since then, the program has helped families book more than 250 complimentary train journeys to and from specialized medical care.

The expanded program will also support families travelling to children’s hospitals in Toronto, Hamilton, Ottawa, Montreal and Quebec City, among other locations along the Quebec City-Windsor corridor.
For families whose children require specialized or ongoing treatment, travelling long distances can add financial, logistical and emotional pressures to an already difficult experience.
VIA Rail says the partnership is intended to reduce some of those barriers by helping families reach the care their children need.
“Connecting people and communities across Canada is at the heart of VIA Rail’s mandate,” said Mathieu Paquette, VIA Rail president and CEO.
He said accessible passenger rail can be an important transportation option for families seeking specialized medical care, as well as people with disabilities or limited transportation options.
Adam Starkman, president and CEO of Canada’s Children’s Hospital Foundations, said the partnership will give hospitals more ways to support families who need to travel outside their home communities.
In 2025, children and families across Canada accessed care at children’s hospitals 3.9 million times, according to the organizations.
The partnership also includes support for children’s hospital foundations in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador.

stories.title: St. Thomas police lay 16 charges in e-bike, e-scooter crackdown
stories.summary: St. Thomas police laid 16 charges and issued seven warnings during an e-bike and e-scooter safety enforcement initiative launched in September.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
St. Thomas police laid 16 charges and issued seven warnings during an e-bike and e-scooter safety enforcement initiative launched in September.

The initiative was launched in response to community concerns and focused on unsafe riding and violations of provincial and municipal laws.

Of the 16 charges, five were for failing to wear a helmet, eight involved other e-bike-related infractions and three were for municipal bylaw violations.

The charges were laid under the Highway Traffic Act and municipal bylaws.

Police are reminding riders to wear required helmets, ensure their vehicles are properly equipped and operate only where permitted. Parents and caregivers are also encouraged to review the rules with young riders before they head out.

stories.title: Rain expected as temperatures begin to cool
stories.summary: Rain is expected to move across the region Wednesday, with 5 to 10 millimetres forecast before cooler temperatures arrive later in the week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Rain is expected to move across the region Wednesday, with 5 to 10 millimetres forecast before cooler temperatures arrive later in the week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Showers are possible this morning, with steadier rainfall expected through the afternoon as a cold front moves through southern Ontario.

Photo Gallery: October Viewer Photos

Atchison says some areas could see heavier pockets of rain, with totals reaching about 15 millimetres near Chatham-Kent.

Temperatures will remain mild Wednesday, reaching a high of 19 C, before dropping to 13 C Thursday under mainly cloudy skies.

A 40 per cent chance of showers is in the forecast Friday, with the risk lingering into Saturday.

Photo Gallery: October Dogs of the Day

Another cold front is expected to bring a further cooldown, with temperatures dropping to 9 C Sunday and Monday, closer to seasonal norms.

Atchison advises residents to bring an umbrella as showers are expected to continue into Wednesday evening.

stories.title: Waterloo battery researcher Linda Nazar awarded Canada’s top science prize
stories.summary: The chemist has spent decades developing materials to make batteries safer, more efficient and affordable
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Linda Nazar always liked science in high school and she was good at it. When she headed off to university, her plan was to aim for medical school.

But then a first-year chemistry course unexpectedly captured her imagination. The more she learned, the more she was drawn to the world of atoms and the elegant geometry that governs their structure and behaviour.

“For some reason it just really clicked,” said Dr. Nazar, who now holds the title of university research professor in chemistry at the University of Waterloo. “It might have been a sense of understanding – or feeling like I understood something about nature at the point of chemical reactions.”

Since then, Dr. Nazar has been on an odyssey of discovery at the atomic level that she has mostly pursued with one key goal in mind: finding materials that can improve how we store and dispense electricity in the form of batteries.

On Wednesday, Dr. Nazar will be recognized for her contributions at a ceremony in Ottawa when she receives the Gerhard Herzberg Canada Gold Medal for Science and Engineering, the country’s most prestigious science prize for non-medical research. It includes $1-million in additional research funding from the federal government.

The award acknowledges Dr. Nazar’s achievements as a scientist and highlights the critical importance of a field that is literally about keeping the lights on for humanity.

At the surface it sounds like a very basic problem, Dr. Nazar said. Every battery consists of separated positive and negative charges that can drive an electric current through whatever device is powered by the battery. The current is balanced by the movement of ions inside the battery through a medium called an electrolyte, which completes the circuit.

The challenge comes in finding materials that can accomplish this efficiently and safely, and that can also be manufactured for a reasonable price at scale.

The solutions vary based on application. Batteries that are lightweight are important for transportation, including in vehicles and aviation. For example, the growing use of drones in defence, agriculture and many other domains underscores why it matters so much to have batteries that can carry a maximum amount of energy within a minimum amount of mass.

For other applications, such as large-scale storage for renewable energy, what matters more is achieving a high-energy density without causing the chemical constituents in a battery to break down. The risk is “thermal runaway” – a process where increasing temperature within a battery accelerates a heat-causing reaction that can lead to an explosion or fire.

The key to solving these challenges is finding materials that can work together in the right way – a field that Dr. Nazar said is still far from being thoroughly explored but is accelerating rapidly.

“There is an amazing amount of stuff that remains to be discovered,” she said. “Companies are starting to use artificial intelligence to design liquid electrolytes, and that May lead to some real changes.”

Dr. Nazar’s work spans multiple applications and approaches, including solid-state batteries, which can store more energy, and those that involve an aqueous electrolyte solution, which tend to be safer and cheaper to produce.

At Waterloo, she is a co-director of the Ontario Battery and Electrochemistry Research Centre, launched in 2024, which aims to provide facilities for academic researchers, startup companies and larger industrial partners to develop and test materials for new kinds of batteries.

She is also part of the Aqueous Battery Consortium, a research collaboration funded by the U.S. Department of Energy that is working toward affordable grid-scale energy storage.

Dr. Nazar grew up in Vancouver and was an undergraduate at the University of British Columbia before earning her PhD at the University of Toronto in 1984, where she worked on methods of depositing metal atoms into polymers and other materials.

This work attracted the attention of Exxon, which hired Dr. Nazar to work as a postdoctoral fellow at its research facility in Annandale, N.J.

At the time, the company employed more than 200 scientists engaged in pure research, based on the model pioneered by Nokia Bell Labs, which drove a revolution in electronics.

Dr. Nazar said the fast pace and dynamic nature of industrial research proved to be incredibly stimulating, including Friday afternoon sessions when young researchers would get together and bounce around ideas, both creative and silly.

It was while working on projects there that Dr. Nazar picked up the electrochemistry that would prove useful for battery research. Following her time at Exxon and a stint at Rutgers University, she returned to Canada to take up a faculty position at the University of Waterloo in 1987.

A few years later, lithium batteries were introduced commercially, transforming how small, portable devices are powered. Dr. Nazar has become one of many researchers looking to take the revolution further with new materials in different configurations.

To colleagues, she is best known for her pioneering discoveries on lithium sulphur batteries, including her most citied paper on the subject, published in 2009. In another highly cited work published in 2016 she showed how vanadium oxide can be applied to making an effective zinc ion battery. Both results have opened up new avenues for research.

But beyond any one innovation, Dr. Nazar has developed a reputation for understanding the chemistry of batteries at a deeper level than almost anyone.

“She gained a lot of respect because she ‘sees’ structure,” said Jillian Buriak, a chemist who specializes in nanomaterials for energy applications at the University of Alberta. “I wonder if she imagines ions navigating solid state materials the way the character Beth Harmon in The Queen’s Gambit visualized chess pieces moving on a chessboard on the ceiling.”

In recent years China has come to dominate the leading edge of battery research while other countries, including Canada, have been slower to appreciate the strategic importance of developing expertise in the area.

That is changing and Dr. Nazar said there is plenty for young researchers entering the field to work on.

“There are so many different aspects that you can get involved in as a physicist, as a chemist, as a chemical engineer, as a mathematician, as a computational scientist,” she said. “Irrespective of what excites you about science and engineering, there’s going to be something in this field that is undiscovered that you can really jump into.”

stories.title: Public menopause care is scarce, and private care is costly. Why Canadians pay either way
stories.summary: Many Canadians turn to private or virtual clinics for help managing symptoms, only to find expensive bills and inconsistent quality
stories.author: Tavia Grant
stories.content:
Angela Rimmer has spent thousands of dollars out of pocket to treat her menopause symptoms.

She’s had no other choice, she says: Her symptoms of brain fog, difficulty sleeping, night sweats, hot flashes, mood changes and exhaustion have been debilitating. As a single mother with four children in the London, Ont., area, she needed help to keep working as a full-time dental assistant and being a caregiver at home.

Initially misdiagnosed by a family doctor, who wanted to prescribe antidepressants, she turned to two different private clinics instead, seeking menopause hormone therapy. She spent $600 for an initial assessment at one clinic, plus $200 for each six-month follow-up appointment, $70 for lab tests, and about $120 per month in prescriptions. She doesn’t have private health insurance, and the province doesn’t cover the treatments. To date, she figures she’s spent more than $5,000.

“I just wish that I didn’t have to access this through private. I wish that it was in the public system, because we’re having to pay so much,” says Ms. Rimmer, 42.

Private care, she says, has been costly and time consuming to find. Access to care, including hormone therapy, which has helped her, “should be readily available for the women who need it without having to reach so far into their pocketbooks at this time in our lives, when we should be saving for retirement and for our kids’ schooling.”

Across the country, more than five million women are between the ages of 40 and 60, and the majority of them will experience menopause symptoms, which can vary from mild to overwhelming. Symptoms range from fatigue to headaches, anxiety, muscle aches and heart palpitations.

Four in 10 Canadian women don’t know where to go to get treatment for their symptoms, according to an Ipsos survey this year for GreenShield. A third of respondents said they waited more than two years to get effective menopause care. And those seeking care face barriers: a shortage of family physicians, doctors who lack training in menopause, long wait times to see specialists, a dearth of research funding in this area and an explosion of misleading online information.

Desperate for treatment, some women are turning to private or virtual clinics. Some are run by physicians or nurse practitioners, while others are operated by naturopaths or tech entrepreneurs. The standard of care varies, women’s health experts say, and so do the prices. Many remedies on offer are costly. Not all are effective or safe.

The proliferation of such clinics is raising questions about why a transition experienced by millions of Canadians is not better managed in the public system. Effective treatments exist that alleviate symptoms, and most cases aren’t so complex that they can’t be handled by a family doctor.

Currently, however, just two provinces – British Columbia and Manitoba – cover the costs of menopausal hormone therapy. Newer, nonhormonal medications such as Veozah or Lynkuet, which alleviate hot flashes and night sweats, are approved by Health Canada but aren’t fully covered by the public system.

As The Globe and Mail recently reported , Canada is behind other countries – such as Britain and Australia – in taking steps to improve access to care.

In June, the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada warned that a two-tiered health system is emerging in which women are forced to pay for basic health care that should be free.

Access to menopause care should be universally available to all Canadians, the Menopause Foundation of Canada says. It started a national campaign last month, urging governments to bolster support for women experiencing menopause.

The foundation says gaps in access are widest for Indigenous, Black and racialized women, along with those living in rural communities, gender-diverse people and those with lower incomes. “Access to safe, evidence-based menopause care should never depend on a person’s ability to pay,” the foundation said in a report that sets out priorities for equitable care.

Jen Gunter, a prominent women’s health advocate, gynecologist and author of The Menopause Manifesto , is among those calling for expanded access.

“Whether you live in Flin Flon, Manitoba or in downtown Toronto, you should be able to get access to excellent first-line menopause care,” just like people should have access to care for other issues such as blood pressure, says Dr. Gunter. “These are things that should be available to everybody.”

Monika Kerschl-Sales hears about menopause all the time.

She is co-owner of Thairapy Beauty Bar in Lindsay, Ont. Hundreds of women in the region sit in her stylist chair and have shared their struggles in getting care. She herself remembers having low moods, fatigue, hot flashes, night sweats and brain fog when she began to experience perimenopause, the phase before menopause when many women start having symptoms. She didn’t feel like herself and couldn’t bring her A-game to work.

She’s feeling better now, and says hormone replacement therapy has been life-changing – but to access it, she has paid thousands of dollars out of pocket. A few years ago, she was spending up to $500 a month on supplements (there is limited evidence showing menopause supplements work, and some may have adverse side effects). And she now spends $200 a visit at a private clinic, every three months.

“I’m fortunate to have access to private care, but I know from conversations I’ve had with others that not everyone is in the same position,” says Ms. Kerschl-Sales, 55. “Every woman deserves access to proper menopause care, regardless of her financial circumstances.”

In Dundas, Ont., Lindsay Deefholts says she started suffering from fatigue and brain fog in her forties.

Now 50, the global communications and advocacy consultant feels grateful – she found a family doctor who listened carefully to symptoms and prescribed Veozah, a nonhormonal treatment she takes for hot flashes. Dozens of private and virtual clinics are springing up to serve demand from people who have been fed up trying to access care through the public system, such as Modern Menopause, Felix and The Menopause Practice.

It can cost $100 to $400 for an initial assessment at such clinics. Further charges for follow-up appointments, products, therapies or monthly membership programs can run thousands of dollars per year. These include services such as access to a life coach, therapist or customized health plan. Many promise little or no wait times for a consult.

Private clinics are growing as practitioners see business opportunities or a better way to serve patients.

National stats are lacking, but one recent study in B.C. found that average out-of-pocket costs on extended health services, among people with no private insurance, amounted to $1,305 in the past year (about a quarter of Canadians don’t have private health insurance).

These services include spending on mental-health professionals, naturopaths, dietitians and kinesiologists.

Another problem is that patients feel that they are not getting adequate care from their providers, says Dr. Brotto, who also works as a psychologist. “They say that they were told, ‘This is a natural stage of life. All women go through it,’ and kind of dismissed in that way,” she says.

“It’s not in keeping with the mandates of our health acts,” says Dr. Brotto.

In Manitoba, Omolayo Famuyide, a physician and founder of the Layo Centre, a publicly funded women’s health clinic in Winnipeg, says she sees long travel times, too. Some patients are driving from as far as Thompson, about an eight-hour trip north, or from Kenora, Ont., a 2.5-hour drive, she says.

Wait times for an appointment are nine to 12 months, says Dr. Famuyide, who is a certified menopause practitioner – a credential that means a health care professional has passed a competency exam on menopause care issued by The Menopause Society, a U.S.-based organization.

“In the last two years, our wait times have grown significantly,” with an increasing number of referrals for women in perimenopause.

There are ways of alleviating the bottlenecks in the public system, she says – if only governments start paying more attention.

Wendy Wolfman has been treating people with menopause symptoms for more than 30 years.

For much of that time, she saw how their suffering was trivialized. But she has recently seen a shift toward women’s experiences and symptoms being more validated, and says there’s been an explosion in women who are seeking care as they feel more empowered to talk about their symptoms.

The wait-list at her clinic at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto is 18 months to two years. She says many people don’t need a specialist or a private clinic, though.

“Many family doctors or nurse practitioners could handle many of the situations we see if they were properly educated and had the clinical experience,” says Dr. Wolfman, who is director of the Weston and O’Born Centre for Mature Women’s Health.

She believes that an experienced clinician could handle many situations virtually, and offer in-person appointments if necessary.

Dr. Wolfman says menopause care can be time consuming, but she firmly believes it should be offered within the public system “because this is a normal part of female aging. Every woman who lives long enough will go through menopause. Every woman.”

Health Canada says it advises consumers to check if health products are authorized. It says unauthorized products haven’t been assessed for safety, efficacy or quality “and may pose a range of serious health risks.” It notes that the delivery of health care – including treatment guidelines – is regulated by provinces and territories.

Ontario’s Health Ministry says it supports access to free, publicly funded drugs, including for menopause, through its drug benefit program. It says it released Canada’s first quality standard for menopause care, last year, to support clinicians in providing evidence-based care.

What’s concerning, Dr. Wolfman says, is that she hears from some patients who are receiving advice from some private virtual clinics that medical professionals would not recommend.

“I have concerns about the people who call themselves menopause experts, many of whom are not experts and many of whom have no clinical experience in the area.”

Some patients have been told to take a barrage of supplements, or high doses of hormone therapy in cases where this would pose additional health risks. Some women are also paying more than they need to for lab tests that may not be necessary, she says. “I would tell people that [if] anybody wants to sell something, be very suspicious,” Dr. Wolfman says.

The Menopause Foundation of Canada offers information on how to assess private clinics, noting, for example, that frequent testing is not generally clinically useful, and cautioning people about unregulated hormone therapy products.

Dr. Jacobson, of Coven Women’s Health, advises people to be wary of misleading claims, particularly around nonmedication health care products. “The misinformation piece that frustrates me is when people sell things, just for the sake of selling them, without really getting what I consider to be informed consent.”

She’s concerned that some of the clinics pushing these claims are tarnishing the reputation of others. “I believe that I’m doing something different here, and I think that we get painted with a lot of the same brush as some of the clinics that I think are a lot less ethical.”

Virtual clinics are simply meeting a demand, some providers say.

In Calgary, Hoda Soboh, co-founder and CEO of Effica Health, says her clinic is helping to solve the access problem. She is an entrepreneur who started the company with Dr. Nese Yuksel, a professor emeritus of pharmaceutical sciences, after experiencing first-hand the gaps and frustrations in getting menopause care.

The virtual menopause clinic started offering privately paid services in May. It now takes referrals for assessments in Alberta, Ontario and B.C. that are publicly insured (meaning patients don’t have to pay out of pocket), as well as offering memberships for $169 a month for access to preventive care services such as appointments with a dietitian or a mental-health counsellor.

“At the end of the day, everybody has a right to make a decision,” Ms. Soboh says.

But the growth of private care has a direct, negative impact on the public system, says Dr. Gunter, the health advocate, author and gynecologist.

“Studies tell us that private care takes away from public care,” she says, because it takes an already limited number of physicians, nurses and administrators out of public health care, exacerbating shortages that lead to longer public wait times. “It creates a two-tier system and makes care worse for the people who can’t pay, and I think that’s un-Canadian.”

Doctors point to other measures that could bolster care in the public system. These include improving remuneration and adding specific billing codes for those providing menopause treatment, so that they’re adequately compensated for their time.

Governments should also provide more research funding on mature women’s health, doctors say. Just 7 per cent of health research grants in Canada goes to female-specific research, according to one 2025 study.

In a brief last month, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research said that menopause remains “substantially underresearched” relative to its prevalence and consequences. After all, fully half of Canadians can expect to go through it as a natural life transition.

For Angela Rimmer, the dental-care worker in Ontario who signed up with two private clinics, it’s rubbing salt into the wound.

“How many women our age have all this stress on us – and then we have to go through this?”

Ms. Rimmer is urging decision-makers to improve coverage, and says she is sharing her experiences publicly because she wants to end the stigma and silence around menopause.

She hopes that if women talk about it openly, the next generation – including her two daughters – will have better access to care.

She didn’t feel like herself and couldn’t bring her A-game to work.

stories.title: As a New Brunswick pulp mill goes quiet, a forestry town waits for the axe to fall
stories.summary: Nackawic, N.B., grapples with uncertainty as India-based AV Group winds down its plant’s operations
stories.author: Lindsay Jones, Photography by Chris Donovan
stories.content:
In the New Brunswick town of Nackawic, the pulp mill across the river emitted what might be its last puff of smoke last week. The town’s mill, its lifeblood and the largest employer for half a century, is shutting down due to “prevailing market conditions,” according to the India-based owner, AV Group New Brunswick.

It’s a devastating blow to the mill’s 350 employees, about a third of whom live here in Nackawic, 65 kilometres west of Fredericton, said Mayor Tim Fox.

“It’s not just the labour force,” said Mr. Fox during a recent interview. “It’s the whole community.”

The town was populated with millworkers soon after the mill opened in the 1970s, the same decade when many of the split-levels and bungalows on the hillside above the riverbank were built. A giant axe sculpture, claiming to be the world’s largest, stands in a park in the heart of the town – a symbol of the province’s mighty forestry industry and a sign of strength many are trying to hold onto as confidence about the mill’s future wanes.

As the plant wound down its operations, millworkers were set to clock off with pink slips on Nov. 4 and the town was bracing for what’s next. Uncertainty looms: The owners of the mill describe the closure as a “temporary idling,” but have declined to answer questions about when or if it might reopen, leaving many unsure about its future.

The closure will put economic pressure on the municipality. The mill represents 10 per cent of the town’s tax base and 14 per cent of its utility revenue. In a worst case scenario – if the mill goes down permanently – Mr. Fox said the town has to figure out a way to replace that revenue, such as fast-tracking new housing developments.

But the effects spread much further than just the town. The closure is expected to have serious and far-reaching consequences for the supply chain, including for woodlot owners, truck drivers and suppliers. The Port of Saint John has said the closure will eliminate up to 10 per cent of container traffic and up to 20 per cent of container exports.

At a strip mall in the town, a pop-up booth for employment counseling has taken over an empty shopfront, while the windows of a drug store are painted with the slogan, “Nackawic Strong.” Several “for sale” signs have popped up on the neat lawns of homes throughout the town.

At Nackawic High School, many of the roughly 250 students have family members who work at the mill, some for multiple generations. It’s been a saving grace that the school district footed the bill for all school fees and some athletic fees this year to ease financial burdens on families, said vice-principal Ross Calder.

“It has made a huge impact so kids can continue to thrive and enjoy what makes the school experience what it is for them,” he said.

Like the mill is to Nackawic, forestry is New Brunswick’s economic backbone, valued at $1.5-billion annually with 9,700 direct and another 14,100 spinoff jobs linked to the sector, according to the province.

But the entire industry is facing declining revenues, thanks to falling market prices for wood and ongoing trade uncertainty, a significant challenge for businesses and the communities the sector supports, said Forestry NB executive director Kim Allen.

AV Group New Brunswick is a subsidiary of the multinational conglomerate Aditya Birla Group, headquartered in Mumbai. Established in 1997, AV Group NB also owns a second mill in northern New Brunswick, and says it manages over 1.6 million acres of company-owned and Crown land.

In September, AV announced the “temporary idling” of its pulp operations in Nackawic and said it would continue to monitor the market situation and business conditions, and assess future scenarios for the facility.

“The temporary idling process continues, as previously announced, and will be conducted in accordance with our regulatory and contractual obligations,” spokesperson Mike Legere wrote in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail. The company declined to be interviewed for this story.

The mill has always been the economic anchor of the town, officially known as Nackawic-Millville Rural Community after a recent amalgamation, except for a stint between 2004 and 2005 when the plant’s previous owner went bankrupt. That’s when AV took over, but many of the mill’s workers lost a significant amount of their pensions during the transition, and a lingering distrust remains.

Now, morale, unsurprisingly, is extremely low, said Grant Charlton, president of Unifor Local 219, which represents 228 workers at the mill.

“We’re continuing to advocate for our members, both for services as they deal with the closure, or idling, as the company would call it, as well as with government to try to look for future opportunities at the mill.”

Some workers are already looking into fly-in-fly-out jobs out west, or considering relocating to other industrial communities, he said.

Like most of his colleagues, Mr. Charlton is unsure what the future holds. He’s worked at the mill for 12 years as a chemical plant operator, helping to dissolve wood into pulp for man-made fabrics such as viscose for the company’s textile plants in India. It’s a job he started after graduating with a bachelor of science from the University of New Brunswick.

Now, he’s contemplating a career change. But the question is whether he can find employment with comparable pay. “That’s where my uncertainty lays.”

He said he still hasn’t told his four-year-old son, who has always been enthralled with the mill where his dad works and its big machinery. “It’ll be hard news to break, to explain to him that I’m not going to work there anymore,” he said.

Unifor, the union that represents Nackawic’s workers, recently held a rally in the town, one of dozens across the country for Forestry National Day of Action, to raise awareness about the perfect storm of trade and economic pressures that is pushing Canada’s forestry workplaces to the brink. Many of the mills at risk of closure are the last ones still operating in their regions.

Along the riverfront in Nackawic, dozens held signs and chanted “protect Canadian jobs.” They called for a national strategy for forestry and immediate transition supports for the workers who will soon be out of a job. New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt addressed the crowd, saying she’s working on finding a solution for the mill. “I’ve been looking at all sorts of options for how we can make sure that we’re best using the site, the wood, the assets and the people that have made Nackawic a strong forestry community and will continue to,” she said.

AV has so far refused to comment on how it plans to idle the mill – whether it will be a cold idle where everything is shut down, or a warm idle that would protect the mill’s machinery, raising the chances of potential new ownership, said Mr. Charlton.

Progressive Conservative MLA Richard Ames, who represents Nackawic, said during throne speech debate in the New Brunswick legislature last week that if the plant isn’t heated, there will be a disastrous outcome. “A harsh reality is now setting in for our community,” he said. “We know that the Birla Group will never start this mill back up again. The time for waiting and hope is over.”
paragraphs: In the New Brunswick town of Nackawic, the pulp mill across the river emitted what might be its last puff of smoke last week. The town’s mill, its lifeblood and the largest employer for half a century, is shutting down due to “prevailing market conditions,” according to the India-based owner, AV Group New Brunswick.
It’s a devastating blow to the mill’s 350 employees, about a third of whom live here in Nackawic, 65 kilometres west of Fredericton, said Mayor Tim Fox.
“It’s not just the labour force,” said Mr. Fox during a recent interview. “It’s the whole community.”

The town was populated with millworkers soon after the mill opened in the 1970s, the same decade when many of the split-levels and bungalows on the hillside above the riverbank were built. A giant axe sculpture, claiming to be the world’s largest, stands in a park in the heart of the town – a symbol of the province’s mighty forestry industry and a sign of strength many are trying to hold onto as confidence about the mill’s future wanes.

As the plant wound down its operations, millworkers were set to clock off with pink slips on Nov. 4 and the town was bracing for what’s next. Uncertainty looms: The owners of the mill describe the closure as a “temporary idling,” but have declined to answer questions about when or if it might reopen, leaving many unsure about its future.

The closure will put economic pressure on the municipality. The mill represents 10 per cent of the town’s tax base and 14 per cent of its utility revenue. In a worst case scenario – if the mill goes down permanently – Mr. Fox said the town has to figure out a way to replace that revenue, such as fast-tracking new housing developments.

But the effects spread much further than just the town. The closure is expected to have serious and far-reaching consequences for the supply chain, including for woodlot owners, truck drivers and suppliers. The Port of Saint John has said the closure will eliminate up to 10 per cent of container traffic and up to 20 per cent of container exports.

At a strip mall in the town, a pop-up booth for employment counseling has taken over an empty shopfront, while the windows of a drug store are painted with the slogan, “Nackawic Strong.” Several “for sale” signs have popped up on the neat lawns of homes throughout the town.

stories.title: Blue wave crashes over American politics in midterm that rebukes Trump policies
stories.summary: Detroit - The world woke up on Wednesday morning to control of the U.S. Congress shifting to Democrats in a clear rejection of President Donald Trump's turbulent second term.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Detroit - The fallout from the Democrat tsunami that crashed over the U.S. Congress was swift on Wednesday, after American voters rejected President Donald Trump’s turbulent second term with a midterm election blowout.

In a stinging rebuke of the second Trump administration, Democrats flipped long-held Republican Senate seats in Texas, Maine and South Carolina. The blue wave also washed over House seats and down-ballot votes, sending shock waves throughout the Republican party.

Trump acknowledged Wednesday that his unpopular war with Iran affected the election but maintained he was committed to the military campaign.

Talking to reporters while walking around the construction site of the new White House ballroom, Trump suggested he was open to working with Democrats before later saying he would use his presidential veto to block their agenda.

Polling before Tuesday’s votes showed that Trump’s approval had plummeted due to rising gas and diesel prices, high inflation and the war with Iran.

The trade war with Canada became a ballot box issue in close contests in Maine and Michigan where Democrats defeated their Republican opponents.

Lifelong Michigander Aaron Corley, 60, said Trump’s attacks on Canada were among the factors driving his vote in Tuesday’s midterms. He said he felt ecstatic as he watched Americans send a message to the “orange man.”

“It was wonderful,” Corley said in Dearborn on Wednesday.

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed — a constant target of Trump and the Republicans — beat GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers.

Trump’s attacks on Canada were unpopular enough in Michigan to force Rogers to distance himself from the president’s trade war.

Trade tensions also upended the Senate race in Maine, where Democrat Troy Jackson ended the nearly 30-year run of Republican Susan Collins.

While Collins had publicly opposed Trump’s tariffs on Canada and lobbied for some exemptions, Jackson accused her of not doing enough to fight the president’s broader tariff regime.

The president even tried to give Collins a boost in the close contest by making changes to 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. The move was not enough to stop the blue wave from sweeping the trade-dependent state, driven in part by high energy prices and a steep drop in Canadian tourism.

The defeat of centrist Republican candidates who pushed back on Trump’s Canada tariffs May convince Democrats and the GOP that fighting with America’s northern neighbour is not a winning strategy, said Matthew Lebo, a political-science professor at Western University in London, Ont.

American lawmakers May be “nicer about Canada” but Trump will still be president, Lebo added.

“As Prime Minister (Mark) Carney has said, this is a ruptured relationship,” Lebo said in a text message. “An election doesn’t undo that. Even if the temperature goes down, Canadians don’t have much reason to trust the U.S. is back on track.”

While the Democrat landslide will change the distribution of power in Washington, the party does not have a large enough majority to override presidential vetoes or remove Trump from office without the help of Republicans.

House Democrats have prepared an ambitious 100-day agenda focused on affordability and conducting sweeping oversight of the Trump administration — but achieving their election promises could prove difficult.

The outcome also has left the Republican party unmoored and looking for leadership.

It’s not clear whether Trump — now the Gop’s unpopular lame duck leader — retains his control over his base.

Voters in some of the most Republican-safe areas showed their frustration with the president and the GOP. In Texas, James Talarico broke a decades-long Democrat losing streak by trouncing Trump-aligned Senate candidate Ken Paxton, while the governor’s race shocked observers when Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousted incumbent Republican Greg Abbott.

“The remaining Republican senators and members of the House will see what happened … and do some recalculating about what will get them re-elected in 2028 and beyond,” Lebo said. “Being too close to Trump was a losing strategy for many.”

In the wake of the election, reports said Republican Mike Johnson of Louisiana would not seek reelection as House speaker.

Vice-President JD Vance, who is widely expected to seek the Republican nomination for president, issued a long post on social media blaming the blowout loss on Trump’s war in Iran.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next (six) years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance said in the post.

“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

When asked about Vance’s possible leadership bid on Wednesday, Trump did not say whether he’d throw his support behind his vice president.

“You don’t know who’s talking about running. You can have people running, you can have a lot of people maybe, or a lot of people running, or maybe nobody’s going to run,” Trump said. “Maybe he won’t run. I don’t know who’s going to run.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: No flooding rinks or making snow: Calgary water restrictions back for final fix
stories.summary: Calgary - Water restrictions are back in Calgary and, along with taking shorter showers, it means there's no flooding outdoor hockey rinks or making snow for ski hills.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Water restrictions are back in Calgary and, along with taking shorter showers, it means there’s no flooding outdoor hockey rinks or making snow for ski hills.

The rules, starting Wednesday for about the next four weeks, will also be in effect during the Grey Cup.

“The timing couldn’t be worse for us, but at the same token since Mother Nature’s not co-operating for us anyway, I guess there’s a little bit of leeway there,” said Dale Oviatt with WinSport, which operates Canada Olympic Park.

Oviatt said with no snow on the ground right now, warmer weather would likely have delayed opening the centre’s ski and snowboarding hill anyway. Right now there’s no opening date, he added, and for the most part season passholders have been understanding.

“We certainly want to get open as soon as we can,” said Oviatt.

“We have ski instructors who are depending on hours to get their paycheques. We have so many other operations that are tied into the hill and we want to get them open.”

It has been described as the last chapter in fixing Calgary’s water woes.

The giant Bearspaw South Feeder Main, which provides 60 per cent of treated water for the 1.6 million residents of Calgary, along with municipalities on its boundaries and the Tsuut’ina Nation, failed in June 2024.

It ruptured again in December last year.

During off-and-on repairs over the two years, Calgarians and those in surrounding communities were asked to restrict their water use.

With a final stretch of repair work, the water main is being temporarily shut down. And residents are again being asked again to take three-minute showers, not flush the toilet until it’s necessary, and hold off on washing clothes or running the dishwasher.

That’s in addition to the ban on outside watering affecting outdoor rinks and ski hills.

“We have one, final, critical stretch ahead of us. To get there we’re going to need Calgarians to come together one more time,” said Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said this week.

“I recognize that we’ve been asking a lot. Over the past couple of years, Calgarians have been through water restrictions, emergency repairs, disruptions to our regular routines and a great deal of uncertainty.

“I know that there is frustration. I know that there is fatigue and, frankly, I share it too.”

Michael Thompson, chief operating officer of water utility for the city, said WinSport had asked for an outdoor watering exemption but one couldn’t be provided.

The restrictions don’t appear to be affecting minor hockey.

“All of our programs operate in indoor facilities, and all facilities are up and running for the year,” Kevin Kobelka, executive director of Hockey Calgary, said in an email.

“As for how (ice) floods are managed, this will be a decision of the facilities. But I have not been informed of any changes or effects to our schedule.”

Oviatt said WinSport has come up with a way to deal with water restrictions in its arenas and office tower.

“In our arena complex, we actually use the ice shavings when we do our cleaning of the ice, and we recycle that water for our toilets in the office tower and arena.”

Thompson said the city is still ready to welcome football fans and that Grey Cup organizers have been sharing the message to comply with the water rules.

The Grey Cup festival starts Nov. 11 and wraps with the championship CFL game on Nov. 15.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Ex-bank worker found guilty after viewing Carney’s data, opening fraudulent accounts
stories.summary: Ottawa — A former Royal Bank of Canada employee has been found guilty of three criminal charges after opening fraudulent accounts and viewing the personal banking information of Prime Minister Mark Carney.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

Posted November 4, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated November 4, 2026 5:12 am.

A former Royal Bank of Canada employee has been found guilty of three criminal charges after opening fraudulent accounts and viewing the personal banking information of Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Ibrahim El-Hakim, who worked at a downtown Ottawa bank branch, was recruited by someone he believed “to be associated with organized crime,” says an agreed statement of facts in the case filed in an Ontario court.

The RCMP began an investigation last year following a complaint from RBC.

The agreed statement says El-Hakim opened at least 43 fraudulent accounts at the bank between November 2023 and June 2025.

In late June 2025, El-Hakim admitted his involvement in the fraud to an RBC corporate security official, saying he was recruited on Telegram, a social media messaging app, by a person using the alias AI World, the statement says.

“Mr. El-Hakim stated that he participated in the scheme because he was experiencing financial difficulties,” it adds.

Court documents show El-Hakim pleaded guilty in August to fraud over $5,000, unauthorized use of a computer and identity theft.

El-Hakim did not turn up for a sentencing hearing late last month.

His lawyer at the time told Ontario Court Justice Norm Boxall that El-Hakim was no longer in Ottawa.

The court has set a new date for sentencing later this month.

The agreed statement of facts says El-Hakim described how he created bank profiles and opened credit products after receiving requests from AI World via Telegram.

AI World would send instructions and personal identifying information, including name, date of birth, social insurance number, driver’s licence information, passport data and customer profile information. It would request that a credit card be linked to a particular account.

El-Hakim would also send identity information back to AI World, including online banking passwords.

El-Hakim received at least $5,000 in compensation — $500 for each account issued in the form of an e-transfer deposited into one of his accounts at other banks, the statement says.

It adds that, shortly after interviewing El-Hakim, RBC became aware he had used his work computer and software to conduct unauthorized queries on customer profiles.

On June 17, 2025, El-Hakim accessed the customer banking profiles of Carney, Justin Trudeau and another individual, the statement says. The Trudeau account he accessed “was determined not to belong to the former prime minister,” the statement adds.

While accessing these profiles, El-Hakim was observed consulting a smart watch, the statement says. On the surveillance video, he was seen at one point taking a cellphone out of his pocket, using it and alternating his gaze between the phone and the computer screen of his bank workstation.

“Mr. El-Hakim committed these offences despite having received training in ethics, privacy, security and fraud prevention as part of his employment at RBC,” the statement says.

“He used customer information provided by third parties, opened fraudulent accounts, attempted to obtain credit products, accessed customer information without authorization, verified and transmitted identifying information, and received compensation for his participation.”

RBC has had to pay $14,634 for 27 clients to receive a two-year credit monitoring service as a result of their identity being stolen, the statement says.

RCMP Cpl. Erique Gasse said in September 2025 the investigation did not lead Mounties to believe there was any threat to Carney’s safety or to national security.

Since the investigation involved the prime minister, it was assigned to the RCMP’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team in Montreal, where the report was made.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Why mosquito season is longer this year in some parts of Canada
stories.summary: Toronto - Canadians who were relieved to be out of mosquito season might be surprised to learn the pesky insects are not gone just yet.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Canadians who were relieved to be out of mosquito season might be surprised to learn the pesky insects are not gone just yet.

Experts say mosquitoes seem to be living longer this fall in parts of southern and eastern Ontario and Eastern Canada, including Nova Scotia, because of warmer-than-usual temperatures.

Mosquitoes typically thrive in warm and humid environments and these conditions have been extended by this year’s strong El Nino — a natural phenomenon that causes global temperatures to spike every few years.

“As long as those mosquitoes haven’t been exposed to temperatures low enough … so cold that it damages them and kills them, then they’ll just stick around,” said Laura Ferguson, an assistant professor in the biology department at Acadia University who studies how ticks and mosquitoes respond to environmental change.

Ferguson, who has been bit by mosquitoes in recent weeks, said overnight temperatures have to dip below freezing for a consistent period of time to have an effect on the insect.

Bill Merryfield, a research scientist at Environment and Climate Change Canada, said El Nino usually affects Canada toward the end of the year, causing unusually mild fall and winter temperatures.

“This year’s event is truly exceptional because this warming has already exceeded three degrees, which is well above that of any previous event and is expected to go even higher before the usual peak of El Nino in November or December,” he said, referring to Pacific Ocean temperatures tied to the weather phenomenon.

“That would consist of warmer-than-usual temperatures coast to coast” in Canada, Merryfield said.

Warmer temperatures May reflect a “new normal” for autumn and winter seasons in Canada as the planet continues to warm at a faster rate than previous years, he added.

In Toronto and surrounding areas of southern Ontario, where mosquitoes were present into late October, temperatures reached the low 20s at the end of the month and in the first week of November. The Weather Network said Toronto hasn’t recorded any temperatures below or at freezing since May 3 this year.

Researchers are still waiting to see how this year’s “super” El Nino will affect mosquito populations next year during warmer seasons, especially across Canada’s 80 diverse mosquito species. Ferguson said this type of weather event could influence how the mosquitoes survive a warmer winter and the size of their populations next spring.

“We definitely expect that they’ll have a longer active season, particularly if spring comes earlier or fall is later and warmer,” she said. “We think we’re seeing some evidence of that.”

Besides the bites and itching that follows, experts are concerned about the possibility of increased disease transmission if mosquitoes’ life spans are prolonged because of unusual weather patterns that lead to a boom in their populations. Temperatures in Canada and around the world are already elevated due to human-caused climate change.

The longer mosquito season is extended in Canada, the more those risks for virus transmission to humans and animals remain, said Carleton University PhD candidate Marc Avramov, who focuses on mosquito-borne diseases such as West Nile virus and eastern equine encephalitis.

“We stop worrying about that as soon as those colder fall conditions start appearing,” he said.

Avramov said new mosquito species could also make their way into Canada, including some that can adapt more easily in the wintertime, and could introduce new emerging diseases if mild weather conditions are sustained.

“That’s one of the risks we always keep an eye out for,” he said.
