stories.title: The midterms are over. Will Trump still want to make a deal with Canada?
stories.summary: Warmer words from Trump have raised hopes for a trade deal, but trade analysts say the real test is tariff relief
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — As U.S. midterm elections loomed over the weekend, Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Donald Trump spoke and publicly suggested that trade talks could restart soon.

Carney said the two countries “will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome.”

Trump went further.

“We have the concept of a very good deal with Canada,” he said in Iowa on Sunday. He said the deal would be “great for our farmers, great for our country, and it’ll be fine for Canada, too” and claimed the long-dead Keystone XL pipeline was being revived — and that Canada would pay for it.

So, will trade talks get underway soon, or was this just political messaging ahead of yesterday’s U.S. midterm elections?

Trade analysts and industry analysts have responded with everything from total skepticism to cautious optimism, but several said Trump’s incentive for negotiating post-election remained the same: unpopular tariffs are squeezing U.S. consumers and businesses.

Jamie Tronnes, executive director of the Center for North American Prosperity and Security, suggested that Trump’s warmer tone this week May reflect exposure on the campaign trail to criticism that his advisers normally filter out.

“The president is now no longer stuck in the Oval Office getting his information filtered through a bubble of advisors,” she said. “He’s been … meeting with candidates and seeing and hearing directly from people on the campaign trail about what’s actually affecting the campaigns.”

Edward Alden, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, also senses a change.

“Americans have come to equate tariffs with rising prices, with hits to their own pocketbook, and I think the administration is recognizing this,” he said. “I’m not going to go out on a limb and predict that a deal is imminent. But I do think the political environment for a deal is considerably better than it was even two, three months ago.”

But, so far, analysts have seen no movement on the biggest sticking points for Ottawa: Trump’s Section 232 tariffs on autos and steel.

Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association and a member of Carney’s Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations, said he had seen no indication that Washington was prepared to improve its previous offer on the auto tariffs, discussed before talks broke down in August. But he does see Trump having an incentive to negotiate after the election, whatever happens, because tariffs are squeezing U.S. automakers, and industry pressure will continue to grow.

“There is a real pressure, a real squeeze on Detroit right now that comes from Washington,” he said.

At the same time, he remained cautious about the warmer rhetoric.

“I think we’re hearing (a warmer tone from Trump) because it’s helpful to speak reasonably during a tough midterm,” said Volpe. “But I haven’t seen any term sheet exchange.”

Volpe said the industry had not yet been engaged in formal consultation, but he remains hopeful and slightly more confident than not that negotiations will restart soon.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc’s office, meanwhile, said the trade minister has no current plans to visit Washington, and no new Washington visit has been publicly confirmed for the chief negotiator, Janice Charette.

Tronnes said her metric for how serious things are getting is “if those guys are on a plane,” but Volpe says talks can happen from anywhere and that it’s the terms that matter most.

According to him, the earlier U.S. offer — a 15 per cent headline tariff with an exemption for U.S. content — would have produced an effective auto tariff of about 7.5 per cent on average. That remained unworkable, he said, because it exceeded the industry’s 2024 Ebitda margin of 6 per cent.

“The math hasn’t changed,” he said. “That tariff has to be materially lower than the profit margin.”

7 times Trump reignited '51st state' rhetoric, suggesting 'that's the only way it works' for Canada

Still, several trade analysts cautioned that Trump’s warmer words did not necessarily signal a broader change in his trade policy.

“He’s had an enormous capacity to disappoint when it comes to critical international relations matters and strategic matters like this,” said Andrew Hale, fellow at Advancing American Freedom in Washington.

A U-turn on auto tariffs could also undermine Trump’s reshoring plans. And since the steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs serve that agenda, Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute, sees major concessions as politically and strategically difficult.

“I would be very surprised if all of a sudden it turns out that the White House is very flexible on (the sectoral tariffs) when they weren’t just a couple of months ago,” he said.

Lawrence Herman, senior fellow at the C.D. Howe Institute, is even more skeptical.

“There’s no indication that Trump and the Maga team are going to give up the power to adjust trade relations on the basis of their own view of US national security interests, and that can be very broadly framed,” he said.

“There May be some accommodation in specific areas. But overall, the trading relationship is going to continue to be a very difficult one.”

Fen Osler Hampson, a professor of international affairs at Carleton University, tends to agree a reversal is unlikely.

“In the best scenario, we see a reduction that we can live with,” he said. But he also pointed to the timing of an electoral issue for Canada. Hampson suggested that Carney May have less room to manoeuvre, especially if a deal involves politically sensitive dairy concessions, until after Dec. 7, when six federal by-elections will be held — three in Quebec, two in Ontario and one in Saskatchewan. “So maybe we get a Christmas surprise here,” Hampson said, noting that the big question of how Trump will act between now and then remains. “Does Trump get to play Santa Claus or the Grinch who stole Christmas?” For Laura Dawson, executive director of the Future Borders Coalition, the opening is encouraging — even if the outcome remains undefined. “I think we’re in the best window for a resolution of some of the major trade irritants,” she said. “But I don’t know what a deal looks like at this point.”

stories.title: More ways to move through Byron: Boler Road improvements are complete
stories.summary: The project adds new cycling and pedestrian connections while replacing the Boler Road watermain.Getting aroun
stories.content:
Getting around Byron by bike just got easier. Boler Road is now open following the completion of the final phase of the Boler Road Cycling and Watermain Improvements project.

A new two-way cycling path along the east side of Boler Road, between Commissioners Road and Southdale Road, gives people another way to travel through the neighbourhood and connect to surrounding areas, including Springbank Park and Lambeth.

The project also added pedestrian crossings, improved sections of sidewalks, upgraded transit stops and a resurfaced road, benefitting people travelling in different ways.

Beneath the road, crews replaced the aging watermain and upgraded water services to nearby properties. Built in 1963, the watermain was in poor condition, undersized for the area's needs and had experienced 14 watermain breaks. Replacing it will help reduce the risk of future breaks and service disruptions.

“By coordinating this work, we were able to make several improvements along Boler Road at the same time, from adding cycling and pedestrian connections to replacing the watermain. This means we can address multiple needs in one project, reducing the chance of returning to dig up the road again for separate work and helping limit future disruptions for the neighbourhood,” said Jennie Dann, Director of Construction and Infrastructure Services.

The work was completed in three phases along Boler Road, between Commissioners Road West and Southdale Road. The final section, between Byron Baseline Road and Commissioners Road West, is now open to traffic.

Crews will return in spring 2027 to complete some remaining work. No traffic disruptions are expected.

stories.title: Additional charges laid
stories.summary: London, ON (November 4, 2026) – A London man who remains in custody in relation to an investigation involving multiple victims is facing 11 additional charges after police seized identity documents belonging to nine people.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 4, 2026) – A London man who remains in custody in relation to an investigation involving multiple victims is facing 11 additional charges after police seized identity documents belonging to nine people.

On Tuesday, October 27, 2026, a man was arrested in relation to a complex investigation by members of the London Police Service (LPS) Criminal Investigation Division and Human Trafficking Unit.

As a result of the ongoing investigation, police seized a bag containing identification belonging to the accused, as well as identity documents belonging to nine other individuals.

The seized documents included driver’s licences, health cards, Social Insurance Number documents and birth certificates.

As a result, police confirmed that at least two of the identity documents had previously been reported stolen. Investigators continue to take steps to contact the remaining individuals associated with the seized documents.

stories.title: Toronto to unveil statue of First World War flying ace William Barker
stories.summary: Monument is part of a broader effort to resurrect appreciation for Canada’s most-decorated service member and the fighting forces he represented
stories.author: Patrick White
stories.content:
No one in Toronto could remember a funeral as large or elaborate as William Barker’s.

Two thousand troops paraded city streets in front of 50,000 mourners. The guest list included the premier, the mayor, federal and provincial cabinet ministers, judges and much of the country’s military brass. A squadron of planes released a shower of rose petals.

The date was March 15, 1930. The country was lurching toward the Great Depression. Unemployment approached 15 per cent. The weary country longed for a hero. In Mr. Barker, they found one.

And then promptly lost him.

Mr. Barker’s wartime heroics were once the stuff of movies, comic books, an Ernest Hemingway short story: 50 enemy aircraft destroyed, 12 gallantry awards, one legendary dogfight with upwards of 15 German Fokkers.

But his memory began to fade from public consciousness in the years after his death, until few but his family and military history buffs could distinguish Mr. Barker from the more renowned ace Billy Bishop.

On Wednesday, admirers and family members of Mr. Barker will gather to unveil a statue of the pilot in midtown Toronto, part of a broader effort to resurrect appreciation for him and the fighting forces he represented.

“If he was an American, you can damn-well bet there’d be a movie about him,” said Capt. Cal Bricker, special adviser to the Commander of the Royal Canadian Navy. “This kid from Dauphin ends up as a national hero and then has a tragic end.”

The script starts in rural Manitoba. Born in a log cabin to farmer parents, he was a quintessential prairie boy, as skilled on a horse as he was with a rifle.

He left for war in 1914 at age 20, enlisting as a trooper in the 1st Canadian Mounted Rifles Regiment. After several months machine-gunning in the foul trenches of Belgium, he decided he’d rather wage war in the skies and volunteered for the Royal Flying Corps as a gunner.

By February 1917, he’d completed pilot training in England. He flew a Sopwith Camel in France, and then Italy, where he earned the “ace” designation given to any aviator who shot down five or more enemy aircraft.

The kills would come in bunches – 22 by April 1918 – but he would also specialize in low-altitude ground assaults, for which one character in Hemingway’s The Snows of Kilimanjaro called him “a bloody murderous bastard.”

His final mission came on the morning of Oct. 27. He shot down a German reconnaissance plane stirring a swarm of enemy aircraft. Fifteen broke off to pursue Mr. Barker, their rounds striking the Canadian in both thighs and the left arm. He fainted, but regained consciousness long enough to crash-land his bullet-riddled plane behind Allied lines.

He survived, adding the Victoria Cross, the British Empire’s highest award for military bravery, to a collection of honours that made him Canada’s most-decorated service member – a designation that remains to this day.

His postwar life was nearly as eventful. A full-on Canadian celebrity, he founded one of the country’s first commercial airlines with his close friend and fellow ace Billy Bishop before becoming the first president of the Toronto Maple Leafs.

In the early 1930s, he became vice-president of Fairchild Aviation Limited of Canada, but died crashing a company biplane into the frozen Ottawa River near the Rockcliffe airfield.

The massive funeral and subsequent naming of Barker Field, an airfield in North York, kept his memory alive. But the field would close in 1953, and his name gradually faded.

“People would think they recognized the name but it would turn out they were thinking of Billy Bishop,” said Ian Mackenzie, Mr. Barker’s grandson.

All that changed in 2009, when veteran pollster John Wright bought a book about Toronto’s Mount Pleasant Cemetery. He intended to keep it in the bathroom. But the entry on Mr. Barker caught his attention. He lives near the cemetery and walked over to have a look at the Barker grave. It proved elusive, lying within a crypt marked with his wife’s maiden name, Smith.

He could hardly believe that the country’s most-decorated service member had no public marker and, with the family’s permission, began a 17-year campaign to cure the national amnesia.

He enlisted a long list of people and organizations to help establish major Barker monuments at Mount Pleasant and Rockcliffe.

On Wednesday, he’ll be on hand to unveil a Barker statue by sculptor Armando Barbon.

At 2:30 p.m., a ceremonial parade will head along Yonge Street – the same street Mr. Barker’s funeral procession followed 96 years ago – ending at Mount Pleasant Cemetery, where more than 400 veterans’ graves will be illuminated.

“This is not just about Barker,” said Mr. Wright. “It’s about all of them, all the veterans, and this provides a convening place where we can all go and remember who they were in the past and who they are today.”

stories.title: Mother, daughter found dead in suspected grizzly bear attack in B.C.
stories.summary: The incident would mark the second grizzly bear attack on humans in Bella Coola in just over a year
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Family members have identified a mother and teenage daughter as the victims of a suspected grizzly attack after both were found dead in the central coast region of British Columbia.

RCMP and search-and-rescue crews located the remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, in the Snooka West Trail area of Bella Coola about 430 kilometres northwest of Vancouver on Monday afternoon, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service and Ms. Balcarras’s brother, Matthew Balcarras. Her 19-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, was found deceased on Tuesday afternoon.

Evidence suggests that a bear was involved, said Inspector Jeff Tyre with the Conservation Officer Service in a video statement on Tuesday. If confirmed, the incident would mark the second grizzly bear attack on humans in the unincorporated community in just over a year.

Family members reported the pair as missing on Sunday after they failed to hear from them as planned.

Mr. Balcarras said his sister, an avid outdoors person, was located a short distance up a trail very close to her home. He suspects that the two had intended to go for a short hike when the attack occurred.

The Conservation Officer Service said it has deployed officers to locate and trap any bears involved and is working to collect and analyze any evidence. The service urged people to avoid the Snooka West Trail both for safety reasons and to allow its staff to do their work.

If a bear is determined to be responsible for the attack, it will be killed “to ensure public safety, as per provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines,” the Conservation Officer Service said.

“Our thoughts are with the family of the victims during this tragic time,” Insp. Tyre said.

BC Emergency Health Services said it was notified at 1:50 p.m. Monday about a possible animal attack incident near the 1100-block of Highway 20 in Bella Coola. An ambulance responded to the scene; no patients were transported to hospital, the agency said in a statement to The Globe and Mail.

Ms. Balcarras worked as an art therapist and spent many years living in coastal communities, including Bella Bella in B.C. and Prince of Wales Island and Juneau in Alaska.

A June 2023 posting from the Hailika’as Heiltsuk Health Centre Society in Bella Bella introducing her as their new art therapist said she had worked with a range of clients, from children to elders, and that she takes a trauma-informed approach in her work.

Her brother said she had always been sensitive to others’ emotional needs.

“My sister’s a smaller woman – she’s petite – but she’s incredibly strong and powerful,” Mr. Balcarras said. “And I think that’s sort of one of her strengths as an art therapist: gentleness with strength.”

Ms. Reed worked as an educational assistant, Mr. Balcarras said. She loved ballet and doted on her cat, Suga, whom she would carry around in a cat backpack with a bubble window.

The incident comes one year after a grizzly bear attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers in the same community.

Eleven people were injured in that attack on Nov. 20, 2025. Four of them – one adult and three children – were badly mauled and airlifted to hospital in Vancouver.

The teachers had standard-issue bear deterrents, including pepper spray and bear bangers, and had tried to fend off the bear, which was believed to be with her two cubs.

At that time, there had been no other record of a similar attack.

Samuel Schooner, elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, offered condolences to the family of Ms. Balcarras and Ms. Reed.

“While the full circumstances are still unfolding, we understand first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims’ family members, the victims of last year’s attack and the community at large,” he said in a statement issued Tuesday.

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson offered his sympathies to the victims’ family, loved ones and the entire Nuxalk Nation.

“The news from Bella Coola is heartbreaking, and at a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day,” Mr. Doerkson said in a statement posted to social media.
paragraphs: Family members have identified a mother and teenage daughter as the victims of a suspected grizzly attack after both were found dead in the central coast region of British Columbia.

RCMP and search-and-rescue crews located the remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, in the Snooka West Trail area of Bella Coola about 430 kilometres northwest of Vancouver on Monday afternoon, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service and Ms. Balcarras’s brother, Matthew Balcarras. Her 19-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, was found deceased on Tuesday afternoon.

Evidence suggests that a bear was involved, said Inspector Jeff Tyre with the Conservation Officer Service in a video statement on Tuesday. If confirmed, the incident would mark the second grizzly bear attack on humans in the unincorporated community in just over a year.
Family members reported the pair as missing on Sunday after they failed to hear from them as planned.

Mr. Balcarras said his sister, an avid outdoors person, was located a short distance up a trail very close to her home. He suspects that the two had intended to go for a short hike when the attack occurred.

The Conservation Officer Service said it has deployed officers to locate and trap any bears involved and is working to collect and analyze any evidence. The service urged people to avoid the Snooka West Trail both for safety reasons and to allow its staff to do their work.

If a bear is determined to be responsible for the attack, it will be killed “to ensure public safety, as per provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines,” the Conservation Officer Service said.
“Our thoughts are with the family of the victims during this tragic time,” Insp. Tyre said.

BC Emergency Health Services said it was notified at 1:50 p.m. Monday about a possible animal attack incident near the 1100-block of Highway 20 in Bella Coola. An ambulance responded to the scene; no patients were transported to hospital, the agency said in a statement to The Globe and Mail.
Ms. Balcarras worked as an art therapist and spent many years living in coastal communities, including Bella Bella in B.C. and Prince of Wales Island and Juneau in Alaska.

A June 2023 posting from the Hailika’as Heiltsuk Health Centre Society in Bella Bella introducing her as their new art therapist said she had worked with a range of clients, from children to elders, and that she takes a trauma-informed approach in her work.
Her brother said she had always been sensitive to others’ emotional needs.

“My sister’s a smaller woman – she’s petite – but she’s incredibly strong and powerful,” Mr. Balcarras said. “And I think that’s sort of one of her strengths as an art therapist: gentleness with strength.”
Ms. Reed worked as an educational assistant, Mr. Balcarras said. She loved ballet and doted on her cat, Suga, whom she would carry around in a cat backpack with a bubble window.
The incident comes one year after a grizzly bear attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers in the same community.
Eleven people were injured in that attack on Nov. 20, 2025. Four of them – one adult and three children – were badly mauled and airlifted to hospital in Vancouver.
The teachers had standard-issue bear deterrents, including pepper spray and bear bangers, and had tried to fend off the bear, which was believed to be with her two cubs.
At that time, there had been no other record of a similar attack.
Samuel Schooner, elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, offered condolences to the family of Ms. Balcarras and Ms. Reed.

“While the full circumstances are still unfolding, we understand first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims’ family members, the victims of last year’s attack and the community at large,” he said in a statement issued Tuesday.
Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson offered his sympathies to the victims’ family, loved ones and the entire Nuxalk Nation.

“The news from Bella Coola is heartbreaking, and at a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day,” Mr. Doerkson said in a statement posted to social media.

stories.title: Saskatoon transportation committee defers expropriating land talks for BRT stations
stories.summary: The committee tasked administration with going back to the negotiation table with six landowners before the next meeting in December
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Saskatoon’s transportation committee has decided to delay discussions on whether the city will move toward taking over small parcels of private land needed for a handful of Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) stations, following stalled negotiations with landowners.

City administrators told the committee Tuesday afternoon that, during the bus station design process, they determined they needed more property to construct their BRT bus stations, consisting of concrete platforms and bus-stopping pads adjacent to the platforms, with electrical wires beneath the platforms.

Terry Schmidt, the city’s transportation and construction general manager, told the committee that the city began consultations with landowners in 2024, has since purchased 10 properties and expects to buy five more. But talks with landowners at six sites have stalled, with the administration noting that many do not want to sell, while others have stopped responding to the city.

Administrators recommended the city move ahead with taking over the six parcels of land at these sites, ranging in size from 30 to 57 square metres. Four of the sites are on 22nd St. W., while the other two are on 8th Street East.

Two of the six landowners resumed talks with the city when they were notified of the motion in front of council on Oct. 28, said Schmidt, adding that the other four will be re-engaged one last time.

Schmidt said administrators did their homework to make sure the bus stations do not interfere with business operations, explaining that planners explored moving the stations up or down the street but found those options were not feasible as they would block access to businesses, require changes to parking lots or cause transit users to walk further.

He also said they have designed narrower platforms with the same amenities as the others along the system, including Cctv cameras.

Business advocates representing west-end landowners voiced concerns at Tuesday’s meeting, saying safety concerns surrounding the bus stations were not specifically addressed by the city.

Karen Kobussen, CEO of the Saskatoon West Business Association, said businesses shared concerns about general access alongside loitering, littering and traffic safety, but the city continued to make offers to purchase the land rather than addressing them.

Meanwhile, Henry Chan, who also spoke on behalf of the Saskatoon West Business Association, questioned the city’s “heavy-handed” approach, noting that expropriation is typically a final resort.

Expropriation of land is covered under Saskatchewan’s Municipal Expropriation Act and is considered a “last resort” that requires reasonable attempts to purchase the land and the passing of a bylaw. Owners must also be formally notified and the province must approve it.

Schmidt said there was a lot of “back and forth” between the administration and landowners, with concerns mainly centred on businesses’ reluctance to face potential social disorder associated with bus stations.

When asked by councillors, Schmidt said the bus stations around 22nd Street West would be fitted with shatter-resistant glass and would have buttons that would need to be pushed to offer heat.

The owners of a used car dealership at 221 22nd St. West shared concerns about a potential land acquisition via written comments to the committee, saying they need the space in front of their business for access and displaying vehicles, which would be impacted by even a small land transfer.

Administrators also presented the committee with another option of building the stations on land they already own, but these were presented as “substandard” as they would lack the shelter and transit user information other BRT stations are fitted with.

Schmidt said these stations would include only a bus stop sign and a concrete pad and would not have a shelter or benches. If there is negative feedback and some desire to retrofit these stops down the road, they would have to restart the negotiation process with landowners, he added.

Coun. Robert Pearce made the deferral motion, calling expropriation a “nuclear response” and seeking more time for the administration to reach out and assess whether there is a desire to continue negotiations.

Meanwhile, Coun. Bev Dubois voted against the deferral motion, saying businesses would have time for consultation within the next couple of weeks before the item would have gone in front of councillors at the end of the month.

The item will now be considered at the next transportation committee meeting at the beginning of December, with Schmidt saying it will not critically delay the BRT project overall.

Administrators say they will begin reaching out to the six property owners as soon as Wednesday.

Construction for the city’s 94 BRT stations started in September 2024, with 41 completed so far. The city expects 14 additional stations to be finished by the end of this year, with the remainder planned for construction next year.

Last month, city council voted through new design plans for a stretch of the BRT on downtown’s 1st Avenue between 19th and 25th streets following five months of stakeholder engagement.

Construction of bus lanes and stations continues on College Drive , modifying traffic lanes and intersections, which snarled commutes for students and hospital-goers in mid-September.

The city expects to launch the BRT system in 2028.

stories.title: ‘When they cry, I’m crying with them’: Local poet shares experience going viral
stories.summary: A London Ont. based poet is sharing her love of writing in the city’s downtown core.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
A London Ont. based poet is sharing her love of writing in the city’s downtown core.

“There’s a long-standing tradition of typewriter poets,” said Vironika Wilde. “They come out to the streets and write custom poems for people.”

Wilde said she believes she is the first typewriter poet in London.

“If you go on TikTok or Instagram, you can find a lot of typewriter poets,” said Wilde. “It’s usually in major big cities.”

Visitors to Wilde’s booth, typically located on Dundas Street, share something meaningful about their life and within minutes a new poem is created.

“There is such an aliveness to typewriter poetry,” said Wilde. “You have to be here, you can’t think about the bills, you can’t think about the kids, you can’t think about anything else, you just have to be here.”

Wilde said the art of poetry has been an outlet for her.

“It’s been a big mental health tool for me,” said Wilde. “I hear these stories and when they cry, I’m crying with them.”

Southwestern Ontario’s Ymca has launched its Woman of Excellence nominations for 2027.

Each year, the Y asks people to nominate women who make a difference in their communities every day.

Winners will be named in each of eight categories, which include “health, science & technology,” “social justice” and “young women of excellence.”

“The awards are to celebrate women who are making a meaningful difference in our community and make sure their contributions are seen and valued,” said Christina Harley the vice president of development marketing and communication at Ymca Southwestern Ontario.

The theme for 2027 is where women thrive communities bloom.

“When women thrive families, workplaces and communities are stronger,” Harley said

Cass Bayley (Credit: Ymca women of excellence page)

London’s Cass Bayley was the 2025 recipent in the “entrepreneur” category.

“It was very lovely and sort of salute to the work that we do,” Bayley said. “It’s a wonderful thing that the Ymca does for women in the London region, supporting women is really important to our community to recognize the great women and the work they’re doing in the London region.”

Bayley is the founder of the Bayley Group , a conference and event management company in London that works across Canada, USA and Europe.

“I’ve been an entrepreneur all my life, I come from a family of entrepreneurs. There have been so many incredible women who have been woman of excellence in London over the years,” Bayley said.

She said the best advice for young entrepreneurs is to think about your long term effect and your legacy. “Taking care of how you operate and the people that you work with is very important from the beginning,” Bayley said. “Maintain your reputation, quality of work and to build a community of like minded people around you.”

Harley stated the event is also the biggest fundraiser for the Ymca has to offer in Southwestern Ontario.

“All funds raised support sending children, families and seniors to Ymca programs and services who can’t afford it.”

She said you can purchase tickets or raffle tickets online in February.

The Ymca has held this event for over 40 years now, the event happens every two years.

Voting opened last week on Oct. 28, you can nominate any women you might know who deserves to be recognized for their work on the website. The deadline for submitting is Dec. 11 and announce the nominees in February. The awards gala will be hosted on May 13, 2027.

stories.title: Smith defends Alberta electoral map against gerrymandering allegations
stories.summary: Premier says proposed boundary changes are reasonable and would give voters better representation
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is rejecting allegations that an independent panel has torqued the province’s electoral map to favour her United Conservative Party, saying the recommended changes to redraw the boundaries are reasonable and would give voters better representation.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Ms. Smith said she also endorses changes to the electoral map in southern Alberta , which have become the greatest source of contention since the province’s proposed boundaries were released publicly the day before.

The new map proposes eliminating one of Lethbridge’s two urban ridings while creating three new districts that mix the city’s suburban neighbourhoods with swaths of rural southern Alberta.

The change has provoked charges of gerrymandering, the U.S.-style practice of manipulating boundaries to give one party an unfair advantage in elections.

“I think Lethbridge would be very well served by having four representatives,” Ms. Smith said, offering her first thoughts on the proposed map since it was published Monday.

Ms. Smith added that she hopes the Alberta Ndp’s promised legal challenge of the map doesn’t come to pass, but that her government would assemble a legal team if necessary. (Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said his party can only file a legal challenge if the government adopts the map.)

The map is expected to be debated on Wednesday afternoon in the Alberta Legislature, where Ms. Smith’s UCP holds a majority of seats.

The electoral map of Alberta is redrawn every eight to 10 years through a process designed to foster compromise and limit political influence. Adopting the recommendations of independent panels, which are often passed with little public scrutiny, has been the standard for provincial legislatures and federal Parliament for decades.

Alberta’s latest redrawing, however, has fuelled accusations of gerrymandering ever since Ms. Smith decided in April to upend the process and reject the recommended map of an earlier independent panel. She then formed a committee to set up a new panel, which delivered a fresh map on Monday.

Alberta’s system dictates that the governing party selects the chair and two panelists while the Official Opposition picks the remaining two.

Of the panelists tasked with drawing the latest map, the two selected by the NDP have added to the accusations of gerrymandering, singling out the changes in Lethbridge.

These two panelists – University of Alberta constitutional law professor Gerard Kennedy and former Okotoks, Alta., town councillor Brent Robinson – wrote in a separate report that they believe some of the new recommended ridings would be “constitutionally fraught” and will likely face a legal challenge.

The remaining three panelists, including panel chair and retired judge Brian O’Ferrall, dismissed their counterparts’ criticisms at several turns through the 300-plus-page report, accusing them of “sanctimonious passing of judgment” and “extreme, unjustified and unnecessary criticisms.”

In the report, Mr. O’Ferrall also singled out political scientists, complaining that they have “preferred to stoke the flames of controversy” instead of contributing “to the public’s understanding of the electoral boundary process.”

Alberta’s next general election is scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027. It is unclear what electoral map would be used for that vote if the NDP launches a legal challenge. Elections Alberta has warned it May not have enough time to prepare for the election, should the new maps be adopted or a legal challenge delays the map from being implemented.

Kara Westerlund, president of Rural Municipalities of Alberta, said on Tuesday that rural leaders are concerned about hybrid ridings, noting the association’s members represent 85 per cent of the province’s land mass but 15 per cent of the population.

“Our main concern is just the fact that we feel that the rural voice and our issues are going to be diluted with [hybrid ridings],” she said.

Politicians from mid-sized cities have cautioned against sweeping hybrid ridings, pointing to the risk that city residents could be represented by people who don’t live in their area or understand their needs.

University of Calgary political scientist Lisa Young said she believes the map is gerrymandered, most clearly underlined by the proposed changes in Lethbridge.

The City of Lethbridge is currently split into two urban electoral districts, with one represented by the NDP and the other by the UCP. Both seats have been competitive since 2015, when the provincial NDP formed government for the first time.

While the NDP would likely win in the city’s new urban riding, the UCP would be heavily favoured to win the three new ridings that extend hundreds of kilometres beyond city boundaries.

“All of this has partisan consequence. It does, to me, look like a deliberate attempt to draw lines on the map in a way that would advantage one party – the governing party – at the expense of the opposition party,” Prof. Young said.

She added that Alberta’s boundary redrawing process May need to be revamped. Other provinces, such as British Columbia, have systems that further remove the process from political influence.

“To have essentially two failed efforts at coming together around a map says that there’s something desperately wrong here,” Prof. Young said.

“It raises the question of whether this sort of bipartisan commission approach that we’ve been using works in a polarized system.”

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: London organizations shine a purple spotlight on abuse
stories.summary: Preventing violence against women is not just a women's issue, says a London organization that works with dome...
stories.author: Georgia Chambers
stories.content:
Preventing violence against women is not just a women’s issue, says a London organization that works with domestic violence victims.

That’s why the London Abused Women’s Centre (Lawc) is calling for men and boys to help make a change this November, which is Woman Abuse Prevention month.

“Violence against women is not a woman’s issue. It is an issue for men, young men and boys to be aware of and learn how to act, learn about behavior and how to treat women,” said Jennifer Dunn, executive director of Lawc.

The centre hopes to raise awareness about violence against women through its 17th annual Shine the Light campaign, which invites organizations and businesses to light up their buildings purple throughout the month of November.

Fanshawe College and Western University are among the buildings that will shine a purple light all month.

Purple was chosen because it’s the colour that’s associated with Women’s Abuse Prevention month but also because, it repersents courage and strength.

The campaign has grown bigger then London, becoming a national and global campaign.

“There are landmarks in Europe that are turning purple for the campaign. There are landmarks in Australia that are turning purple for the campaign. In Montreal, we just had heard about the big skywheel in Montreal is turning purple for the campaign,” Dunn said.

Dunn said their goal is to encourage Londoners to think about what they can do to help bring awareness and prevent violence against women. That could mean either starting a conversation or giving people that need support reasources to help.

“If there is one woman that reaches out for support during the month of November because she’s heard about the campaign then that makes it all worth it to us,” Dunn said.

Lawc provides long-term counselling and support for women and girls, twelve and up, who have gone through abuse, sexual assualt or intimate partner violence.

The organization does not offer places to stay but will help women make safety plans and connect them with other reasources in the community.

Londoners can participate in Wear Purple Day on November 15 by wearing purple.

That’s why the London Abused Women’s Centre (Lawc) is calling for men and boys to help make a change this November, which is Woman Abuse Prevention month.

“Violence against women is not a woman’s issue. It is an issue for men, young men and boys to be aware of and learn how to act, learn about behavior and how to treat women,” said Jennifer Dunn, executive director of Lawc.

The centre hopes to raise awareness about violence against women through its 17th annual Shine the Light campaign, which invites organizations and businesses to light up their buildings purple throughout the month of November.
Fanshawe College and Western University are among the buildings that will shine a purple light all month.
Purple was chosen because it’s the colour that’s associated with Women’s Abuse Prevention month but also because, it repersents courage and strength.
The campaign has grown bigger then London, becoming a national and global campaign.

“There are landmarks in Europe that are turning purple for the campaign. There are landmarks in Australia that are turning purple for the campaign. In Montreal, we just had heard about the big skywheel in Montreal is turning purple for the campaign,” Dunn said.

Dunn said their goal is to encourage Londoners to think about what they can do to help bring awareness and prevent violence against women. That could mean either starting a conversation or giving people that need support reasources to help.
“If there is one woman that reaches out for support during the month of November because she’s heard about the campaign then that makes it all worth it to us,” Dunn said.
Lawc provides long-term counselling and support for women and girls, twelve and up, who have gone through abuse, sexual assualt or intimate partner violence.
The organization does not offer places to stay but will help women make safety plans and connect them with other reasources in the community.
Londoners can participate in Wear Purple Day on November 15 by wearing purple.

stories.title: Canadians, Londoners await U.S. midterm results
stories.summary: U.S midterm elections got under way Tuesday, with many on this side of the border watching results. As polls p...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
U.S midterm elections got under way Tuesday, with many on this side of the border watching results.

As polls predicted Democrats could take the win, many Londoners were paying close attention.

“We are very interested because of some priorities of the Trump administration affect Southwestern Ontario; most notably undermining the North Atlantic Trade Organization (Nato), and also imposing trade restrictions directly impacts businesses here in London,” said Matt Farrell, a professor of political science at Fanshawe College.

“We are going to be watching for a change in the House or the Senate or both, as that could have the potential to push b

Matt Farrell, political science professor at Fanshawe College (Benjamin McFadden/XFM News) ack against the president’s tariff’s.”

Businesses that import to the U.S., such as London’s General Dynamics Land Systems (Gdls) are directly and often financially affected by U.S. policy.

The first polls closed in Kentucky and Indiana around 6 p.m.

“One thing Londoners should watch for is districts that are more divided between Democrat and Republican and see who wins where, as this will show across the board what direction it is going,” said Farrell.

This comes at a critical time as tensions between Canada and the United States continue to grow.

stories.title: New Winnipeg city council takes office, sets agenda at inaugural meeting
stories.summary: Mayor Scott Gillingham and the 15 freshly elected representatives on Winnipeg city council took the Declaration of Office Tuesday.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Winnipeg’s new city council has officially taken the reins after being sworn in at city hall Tuesday.

Nine new faces are sitting on Winnipeg’s freshly elected city council alongside six incumbent city councillors. Mayor Scott Gillingham also retained his role in last week’s election and is set to begin his second term.

He will lead the council alongside 15 city councillors, including St. James representative Kelly Ryback, who will serve as the presiding officer, which is the city’s equivalent of the speaker.

The 14 other ward representatives include: Evan Duncan, Cindy Gilroy, Emma Durand Wood, Jeff Palmer, Natalie Smith, Jeff Browaty, Greg McFarlane, Vivian Santos, Sara MacArthur, Matt Allard, Ray Dubois, Chris Sigurdson, Lora Meseman and Jasmine Brar.

The councillors were sworn in at Winnipeg city hall during the inaugural meeting on Tuesday evening. All the elected officials took the Declaration of Office, vowing to represent Winnipeggers and their ward residents fairly. They also swore they would not take bribes or engage in other corruption.

“In this town, change is always necessary but it’s never easy. New faces and new laws, and new promises can create exciting opportunities for change. But on their own, they’re not enough. Lasting change takes hard work, determination, risk, (and) follow through,” Gillingham said, addressing the councillors after they took the declaration.

“Let’s approach the next four years with determination, with humility, and a willingness to work together.”

Among the items on his new council’s agenda is further developing downtown to attract new residents, investments and businesses. The city will also respond to riders’ feedback by improving upon Winnipeg Transit, Gillingham said.

“We can bring new life to old streets. It’s been a struggle for decades, like (at) north Main Street,” the mayor continued, noting that new life would involve the city having “to address homelessness, mental health and addictions.”

“Bringing housing, treatment, outreach and ongoing supports together while improving public safety.”

On Wednesday, he will get to work by establishing his new executive policy committee. The EPC consists of a handful of city councillors who will join the mayor’s equivalent of a cabinet. The mayor will serve as that committee’s chair.

stories.title: Manitoba producers hopes for stability from U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Manitobans are watching the U.S. midterms closely on Tuesday evening hoping for some relief after tariffs continue to hamper the agricultural industry.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Manitobans are watching the U.S. midterms closely on Tuesday evening hoping for some relief after tariffs continue to hamper the agricultural industry.

“What a nightmare it is buying fuel right now to close out the season, as we get colder temperatures our equipment use more fuel,” said Curtis McRae, a farmer in St. Andrews, Man. “It makes it very difficult for me to plan years in advance. When you farm you need to plan a couple years out.”

McRae paid 30 per cent more for fertilizer and nearly a 100 per cent increase for diesel, he says.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: McGill confirms convicted murderer no longer enrolled as a law student
stories.summary: McGill's provost, Angela Campbell, informed students and staff about the news in a statement sent on Monday.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Montreal’s McGill University says a man who was convicted of murder and attempted murder for attacks committed in 1984 is no longer a student.

McGill’s provost, Angela Campbell, informed students and staff about the news in a statement sent on Monday.

“McGill’s principal obligation is our duty of care to everyone who learns, works and lives on our campuses,” Campbell wrote.

Campbell sent the message after news from October about Jeffrey George Ewart’s enrolment in law classes while on parole sparked concern about student safety and debate over whether or not he should be allowed to attend.

Ewert, now in his 60s, was sentenced to two life sentences after he sexually assaulted and strangled two women in British Columbia in separate 1984 incidents that left one victim dead and the other severely disabled.

Campbell’s note did not identify Ewart by name, but said a person on day parole who was admitted to its law faculty this fall is no longer enrolled.

“Each student and colleague deserves a learning and research environment that is safe, respectful, inclusive, and conducive to their flourishing and success'” Campbell said.

Campbell said the university has launched an independent review of admissions processes and protocols that will take several months to complete.

“The goal of this review is to make sure existing procedures are sufficiently rigorous, set clearly defined responsibilities, and reflect our values, our academic mission, and our duty of care,” she wrote.

Campbell said the school is also committed to “dignity and second chances.”

“We believe in rehabilitation and in education’s power to transform lives,” the statement read. “Accordingly, past convictions do not, ON their own, bar anyone from studying here.”

Campbell also acknowledged that students have been under strain due to media attention generated by the case, and that “differing views about recent events have created tensions within our community.”

The statement did not say whether Ewert’s enrolment was revoked by the school or whether he withdrew. The Canadian Press could not immediately reach his lawyer for comment.

Correctional Service Canada confirmed that it had issued a warrant to suspend Ewert’s conditional release and said he has returned to custody while the situation is being reviewed.

The agency said it can move to return someone to custody “when there are reasonable grounds to believe that the offender has breached a condition of release or that the risk they present can no longer be safely managed in the community.”

The agency said it can either cancel the suspension within 30 days or refer the case to the Parole Board of Canada for a post-suspension review.

McGill said it could not comment on specific cases for privacy reasons. However, it said that while criminal background checks are not typically part of Canadian universities’ admissions processes, the school “would act quickly and decisively should concerning information be brought forward about a student’s background or behaviour on campus.”

McGill said its procedures also include consulting relevant government bodies and its own policies to remove the individual from campus and to review its admission processes to ensure the situation isn’t repeated.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

stories.title: National campaign fighting migrant worker exploitation wins $50,000 prize
stories.summary: The campaign to stop deportations and win labour rights, led by Migrant Workers Alliance for Change, wins the Atkinson Foundation’s Good Fight prize.
stories.author: Elissa Mendes
stories.content:
A campaign uniting migrant workers in Canada to battle exploitation has won a prestigious social justice award from the Atkinson Foundation.

The United We Are Stronger initiative has advocated for migrants in essential sectors across the country, fighting to stop deportations, secure work permit extensions and win labour protections.

The campaign, led by Migrant Workers Alliance for Change, will receive $50,000 with this year’s Good Fight prize.

The award recognizes exemplary work toward economic and social justice — a struggle that legendary Toronto Star founder and publisher Joseph Atkinson termed “the good fight.”

Canadian migrant workers face systemic exclusion and unequal rights, said Colette Murphy, CEO of the Atkinson Foundation and a member of the Good Fight prize jury.

“But it’s wonderful, for just one night, to stand back and take in the exceptional efforts to fight for working people in a world buckling under the weight of extreme wealth concentration.”

Murphy added, “At its core, the United We Are Stronger campaign recognizes that labour rights and immigration status are deeply connected — when a person’s ability to stay in the country depends entirely on their boss, standing up for fair treatment is difficult if not dangerous.”

The campaign has largely supported workers in the food and care industries , finding them allies in unions, researchers and faith groups, said Syed Hussan, executive director of Migrant Workers Alliance for Change.

“We’re all struggling with the high cost of rent, the high cost of groceries and low wages, whether you’re a migrant or a citizen,” said Hussan.

“It’s necessary for us to unite and deal with the government policies and corporate profiteering that are causing this crisis.”

Organizers advocated for migrant workers as essential community members who are increasingly being scapegoated for the country’s housing crisis, health-care shortages and social tensions.

Hussan said he is proud to have helped two Mexican temporary foreign workers secure a lost wages settlement from a New Brunswick lobster processor, even though they didn’t have visas to return to Canada.

“To me, this is a story of the enormous systemic ways in which migrants are denied justice,” he said.

“But it’s also a story of racialized working-class people standing up and fighting not just for themselves, but for the rights of others.”

Two other finalists each won $25,000 for their “good fight” efforts: a renoviction resistance campaign by Acorn Canada, and a coalition to bring employee ownership trusts to Canada.

“The Migrant Workers Alliance for Change’s impactful advocacy and organizing, alongside that of our two additional finalists, only reinforces our decision to recognize and support decent work campaigns year after year,” said Murphy.

This article was updated to make clear that Migrant Workers Alliance for Change got settlements for two Mexican workers even though they weren’t able to get them visas to return to Canada for their day in court.

stories.title: B.C. First Nation buys major Sunshine Coast forestry operation in $80M deal
stories.summary: Powell River - Western Forest Products and the Tla'amin Nation say they have completed a deal that transfers ownership of a major forestry operation to the First Nation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Powell River - Western Forest Products and the Tla’amin Nation say they have completed a deal that transfers ownership of a major forestry operation to the First Nation.

A joint statement says the Tla’amin forestry arm has acquired a 100 per cent ownership interest in the Stillwater Forest Operation near Powell River, B.C., for about $80 million after adjustments.

stories.title: NFB filmmaker Anne Claire Poirier focused her lens on women’s stories
stories.summary: A pioneer of Quebec cinema, she is best known for her groundbreaking film Mourir à tue-tête, which examines in excruciating detail the rape of a nurse in Montreal
stories.author: James Cullingham
stories.content:
Anne Claire Poirier, who died in Montreal on Sept. 27 at age 94, was a singular force in Quebec cinema. She set a standard for documentary, fiction and experimental hybrid films working for the National Film Board of Canada (known in French as the Office national du film du Canada, or ONF). The films she made were distinctive and highly influential. Her drama Mourir à tue-tête was selected for the 1979 Cannes Film Festival. As a producer at the NFB, she also oversaw a strand of feminist films that nurtured the careers of emerging female filmmakers.

Marc St-Pierre, collection curator at the NFB, calls Ms. Poirier “one of the pioneers of Quebec cinema.” He said she was a peer of film visionaries Michel Brault, Claude Jutra, Pierre Perrault, Gilles Groulx and Jacques Godbout. “What’s more exceptional, he added, “is that she was a woman – in fact, the only [francophone] woman directing and producing films at the NFB when she first emerged.”

Anne Claire Poirier was born into a Catholic middle-class family on June 6, 1932, in Saint-Hyacinthe in southwestern Quebec, just east of Montreal. Her father, Émile Poirier, ran an upscale clothing store for women. Her mother, Berthe Poirier (née Latraverse), also worked in the store.

Ms. Poirier moved to Montreal where she studied dramatic arts and then law. She began her chosen career at Radio-Canada, but moved to the NFB in 1960, where she first worked in dubbing and received her film education by watching NFB productions in English and French. When she became an editor, she worked almost exclusively with male peers; she later joked that she became “one of the boys.” Convinced she could direct her own films, she prevailed upon her male bosses to give her a chance.

The first opportunity was 30 Minutes, Mister Plummer (1963), which put her theatrical training to good use. The documentary is a closely observed look at Christopher Plummer and Kate Reid preparing to go on stage at the Stratford Festival. The film foreshadows Ms. Poirier’s signature interests in its observation of how Ms. Reid balanced her roles as actor and mother of young children.

The following year saw Ms. Poirier branch into experimental short drama with La fin des étés, co-written with filmmaker and novelist Hubert Aquin and featuring the emerging star Geneviève Bujold.

In 1973, Ms. Poirier and other francophone women at the NFB launched En tant que femmes, a groundbreaking series of six French-language films by women about women’s issues. (The following year, the NFB launched its Studio D, which produced films exclusively by women – mostly in English – over a period of 22 years.)

Ms. Poirier ’s Les filles du Roy (1974), the fifth of the En tant que femmes films, is a richly visualized examination of the lot of Quebec women. Industrial textile workers, nuns, waitresses, farmers, topless dancers, artisanal weavers and clerical workers are among the subjects depicted. The uniquely stylized film is underscored with motifs of the landscapes of Quebec and echoes of Indigenous and colonial influences. In the 2003 NFB documentary Entretien avec Anne Claire Poirier, by Nicole Giguère, Ms. Poirier put Les filles du Roy into the context of the overall mission of the series she was producing, saying she wanted her film, “to broaden the daily life of women into the history of women of Quebec. It’s not exactly an historical film, but the meaning of the history of women is the primary source material.”

Ms. Giguère, who began creating documentary and fictional films with a video production collective in Quebec City, is among the female filmmakers who were motivated by and found opportunity because of the En tant que femmes series. She was one of the founders of Réalisatrices équitables, a non-profit group that came together in 2007 to champion funding and opportunity for female filmmakers.

Anne Claire Poirier was the organization’s first guest speaker. In working with Ms. Poirier on the film about her career, Ms. Giguère found her subject to be “agreeable, full of humour and frequently laughing” as she described a career path that Ms. Giguère described as “audacious.”

Ms. Poirier made perhaps her boldest, most disturbing and enduring film in 1979 with Mourir à tue-tête ( A Scream from Silence ) filmed by Mr. Brault. This work of docu-fiction, as Ms. Poirier called it, is often considered her masterpiece. It examines in excruciating detail the rape of a nurse in downtown Montreal. Mr. St-Pierre says its depiction of the rape in the back of a van from the point of view of the victim is, “one of the most powerful scenes in the history of the NFB.”

Julie Vincent auditioned for the role of the rape victim when she was studying at the National Theatre School, in Montreal. She recalled that she was nervous when first meeting the director. “I was even trembling a bit,” she said. “[Ms. Poirier] told me that nervousness could help in the role. She said, ‘What matters is your attitude and the light in your gaze; emotion must stay inside of you, in your belly. And your thought, which comes from what you feel – injustice – that thought is in your eyes.’ ”

Mourir à tue-tête was shown at the Cannes Film Festival and was lauded at the Chicago Film Festival. As she told Ms. Giguère, Ms. Poirier found some aspects of making the film to be soul-wrenching. Being on set was not a problem, because the camera and actors helped create a sense of distance from the violent act; the excruciating part for her came before that, when she interviewed rape victims about their experiences.

“It was the research that was dreadful,” Ms. Poirier said. “It was the only time on all the films I made – and on that occasion it was very acute – that I had a sense of regret for opening that door. I was saying this to myself, ‘I never knew of a woman who volunteered to be raped,’ but I had a sense of doing that myself.”

Ms. Vincent, now an established actor, producer, writer and artistic director of the theatre company Singulier Pluriel says that in the 47 years since the film’s release, hardly a week has gone by without someone mentioning the film to her. Ms. Vincent thinks that Ms. Poirier’s legal training was vital to her approach. “That was very important,” Ms. Vincent said. “She paid great attention to facts [in her research] and believed in justice and democracy.”

That capacity for research was put to a horrendous test with Tu as crié LET ME GO (1996). Ms. Poirier’s final feature documentary recounts the circumstances and context of the 1992 murder of her daughter, Yanne Cornu Poirier, who had struggled with heroin addiction. The film is a hauntingly personal testament and a rigorous examination of heroin addiction and its effects on users and their family members.

Ms. Poirier’s husband, André Cornu, died in grief within two years of Yanne’s murder. The couple also had a son, Frédéric Cornu, now a realtor, who says his mother’s faith was tested by his sister’s death. Although Ms. Poirier had been raised a Catholic and had long taken an interest in world religions, she became an atheist.

“She couldn’t understand how a loving God could let such a thing happen,” Mr. Cornu said. Tu as crié LET ME GO was her means of trying to come to peace and to help others.

Like Ms. Vincent, Mr. Cornu stressed that Ms. Poirier was full of zest for life even after the losses she suffered. She gave workshops to aspiring actors and filmmakers, read voraciously, saw her friends and grandchildren and enjoyed lunch with her son every Tuesday for more than 30 years.

As Frédéric and Yanne grew up in Outremont, their parents often had parties. The children would ask their parents to leave their doors open so they could sit on the stairs to see the dancing. “Maman used to say that a party wasn’t over until there was dew on the grass outside. Sometimes she would go check at about 4:30 in the morning!”

She was also willing to discuss the challenging subject matter of her films. Frédéric was a teenager when he attended the premiere of Mourir à tue-tête in Montreal.

“It was gobsmacking. We had some long discussions about it. She brought important things to light. She was our heroine.”

Music and literature were Anne Claire Poirier’s constant companions. She loved jazz, particularly by Miles Davis, and shared an admiration of chansonniers with her French-born husband. Of Montreal artists, she was devoted to the work of Diane Dufresne and Leonard Cohen. Albert Camus was her favourite writer; Ms. Vincent says his book L’homme révolté ( The Rebel ) was especially important to her as it helped her navigate her way back to life after Yanne’s death.

Ms. Poirier and Ms. Vincent remained close after Mourir à tue-tête . Ms. Vincent strives to emulate Ms. Poirier’s rigour and collegial, supportive nature. “She would tell me, ‘You’re great!’ She gave confidence to others. Damn, but that’s rare in our business!”

In 1988, Anne Claire Poirier won the Prix Albert-Tessier; in 1997 Tu as crié LET ME GO won a Genie Award for Best Feature-Length Documentary. In 2001, she won a Governor-General’s Performing Arts Award for Lifetime Achievement and in 2003, she was named an officer of the Order of Canada.

She leaves her son, Frédéric Cornu; grandchildren, Gabriel and Frédérique; two great-grandchildren; five stepchildren; and extended family.

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

To submit a memory about someone we have recently profiled on the Obituaries page, e-mail us at obit@globeandmail.com .

Like Ms. Vincent, Mr. Cornu stressed that Ms. Poirier was full of zest for life even after the losses she suffered. She gave workshops to aspiring actors and filmmakers, read voraciously, saw her friends and grandchildren and enjoyed lunch with her son every Tuesday for more than 30 years.

As Frédéric and Yanne grew up in Outremont, their parents often had parties. The children would ask their parents to leave their doors open so they could sit on the stairs to see the dancing. “Maman used to say that a party wasn’t over until there was dew on the grass outside. Sometimes she would go check at about 4:30 in the morning!”
She was also willing to discuss the challenging subject matter of her films. Frédéric was a teenager when he attended the premiere of Mourir à tue-tête in Montreal.
“It was gobsmacking. We had some long discussions about it. She brought important things to light. She was our heroine.”

Music and literature were Anne Claire Poirier’s constant companions. She loved jazz, particularly by Miles Davis, and shared an admiration of chansonniers with her French-born husband. Of Montreal artists, she was devoted to the work of Diane Dufresne and Leonard Cohen. Albert Camus was her favourite writer; Ms. Vincent says his book L’homme révolté ( The Rebel ) was especially important to her as it helped her navigate her way back to life after Yanne’s death.

Ms. Poirier and Ms. Vincent remained close after Mourir à tue-tête . Ms. Vincent strives to emulate Ms. Poirier’s rigour and collegial, supportive nature. “She would tell me, ‘You’re great!’ She gave confidence to others. Damn, but that’s rare in our business!”

In 1988, Anne Claire Poirier won the Prix Albert-Tessier; in 1997 Tu as crié LET ME GO won a Genie Award for Best Feature-Length Documentary. In 2001, she won a Governor-General’s Performing Arts Award for Lifetime Achievement and in 2003, she was named an officer of the Order of Canada.
She leaves her son, Frédéric Cornu; grandchildren, Gabriel and Frédérique; two great-grandchildren; five stepchildren; and extended family.

content_blocks.text: Anne Claire Poirier, who died in Montreal on Sept. 27 at age 94, was a singular force in Quebec cinema. She set a standard for documentary, fiction and experimental hybrid films working for the National Film Board of Canada (known in French as the Office national du film du Canada, or ONF). The films she made were distinctive and highly influential. Her drama Mourir à tue-tête was selected for the 1979 Cannes Film Festival. As a producer at the NFB, she also oversaw a strand of feminist films that nurtured the careers of emerging female filmmakers.

content_blocks.text: Marc St-Pierre, collection curator at the NFB, calls Ms. Poirier “one of the pioneers of Quebec cinema.” He said she was a peer of film visionaries Michel Brault, Claude Jutra, Pierre Perrault, Gilles Groulx and Jacques Godbout. “What’s more exceptional, he added, “is that she was a woman – in fact, the only [francophone] woman directing and producing films at the NFB when she first emerged.”

content_blocks.text: Anne Claire Poirier was born into a Catholic middle-class family on June 6, 1932, in Saint-Hyacinthe in southwestern Quebec, just east of Montreal. Her father, Émile Poirier, ran an upscale clothing store for women. Her mother, Berthe Poirier (née Latraverse), also worked in the store.

content_blocks.text: Ms. Poirier moved to Montreal where she studied dramatic arts and then law. She began her chosen career at Radio-Canada, but moved to the NFB in 1960, where she first worked in dubbing and received her film education by watching NFB productions in English and French. When she became an editor, she worked almost exclusively with male peers; she later joked that she became “one of the boys.” Convinced she could direct her own films, she prevailed upon her male bosses to give her a chance.

content_blocks.text: The first opportunity was 30 Minutes, Mister Plummer (1963), which put her theatrical training to good use. The documentary is a closely observed look at Christopher Plummer and Kate Reid preparing to go on stage at the Stratford Festival. The film foreshadows Ms. Poirier’s signature interests in its observation of how Ms. Reid balanced her roles as actor and mother of young children.

content_blocks.text: In 1973, Ms. Poirier and other francophone women at the NFB launched En tant que femmes, a groundbreaking series of six French-language films by women about women’s issues. (The following year, the NFB launched its Studio D, which produced films exclusively by women – mostly in English – over a period of 22 years.)

content_blocks.text: Ms. Poirier ’s Les filles du Roy (1974), the fifth of the En tant que femmes films, is a richly visualized examination of the lot of Quebec women. Industrial textile workers, nuns, waitresses, farmers, topless dancers, artisanal weavers and clerical workers are among the subjects depicted. The uniquely stylized film is underscored with motifs of the landscapes of Quebec and echoes of Indigenous and colonial influences. In the 2003 NFB documentary Entretien avec Anne Claire Poirier, by Nicole Giguère, Ms. Poirier put Les filles du Roy into the context of the overall mission of the series she was producing, saying she wanted her film, “to broaden the daily life of women into the history of women of Quebec. It’s not exactly an historical film, but the meaning of the history of women is the primary source material.”

She was one of the founders of Réalisatrices équitables, a non-profit group that came together in 2007 to champion funding and opportunity for female filmmakers.

This work of docu-fiction, as Ms. Poirier called it, is often considered her masterpiece. It examines in excruciating detail the rape of a nurse in downtown Montreal. Mr. St-Pierre says its depiction of the rape in the back of a van from the point of view of the victim is, “one of the most powerful scenes in the history of the NFB.”

She recalled that she was nervous when first meeting the director. “I was even trembling a bit,” she said. “[Ms. Poirier] told me that nervousness could help in the role. She said, ‘What matters is your attitude and the light in your gaze; emotion must stay inside of you, in your belly. And your thought, which comes from what you feel – injustice – that thought is in your eyes.’ ”

Being on set was not a problem, because the camera and actors helped create a sense of distance from the violent act; the excruciating part for her came before that, when she interviewed rape victims about their experiences.

stories.title: Carney says ‘more intense’ trade negotiations with U.S. have begun
stories.summary: The prime minister said Tuesday the two sides have made progress on the issue of restricting Canada's ability to negotiate trade deals with other countries.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says “more intense” trade negotiations with the United States have already begun, following his call with President Donald Trump last weekend.

Taking questions from reporters in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda today, Carney said some of Canada’s “red lines” have been taken off the table, including language, culture and the ability to negotiate trade deals.

Carney called off formal trade talks with the United States in August at the 11th hour as the two sides worked to finalize a deal before a new round of U.S. tariffs was imposed on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.

The prime minister said Tuesday the two sides have made progress on the issue of restricting Canada’s ability to negotiate trade deals with other countries.

Carney said there are still other important issues that need to see progress in negotiations but he didn’t say what those are.

He said the United States is asking less of Canada and offering more.

stories.title: Galloway accuser reported allegations to RCMP but retracted statement out of fear, says professor
stories.summary: Galloway filed lawsuit against A.B. and several other defendants in 2018 for online statements alleging assaults which he has denied
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A University of British Columbia professor has testified about a colleague’s decision to call police to visit Steven Galloway after he was accused of sexual assault, describing it as an “act of care” toward the author, who had spoken of killing himself.

Galloway, who is suing his accuser and others in a defamation trial centred on the unproven allegations, has described his subsequent committal to a hospital in the United States as “terrifying.”

But creative writing professor Annabel Lyon testified on Tuesday in the defamation lawsuit that calling 911 about Galloway had been unfairly “twisted as some sadistic act.”

Galloway, the award-winning author of The Cellist of Sarajevo was never charged over the allegations, and his accuser, a former student known as A.B. with whom Galloway had an affair, is not defending the alleged defamatory statements as true.

Her defence does not allege she was sexually assaulted, but only that she reported the assaults.

Lyon, who is now the director of the university’s school of creative writing, is the first witness for A.B., who cannot be named under a publication ban.

The professor told the B.C. Supreme Court that A.B. had given a statement to police but retracted it a short time later out of concern they would contact Galloway.

Lyon later described how she first learned of the allegations against Galloway from a fellow professor in November, 2015.

She then spoke on the phone with A.B. before Lyon and others met to discuss what to do on Nov. 15 and 16, 2015.

Lyon described meeting with two colleagues when Galloway began calling them all from Ohio. They did not immediately answer.

Lyon said she eventually spoke to Galloway and it sounded like he was crying. He said, “I should just kill myself,” she testified.

One of Lyon’s colleagues called 911 and the court heard police showed up at the author’s hotel room after getting a report he was suicidal.

Lyon said Ohio police had called her, saying Galloway didn’t seem suicidal, but she told them that he was “manipulative” and she later learned he’d been taken to hospital.

“Those events have been massively twisted and misunderstood, and it hurts me to my core,” Lyon said.

“It was an act of care. We made that call as an act in care. And when I heard that the police were there, and when I hear that he was in a hospital, I was relieved because I thought, ‘He is safe. At least for tonight, he’s safe.’”

Galloway testified last month that being put into hospital as a result of the call “was the most terrifying place I’ve ever been in my life.”

Under cross-examination on Tuesday from Galloway’s lawyer Daniel Burnett, Lyon said she didn’t follow up afterwards because she’d been told not to communicate with Galloway.

“The only reason I broke that rule in allowing him to phone me that night and picking up the phone was because of what my administrator had said; that if he was any danger to himself and we had not answered that we would not be able to live with ourselves,” she said.

“I felt that I had done what I could do from the distance that I was at.”

But creative writing professor Annabel Lyon testified on Tuesday in the defamation lawsuit that calling 911 about Galloway had been unfairly “twisted as some sadistic act.”

She then spoke on the phone with A.B. before Lyon and others met to discuss what to do on Nov. 15 and 16, 2015.

stories.title: More intense U.S. trade negotiations have started, Carney says
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says "more intense" trade negotiations with the United States have already begun, following his call with President Donald Trump last weekend.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
ST John’s — Prime Minister Mark Carney says “more intense” trade negotiations with the United States have started since his call with President Donald Trump last weekend.

“We’ve made progress but we haven’t finished,” Carney told reporters Tuesday in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda.

Carney said some of Canada’s “red lines” have been taken off the table, including language, culture and Canada’s ability to negotiate trade deals with other markets.

“They’re asking less and they’re offering more but we’re not quite there,” he said.

Trump told Fox News in an interview Tuesday that a deal with Canada is imminent.

“Canada is very good, we’re going to make a deal with Canada very soon. We’re going to make ⁠a great deal,” he said.

He also claimed Canada would provide fertilizer to the United States tariff-free. Canada does not charge any export tariffs on fertilizer or its components, including potash.

Carney called off formal trade talks with the United States in August at the eleventh hour as the two sides worked to finalize a deal before a new round of U.S. tariffs was imposed on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.

The prime minister said Tuesday there are still important issues that need to see progress in negotiations but didn’t say what those are. He also did not say when Canada’s chief negotiator is likely to return to Washington.

“Because we have made progress, it was felt (to be) important to acknowledge that publicly,” he said. “It’s not always necessary to have the trade negotiators go in formally into the U.S. trade representative’s offices or the Department of Commerce.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

— With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press
