stories.title: Mexico, Caribbean and Central America top vacation destinations for Canadians: poll
stories.summary: Nearly half of Canadians are planning to take a vacation over the next six months, with Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean leading the list of destinations, according to a new poll. The Canada Pulse Insights survey found 49 per cent of Canadians plan to take one or more vacations between now and April 2027, […]
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
By Joseph Ryan

Posted November 3, 2026 5:17 pm.

Nearly half of Canadians are planning to take a vacation over the next six months, with Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean leading the list of destinations, according to a new poll.

The Canada Pulse Insights survey found 49 per cent of Canadians plan to take one or more vacations between now and April 2027, including March Break. Fifty-one per cent of Canadians do not have any vacation plans by next April.

Among those planning a trip, 30 per cent said they expect to travel to Mexico, Central America or the Caribbean.

Domestic destinations also ranked ahead of the United States, with 22 per cent planning to visit another province or territory and 21 per cent expecting to travel within their own province or territory.

Europe was named by 17 per cent of vacation planners, followed by the United States at 16 per cent. Asia, including Southeast Asia, was named by 14 per cent.

The poll found 29 per cent of Ontario vacation planners expect to travel to Mexico, Central America or the Caribbean, compared with 17 per cent who plan to visit the United States.

The low perentage of travelers to the U.S. comes at a time where tensions between the two nations are high amid a tariff war and ongoing trade talks.

Vacation intentions were highest in Alberta and British Columbia, where 57 per cent and 55 per cent of residents, respectively, plan to take a vacation over the next six months.

Ontario followed at 49 per cent, while 45 per cent of Quebec residents and 32 per cent of Atlantic Canadians plan to take a trip.

The survey also found vacation plans vary significantly by household income. Only 24 per cent of Canadians in households earning less than $50,000 plan to take a vacation, compared with 73 per cent of those earning $150,000 or more.

Vacation planners also vary heavily by age. Among Canadians aged 18 to 34, 55 per cent plan to take a vacation, compared with 44 per cent of those aged 55 and older.

Canadians are still keeping domestic destinations as part of their vacation plans, according to the poll.

Among those planning a vacation, 41 per cent of Atlantic Canadians expect to visit another province or territory, while 42 per cent plan to travel within their own province or territory.

In Ontario, 20 per cent of vacation planners expect to visit another province or territory, while 18 per cent plan to travel within the province.

The United States was named by 20 per cent of vacation planners in Alberta, 19 per cent in Saskatchewan-Manitoba, 17 per cent in both British Columbia and Ontario, 13 per cent in Quebec and five per cent in Atlantic Canada.

The survey was conducted online from October 1 to 8, 2026, with 1,531 Canadian adults. The results were weighted to Statistics Canada population estimates. The poll’s margin of error for a comparable probability-based random sample of the same size is plus or minus 2.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. The findings reflect travel intentions, not confirmed bookings. Respondents could select multiple destinations, meaning the destination percentages add up to more than 100 per cent.

stories.title: One dead, one missing in suspected grizzly bear attack in B.C.
stories.summary: Remains of one person found near Bella Coola on Monday, while search continues for second person, says B.C. Conservation Officer Service
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Family members have identified a mother and teenage daughter as the victims of a suspected grizzly attack after both were found dead in the central coast region of British Columbia.

RCMP and search-and-rescue crews located the remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, in the Snooka West Trail area of Bella Coola about 430 kilometres northwest of Vancouver on Monday afternoon, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service and Ms. Balcarras’s brother, Matthew Balcarras. Her 19-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, was found deceased on Tuesday afternoon.

Evidence suggests that a bear was involved, said Inspector Jeff Tyre with the Conservation Officer Service in a video statement on Tuesday. If confirmed, the incident would mark the second grizzly bear attack on humans in the unincorporated community in just over a year.

Family members reported the pair as missing on Sunday after they failed to hear from them as planned.

Mr. Balcarras said his sister, an avid outdoors person, was located a short distance up a trail very close to her home. He suspects that the two had intended to go for a short hike when the attack occurred.

The Conservation Officer Service said it has deployed officers to locate and trap any bears involved and is working to collect and analyze any evidence. The service urged people to avoid the Snooka West Trail both for safety reasons and to allow its staff to do their work.

If a bear is determined to be responsible for the attack, it will be killed “to ensure public safety, as per provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines,” the Conservation Officer Service said.

“Our thoughts are with the family of the victims during this tragic time,” Insp. Tyre said.

BC Emergency Health Services said it was notified at 1:50 p.m. Monday about a possible animal attack incident near the 1100-block of Highway 20 in Bella Coola. An ambulance responded to the scene; no patients were transported to hospital, the agency said in a statement to The Globe and Mail.

Ms. Balcarras worked as an art therapist and spent many years living in coastal communities, including Bella Bella in B.C. and Prince of Wales Island and Juneau in Alaska.

A June 2023 posting from the Hailika’as Heiltsuk Health Centre Society in Bella Bella introducing her as their new art therapist said she had worked with a range of clients, from children to elders, and that she takes a trauma-informed approach in her work.

Her brother said she had always been sensitive to others’ emotional needs.

“My sister’s a smaller woman – she’s petite – but she’s incredibly strong and powerful,” Mr. Balcarras said. “And I think that’s sort of one of her strengths as an art therapist: gentleness with strength.”

Ms. Reed worked as an educational assistant, Mr. Balcarras said. She loved ballet and doted on her cat, Suga, whom she would carry around in a cat backpack with a bubble window.

The incident comes one year after a grizzly bear attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers in the same community.

Eleven people were injured in that attack on Nov. 20, 2025. Four of them – one adult and three children – were badly mauled and airlifted to hospital in Vancouver.

The teachers had standard-issue bear deterrents, including pepper spray and bear bangers, and had tried to fend off the bear, which was believed to be with her two cubs.

At that time, there had been no other record of a similar attack.

Samuel Schooner, elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, offered condolences to the family of Ms. Balcarras and Ms. Reed.

“While the full circumstances are still unfolding, we understand first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims’ family members, the victims of last year’s attack and the community at large,” he said in a statement issued Tuesday.

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson offered his sympathies to the victims’ family, loved ones and the entire Nuxalk Nation.

“The news from Bella Coola is heartbreaking, and at a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day,” Mr. Doerkson said in a statement posted to social media.

stories.title: UBC professor says calling police on Galloway was 'act of care' after suicide remark
stories.summary: Vancouver - A University of British Columbia professor has testified about a colleague's decision to call police to visit Steven Galloway after he was accused of sexual assault, describing it as an "act of care" toward the author, who had spoken of killing himself.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A University of British Columbia professor has testified about a colleague’s decision to call police to visit Steven Galloway after he was accused of sexual assault, describing it as an “act of care” toward the author, who had spoken of killing himself.

Galloway, who is suing his accuser and others in a defamation trial centred on the unproven allegations, has described his subsequent committal to a hospital in the United States as “terrifying.”

But creative writing professor Annabel Lyon testified on Tuesday in the defamation lawsuit that calling 911 about Galloway had been unfairly “twisted as some sadistic act.”

Galloway, the award-winning author of “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” was never charged over the allegations, and his accuser, a former student known as A.B. with whom Galloway had an affair, is not defending the alleged defamatory statements as true.

Her defence does not allege she was sexually assaulted, but only that she reported the assaults.

Lyon, who is now the director of the university’s school of creative writing, is the first witness for A.B., who cannot be named under a publication ban.

The professor told the B.C. Supreme Court that A.B. had given a statement to police but retracted it a short time later out of concern they would contact Galloway.

Lyon later described how she first learned of the allegations against Galloway from a fellow professor in November 2015.

She then spoke on the phone with A.B. before Lyon and others met to discuss what to do on Nov. 15 and 16, 2015.

Lyon described meeting with two colleagues when Galloway began calling them all from Ohio. They did not immediately answer.

Lyon said she eventually spoke to Galloway and it sounded like he was crying. He said “I should just kill myself,” she testified.

One of Lyon’s colleagues called 911 and the court heard police showed up at the author’s hotel room after getting a report he was suicidal.

Lyon said Ohio police had called her, saying Galloway didn’t seem suicidal, but she told them that he was “manipulative” and she later learned he’d been taken to hospital.

“Those events have been massively twisted and misunderstood, and it hurts me to my core,” Lyon said.

“It was an act of care. We made that call as an act in care. And when I heard that the police were there, and when I hear that he was in a hospital, I was relieved because I thought, ‘He is safe. At least for tonight, he’s safe.’”

Galloway testified last month that being put into hospital as a result of the call “was the most terrifying place I’ve ever been in my life.”

She said the suspension of Galloway would make it safe for others to come forward if they wanted to.

“The university had put me in that role,” she said. “I tried very hard to be neutral in all of this.”

stories.title: National Ballet’s Romeo and Juliet review: A thrilling, daredevil vision of first love
stories.summary: Company, which is marking 75 years, first performed John Cranko’s version in 1964
stories.author: Martha Schabas
stories.content:
Title: Romeo and Juliet

Choreographer: John Cranko

Company: National Ballet of Canada

Venue: Four Seasons Centre for the Arts

City: Toronto

Year: To Nov. 8, 2026

Shakespeare’s star-crossed lovers, destined for tragedy, had a secondary destiny: to be immortalized in ballet. That feeling of artistic kismet reverberated through a sold-out Four Seasons Centre this past weekend as the National Ballet of Canada opened its 75th season with a beautiful revival of John Cranko’s Romeo and Juliet.

It’s a symbolic production for the company, which managed to nab the North American rights to the ballet in 1964 and premiere it that year at the O’Keefe Centre, their new home. With Sergei Prokofiev’s idiosyncratic score, Cranko’s alternately playful and powerful choreography, and a timeless story audiences know and adore, the National Ballet had a major hit on its hands. The production put the young company on the cultural map.

It’s easy to see why. Romeo and Juliet makes so much sense as a ballet because it capitalizes naturally on the form’s most definitive feature: the pas de deux. While dance adaptations of Romeo and Juliet date back to the 18th century, everything changed when Prokofiev returned to the Soviet Union in 1935 and wrote his own version of the ballet. It’s one of the most stirring and inventive works of 20th-century music, grazing the colour, depth and beauty of Shakespeare’s words.

Compositionally, it’s wildly eclectic, full of tremulous woodwinds, pizzicato strings and menacing brass. Unsurprisingly, several choreographers in the 1940s and 50s used it for their productions. But Cranko’s 1962 version was special. Then artistic director at the Stuttgart Ballet, the South African-born choreographer was a rule-breaker in both life and art. He was ready to shake up the conventional understanding of the pas de deux – and what better opportunity than a ballet about irrepressible teenage passion.

Audiences at the O’Keefe Centre in 1964 must have adored the heady danger of Cranko’s romantic duets, in which Juliet throws herself from various heights and directions into Romeo’s arms.

It’s still a thrill all these decades later to see this carefree evocation of first love, in which the ballerina executes one daredevil act after another, falling backward blindly and jumping into Axel-like spins that end in fish dives. To do this well, and make it seem like a natural extension of emotion and not just a virtuosic figure-skating routine, the lead dancers must be connected at an instinctive level, fully in sync and anticipating each other’s next move.

At the Sunday matinee, principal dancers Agnes Su and Ben Rudisin seemed telepathically in tune. Su, who joined the National Ballet last season, brings with her several decades of experience with Cranko’s repertoire: She’s a graduate of the John Cranko School and spent 13 years at Stuttgart Ballet performing his foundational ballets. As Juliet, her ease with Cranko’s breathless partnering is riveting.

A dancer with naturally expressive lines and a stunning arabesque, Su has a subtle wild side that shines in this neoclassical vocabulary. There’s a beautiful looseness to her movement that can look playful one moment and full of teenage rage or yearning the next. You never get the sense she’s acting; every emotion seems deep and genuine, stirred to life as she moves.

Rudisin has an incredible stage presence no matter the role, and his Romeo delivers a lovely mix of tenderness and masculinity. Cranko creates quite the physical marathon for his male lead, and Rudisin rises to every tonal and athletic challenge. In Act 1, while getting into trouble with his bros he performs a veritable workout of squats and rolls before the difficult leaps and tours en l’air that come later.

The ensemble scenes in Cranko’s version are where its age starts to show. Visually, there is much to admire. Susan Benson’s opulent costumes of velvet and brocade look painterly against her stone rendering of Verona. And there are playful sequences performed by the mischief-making triumvirate of Romeo, Benvolio (Tom Cape) and Mercutio (Kota Sato) that consistently charm. Sato is particularly compelling as the caddish Mercutio, a perfect foil to Chase O’Connell’s towering, imperious Tybalt.

But there’s a staidness to the storytelling in these sections that keeps the plot and the dancing separate, rather than braided together as they are in the pas de deux. This approach was more common in older story ballets and brings to mind the fact that the National Ballet has another landmark Romeo and Juliet in its repertoire – arguably a better one.

In 2011, Karen Kain commissioned Alexei Ratmansky, then a rising choreographic star who had just ended his leadership of the Bolshoi Ballet, to make a Romeo and Juliet for the company, which was awash with new talent. Not only does Ratmansky’s version feel more of the moment and kinetically inventive, it also finds poetic ways to distill the storytelling, creating striking theatrical images and ideas.

When Juliet first sees Romeo at the Capulet ball, for example, he keeps popping up in front of her no matter where she turns, as though we’re getting her internalized experience of the episode. Cranko’s choices, meanwhile, are typically literal and direct. And while you can’t deny Cranko’s musicality, here again Ratmansky offers a sensibility that feels fresher and more attuned to Prokofiev’s jazzy staccato and slippery echoes.

Still, Cranko’s version has real theatrical energy; this is not just a pretty artifact unearthed for the company’s birthday. In fact, one part feels racy by today’s standards. Shakespeare never suggested anything untoward was happening between Lady Capulet (Heather Ogden) and her nephew Tybalt. But after Romeo kills Tybalt, Cranko has his haughty matriarch let down her hair, rip open her bodice and straddle her nephew’s corpse as it is carried off stage. Maybe that spoke to a free-loving sixties crowd.

It’s one of the most stirring and inventive works of 20th-century music, grazing the colour, depth and beauty of Shakespeare’s words.

content_blocks.text: Compositionally, it’s wildly eclectic, full of tremulous woodwinds, pizzicato strings and menacing brass. Unsurprisingly, several choreographers in the 1940s and 50s used it for their productions. But Cranko’s 1962 version was special. Then artistic director at the Stuttgart Ballet, the South African-born choreographer was a rule-breaker in both life and art. He was ready to shake up the conventional understanding of the pas de deux – and what better opportunity than a ballet about irrepressible teenage passion.

content_blocks.text: It’s still a thrill all these decades later to see this carefree evocation of first love, in which the ballerina executes one daredevil act after another, falling backward blindly and jumping into Axel-like spins that end in fish dives. To do this well, and make it seem like a natural extension of emotion and not just a virtuosic figure-skating routine, the lead dancers must be connected at an instinctive level, fully in sync and anticipating each other’s next move.

Su, who joined the National Ballet last season, brings with her several decades of experience with Cranko’s repertoire: She’s a graduate of the John Cranko School and spent 13 years at Stuttgart Ballet performing his foundational ballets. As Juliet, her ease with Cranko’s breathless partnering is riveting.

content_blocks.text: A dancer with naturally expressive lines and a stunning arabesque, Su has a subtle wild side that shines in this neoclassical vocabulary. There’s a beautiful looseness to her movement that can look playful one moment and full of teenage rage or yearning the next. You never get the sense she’s acting; every emotion seems deep and genuine, stirred to life as she moves.

content_blocks.text: Rudisin has an incredible stage presence no matter the role, and his Romeo delivers a lovely mix of tenderness and masculinity. Cranko creates quite the physical marathon for his male lead, and Rudisin rises to every tonal and athletic challenge. In Act 1, while getting into trouble with his bros he performs a veritable workout of squats and rolls before the difficult leaps and tours en l’air that come later.

content_blocks.text: The ensemble scenes in Cranko’s version are where its age starts to show. Visually, there is much to admire. Susan Benson’s opulent costumes of velvet and brocade look painterly against her stone rendering of Verona. And there are playful sequences performed by the mischief-making triumvirate of Romeo, Benvolio (Tom Cape) and Mercutio (Kota Sato) that consistently charm. Sato is particularly compelling as the caddish Mercutio, a perfect foil to Chase O’Connell’s towering, imperious Tybalt.

This approach was more common in older story ballets and brings to mind the fact that the National Ballet has another landmark Romeo and Juliet in its repertoire – arguably a better one.

content_blocks.text: In 2011, Karen Kain commissioned Alexei Ratmansky, then a rising choreographic star who had just ended his leadership of the Bolshoi Ballet, to make a Romeo and Juliet for the company, which was awash with new talent. Not only does Ratmansky’s version feel more of the moment and kinetically inventive, it also finds poetic ways to distill the storytelling, creating striking theatrical images and ideas.

content_blocks.text: When Juliet first sees Romeo at the Capulet ball, for example, he keeps popping up in front of her no matter where she turns, as though we’re getting her internalized experience of the episode. Cranko’s choices, meanwhile, are typically literal and direct. And while you can’t deny Cranko’s musicality, here again Ratmansky offers a sensibility that feels fresher and more attuned to Prokofiev’s jazzy staccato and slippery echoes.

content_blocks.text: Still, Cranko’s version has real theatrical energy; this is not just a pretty artifact unearthed for the company’s birthday. In fact, one part feels racy by today’s standards. Shakespeare never suggested anything untoward was happening between Lady Capulet (Heather Ogden) and her nephew Tybalt. But after Romeo kills Tybalt, Cranko has his haughty matriarch let down her hair, rip open her bodice and straddle her nephew’s corpse as it is carried off stage. Maybe that spoke to a free-loving sixties crowd.

stories.title: Alberta bill to limit institutional speech, comments from post-secondary schools
stories.summary: The policies would bar Alberta post-secondary institutions from making official statements on global political, social and ideological issues outside of their 'academic mission.'
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
Alberta is proposing a new law that would restrict post-secondary schools from being able to weigh in on social and political issues.

Myles McDougall, Alberta’s Advanced Education Minister, tabled the Advanced Education Statues Amendment Act Tuesday afternoon.

If passed, it will require post-secondary schools to develop and implement institutional neutrality and freedom of expression policies, which McDougall could review.

The policies would bar post-secondary institutions, like universities and colleges, from making official statements on global political, social and ideological issues outside of their “academic mission.”

Beyond that, the bill has wide-reaching policy changes that would also authorize McDougall to set maximum tuition amounts for programs or groups of programs and enable the government to set minimum requirements for student codes of conduct.

As far as making official university statements, McDougall said there are some instances, like the loss of life, where the university could make an expression of sorrow or support but would not be able to explore any related politics.

“Underlying some tragedies there can be some political issues, and what we’re saying is that’s not the role for the institution to get into that area,” McDougall told a news conference before tabling the bill.

The Israeli-Palestine conflict is “obviously political,” he said, and institutions could not show support for either side, though those rules wouldn’t apply to university officials, staff or students. Private institutions and First Nations would also not be bound by the new rules.

In a statement, Premier Danielle Smith said “our universities and colleges should teach students how to think, not what to think. Alberta will protect that freedom and keep a great education within reach for everyone.”

British Columbia has seen a court challenge on that front.

Last year, several professors and a graduate student from the University of British Columbia filed a petition against the school over what they deemed “political activity.”

They said the activity violates legislation that the school remain non-political, citing issues with the university’s diversity, equity and inclusion policy, its public stance on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and its Indigenous land acknowledgement, which declared the university was on “unceded Indigenous” land.

McDougall said there will have to be consequences if schools don’t follow the rules, but said those details are not prepared yet and he doesn’t expect it will be an issue.

David Eggen, the Opposition Ndp’s advanced education critic, told reporters that much of the government’s bill was a waste of time.

He said the government’s focus on “culture war garbage” was merely a distraction from real issues affecting post-secondary schools and students, like stable funding and affordability.

“The government has not had a coherent policy for advanced education for seven years,” Eggen said.

“We can do better. We must do better.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We can do better. We must do better."

All the tuition changes in the bill apply to domestic students.

The bill would enable McDougall to replace annual tuition growth caps with maximum amounts.

The province did not say which groups or programs would be affected and did not respond to an emailed question about whether it aims to cut tuition costs or increase them.

McDougall said a combination of factors will determine the change in tuition, including the cost to offer the program.

Students already in their programs, though, will have tuition capped at two per cent next year.

Last year, an expert-panel estimated that two-thirds of Alberta’s tuition fee revenue come from domestic students while most other provinces rely more heavily on international students. Saskatchewan was the only province that relied slightly more heavily on domestic students for tuition dollars.

Statistics Canada data shows Alberta’s domestic tuition fees across all programs rose by 35 per cent from 2020 to 2027, the most of any province in Canada.

However, Alberta’s average domestic tuition cost of $8,260 is not the highest in Canada. In New Brunswick, it’s $10,373.

— With files from Jack Farrell, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian film financier Jason Cloth defrauded investors, capital markets tribunal finds
stories.summary: Joker, House of Gucci producer and his defunct company found to have misappropriated funds, including by diverting $53.8-million to real estate projects
stories.author: Alexandra Posadzki
stories.content:
Ontario’s Capital Markets Tribunal has found that Toronto film financier Jason Cloth and his now-defunct company Creative Wealth Media Finance Corp. perpetrated securities fraud by misappropriating investors’ funds, including by diverting $53.8-million to real estate projects.

The tribunal also found that Mr. Cloth, who has executive producer credits on films such as Joker and House of Gucci , used investors’ funds to repay other investors, and sometimes raised more money than the maximum specified in investment agreements.

A hearing to consider costs and sanctions against Mr. Cloth and Creative Wealth will be held no later than Nov. 30, the tribunal’s decision said.

The 60-year-old film producer was the sole director and officer of Creative Wealth, a private company that financed film and TV productions through loans to independent producers. The loans were financed by investors, and Creative Wealth charged a fee, calculated as a percentage of the amount invested, for facilitating the transactions.

The Ontario Securities Commission had argued that from 2018 onward, Creative Wealth was sustained “through Ponzi-like payments.” A Ponzi scheme is one in which the source of distributions to investors is not the underlying value of any investments, but rather money that has been obtained from new investors.

“Cloth was well aware of what he was doing,” reads Tuesday’s decision from the three adjudicators at the Capital Markets Tribunal, an independent division of the OSC that conducts hearings under the Ontario Securities Act.

“He also admitted that ‘I fully understand that some of the things that went on were not right, but at the time of evaluating what my options were, in my mind, it was the better option.’”

Mr. Cloth, who did not attend the hearing in person, could not be reached for comment.

Although Andrew Guaglio, a lawyer at Fenton Law Barristers, attended the hearings as Mr. Cloth’s counsel, he did not cross-examine any witnesses or make substantive submissions on any of the issues that arose. Shortly before the scheduled date for oral closing submissions, Mr. Guaglio sought to be removed as counsel of record for Mr. Cloth, citing a breakdown in the solicitor-client relationship. The tribunal granted the motion.

The decision from the Capital Markets Tribunal follows Mr. Cloth’s arrest in the United States in July on seven counts of wire fraud, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Illinois. Each count is punishable by up to 20 years in federal prison.

Mr. Cloth was released on bail, and the allegations levied against him by U.S. prosecutors have not been proven in court.

The tribunal found that the OSC successfully established that Mr. Cloth and his company “improperly diverted” $53.8-million of investors’ funds, which had been raised for other purposes, to a real estate development company called Conacher Kingston and a construction company, Olympus Home.

Mr. Cloth admitted to the commission that he used money he had raised for films to invest in real estate without informing investors, the ruling states.

The tribunal also found that between October 2018 and the end of 2021, Mr. Cloth used money raised for specific media projects to fund other media projects.

He also diverted investors’ funds to repay other investors on more than one occasion, the tribunal found. For instance, out of approximately US$7.9-million that Creative Wealth had raised from investors in a Series E financing round, at least $4.19-million went to repaying earlier investors in other projects.

Creative Wealth eventually collapsed, entering bankruptcy proceedings in October 2023.

OSC spokesperson Curtis Lindsay said in a statement on Tuesday that the commission was “pleased with the Tribunal’s decision in this case in finding Jason Cloth perpetrated fraud. Mr. Cloth’s actions took advantage of investors, and even personal relationships at times of vulnerability. We await the Tribunal’s decision on sanctions in due course.”

stories.title: Oxford County ready for another mega-dump battle
stories.summary: Local leaders and citizen activists in Oxford County say they’re ready to go to battle over proposed mega-dumps all over again. This, as the province considers changes that would allow large landfills without a willing host.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Local leaders and citizen activists in Oxford County say they’re ready to go to battle over proposed mega-dumps all over again. This, as the province considers changes that would allow large landfills without a willing host.

“The community rejected the idea that people would bring a dump and bring stuff into our water table and poison our water. That was pretty clear, and that thinking hasn’t changed,” said Bryan Smith, an activist with the now disbanded Oxford People Against Landfills (Opal).

Six years ago citizens groups and civic leaders won a drawn-out battle preventing a proposed mega-landfill on Ingersoll’s doorstep. Walker Environmental would eventually walk away from plans to convert a limestone quarry into a dump designed to hold 17 million tonnes of waste.

But a new battle over refusal is about to start. The province is considering rolling back Bill 197. A legislation that gives municipalities the right to approve or deny landfills in their own communities, or within 3.5 kilometres.

“Industry hasn’t really responded by reducing the quantities of garbage. They’re hauling it, and right now they’ve got a problem with where they haul it. Hauling it to Michigan is problematic now,” Smith said.

Proposed changes to the Environmental Assessment Act were made public Oct. 27, the day after province-wide municipal elections.

Mayors of Oxford County, including those newly-elected have issued a statement calling on the province to maintain the rights of municipalities to approve future landfills.

“I wish there was more time to comment, but frankly, we’re ready,” exclaimed Oxford County Warden and Zorra Township Mayor Marcus Ryan. “We’ve been ready on this from the time we got this legislative change years ago. This was always going to come back at some point. Because again, the industry was not going to let it lie,” he said.

Landfills across Ontario are getting closer to reaching their capacity. The government points out that there hasn’t been a new large landfill approved in Ontario in 20 years. The province also says no other jurisdiction has a mandatory municipal support requirement for landfills.

Other proposed changes include pushing out some organic waste diversion targets, along with changes to recycling for the Industrial, Commercial, and Institutional sector.

“Some of the changes are potentially going to make less items recyclable,” said Ryan.

“When it comes to incinerating waste, philosophically, not probably a bad thing to try and recover some energy from that waste,” he added.

The comment period on the proposed changes is 30 days, closing Nov. 26.

“This is not really a fair process. This is loaded so that they can push it through fast,” Smith said.

stories.title: B.C. ostrich farms files lawsuit against food inspection agency and RCMP over cull
stories.summary: More than 300 ostriches were culled by the Cfia in November 2025 after avian flu was discovered on the Universal Ostrich Farm
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
The owners of a B.C. ostrich farm that was the site of a controversial cull a year ago is suing the federal government and RCMP.

In a civil lawsuit filed Friday, Universal Ostrich Farm and its parent company make several claims against the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) and the RCMP.

More than 300 ostriches were culled at the farm in November 2025 after avian flu was discovered there almost a year before. But when the farmers refused to carry out a cull, the Cfia moved in with support from the RCMP to slaughter the birds.

The lawsuit claims that the Cfia offered Universal Ostrich $942,000 in lieu of the loss of 314 birds, but states that didn’t reflect the fair market value of the flock. A claim is made that there were 351 birds on the property with the Cfia entered it.

“The full extent of missing birds has not been disclosed to Universal, and Cfia has provided no satisfactory explanation for the discrepancy,” states the lawsuit.

It also alleges the Cfia seized 1,200 ostrich eggs from the farm in an “entirely separate unlawful act” and that the eggs were never returned.

Farm owners claim the eggs were the “core biological input” for a new dietary supplement they were developing, and that the product had been about to launch commercially to generate an estimated $200 million in revenues.

“The Cfia’s unlawful seizure of Universal’s eggs entirely and irreversibly destroyed this commercial enterprise and eliminated all associated revenues, investments, and business opportunities,” states the lawsuit.

The farm’s lawsuit is seeking several types of damages and an order that the Cfia account for all items and birds removed from the property.

In a statement posted on X , farm spokesperson Katie Pasitney and her mother, farm co-owner Karen Espersen, said they filed the lawsuit to seek “justice, accountability, and meaningful policy change.”

“Virus control and animal cruelty should never go hand in hand. Science must come before destruction, and government power must never be above accountability,” the statement said.

“The outcome at our farm does not erase responsibility. When enforcement shortcuts due process, everyone becomes vulnerable.”

The prospect of an ostrich cull was fought through several court levels over the past two years, with the farm challenging the Cfia’s cull order. The Federal Court of Appeal ruled that the Cfia had the right to cull the birds.

The matter was appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada, which declined to hear the case.

Canada’s Agricultural Review Tribunal both upheld and threw out separate $10,000 fines the farm received from the Cfia over their response to the cull.

The entire cull operation ended up costing taxpayers $6.8 million according to parliamentary documents.

American billionaire John Catsimatidus was a strong supporter of the farm, in its determination to have the ostriches tested before they were killed.

“I was disappointed that the Cfia (Canadian Food Inspection Agency) did not have enough respect to allow Secretary Kennedy, Dr. Oz, or the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), one of the world’s leading health agencies, to test the ostriches as they had requested,” he wrote in a statement posted on X .

None of the allegations made in the lawsuit have been proven in court.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Great blue heron hit by plane at YVR makes full recovery, released
stories.summary: A wildlife rescue group says a great blue heron has made a full recovery after being hit by a plane at Vancouver's airport.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A wildlife rescue group says a great blue heron has made a full recovery after being hit by a plane that was lifting off at Vancouver’s airport.

The Wildlife Rescue Association of BC’s advancement director Marina Schwarz said the heron suffered a suspected concussion, an eye injury, bruises and scratches when it collided with the Dash 8 plane operated by Air Canada Jazz.

Pilot Alex Toporowski said it’s been a “roller-coaster of emotions” but he’s relieved the bird recovered after the collision on Sept. 29.

He said he was about to take off for Toronto when the first officer alerted him to the large water bird flying toward them.

Toporowski said he hit the brakes and watched the bird “bounce up off the wing.”

“It (the plane) was at a very low speed, so it wasn’t too dramatic in that sense, but as for the bird, I felt really badly,” said Toporowski.

Toporowski said he asked air traffic control to check whether they found the bird’s “carcass,” and was told that they located it.

“I was very sad, but then when we were waiting to get going again, Vancouver Airport Wildlife, they said that they had the bird, still alive, in one of their trucks,” said Toporowski, adding that hearing the bird still has its legs and wings brought him tremendous relief.

A maintenance crew found no damage to the plane and it took off an hour later, he said.

The bird was taken to the Wildlife Rescue Association, before being released at Gilbert Beach in Richmond, B.C., ON Oct. 5.

Jackie McQuillan, program director for the association, said when the heron first arrived at the facility it was “banged up” with a bruised left leg and an ulcer on its eye.

The heron had received medication and monitoring over seven days.

McQuillan, who has been working with the rescue association for decades, said the centre takes care of many birds with concussions that fly into windows or that are hit by vehicles, but it’s only the second time she’s seen a bird brought in that was hit by a plane.

“This is really a very unique case. Incredible that this bird survived,” said McQuillan.

Great blue herons, standing up to 1.3 metres tall, are listed as a vulnerable species by the B.C. government, which said they number between 5,000 to 6,000 in the province.

Toporowski, who has been flying commercially for about 10 years, said bird strikes are “fairly common,” and they usually don’t cause issues.

“But every time it does happen, we have to get an inspection from maintenance, and they make sure that there’s nothing damaged on the aircraft.”

Toporowski said he asked to visit the bird in-person but was rejected due to the sensitive nature of its rehabilitation.

He said the rescue association shared a video of the bird’s release with him, and it was “a beautiful full-circle moment to see the bird flying off into the distance.”

“All I can do is hope that he stays away from airports in the future,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

stories.title: De Havilland getting up to $2.5B in federal financing to ramp up water bomber production
stories.summary: The up to $2.5 billion in federal financing for Canadair water bomber maker De Havilland will allow for a second assembly line in Alberta to make the iconic firefighting aircraft.
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds
stories.content:
The federal government has pledged up to $2.5 billion in financing for Canadair water bomber maker De Havilland Canada in a bid to ramp up production of the iconic firefighting aircraft.

The money will allow for a second assembly line in Alberta, the federal Department of Finance said. And it will provide the means to double production capacity to an eventual 20 water-scooping planes per year, according to De Havilland.

The manufacturer, whose “super scoopers” can suck up more than 6,000 litres of water in 12 seconds and dump it on wildfires , also says it will put the cash toward new staff and production in Victoria, Calgary and Ontario.

The funding is expected to take the form of loans and loan guarantees, delivered by Export Development Canada, said Finance Department spokesperson Benoit Mayrand.

The interest rates and repayment terms are confidential.

Demand for amphibious firefighting aircraft is on the rise as the scale and intensity of wildfires increases and the need for tools to fend off climate disasters grows more urgent.

The yellow Canadair turboprops serve as the only aircraft of their kind currently in production built from the outset for that purpose, rather than being retrofitted to douse flames.

However, competition is hot on their tail fin.

Aerospace companies such as Positive Aviation, Kepplair Evolution and Hynaero of France are all developing water bombers.

Italy’s 19-01 Holding aims to roll out its first prototype, which can scoop roughly twice the water volume of the DHC-515, by 2028.

De Havilland revived production of the Canadian-made planes in 2022 after several European countries placed orders for the program.

The assembly line had halted in 2015, when it was run by Bombardier Inc.

Revving up has been a challenge, and the company has yet to churn out a single aircraft.

The years-long hiatus meant a supply chain that drew on 60,000 parts had evaporated. Procurement hurdles have helped push the projected delivery date for the first Canadair DHC-515 (formerly called the CL-515) to early 2028.

Until last week it was sold out through 2034, though the fresh financing will now let more planes be assembled simultaneously starting in 2030, the company said in a release.

Even as it struggles to meet demand from other countries, De Havilland has been calling for a national fleet of water bombers at home.

Neil Sweeney, the company’s vice-president of corporate affairs, said in a recent interview that an order for 50 new water bombers from the federal government or the provinces would give it the financial runway — billions of dollars — to launch a second production line at the assembly plant currently under construction 30 minutes east of Calgary in Wheatland County.

Something comparable to that goal seemed on the cusp of fruition in September, when a draft joint statement from the Canada-European Union summit and seen by The Canadian Press pledged an order for 50 De Havilland water bombers.

However, the final joint statement last week stuck with the 24 planes already ordered by European countries, with no fresh batch of orders emerging.

Questions around financial liability and production capacity persist.

“My question is, who carries the risk if there’s an issue with De Havilland being able to build these airplanes at scale,” said John Gradek, who teaches aviation management at McGill University.

“De Havilland’s never built one of these airplanes.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "De Havilland's never built one of these airplanes."

Industry insiders have also highlighted the pace of production for the water bombers, which will be riveted by hand and roll off the line at a projected rate of 10 per year — 20 eventually — partly due to a lack of automation.

“De Havilland is building this airplane the way Canadair built it in the 1960s,” Gradek said, referring to the Montreal-based company that was nationalized in the 1970s before its purchase by Bombardier in 1986.

Decades later, automation typically plays a much greater role aircraft production, he noted.

“I want to know where this money is going, and I want to make sure that … they’re not just replicating a hand-built or a hand-assembled airplane.

“That’s not the way we build airplanes in 2026.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That's not the way we build airplanes in 2026."

De Havilland did not respond to a request for comment.

However, CEO Brian Chafe has framed the facility now under construction as a “world-class aerospace hub” and a “state-of-the-art campus.”

“De Havilland Canada will use this financing to hire new staff and invest in additional production capacity across its Canadian sites in Victoria, Calgary, Toronto, Kitchener and Fort Erie with supply chain jobs being created from Newfoundland to British Columbia,” it said in a release Friday.

The Finance Department did not lay out any potential reporting requirements.

“Specific commercial terms and conditions, including applicable interest rates and repayment terms, are subject to commercial confidentiality,” Mayrand said.

There are about 160 water bombers currently in service across the globe, mainly in Canada, the United States and Europe.

The 38 new planes now on the order book comprise 24 for six European countries as well as six for Ontario, five for Alberta — for $400 million, or $80 million apiece — and three for Manitoba, according to De Havilland.

content_blocks.text: Until last week it was sold out through 2034, though the fresh financing will now let more planes be assembled simultaneously starting in 2030, the company said in a release.
Even as it struggles to meet demand from other countries, De Havilland has been calling for a national fleet of water bombers at home.

Neil Sweeney, the company’s vice-president of corporate affairs, said in a recent interview that an order for 50 new water bombers from the federal government or the provinces would give it the financial runway — billions of dollars — to launch a second production line at the assembly plant currently under construction 30 minutes east of Calgary in Wheatland County.

content_blocks.alt: An artists rendition of the new aircraft manufacturing plant that De Havilland Canada is building in Wheatland County, about 30 minutes east of Calgary.
content_blocks.caption: An artists rendition of the new aircraft manufacturing plant that De Havilland Canada is building in Wheatland County, about 30 minutes east of Calgary. Courtesy: De Havilland

content_blocks.text: Something comparable to that goal seemed on the cusp of fruition in September, when a draft joint statement from the Canada-European Union summit and seen by The Canadian Press pledged an order for 50 De Havilland water bombers.
However, the final joint statement last week stuck with the 24 planes already ordered by European countries, with no fresh batch of orders emerging.
Questions around financial liability and production capacity persist.
“My question is, who carries the risk if there’s an issue with De Havilland being able to build these airplanes at scale,” said John Gradek, who teaches aviation management at McGill University.
“De Havilland’s never built one of these airplanes.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "De Havilland's never built one of these airplanes."

content_blocks.text: Industry insiders have also highlighted the pace of production for the water bombers, which will be riveted by hand and roll off the line at a projected rate of 10 per year — 20 eventually — partly due to a lack of automation.

“De Havilland is building this airplane the way Canadair built it in the 1960s,” Gradek said, referring to the Montreal-based company that was nationalized in the 1970s before its purchase by Bombardier in 1986.
Decades later, automation typically plays a much greater role aircraft production, he noted.
“I want to know where this money is going, and I want to make sure that … they’re not just replicating a hand-built or a hand-assembled airplane.
“That’s not the way we build airplanes in 2026.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That's not the way we build airplanes in 2026."

content_blocks.text: De Havilland did not respond to a request for comment.

content_blocks.text: However, CEO Brian Chafe has framed the facility now under construction as a “world-class aerospace hub” and a “state-of-the-art campus.”

“De Havilland Canada will use this financing to hire new staff and invest in additional production capacity across its Canadian sites in Victoria, Calgary, Toronto, Kitchener and Fort Erie with supply chain jobs being created from Newfoundland to British Columbia,” it said in a release Friday.
The Finance Department did not lay out any potential reporting requirements.
“Specific commercial terms and conditions, including applicable interest rates and repayment terms, are subject to commercial confidentiality,” Mayrand said.
There are about 160 water bombers currently in service across the globe, mainly in Canada, the United States and Europe.

The 38 new planes now on the order book comprise 24 for six European countries as well as six for Ontario, five for Alberta — for $400 million, or $80 million apiece — and three for Manitoba, according to De Havilland.

By Emily Leighton,

A life-saving treatment pioneered by Fred Possmayer has helped generations of at-risk premature babies survive their first days of life. Now, he’s being recognized among Canada’s medical leaders.

When the biochemist began his research at Western University in the 1970s, more than half of premature babies who developed respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) died from the condition.

Today, the surfactant treatment Possmayer helped develop has been used to treat more than 160,000 premature babies in Canada and around the world.

For his contributions to neonatal medicine, the professor emeritus at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry is among the Canadian Medical Hall of Fame’s 2027 inductees.

It is an unexpected honour for Possmayer.

“I didn’t do anything spectacular,” he reflected. “It was serendipity – a well-prepared mind and being in the right place, at the right time, with the right people.”

At the heart of RDS is a lack of sufficient pulmonary surfactant, a substance that helps keep the tiny air sacs in the lungs open. Without enough surfactant, the lungs become stiff and can collapse with each breath, making it extremely difficult for newborns to breathe.

American paediatrician Dr. Mary Ellen Avery first identified the cause of RDS in 1957. Possmayer, whose research had focused on phospholipid metabolism in the liver and brain, joined a select group of scientists around the world in the search for a treatment.

Collaborations with Dr. Goran Enhorning at the University of Toronto led him to develop a methods for isolating and preparing surfactant extracts from bovine lungs which could be used in premature infants.

The resulting treatment, known as bovine lipid extract surfactant (BLES), was tested in clinical trials, with Canadian findings published in 1983. It was subsequently made available in Canadian hospitals before receiving formal drug approval in the late 1990s.

BLES is now used across Canada and in more than 20 other countries, and surfactant replacement therapy has become a cornerstone of modern neonatal intensive care.

Throughout his career, Possmayer has emphasized the collective nature of scientific progress, crediting the researchers and clinicians whose work helped make surfactant therapy possible.

He also remains a champion of scientific curiosity, persistence and the willingness to challenge assumptions.

“You need to have a strong desire to understand, to obtain data to show your ideas are correct. Or better yet, that they are wrong, because that can generate new directions and real progress,” he said in an interview for The Impact Project.

His contributions have earned numerous honours, including the Order of Ontario in 2024. BLES has also been recognized by the Council of Ontario Universities as one of the province’s top five medical breakthroughs.

“I have to be pleased and even proud that our work has benefitted many babies and their families,” he said.

stories.title: Alberta tables bill to end tuition hike cap, bar schools from expressing ideological positions
stories.summary: There will likely be consequences for schools that break the rules, minister says
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
Universities and colleges in Alberta won’t be allowed to take official positions on sensitive ideological and political matters under proposed legislation that would also pave the way for lifting the province’s 2-per-cent cap on average annual domestic tuition increases.

Myles McDougall, Alberta’s minister of advanced education, tabled a bill Tuesday that would require postsecondary schools to establish “institutional neutrality and freedom of expression” policies. Neutrality policies would apply to schools themselves, not to individuals expressing their views in class and on campus. The bill would also set minimum standards for student codes of conduct.

“When an institution speaks officially, we expect it to stay neutral on political, social and ideological issues,” Mr. McDougall told a news conference before introducing the bill. “That leaves the debate where it belongs: with students, faculty and staff.”

Mr. McDougall proposed the new legislation, Bill 38, a little more than a year after releasing an expert panel’s report on Alberta’s college and university sector. That report, led by University of Calgary economist Jack Mintz, focused mainly on creating a predictable funding formula for postsecondary institutions, but also included a recommendation in favour of institutional neutrality and against most diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives.

On Tuesday, the opposition New Democratic Party accused Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party government of focusing on institutional neutrality to distract from a lack of action on postsecondary funding.

“This government is trying to bring forward this culture war garbage that they imported from the United States, and to divert attention from the fact that they are underfunding advanced education – our colleges, our universities and our polytechnics – and students are suffering as a result,” said David Eggen, the NDP critic for advanced education.

Mr. McDougall said Tuesday that a new funding framework for the sector would be rolled out in next year’s Alberta budget.

In the meantime, domestic tuition increases would continue to be capped at two per cent for the 2027-28 school year while the government develops new maximum tuition rates for specific programs and groups of programs. Postsecondary institutions would set their own tuition rates beneath those ceilings.

Alberta’s current tuition regulations bar institutions from raising average domestic tuition rates by more than 2 per cent a year and the tuition for any one program by more than 10 per cent a year.

Also on Tuesday, Mr. McDougall unveiled a change to Alberta’s student financial aid rules, separate from Bill 38. Applications for government-financed student loans will stop taking parental income into account, he said.

“Students and families told us that counting parental income in student aid assessments did not always reflect the support parents could actually provide. We listened,” he told the news conference. “For the 2026-27 academic year, we are removing parental income from provincial student aid assessments.”

The minister made no mention of increasing non-repayable grants and scholarships to Alberta postsecondary students, a measure the Mintz report recommended.

When it comes to institutional neutrality, Mr. McDougall said there will likely be consequences for institutions that break the rules.

“What specific penalties have been established? That will be done by regulation, and we will continue to work with the postsecondary stakeholders in determining what would be reasonable,” he said.

Lee Easton, president of the Confederation of Alberta Faculty Associations, said it would be “hugely concerning” if the province were to enact punishments such as withholding funding to postsecondary institutions that violate the neutrality principle.

“We’re really worried about who gets to decide, at the end of the day, what constitutes openness, what constitutes neutrality,” he said.

The minister, in his news conference, elaborated on what would and wouldn’t violate the proposed new law.

As an example, he said the president of a university would be free to share his or her personal opinions, but not to have the institution adopt them as official policy. He also said colleges and universities wouldn’t be penalized for speaking in an official capacity about government decisions that affect their operations.

He added that schools could make official statements of sympathy for victims of tragedies.

Asked by a reporter if it would be okay for an institution to say, “prayers for Ukraine or Gaza,” Mr. McDougall replied: “For me, it’s okay. Anywhere people are, in this case, dying, one deserves perspectives of support and prayers. You know, the underlying political reasons for why these types of things happen – that’s not for the institution to weigh in.”

Mr. Mintz, in an interview with The Globe and Mail on Tuesday, said he was pleased that the Alberta government seems to be taking the panel’s recommendations for a new postsecondary funding formula seriously.

He also said he supported the government’s plan to enforce institutional neutrality through a law, despite his expert panel reporting that all publicly funded postsecondary institutions in Alberta had already adopted the neutrality principle as originally espoused by the University of Chicago in 1967.

“The argument, I think, for legislation, is to make sure that this is going to be binding,” Mr. Mintz said.

stories.title: Barn fire kills 50+ chickens and crushes local small farm business
stories.summary: On Monday, a barn housing close to 90 chickens and nine pigs caught fire on Sparta Line, directly across from the elementary school.
stories.content:
A barn fire in Sparta, Ont., has killed dozens of chickens and destroyed a small farm business.

On Monday, a barn housing close to 90 chickens and nine pigs caught fire on Sparta Line, directly across from the elementary school.

By Tuesday morning, Vera Davey, owner of Quaker Springs Farm, estimated more than 50 egg-laying chickens had been lost in the fire.

A neighbour managed to let the nine pigs out of the barn as the fire started, and Davey said she had recovered two of them. The other seven remain unaccounted for in the fields surrounding her home.

Davey said freezers full of butchered meat, chickens and pork products were destroyed in the blaze.

Her entire inventory for the Horton Street Christmas Market in St. Thomas was also lost.

Yarmouth Centre Fire Department responded to the fire with assistance from the Elgin County OPP, which closed Sparta Line as crews battled the blaze.

Due to the timing of the fire and its proximity to the school, police helped facilitate the pickup of students at the end of the school day.

London fire crews battle barn fire

Hours after the blaze in Elgin County, London fire crews were battling a barn fire in south London.

Crews were called to a shop/shed at the intersection of Scotland Drive and Wellington Road shortly before midnight.

London fire officials said the extent of the fire damage caused the structure to begin failing, with a roof collapse and a partial wall collapse reported.

Fire operations shifted to a defensive strategy, with a water shuttle used to support suppression efforts.

All occupants were accounted for and no injuries were reported.

stories.title: ‘It’s staggering’: One in three Canadians report skipping meals due to high cost of groceries
stories.summary: Results from a new survey are shedding light on the growing issue of food affordability in Canada.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg — Results from a new survey are shedding light on the growing issue of food affordability in Canada.

The Salvation Army’s 2026 Poverty and Socioeconomic Analysis found 31 per cent of the 1,500 Canadians surveyed skipped meals or reduced portion sizes because they couldn’t afford groceries. This is up from 27 per cent last year.

The number turning to community supports, including food banks, also rose from 11 per cent to 15 per cent this year.

“It’s staggering when we think about those that are coming to the doors of The Salvation Army each and every day, arriving at our food banks or our community service locations, many of whom who have past donated to The Salvation Army and find themselves in need,” said Glenn van Gulik, who is the national spokesperson for The Salvation Army.

“Skipping a meal in order to make sure their children might be able to have a dinner or a lunch to go to school with is just staggering.”

The findings also reveal younger Canadians are particularly impacted.

Forty-one per cent of Canadians aged 18-34 reported skipping or reducing meals; 23 per cent of younger Canadians in the same category accessed community food supports; and 76 per cent in that age range report challenges managing limited financial resources, compared with 55 per cent of those aged 55 and older.

“They’re on fixed income, and needing to avail themselves of family supports or friends supports just to get by and so seeing them at the doors of a Salvation Army location, asking for help, it is really surprising and difficult to see on a daily basis, those numbers rising,” van Gulik said.

Van Gulik says the survey also suggests that Canadians are more concerned about U.S. tariffs and their effect on the economy than last year, with nearly 90 per cent saying they were worried the trade war would spike prices for everyday goods.

‘Really impacting Canadians’

Three in five surveyed reported their household was already feeling the impacts from U.S. tariffs.

“These are the concerns that we’re seeing on the front line, and that trickles down into things like food insecurity,” he said.

“All of these ripple effects are really impacting Canadians.”

At Harvest Manitoba in Winnipeg, which is the province’s largest charitable food relief organization, is also seeing more people relying on food supports.

Meaghan Erbus, who is the VP of advocacy and stakeholder relations with Harvest Manitoba, says the organization serves around 60,000 people per month, with half of them being children.

“That’s 50 per cent more than what we’ve seen since 2021,” said Erbus.

“So we’ve really seen things hitting people harder than before.”

Erbus says there are several reasons for this, but says increased costs are making things extremely hard for many.

“Affordability, groceries have gone up. Transportation has gone up. All of those costs, coupled with wages not increasing as well, can create that perfect storm for folks needing to access a food bank,” she said.

Seventeen-year-old Daisy Adesokan, a volunteer at Harvest Manitoba who helps pack food hampers, is also concerned about affordability, even at her age.

“It’s like really expensive. One box of granola bars would be at least $5, and that’s kind of crazy, but it’s economics nowadays, and everything is going up,” she said.

“I’m concerned too because I also go to the store every day to buy food, and I know it’s going to get more expensive.”

As more Canadians struggle to afford the basics, volunteers like Adesokan are helping make sure families have one less thing to worry about.

She says volunteering is a way to turn her concern into action, helping families facing the same rising costs she worries about herself.

“I will continue to do this because it’s good, like you’re doing something meaningful for the community,” she said.

“If I contribute into this, it’s like you’re doing a good thing, like you’re sowing a good seed for others.”

Salvation Army’s Canadian Poverty and Socioeconomic Analysis national survey of 1,525 Canadians from the online Angus Reid Forum, balanced and weighted by age, gender and region. Conducted by Edelman Intelligence from Sept. 11 to 18, 2026. Margin of error of approximately ±2.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Novacap fund acquires OSI Maritime Systems, keeping Nato provider in Canada
stories.summary: B.C. company’s navigation tech has been installed or contracted on more than 1,000 vessels around the world
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
A Canadian navigation technology company has been acquired by a consortium of largely domestic investors, keeping the nearly 50-year-old operation serving Nato in Canada after similar recent acquisitions by foreign investors.

The consortium acquiring Burnaby, B.C.-based OSI Maritime Systems is led by Montreal-based private equity investment firm Novacap and includes Crown corporations Export Development Canada and the Business Development Bank of Canada. The consortium is entirely Canadian, save for one Scandinavian investor.

David Armstrong, a senior partner at Novacap, said the firm began speaking with OSI more than a year ago and was initially surprised by the scope and size of the business.

OSI was founded in 1979 and develops electronic chart software, as well as navigation systems for ships and submarines. It serves 27 Nato and allied navies, including the Royal Canadian Navy, and its technology has been installed or contracted on more than 1,000 vessels, according to OSI.

“This was a company that ticked all the boxes for us. We think we can help invest to grow the business internationally. We want to invest in new products. We think they’re really fundamental to autonomous operations,” Mr. Armstrong said in an interview.

“This is exactly the type of company that we look for in the mid-market to invest behind and grow.”

The acquisition marks Novacap’s first investment through its US$3.8-billion technology fund, which closed in February . Chief executive officer Pascal Tremblay told The Globe and Mail at the time that Canada’s growing investment in defence would be a huge opportunity for the fund.

That opportunity has since caught the attention of foreign investors as well, especially in the underwater technology space, in which Canada has a unique advantage given its lengthy coastlines.

On Oct. 20, Israeli defence company Elbit Systems Ltd. completed its acquisition of International Submarine Engineering Ltd., a Port Coquitlam, B.C.-based company specializing in underwater autonomous and remotely operated vehicles. Then, ON Sunday, U.S. defence giant Lockheed Martin Corp. acquired Nova Scotia-based anti-submarine warfare company Ultra Maritime for $3.45-billion.

The financial terms of Novacap’s acquisition of OSI were not disclosed.

In June, OSI signed a memorandum of understanding with Tkms, the German submarine company that is currently negotiating with the federal government for a contract for up to 12 of its vessels. Mr. Armstrong said Osi’s working relationship with Tkms remains strong.

This summer, the B.C.-based company also completed its compliance testing against Nato’s most recently released standard for electronic chart display and information systems in warships. Currently, it’s working on an autonomy centre of excellence to support its work with the Royal Canadian Navy, through which it has previously developed products.

“When a navy chooses a navigation system, it is making a 30-year decision, so continuity and reliability matter more in our market than in almost any other segment of systems and software,” Jim Girard, president and CEO of OSI, said in a written statement.

stories.title: Rising antisemitism in Canada is ‘very disappointing’ but ‘we do have power’: Holocaust survivor
stories.summary: Antisemitism today is 'violent,' says Nate Leipciger. Prayer scrolls were ripped off of doors and synagogues are being shot at
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
The Canada that Nate Leipciger sees today is “very disappointing,” he says, compared to how it was when he moved here decades ago.

The 98-year-old arrived in Toronto in 1948 after surviving the Holocaust, including time at notorious concentration camp, Auschwitz-Birkenau. The antisemitism of Canada’s past was “gentle,” as he put it.

Jewish people were quietly told they couldn’t rent a house or stay at a hotel. But now, antisemitism is “violent.”

Mezuzahs, or prayer scrolls, are ripped off of doors. There are shootings at synagogues.

“The prime minister (Mark Carney) has offered $100 million to Hamas — the enemy that caused the terrific destruction of October 7,” he told National Post on Tuesday, before a speaking engagement at the Toronto Holocaust Museum for Neuberger Holocaust Education Week .

In September, Carney said he would send that amount as aid for Palestinians. But terror group Hamas has not left Gaza, and an election that was expected in November has been postponed by nearly a year.

Meanwhile, said Leipciger, Hamas’ goal “to destroy the Jewish people” remains.

“Once, there was one person that said, ‘I’m going to destroy the Jewish nation.’ Nobody believed him,” he said.

“Today, we don’t have the luxury of saying, ‘Well, maybe it won’t happen.'”

In 1939, when Leipciger was 11 years old, Nazi Germany invaded Poland. His family was forced out of their home. They were first moved to the Sosnowiec ghetto and then the Srodula ghetto, where he shared half a room with his parents and sister.

It was at this location, in 1942, where Leipciger and others in the Jewish community started to build hiding places to avoid Nazi soldiers who would make random arrests and deport people.

After being tipped off that a Nazi raid was imminent, Leipciger, his family and others hid on a rooftop. A woman carrying a newborn baby begged to join. Many were reluctant to let her, worried the baby would cry, but she joined anyway.

The Nazi search came to an end. As Leipciger left the hiding spot, he heard the woman screaming. Somebody beside her had smothered the baby out of fear of being discovered.

This story only represents one life on top of the six million Jews who were killed in the Holocaust, said Leipciger, but it stuck with him because it was the “most terrible thing” he can think of that happened to the Jewish people as a nation.

“Not only did they murder us, but the Nazis made murderers out of us,” he said. “Our morality was so low that we could murder a child in order to survive a few hours.”

Marty York: Motion will urge creation of antisemitism task force at TMU law school

Terry Newman: Pro-Palestine student group proves anti-Zionism is often antisemitism

Leipciger was not able to avoid deportation forever.

At 15, he was loaded into a cattle car with his family and taken to Auschwitz-Birkenau.

Leipciger and his father were sent to work camps where “life was hard but manageable,” he said. There was “hope” as rumours spread of the war coming to an end.

As Allied forces neared, Leipciger and his father took part in a death March, or forced evacuation. They would walk from camp to camp — many kilometres away — in an effort by the Nazis to keep prisoners from being liberated.

Many were “taken out of line and unceremoniously shot and left by the side of the road,” said Leipciger.

He ended up at a subcamp of the Dachau concentration camp in late April 1945.

Days later, American soldiers arrived. But it was an “empty victory,” he said, because he did not know who among his family had survived. He later learned his sister, mother, and many of his aunts, uncles and cousins were killed.

After moving to Canada with his father, Leipciger made it his life’s mission to educate young people about the Holocaust. He returned to Auschwitz-Birkenau for the first time in 1975 and has gone back to give tours more than 20 times.

He said he sees Jew hatred today as “more than antisemitism.” It’s also “anti-Western culture.”

“This is why we have to stand up. We live in a free society, and we are not powerless. We do have power. We can vote out our government that allocated $100 million to Hamas,” he said. “We can fight it at the ballot box, and we can take people to court who are committing acts of violence against us.”

He recalled a scene prior to his deportation to Auschwitz, when the Jewish community was led to the train station in front of other Polish citizens — regular men, women and children. It was not done in a vacuum, he said.

There were people witnessing what was happening. They were also unable to help in any way, he said, but some showed compassion.

He said he remains hopeful that the next generation will be proactive and squash hate wherever they see it.

“Today we are very fortunate that we have many non-Jewish people who are helpful, who understand that (we’re) not necessarily the only group this can happen to, and they feel for us, and that is the big difference,” he said.

stories.title: How the Midterm results could impact financial markets and your retirement
stories.summary: The U.S. Midterm elections could have implications for investors, including Canadians' retirement savings, and experts say financial markets could react strongly to the results.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections could have implications for investors, including Canadians’ retirement savings , and experts say financial markets could react strongly to the results.

A shift in control of the U.S. Congress could change the direction of, or even reverse, some key policies, including U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and trade measures.

An unexpected election result could trigger market volatility, while a predictable outcome May bring some relief by reducing political uncertainty.

Recent U.S. polling suggests Democrats will likely regain control of the House, and potentially the Senate. Much of this outcome May already be reflected in market prices, which means markets on Wall Street and Bay Street could sell off if the results differ from investors’ expectations.

“I guarantee you that there are bets being made and expectations are being priced into the market. So the challenge is not what the outcome is today. It’s how much that outcome lines up with the expectations priced into the market,” says Colin White, president and CEO of Veracan Capital Management.

“Markets hate uncertainty, and some of that uncertainty is going to get removed tonight. How much uncertainty gets replaced? That’s the unanswered question.”

U.S. President Donald Trump’s Republicans currently control both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, which has helped his administration push through hundreds of new policies and policy changes, including his infamous trade war and tariffs.

“It’s been known for some time that the Democrats are going to take control, at least of the House; it’s looking increasingly likely that they’re going to take control of the Senate as well,” says economics professor Moshe Lander of Concordia University.

“As long as those results play out as expected, that’s already priced into markets, and I think that’s why you’re seeing there’s very little movement in the markets today.”

“If something unanticipated happens — that’s where the markets are going to react.”

Most investors who want to minimize risk allocate their money into different investment products, such as stocks and bonds, and strategize which products to invest in based on careful analysis.

For Canadians building for their retirement, this means some of these investments could be impacted by the midterm results if there is a sudden, drastic market reaction.

“The challenge is not what the outcome is today, it’s how much that outcome lines up with the expectations priced into the market,” says White.

“Once the election’s done and then we know what the results are, historically, you’re gonna see a little bit of a relief rally. This uncertainty is removed. We can stop guessing, we know what we’re dealing with, and markets hate uncertainty more than anything else.”

If Republicans surprise markets by remaining in control of one or both the House and the Senate, that would technically work against the expectations of stock markets right now for a mostly Democratic victory. However, that wouldn’t necessarily trigger a sell-off.

That’s because American politics would essentially return to the status quo, which means investors have a more predictable path forward.

White says markets tend to like political gridlock, where opposing parties in Congress creates political resistance that can delay policy changes.

“If you’re allocating capital or running a business, you like to know the rules. And if you think the rules are solid, and aren’t going to change every couple of months, then you can behave a little bit better,” says White.

“The best outcome here is a kind of a deadlock or gridlock, of some description, because giving either side the ability to make quicker radical changes, that’s more difficult to plan with.”
