stories.title: Canada’s aid efforts make it ‘humanitarian superpower,’ says UN’s relief head
stories.summary: Tom Fletcher says Canada’s advocacy and funding is ‘saving millions of lives’ across the globe every year
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
The United Nations’ global head of humanitarian issues is praising Canada for helping the world’s most vulnerable even as he calls for accountability for the wars driving suffering worldwide.

“Canada has become a humanitarian superpower,” Tom Fletcher said in an exclusive interview with The Canadian Press during a Monday visit to Ottawa.

“I really hope that Canada continues to hold the line.”

Fletcher leads the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. For two years he has visited the front lines in Ukraine and Gaza while urging the world not to forget about ongoing crises in Sudan, Afghanistan and Mali.

His term started just weeks before the U.S. made deep cuts to foreign aid – though Fletcher praised the United States for restoring some of that funding over the past year.

Pointing to the conflicts in Sudan and Gaza, Fletcher said the funding shortfall is being compounded by wars that are spreading hunger and blocking humanitarian relief.

Roughly 19 million people in Sudan are living with acute hunger, and Fletcher warns their plight could be made worse by changing weather patterns and the U.S. war in Iran blocking supply routes.

Sudan’s warring parties in the now three-year-old civil war have banned aid workers from certain areas based on how they perceive the local population’s loyalties.

Fletcher said he worries about normalizing practices the Israeli government has implemented in Gaza, such as barring journalists from the territory and drastically restricting aid flows.

“It’s sort of infectious, in the way that it undermines international law elsewhere, and creates or adds to this climate of impunity that we’re seeing across all the crises we work in,” he said.

Fletcher has faced sustained criticism from supporters of Israel who say the UN is downplaying groups like Hamas diverting aid or embedding themselves among civilians.

The United Nations' global head of humanitarian issues is praising Canada as a leader in helping the world's most vulnerable, while urging accountability for the wars driving sufferi…

Fletcher said it’s important not to bow to that pressure, which he said comes from people who don’t want the world to see the extent of suffering inside Gaza.

“We’re being told, ‘Well, you’ll get more access if you change your reporting, or if you reduce your criticism or your advocacy, or if you spend less time talking about international law,’ and so on,” he said. “We just have to be consistent here.”

Technology is also making wars easier to fight. Fletcher said drones are being used more frequently against civilians in Sudan, Ukraine, Gaza and Lebanon.

“The way in which humans are using their ingenuity to find new ways to kill civilians is terrifying,” he said. “We need the member states to be holding themselves and each other to account.”

Fletcher praised Canada for its advocacy and its foreign aid funding, which he said “is saving millions of lives every year from Sudan to Afghanistan, to Gaza, to Ukraine, to Haiti and beyond.”

“We’re in a world right now where we’re underfunded, we’re overstretched, we’re literally under attack – a thousand dead humanitarians in three years,” he said.

“And at each point at which I’ve felt particularly exposed and where we as humanitarians feel exposed, we do look behind us and we find that Canada does have our back. And that means a huge amount.”

On Tuesday, Fletcher met with Randeep Sarai, Canada’s secretary of state for international development, who announced the renewal of $6-million in federal funding to help co-ordinate global emergency responses.

But Canada has changed its approach to foreign aid since Prime Minister Mark Carney took office. It cut funding for global health programs, is pushing for more private-sector investments in aid programs and spinoffs for Canadian companies, and dropped the “feminist” label from its foreign policy.

The aid sector has criticized this shift. They argue it prioritizes domestic growth over aid intended to address the issues which drive migration and conflict, and does not support the world’s most vulnerable people.

Ottawa has insisted it can fight poverty abroad while boosting Canadian companies at home.

Cooperation Canada, a coalition of most Canadian aid groups operating abroad, said the sector supports reforms but is urging Ottawa not to cut development and humanitarian funding further.

Coalition head Kate Higgins said during a Monday reception for Fletcher that the government’s recent national security strategy called for “strong international partnerships and a disciplined foreign policy.”

“Canada can give practical expression to that ambition through sustained humanitarian funding, principled diplomacy and consistent leadership in upholding international humanitarian law,” she said.

Next July, Canada will chair a donor support group which consults with other rich countries on how the UN uses its humanitarian funding.

Fletcher said that’s an opportunity for a “reimagination” of what humanitarian aid looks like in an era when governments aren’t meeting the needs.

“I’d like to reach out beyond just traditional humanitarian development partners, actually towards technology companies, to the private sector, to really get their sense of how we can together deal with these crises,” he said.

Fletcher said UN agencies and large organizations have a crucial role to play in addressing complex problems like the hunger crisis in Darfur.

But he said places with internet connectivity and a functioning market might benefit more from cash transfers to individuals, or from health care programs where private companies can help while making a profit.

stories.title: How menopause symptoms affects women and the economy, according to our experts
stories.summary: Readers asked how to talk to a doctor about symptoms, how it affects women’s careers and how governments could create better supports
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
How does menopause affect the economy? Investigative reporter Tavia Grant and Dr. Sheila Wijayasinghe answered reader questions on the stigma around menopausal symptoms , the options available for seeking treatment and the impact it has on Canada’s work force.

Menopause symptoms hit the majority of women between the ages of 45 and 55, and can include hot flashes, depression, anxiety, trouble sleeping and heart issues. And despite being a normal part of life, many women feel it’s taboo to bring up symptoms with their doctors, or struggle getting their physicians to understand what they’re dealing with.

The stigma around menopause has taken a heavy toll on working women and the economy as a whole. Menopause symptoms cause some women to reduce their hours, avoid promotions, change careers or drop out of the labour force altogether, according to the Menopause Foundation of Canada, causing ripple effects for their financial security and retirement savings.

Readers asked how to talk to a doctor about their symptoms, how it affects women’s careers and how governments could create better supports. Here are some highlights from the Q&A.

When does menopause start? When does it end?

Dr. Sheila Wijayasinghe: First, it’s helpful to understand that menopause isn’t a single phase, but part of a transition.

Perimenopause is the time leading up to menopause, when hormone levels fluctuate and symptoms can begin. It often starts in our 40s, sometimes earlier, and can last several years. You May notice changes in your periods, hot flashes, sleep disturbances or mood changes.

Menopause is officially reached when you’ve gone 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period (assuming there’s no other cause). The average age in Canada is around 51. This is considered a natural transition but can also occur overnight for those who have had something called surgical menopause if the ovaries are removed.

Post-menopause is everything that comes after! There’s no specific age when menopause symptoms end. For some, symptoms improve within a few years, while others experience them for much longer. Vaginal and urinary symptoms can actually develop or worsen over time without treatment. The key piece to remember is that we are all unique in our journeys, with some starting earlier, others later and some with mild symptoms and others with more severe. And there are options for support during each of these phases.

Is weight gain and hair loss normal during menopause? How can I curb these effects?

Dr. Wijayasinghe: Yes, both are common concerns during perimenopause and menopause. With weight, it’s important to distinguish between aging and menopause itself. Weight gain becomes more common as we get older, partly because of changes in muscle mass, activity and metabolism. Menopause also changes where we tend to store fat, with more accumulating around the abdomen. My advice is to focus less on the number on the scale and more on maintaining muscle and supporting your overall health. Strength training, regular physical activity, adequate protein, good sleep and sustainable eating habits can all help. And remember, menopause hormone therapy isn’t a weight-loss treatment.

Hair thinning can also become more noticeable around menopause, partly due to hormonal changes, aging and genetics. It’s important to ensure there is no other cause so your clinician can rule out iron deficiency, thyroid conditions and other causes, especially if hair loss is significant or sudden. For hair thinning, treatments such as topical minoxidil May help, depending on the cause. How does the lost labour due to menopause actually materialize? What does it look like in a company?

Tavia Grant: There is a need for more research in this area. We do know the labour force participation rate for women in Canada drops off to 73.3 per cent by age 59. The survey doesn’t capture the impact of menopause specifically, but this could be one factor among several.

Other surveys show some of the impacts in the workplace . One found that two-thirds of women wouldn’t feel comfortable speaking to their supervisor about what they were experiencing; nine in 10 working women feel their employer doesn’t provide support related to menopause.

Have women who have left their jobs due to bad symptoms returned? How did they do it and what was it like for them?

Grant: I have spoken with many women who have returned to work, or stayed at work and flourished. Why did you choose to focus on the economic impact of menopause for your article?

Grant: Menopause has become a huge topic in health coverage, but the economic and workplace side hasn’t been reported much in Canada. Millions of women in Canada are in their forties and fifties, when symptoms can hit – at the top of their game in skills, experience and seniority. Workplaces can do a lot to break stigma and offer supports to employees; by doing so they retain and engage these experienced, knowledgeable people.

Talking about both the economic and health aspects of this is important as these discussions can help in forming public policies.

Dr. Wijayasinghe: It’s important to look at the economic impact of menopause not just from a broader societal perspective, but also at the individual level. In my practice, I see how symptoms can affect people’s ability to work, their confidence, their financial security and ultimately their quality of life. For some, it means taking unpaid time off, reducing their hours, turning down opportunities or even leaving jobs they love. And for others, particularly those working multiple jobs or living paycheque to paycheque, those choices May not even be possible. Add in the costs of medications, appointments and treatments that May not be covered, and the financial burden can be significant.

The larger economic numbers help us understand why this matters to employers, policy-makers and our health care system. But behind every statistic is a person whose life, livelihood and financial independence May be affected. That’s the part I see in my patients, and why I think we need to pay attention to both while also addressing the gaps in care and physical/emotional/cognitive symptoms of menopause.

How does menopause impact the regular working class?

Grant: I’ve spoken to women across Canada who work in regular jobs – such as in restaurants or social services – who are experiencing symptoms and struggling at work.

One described having migraines and muscle aches, but not having access to paid sick days. Others have said they don’t feel comfortable raising this with their manager. Many have described paying out of pocket, hundreds and sometimes thousands of dollars, for care, even though it’s difficult to afford, just so they can continue to work and manage their responsibilities at home.

Health care is primarily a provincial responsibility. What would a national strategy do in practice?

Grant: Some feel that a national strategy would help ensure access to care and supports for those experiencing menopause, regardless of where people live in Canada.

Right now, that access and coverage is uneven – for example, only two provinces, B.C. and Manitoba, cover the costs of menopause hormone therapy. The Menopause Foundation of Canada is calling for treatment to become more accessible and affordable, across Canada.

As well, a proposed bill about women’s health, Bill S-243 , had its second reading in the Senate. It aims to establish a national framework for women’s health that will bolster investment in health research, including on menopause, and strengthen primary health care services for women.

What role can men play? How can we better help the women around us?

Grant: Many symptoms are invisible, but they can be utterly debilitating – for example, a lack of sleep and exhaustion, brain fog and a loss of confidence. And though conversations around this are helping to normalize this topic, many women are still suffering in silence for fear of stigma.

Australia has a national health campaign under way right now. Part of this is just building awareness, and offering brochures about how to support someone going through this. It would be helpful to see a similar type of initiative in Canada.

Dr. Wijayasinghe: Men have such an important role to play, whether as partners, friends, colleagues, family members or leaders in the workplace.

I gently suggest: start by listening, learning and taking symptoms seriously. Ask what would be helpful rather than making assumptions. That might mean supporting someone who’s struggling with sleep, being flexible at work, or simply making space for an open conversation without jokes or judgment.

And here’s my gentle call-out to the men in our lives: Take care of yourselves, too! So often, women are carrying the mental load of managing everyone else’s health, appointments and well-being. Book your own appointments, stay on top of your health, and take responsibility for your share of the household and caregiving work without waiting to be asked. Menopause isn’t just a women’s issue. The more we can share the responsibility for care, both at home and in our communities, the better supported everyone will be.

What can we do to convince employers that making accommodations for menopausal symptoms is worth doing?

Grant: Some workplaces are introducing policies and support groups, offering webinars and educating managers. They’re still in the minority in Canada, but this is changing.

One interesting point that Professor Pnina Alon-Shenker at Toronto Metropolitan University told me is that workplace accommodations can be very effective, but they needn’t cost much – for example, giving employees access to cold water, allowing some breaks or hybrid work or modified clothing requirements.

The U.K., recognizing that this is an economic issue, is nudging employers to take action. As of this year, the British government is encouraging large employers to have action plans that support people experiencing menopause. This will become mandatory next year.

content_blocks.text: Grant: Menopause has become a huge topic in health coverage, but the economic and workplace side hasn’t been reported much in Canada. Workplaces can do a lot to break stigma and offer supports to employees; by doing so they retain and engage these experienced, knowledgeable people.

stories.title: Head of UN relief praises Canada, calls for accountability in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan
stories.summary: The United Nations’ global head of humanitarian issues is praising Canada for helping the world’s most vulnerable even as he calls for accountability for the wars driving suffering worldwide.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The United Nations’ global head of humanitarian issues is praising Canada for helping the world’s most vulnerable even as he calls for accountability for the wars driving suffering worldwide.

“Canada has become a humanitarian superpower,” Tom Fletcher said in an exclusive interview with The Canadian Press during a Monday visit to Ottawa.

“I really hope that Canada continues to hold the line.”

Fletcher leads the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. For two years he has visited the front lines in Ukraine and Gaza while urging the world not to forget about ongoing crises in Sudan, Afghanistan and Mali.

His term started just weeks before the U.S. made deep cuts to foreign aid — though Fletcher praised the United States for restoring some of that funding over the past year.

Pointing to the conflicts in Sudan and Gaza, Fletcher said the funding shortfall is being compounded by wars that are spreading hunger and blocking humanitarian relief.

Roughly 19 million people in Sudan are living with acute hunger and Fletcher warns their plight could be made worse by changing weather patterns and the U.S. war in Iran blocking supply routes.

Sudan’s warring parties in the now three-year-old civil war have banned aid workers from certain areas based on how they perceive the local population’s loyalties.

Fletcher said he worries about normalizing practices the Israeli government has implemented in Gaza, such as barring journalists from the territory and drastically restricting aid flows.

“It’s sort of infectious, in the way that it undermines international law elsewhere, and creates or adds to this climate of impunity that we’re seeing across all the crises we work in,” he said.

Fletcher has faced sustained criticism from supporters of Israel who say the UN is downplaying groups like Hamas diverting aid or embedding themselves among civilians.

Fletcher said it’s important not to bow to that pressure, which he said comes from people who don’t want the world to see the extent of suffering inside Gaza.

“We’re being told, ‘Well, you’ll get more access if you change your reporting, or if you reduce your criticism, or your advocacy, or, if you spend less time talking about international law,’ and so on,” he said. “We just have to be consistent here.”

Technology is also making wars easier to fight. Fletcher said drones are being used more frequently against civilians in Sudan, Ukraine, Gaza and Lebanon.

“The way in which humans are using their ingenuity to find new ways to kill civilians is terrifying,” he said. “We need the member states to be holding themselves and each other to account.”

Fletcher praised Canada for its advocacy and its foreign aid funding, which he said “is saving millions of lives every year from Sudan to Afghanistan, to Gaza, to Ukraine, to Haiti and beyond.”

“We’re in a world right now where we’re underfunded, we’re overstretched, we’re literally under attack — a thousand dead humanitarians in three years,” he said.

“And at each point at which I’ve felt particularly exposed and where we as humanitarians feel exposed, we do look behind us and we find that Canada does have our back. And that means a huge amount.”

Fletcher met Tuesday with Randeep Sarai, Canada’s secretary of state for international development, who announced the renewal of $6 million in federal funding to help co-ordinate global emergency responses.

But Canada has changed its approach to foreign aid since Prime Minister Mark Carney took office. It cut funding for global health programs, is pushing for more private-sector investments in aid programs and spinoffs for Canadian companies, and dropped the “feminist” label from its foreign policy.

The aid sector has criticized this shift. They argue it prioritizes domestic growth over aid intended to address the issues which drive migration and conflict, and does not support the world’s most vulnerable people.

Ottawa has insisted it can fight poverty abroad while boosting Canadian companies at home.

Co-operation Canada, a coalition of most Canadian aid groups operating abroad, said the sector supports reforms but is urging Ottawa not to cut development and humanitarian funding further.

Coalition head Kate Higgins said during a Monday reception for Fletcher that the government’s recent national security strategy called for “strong international partnerships and a disciplined foreign policy.”

“Canada can give practical expression to that ambition through sustained humanitarian funding, principled diplomacy, and consistent leadership in upholding international humanitarian law,” she said.

Next July, Canada will chair a donor support group which consults with other rich countries on how the UN uses its humanitarian funding.

Fletcher said that’s an opportunity for a “reimagination” of what humanitarian aid looks like in an era when governments aren’t meeting the needs.

“I’d like to reach out beyond just traditional humanitarian development partners, actually towards technology companies, to the private sector, to really get their sense of how we can together deal with these crises,” he said.

Fletcher said UN agencies and large organizations have a crucial role to play in addressing complex problems like the hunger crisis in Darfur.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Toronto AI chatbot firm Ada to merge with U.S. company Dialpad in $600-million deal
stories.summary: Valuation is down significantly from unicorn-level peak in 2021
stories.author: Sean Silcoff, Vanmala Subramaniam, Murad Hemmadi
stories.content:
Ada Support Inc., the Toronto-based company that makes AI customer service software for businesses, has agreed to combine with U.S. company Dialpad Inc. in an all-share deal valuing the Canadian enterprise at around $600-million, or about US$430-million, two sources familiar with the matter said.

That’s down from Ada’s US$1.2-billion valuation when it raised money at the peak of the pandemic technology bubble in a US$130-million financing round led by Silicon Valley venture capital firm Spark Capital. At the time, that financing made it part of a cohort of Canadian “unicorns,” or privately held technology companies that achieve a valuation of US$1-billion or more.

Tech valuations subsequently plummeted starting in late 2021 and those of legacy software providers have remained depressed owing to lingering questions about how much large language model-powered (LLM) artificial-intelligence software will disrupt the market. Like other emerging technology companies, Ada went on to make a series of layoffs and cost cuts, including eliminating half its marketing team in July and laying off 25 employees last week, two other sources told The Globe and Mail.

The Globe is not identifying the sources as they are not authorized to discuss the matters.

Chief executive officer Mike Murchison and David Hariri co-founded Ada in 2016 after launching an earlier social-media startup. The firm sold a software system that let businesses set up their own customer service chatbots, initially using elaborate prewritten scripts.

In addition to answering questions, Ada’s technology connects to clients’ other software systems to do tasks such as updating contact information, changing bookings or issuing refunds.

The firm’s website lists customers including Caribbean telecom provider Digicel, Canadian retailer Indigo Books & Music Inc. and Asian consumer superapp Grab. It’s also counted Shopify Inc., AirAsia Group BHD and Telus Corp. among its clients.

Mr. Murchison did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the transaction.

Ada grew rapidly in its early years, generating tens of millions of dollars in annual revenue by the early 2020s, and raising money from several leading Canadian venture capital firms as well as U.S. heavyweights Accel, Bessemer Venture Partners, FirstMark Capital and Tiger Global Management.

While Ada was early to the business of AI chatbots, it’s faced increasing competition in recent years, particularly following OpenAI’s launch of ChatGPT in November 2022.

Ada rebuilt its technology to use LLMs, letting the bots more dynamically take in and respond to users’ questions. In April 2023, it rolled out voice agents that could answer customer-service phone calls. That led to a rapid decline in revenues from its older products but an equally quick expansion of its LLM-based offering. But the net result, said the two sources familiar with the deal terms, was that Ada’s overall revenue expansion has not kept pace with other rapidly growing AI-based companies and was recently running at about US$50-million in revenues on an annual basis.

Dialpad is a privately held San Francisco Bay Area software company that sells contact-centre software to businesses and has been in operation since 2011. It’s much larger than Ada, which has roughly 200 employees. Dialpad, which like Ada achieved unicorn status during the pandemic, also has a deep bench of top-flight U.S. early-stage investors, including Andreessen Horowitz, Google Ventures, SoftBank Corp., Iconiq Capital and Salesforce Ventures, as well as the growth equity arm of the Ontario Municipal Employees’ Retirement Systems.

Last October, Dialpad launched an agentic AI platform, supplying the software for businesses to build autonomous voice-and-text AI agents. Some of its clients include Randstad, Nasdaq and T-Mobile. AI agents make decisions or execute on actions autonomously on behalf of human users.

One of the sources familiar with the deal said Dialpad has a strong user base in enterprise telephony for internal and customer support, and that the deal is seen as a way to help both companies generate continued market growth with Ada’s advanced technology.

The deal is expected to close as soon as next week.

There have been significant shifts in Ada’s work force in recent months. In a recording of the July layoffs, obtained by The Globe, Mr. Murchison can be heard telling employees that his decision to terminate their employment was related to a “change we are making around how Ada is building products.” Two of those laid-off employees, who spoke to The Globe on condition of anonymity, said that Mr. Murchison had been keen on amplifying the use of the AI agent Claude in workflows, especially on the marketing team, to cut costs. They believed that their layoffs were the direct impact of AI use within the company.

Ada co-founder Mr. Hariri left the firm in July for a product management role at Shopify, according to his LinkedIn profile, although he remains on the board. Ada’s chief marketing officer and chief customer officer have also exited this year.

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge victim Maya Gebala recognized with heroism award
stories.summary: The 13-year-old girl, who was badly injured during the mass shooting, is the first recipient of the award outside of the United States
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Maya Gebala, who was badly injured during the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has received the first international award from a U.S.-based charity that was formed in the aftermath of another school shooting.

The Youth Peace and Justice Foundation, also known as The Uvalde Foundation For Kids, says it has recognized the 13-year-old girl with its Youth Heroism Award, making her the first recipient outside the United States.

The award recognizes young people who demonstrate “exceptional courage, leadership, compassion, or selfless action” in helping others, and Gebala is being singled out for her courage during the Feb. 10 attack as well as “her determination throughout the difficult recovery.”

The foundation was formed following the mass shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, in May, 2022 that killed 19 children and two teachers.

Gebala was gravely injured in the Tumbler Ridge shooting where Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight people before shooting herself.

The girl was released from BC Children’s Hospital in Vancouver last week, more than eight months after being shot three times in the attack.

“According to accounts shared by her family, she attempted to secure the school library door to help protect other students as the attack unfolded, the foundation’s announcement says.

The group’s president Daniel Chapin says that “heroism is not defined by age” or whether they walked away unharmed.

“Maya was a young girl facing an unimaginable situation, and she showed courage in the midst of it,” Chapin says in a statement. “We are honoured to recognize her.”

stories.title: Toys ‘R’ Us Canada to open in 300 Staples stores
stories.summary: By the end of 2027, the companies hope they will have opened Toys "R" Us and Parties "R" Us locations at roughly 300 Staples stores.
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
The new owner of Toys “R” Us Canada will revive the brand by opening dedicated shopping areas within Staples Canada stores.

The office supplies retailer says it has reached a deal with Next Century Ipco Can ULC to bring Toys “R” Us and new Parties “R” Us departments to Staples locations.

The partnership will start with a pilot launching on Nov. 14 at a Staples in Richmond Hill, Ont.

By the end of 2027, the companies hope they will have opened Toys “R” Us and Parties “R” Us locations at roughly 300 Staples stores.

Next Century bought 150 of Toys “R” Us Canada’s trademarks earlier this year, when the retailer run by Ancaster, Ont.-based entrepreneur Doug Putman filed for creditor protection.

Next Century is an affiliate of Ad Populum, a U.S. firm that owns Party City, manages several toy companies, and is involved with Graceland, the Elvis Presley attraction in Tennessee.

stories.title: Smith defends proposed Alberta riding redraw despite NDP accusations of gerrymandering
stories.summary: Opposition says many changes suggested in report are designed to give Smith’s UCP an unfair advantage heading into 2027 election
stories.author: Jack Farrell and Lisa Johnson
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is rejecting allegations that an independent panel has torqued the province’s electoral map to favour her United Conservative Party, saying the recommended changes to redraw the boundaries are reasonable and would give voters better representation.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Ms. Smith said she also endorses changes to the electoral map in southern Alberta , which have become the greatest source of contention since the province’s proposed boundaries were released publicly the day before.

The new map proposes eliminating one of Lethbridge’s two urban ridings while creating three new districts that mix the city’s suburban neighbourhoods with swaths of rural southern Alberta.

The change has provoked charges of gerrymandering, the U.S.-style practice of manipulating boundaries to give one party an unfair advantage in elections.

“I think Lethbridge would be very well served by having four representatives,” Ms. Smith said, offering her first thoughts on the proposed map since it was published Monday.

Ms. Smith added that she hopes the Alberta Ndp’s promised legal challenge of the map doesn’t come to pass, but that her government would assemble a legal team if necessary. (Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said his party can only file a legal challenge if the government adopts the map.)

The map is expected to be debated on Wednesday afternoon in the Alberta Legislature, where Ms. Smith’s UCP holds a majority of seats.

The electoral map of Alberta is redrawn every eight to 10 years through a process designed to foster compromise and limit political influence. Adopting the recommendations of independent panels, which are often passed with little public scrutiny, has been the standard for provincial legislatures and federal Parliament for decades.

Alberta’s latest redrawing, however, has fuelled accusations of gerrymandering ever since Ms. Smith decided in April to upend the process and reject the recommended map of an earlier independent panel. She then formed a committee to set up a new panel, which delivered a fresh map on Monday.

Alberta’s system dictates that the governing party selects the chair and two panelists while the Official Opposition picks the remaining two.

Of the panelists tasked with drawing the latest map, the two selected by the NDP have added to the accusations of gerrymandering, singling out the changes in Lethbridge.

These two panelists – University of Alberta constitutional law professor Gerard Kennedy and former Okotoks, Alta., town councillor Brent Robinson – wrote in a separate report that they believe some of the new recommended ridings would be “constitutionally fraught” and will likely face a legal challenge.

The remaining three panelists, including panel chair and retired judge Brian O’Ferrall, dismissed their counterparts’ criticisms at several turns through the 300-plus-page report, accusing them of “sanctimonious passing of judgment” and “extreme, unjustified and unnecessary criticisms.”

In the report, Mr. O’Ferrall also singled out political scientists, complaining that they have “preferred to stoke the flames of controversy” instead of contributing “to the public’s understanding of the electoral boundary process.”

Alberta’s next general election is scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027. It is unclear what electoral map would be used for that vote if the NDP launches a legal challenge. Elections Alberta has warned it May not have enough time to prepare for the election, should the new maps be adopted or a legal challenge delays the map from being implemented.

Kara Westerlund, president of Rural Municipalities of Alberta, said on Tuesday that rural leaders are concerned about hybrid ridings, noting the association’s members represent 85 per cent of the province’s land mass but 15 per cent of the population.

“Our main concern is just the fact that we feel that the rural voice and our issues are going to be diluted with [hybrid ridings],” she said.

Politicians from mid-sized cities have cautioned against sweeping hybrid ridings, pointing to the risk that city residents could be represented by people who don’t live in their area or understand their needs.

University of Calgary political scientist Lisa Young said she believes the map is gerrymandered, most clearly underlined by the proposed changes in Lethbridge.

The City of Lethbridge is currently split into two urban electoral districts, with one represented by the NDP and the other by the UCP. Both seats have been competitive since 2015, when the provincial NDP formed government for the first time.

While the NDP would likely win in the city’s new urban riding, the UCP would be heavily favoured to win the three new ridings that extend hundreds of kilometres beyond city boundaries.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Ms. Smith said she also endorses changes to the electoral map in southern Alberta , which have become the greatest source of contention since the province’s proposed boundaries were released publicly the day before.
The new map proposes eliminating one of Lethbridge’s two urban ridings while creating three new districts that mix the city’s suburban neighbourhoods with swaths of rural southern Alberta.
The change has provoked charges of gerrymandering, the U.S.-style practice of manipulating boundaries to give one party an unfair advantage in elections.
“I think Lethbridge would be very well served by having four representatives,” Ms. Smith said, offering her first thoughts on the proposed map since it was published Monday.

Ms. Smith added that she hopes the Alberta Ndp’s promised legal challenge of the map doesn’t come to pass, but that her government would assemble a legal team if necessary. (Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said his party can only file a legal challenge if the government adopts the map.)
The map is expected to be debated on Wednesday afternoon in the Alberta Legislature, where Ms. Smith’s UCP holds a majority of seats.

The electoral map of Alberta is redrawn every eight to 10 years through a process designed to foster compromise and limit political influence. Adopting the recommendations of independent panels, which are often passed with little public scrutiny, has been the standard for provincial legislatures and federal Parliament for decades.

Alberta’s latest redrawing, however, has fuelled accusations of gerrymandering ever since Ms. Smith decided in April to upend the process and reject the recommended map of an earlier independent panel. She then formed a committee to set up a new panel, which delivered a fresh map on Monday.
Alberta’s system dictates that the governing party selects the chair and two panelists while the Official Opposition picks the remaining two.
Of the panelists tasked with drawing the latest map, the two selected by the NDP have added to the accusations of gerrymandering, singling out the changes in Lethbridge.

These two panelists – University of Alberta constitutional law professor Gerard Kennedy and former Okotoks, Alta., town councillor Brent Robinson – wrote in a separate report that they believe some of the new recommended ridings would be “constitutionally fraught” and will likely face a legal challenge.

The remaining three panelists, including panel chair and retired judge Brian O’Ferrall, dismissed their counterparts’ criticisms at several turns through the 300-plus-page report, accusing them of “sanctimonious passing of judgment” and “extreme, unjustified and unnecessary criticisms.”

In the report, Mr. O’Ferrall also singled out political scientists, complaining that they have “preferred to stoke the flames of controversy” instead of contributing “to the public’s understanding of the electoral boundary process.”

Alberta’s next general election is scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027. It is unclear what electoral map would be used for that vote if the NDP launches a legal challenge. Elections Alberta has warned it May not have enough time to prepare for the election, should the new maps be adopted or a legal challenge delays the map from being implemented.

“Our main concern is just the fact that we feel that the rural voice and our issues are going to be diluted with [hybrid ridings],” she said.

Politicians from mid-sized cities have cautioned against sweeping hybrid ridings, pointing to the risk that city residents could be represented by people who don’t live in their area or understand their needs.
University of Calgary political scientist Lisa Young said she believes the map is gerrymandered, most clearly underlined by the proposed changes in Lethbridge.

She added that Alberta’s boundary redrawing process May need to be revamped. Other provinces, such as British Columbia, have systems that further remove the process from political influence.
“To have essentially two failed efforts at coming together around a map says that there’s something desperately wrong here,” Prof. Young said.
“It raises the question of whether this sort of bipartisan commission approach that we’ve been using works in a polarized system.”

stories.title: RCMP investigate photo of man in Nazi uniform while trick-or-treating in Nova Scotia
stories.summary: Cole Harbour - Police in Nova Scotia are investigating a complaint about a social media post showing a man wearing a swastika while trick-or-treating on Halloween.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Cole Harbour - A mother in the Halifax region says she was shocked to see a man trick-or-treating on Saturday wearing what appeared to be a Nazi uniform.

Paige Hoveling said her community of Cole Harbour, N.S., about 10 kilometres east of Halifax, is diverse and tightly knit. She said she was confused and then alarmed when she saw the man in a dark uniform wearing a red armband emblazoned with a swastika amid happy families on Halloween.

“Millions of people died because of people that wore these uniforms,” she said in an interview Tuesday.

“I want people to be aware that this is not OK. It’s not OK to spread hate in our community, and it’s not OK to make your neighbours feel unsafe in the place where they live.”

Hoveling said her son spotted the man as they were trick-or-treating with friends. The boy thought the man was dressed as a German general, but she and her husband explained he was wearing Nazi regalia.

“We just kind of went, ‘Um, no, buddy, that’s a Nazi, and that’s not OK,’” she said.

She snapped a picture of the man so she could alert her neighbours. She and her group discussed whether to approach him. Surrounded by children, they decided to stay away, she said.

The Canadian Press viewed her photo of the man. His outfit includes a dark peaked cap and dark pants tucked into laced, black boots. There is a dark leather strap over the man’s right shoulder. A red band with a black swastika encircles his left arm.

Hoveling said he was pushing a stroller.

The Nazis killed an estimated six million European Jews during the Holocaust, which was the mass murder of Jews and other groups before and during the Second World War.

RCMP confirmed Tuesday that they were investigating a complaint about a social media post showing a man wearing a swastika while trick-or-treating on Halloween. A spokesperson encouraged Nova Scotians to report any behaviour that “appears motivated by bias or prejudice.”

“The RCMP takes all reports of suspected hate-motivated incidents and hate crimes seriously,” Cpl. Mandy Edwards said in an email. “Speaking up helps protect the well-being of everyone in the community.”

Ben Sichel with Independent Jewish Voices in Halifax said it was disturbing that someone thought it was OK to dress as a Nazi for Halloween. He said expressions of hate from far-right groups are becoming more normalized, pointing to recent demonstrations by white nationalists in Canada, including in Halifax and a First Nation in British Columbia.

“Nazi symbols are of course deeply antisemitic, but incidents like this are also connected to anti-Muslim bigotry, Residential School denialism and other forms of bigotry, which we experience right here in Nova Scotia,” Sichel said in an email. “All must be loudly condemned.”

Andy Fillmore, mayor of the Halifax Regional Municipality, said the uniform’s symbols represent “hatred, antisemitism and atrocities.”

In an emailed statement, he encouraged the man in the photograph to think about the harm the symbols represent and how his decision to promote them May have affected the people around him.

“Halifax is a welcoming and inclusive community, and everyone who calls it home deserves to feel safe, respected and valued,” he said. “We all have a responsibility to stand against hatred and intolerance wherever we encounter it.”

Trish Purdy, the Halifax Regional Municipality councillor for the district, said she was appalled.

In an email, Purdy said wearing a Nazi uniform as a costume is “morally repugnant.” In April, Jewish advocacy group B’nai Brith said it logged 6,800 antisemitic incidents in Canada last year — the highest number recorded since the group began collecting the data in 1982.

Earlier this year, the Canadian government passed the Combatting Hate Act, creating new Criminal Code offences for hate-motivated intimidation of identifiable groups, including through the intentional display of certain Nazi symbols.

In 2024, a volunteer fire department in North Sydney, N.S., apologized after a group said to be unaffiliated attended a Halloween party at the local firefighters club dressed as members of the Ku Klux Klan.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

— By Sarah Smellie in St. John’s, N.L., with files from The Associated Press

stories.title: One dead, one missing in suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola, B.C.
stories.summary: Bella Coola - The British Columbia Conservation Officer Service says one person is dead and another is missing after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the Bella Coola area.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Two people are dead after a suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola, B.C., a year after an attack on a group of schoolchildren in the same community.

An initial statement from the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service on Tuesday said the remains of one person had been found in the west trail area of the Snooka trail system on Monday, while a search was underway for a second person.

That person was found dead later Tuesday, a representative of the B.C. government said.

The Conservation Officer Service said family members had reported the pair missing on Sunday.

Art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her daughter were reported missing by relatives.

Kara Balcarras, who identified herself as Jenny Balcarras’s sister-in-law, issued a Facebook post about the missing pair and later updated it with the Conservation Officer Service’s statement about the apparent attack.

The post said the pair’s vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, located nearly 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver by road.

Insp. Jeff Tyre with the Conservation Officer Service said evidence at the scene where human remains were found suggested a bear May have been involved.

“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time. We are working to support the family as our investigation continues,” he said in a video statement.

The apparent attack comes nearly a year after a grizzly attacked a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers in Bella Coola, leaving an adult and three children badly injured last November.

There was an extensive effort to catch that bear, but while several grizzlies were trapped, DNA tests showed they did not include the bear involved in that attack.

Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, issued a statement Tuesday saying the full circumstances of the latest suspected attack were still unfolding, but he understood “first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims’ family members, the victims of last year’s attack, and the community at large.”

Emergency Health Services spokesman Brian Twaites said at the time of the attack a year ago that it happened on a trail near Highway 20.

A map on the Bella Coola Community Forest website shows the Snooka trail system, the site of the latest suspected attack, is just south of Highway 20.

Tyre said the Conservation Officer Service was urging people to stay away from the Snooka trails due to the potential danger and to allow officers to conduct their work.

He said efforts were underway to find and trap any bears involved.

Any captured bears would be assessed to determine next steps, the service said.

“If the bear is determined to be the bear responsible for the attack, it will be dispatched to ensure public safety, as per provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines,” it said in a post on social media.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version incorrectly spelled the surname of Jenny Balcarras and Kara Balcarras.

stories.title: ‘Musical Olympics’: Meet the five finalists hoping to make history as Canada makes Eurovision debut
stories.summary: Canadians still have time to vote for the musician they think should represent the country on the Eurovision stage. Known as the world’s largest live annual televised music competition, Canada is set to make it’s Eurovision debut next year – the first new country to join since Australia in 2015. Five musicians are in the […]
stories.author: Pamela Pagano
stories.content:
By Pamela Pagano

Posted November 3, 2026 2:14 pm.

Canadians still have time to vote for the musician they think should represent the country on the Eurovision stage.

Known as the world’s largest live annual televised music competition, Canada is set to make it’s Eurovision debut next year – the first new country to join since Australia in 2015.

Five musicians are in the running to represent Canada: William Cloutier, Josiane, Talk, Tyler Shaw, and Rêve.

“Eurovision is the musical Olympics,” said Rêve. “I’m not much of an athlete so this is the musical version of that. It’s a scale beyond my wildest dreams.

“To be the first representative that Canada puts forward would just be such a proud Canadian moment for me and for any of us five finalists.”

Rêve, the Juno Award-winning artist from Montreal, has amassed more than 175 million global streams with songs including “CTRL + ALT + DEL,” “Contemporary Love,” and “Whitney.”

As for Tyler Shaw, the Vancouver-born Chinese Canadian pop artist’s song “Kiss Goodnight” reached Platinum in 2012. And his song “With You” was 2019’s most-played single on Canadian radio by a Canadian artist.

“I have been able to have been fortunate enough to live in a lot of different places in this country and a lot of these places I do feel like I am able to call home,” said Shaw. “Growing up in Vancouver, going to university in PEI, living in Toronto for 10 years, building the music career. Now I live in Ottawa, my grandparents own a home in Saskatchewan.

“So I feel like my home is literally across Canada.”

Talk, who was raised in Ottawa, won the 2024 Juno for breakthrough artist of the year. He’s had new music dropping year-round and is set to tour Canada later this year.

“Seeing it come to life as this manifestation I’ve had has been really magical and I’m really proud of myself, my team and really all of the finalists.”

From New Brunswick, Acadian singer-songwriter Josiane makes bilingual pop. Her song “Lose It All” has surpassed six million streams.

She won Quebec’s version of The Voice — La Voix – in 2020.

“It’s bigger than anything I could ever dream for and hope for for myself,” she said. “For me, it’s an amazing opportunity also to represent Canada; I’m such a proud Canadian.”

Nominated for song of the year alongside artists like Céline Dion, Charlotte Cardin and Angine de Poitrine at the Gala de l’ADISQ this Sunday for “Où on dansait autrefois” is William Cloutier.

From Drummondville, Que., he won Mixmania at 16, then Star Académie in 2021.

“What I love to be is on stage and it’s my house. So for me it’s absolutely a dream,” he said.

Back in 1988, Céline Dion won the Eurovision Song Contest representing Switzerland.

As for who will take Canada’s inaugural spot, votes can be cast online , once a day, until Thursday.

stories.title: ‘Mining-induced event’ suspected cause of Saskatchewan tremor: Earthquakes Canada
stories.summary: Esterhazy, Sask., was awoken by seismic activity Tuesday morning after a suspected mining-induced event triggered a tremor, Earthquakes Canada said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A tremor felt in parts of southeastern Saskatchewan Tuesday morning is suspected to have been caused by mining activity, according to Earthquakes Canada.

A 3.4 magnitude seismic event occurred around 7:04 a.m. local time in an area northeast of Esterhazy, Sask., according to the federal agency. Esterhazy is approximately 230 kilometres east of Regina.

Earthquakes Canada said moderate shaking started about one kilometre underground, and was triggered by human activity in the form of a “suspected mining-induced event.”

In an emailed statement, Mosaic Canada confirmed that seismic activity was felt near its potash mine just outside of Esterhazy.

“The event occurred in a mined-out area of the older workings of the K3 Mine,” the statement from Mosaic said.

All roughly 1,200 Mosaic employees have been accounted for, and operations in Esterhazy are continuing as normal. No safety concerns remain as a result of the tremor, the company said.

“Mining induced seismic activity in this area is common, and our facilities are engineered with seismic loading in mind,” Mosaic added. “We continue to advance our understanding of the geological properties of the K3 ore body and will work with external experts to review seismic activity.”

At the time of publication, 22 people reported having felt the tremor to Earthquakes Canada. It noted that details have been reviewed by the agency but have not yet been finalized.

content_blocks.html: Earthquakes Canada said moderate shaking started about one kilometre underground, and was triggered by human activity in the form of a “suspected mining-induced event.”

content_blocks.text: In an emailed statement, Mosaic Canada confirmed that seismic activity was felt near its potash mine just outside of Esterhazy.
content_blocks.html: In an emailed statement, Mosaic Canada confirmed that seismic activity was felt near its potash mine just outside of Esterhazy.

content_blocks.text: “The event occurred in a mined-out area of the older workings of the K3 Mine,” the statement from Mosaic said.
content_blocks.html: “The event occurred in a mined-out area of the older workings of the K3 Mine,” the statement from Mosaic said.

content_blocks.text: All roughly 1,200 Mosaic employees have been accounted for, and operations in Esterhazy are continuing as normal. No safety concerns remain as a result of the tremor, the company said.

“Mining induced seismic activity in this area is common, and our facilities are engineered with seismic loading in mind,” Mosaic added. “We continue to advance our understanding of the geological properties of the K3 ore body and will work with external experts to review seismic activity.”
At the time of publication, 22 people reported having felt the tremor to Earthquakes Canada. It noted that details have been reviewed by the agency but have not yet been finalized.

stories.title: Boycott grows against Russia hockey reinstatement, leaves questions about World Juniors
stories.summary: Sweden, Finland, Czechia and Latvia have said they will not play Russia in international competition while Norway, Denmark and Austria have also expressed opposition.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Growing protests in international hockey over Russia’s return to competition could impact the upcoming world junior championship in Alberta.

Sweden, Finland, Czechia and Latvia are refusing to play against Russia in international competition.

Norway said it will not play the Russians at the men’s world championship in 2027, Austria oppose Russia’s return but has made no mention of not competing, and Denmark has also reportedly refused to play Russia.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled last week that the International Ice Hockey Federation (Iihf) must reinstate Russian teams, beginning with the world juniors , which start Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer.

Hockey Canada said Friday it was seeking clarity from the Iihf on how Russia’s return would impact the competition. The organization did not immediately respond Tuesday to a request for comment.

Following the decision on October 30th, Canada’s Secretary of Sport Adam van Koeverden said the federal government strongly opposes the court’s decision.

“We take great pride in welcoming the world to compete at the highest level and sharing the hospitality and spirit that define us as Canadians. But with that pride also comes a responsibility to uphold our principles and values,” he said in a statement on Friday afternoon.

Canada’s stance on Russia’s actions has not changed, the minister said.

“Canada maintains, as it has since 2022, that Russia should not be represented in international sport competitions while Russia’s illegal and unjustifiable full-scale invasion against Ukraine continues,” van Koeverden said.

“Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable.”

German federation board chair Frank H. Lutz wrote on the organization’s website, “We reject the return of Russian national teams to international ice hockey tournaments.”

Germany is the host of the 2027 men’s world championship, and Ukraine is a participating country.

“Allowing Russia to participate would have significant security, political, and economic consequences for us as hosts,” Lutz said last week.

Canada’s federal government has said it opposes Russia’s return and will maintain restrictions on Russian athletes at events in Canada that receive federal funding. Hockey Canada confirmed the world juniors has no federal funding. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said the province would comply with the CAS ruling.

stories.title: Bank of Canada maintains stance on rate hike ahead of Nov. 5 budget release
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada is standing by its decision last week to hike interest rates for the first time in three years, and as Ottawa gets set to table its budget.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The Bank of Canada is standing by its decision last week to hike interest rates for the first time in three years, even though it could mean many Canadians and businesses will pay more for some mortgages and other loans.

This also comes as the federal government plans to release its next budget on Nov. 5, which is expected to include tax incentives for small and medium-sized businesses to reinvest.

Governor Tiff Macklem spoke Tuesday before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance.

“Last week, we raised the policy interest rate by 25 basis points, bringing it to 2.5 per cent. This was the first interest rate increase since July 2023,” said Macklem in his opening statement.

“With the outlook for inflation substantially higher and the economy showing resilience, an increase in the policy rate was needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalized inflation.”

Interest rates that Canadians and businesses are charged by commercial banks and other lenders are based mainly on the overnight rate set by the Bank of Canada, particularly with variable rate loans. In other cases, fluctuations in bond market yields can also determine more long-term products like fixed-rate options.

The central bank raised its benchmark last week in anticipation of higher inflation, especially as higher oil and energy prices drive up prices for goods and services beyond gasoline.

Macklem said there was mounting pressure to raise rates as the Iran war leads continues to see surging global energy prices and supply chain shocks.

“With the war in the Middle East persisting, global oil prices have increased and are expected to remain higher for longer. This is hitting Canadians at the gas pump and increasing costs for many businesses,” said Macklem.

“The prices of gasoline, diesel and heating oil are elevated and are expected to remain higher for longer. This is hitting consumers directly and raising business costs for production and transportation.”

“While businesses have mostly absorbed higher input costs so far, past experience and Bank surveys suggest that cost pass-through will increase over the next year.”

Macklem was then asked by Kent MacDonald — Liberal MP for Cardigan, PEI — about how the federal government’s newest incentives, including the so-called productivity mega-deduction , are supposed to appeal to Canadian businesses while interest rates are rising.

“We totally understand that there is no immediate benefit of raising interest rates, but that’s the tool we have to moderate this pass through of costs to get inflation back to target,” Macklem said in response.

“If we don’t do it, what it means for consumers is that the prices of everything will be going up, not just gasoline, and that’s exactly what we want to avoid.”

Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers at the central bank also responded.

“A lower interest rate might help, ON balance, with the incentive investing, but not if it comes with increasing inflation.”

“So if we kept interest rates low, and the trade off was inflation got away on us, then I don’t think that’s an environment where they would feel comfortable investing either.”

2:05 Business Matters: Inflation rate rises to 3.1% in September

The exchange also highlighted the broader relationship between the Bank of Canada’s monetary policy and the federal government’s economic agenda — although the Bank of Canada stresses that it operates independently of the federal government.

Macklem told members of Parliament on Tuesday he doesn’t think the federal government’s fiscal policy is at odds with the central bank’s efforts to control inflation.

Conservative finance critic Michael Chong asked Macklem for his opinion on the government’s affordability efforts. The central bank governor declined to answer directly.

He said he only comments on the government’s fiscal policy when spending is approaching unsustainable levels, or when the government’s actions are working against the Bank of Canada’s efforts to tame inflation.

“In the current circumstances, I don’t think either of those criteria are met,” he said.

Macklem did comment publicly on the pace of government spending three years earlier. He warned at the time that fiscal spending was adding to demand faster than it was increasing supply, which was “not helpful” for getting inflation back under control.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre regularly rails against the Liberal government over what he calls inflationary spending. He has urged the government to slash spending ahead of Thursday’s budget to help get costs under control for Canadians.

– with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge victim Maya Gebala recognized with heroism award from U.S. foundation
stories.summary: Tumbler Ridge - Maya Gebala, who was badly injured during the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has received the first international award from a U.S.-based charity that was formed in the aftermath of another school shooting.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Tumbler Ridge - Maya Gebala, who was badly injured during the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has received the first international award from a U.S.-based charity that was formed in the aftermath of another school shooting.

The Youth Peace and Justice Foundation, also known as The Uvalde Foundation For Kids, says it has recognized the 13-year-old girl with its Youth Heroism Award, making her the first recipient outside the United States.

stories.title: TransAlta gathering community input on potential new Parkland County data centre
stories.summary: The site, directly south of TransAlta's existing gas-fired Keephills Generating Station, has been granted 230 megawatts through Alberta's grid operator for an initial phase.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Teams with TransAlta Corp. have been busy fielding questions from rural residents west of Edmonton, where the power generator, Brookfield and CPP Investments aim to build a new data centre.

The three partners signed a memorandum of understanding in February to evaluate a large-scale project in Parkland County called the Boreal Technology Hub .

The site, directly south of TransAlta’s existing gas-fired Keephills Generating Station, has been granted 230 megawatts through Alberta’s grid operator for an initial phase.

At full build out, it could be as large as 1,600 megawatts — more than what the City of Edmonton consumes at any given moment.

TransAlta CEO Joel Hunter said Tuesday that a community open house a month ago went well, running four hours and attracting some 180 attendees.

“The takeaway was, they want to understand more around data centres. Even though we talk a lot about data centres, it’s still relatively new and they have questions around ‘What’s the amount of noise that will come from the facility? What’s the amount of water that would be used?'” he told analysts on a conference call to discuss third-quarter results.

“There were no protests or anything like that. It was really people just trying to get more information.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "There were no protests or anything like that. It was really people just trying to get more information."

TransAlta, previously a major coal-fired power producer, has been present in the region for more than 70 years, so it has a long history engaging with nearby residents, Hunter added.

Another session is scheduled for next week at the community hall in the hamlet of Keephills, where residents can take a deeper dive into the technical aspects of the project, the regulatory process and community benefits.

The Alberta government has been looking to attract data centre developers to the province, which has plentiful natural gas and land. But it has also been mindful of not overburdening the provincial electrical system, requiring entrants to provide their own power and capping how much can initially be drawn from the grid.

Hunter praised the province’s approach. In some U.S. jurisdictions, for example, development has raced ahead too fast, driving up consumers’ power bills, which in turn has led to abrupt reversals in the form of moratoriums.

“(The province) has been very deliberate and very focused on ensuring they don’t want to compromise reliability or affordability here for Albertans,” Hunter said.

“At times, people might feel a bit frustrated by that. But I think it’s actually very intentional and being very focused not only on the medium term but the long term.”

Earlier Tuesday, the Calgary-based company said it earned a profit attributable to common shareholders of $63 million or 20 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

The result compared with a loss of $62 million or 20 cents per diluted share for the same quarter last year.

On an adjusted basis, TransAlta says it earned 18 cents per share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted loss of two cents per share in the third quarter of 2025. Revenue for the quarter totalled $536 million, down from $615 million a year earlier.

stories.title: Ontario won't make career college Osap audit public, minister says
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's colleges and universities minister says he will not be releasing a government-commissioned audit into student financial aid usage at career colleges.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario’s colleges and universities minister said Tuesday he will not be releasing a government-commissioned audit into student financial aid usage at career colleges.

Nolan Quinn announced last month that he had engaged Kpmg to audit the sector following concerns about rising usage in the Ontario Student Assistance Program. Preliminary findings from that audit alarmed the government enough to refer the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police.

stories.title: X says B.C. law can’t force the platform to delete intimate image. Tribunal agrees
stories.summary: Social media platform argued that removing the image from Canadian view was sufficient
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A British Columbia Tribunal has ruled that X, the social media platform formerly known as Twitter, does not need to remove an intimate image of a B.C. woman that was posted non-consensually.

The woman, referred to as TR due to a publication ban on her name, had complained last year about the image, and in March an order had been issued by Eric Regehr, vice chair of the B.C. Civil Resolution Tribunal (CRT), to remove it from the platform.

“I will refer to it as the protection order decision,” he wrote in a followup decision, referring to the order to remove the image. “The applicant in that unpublished decision, who I will call TR, says X Corp. did not comply with the protection order. TR asks me to order X to pay an administrative monetary penalty for its failure to comply.”

He added: “X says that it complied with the order by restricting access to the intimate image within Canada, a practice it calls geofencing. It argues B.C. law cannot compel it to take any further steps.”

Regehr found this insufficient, and ordered X to pay the maximum $100,000 administrative penalty under the law.

However, in a new decision published on Monday, Regehr wrote that TR had asked for an additional $100,000 penalty since the image remains visible outside Canada.

“As I noted in the previous decision, X had provided very little evidence and raised only one legal issue with very brief submissions,” he wrote. “Here, X has provided considerably more detailed evidence and submissions and has raised new issues. It is unfortunate that X did not put its full case forward the first time it was before the CRT.”

He noted that, in its submission, X admitted that the image remains visible outside of Canada, but that “it is a global platform subject to many different legal regimes about what people are allowed to post.”

He continued: “X argues that it would be unreasonable to expect it to strictly comply with B.C. law by deleting the image, with global effect, when United States law would not require it to remove the image.”

He brought up “the comity of nations,” noting: “When laws could impact the sovereignty of other countries, the principle of comity affects how those laws are interpreted … In short, comity May operate to limit a law’s application outside Canada.”

“I appreciate that it May seem odd that an internet intermediary May avoid an administrative penalty despite not complying with the strict terms of a protection order,” Regehr wrote. “However, I agree with X that for the defence to have real force, it must be able to operate when there has been imperfect compliance with a protection order.”

X had requested that TR pay its legal fess, but Regehr denied that, saying it “would be contrary to the Crt’s mandate and unfair to TR to order her to pay any of X’s legal fees in these circumstances,” reported to be US$119,000

He also noted that TR had brought her case forward in good faith.

“Overall, I find that TR had a reasonable belief, backed by evidence, that the protection order required X to delete her intimate image. She therefore had a rational and good faith basis for prosecuting this application.”

X is said to have filed for a judicial review of the previous $100,000 penalty.

stories.title: Crook admits Facebook post ‘went too far’ after appearance on CTV News
stories.summary: A day after Ward 13 runner-up Andrew Crook defended a recent Facebook post about his experience as a candidate in the municipal election, he said the comments were a call for “political accountability, not violence.”
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A day after Ward 13 runner-up Andrew Crook defended a recent Facebook post about his experience as a candidate in the municipal election, he said the comments were a call for “political accountability, not violence.” Crook wrote in a follow-up post Tuesday morning: “I entered this election believing London needed change.

Now that it’s over, I believe we also need to change how we disagree. That includes me.” His original post referred to some elected politicians as sociopaths and stated, “The rope is useless unless we are prepared to use it to hang them.” Crook now says his words crossed a line.

“My language went too far, particularly the reference to using someone’s own ‘rope’ against them. I should have expressed myself differently,” he wrote. He added the post stemmed from “frustration with the hostility I witnessed during the election, including personal attacks, intimidation and vandalism experienced by me and other candidates.” In the Oct.

26, 2026, municipal election, incumbent David Ferreira received 4,308 votes, or 69.54 per cent, in Ward 13. Crook finished a distant second with 735 votes, or 11.86 per cent. His follow-up post reads: “I want to thank Daryl Newcombe and CTV News for the opportunity to address my recent Facebook comments.

“I entered this election believing London needed change. Now that it’s over, I believe we also need to change how we disagree. “That includes me. “We can start with common ground, disagree honestly, and hold people accountable without treating one another as enemies.

“The comments in question came from frustration with the hostility I witnessed during the election, including personal attacks, intimidation and vandalism experienced by me and other candidates. “My language went too far, particularly the reference to using someone’s own ‘rope’ against them.

I should have expressed myself differently. I was calling for political accountability, not violence. I do not advocate threats or physical harm against anyone. “I can stand my ground on the need for accountability while recognizing that I can do better in how I communicate it.

“The election is over. My responsibility to participate continues.”

stories.title: N.B. introduces law to protect youth from misleading online business practices
stories.summary: Fredericton - The New Brunswick government has introduced legislation that it says will make the province the first in Canada to protect young consumers from unfair online business practices.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Fredericton - The New Brunswick government has introduced legislation that it says will make the province the first in Canada to protect young consumers from unfair online business practices.

Justice Minister Robert McKee tabled the proposed law Tuesday. It includes the new Young Consumers in Digital Markets Act, which prohibits companies from engaging in misleading, deceptive or other unfair practices involving consumers under 16 years old.

“This includes misleading young consumers or hiding important information from them, using pressure or urgency to encourage a young consumer to make a purchase or agree to something,” McKee told a news conference.

The legislation also takes aim at business practices that make it difficult for young consumers to understand what they are agreeing to, or ads that unfairly influence young consumers’ decisions.

The minister, who is also responsible for addictions and mental health services, gave an example of a young person who might start playing a game on a free trial, only to be charged for a one-year subscription when the trial expires.

The new rules would apply to sellers of digital goods, such as ebooks and software, as well as providers of digital services including streaming, social media or artificial intelligence products.

It would also apply to digital platforms that connect users to goods and services, including TikTok, Snapchat and Roblox.

The act would be administered and enforced by the province’s Financial and Consumer Services Commission. McKee said he was confident the commission could take on this new role without any budget increase.

The minister said investigations will be complaint-based and will apply to any company, regardless of where they are based.

Proposed remedies could include cancelling an agreement without cost or penalty, cancelling future payments or ordering full refunds. In some cases, the commission could issue fines of up to $25,000 without a hearing.

In more serious cases requiring a tribunal, penalties could include fines of up to $5 million and imprisonment of almost five years for an individual. Fines of up to $5 million are also possible for a business.

“Sometimes these platforms will use tactics that, whether intentionally or not, pressure kids to spend money on an app or agree to a feature by using language they don’t understand,” said McKee.

The government says it’s the first law of its kind in Canada, but similar legislation exists in Australia and Europe.

The minister said the legislation will complement the federal government’s Bill C-34, which would force social media platforms to block access for children under 16. Introduced in June, the federal bill is making its way through Parliament.

New Brunswick is also amending legislation to codify its previously announced ban on personal electronic devices in schools across all grade levels.

That ban, which mainly applies to cellphones and tablets, went into effect in September for children in daycares and students from kindergarten to Grade 8. It will be expanded to students in grades 9 to 12 at the start of the second semester in February.

Teachers can still use electronic devices to deliver curriculum content. There are also exceptions to the policy for medical reasons, such as a diabetic student keeping track of blood sugar levels.

— By Devin Stevens in Halifax.
