content_blocks.caption: A mug shot of Durante King-Mclean, 25, after his U.S. arrest in 2023. Pennsylvania State Police

content_blocks.text: “The driver knew least amount of knowledge possible that I could tell him because this was a big job,” Chaudhary said. “Money like that … you don’t know what the person’s going to do.” In other words, he was afraid that if King-Mclean knew the value of the crate he would have in the truck, he might just keep on driving.
Finally, Chaudhary arranged for a quiet spot where the loot could be taken off the truck and divided. He settled on a farm near Acton, Ont., a 50-minute drive west of the airport.

“It was through a friend who I knew that said I could do something over there. It was, like, they had a little shed there that I could pay him to rent.… I just needed a shed to move the gold from one truck to another.… and I paid him, like a hundred bucks.” Prasath Paramalingam, 34, another friend from Brampton, helped him rent it, he said.
By late March Chaudhary had arranged for the truck, the driver and the destination. He just needed to wait until his inside man found an irresistible target.

That came on April 17, 2023, when heavy incoming air freight from a precious metal refinery in Zurich was destined for Toronto. News of that shipment ignited hundreds of phone calls, group chats, texts and encrypted messages firing back and forth.

“Gooooood morning it is,” an early-morning text that day pinged on the phone of Parmpal Sidhu, a 53-year-old Air Canada cargo employee known as Paul who worked under Panesar but was also his friend. The text was from Panesar’s phone, court heard. It was followed by, “We looking good anyways for today.”
On the day of the heist, Chaudhary set up at the Four Points by Sheraton hotel, just four kilometres from the airport.

Phone records show Chaudhary was in contact with King-Mclean 16 times that day, with Panesar eight times, with Grover seven times, with Grover’s trucking business twice, with Sidhu three times, and with Paramalingam once.

As the Air Canada plane was over the Atlantic, from inside the large Air Canada facility a series of computer transactions discreetly changed the instructions for what the airline’s automated cargo sorting system was to do with that crate of gold. The login credentials of an Air Canada manager were used to delete a code flagging the crate as a high-value shipment. That meant that when it arrived, instead of being sent to a locked and guarded storage room it was treated as general cargo.

Under the login credentials for a different Air Canada manager the computer was then told the crate was not to be unpacked by cargo staff and divided for its two customers — TD Bank collecting the gold and a Vancouver foreign exchange picking up the currency — but kept intact instead. That meant no one would open the crate to see its contents, and the gold and the cash would be kept together for the heist.

content_blocks.alt: Parmpal Sidhu
content_blocks.caption: Parmpal Sidhu, who is accused in the 2023 gold heist at Toronto’s Pearson airport, outside court during his trial in Brampton, Ont., on TOct. 6, 2026. Peter Power / Postmedia

content_blocks.text: Court heard that the two managers whose credentials were used were not working that day and were not involved in the heist. At the time, Air Canada’s computer security at the warehouse was poor, with login credentials routinely shared among employees.
The flight touched down in Toronto nine minutes early, shortly before 4 p.m.

Chaudhary said that Panesar gave him a legitimate Air Canada air waybill that had been carefully doctored to allow a customer to collect the targeted crate, and Chaudhary gave it to King-Mclean. Court heard that Sidhu’s log-in credentials were used to print it off.

The cargo automation faultlessly followed its new instructions and the crate of gold moved unnoticed around the warehouse on a device like an enormous baggage carousel, taking it where the new codes told it to and dropping it into a cavernous sorting area known as a pit.
At 6:30 p.m., King-Mclean backed a white truck into loading bay 12 at Air Canada’s cargo warehouse on Brittania Road East. The heist was truly underway.

Wearing a facemask, hat, gloves, work boots and a safety vest, King-Mclean handed the doctored waybill to an Air Canada employee who passed it to cargo handlers to retrieve the crate. The driver paced about waiting before moving into the loading bay to open the back of his truck.

content_blocks.alt: Durante King-Mclean talking to a worker
content_blocks.caption: The accused driver in the Toronto airport gold heist, Durante King-Mclean, standing, telling an unwitting Air Canada cargo worker where his truck is waiting before a crate of gold and cash worth more than $22.5 million was stolen, April 17, 2023. Court exhibit

content_blocks.text: John Iheme, a station attendant at the warehouse, went to help the waiting customer. He said he was unaware of the heist plot and didn’t know of his unwitting role until Peel Regional Police investigators showed him internal security video showing their interaction, he said. Iheme greeted the driver with a fist bump, after which King-Mclean removed the heavy-duty work glove from his right hand.

Iheme found the crate matching the number written on the waybill in the pit. He loaded it onto a forklift, whirled it out to the waiting driver and even helped King-Mclean load it onto the truck. The driver gave Iheme an appreciative fist bump before climbing back behind the wheel and driving off.
Chaudhary had told King-Mclean to head west and then north to get to the farm he had arranged. Chaudhary drove close to the truck all the way.
Not everyone involved in the heist knew exactly what they had stolen.

The shipping manifest said it was high-value goods, provided the weight of the crate and said it contained gold and currency but didn’t specify much else. Some of the heft could have come from bags of pennies.
They didn’t know how successful their heist was until they met up at the farm and opened the crate.
It is hard to imagine there wasn’t a moment of dumbfounded ecstasy.

Inside they saw thousands of small strips or bars of gold — not the brick-sized gold ingots seen in movies. Chaudhary called them biscuits. Each was stamped with the TD logo of the Toronto Dominion Bank and a serial number. Stacks of biscuits were inside hardshell boxes with a lid that pulled off, like old sewing machine cases, he said.

Chaudhary, Panesar and King-Mclean unloaded the boxes of gold and cash and divided it between the two masterminds, Chaudhary alleged. They did a rough split by eyeball rather than counting individual biscuits and bills. Chaudhary said he trusted Panesar to make sure he got a full 30 per cent.
“He trusted me with everything, so I had to trust him with something. Without trust, we couldn’t make this happen,” Chaudhary said. He loaded his cut into his Range Rover.
By 9:30 p.m., when armed Brink’s guards arrived at the Air Canada warehouse expecting to pick up a crate of gold, the crooks were unloading the loot 50 kilometres away.

By 10 p.m., as Air Canada staff were searching for the crate with increasing alarm, the crooks were leaving the farm and going their separate ways. Chaudhary headed to a condo he rented for a stash house so his loot wasn’t stored where he slept.

“The plan was to basically clear the gold out, melt it, get the money, pay everyone out … everyone will be quiet about it because everyone got paid, and that’s it. Normal life, pretty much,” Chaudhary said.
The endgame proved the diciest part of the heist.

content_blocks.alt: Gold bangles
content_blocks.caption: These six gold bangles are believed to have been made with the stolen gold. Peel Regional Police

content_blocks.text: “I knew I needed help to melt the gold,” Chaudhary said.

Chaudhary had made many trips back to Pakistan over the years, and he got to know a man there named Ibrahim who had connections. He’d known him for about 12 years. Chaudhary asked Ibrahim if he could get him gold melting machines. Ibrahim, who was in Pakistan, arranged for him to meet with someone in Canada who got him the equipment, Chaudhary said. He started melting gold in his condo after watching how-to videos on YouTube.
“It’s not brain surgery. It’s pretty simple: Put it on, heat it up, put it in there. It melts,” he said. Melting it destroyed the logos and serial numbers. “No one could tell where it came from.”

Chaudhary said he reached out to another friend, this one in Canada, to help him sell the reforged gold. He had been close friends with 39-year-old Amit Jalota for at least 15 years. Jalota was an actuary and made good money.

content_blocks.text: “He had some contacts,” Chaudhary said. “I made up a story… and asked him if he could get it exchanged for some cash for me. He’s a friend, so I didn’t really have to tell him a lot.”

content_blocks.caption: The accused driver in the Toronto airport gold heist, Durante King-Mclean, on the right, gives an unwitting Air Canada cargo worker a fist bump for helping load a crate of gold being stolen, April 17, 2023. Court exhibit

content_blocks.text: Chaudhary gave gold to Jalota in increments — about three of his forged bars at a time — and Jalota took the gold to Ali Raza court heard. Raza was the 36-year-old proprietor of Mashallah Jewellers, a store near the airport in a retail hub catering to South Asian and Middle Eastern interest in gold. It was an easy sale.
“They took all of it,” Jalota texted Chaudhary on June 9, 2023. “They get horny when they see it hahahah. They can’t let it go.”
“I didn’t know who Ali Raza was. It was not my person,” Chaudhary said. “Only time I find out who Mr. Raza was when the newspapers came out,” with news of arrests for the heist.
Chaudhary said he got more than a million in cash back.
“I knew the money couldn’t stay in this country,” he said.

He turned again to Ibrahim in Pakistan. Ibrahim helped him transfer the money out of Canada and into Pakistan using underground banking, or, as Chaudhary called the service, “Ibrahim’s guy.” Chaudhary then flew to Pakistan to collect it. “I give the guy money (in) Canada and receive it in Pakistan.”
Chaudhary thought he had found the key to unlocking the cash value trapped in his stolen gold without drawing attention from police in Canada.

While Chaudhary was still in Pakistan, however, Ibrahim figured out what he was up to — wanting gold melting machines and then help to move huge sums of cash all while the Toronto airport gold heist made headlines around the world was a giveaway. Chaudhary said he was betrayed.

“All of a sudden, I was kidnapped,” Chaudhary said. “I was kidnapped by the police over there.… They blindfolded me, and they took me to a place that I don’t know where I was. And they told me they would torture me, do things with me, leave my body where no one will ever find me again, and it’ll be the last time I see anyone.
“They told me that they wouldn’t let me go until they had everything,” he said. “What’s the point of all this money when you can’t even live.”

His kidnappers connected him on FaceTime video calls to their colleagues in Canada; Chaudhary told them where to go to scoop up the rest of his hidden gold, and then to a family member’s home to take his cash.

“They held me until they grabbed everything.” Once his kidnappers’ colleagues in Canada had their hands on the loot they blindfolded him again and drove him into town, told him to lie on the road and count to 30 before looking up. When he took off his blindfold, they were gone.
He thinks they stole at least $5 million worth of gold and a million or more in cash, and left him with post-traumatic stress disorder.
“Trust me, it’s a movie, but it’s a horrifying movie to me,” he said. “It’s a very scary experience for me.”
He flew back home to Canada as soon as he could.

There he faced a different problem. The driver, King-Mclean, was the most likely to be linked to the heist because of the video surveillance. He had also left fingerprints behind after he took his glove off at the warehouse. Police were looking for him.

Grover returned to Canada in May 2024 and Chaudhary this January. Both were arrested as they got off a plane at Pearson airport. Grover is scheduled for trial next year on charges of theft and conspiracy. He is also wanted in the United States in the gun-running case.

Chaudhary quickly agreed to plead guilty to theft, and this past April, a week before the third anniversary of the heist, he was sentenced to four years imprisonment. It was evidence by Chaudhary that led to charges against Jalota, Ammad Chaudhary, and Raza being withdrawn, because he insisted they had no knowledge of the heist.
At a large media conference called by Peel police on the first anniversary of the heist, it was announced that nine men were accused of involvement in the gold heist.
Paramalingam was arrested in the original sweep but disappeared after his release on bail. He is considered a fugitive. He is also wanted for the U.S. gun case.
Evidence and submissions wrapped up Monday at Sidhu’s trial in Brampton on theft and conspiracy charges. He is free on bail while he waits for a verdict.
Which leaves Panesar, the alleged mastermind.

Panesar is in India, authorities said, where India’s national finance police suspect he brought gold or cash from the heist into their country, documents allege. His lawyer in Canada, Greg Lafontaine, said the Indian investigation prevents his client from returning to Canada to face his charges. Panesar’s wife is a singer and actress, and in India they have been working on video and music productions.
If Chaudhary told the truth about Panesar driving off with the lion’s share of the loot, then what happened to that part of the gold is a story yet to be revealed.

stories.title: No charges for London officer after teen bitten by police dog
stories.summary: Ontario’s Special Investigations Unit (SIU) says there are no reasonable grounds to believe a London police officer committed a criminal offence after a 16-year-old boy was bitten by a police dog in July.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Ontario’s Special Investigations Unit (SIU) says there are no reasonable grounds to believe a London police officer committed a criminal offence after a 16-year-old boy was bitten by a police dog in July.

The incident happened July 5, 2026, after police received a report that two masked males had broken into a property near Quarrier and Pelkey roads, the SIU said.

The two attempted to flee and hide from police. An officer and police dog arrived to help locate them. One of the males surrendered, while the other tried to run away and ignored police commands.

The police dog knocked the teen to the ground and bit his left thigh.

SIU Director Joseph Martino found the officer’s decision to use the dog was reasonable, saying it increased the likelihood of capturing the teen while temporarily placing him in a compromised position and reducing the risk he posed as officers moved in to arrest him.

stories.title: If the Democrats win the U.S. midterms, what would change for Canada?
stories.summary: Democratic candidates have seized on U.S. President Donald Trump's tariff policies and trade war against Canada, linking them to affordability struggles.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
American voters are heading to the polls on Tuesday for the U.S. midterms and many in Ottawa will be watching the results closely for what it means for the future of U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats against Canada.

Since he took office for his second term in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly escalated his economic attacks against Canada. Democratic candidates have seized on his tariff policies and trade war against Canada, linking them to affordability struggles.

Democrats appear to be surging across the country, with some polls predicting Democratic control of the House of Representatives and the Senate being in play.

However, would anything change for Canada if Democrats sweep both chambers and win the midterms?

While Canada “historically has never been an election issue,” in the U.S., that appears to have changed this year, said University of Ottawa political science professor Emily Regan Wills.

“Canada is an election issue because Trump has made Canada into an enemy. A lot of people are like, why would you antagonize the nice guys?” she said.

Democratic candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, have tried to link Trump’s tariffs against Canada with higher costs for American consumers.

“If you’re picking a fight with Canada, you’re the asshole,” El-Sayed told reporters last month.

But the cloud of uncertainty around Trump’s Canada trade policy is “unlikely” to change even if the Democrats sweep the election, said University of Guelph political science professor Julie Simmons.

The two major sets of tariffs – the Section 232 sectoral tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos as well as the sweeping 50 per cent Section 338 tariffs – were imposed via executive order, not Congress.

Trump simply circumvented the U.S. Congress in imposing his tariffs on Canada.

“He can bypass Congress with his use of things like the Trade Expansion Act and the Trade Act of 1930, which have been two tools that he has used thus far. It’s unlikely that that will change,” Simmons said.

While Congress does need to approve any new treaties the U.S. enters, it can do little to curb Trump’s use of executive power to impose tariffs the way he has, Wills said.

Trump has signaled he will become more confrontational in executing his agenda in the event of a Democratic sweep.

“I guess I’ll become Mr. Veto,” Trump told the New York Post in a podcast that released on Monday.

“In order to override that veto, the Democrats would have to have two-thirds majority in a vote. It’s unlikely that even if they do take back both the House of Representatives and the Senate, that they would have that kind of a supermajority,” Simmons.

However, the Democrats do have a big tool in their toolbox in stopping Trump’s agenda.

“A Democratic sweep does put impeachment of Donald Trump on the table,” Wills said.

“However… there’s no guarantee that an impeachment would lead to his removal from office,” she added.

Trump was impeached twice during his first time. First in 2019, for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress in 2019. Later in January 2021, a week before his term ended, for inciting an insurrection.

In both instances, he was not removed from office because of the impeachment. A simple majority in the House is enough to impeach a president, but only a two-thirds vote by the Senate can remove a president from office.

Whether Democrats win both chambers or just one, Canadians should be cautious in assuming they would all be opposed to tariffs, Simmons said.

“We also have to remember that even if Congress were to become Democratic in both houses, we can’t assume that Democratic representatives would want to remove all tariffs,” she said.

“It’s incumbent upon trade negotiators in Canada to think of ways to pitch to their Democratic colleagues across the border ways in which reduced tariffs can somehow be in the interests of American voters and also American business owners,” she said.

It is also likely that Trump could become more hostile, not less, if Republicans lose control of Congress, she said.

“If the Republicans are to lose both houses, that given Mr. Trump’s narratives of the past, we can anticipate that he May turn and blame Canada for those outcomes,” Simmons said.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has said American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of the midterm elections.

Prime Minister Mark Carney rebutted Hoekstra and said there was “no merit” in the claims that Canada was looking to interfere in American elections.

stories.title: Unseasonably warm temperatures before weekend cooldown
stories.summary: Unseasonably warm temperatures are expected across the region Tuesday, with a high of 21 C before cooler conditions move in later this week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Unseasonably warm temperatures are expected across the region Tuesday, with a high of 21 C before cooler conditions move in later this week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

The day will start with some cloud cover before skies clear and sunshine returns in the afternoon. South winds are expected to pick up to 20 km/h, with gusts reaching 40 km/h around noon.

The mild weather will continue Wednesday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a high of 21 C. The chance of rain increases to 60 per cent Wednesday night as a cold front moves through.

Temperatures will drop to 16 C Thursday, with another chance of showers Friday.

Cooler conditions are expected over the weekend, with daytime highs around 8 C.

Atchison says the region will hold on to the warmer temperatures through the workweek before cooler air settles in for the weekend.

stories.title: She makes chili oil. He’s an architect. They threw a disco-themed pizza party
stories.summary: The couple DIYed many elements of their wedding and even brought in artwork from their own home, keeping costs low
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
In our new Weddings series, Canadian couples tell us how they went from first dates to walking down the aisle.

Alex Nankivell, 33, grew up in Ottawa but moved to Sydney, Australia, in 2015 to get his master’s in architecture. After graduating, he stayed in the city, where he ran in the same social circles as Sydney-born human resources professional Nicola Scott, also 33. Despite attending the same house parties and music festivals, the two didn’t interact much for a few years.

“I thought she was probably a bit out of my league,” Nankivell said.

In the fall of 2019, they sat next to each other at a friend’s birthday dinner and hit it off. “I distinctly remember Alex dropping the cauliflower on the ground because he was so nervous to talk to me,” Scott said.

Nankivell had been planning to move to London, but as he and Scott got to know each other, he decided to stay in Sydney to see where their relationship might lead. The pair had a lot in common. They were both well-travelled and their childhoods shared a connection to Hong Kong: Nankivell was born there to a diplomat father and raised in Beijing. Meanwhile, Scott’s mother, originally from Britain, was born and raised in Hong Kong, an experience Scott says had a significant influence on her own upbringing.

“Alex is very curious about the world around him,” Scott said. “The thing that attracted me the most to him was the unique ability of using both sides of his brain. He’s quite a creative person, but he’s also very rational and analytical.”

Nankivell was equally enamoured. “Nicola really knows how to light up a room,” he said. “She’s very gregarious and so full of life.”

After dating Scott for six months, Nankivell returned to Canada in March, 2020, to renew his Australian work visa – just before the COVID-19 pandemic hit. With Nankivell unable to return, the couple dated long-distance. But they saw the pandemic as a fortuitous time to get to know each other.

The two would set up cooking dates while Scott prepared her breakfast and Nankivell made his dinner. They had Teleparties on Netflix so they could watch the same movie at the same time. It wasn’t unusual for the couple to spend up to six hours talking on the phone.

Australia’s border closings were stricter than Canada’s at the time, and Scott was considering a career change. The couple figured they’d try living together in Toronto, where Nankivell’s parents live. In March, 2021, Scott came to the city for a three-month visit.

“It was a very good test for being in a pressure-cooker environment,” she said. “It reinforced to me that Alex was the right person to be making such a big change to my life.” She moved to Toronto for good the following spring.

The pair rented an apartment in the city’s Little Italy neighbourhood, co-habiting with Scott’s cat, Hendrix, who she brought with her. On a trip to Ottawa a year and a half later, they began talking seriously about the future.

“We both wanted to get married,” Nankivell said. “We were talking about starting a family, what that would look like and what conditions we’d want to be in place to be able to do that.”

In the summer of 2024, Scott started her own business, a chili oil company called Rippah, inspired by her mother’s upbringing in Asia. Her days were consumed by producing the oil and promoting her business, but she hadn’t forgotten about her desire to get married. She let Nankivell know she hoped to be engaged by the end of the year.

“The running joke in our relationship was that Alex is a procrastinator, so he was going to wait until New Year’s Eve to do it,” Scott said.

Nankivell found a ring – a bezel-set diamond on a gold band – from British jeweller Le Mela, but a postal strike halted delivery. He was eager to buck Scott’s expectation of a New Year’s Eve proposal and pop the question on Christmas, so he bought a placeholder ring from Mejuri.

He wrote a poem about the couple’s relationship and drew accompanying illustrations, displaying them in a PowerPoint presentation on their TV. “I wasn’t surprised by the proposal, but I was surprised by when it happened and how it happened,” Scott said. “It was very personal and considerate.”

A wedding in the summer of 2025 felt too rushed for loved ones from Australia to make the trip, so the couple picked a date in August of this year. They envisioned an informal gathering of about 50 guests, with a short ceremony and a disco-themed pizza party and cocktail reception. “We wanted it to feel like a casual house party that was colourful and kitschy,” Scott explained.

For their venue, they chose a small event and production space in Toronto’s west end called Sixteen Eleven Studios, which they described as “a living room-slash-speakeasy-slash-bar that had disco vibes.”

The couple DIYed many elements of their wedding, sourcing second-hand knickknacks, serveware from local stores, including Value Village, Bazaar and Arts Market. They also brought in artwork from their own home, including the illustrations Nankivell used to propose. A decal illustration of the couple with Hendrix, also made by Nankivell, decorated the venue’s exterior.

All of this helped the couple keep costs low. They spent around $15,000 all-in, including photography by venue owner Kelsi Gayda and florals by Nina Caputo, who assembled a bouquet and sculptural arrangements of carnations, roses and anthuriums inspired by colours of the sunset.

Scott scored her dress, a vintage draped satin gown with a low back, from Space Vintage for $280. “It was so sexy and it felt very timeless, like a nod to the seventies,” she said. Nankivell wore a double-breasted Hugo Boss suit from Simons with a subtle plaid pattern and a flared collar, fitting with the retro theme.

The couple hosted a welcome dinner the day before the event at Nankivell’s parents’ house in High Park, with catering from Parallel Brothers, which serves Middle Eastern food. On the day-of, industry friends helped assemble the food, and other friends pitched in with decor and set-up. Nankivell was on co-ordination duty while Nicola got ready at their apartment. He then joined her to change into his suit.

“We ordered ourselves an Uber Black to get to the wedding,” he said. “It was the peak of luxury.”

They enjoyed a preceremony cocktail hour with guests before the ceremony, which was held in the venue’s back room. It was a short but emotional 15 minutes in which the couple exchanged personal vows about the joy they find in everyday moments and their shared quirky sense of humour.

By the time guests returned to the main lounge, pies from Mac’s Pizza – including one with “Just Married” written in ricotta – had arrived. Pizza was accompanied by a grazing table the couple put together using ingredients they’d purchased themselves, with the help of family and friends in the days and hours leading up to the wedding. Guests returned to the ceremony area for speeches before it was time for dancing back in the main space. The DJ played everything from cross-generational classics to late-nineties rave tunes.

The next day, they had scheduled a brunch at Trinity Bellwoods Park but they relocated the gathering to Nankivell’s parents’ house because of rain. The couple supplied sandwiches from Dad’s Breakfast and Kettleman’s Bagels. “A lot of the same characters showed up, so it was nice to catch up with everyone,” Nankivell said.

The following day, the newlyweds, along with four of Scott’s friends from Australia, travelled to Bracebridge, about a two-hour drive north of Toronto, for a mini-honeymoon at Nankivell’s family cottage.

“We were going kayaking, having drinks and nibbles on the dock and drinking Champagne while swimming,” Scott said. “It was a nice way to decompress and relax after the wedding.”

The pair feel like they’re still in the honeymoon period.

“I look at you and think, ‘I’m so in love with you,’” Scott said. “Nothing and everything changes because we live together and we’ve got our routines and rituals, but having that level of commitment, you just see each other in a different light.”

paragraphs: In our new Weddings series, Canadian couples tell us how they went from first dates to walking down the aisle.

Alex Nankivell, 33, grew up in Ottawa but moved to Sydney, Australia, in 2015 to get his master’s in architecture. After graduating, he stayed in the city, where he ran in the same social circles as Sydney-born human resources professional Nicola Scott, also 33. Despite attending the same house parties and music festivals, the two didn’t interact much for a few years.
“I thought she was probably a bit out of my league,” Nankivell said.

In the fall of 2019, they sat next to each other at a friend’s birthday dinner and hit it off. “I distinctly remember Alex dropping the cauliflower on the ground because he was so nervous to talk to me,” Scott said.

Nankivell had been planning to move to London, but as he and Scott got to know each other, he decided to stay in Sydney to see where their relationship might lead. The pair had a lot in common. They were both well-travelled and their childhoods shared a connection to Hong Kong: Nankivell was born there to a diplomat father and raised in Beijing. Meanwhile, Scott’s mother, originally from Britain, was born and raised in Hong Kong, an experience Scott says had a significant influence on her own upbringing.

“Alex is very curious about the world around him,” Scott said. “The thing that attracted me the most to him was the unique ability of using both sides of his brain. He’s quite a creative person, but he’s also very rational and analytical.”
Nankivell was equally enamoured. “Nicola really knows how to light up a room,” he said. “She’s very gregarious and so full of life.”

After dating Scott for six months, Nankivell returned to Canada in March, 2020, to renew his Australian work visa – just before the COVID-19 pandemic hit. With Nankivell unable to return, the couple dated long-distance. But they saw the pandemic as a fortuitous time to get to know each other.

The two would set up cooking dates while Scott prepared her breakfast and Nankivell made his dinner. They had Teleparties on Netflix so they could watch the same movie at the same time. It wasn’t unusual for the couple to spend up to six hours talking on the phone.

Australia’s border closings were stricter than Canada’s at the time, and Scott was considering a career change. The couple figured they’d try living together in Toronto, where Nankivell’s parents live. In March, 2021, Scott came to the city for a three-month visit.

“It was a very good test for being in a pressure-cooker environment,” she said. “It reinforced to me that Alex was the right person to be making such a big change to my life.” She moved to Toronto for good the following spring.

The pair rented an apartment in the city’s Little Italy neighbourhood, co-habiting with Scott’s cat, Hendrix, who she brought with her. On a trip to Ottawa a year and a half later, they began talking seriously about the future.
“We both wanted to get married,” Nankivell said. “We were talking about starting a family, what that would look like and what conditions we’d want to be in place to be able to do that.”

In the summer of 2024, Scott started her own business, a chili oil company called Rippah, inspired by her mother’s upbringing in Asia. Her days were consumed by producing the oil and promoting her business, but she hadn’t forgotten about her desire to get married. She let Nankivell know she hoped to be engaged by the end of the year.
“The running joke in our relationship was that Alex is a procrastinator, so he was going to wait until New Year’s Eve to do it,” Scott said.

Nankivell found a ring – a bezel-set diamond on a gold band – from British jeweller Le Mela, but a postal strike halted delivery. He was eager to buck Scott’s expectation of a New Year’s Eve proposal and pop the question on Christmas, so he bought a placeholder ring from Mejuri.

He wrote a poem about the couple’s relationship and drew accompanying illustrations, displaying them in a PowerPoint presentation on their TV. “I wasn’t surprised by the proposal, but I was surprised by when it happened and how it happened,” Scott said. “It was very personal and considerate.”

A wedding in the summer of 2025 felt too rushed for loved ones from Australia to make the trip, so the couple picked a date in August of this year. They envisioned an informal gathering of about 50 guests, with a short ceremony and a disco-themed pizza party and cocktail reception. “We wanted it to feel like a casual house party that was colourful and kitschy,” Scott explained.

For their venue, they chose a small event and production space in Toronto’s west end called Sixteen Eleven Studios, which they described as “a living room-slash-speakeasy-slash-bar that had disco vibes.”

The couple DIYed many elements of their wedding, sourcing second-hand knickknacks, serveware from local stores, including Value Village, Bazaar and Arts Market. They also brought in artwork from their own home, including the illustrations Nankivell used to propose. A decal illustration of the couple with Hendrix, also made by Nankivell, decorated the venue’s exterior.

All of this helped the couple keep costs low. They spent around $15,000 all-in, including photography by venue owner Kelsi Gayda and florals by Nina Caputo, who assembled a bouquet and sculptural arrangements of carnations, roses and anthuriums inspired by colours of the sunset.

Scott scored her dress, a vintage draped satin gown with a low back, from Space Vintage for $280. “It was so sexy and it felt very timeless, like a nod to the seventies,” she said. Nankivell wore a double-breasted Hugo Boss suit from Simons with a subtle plaid pattern and a flared collar, fitting with the retro theme.

The couple hosted a welcome dinner the day before the event at Nankivell’s parents’ house in High Park, with catering from Parallel Brothers, which serves Middle Eastern food. On the day-of, industry friends helped assemble the food, and other friends pitched in with decor and set-up. Nankivell was on co-ordination duty while Nicola got ready at their apartment. He then joined her to change into his suit.
“We ordered ourselves an Uber Black to get to the wedding,” he said. “It was the peak of luxury.”

They enjoyed a preceremony cocktail hour with guests before the ceremony, which was held in the venue’s back room. It was a short but emotional 15 minutes in which the couple exchanged personal vows about the joy they find in everyday moments and their shared quirky sense of humour.

By the time guests returned to the main lounge, pies from Mac’s Pizza – including one with “Just Married” written in ricotta – had arrived. Pizza was accompanied by a grazing table the couple put together using ingredients they’d purchased themselves, with the help of family and friends in the days and hours leading up to the wedding. Guests returned to the ceremony area for speeches before it was time for dancing back in the main space. The DJ played everything from cross-generational classics to late-nineties rave tunes.

The next day, they had scheduled a brunch at Trinity Bellwoods Park but they relocated the gathering to Nankivell’s parents’ house because of rain. The couple supplied sandwiches from Dad’s Breakfast and Kettleman’s Bagels. “A lot of the same characters showed up, so it was nice to catch up with everyone,” Nankivell said.

The following day, the newlyweds, along with four of Scott’s friends from Australia, travelled to Bracebridge, about a two-hour drive north of Toronto, for a mini-honeymoon at Nankivell’s family cottage.
“We were going kayaking, having drinks and nibbles on the dock and drinking Champagne while swimming,” Scott said. “It was a nice way to decompress and relax after the wedding.”
The pair feel like they’re still in the honeymoon period.

“I look at you and think, ‘I’m so in love with you,’” Scott said. “Nothing and everything changes because we live together and we’ve got our routines and rituals, but having that level of commitment, you just see each other in a different light.”

stories.title: Being connected to primary care is not care – but it’s a start
stories.summary: Wait times remain long and other parts of the medical system need work, too
stories.author: André Picard
stories.content:
Fourteen million two hundred and fifty-nine thousand Ontarians are now connected to a primary care provider.

That’s 511,000 people more than in January, 2025, when the government launched its Primary Care Action Plan with much fanfare, vowing that everyone would have a primary care provider by 2029.

This is progress. The provincial government is putting money into this effort, $3.4-billion and counting so far. The efforts of Jane Philpott, chair of the action team, seem to be paying off.

But. There’s always a “but” or two.

First, there is the practical mathematical challenge.

There are still roughly 1.8 million Ontarians without a health-care provider, and that number will continue to grow.

The province’s population is increasing, and aging, burned out family doctors and nurse practitioners are retiring, or planning to, in droves. Practitioners are leaving in such large numbers, we are struggling to replace them, and newer recruits practise differently.

Hundreds of multidisciplinary health teams called Family Health Organizations (FHOs) are being formed, creating a robust “medical home” model. But the average doctor has a panel of 1,350 patients, respectively, and FHOs have panels of 2,400 to 4,000 patients cared for by three to five family physicians. Many more teams are needed.

The larger, more important issue is that “attachment” is the easy part of the process. Signing up a patient and opening a file for them doesn’t take much effort at all.

Providing access to care is quite another matter.

Dr. Philpott’s mandate is to ensure that “100% of people in Ontario are attached to a family doctor or a primary care nurse practitioner working in a publicly funded team, where they receive ongoing, comprehensive, and convenient care,” and to do so by 2029.

Let’s start with “convenient.” Practically, that means being able to book an appointment the same day or the next day when you’re sick, as well as evenings and weekends.

According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information , only 30.4 per cent of Ontario adults are able to do so. While that’s better than the Canadian average, 26.3 per cent, it is still a poor showing.

In comparative studies of wealthy countries done by the Commonwealth Fund , Canada consistently ranks last in measures of access, including same-day or next-day appointments.

So, what do patients do when they are told – if someone actually answers the phone – that the first available appointment is in a week or a month? They go to their local hospital emergency department, where waits are often punishing , with one in 10 patients waiting more than 14 hours care and those requiring admission to hospital sometimes waiting more than three times longer.

There there’s comprehensiveness, which is hard to deliver with 10-to-15-minute visits. Many physicians and clinics also have strict “one issue per visit” policies and refuse to do some standard procedures like gynecological exams.

Comprehensive care doesn’t end with the family doc or NP either. Continuity and timeliness of care matter.

Yet, primary care providers often struggle to make referrals to specialists. Wait times for specialist appointments are often measured in weeks and months, and the subsequent waits for surgery can stretch out for more months, or even years.

Many family physicians are reluctant to take on complex patients, such as elderly people with multiple chronic conditions, because they take a lot of extra time, which is poorly remunerated.

While the Ontario government was quick to highlight that the number of unattached patients in the province is coming down, we have very little information about which patients are being added to rosters.

The priority needs to be complex patients, not young healthy ones.

That there are at least 24,000 registrants on Ontario’s HealthCare Connect list who have been waiting more than six months for a referral suggests that there is some cherry-picking going on.

One can’t overstate the importance of a robust primary care system, one where every single citizen has a primary care practitioner who delivers comprehensive care. A health system needs a solid foundation.

A spot on a roster is not care, it’s the promise of care. There needs to be performance indicators to ensure care – quality care – is being delivered. Ontario has promised standards and measures but has not yet delivered.

The good intentions seem to be there.

But, after decades of neglect, actually delivering on primary care for all remains a Sisyphean task, and one that needs to be matched by similar efforts in other parts of the system, including hospitals, long-term care, and home care.

That’s 511,000 people more than in January, 2025, when the government launched its Primary Care Action Plan with much fanfare, vowing that everyone would have a primary care provider by 2029.
This is progress. The provincial government is putting money into this effort, $3.4-billion and counting so far. The efforts of Jane Philpott, chair of the action team, seem to be paying off.
But. There’s always a “but” or two.
First, there is the practical mathematical challenge.
There are still roughly 1.8 million Ontarians without a health-care provider, and that number will continue to grow.

The province’s population is increasing, and aging, burned out family doctors and nurse practitioners are retiring, or planning to, in droves. Practitioners are leaving in such large numbers, we are struggling to replace them, and newer recruits practise differently.

Hundreds of multidisciplinary health teams called Family Health Organizations (FHOs) are being formed, creating a robust “medical home” model. But the average doctor has a panel of 1,350 patients, respectively, and FHOs have panels of 2,400 to 4,000 patients cared for by three to five family physicians. Many more teams are needed.
The larger, more important issue is that “attachment” is the easy part of the process. Signing up a patient and opening a file for them doesn’t take much effort at all.
Providing access to care is quite another matter.

Dr. Philpott’s mandate is to ensure that “100% of people in Ontario are attached to a family doctor or a primary care nurse practitioner working in a publicly funded team, where they receive ongoing, comprehensive, and convenient care,” and to do so by 2029.

According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information , only 30.4 per cent of Ontario adults are able to do so. While that’s better than the Canadian average, 26.3 per cent, it is still a poor showing.
In comparative studies of wealthy countries done by the Commonwealth Fund , Canada consistently ranks last in measures of access, including same-day or next-day appointments.

While the Ontario government was quick to highlight that the number of unattached patients in the province is coming down, we have very little information about which patients are being added to rosters.
The priority needs to be complex patients, not young healthy ones.
That there are at least 24,000 registrants on Ontario’s HealthCare Connect list who have been waiting more than six months for a referral suggests that there is some cherry-picking going on.

One can’t overstate the importance of a robust primary care system, one where every single citizen has a primary care practitioner who delivers comprehensive care. A health system needs a solid foundation.

A spot on a roster is not care, it’s the promise of care. There needs to be performance indicators to ensure care – quality care – is being delivered. Ontario has promised standards and measures but has not yet delivered.

stories.title: In new memoir, Harper says he offered Carney a job — but not finance minister
stories.summary: Former prime minister Stephen Harper says he offered Mark Carney, then the governor of the Bank of Canada, a role in his Conservative government in 2012 — though not as finance minister. Not right away, at least.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Former prime minister Stephen Harper says he offered Mark Carney, then the governor of the Bank of Canada, a role in his Conservative government in 2012 — though not as finance minister. Not right away, at least.

In his new book “Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister,” Harper says he told Carney the finance position was already taken but indicated that he would be next in line for the job when it became vacant.

“Obviously, I did not offer him the post of minister of finance, as it was then not available. However, I indicated that, if he chose to join the government, he would be the leading candidate should the post come open,” Harper writes.

Carney said in an interview on CBC during the 2025 Liberal leadership race that Harper had “asked me if I would be his finance minister in 2012.” He said at the time it wouldn’t be appropriate to go directly from the Bank of Canada governorship to party politics.

In his book, released Tuesday, Harper says while Carney was “highly effective” as bank governor, his finance minister Jim Flaherty was “increasingly” worried in the wake of the 2011 election that Carney was nurturing political ambitions and might wish to seek the Liberal party leadership — something widely rumoured at the time.

“This was a serious concern for us,” Harper writes.

Harper says he brought it up with Nigel Wright, his chief of staff, who suggested a job offer would either secure Carney’s services for the government or force him to rule out a Liberal leadership bid, since he was in the non-partisan role of bank governor.

“Mark took some time to reflect on the opportunity, ultimately declaring that he should stay out of partisan politics,” he said, noting Carney left soon after for the top job at the Bank of England.

The mention of Carney is just a small aside in the nearly 650-page memoir. Harper says he felt he should address the issue since it has “occasionally cropped up in the media.”

The book offers Harper’s perspective on his tenure in Canadian politics from start to finish, from uniting the right under the modern Conservative party through a decade in government.

It also contains a rare first-person account of Harper’s final election campaign and the defeat of his government in 2015.

The former prime minister writes that he debated stepping down from the leadership in the summer of 2014 to rejuvenate the party.

Harper says after deciding to remain at the helm and lead his party into what he knew would be a tough race, he decided he would serve until just after the 150th anniversary of Confederation on July 1, 2017, then call a leadership race.

Harper also says he only learned of one of the most controversial episodes of the 2015 election — his party’s embrace of a “barbaric cultural practices hotline” — during his preparation for the French leaders’ debate in Montreal when the news “flashed across my screen.”

The announcement of the proposed tip line — which frustrated Red Tories and hindered the party’s outreach efforts with multicultural communities years after the fact — was fronted at the time by former cabinet ministers Kellie Leitch and Chris Alexander.

Harper writes he was “furious” upon learning about the policy, which he says he was not consulted on and had to defend on the campaign trail.

The book spans decades of Canadian political history. It includes Harper’s description of face-to-face standoffs with Russian President Vladimir Putin at G8 meetings, his reaction to the 2008 parliamentary crisis — when opposition parties attempted and failed to form a coalition government to oust the Conservatives — and Harper’s personal experience during the 2014 shooting on Parliament Hill, which happened when he was without his normal personal protective detail.

The former prime minister also offers up occasional reflections on current matters. While he attended the World Economic Forum in Davos twice during in his time in office, he now says he opposes it.

If he were prime minister today, Harper writes, he would end the Canadian government’s participation in the WEF, an event he describes as a once-useful forum that has become a club for advancing the “narrow interests of its globalist, elitist attendees.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Retired Air Force Pilot with ALS is pushing for research funding in federal budget
stories.summary: Studies have found a potential link between ALS diagnoses and military service
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Bob Gibson flew all over the world during his 12 years as a pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force, but when he travelled to Ottawa from Guelph, Ont., last week, he was on a different mission.

Mr. Gibson was diagnosed with Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, in December, 2023, years after he started to have trouble moving his right foot, an issue medical providers initially attributed to back issues. He has since learned about several studies from multiple countries that found veterans appear to be diagnosed with ALS at rates higher than the general population.

The reason for the association remains a mystery.

In a 2013 policy document , Veterans Affairs Canada noted while the cause of ALS is largely unknown in the majority of cases, some scientific theories exist about potential triggers, including, but not limited to, exposure to neurotoxic substances, viral infections, dietary deficiencies, heavy labour and physical trauma.

Mr. Gibson is working with the ALS Society of Canada to try and secure $50-million in research funding from the federal government in Thursday’s budget to better understand the disease, including its potential link to military service.

He said in an interview that Canada needs to support further research on ALS, similar to other countries. In February, the U.S. Congress approved new federal funding for ALS research totalling US$315-million. ALS Canada says Australia and Britain also recognize the need for research spending.

The advocacy organization says the federal government has never offered specific funding for ALS research in past budgets.

“We’ve got a good group of people here,” Mr. Gibson said, referring to Canadian researchers. “Use them and get going.”

Mr. Gibson, 69, knows future research efforts won’t change the fact that ALS, which affects muscles involved in key functions such as breathing, will eventually take his life.

But the grandfather, known by his family for his stubborn streak, is determined to push ahead while he can.

After being diagnosed with ALS, Mr. Gibson said he had a choice to make: He could either feel bad about his situation or he could do whatever he could with his “last bit of time.”

Tammy Moore, chief executive officer of ALS Canada, is urging the government to fund research that could be used to evaluate the demographics of patients across the country and ensure they have access to clinical trials. Additionally, new funding would offer a chance to examine differences in outcomes, such as patients who live months compared with years.

Ms. Moore added that Canadian research could help answer outstanding questions about findings that veterans seem more likely to develop ALS. “We need to understand why,” she said.

ALS Canada said the first major signal of a pattern between ALS diagnoses and military service was found in 2003. Researchers had examined approximately 2.5 million U.S. military personnel who served worldwide during the Gulf War. Veterans who had deployed to the region were found to have nearly twice the risk, 92 per cent higher, of developing ALS compared with those who had not.

This summer, a study led by researchers at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health was published in Neurology, a peer-reviewed medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology. It looked at nearly 9.2 million male veterans who received care through the U.S. Veterans Health Administration from 2000 to 2024 and found ALS diagnosis rates varied based on which branch of the military a patient had served in, suggesting a potential link to environmental exposures.

Among the U.S. veterans, the study found 13,935 developed ALS. Compared with army veterans, those who served in the air force had a 29 per cent higher rate of the disease, coast guard veterans had a 26 per cent higher rate and navy veterans had a 15 per cent higher rate. Marine veterans had a 22 per cent lower rate, the study found.

“Officers and those serving in the Air Force, Navy, or Coast Guard May incur exposure to military environments that increase risk of ALS,” it said. “It is imperative to identify relevant exposures to reduce harm to service members and, potentially, civilians with similar exposures,” the study said.

Defence Minister David McGuinty has expressed concern about the potential link between disease and military service, and pledged last week that Ottawa would look into the matter in relation to ALS.

In the House of Commons last week, Conservative MP Michael Barrett raised Mr. Gibson’s case and said he supports the ALS community’s call for $50-million in federal spending on research.

Amid their push for research funding, Mr. Gibson and his wife Charmaine Gibson worry the same diagnosis will land on their son, Kyle, a 39-year-old who spent 17 years as a pilot in the Air Force.

Veterans deserve to know about the risk of developing the disease, Ms. Gibson said, adding it is not sufficient to compensate former service members who develop ALS. There must be answers, she said.

Before he learned his father had ALS, Kyle Gibson said that he never thought his time in the military could be linked to a heightened risk for the disease.

Kyle said it has been a shock to see how debilitating ALS is for his dad and the thought of developing the condition himself lives in the back of his mind.

He applauds his father for pushing the federal government to fund scientific research that could help other patients.

“I think it’s kind of shameful that he has to fight that hard for it, though.”
paragraphs: Bob Gibson flew all over the world during his 12 years as a pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force, but when he travelled to Ottawa from Guelph, Ont., last week, he was on a different mission.

Mr. Gibson was diagnosed with Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, in December, 2023, years after he started to have trouble moving his right foot, an issue medical providers initially attributed to back issues. He has since learned about several studies from multiple countries that found veterans appear to be diagnosed with ALS at rates higher than the general population.
The reason for the association remains a mystery.

In a 2013 policy document , Veterans Affairs Canada noted while the cause of ALS is largely unknown in the majority of cases, some scientific theories exist about potential triggers, including, but not limited to, exposure to neurotoxic substances, viral infections, dietary deficiencies, heavy labour and physical trauma.

Mr. Gibson is working with the ALS Society of Canada to try and secure $50-million in research funding from the federal government in Thursday’s budget to better understand the disease, including its potential link to military service.

He said in an interview that Canada needs to support further research on ALS, similar to other countries. In February, the U.S. Congress approved new federal funding for ALS research totalling US$315-million. ALS Canada says Australia and Britain also recognize the need for research spending.
The advocacy organization says the federal government has never offered specific funding for ALS research in past budgets.
“We’ve got a good group of people here,” Mr. Gibson said, referring to Canadian researchers. “Use them and get going.”
Mr. Gibson, 69, knows future research efforts won’t change the fact that ALS, which affects muscles involved in key functions such as breathing, will eventually take his life.
But the grandfather, known by his family for his stubborn streak, is determined to push ahead while he can.
After being diagnosed with ALS, Mr. Gibson said he had a choice to make: He could either feel bad about his situation or he could do whatever he could with his “last bit of time.”

Tammy Moore, chief executive officer of ALS Canada, is urging the government to fund research that could be used to evaluate the demographics of patients across the country and ensure they have access to clinical trials. Additionally, new funding would offer a chance to examine differences in outcomes, such as patients who live months compared with years.
Ms. Moore added that Canadian research could help answer outstanding questions about findings that veterans seem more likely to develop ALS. “We need to understand why,” she said.

ALS Canada said the first major signal of a pattern between ALS diagnoses and military service was found in 2003. Researchers had examined approximately 2.5 million U.S. military personnel who served worldwide during the Gulf War. Veterans who had deployed to the region were found to have nearly twice the risk, 92 per cent higher, of developing ALS compared with those who had not.

This summer, a study led by researchers at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health was published in Neurology, a peer-reviewed medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology. It looked at nearly 9.2 million male veterans who received care through the U.S. Veterans Health Administration from 2000 to 2024 and found ALS diagnosis rates varied based on which branch of the military a patient had served in, suggesting a potential link to environmental exposures.

Among the U.S. veterans, the study found 13,935 developed ALS. Compared with army veterans, those who served in the air force had a 29 per cent higher rate of the disease, coast guard veterans had a 26 per cent higher rate and navy veterans had a 15 per cent higher rate. Marine veterans had a 22 per cent lower rate, the study found.

“Officers and those serving in the Air Force, Navy, or Coast Guard May incur exposure to military environments that increase risk of ALS,” it said. “It is imperative to identify relevant exposures to reduce harm to service members and, potentially, civilians with similar exposures,” the study said.
Defence Minister David McGuinty has expressed concern about the potential link between disease and military service, and pledged last week that Ottawa would look into the matter in relation to ALS.
In the House of Commons last week, Conservative MP Michael Barrett raised Mr. Gibson’s case and said he supports the ALS community’s call for $50-million in federal spending on research.
Amid their push for research funding, Mr. Gibson and his wife Charmaine Gibson worry the same diagnosis will land on their son, Kyle, a 39-year-old who spent 17 years as a pilot in the Air Force.
Veterans deserve to know about the risk of developing the disease, Ms. Gibson said, adding it is not sufficient to compensate former service members who develop ALS. There must be answers, she said.
Before he learned his father had ALS, Kyle Gibson said that he never thought his time in the military could be linked to a heightened risk for the disease.
Kyle said it has been a shock to see how debilitating ALS is for his dad and the thought of developing the condition himself lives in the back of his mind.
He applauds his father for pushing the federal government to fund scientific research that could help other patients.
“I think it’s kind of shameful that he has to fight that hard for it, though.”

stories.title: Former Alberta junior hockey executive charged with sex offences against players
stories.summary: King had worked with various teams across Alberta, Ontario and BC, including the Okotoks Oilers with the British Columbia Hockey League.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A former junior hockey executive in Alberta has been charged with sexually exploiting three players.

Tyler King, 39, was arrested Friday at a U.S. border crossing in Ontario, RCMP announced Monday.

He had been working with the State University of New York campus at Oswego in New York state.

RCMP said the 39-year-old is to be returned later this week to Alberta to face charges of luring, sexual exploitation and making child pornography.

The three complainants, all under 18 at the time of the allegations, were junior A players from Saskatchewan and Alberta.

“We are still actively investigating the span of the time that (these offences) happened,” Cpl. Daniel Campbell said during a virtual news conference.

“Given the seriousness of the accusations and to protect the integrity of the investigation, it was important that we proceed carefully and thoroughly at every stage.”

King had worked with various teams across Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia, including the Okotoks Oilers with the British Columbia Hockey League.

Mounties said the Alberta-based Oilers reported in June 2024 that a former employee had allegedly solicited and compensated players for intimate images and sexual videos.

A statement published on the team’s website around the same time announced King was leaving his job.

“The Okotoks Oilers would like to thank Tyler Kingfor his tireless efforts during his three seasons in our organization as Assistant GM, Business Operations,” said the June 2024 statement.

It said King had been in charge of overseeing all off-ice operations.

“During his second and third seasons with the Oilers, Tyler served as the main play-by-play voice of the team on The Eagle 100.9 FM in Okotoks and online streaming platforms,” it added.

The Oilers said in a statement Monday that it became aware of the allegations against King after he left the team.

“After his departure, we received information that, while unverified at the time, raised enough concern that we felt it needed a closer look,” said Brent Lauinger, the team’s chairman and governor

“We reviewed it carefully and passed it to the RCMP.”

The university in New York state said King joined the school in 2025 as a professor of practice with its communications studies department.

“We are aware of the arrest in Canada and are co-ordinating with law enforcement,” it said in an email. “Because this is an ongoing criminal matter involving a university employee, we cannot comment further at this time.”

Campbell said the Oilers have also been co-operative with investigators.

“They’re obviously very concerned for their players,” he said.

stories.title: Blue Jays decline $8M club option for outfielder Myles Straw
stories.summary: The option was for $8 million and would have been the fourth season of the 32-year-old's five-year, $25 million deal.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Toronto Blue Jays have declined the 2027 club option for outfielder Myles Straw, the MLB club announced Monday.

The option was for US$8 million and would have been the fourth season of the 32-year-old’s five-year, $25 million deal.

Straw had three home runs and 26 RBIs while batting .241 in 147 games for Toronto this past season.

Meanwhile, outfielder Rudy Martin Jr. elected for free agency and right-hander CJ Van Eyk has cleared waivers and been assigned to triple-A Buffalo.

The Blue Jays also reinstated a host of players from the injured list.

Outfielders Anthony Santander, Jonatan Clase and Addison Barger and right-handers Jose Berrios, Jake Bloss, Cody Ponce and Bowden Francis were all taken off the 60-day IL.

stories.title: How a New Brunswick island is caught in the middle of the Canada-U.S. trade war
stories.summary: A Canadian island reliant on the U.S. for everyday necessities is caught in the middle as tensions strain a centuries-old relationship.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Jeff Semple
stories.content:
For most Canadians, avoiding the United States amid a bitter trade war might mean skipping a cross-border shopping trip or choosing a vacation closer to home.

But for the roughly 900 people who live on Campobello Island , N.B., it’s not that simple.

The Canadian island sits just off Lubec, Maine, and is cut off by road from the rest of Canada. Its only bridge leads to the United States, making crossing the border a part of everyday life.

There’s no gas station on Campobello and grocery options are limited, sending residents across the border for basic necessities.

“It’s kind of unique,” said American fisherman Dana Barker, who has lived on Campobello Island with his Canadian wife for 50 years. “There’s not a gas station (on the island).”

For one student who lives on the island but attends high school in the U.S., crossing an international border is simply part of the morning routine. “Yeah, I cross the border almost every morning,” she told Global News.

“And there aren’t a lot of grocery store options, so we have to do most of our shopping over (in Maine).”

That closeness between the two countries is woven into the island’s history.

British loyalists fled to Campobello after the American Revolution. The United States later relinquished its claim to the island following the War of 1812 in exchange for other islands.

Beginning in the 1880s, Franklin D. Roosevelt’s family spent summers at a home on Campobello, a tradition that continued during his presidency.

Today, the historic site is jointly owned and operated by Canada and the United States, a symbol of a friendship that has connected the two countries for generations.

“The park’s primary purpose and mission is the friendship, unity, and mutual respect that both nations have for each other,” said John Southern of Roosevelt Campobello International Park.

But that relationship has become increasingly complicated as tensions between Canada and the United States spill across the border.

Canadian tourism to Maine was cut in half last year following U.S. President Donald Trump’s taunts and tariffs.

On Campobello, the impact has been even harder to escape.

Residents were forced to pay a 25 per cent tariff on U.S. goods brought across the border until Ottawa announced a special exemption for the island.

Last month, a truckload of supplies was turned back by U.S. border officials. A Campobello brewery has also shut down because of the tariffs.

“So decisions that are made in capitals far away have an impact immediately on Campobello,” New Brunswick MP John Williamson said.

On the other side of the bridge, some Americans say the political tensions risk damaging a relationship that has long defined their neighbouring communities.

“There’s no reason to be causing bad blood among good neighbours,” Lubec resident Nelson Meaker said. “It’s just crazy.”

Lubec, the easternmost municipality on the U.S. mainland, usually votes Republican. But pollsters are predicting a closer race in the midterm elections, with voters concerned about the cost of living and the trade war with Canada.

For Campobello residents, whatever happens in Washington or Ottawa has a way of quickly reaching their small island.

But Barker believes the ties connecting the two sides of the border are stronger than the political dispute dividing them.

“Oh yeah, we’re gonna work it out,” he said. “We’re too close.”

Then, with one exception: “Except for hockey!”

stories.title: Former Junior A hockey executive charged with child luring, sexual exploitation in Alberta
stories.summary: A former Junior A hockey broadcaster and executive who worked with teams across Western Canada is facing five charges related to alleged sexual offences involving underage male hockey players from Alberta and Saskatchewan, as RCMP investigate whether there are additional victims.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
“Our investigation is solely focused on our three (victims) as of right now,” said RCMP Cpl. Dan Campbell. “We’ll be welcoming anyone that believes that they were a victim as well to come forward.”

Tyler Robb King, 39, has been charged with three counts of child luring, one count of sexual exploitation and one count of making child pornography.

RCMP say the three alleged victims were male hockey players from Alberta and Saskatchewan who were under 18 at the time of the alleged offences. All three played hockey within the Okotoks Oilers Athletic Association.

According to court documents, the three child-luring charges involve separate alleged victims, with offences said to have occurred at or near Okotoks, Alta.

The first allegedly occurred between June 2021 and April 2023, the second between January 2021 and October 2024, and the third between September and October 2022.

The investigation began after the organization contacted police about a former employee.

Campbell said the Okotoks Oilers reported “that one of their former employees was soliciting and compensating players for intimate images and sexual videos.”

In a statement Monday, the Okotoks Oilers said they were “not aware of these allegations while this individual was with our organization.”

“After his departure, we received information that, while unverified at the time, raised enough concern that we felt it needed a closer look. We reviewed it carefully and passed it to the RCMP.”

The organization said it is co-operating with investigators and that the safety and well-being of its players remain its highest priority.

King joined the Okotoks Oilers in 2021, where he spent three seasons before moving to British Columbia to work with the Nanaimo Clippers as vice-president of business operations.

The Brooks Bandits also issued a statement Monday, saying the organization is aware of the case and will co-operate with local RCMP.

In 2025, King joined the State University of New York at Oswego as a professor of practice specializing in multimedia journalism and sports, according to his university biography. The biography also identifies him as a faculty adviser to the campus television station.

Police say King was arrested Friday at the Lansdowne border crossing near Kingston, Ont., after living and working in the United States.

He was remanded into custody following a judicial interim release hearing and is expected to be returned to Alberta to face the charges.

The RCMP investigation remains ongoing, with police working alongside other jurisdictions as they seek to identify any additional potential victims.

None of the allegations have been proven in court.

‘If bad adults are in positions of power, bad things can happen’

For Greg Gilhooly, a lawyer and survivor of sexual abuse by former junior hockey coach Graham James, the allegations bring back painful memories.

“The decades kind of fall away. And I’m taken back to when I was a teen and, you know, trying to remember just how vulnerable I was at the time,” he said.

Gilhooly said young athletes can be particularly vulnerable when adults hold significant influence over their futures.

“Because so much is at play and adults have control over your future, if bad adults are in positions of power, bad things can happen.”

Doug King, a professor of justice studies at Mount Royal University, said the allegations highlight the seriousness of potential abuses of trust and authority.

“If you are under the age of 18 and a person in power, trust or authority uses that power, trust, authority to exploit you, that’s serious,” he said.

Gilhooly also warned against dismissing allegations simply because someone is well regarded in the community.

“Anybody is capable of everything, and you don’t ever really know anybody,” he said.

For anyone considering reporting past abuse, Gilhooly said the decision must remain their own.

“I would never tell somebody to come forward who wasn’t comfortable coming forward. But I would say that coming forward has been a good thing for me in terms of my recovery.”

stories.title: Leonard Cohen lives on as his son and grandson mark 10 years since singer’s death
stories.summary: Ten years after losing his father, Adam Cohen spots him everywhere.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

Posted November 3, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated November 3, 2026 5:02 am.

Ten years after losing his father, Adam Cohen spots him everywhere.

“I happen to have inherited his body type and his voice, and when I catch a glimpse of myself in the mirror, I see him,” says the 54-year-old singer-songwriter.

Beyond that, the world brings its own reminders: songs playing in taxis and restaurants, buskers singing on street corners, videos of weddings and funerals set to his father’s music.

“I don’t know that there’s been a single day that I haven’t thought of him and that the world hasn’t provoked me to do it.”

Now, he’s seeking a more deliberate connection, gathering his own son and fellow artists for a concert marking a decade since his father’s death.

“Everybody Knows Leonard Cohen: The Official 10th Anniversary Concert Celebration” is a family-led tribute bringing the bard of Montreal’s music to Canadian stages this month before heading to Europe in early 2027.

Created and directed by Adam Cohen, the production combines performances with archival footage. Feist, Rufus Wainwright and Serena Ryder are among the guests announced for Toronto’s Meridian Hall on Nov. 7, exactly 10 years after Leonard Cohen’s death.

Over a career spanning five decades, Cohen was one of Canada’s most revered artists, bringing a poet’s sensibility and a distinctive baritone to enduring songs such as “Hallelujah” and “Suzanne.”

Adam Cohen and his 19-year-old son, Cassius, have been working through Leonard’s songs in the family home in Montreal, a bittersweet way of reconnecting with the late singer-songwriter.

“Just playing his songs and really studying them word for word, chord for chord is the closest thing to the grief that I remember of having lost him,” he says in an interview from the kitchen where they shared countless meals.

“It’s accompanied with a kind of deliciousness and deep appreciation for the man that you can only have when you’re practising someone’s song.”

The production also serves a more immediate parental concern: putting his own son to work.

After Cassius Cohen dropped out of college last summer and announced he wanted to be a musician, Adam hired him as his bass player for performances in Germany and Greece.

“If he’s not going to go to college, then he should be working with the same appetite and rigour that school was expecting of him, but in music,” he says.

Now, hearing his son perform his father’s songs brings back memories of three generations sitting at the dinner table.

“The whole thing is beautiful and touching and emotional.”

And while it could easily become sentimental, he says Cassius’s musicianship gives him plenty other reasons to be proud.

“He’s far more accomplished technically than I am.”

Adam Cohen knows a thing or two about seeking a father’s approval through music.

He recalls the bard saying he wanted his son to become something more important in society.

“He would often joke that he wanted me to be prime minister of Canada and he referred to the music business as a racket, a cesspool,” he says.

“There was a kind of disappointment that I’d followed in his footsteps.”

But being chosen to produce 2016’s “You Want It Darker,” Leonard Cohen’s final album released during his lifetime, offered Adam a chance to prove himself.

Revisiting the catalogue now, Cohen says he’s struck by the painstaking choices behind it: every chord, adjective and cadence.

“The common expression is that they don’t make things the way they used to,” he says.

“His work lasts because it’s imbued with a kind of devotional labour. It aims for a kind of excellence that is a triumph over planned obsolescence.”

The tribute, which also hits Montreal this week, aims to summon Leonard Cohen’s presence, including the humour that accompanied his wisdom. Adam says it’s less about revealing an unknown side of his father than remembering the qualities audiences already cherish.

“We’ll do our best to capture the entirety of the man.”

One might imagine that aura of effortless cool occasionally gave way to a corny dad moment behind closed doors. But Adam has no such anecdotes.

“Not even when he was being extremely funny or light or jovial was there anything inconsistent,” he says.

“He did it in his inimitable style, and there was a throughline of elegance and humility and generosity and intelligence and presence. He was molecularly charged in a way that was very palpable to anyone who came in his midst.”

“I happen to have inherited his body type and his voice, and when I catch a glimpse of myself in the mirror, I see him,” says the 54-year-old singer-songwriter.
Beyond that, the world brings its own reminders: songs playing in taxis and restaurants, buskers singing on street corners, videos of weddings and funerals set to his father’s music.
“I don’t know that there’s been a single day that I haven’t thought of him and that the world hasn’t provoked me to do it.”
Now, he’s seeking a more deliberate connection, gathering his own son and fellow artists for a concert marking a decade since his father’s death.

“Everybody Knows Leonard Cohen: The Official 10th Anniversary Concert Celebration” is a family-led tribute bringing the bard of Montreal’s music to Canadian stages this month before heading to Europe in early 2027.

Created and directed by Adam Cohen, the production combines performances with archival footage. Feist, Rufus Wainwright and Serena Ryder are among the guests announced for Toronto’s Meridian Hall on Nov. 7, exactly 10 years after Leonard Cohen’s death.
Over a career spanning five decades, Cohen was one of Canada’s most revered artists, bringing a poet’s sensibility and a distinctive baritone to enduring songs such as “Hallelujah” and “Suzanne.”
Adam Cohen and his 19-year-old son, Cassius, have been working through Leonard’s songs in the family home in Montreal, a bittersweet way of reconnecting with the late singer-songwriter.
