“It’s accompanied with a kind of deliciousness and deep appreciation for the man that you can only have when you’re practising someone’s song.”
The production also serves a more immediate parental concern: putting his own son to work.
After Cassius Cohen dropped out of college last summer and announced he wanted to be a musician, Adam hired him as his bass player for performances in Germany and Greece.

stories.summary: ST John's - Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Antigua and Barbuda today for a meeting of Commonwealth heads of government.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:

By Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press

ST John’s - Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is a voice “for justice” as the United Kingdom considers offering a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade.

Carney was in the Caribbean nation of Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday for a meeting of Commonwealth leaders, where calls for reparations from the U.K. for its role in the slave trade were prominent.

Days before the summit began, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his government would consider apologizing for the first time for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but said reparations were not on the table.

In his opening speech to the summit Tuesday, Antigua Prime Minister Gaston Browne noted the last Commonwealth meeting in Samoa in 2024 included an agreement that “the time had come for a meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation on reparatory justice.”

“We must now carry that commitment forward through structured, inclusive dialogue on the enduring consequences of slavery and colonialism, with a determination to make progress and a willingness to build consensus,” Browne said.

In his speech at the summit, King Charles called the transatlantic slave trade a “shameful chapter of history” but did not issue an apology.

“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us. We can however learn from the past,” the King said.

“The transatlantic trade and enslaved persons still cast a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth. As I’ve said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.”

Hours later, when asked by reporters about the calls for an official apology and reparations, Carney said Ottawa is always speaking up for “justice” and wants to play a role in building consensus.

He said Burnham spoke to the issue in the room during Tuesday’s meetings and it would be addressed in a joint statement.

“You will see in the final communiqué a reflection of the consensus, the impact of his words and the process being put in place to move forward amongst the Commonwealth,” Carney said. “We’re supportive of that and that’s part of the role we can play in hearing all voices and moving towards consensus.”

The final summit communiqué welcomed the British government’s pledge “to engage in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms.”

Protesters demanding reparations set up outside the meeting. Carney and Burnham were among the world leaders who had to walk past them into the opening ceremony on Tuesday.

“Technically, we’re free, but mentally a lot of us aren’t,” said protester Shana Michelle of Antigua. “If you look at the way we speak about ourselves, our skin, our hair, how we describe ourselves, you can see we still have those vestiges of colonialism in our speech, and we have to get away from that.”

Countries in Caricom, an intergovernmental organization representing Caribbean nations, have proposed a 10-point plan for reparations.

Earlier in the day, Carney told Commonwealth leaders at a working breakfast meeting that Canada and the Caribbean have barely begun to realize what’s possible in their trading relationship.

“There’s more than a million people in Canada who trace their roots back to the region,” Carney told the assembled leaders before attending the opening of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in the capital St. John’s.

“There is growing trade, $4 billion a year more broadly … It scratches the surface of what’s possible.”

Carney began his day with a meeting with Browne, who told Carney at the start of their meeting that Canada “as a middle power is very influential in the Commonwealth globally.”

He said Canada can help “make the Commonwealth more consequential.” Carney replied that the gathering was “an extraordinarily important meeting at a crucial time.”

Carney’s office said in a readout that he discussed with Browne ways to do more in “trade and investment, energy, climate resilience, youth, tourism, people to people ties and the priorities of small island developing states.”

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand joined Carney at the working breakfast, where the prime minister gave each of the assembled Caribbean leaders a bottle of maple syrup with his own brand on it.

Heads of state and foreign ministers from Antigua, the Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Dominica, Grenada, Guyana, Jamaica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Trinidad and Tobago were in attendance, along with the secretary-general of Caricom.

“We all know how much the world has changed. We’re all responding to it. We all know that the best response is to build out the close ties of friendship,” Carney said in his opening remarks at the breakfast.

After the breakfast, Carney and the Caribbean leaders walked together to the venue where the Commonwealth heads of government meeting was being held, just a few minutes away.

Later in the day, Carney also met with Guyana President Mohamed Irfan Ali, who thanked Carney for his “enormous global leadership” and for expanding trade, security and biodiversity co-operation with Caribbean countries. Carney also met with the leaders of Australia and Ghana.

He later told reporters that leaders discussed trade and investment opportunities, strengthening supply chains and fostering sustainable economic growth.

“This is the moment when you pivot, and then you move in that direction,” Carney told reporters. He said his one-day visit started “to put in place some of the mechanisms that make that direction possible.”

In a press release following the meeting, the government said the prime minister had announced more than $70 million in new investments in Commonwealth countries, including the Caribbean. The release said the investments would go towards infrastructure, emergency preparedness, restoring forest ecosystems, and the fast dispatch of emergency relief.

Carney described talks on clean energy and mining collaboration and financing to deal with climate change — a cause Canada has championed in recent years and one that Caribbean leaders cite as one of their most pressing challenges.

Carney addressed Commonwealth leaders at a roundtable session titled “financing for development,” but his remarks were closed to media and the Prime Minister’s Office declined to provide a copy of his speech.

Carney also attended a lunch hosted by King Charles for new heads of government in the Commonwealth. The leaders of Gabon, Ghana, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia and the U.K. were also expected to attend the lunch, a spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office said.

Carney is attending a dinner also hosted by King Charles before he flies back to Ottawa late Tuesday. Neither event with the king, nor the King’s speech at the meeting, were accessible to Canadian media.

The Commonwealth is a voluntary coalition of 56 countries. Most of them have ties to the former British Empire. The leaders’ meeting is held every second year and is the first since Carney took office in March 2025.

The modern Commonwealth was established in 1949 and Commonwealth countries together represent 2.7 billion people. Commonwealth members include large countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, India and Nigeria, and many of the world’s smallest countries — such as Tuvalu, a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean with a population of about 10,000.

Experts say ties with Commonwealth countries can help Canada win support in multilateral forums like the United Nations, a strategy Canada has used in the past.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

— With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

stories.title: 'Screwed either way': Republican senator fights backlash over Trump tariffs in Maine
stories.summary: Fredericton - U.S. tariffs on Canada have played an outsized role in the Senate race in Maine, but experts say there May not be any relief coming for Canadians regardless of the outcome of Tuesday’s midterms.
stories.author: Eli Ridder The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Bangor - Maine Democrat Troy Jackson has ousted longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins to cap a U.S. Senate race that was, in part, shaped by the trade war between Canada and the United States.

It added to a blue wave that propelled the Democrats to take control of the Senate and punished allies of President Donald Trump.

“We have to stand up to Donald Trump. We have to stand up for our democracy,” Jackson told supporters in a victory speech.

Maine, a Northeastern state that borders New Brunswick and Quebec, imports billions of dollars in products from Canada, such as electricity, seafood and plastics.

Polling showed a majority of voters in Maine were unhappy with Trump policies that have pushed up energy prices and caused Canadian tourism to plummet.

Collins publicly opposed Trump’s tariffs on Canada and lobbied for some exemptions, though Jackson said she hadn’t done enough to fight the president’s broader tariff regime.

Many voters who spoke to The Canadian Press on Tuesday hoped for an end to the tariff skirmish between the two countries that Trump started after coming into office last year.

Sydney Olson said she doesn’t see why the United States would wage a trade war with Canada. She said the economy played into her vote for Jackson.

“There’s hardly any Americans who want Canadians to be antagonized and want to be in a trade war with Canada,” Olson said outside a Bangor polling station Tuesday.

“We have no problem with Canada. We love Canada. Why bother?”

Michael Furrow, a retired military officer, said he voted for Collins because of her ability to get federal backing for projects critical to Maine’s economy.

The 23-year-old said he also wanted to see an end to Trump’s tariffs on Canadian imports.

“Trade needs to be open and free across the border,” Furrow said outside the arena where he voted Tuesday.

“We got two great countries. Work together and I think we can do wonderful things.”

“Canada’s our friend and neighbour. Why should we be treating them like we’re treating them?” Dan O’Connell asked as he headed into a polling station in Brewer, Maine.

While he voted for Collins in the past, O’Connell said this year he was ready to back her opponent, in part so a Democrat-controlled Senate could rein in Trump’s tariffs.

Some Republican voters on Tuesday said they wanted the levies on Canadian imports to remain, at least to some extent.

“I’d like to see a level playing field,” Mark McPherson said after marking his ballot for Collins.

McPherson said he agreed with Trump’s claim that the U.S. has been “ripped off” through global trade.

Some voters said Canada was top of mind at the ballot box.

Donna Twombly, who was born in Maine, said her grandparents were Danish citizens who immigrated to Canada before settling in the U.S.

Twombly said she was angry when Trump imposed his first wave of levies on Canada and other countries.

“I went out and bought a Canadian flag,” she said.

“I only found a small one when I went shopping but I put it up on my home.”

Federal government figures show Maine imports $4.1 billion in goods from Canada each year, making it the state’s largest trading partner.

That includes $2 billion in heating oil, more than half a billion dollars in forestry products, and $263 million in electricity from New Brunswick.

In a column earlier this year, Maine Gov. Janet Mills said the state’s forest product exports to Canada had dropped 20 per cent since Trump started his trade war, causing job losses.

The number of trips by Canadians to Maine dipped sharply last year, according to an analysis of border data by the Maine Center for Economic Policy.

U.S. tariffs have strained New Brunswick’s forestry sector and manufacturing base and have cut into the bottom lines of breweries.

Political watchers said it was not clear which result would offer a win for Canada, or whether a win was even likely.

Collins pitched herself as an independent not afraid of breaking from her party and voting against Trump on tariffs she had long opposed.

Jackson, meanwhile, said Collins hadn’t done enough as a Republican to push back against the levies.

At a debate last month, Collins said she lobbied the White House to get Canadian concrete, pulp and road salt removed from the tariff list.

Jackson snapped back, saying, “We can’t eat road salt.”

The exchange went viral and spurred the sharing of “let them eat road salt” memes among progressives.

And less than two weeks before the midterm elections, Collins announced the U.S. would lift tariffs on nine categories of Canadian goods she said were crucial to Maine’s hard-hit agricultural industries.

It was seen as an attempt by Trump — who did not campaign in Maine this election cycle — to help Collins retain her seat.

But in the same executive order lifting some of the tariffs, Trump imposed levies on dozens of new categories, such as cocoa powder, paints and varnishes, shampoos, vinyl flooring, archery equipment and carpets.

Trump’s levies on a swath of countries triggered retaliatory tariffs by Ottawa and a trade war that has damaged industries and raised costs on both sides of the border.

The previous round of trade talks between the two sides broke down in August, though Trump said Sunday that Canada and the United States were close to reaching a “very good” trade deal.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada has since started “more intense” trade negotiations with the United States after speaking with Trump over the weekend.

“We’ve made progress but we haven’t finished,” he told reporters Tuesday during a trip to Antigua and Barbuda.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

— With files from Kelly Geraldine Malone in Detroit and The Associated Press

stories.title: Ottawa’s focus groups report low awareness of federal deficit, budget updates
stories.summary: Ottawa — The Liberal government is getting ready to table its 2026 budget on Thursday — but Ottawa's own focus groups suggest Canadians aren't watching the state of the federal purse too closely.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Liberal government is getting ready to table its 2026 budget on Thursday — but Ottawa’s own focus groups suggest Canadians aren’t watching the state of the federal purse too closely.

Finance Canada commissioned market research firm Environics to host a series of roundtables with Canadians roughly a week after Ottawa tabled its spring economic update on April 28.

Mid-year fiscal updates offer Canadians a glimpse of federal finances between budgets and sometimes include announcements of new items or spending priorities.

Over the course of a week, Environics conducted 10 online focus groups across the country involving 73 people, divided between younger and older Canadians.

A final report from the focus groups was delivered by Environics on June 4, a month before the federal government embarked on pre-budget consultations for the summer. The report was only recently published online.

The report suggests Canadians tend to tune out fiscal updates.

“Top of mind awareness of the spring economic update was very low, even after participants had been prompted about it having taken place,” the report found.

Since the 2025 federal election, the Liberals have broadly deepened deficits with new spending to pivot Canada’s economy away from reliance on the United States. The April fiscal update showed a general improvement in near-term deficits, thanks mostly to stronger-than-expected economic results at the end of last year.

Regardless of the state of the borrowing track, the report noted focus group participants expressed “little concern about the deficit.” Most participants felt there was no point in trying to balance the budget quickly, given disruptions from U.S. tariffs and the war in the Middle East.

“For most, the deficit is just a number and they had little sense of what that really meant or how it affected their personal lives or standard of living,” the report stated.

Among other consequences, prolonged deep government deficits require more federal money to service interest costs. A tighter fiscal situation can eventually restrict a government’s ability to respond to economic shocks.

Many participants did tell Environics they understood on some level that running deep deficits can harm the economy and there should be a plan to bring borrowing under control.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre regularly rails against the Liberals over deficits and is urging the government to cut wasteful spending ahead of Thursday’s budget.

The Liberal government claims its fiscal guardrails — shrinking the deficit as a share of the economy and borrowing only for capital investment starting next year — are keeping it on a sustainable track.

Some roundtable participants did say they were aware of a few specific items highlighted in the update. But awareness was low even when it came to the Liberals’ landmark affordability measures, Environics found.

Few participants reported knowing about the Liberals’ grocery and essentials payment, which replaced and expanded the previous GST benefit for lower-income households.

A pause on the federal fuel excise tax was viewed positively, Environics reported, but some confused it with the Liberals’ move to kill the consumer carbon price a year earlier.

The spring economic update also included a plan to spend nearly $6 billion to foster more careers for young Canadians in the skilled trades.

“Most participants had not heard anything” about such a plan, the report said, adding most reacted favourably when informed about it.

Finance Canada uses regular roundtables to get a sense of how the public is responding to its efforts to guide the economy. Environics noted these focus groups offer a range of opinions but the firm does not weigh those findings as a traditional poll might.

“The use of qualitative research allows the department to get a clear and current sense of the evolution of the public mood towards the state of the economy, the sense of personal economic well-being and government actions in the economic sphere,” the report states.

This week’s budget will show whether a tailwind from higher global oil prices has offset the surge in federal spending commitments since the spring economic statement.

When Prime Minister Mark Carney took office in 2025, he reversed the federal government’s fiscal schedule — the budget is now tabled in the fall, and mid-year updates in the spring.

Only two or three older participants who labelled themselves as “news junkies” reported being aware of a spring economic update, the Environics report noted.

There was stronger awareness of Carney’s travels overseas to find new trading partners for Canada, and a broader recognition of American news stories over Canadian ones.

That was particularly true among younger participants, who reported getting more of their news from TikTok and Instagram, where Environics noted U.S. news is more prevalent.

Despite the low awareness of the spring economic update, Environics said that after they were told about the contents of the plan, participants’ “opinions were mixed but generally neutral to positive.”

“Many participants noted that they did not have high expectations from the federal government in the first place,” the report said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Americans head to the polls for midterm election referendum on Trump's tenure
stories.summary: Detroit - Americans head to the polls Tuesday to vote in U.S. midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump's chaotic and controversial second term.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Detroit - A blue wave crashed over the American political system in Tuesday’s midterm elections as voters sent a message rebuking President Donald Trump’s chaotic and controversial second term.

Democrats took control of the House and the Senate during the election that will reorder control of Congress and bring a check on Trump’s unprecedented use of executive power over the remainder of his time in office.

Key races in Maine and Michigan, where Trump’s trade war with Canada has soured voters, solidified the Democrats’ triumph.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A Landslide!” Trump posted on social media just before 11 p.m. ET.

Republicans were on the defensive throughout the turbulent midterm campaign season, with polls showing Trump’s approval plummeting due to rising gas and diesel prices, high inflation and the unpopular war with Iran.

Trump’s closing arguments Monday did little to shore up enthusiasm.

He defended his administration’s policies and claimed his second term had seen the “best” economy ever, despite widespread voter disapproval of his handling of pocketbook issues.

Voters in some of the most Republican-safe areas showed their frustration with the president and the GOP, including in Texas, where James Talarico broke a decades-long Democrat losing streak by trouncing Trump-aligned Ken Paxton.

In Michigan, Democrats faced a key test during a shocking eleventh-hour party fracture in a tight Senate race when Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

Alan Latham, a 44-year-old attorney and lifelong Michigander, said he worried about affordability but was more motivated to back a candidate who promised progress over polarization.

“For me the candidate that’s going to push us forward in a positive direction as a country, as a people, unify us, is what really brought me out to the polls and what really is important to me as a voter and as a citizen,” Latham said after casting a ballot in White Lake for El-Sayed.

At the same polling station, Mark Pospisil, 43, said he’s pretty neutral on political issues. He said he voted for Rogers because the Republican would “honour and fear God and be best to implement good laws for our community.”

Michigan’s economy is tightly integrated with Canada and has been hit hard by tariffs. Rogers last month broke ranks with Trump over the tariffs slapped on Canada, and El-Sayed has long called the trade war nonsensical.

As counts slowly came in late Tuesday, Rogers and El-Sayed’s chances remained close. At a Republican event in Detroit, Rogers’ wife Kristi told supporters to “stick with us.”

“It’s going to be good,” she said.

Some spectators whispered concerns when Democrat Roy Cooper won North Carolina’s Senate race and Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff was re-elected in Georgia, even as GOP staffers encouraged supporters to stay optimistic.

Rogers’ defeat was solidified early Wednesday with El-Sayed set to become the nation’s first Muslim Senator.

The tight race in Maine saw Democrat Troy Jackson end the nearly 30-year run of Republican Susan Collins.

Trump last month attempted to give Collins a boost in the tough contest by making changes to 50 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods to offer a reprieve to industries hit hard in Maine. The move was not enough to stop the blue wave from sweeping the state in response to high energy prices and a plummet in Canadian tourism.

“We have to stand up to Donald Trump. We have to stand up for our democracy,” Jackson told supporters early Wednesday.

Tyler Levesque, who cast his ballot in Bangor, said: “Canada is our partner.”

“It’s not fair to us as Mainers, as a community, to suffer because of failed economic policy,” Levesque said Tuesday.

Many Americans were angered by Trump’s policies, which have driven up costs at gas stations and grocery stores.

Trump returned to the White House after promising to boost the economy, reduce inflation and keep the United States out of foreign wars. He made gains among young men, the Hispanic community and Black men based on those pledges.

Halfway through his second term, many of those same voters said they feel duped.

Dylan Raford supported Trump in 2024 — though he was too young to vote at the time — and hyped up the president to family and friends. The 19-year-old from South Carolina described himself as a business owner, entrepreneur and “big free market type of guy.”

Raford said he felt betrayed.

“I did like Trump. I did. As a Black person, I got so much hate for it,” Raford said.

“He made me a fool. He made all those people right.”

Like many voters who turned out for Trump in 2024, Raford said he had no party affiliation. He said he was voting Democrat because he wanted Trump to face restraints.

Democrat Annie Andrews flipped Lindsey Graham’s old seat in the historically red South Carolina Senate race.

It was a sharp rejection of Trump’s hand-picked candidate, Darline Graham Nordone, who was criticized for her lack of experience and multiple fumbles on the campaign trail as she sought to take her late brother’s seat.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

— With files from Eli Ridder in Bangor and The Associated Press
paragraphs: Detroit - A blue wave crashed over the American political system in Tuesday’s midterm elections as voters sent a message rebuking President Donald Trump’s chaotic and controversial second term.

Democrats took control of the House and the Senate during the election that will reorder control of Congress and bring a check on Trump’s unprecedented use of executive power over the remainder of his time in office.
Key races in Maine and Michigan, where Trump’s trade war with Canada has soured voters, solidified the Democrats’ triumph.
“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A Landslide!” Trump posted on social media just before 11 p.m. ET.

Republicans were on the defensive throughout the turbulent midterm campaign season, with polls showing Trump’s approval plummeting due to rising gas and diesel prices, high inflation and the unpopular war with Iran.
Trump’s closing arguments Monday did little to shore up enthusiasm.
He defended his administration’s policies and claimed his second term had seen the “best” economy ever, despite widespread voter disapproval of his handling of pocketbook issues.

Voters in some of the most Republican-safe areas showed their frustration with the president and the GOP, including in Texas, where James Talarico broke a decades-long Democrat losing streak by trouncing Trump-aligned Ken Paxton.

In Michigan, Democrats faced a key test during a shocking eleventh-hour party fracture in a tight Senate race when Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican candidate Mike Rogers.
Alan Latham, a 44-year-old attorney and lifelong Michigander, said he worried about affordability but was more motivated to back a candidate who promised progress over polarization.

“For me the candidate that’s going to push us forward in a positive direction as a country, as a people, unify us, is what really brought me out to the polls and what really is important to me as a voter and as a citizen,” Latham said after casting a ballot in White Lake for El-Sayed.

At the same polling station, Mark Pospisil, 43, said he’s pretty neutral on political issues. He said he voted for Rogers because the Republican would “honour and fear God and be best to implement good laws for our community.”

Michigan’s economy is tightly integrated with Canada and has been hit hard by tariffs. Rogers last month broke ranks with Trump over the tariffs slapped on Canada, and El-Sayed has long called the trade war nonsensical.
As counts slowly came in late Tuesday, Rogers and El-Sayed’s chances remained close. At a Republican event in Detroit, Rogers’ wife Kristi told supporters to “stick with us.”
“It’s going to be good,” she said.

Some spectators whispered concerns when Democrat Roy Cooper won North Carolina’s Senate race and Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff was re-elected in Georgia, even as GOP staffers encouraged supporters to stay optimistic.
Rogers’ defeat was solidified early Wednesday with El-Sayed set to become the nation’s first Muslim Senator.
The tight race in Maine saw Democrat Troy Jackson end the nearly 30-year run of Republican Susan Collins.

Trump last month attempted to give Collins a boost in the tough contest by making changes to 50 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods to offer a reprieve to industries hit hard in Maine. The move was not enough to stop the blue wave from sweeping the state in response to high energy prices and a plummet in Canadian tourism.
“We have to stand up to Donald Trump. We have to stand up for our democracy,” Jackson told supporters early Wednesday.
Tyler Levesque, who cast his ballot in Bangor, said: “Canada is our partner.”
“It’s not fair to us as Mainers, as a community, to suffer because of failed economic policy,” Levesque said Tuesday.
Many Americans were angered by Trump’s policies, which have driven up costs at gas stations and grocery stores.

Trump returned to the White House after promising to boost the economy, reduce inflation and keep the United States out of foreign wars. He made gains among young men, the Hispanic community and Black men based on those pledges.
Halfway through his second term, many of those same voters said they feel duped.

Dylan Raford supported Trump in 2024 — though he was too young to vote at the time — and hyped up the president to family and friends. The 19-year-old from South Carolina described himself as a business owner, entrepreneur and “big free market type of guy.”
Raford said he felt betrayed.
“I did like Trump. I did. As a Black person, I got so much hate for it,” Raford said.
“He made me a fool. He made all those people right.”
Like many voters who turned out for Trump in 2024, Raford said he had no party affiliation. He said he was voting Democrat because he wanted Trump to face restraints.
Democrat Annie Andrews flipped Lindsey Graham’s old seat in the historically red South Carolina Senate race.

It was a sharp rejection of Trump’s hand-picked candidate, Darline Graham Nordone, who was criticized for her lack of experience and multiple fumbles on the campaign trail as she sought to take her late brother’s seat.

stories.title: Little evidence AI is to blame for decline in youth hiring, new StatCan study finds
stories.summary: A recent study from Statistics Canada suggests that while it May be more difficult for youth to land a job, AI is not necessarily to blame.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

Posted November 3, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated November 3, 2026 5:02 am.

A recent study from Statistics Canada suggests that while it may be more difficult for youth to land a job, AI is not necessarily to blame.

The study published last week said it found “no broad evidence” that the rise of AI has led to substantial decreases in hiring or increases in job separation rates — which account for voluntary and involuntary ending of employment — in Canada since November 2022, when ChatGPT publicly launched.

It also noted this was the case for younger workers and people in jobs it classified as potentially more susceptible to AI substitution, like data-entry clerks or computer coding-intensive occupations.

“AI is no doubt reshaping sort of workflows and redefining jobs right now. I have no doubt about that,” said Tahsin Mehdi, a senior research economist at the agency and study co-author. “It’s just, it may not be eliminating entire jobs right now.”

Statistics Canada noted hiring and job separation rates, which account for layoffs, from the six months before November 2022 to the six months ahead of August 2026 were “generally within historical ranges or represented a continuation of pre-existing trends.”

The study examined data from labour force surveys for workers aged 15 to 64 in Canada between January 2006 and August 2026 and classified jobs based on potential exposure to and complementarity with AI, which measured how the technology affects different jobs and if AI is a tool that can enhance a worker’s output or be a substitute for human tasks.

Mehdi said hiring and job separation rates were used because they can offer “early signals of shifts in the labour market” whether due to trade dynamics, economic factors, tech disruptions or AI.

YOUTH JOB MARKET

He said data showed a decline in hiring for young workers across industries, including jobs generally seen as less impacted by AI.

“It’s hard to sort of differentiate (or) sort of tease out, well, if it’s happening across the economy, then how can we really say that AI is definitely impacting certain jobs?” Mehdi said.

For example, the study noted that in jobs with low exposure to AI, the hiring rate for employees aged 15 to 29 decreased from four per cent in the six months before November 2022 to 3.3 per cent in the six months before August 2026. Meanwhile, over that same period, youth hiring rates in jobs more vulnerable to AI substitution edged down from 3.2 per cent to three per cent.

“We have a lot of competing economic forces out there,” Mehdi said. “AI is another layer of complexity, but we have trade dynamics, U.S. tariffs, we have immigration shocks over the past couple of years, the rapid growth in population, which had an impact on the labour. It’s sort of hard to tease out how AI fits into all that when we have so many things going on.”

The study also indicated hiring rates in coding-intensive jobs decreased from 2.5 per cent to 1.9 per cent in the 2022 to 2026 time span, but Mehdi said hiring in that field rose to above five per cent around 2020 and 2021, and firms may have over-hired during the pandemic.

“Often people sort of mischaracterize that as an AI effect, when in reality it could have been firms just simply adjusting their workforce,” he said.

Employment growth for younger workers was relatively weak — regardless of potential exposure to AI — in the post-pandemic period, according to the research.

“After the pandemic, the labour market did shift in a substantial way, and some groups of the population, such as youth, they might be still sort of feeling the reverberations and aftershocks from the pandemic,” Mehdi said.

DETECTING AI’S IMPACT

Still, the study lands amid ongoing fear over AI’s possible impact on jobs. Last week, The Associated Press reported Microsoft was offering voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States as the company spends heavily on AI.

Viet Vu, the manager of economic research at The Dais, a think tank at Toronto Metropolitan University, said he’s not surprised by Statistics Canada’s findings and it’s part of a growing body of evidence — including in his own research — that shows “you just can’t detect AI’s impact on the Canadian labour market just yet.”

Vu suggested fear over AI can arise from the fact that it has the potential to impact every sector of the economy and is changing at a pace faster than our labour market is accustomed to.

But he suggested a greater fear among young people comes from the notion that AI can “change the fundamental social contract of work.”

Most people go to school, gain experience in their respective field and use that to land a first job, which leads to future jobs until retirement, Vu explained.

“If any of these middle steps disappear, such as the step in which you’re getting your first job, where you no longer have the opportunity to translate what you learned in school, to leverage that into a career, then that spells a lot of trouble,” he said.

DISPELING FEAR AROUND AI

Studies like this one can “help dispel some of that immediate fear and counter some of the existing fearmongering” around AI’s impact on the workforce, Vu said, but it doesn’t address the unease people may have about the future.

“But these kinds of studies are really the only way for us to actually understand if those future scary worlds may actually come to be, and if it does come to be, for us be able to respond appropriately,” he said.

The study’s authors noted the insights represented early findings.

“As AI adoption accelerates, it will be essential to continue monitoring labour market trends to better understand how technological changes are reshaping the economy — and for whom,” the study said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Harper memoir says he never offered Carney finance ministry, despite prime minister’s claims
stories.summary: The possibility of Mark Carney becoming a political opponent was 'a serious concern for us,' writes Stephen Harper
stories.author: Stuart Thomson
stories.content:
Ottawa — Former prime minister Stephen Harper says he didn’t offer Mark Carney the job of finance minister in 2012, rebuffing a claim Carney made in an interview last year while he was running for Liberal leader.

In his newly released memoir, Harper writes that he did invite Carney to join his government and suggested that he would be the top candidate for the finance job if it opened up. But at the time, the job was held by Jim Flaherty, who was in his sixth year of what would be an eight-year tenure heading the Finance Department.

“Obviously, I did not offer him the post of minister of finance, as it was then not available. However, I indicated that, if he chose to join the government, he would be the leading candidate should the post come open,” writes Harper in the final chapter of Here for Canada, which was released Tuesday.

In the interview with CBC in February 2025, Carney said that Harper had directly asked him to be his finance minister.

“I have been offered positions in the past. For example, Prime Minister Harper asked me if I would be his finance minister in 2012,” Carney said.

Carney said he refused the job because it wouldn’t have been “appropriate” to “go directly from being governor into elective politics.”

In fact, Harper writes that it was Flaherty who kicked off the discussion in the prime minister’s office about Carney, when he told Harper that Carney “was nurturing political ambitions” that could lead him to run for the leadership of the federal Liberals.

Harper writes that his offer to Carney, who was Bank of Canada governor from 2007 to 2013, was partly an attempt to smoke out Carney’s aspirations.

The possibility of Carney becoming a political opponent was “a serious concern for us,” writes Harper. As the rumours gained steam, Harper’s then chief of staff Nigel Wright suggested that offering him a job would be a win-win scenario for the government because Carney would be hamstrung if he refused.

Exclusive: How I faced down the 'coalition coup' — by Stephen Harper

Harper says Canada could have become an energy superpower over a decade ago, blames Trudeau's policy choices

“The idea was inspired. If Carney accepted the offer, it would be good for the government. But, if he refused, he would have to say it was because the (central bank) governor should not enter partisan politics. Indeed, he could not expect to maintain Liberal aspirations and remain governor for our government,” writes Harper.

“Mark took some time to reflect on the opportunity, ultimately declaring that he should stay out of partisan politics,” writes Harper.

Although the brief section of the book is mostly a rebuke of Carney’s claim about the finance minister overture, Harper does offer some praise for Carney’s performance as Bank of Canada governor.

“Governor Carney was highly effective in his responsibilities and, in addition, provided the Government with solid advice on broader macroeconomic matters,” Harper writes.

It’s the first time Harper has addressed Carney’s claim, although Harper last year did criticize Carney for making certain claims about his role as bank governor during the 2008 financial crisis.

As the federal Liberal leadership race drew to a close in early March 2025, Harper lambasted Carney in a letter to Conservative members, accusing him of trying “to take credit for things he had little or nothing to do with.”

Harper wrote that Carney was significantly inflating his role in the crisis when Carney had said that he had “guided Canada through one of the most turbulent economic periods in modern history.”

Harper said he had listened in “disbelief” to Carney’s claims and accused him of taking credit for the work of Flaherty, who was finance minister during the financial crisis.

“Carney’s experience is NOT the day-to-day management of Canada’s economy during the global financial crisis,” wrote Harper.

Since then, Harper has refrained from criticizing Carney’s government, and their relationship has sometimes even appeared friendly, with the two men sharing a stage on two occasions.

Carney spoke earlier this year when Harper’s official portrait was unveiled in Ottawa , saying that “in a political climate increasingly buffeted by noise, he brought composure, intellect and decisiveness to public life.”

Harper also delivered a keynote speech at the government’s Canada Investment Summit in Toronto in September, where he defended Carney’s decision to walk away from trade talks with the U.S. and praised his efforts to fast-track major energy projects .

stories.title: Saskatoon committee to weigh expropriating land for BRT stations
stories.summary: The leader of a Saskatoon business association says her members were taken by surprise that expropriation is on the table for the construction of six bus rapid transit sites.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Saskatoon’s transportation committee will decide Tuesday whether to move toward expropriating small pieces of private land administrators say are needed for a handful of Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) stations after negotiations with six property owners stalled.

A report from city administration recommends the city move ahead with taking over six parcels of land near sites set aside for concrete BRT platforms on 22nd Street West and 8th Street East.

Each site requires around 30 to 57 square metres of land, according to the report.

The city says it began talks with landowners in 2024, has since purchased 10 properties for stations and expects to buy five more. For the six remaining sites, administration says some owners do not want to sell, while others have stopped responding to the city.

But the leader of an association representing businesses in Saskatoon’s west end says the agenda item before the city’s transportation committee surprised landowners.

“The ones I’ve spoken to have received emails on Friday, just basically saying consult your lawyer and here’s the meeting notice,” said Karen Kobussen, CEO of Saskatoon West Business Association. “And so we’ve all been scrambling since Friday to try to put some thoughts together.”

Kobussen says owners are raising concerns about potential land loss and how it will affect their businesses’ operations — including reduced parking spaces, with others potentially having to reconfigure their drive-thru setups.

“Why now? Why so much land? Have you consulted on other impacts to the business community that this could have?” she said.

In the report, administrators say they explored moving the stations up or down the street but found those options were not feasible as they would block access to businesses, require changes to parking lots or cause transit users to walk more.

Administrators are also presenting the committee with another option of building the stations on land the city already own. But the report refers to this option as “substandard,” saying the stops would not have shelter or transit user information and could lead to expropriation down the line if there is negative public feedback.

Expropriation of land is covered under Saskatchewan’s Municipal Expropriation Act and is considered a “last resort” that requires reasonable attempts to purchase the land and the passing of a bylaw. Owners must also be formally notified and the province must approve it.

Kobussen says owners have also raised safety concerns about the stations.

“General traffic safety, general pedestrian safety and the fact that perhaps the bus shelters, from a community safety perspective, might be cause for concern,” Kobussen said.

Coun. Bev Dubois, who is the chair of the transportation committee, says she expects many people to speak at Tuesday’s meeting. She says some owners had been working with the city on adjustments to their land before communication stopped.

“There were some that were having some adjustments made already to that piece of land with the city, or discussions about possible adjustments, and then the conversation with the business just stopped,” Dubois said. “They stopped responding to the City of Saskatoon employees.”

She says the outcome is not certain, with the possibility of additional meetings with landowners before the item goes to council at the end of November.

“You never know with negotiations and deliberations on anything, there’s always a chance something could happen,” Dubois said.

Kobussen says she supports BRT but hopes the city will keep talking with owners before expropriating and consider smaller platforms instead.

“We absolutely agree that BRT and transit in general is very important for Saskatoon,” she said. “But what can we look at so that both sides can say, yes, I can live with that and this is a great, happy medium.”

The committee’s recommendation will go to city council for a final decision.

“We absolutely agree that BRT and transit in general is very important for Saskatoon,” she said. “But what can we look at so that both sides can say, yes, I can live with that and this is a great, happy medium.”
The committee’s recommendation will go to city council for a final decision.

stories.title: Cranbrook Manor Continues Halloween Tradition for 24th Year
stories.summary: Every October, a residential property on Cranbrook Road in London transforms into an elaborate Halloween displ...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
Decorations shown at Cranbrook Manor on Oct. 31. Callum Contursi/XFM News

Every October, a residential property on Cranbrook Road in London transforms into an elaborate Halloween display, drawing visitors to one of the city’s seasonal haunted attractions.

The Styles family runs Cranbrook Manor, located at 644 Cranbrook Road, which they have developed into an extensive Halloween experience featuring themed decorations, animatronics, lighting, and sound effects.

The attraction includes a walk-through experience designed around traditional horror themes. Visitors encounter different scenes featuring costumed characters and special effects, creating an environment intended to simulate a haunted house.

The display also accommodates visitors who prefer a less frightening experience. Designated family-friendly hours allow younger visitors to view the decorations without the full scare experience.

“It’s really cool to see people who came here as children bring their children here.” Kim Styles, who decorates Cranbrook Manor with her husband Rob Styles, said.

In addition to its Halloween activities, Cranbrook Manor has incorporated community fundraising into its annual operations. Donations collected at the attraction have supported the Humane Society of London and Middlesex.

According to Global News reporting, the display raised $4,000 for the organization in 2022. The fundraising initiative provides an opportunity for the annual Halloween event to contribute to a local charitable organization.

The attraction requires significant preparation, with decorations, mechanical features and themed environments assembled ahead of October.

Its continued development reflects the growing interest in elaborate residential Halloween displays.

Decorations shown at 644 Cranbrook Rd. on Saturday, Oct. 31. Callum Contursi/XFM News

stories.title: Stephen Harper’s new memoir revisits Mark Carney rivalry, Pierre Poilievre and a day of fear on the Hill
stories.summary: In ‘Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister,’ the former prime minister disputes a key claim about the 2012 finance minister offer and reflects on regrets from his decade in power
stories.author: Tonda MacCharles
stories.content:
Ottawa—In a massive 645-page memoir, Stephen Harper aims to set the record straight.

Publishing Tuesday, “Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister” is clearly written for the history books, but for readers and chroniclers of today’s events, the former Conservative party leader’s memoir reveals where he thinks the mainstream media got it wrong, not least when it comes to his ties to current Prime Minister Mark Carney .

Harper says he never offered the Liberal prime minister the job of finance minister in his Conservative government, contrary to what Carney has said publicly.

Although Harper respects Carney’s performance as central bank governor — he appointed Carney to lead the Bank of Canada — the Conservative says he only dangled the finance job in front of Carney as a possibility, conditional upon the central banker jumping into Harper’s side of politics.

By that time, Harper says he and then-finance minister Jim Flaherty already suspected Carney was a Liberal. Harper casts his offer to Carney as intended to either flush him out or commit him to staying within the non-partisan guardrails of his office. “Minister Flaherty increasingly brought concerns to my attention. These mostly revolved around his belief that the governor was nurturing political ambitions, including the possibility of running for leader of the Liberal party,” Harper writes, calling it a “serious concern for us.”

Harper said it was “evident there was something to it,” and discussed it with Nigel Wright, his chief of staff then on leave from investment giant Onex.

In his massive 645-page memoir, “Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister” Stephen Harper aims to set the record straight.

“Nigel had known Governor Carney for many years. He suggested that the way to deal with this was to offer Mark the possibility of joining the Conservative government instead. The idea was inspired,” Harper writes. “If Carney accepted the offer, it would be good for the government. But, if he refused, he would have to say it was because the governor should not enter partisan politics. Indeed, he could not expect to maintain Liberal aspirations and remain governor for our government.”

Harper said he raised it with Carney in mid-2012. “Obviously, I did not offer him the post of minister of finance, as it was then not available. However, I indicated that, if he chose to join the government, he would be the leading candidate should the post come open.

“Mark took some time to reflect on the opportunity, ultimately declaring that he should stay out of partisan politics. Carney would soon depart for the governorship of the Bank of England. In this case, the rest really is history!”

On Nov. 26, 2012, Carney was appointed as governor of the Bank of England, a post he held from July 2013 to March 15, 2020. He went on to become UN special envoy on sustainable climate finance and later Brookfield Asset Management chair, and slowly entered Liberal politics . In 2024, after Justin Trudeau’s grip on the Liberal leadership faltered, launching a leadership race in early 2025, Carney jumped in.

Although Carney has not offered a detailed recounting of what specifically was said between them, in February 2025, when he was campaigning for the Liberal leadership, Carney told CBC host Rosemary Barton, “I have been offered positions in the past. I was offered, for example, Prime Minister Harper asked me if I would be his finance minister in 2012.”

Carney said it “wasn’t appropriate to proceed with that. I didn’t.” He said as a central banker, he did not feel it would be right to “go directly from being governor into elected politics.”

In excerpts from his new memoir, former prime minister Stephen Harper shares stories of Paul McCartney and Yo-Yo Ma.

Harper does suggest he and Carney were aligned during the years Carney was at the Bank of Canada, including on monetary policy during the global financial crisis of 2008-09. But he says Flaherty, his late friend, was “the most important person by far in Canada’s successful response to the global financial crisis, inside or outside of Cabinet.”

Harper does not further discuss his and Carney’s current relationship, which the Star first reported is warm, involves regular contact and lately has featured Harper addressing Carney’s investment summit and appearing at the Canada-EU summit dinner last week in Montreal.

Harper makes only a brief reference to the current Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre , noting he named him democratic reform minister in a 2013 cabinet shuffle that promoted a range of caucus members.

The former prime minister’s memoir is at its core a first-hand account by the modern party’s philosophical pathfinder of more than a decade in federal politics.

It is also revealing as much for the mistakes that he now admits to as for the ones he does not, and notable for his views on some of the pressing issues Canada still faces, although he does not directly comment on headlines of the day.

He is critical of China not just for trade imbalances but for “widespread trade abuse, not merely controlling market access but also engaging in intellectual property theft, industrial espionage, cyber warfare, capital controls, and currency manipulation. These are not issues restricted to Canada.”

He criticizes Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, saying he is not, as some thought, “a Western ally with a foot in the Islamic world. He is a political Islamist and Sunni sectarian leader using the West when it suits him to do so.”

He praises Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu as “probably the smartest, best-read, most-articulate foreign leader I have met” and says love him or hate him, once he is no longer in office, his successors will “deviate little from the course Bibi has charted on a range of domestic and foreign affairs.”

On Canada-U.S.-Mexico relations:

The former prime minister says the deepened trilateral Canada-U.S.-Mexico integration that came about following the North American Free Trade Agreement is “the biggest foreign policy mistake our country has made in modern times. Our relationship with the Americans is special in a way the Mexican one with their neighbours is not.” He writes that “folding our bilateral talks with the Americans into a largely trilateral partnership, particularly given the emphasis in recent years on border security, has been very unhelpful for this country.”

On Canada-EU summits:

Harper expresses impatience with Canada-EU summits as being among the most frequent on his overloaded international travel schedule, “also among the most useless,” but describes how he leveraged refusal to attend one to galvanize progress on launching talks to reach a Canada-European free trade agreement, later concluded by the Liberals.

On Fixed Election dates:

Harper says establishing a law that fixes a federal election for every four years — in October — “has essentially lengthened the electoral period. Full campaigning can be undertaken very early, given certain knowledge of the election date. That includes high-profile, well-funded, well-coordinated advocacy campaigns by groups strongly aligned with particular political parties.” Harper concludes that “the fixed election date was the wrong solution to the problem … All that really had to be done to address that problem was to lengthen the minimum campaign period.”

Regrets about the Federal Accountability Act

Harper says that in hindsight, his five-year ban on public office-holders from lobbying government is unnecessary because it is longer than the lifespan of most governments, and when political parties in office change, such a lengthy ban is not needed to avoid the conflicts once feared. Harper also writes it was unwise to bar smart political staffers from entering the ranks of the public service.

Regrets about changes to the Supreme Court of Canada nomination process

Harper does not write specifically about his failed appointment of a federal court judge, Marc Nadon, to a Quebec seat on the high court — deemed unconstitutional by the court after a lawsuit — nor about his high-profile battle with then-chief justice Beverley McLachlin after a string of federal losses at the top court.

However, Harper does rue a change he made to require Supreme Court appointees to face questioning at a parliamentary committee before their appointment is confirmed. “Critics … warned that we risked politicizing the judicial appointment process — potentially moving toward U.S.-style hearings of confrontation, spin, and prime-time theatrics. In the end, that did not happen, and we used a similar process for each Supreme Court nominee.

“That said, I would not use such a process again. While the crass politicization feared never happened, some warning signs of it did appear as time went on. More importantly, the benefits of the process were virtually nonexistent. There was wide-ranging questioning that the candidates would not, or could not, answer. Ultimately, there was little scrutiny and little utility to the exercise.”

On the 2014 Parliament Hill Attack

Trained by a former RCMP bodyguard to exit an attack situation or hide, Harper says he contemplated the prospect of a gunman entering the Conservative caucus room, knowing “there would be little possibility of survival. It was a uniquely chilling moment. I said a little prayer and prepared myself to die, if things were going to come to that.” He said that brought a strange peace to his mind. They barricaded themselves, and Harper writes, he “was asked to take cover in a small utility closet. I was the number one target, without a security detail, and, as step two instructed, needed to be concealed.” Minutes later, RCMP guards escorted Harper out, but his caucus was forced to remain until the early evening.

“One of my great regrets about the whole event was that I did not override the RCMP and order them evacuated,” Harper writes.

content_blocks.text: Harper does suggest he and Carney were aligned during the years Carney was at the Bank of Canada, including on monetary policy during the global financial crisis of 2008-09. But he says Flaherty, his late friend, was “the most important person by far in Canada’s successful response to the global financial crisis, inside or outside of Cabinet.”

content_blocks.text: The former prime minister’s memoir is at its core a first-hand account by the modern party’s philosophical pathfinder of more than a decade in federal politics.

content_blocks.text: It is also revealing as much for the mistakes that he now admits to as for the ones he does not, and notable for his views on some of the pressing issues Canada still faces, although he does not directly comment on headlines of the day.

content_blocks.text: He is critical of China not just for trade imbalances but for “widespread trade abuse, not merely controlling market access but also engaging in intellectual property theft, industrial espionage, cyber warfare, capital controls, and currency manipulation. These are not issues restricted to Canada.”

content_blocks.text: He criticizes Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, saying he is not, as some thought, “a Western ally with a foot in the Islamic world. He is a political Islamist and Sunni sectarian leader using the West when it suits him to do so.”

content_blocks.text: He praises Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu as “probably the smartest, best-read, most-articulate foreign leader I have met” and says love him or hate him, once he is no longer in office, his successors will “deviate little from the course Bibi has charted on a range of domestic and foreign affairs.”

content_blocks.html: On Canada-U.S.-Mexico relations:

content_blocks.text: The former prime minister says the deepened trilateral Canada-U.S.-Mexico integration that came about following the North American Free Trade Agreement is “the biggest foreign policy mistake our country has made in modern times. Our relationship with the Americans is special in a way the Mexican one with their neighbours is not.” He writes that “folding our bilateral talks with the Americans into a largely trilateral partnership, particularly given the emphasis in recent years on border security, has been very unhelpful for this country.”

content_blocks.text: Harper expresses impatience with Canada-EU summits as being among the most frequent on his overloaded international travel schedule, “also among the most useless,” but describes how he leveraged refusal to attend one to galvanize progress on launching talks to reach a Canada-European free trade agreement, later concluded by the Liberals.

content_blocks.text: On Fixed Election dates:
content_blocks.html: On Fixed Election dates:

content_blocks.text: Harper says establishing a law that fixes a federal election for every four years — in October — “has essentially lengthened the electoral period. Full campaigning can be undertaken very early, given certain knowledge of the election date. That includes high-profile, well-funded, well-coordinated advocacy campaigns by groups strongly aligned with particular political parties.” Harper concludes that “the fixed election date was the wrong solution to the problem … All that really had to be done to address that problem was to lengthen the minimum campaign period.”

content_blocks.text: Harper says that in hindsight, his five-year ban on public office-holders from lobbying government is unnecessary because it is longer than the lifespan of most governments, and when political parties in office change, such a lengthy ban is not needed to avoid the conflicts once feared. Harper also writes it was unwise to bar smart political staffers from entering the ranks of the public service.

content_blocks.text: Harper does not write specifically about his failed appointment of a federal court judge, Marc Nadon, to a Quebec seat on the high court — deemed unconstitutional by the court after a lawsuit — nor about his high-profile battle with then-chief justice Beverley McLachlin after a string of federal losses at the top court.

content_blocks.text: However, Harper does rue a change he made to require Supreme Court appointees to face questioning at a parliamentary committee before their appointment is confirmed. “Critics … warned that we risked politicizing the judicial appointment process — potentially moving toward U.S.-style hearings of confrontation, spin, and prime-time theatrics. In the end, that did not happen, and we used a similar process for each Supreme Court nominee.

content_blocks.text: “That said, I would not use such a process again. While the crass politicization feared never happened, some warning signs of it did appear as time went on. More importantly, the benefits of the process were virtually nonexistent. There was wide-ranging questioning that the candidates would not, or could not, answer. Ultimately, there was little scrutiny and little utility to the exercise.”

content_blocks.text: On the 2014 Parliament Hill Attack
content_blocks.html: On the 2014 Parliament Hill Attack

content_blocks.text: Trained by a former RCMP bodyguard to exit an attack situation or hide, Harper says he contemplated the prospect of a gunman entering the Conservative caucus room, knowing “there would be little possibility of survival. It was a uniquely chilling moment. I said a little prayer and prepared myself to die, if things were going to come to that.” He said that brought a strange peace to his mind. They barricaded themselves, and Harper writes, he “was asked to take cover in a small utility closet. I was the number one target, without a security detail, and, as step two instructed, needed to be concealed.” Minutes later, RCMP guards escorted Harper out, but his caucus was forced to remain until the early evening.

stories.title: Assault investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (November 3, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Patrol Operations Investigative Section have charged three youths after a disturbance led to an assault in the south end late last month.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 3, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Patrol Operations Investigative Section have charged three youths after a disturbance led to an assault in the south end late last month.

On Friday, October 23, 2026, at approximately 10:35 p.m., multiple youths were observed in area of Osgoode Drive and Adelaide Street South, setting off fireworks towards residences and vehicles. A group of youths assaulted two adults who were outside of a residence on Osgoode Drive.

Police attended, identified and arrested three suspects.

The victims were transported to hospital by paramedic services with serious, but non-life-threatening injuries.

As a result of the investigation, three 15-year-old females, who cannot be named under provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act, have been jointly charged with assault cause bodily harm.

While three females have been arrested and charged, investigators are seeking the public’s assistance in identifying three additional teenaged male suspects.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 10 p.m. – 11 p.m., and May have witnessed the assault, or who has dashcam, residential, or business surveillance footage, to please contact us.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

Westminster Secondary School students and teachers are rolling up their sleeves to give the gift of life-saving blood to those in need.

The school has sent around 200 potential donors to the Canadian Blood Services clinic in London since June 2022.

Canadian Blood Services sends a 21-passenger bus to the school two to three times per year, and the school community typically fills the bus each time.

“It reflects highly on the school community that we have so many students who are willing to donate,” said Wesley Chick, a Westminster teacher who, along with fellow teacher Kathryn Farrow, took over organizing the trips in 2022.

The school recently completed a trip in October and has two more donation drives planned for January and April.

Students and staff hope Westminster Secondary School’s success will inspire other school communities to roll up their sleeves as well.[](https://tvdsbo365-my.sharepoint.com/:v:/g/personal/tv59820_tvdsb_ca/IQBmmVGUXk62R79P58vX66itAa8a_OVYHR62RP7AbMPWCI4?e=pmMLH5)

stories.title: Thames Valley Highlights - November 3, 2026 | Issue #79
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
General News

All Notices and Updates

Read the Full Newsletter Subscribe

Dear Thames Valley Community,

Since the first day of school, it’s been an honour to witness school communities come together, especially during days of significance.

Days such as the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation (also known as Orange Shirt Day) are important reminders of Thames Valley’s ongoing commitment to Indigenous Education. I encourage you to continue accessing Indigenous Education resources , available through the board’s website, throughout the year, so that we can honour Residential School survivors and those who did not make it home.

Small actions, such as incorporating new resources or questioning our previous understanding, can make a big difference in the lives of students and the greater community. This month’s newsletter highlights several instances where Thames Valley staff and students achieved excellence in education through their creativity, ingenuity, and dedication.

Thank you to everyone who helped make “good news stories” like the ones featured this month possible. Your hard work and commitment continue to showcase learning at its best. In particular, I wish to extend my sincere appreciation for Custodians, Child Care Workers, Early Childhood Educators and Teachers, who were celebrated during their respective days of recognition in October.

To Thames Valley staff – thank you for sharing your stories! I hope you continue submitting your achievements to Share Your Story, so that we can recognize your incredible work across the system every month.

With gratitude,

Kevin Auckland CEO, Thames Valley District School Board

London teenage band takes centre stage in new documentary premiere at Forest City Film Festival

Three H.B. Beal Secondary School students are taking their growing music career to stages across Canada, and now to the big screen.

Thunder Queens, a punk rock band featuring Grade 11 and 12 students Violet Bruneel, Clara Magnan and Lola Good, have already achieved the kind of success to which many established musicians aspire. The trio has toured Canada and shared bills with major artists including Sheryl Crow, The Beaches, Sloan and 54-40.

Earlier this year, Thunder Queens recorded their second studio album, Deep Below, in Toronto with Grammy-winning producer Dave Schiffman, whose credits include work with Smashing Pumpkins and Alanis Morissette. During a recent appearance on CBC Radio’s Q with Tom Power , Power described Deep Below as one of the best new records of the year.

Now, their journey is the subject of a new documentary, Thunder Queens , which recently celebrated its world premiere at the Forest City Film Festival. The film explores the band’s story while highlighting women in music, the importance of community and the potential of today’s youth.

Students and staff from Beal attended the premiere, where the film was met with standing ovations. "It was an unforgettable evening filled with emotion, tears and laughter," said Andrew Parr, a teacher at Beal and staff lead for the school's Rock Band Club. "Lola, Violet and Clara are navigating this exciting journey with immense grace and maturity, and we are so fortunate to have them as Raiders! In this film they show us that their generation is to be heard and respected. I left the theatre bursting with pride and grateful to be a part of the Thunder Queens community. I encourage everyone to go see the film – you will leave inspired!"

On top of their incredible music career as Thunder Queens, Violet, Clara and Lola are also dedicated students at H.B. Beal art teacher receives national recognition for excellence in art education

Thames Valley District School Board congratulates Kim Davy, a valued art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary School, for receiving the prestigious Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award from the Canadian Society for Education through Art (CSEA/SCEA) and the journal Canadian Art Teacher (CAT).

Kim Davy is one of just five educators from across Canada named as award recipients this fall, and the only recipient representing Ontario. The Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award is a national recognition program that celebrates outstanding K-12 art educators who contribute to sharing knowledge and fostering meaningful learning through the visual arts.

Kim was nominated for the award by a BealArt alumna who wanted to honour the exceptional impact she has had on students through her work in the classroom.

"I am deeply passionate about the power of Art Education to drive personal growth and development," said Kim Davy. "As an educator, my primary mission is to support and empower students as they find their voice, build technical skills, and expand their creative awareness. I encourage them to focus on their unique artistic journeys—where "mileage on the hands" reflects a dedication to practice, and deep research fosters an authentic voice. By inviting students to take risks, I help them learn to trust the creative process. Within the Bealart community, staff and students uplift one another through coordinated teamwork, critical dialogue, technical growth, and conceptual exploration. Ultimately, my hope is that our students cultivate lifelong skills that extend far beyond the classroom, shaping them into future creators and engaged community members."

As part of the recognition, Kim participated in a CAT Conversation on October 15, joining fellow award recipients in an 80-minute discussion focused on creative programming and art education.

Congratulations to Kim Davy on this outstanding achievement and recognition of her work in art education!

Dear Thames Valley Community,
Since the first day of school, it’s been an honour to witness school communities come together, especially during days of significance.

Days such as the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation (also known as Orange Shirt Day) are important reminders of Thames Valley’s ongoing commitment to Indigenous Education. Small actions, such as incorporating new resources or questioning our previous understanding, can make a big difference in the lives of students and the greater community. This month’s newsletter highlights several instances where Thames Valley staff and students achieved excellence in education through their creativity, ingenuity, and dedication.

Thank you to everyone who helped make “good news stories” like the ones featured this month possible. Your hard work and commitment continue to showcase learning at its best. In particular, I wish to extend my sincere appreciation for Custodians, Child Care Workers, Early Childhood Educators and Teachers, who were celebrated during their respective days of recognition in October.

To Thames Valley staff – thank you for sharing your stories! I hope you continue submitting your achievements to Share Your Story, so that we can recognize your incredible work across the system every month.
With gratitude,
Kevin Auckland CEO, Thames Valley District School Board
London teenage band takes centre stage in new documentary premiere at Forest City Film Festival
Three H.B. Beal Secondary School students are taking their growing music career to stages across Canada, and now to the big screen.

Thunder Queens, a punk rock band featuring Grade 11 and 12 students Violet Bruneel, Clara Magnan and Lola Good, have already achieved the kind of success to which many established musicians aspire. The trio has toured Canada and shared bills with major artists including Sheryl Crow, The Beaches, Sloan and 54-40.

Earlier this year, Thunder Queens recorded their second studio album, Deep Below, in Toronto with Grammy-winning producer Dave Schiffman, whose credits include work with Smashing Pumpkins and Alanis Morissette. During a recent appearance on CBC Radio’s Q with Tom Power , Power described Deep Below as one of the best new records of the year.

Now, their journey is the subject of a new documentary, Thunder Queens , which recently celebrated its world premiere at the Forest City Film Festival. The film explores the band’s story while highlighting women in music, the importance of community and the potential of today’s youth.

Students and staff from Beal attended the premiere, where the film was met with standing ovations. "It was an unforgettable evening filled with emotion, tears and laughter," said Andrew Parr, a teacher at Beal and staff lead for the school's Rock Band Club. "Lola, Violet and Clara are navigating this exciting journey with immense grace and maturity, and we are so fortunate to have them as Raiders! In this film they show us that their generation is to be heard and respected. I left the theatre bursting with pride and grateful to be a part of the Thunder Queens community. I encourage everyone to go see the film – you will leave inspired!"

On top of their incredible music career as Thunder Queens, Violet, Clara and Lola are also dedicated students at H.B. Beal Secondary School, where they participate in the school band as well as a number of other extracurriculars and are currently considering post-secondary education pathways in music.

Thunder Queens' accomplishments showcase the remarkable creativity and talent of Thames Valley students and demonstrate what young people can achieve when passion, opportunity and community come together.
