content_blocks.text: Beal art teacher receives national recognition for excellence in art education
content_blocks.html: Beal art teacher receives national recognition for excellence in art education

content_blocks.alt: H.B. Beal Secondary School art teacher Kim Davy

content_blocks.text: Thames Valley District School Board congratulates Kim Davy, a valued art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary School, for receiving the prestigious Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award from the Canadian Society for Education through Art (CSEA/SCEA) and the journal Canadian Art Teacher (CAT).
content_blocks.html: Thames Valley District School Board congratulates Kim Davy, a valued art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary School, for receiving the prestigious Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award from the Canadian Society for Education through Art (CSEA/SCEA) and the journal Canadian Art Teacher (CAT).

content_blocks.text: Kim Davy is one of just five educators from across Canada named as award recipients this fall, and the only recipient representing Ontario. The Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award is a national recognition program that celebrates outstanding K-12 art educators who contribute to sharing knowledge and fostering meaningful learning through the visual arts.
content_blocks.html: Kim Davy is one of just five educators from across Canada named as award recipients this fall, and the only recipient representing Ontario. The Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award is a national recognition program that celebrates outstanding K-12 art educators who contribute to sharing knowledge and fostering meaningful learning through the visual arts.

content_blocks.text: Kim was nominated for the award by a BealArt alumna who wanted to honour the exceptional impact she has had on students through her work in the classroom.
content_blocks.html: Kim was nominated for the award by a BealArt alumna who wanted to honour the exceptional impact she has had on students through her work in the classroom.

content_blocks.text: "I am deeply passionate about the power of Art Education to drive personal growth and development," said Kim Davy. "As an educator, my primary mission is to support and empower students as they find their voice, build technical skills, and expand their creative awareness. I encourage them to focus on their unique artistic journeys—where "mileage on the hands" reflects a dedication to practice, and deep research fosters an authentic voice. By inviting students to take risks, I help them learn to trust the creative process. Within the Bealart community, staff and students uplift one another through coordinated teamwork, critical dialogue, technical growth, and conceptual exploration. Ultimately, my hope is that our students cultivate lifelong skills that extend far beyond the classroom, shaping them into future creators and engaged community members."

Ultimately, my hope is that our students cultivate lifelong skills that extend far beyond the classroom, shaping them into future creators and engaged community members."

content_blocks.text: As part of the recognition, Kim participated in a CAT Conversation on October 15, joining fellow award recipients in an 80-minute discussion focused on creative programming and art education.

stories.title: Shelter-in-place issued for University of Toronto Mississauga campus
stories.summary: Emergency responders are at the scene at McLuhan Court residence
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police just west of Toronto say there’s no threat to public safety after officers responded late Monday to a dangerous weapons call at a dormitory on the University of Toronto’s Mississauga campus.

The school issued a shelter-in-place order for students near McLuhan Court residence, a complex that houses hundreds of first-year students.

Peel Regional Police, describing the matter on social media as a dangerous weapons call, has urged the public to keep away from the area.

Investigators said the situation was contained to a single residential unit and there had been no reports of physical injuries.

In an update early Tuesday, police said the matter had been resolved and officers would remain on scene overnight.

Images from the scene showed police vehicles blocking roadways near the dormitory and officers directing traffic.

“Further information will be provided as it becomes available,” Peel Police said in a social media post.

In an updated alert, the school said some areas remain cordoned off at the residence.

The alert also said mental health and counselling supports are available for those impacted.

A spokesperson for Peel Regional Paramedic Services said Monday night that police had asked them to stage nearby. The official noted that paramedics had not taken any patients to hospital.

stories.title: The Globe and Mail wins four Jack Webster Awards
stories.summary: Globe journalists were recognized for coverage of the Tumbler Ridge school shooting, the complexity of bail reform in Canada and the necessity of protecting wilderness in British Columbia
stories.author: Temur Durrani
stories.content:
The Globe and Mail has won four prestigious Jack Webster Awards for work on topics that include extensive coverage of the Tumbler Ridge school shooting, the complexity of bail reform in Canada and the necessity of protecting wilderness in British Columbia.

The accolades, which honour excellence in journalism across B.C., were announced at the ceremony’s 40th annual iteration in downtown Vancouver on Monday. Globe journalists were nominated in eight categories and won in four of them, making the publication the leading news outlet at the event two years in a row.

Justine Hunter, The Globe’s Victoria-based legislative reporter , received three awards – one as part of a team, and two for her feature stories on environmental protection.

This past February, Ms. Hunter worked alongside a substantial number of Globe staff who mobilized immediately in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C.

Canadian news outlets have significantly less experience covering deadly gun attacks in schools than their U.S. counterparts. But when violence erupted in the small town tucked in the foothills of the Canadian Rockies, The Globe drew on the entirety of its reporters in the B.C. bureau , as well as journalists in Calgary, Edmonton and Toronto.

The Tumbler Ridge coverage included exclusive stories with vivid language and meticulous reporting, much of which was published just hours after the shooting – such as a piece on a 12-year-old student who hid in a closet with classmates; how the shooter suffered from crucial mental-health challenges and had a history with psychedelic mushrooms; and details about the disturbing social-media messages that foreshadowed the violence.

For their work on the tragedy, Ms. Hunter and the Globe team of Nathan VanderKlippe , Mike Hager , Andrea Woo , Jana G. Pruden , Tu Thanh Ha and Patrick White took home the prize of Best News Reporting of the Year.

“Congratulations to all the winners and nominees. What is particularly validating is the jurors recognized brave, independent work,” said Globe and Mail editor-in-chief David Walmsley.

Ms. Hunter also won a Webster for her interactive story with visual journalist Jeremy Agius about how a moratorium has mostly kept tankers out of B.C.’s Hecate Strait, though Canada’s ambitions to ship oil to new markets could be perilous in what’s been called the fourth-most dangerous body of water in the world.

Additionally, Ms. Hunter’s personal expedition retracing the steps of an adventurous 20-year-old woman who helped map the protected Strathcona Provincial Park in the summer of 1910 won for excellence in feature reporting.

Vancouver-based Globe justice reporter David Ebner was awarded the top prize in the legal category for his piece examining Prime Minister Mark Carney’s promises toward stricter bail rules. Despite the apparent political consensus that bail in Canada is too lenient, data show that a record number of people are not being released through that system, Mr. Ebner reported.

Monday’s ceremony was co-hosted by CBC journalists Dan Burritt and Jason D’Souza.

Environment-focused publication The Narwhal received three top honours, one of which was a partnership with the non-profit Investigative Journalism Foundation; while the CBC and IndigiNews, the Indigenous-led online outlet, each won in two categories.

The awards are handed out by the Jack Webster Foundation, named after the influential late reporter from Western Canada. The foundation says its annual celebration is meant to create a community where B.C. journalism thrives.

stories.title: Lawc marks 17th annual ‘Shine the Light on Women Abuse’ campaign
stories.summary: A tree in Victoria Park will be lit purple for the entire month of November to raise awareness and stand in solidarity with survivors of gender-based violence.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
A tree in Victoria Park will be lit purple for the entire month of November to raise awareness and stand in solidarity with survivors of gender-based violence.

“Women need to know they are not alone,” said Jennifer Dunn with the London Abused Women’s Centre (Lawc). “Women need to know that they have a community of support behind them.”

It’s part of the 17th annual “Shine the Light on Women Abuse’ campaign launched by the Lawc.

“The goals of the campaign remain the same, to raise awareness of violence against women and to shift any shame or blame that they might feel to the shoulders of the perpetrator of the violence and the abuse,” said Dunn. “The Shine a Light campaign was built to mobilize communities and institutions to take concrete action toward ending violence against women.”

This year’s campaign theme is focused on intimate partner violence and coercive control.

“Coercive control might be new to you but it is not a new kind of abuse,” said Dunn. “Coercive control is a pattern of acts such as threats or intimidation.”

November is recognized in Canada as Woman Abuse Prevention Month, as well as Domestic Violence Awareness Month

stories.title: Second Nova Scotia teen pleads guilty to sexual assault in hockey hazing case
stories.summary: The victims’ families called the guilty pleas an important recognition of the harm experienced by their children
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
A second teenaged boy pleaded guilty to sexual assault with a weapon in a Nova Scotia youth court Monday in relation to a violent hockey hazing incident at a team gathering last fall. The boy, now aged 15, also pleaded guilty to two counts of sexual assault.

In the Truro courtroom, the teen stood squeezing his eyes open and shut as he leaned down into the microphone and said “guilty” to the three charges read out by Judge Jennifer MacLellan. Family members of the victims listened intently on the opposite side of the courtroom as the details of the violent sexual assault at a team sleepover party were read aloud from the agreed statement of facts.

The identities of the victims and accused cannot be named under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

In September, the other accused teen, also 15, pleaded guilty to sexual assault with a weapon.

News of the assault struck a chord nationwide as hockey and the sports bodies that regulate it have faced a reckoning in recent years for a culture of silence and toxic masculinity. Hockey Canada, which governs amateur hockey, opened an investigation into the Nova Scotia incident, but the sports body said it is confidential.

The court heard that on the evening of Oct. 3, 2025, the under-15 triple ‘A’ boys’ hockey team gathered at a teammate’s house for a team-building and social event in Colchester County, N.S. The gathering had been organized so the more senior players could get to know the rookies.

According to the agreed statement of facts read in court by senior Crown attorney Patrick Young on Monday, the players’ parents gathered downstairs, while the boys socialized upstairs in two bedrooms. During the evening, a 13-year-old rookie player was lying on a bed face down on his stomach, scrolling on his phone when two older players, who were 14 at the time, pinned him down and immobilized him. They pulled down his pants and underwear and exposed his buttocks. The co-accused approached the rookie with the view of “initiating” him as a “full-fledged member of the hockey team by inserting a mini stick in his buttocks.”

One of the co-accused inserted a mini stick in the boy’s buttocks while he was pinned down. The rookie shouted for them to stop and started crying, later telling authorities that the assault lasted 15 to 20 seconds, but it “felt like forever.”

After the assault, two older boys ushered two other rookies into the same room, pinned them down and pulled down their pants, partially removing their underwear. But the younger boys kicked themselves free of their attackers.

The court heard that the first victim always planned to tell his parents but didn’t know how to raise the subject and he didn’t want to get anyone in trouble. The first victim’s father eventually heard about the incident, went to the RCMP on Jan. 30 and filed a complaint, according to the statement of facts.

A sentencing hearing for the teenage assailant who pleaded guilty Monday is scheduled for February, 2027. The defence and the Crown attorney told the court they would be recommending a joint sentencing submission for the boy’s three charges. A fourth charge was dismissed as part of a plea negotiation process, Mr. Young said. In court, it was agreed that a psychological assessment of the assailant would be presented to the court prior to sentencing.

Mr. Young told reporters a sentence for sexual assault with a weapon can range from three years in custody and a supervision order, to a reprimand or period of probation, but it all hinges on the accused’s personal circumstances.

In a statement issued through their lawyer Tara Miller, the victims’ families said: “While nothing can undo what happened or the impact it has had on our children, the guilty pleas mean they will not have to endure the additional stress and trauma of a trial. There is also real significance in having a public acknowledgment of responsibility and accountability for the harm caused. Our children have been heard, and the guilty pleas represent an important recognition of their experiences.”

The families added that they hope the outcome allows them and their children to move forward, knowing that accountability has been accepted.

Hockey Canada has been embroiled in controversy over its handling of sexual assault allegations made against five members of the 2018 national junior team (they were found not guilty in a criminal court last year), and for quietly using registration fees from players across the country to settle such cases.

In response to that scandal, Hockey Canada launched a new independent third-party (ITP) process in 2022 for confidentially handling hockey-related maltreatment complaints, and to ensure possible Criminal Code offences are reported to law enforcement and child protection services.

Hockey Nova Scotia, a branch of Hockey Canada and the organization that governs the sport in the province, initially suspended and later disbanded the team involved in last year’s hazing incident. The Globe and Mail is not naming the team to protect the identities of the victims and accused.

The incidents of sexual violence involving the team were reported to Hockey Canada’s ITP and an investigation into allegations of maltreatment was launched earlier this year, Hockey Canada chief of staff Jeremy Knight said.

These resulted in adjudication processes in accordance with Hockey Canada’s Maltreatment Complaint Management Policy, which are now fully concluded, said Jahmiah Ferdinand-Hodkin of Sport Dispute Management, the organization that runs the ITP, in a statement.

An adjudicator can issue sanctions against players, ranging from warnings to permanent lifetime bans from Hockey Canada activities.

“These complaints resulted in multiple decisions pertaining to multiple participants, some of whom are minors. Some were sanctioned and some were fully exonerated,” said Ms. Ferdinand-Hodkin.

The adjudicator in this case decided to not to make the decisions related to Truro incident public, but it was shared with the people involved and Hockey Nova Scotia.

stories.title: ‘No failure’ in Bridle Path home invasion probe, Toronto Police chief says
stories.summary: Officers did not detain wounded man in hospital later identified as suspect because they lacked evidence, Chief Myron Demkiw says
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
Toronto’s police chief says there was “no failure” when officers did not detain a man in hospital with a gunshot wound who was later identified as a suspect in a violent home invasion that injured a family of four.

The man, who left the hospital, is now the subject of a Canada-wide warrant in connection with the early-morning robbery last Thursday in Toronto’s Bridle Path neighbourhood, one of the city’s wealthiest areas. Police say masked assailants shot three members of the family and attacked another with a hammer.

Police revealed over the weekend that the suspect ended up in hospital just hours after the attack. Officers confronted the man in hospital but did not detain or arrest him. Investigators say they now believe he was accidentally shot by one of the other home invasion suspects.

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw said the officers could not have detained the man because they lacked evidence and did not know at the time that any of the suspects in the home invasion had a gunshot wound. The man was in the hospital for just a few hours before he was discharged.

“From my perspective, there has been no failure,” Chief Demkiw told reporters at a news conference on Monday. “There has been nothing but exceptional policework.”

Police now say the man who was in hospital, identified as 23-year-old Daijohn Richards, is wanted and should be considered armed and dangerous. He has a gunshot wound to the right shoulder, police said.

Chief Demkiw said there was no information in the hours after the attack that any of the suspects had been shot.

“The home invasion happens in the middle of the night and a short time – a very short time – later an individual shows up in the hospital with a gunshot wound,” the chief said.

“What’s important to note is that in the home invasion investigation there is no information that suggested to investigators an assailant had been shot.”

The home invasion robbery has drawn attention to an increase in such crimes in Toronto. Shootings and homicides have dramatically declined in the city in 2025 and 2026. But police say Toronto has had 119 home invasions in 2026, up 35 per cent from the same time last year.

The victims are real estate executive David Morton, 75; his wife Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64; and the couple’s two adult daughters in their 20s, Cristina and Maggie.

Police were called to the hospital because that is the standard protocol when someone is treated for gunshot wounds.

In Ontario, such ground rules are spelled out in the 2005 Mandatory Gunshot Wounds Reporting Act. But one legal expert said the law only gives police notifications about hospitalized people, and no heightened ability to detain or interview anyone.

“It doesn’t give police new powers – it doesn’t say that if someone is reported, police can arrest them on reasonable suspicion,“ said Andrew Flavelle Martin, a law professor at Dalhousie University’s Schulich School of Law.

Police previously said they were looking for three suspects. Investigators have said the assailants entered the house through its back entrance while the family was sleeping. The masked men attacked the family as they demanded valuables, police said.

Chief Demkiw said the investigation remains “very active” and is being handled by the force’s best investigators.

“We are following the evidence as it becomes available,” he said. “Had there been evidence to allow us to do something different, that’s what would have happened.”

Police were called to the family’s home on Hyde Park Circle shortly before 4 a.m. on Thursday.

Investigators have said they did not develop grounds for an arrest warrant until Friday evening. On Saturday morning, police publicly identified Mr. Richards as a suspect. He is now wanted for four counts of discharging a firearm with intent to wound, four counts of robbery with a firearm and three counts of aggravated assault.

With files from Kelly Grant

stories.title: Election runner-up defends online post criticized for potentially inciting violence against council
stories.summary: Writing about his experience as a candidate, Ward 13 runner-up Andrew Crook’s Facebook post begins, “I would only consider running again if we organized a machine of citizens and supporting organizations who aggressively and unapologetically attack the far left progressive machine. We must fight fire with fire to upend the sociopaths from power.”
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Writing about his experience as a candidate, Ward 13 runner-up Andrew Crook’s Facebook post begins, “I would only consider running again if we organized a machine of citizens and supporting organizations who aggressively and unapologetically attack the far left progressive machine. We must fight fire with fire to upend the sociopaths from power.”

Later in the post he writes, “The rope is useless unless we are prepared to use it to hang them.”

On Monday, Crook defended his weekend post and challenged those criticizing his words online, “First of all, this is Facebook. Second of all, it’s an old saying. So, if you don’t recognize an old saying then that’s something you need to Google yourself.”

CTV News entered the quote about hanging into Google’s search engine, but the only result was a link to Crook’s original Facebook post.

In addition, Google’s Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool referred to the quote as, “Highly aggressive, politically charged rhetoric”.

While being interviewed, Crook alluded to an idiom that references both rope and hanging.

“It’s a common saying that if you basically let people speak, they can get themselves in hot water. And then if they do things that compile and build-up, that eventually gets them into a situation where you can let them hang themselves,” he explained.

Asked if he actually meant, giving someone enough rope to hang themselves, he agreed, “That’s it. That’s the saying.”

In response to the significant difference between that saying and the words he posted on Facebook he said, “That’s the spirit of what I was focussing on.”

Crook added, “The intention, again, was to make it very clear that people need to be held to account and that if they’re getting a rope, we need to actually use that. We actually need to make them feel the burn. And if we don’t, then it’s meaningless. It’s pointless. People just get away with whatever they want to do and that doesn’t work.”

In the Oct. 26, 2026 municipal election, Ward 13 incumbent David Ferreira received 4,308 votes, or 69.54 per cent.

Crook finished a distant second with 735 votes, or 11.86 per cent.

Coun. Skylar Franke believes Crook’s choice of words is unacceptable, “We’ve seen that kind of online discourse be used to catalyze people to take action and to commit violence against elected officials. So, I really think it’s unacceptable. And I hope that Mr. Crook sees that and apologizes.”

She emphasizes that political debate must remain civil, “We can disagree on policy, ON programs, ON funding, ON budgets. That’s fine and that’s healthy. That’s part of a normal debate, normal democracy.”

Crook asserts that his post was not threatening, “There is no physical threat or reference to that whatsoever. Anybody who wants to misconstrue that is somebody looking to just strum up stuff, make things up just to cause more B.S., quite frankly.”

Crook’s entire Facebook post reads:

“I would only consider running again if we organized a machine of citizens and supporting organizations who aggressively, and unapologetically attack the far left progressive machine. We must fight fire with fire to upend the sociopaths from power.

That means endless integrity complaints, lawsuits against the city and councillors and their supporters. That means strategic boycotts of supporting organizations, and general civil disobedience to block any far left initiatives. We must grind the gears of the enemy, which will require heavy financial backing from freedom loving organizations and people.

The rope is useless unless we are prepared to use it to hang them. That is the cold, hard truth. That isn’t going to be pretty, or nice, but it is what must be done. We should set a goal of forcing a couple of the councillors/mayor to resign in disgrace during this term. That will require many eyes and ears to capture sensitive data inside and out of city hall.

(Redacted) isn’t the only corrupt pervert at city hall, find more, expose them and use public shame to break them. That is how you prepare the city for real change. Gloves off.”

stories.title: ‘An art as well as a science’: Burn nurses provide crucial recovery care to victims of CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: Specialists are the backbone of burn care, spending nearly every moment at the bedside of the wounded, doctor says
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
It can take hours for a nurse specialized in burn care to change the dressing on severe wounds, carefully removing layers of bandages before cleaning the damaged area, applying necessary anti-infection treatments and covering with a new wrapping.

Ashley Callahan, who has been involved in burn care for nearly two decades and now manages a team of specialized nurses at Ontario’s Ross Tilley Burn Centre, describes the process as “a bit of an art as well as a science.” She said the job of a burn nurse is not just physically demanding but also mentally challenging as they often treat patients during the worst days of their lives.

“A burn nurse is not just an expert in wounds; they’re an expert in everything that is involved in that very long journey of recovery,” said Ms. Callahan. “For most of us, it really is a calling. You do not move into this work without loving it and feeling like you have purpose.”

The fast-moving fire that killed four and injured dozens at a military base in Wainwright, Alta., ON Oct. 17 has drawn attention to the specialized field of burn care, which blends emergency and critical medicine, reconstructive surgery, rehabilitation as well as supports for nutrition and mental health. Of the 39 soldiers who were injured, more than half still remain in hospital.

The extent of the injuries varies among the military members, but the majority suffered severe burns. Those with skin so scorched that it cannot heal on its own have required skin grafts, which is a surgical procedure where donated skin or a patch of healthy skin from another part of the patient’s body is removed and transplanted to the area needing repair.

Because of the expertise required for burn care, 28 health care professionals, mostly nurses, arrived in Alberta last month from Ontario to help treat the fire victims. This includes specialists from Toronto’s Ross Tilley Burn Centre at the Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children and Hamilton Health Sciences.

Requests to Ontario’s Ministry of Health and Alberta Health Services to interview these burn specialists have been denied.

Alan Rogers, a burn surgeon at Ross Tilley since 2014, said he is in touch with 10 of his nursing colleagues and another surgeon who quickly raised their hands to travel to Alberta to help treat the Wainwright patients. He said they are managing a large number of dressings daily and have been warmly received by hospital staff.

Ross Tilley is Canada’s largest burn centre with a 14-bed intensive care unit, two operating rooms and an outpatient service. Yearly, between 350 and 450 patients are treated and upward of 700 surgeries are performed – a substantial increase since 2014, said Dr. Rogers.

Patients are admitted to the unit when they have suffered severe, acute burn injuries or complex soft tissue wounds that require critical care. Dr. Rogers said admission is not just based on the degree of burn, its depth and extent, but whether the injury involves sensitive areas of the body, such as the face, hands or genitalia.

The Alberta victims, he said, fit these criteria.

“We often admit some of the worst, most extensive and most challenging wound cases at the burn centre,” he said, related to such causes as fire, frostbite and flesh-eating diseases.

Infection is the leading cause of death for burn victims because the body no longer has its natural armour.

Inside the operating room for a skin graft, surgeons meticulously remove damaged skin to reveal a healthy wound bed where a thin layer taken from another part of the body is then placed. This skin can be stretched to cover bigger surfaces.

If successful, it will bind to the body and acquire its own blood supply.

Should cryopreserved cadaver skin need to be used, it will be thawed and placed on the damaged area. The body will eventually reject this skin, but it can help to prevent infection while a patient heals and acts as a bridge until a permanent graft can be placed.

Dr. Rogers said specialized nurses are the backbone of burn care, spending nearly every moment at the bedside of the wounded.

Severe burn victims are not able to regulate their own temperature, so nurses must work in rooms that “feel like a sauna” while wearing head to toe personal protective equipment to shield their patients from outside hazards, explained Ms. Callahan.

These nurses are responsible for pain and fluid management, changing dressings, infection control, co-ordinating therapy and, more generally, helping comfort and educate patients and their families on the long road ahead. Multiple surgeries are often required, in addition to daily physical and occupational therapy.

Some patients are in such critical condition that they are hooked up to a ventilator or on dialysis while burn care is performed, sometimes completely sedated.

For every 1 per cent of total body surface area burned, Ms. Callahan said a patient should expect to spend one to two days in hospital. Some of the injured soldiers in Alberta will likely require months of care.

“So, you can imagine the relationship we develop with our patients and families,” she said. “Burn nurses and burn centres save lives and ensure people can return to their highest quality of life.”

stories.title: Belleville synagogue members call for increased focus on counter-radicalization
stories.summary: Survivors of September shooting say antisemitic incidents have continued more than a month after attack
stories.author: Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
Members of a Belleville, Ont., synagogue are urging the federal government to escalate counter-radicalization efforts, pointing to antisemitic incidents continuing in their community more than a month after a shooter attacked their congregation on the holiest day in the Jewish year.

Two members of the Sons of Jacob congregation were in Ottawa on Monday raising concerns that rising levels of hate in the country are going unchecked. In September, a shooter attacked the synagogue as members were gathering to worship in what police called a targeted act of antisemitism.

“What the attack on Sons of Jacob demonstrated is that acts of violence and hatred caused by extremism and radicalization have a profound and far-reaching impact, not only on us, but on those who protect and serve, ON our neighbours, communities and Canadian society at large,” said Shima Vigoda, the vice-president of the synagogue, who was present the night of the shooting.

“It is imperative that we address not only the immediate threats to our collective safety but also the extremist ideologies and radicalization that lead to such violence,” he told an Ottawa news conference.

The Globe and Mail reported last week that security officials are growing increasingly concerned about the speed and pace of radicalization, saying that the threats faced by the Jewish community in Canada have reached unprecedented levels.

The officials cited a range of sources for the threats: white nationalists, people inspired by Islamic terrorist groups, threats from Iran and online communities that specifically target young people to persuade them to carry out violent acts.

Some media outlets have reported the Belleville shooter, identified as Sean Ward, was active in online forums that trafficked in conspiracy theories blaming Jews for the COVID-19 pandemic and other issues.

Police have yet to release specific details on his history or motivations.

The shooter arrived at the Sons of Jacob synagogue as community members were gathering on Sept. 20 to pray at the start of Yom Kippur.

He opened fire on a police officer stationed outside the building, yelling, “You are going to die for the Jews,” and a gun battle followed.

Constable Jeff Smith was wounded in the incident. The shooter died the next day. No one inside the building was hurt by the gunfire.

Douglas Lobel, who was inside the synagogue that evening, said in the weeks after, antisemitic flyers appeared in the community blaming Jews for various conspiracies, and antisemitic slurs were yelled at people standing outside the synagogue.

“What makes this more painful is that the warning signs were already there, even in our own community,” he said.

“Long before Sept. 20, we witnessed Holocaust denial, conspiracy theories about Jewish power and control, and hateful images, and centuries-old stereotypes designed to dehumanize the Jewish people, circulating openly in local social-media groups.”

Mr. Lobel said the government must move swiftly because the next incident could be much worse.

The government released a strategy on countering radicalization to violence in 2018.

The implementation of it falls to the Canada Centre for Community Engagement and Prevention of Violence. The Canada Centre, as it is known, has distributed millions in grants for counter-radicalization programming in the last eight years.

But the funding streams for the programs appear scheduled to soon dry up.

The Public Safety Department’s 2026-27 departmental plan, for example, notes the “maturation” of funding for the Canada Centre as being linked to the loss of 17 full-time equivalent positions.

Noah Shack, the chief executive officer of the advocacy group Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, said at the news conference that he hopes Thursday’s federal budget renews and increases the funding.

He said those who work in counter-radicalization efforts say a common thread among those susceptible to violent extremism is hatred of Jews.

“So we know that in confronting antisemitism, we are getting at the root of a larger problem,” he said.

stories.title: CTV News in Latvia: Canadian soldiers in defensive battle-ready position near the Russian border
stories.summary: For the first time ever, Nato’s entire Canadian-led military brigade stationed in Latvia is deploying east this week, near the border of both Russia and Belarus.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Rezekne, Latvia - For the first time ever, Nato’s entire Canadian-led military brigade stationed in Latvia is deploying east this week, near the border of both Russia and Belarus.

Tanks, infantry, medics and engineers are pushing east from their base in Adazi, Latvia to take part in a multi-day exercise that will include building out defensive positions along Nato’s eastern front.

Lativa is home to Canada’s largest oversees military deployment. Since 2017. Canada has been leading Nato’s multinational brigade in the country under Operation Reassurance.

The base in Adazi is home to roughly 3,000 soldiers from 14 Nato nations, out of which approximately 2,000 are members of the Canadian Armed Forces. Nearly all of them are taking part in this week’s mass mobilization of troops east.

CTV News is embedded with members of the Canadian Armed Forces in Latvia, getting an exclusive look at the largest Nato operation ever conducted in the country.

Canadian Armed Forces Lt.-Col. Simon Mailloux, who is the commander of the multinational battle group, leading infantry troops through the operation, shares that Canada’s military posture in the east has changed.

“Back when we began leading Nato presence in Latvia in 2017, we were in a reassurance posture that evolved to a deterrence posture and now we’re in a ready-to-defend posture,” says Lt.-Col. Mailloux.

Concerns of Russian aggression in this region have only increased following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Kremlin has been accused of carrying out “hybrid warfare” across the region, from drone incursions to cyber attacks.

Over the last week, the sounds of artillery, tanks and infantry soldiers calling out commands have echoed across a training field in Adazi. The Canadian-led brigade has been performing a combat readiness evaluation ahead of their current deployment to eastern Latvia.

Lt.-Col. Mailloux says his battle group is ready for whatever they May encounter.

“We’re conducting the exercise to ensure the battle group is ready to fight. We want to see if our drills and tactics are updated to the day. We see what’s happening in Ukraine, things are evolving. We want to be on the edge, we want to be ready if it comes to that.”

Both Russia and Belarus line Latvia’s eastern border, along with Estonia and Lithuania, Latvia makes up Nato’s eastern flank.

In July, at the Nato summit in Ankara, Turkiye, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced “the extension of Operation Reassurance in Latvia,” as he shared Canada’s plans to shoulder more responsibility in the region in the face of “the threats that we face” from Russia.

Russia has also been conducting similar military readiness exercises across the border.

Members of the Canadian-led Nato brigade hope their presence and preparedness in this region serve as a strong deterrent and that peace prevails in Latvia.

stories.title: Businesses adjust to darker mornings and schedules in new Manitoba Standard Time
stories.summary: Manitobans are adapting to a new time zone, impacting IT teams and scheduling issues for construction workers due to darker mornings.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Manitobans are adapting to a new time zone impacting IT teams and scheduling issues for construction workers due to darker mornings.

“You woke up and that map of North America was a lot uglier than it was back in October, but business adjusts, we will find ways to adapt,” said Loren Remillard, president and CEO of the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce. “But ultimately this is what Manitobans decided.”

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew announced the province won’t fall back during an interview with 680 Cjob on Sept. 17.

Manitoba joins Alberta, B.C., Northwest Territories, and parts of Northwestern Ontario who also ditched the time change.

Ninety-two per cent of Manitobans wanted to end seasonal time changes, according to the province.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: Ontarians look to social media for medical specialists because of long waits, association says
stories.summary: The Ontario Medical Association is calling on the province to create a centralized referral program to enable faster care
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Getting a timely referral to a medical specialist now takes so long in Ontario that patients are reduced to scouring Facebook and WhatsApp groups to find where help is available, the association representing the province’s physicians says.

In a media briefing Monday, the Ontario Medical Association said that access to specialists has worsened, as patients with chronic conditions wait months to see a specialist while their family doctors resort to making multiple referrals in an attempt to cut through the delays.

“These delays have real consequences, and people are growing frustrated,” said OMA president Rebecca Hicks, a family physician.

She presented the results of a poll where one in five respondents reported waiting six months or longer to see a specialist, and another 8 per cent were still waiting for an appointment.

The Ipsos poll was conducted for the OMA and questioned 1,156 people between Oct. 13 and 19. It is considered accurate to within 3.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

About 14 per cent of respondents said their households considered seeking specialist care outside Canada.

The medical association called on the Ontario government to create a centralized referral program that would enable patients and doctors to be informed of the best options possible when seeking specialists, such as cardiologists, oncologists or orthopedic surgeons.

The OMA also said the province should expand its team-based model to include independent, community-based specialists, who often struggle with overhead, paperwork and staffing issues.

(Since 2024, Ontario has expanded access to primary care through a team-based approach that partners family doctors, nurse practitioners and other health care professionals to reduce administrative burdens and widen geographic coverage.)

The previous OMA president, Zainab Abdurrahman, is a pediatric allergy specialist based in Mississauga, but she told the media briefing that her patients come from as far away as Thunder Bay because they had trouble finding specialist care.

One family from Peterborough came to her because there was a year-long wait in their community to see a specialist for their child, who had a life-threatening allergy. They had heard of Dr. Abdurrahman’s availability through word of mouth and afterward told her that they would add her name to a Facebook page for Peterborough families seeking specialists.

“Our patients and our physicians are using Facebook groups, WhatsApp groups to find community-based specialists to connect patients to care,” Dr. Abdurrahman said. “We need a centralized system that’s going to allow for patients to be able to, if they can go further, get faster care.”

Jane Purvis, a rheumatologist from Peterborough, said referrals are currently made in an ad-hoc, inefficient manner.

“The family physician or other specialist who wants to make a referral refers into a black box of unknowns,” she said at the briefing. “Nobody knows what the waiting lists are like. You might get referred to somebody whose waiting list is a year longer than a similar physician just down the street.”

As a result, physicians often send out four or five different referrals for the same patient for the same problem, “hoping that one of them will stick,” Dr. Purvis added.

Finding a specialist is particularly challenging for mental-health patients, who have trouble managing phone calls and e-mails.

Tania Tajirian, chief health information officer at Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, spoke at the briefing about a female patient living with schizophrenia who needed to see a cancer specialist. “Unfortunately her phone has been disconnected. After a few missed calls … no one in the system is responsible for following up, and her family doctor was never told.”

Questioned by reporters about the Oma’s concerns, Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones noted that the province already has a referral system for family doctors. “The next step, of course, is making sure that on the specialist side, we do the same thing.”

She would not say when a specialists’ referral system would be in place. “I’m not going to give you a timeline because it is something that physicians have to make the decision if they want to participate.”

Quebec doesn’t have a central referral system either, but there are dispatch centres in each health region, where requests for 26 main specialties are received, prioritized and directed to where service is available.

With files from Jeff Gray and Laura Stone
paragraphs: Getting a timely referral to a medical specialist now takes so long in Ontario that patients are reduced to scouring Facebook and WhatsApp groups to find where help is available, the association representing the province’s physicians says.

In a media briefing Monday, the Ontario Medical Association said that access to specialists has worsened, as patients with chronic conditions wait months to see a specialist while their family doctors resort to making multiple referrals in an attempt to cut through the delays.
“These delays have real consequences, and people are growing frustrated,” said OMA president Rebecca Hicks, a family physician.
She presented the results of a poll where one in five respondents reported waiting six months or longer to see a specialist, and another 8 per cent were still waiting for an appointment.
The Ipsos poll was conducted for the OMA and questioned 1,156 people between Oct. 13 and 19. It is considered accurate to within 3.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
About 14 per cent of respondents said their households considered seeking specialist care outside Canada.

The medical association called on the Ontario government to create a centralized referral program that would enable patients and doctors to be informed of the best options possible when seeking specialists, such as cardiologists, oncologists or orthopedic surgeons.
The OMA also said the province should expand its team-based model to include independent, community-based specialists, who often struggle with overhead, paperwork and staffing issues.

(Since 2024, Ontario has expanded access to primary care through a team-based approach that partners family doctors, nurse practitioners and other health care professionals to reduce administrative burdens and widen geographic coverage.)

The previous OMA president, Zainab Abdurrahman, is a pediatric allergy specialist based in Mississauga, but she told the media briefing that her patients come from as far away as Thunder Bay because they had trouble finding specialist care.

One family from Peterborough came to her because there was a year-long wait in their community to see a specialist for their child, who had a life-threatening allergy. They had heard of Dr. Abdurrahman’s availability through word of mouth and afterward told her that they would add her name to a Facebook page for Peterborough families seeking specialists.

“Our patients and our physicians are using Facebook groups, WhatsApp groups to find community-based specialists to connect patients to care,” Dr. Abdurrahman said. “We need a centralized system that’s going to allow for patients to be able to, if they can go further, get faster care.”
Jane Purvis, a rheumatologist from Peterborough, said referrals are currently made in an ad-hoc, inefficient manner.

“The family physician or other specialist who wants to make a referral refers into a black box of unknowns,” she said at the briefing. “Nobody knows what the waiting lists are like. You might get referred to somebody whose waiting list is a year longer than a similar physician just down the street.”
As a result, physicians often send out four or five different referrals for the same patient for the same problem, “hoping that one of them will stick,” Dr. Purvis added.
Finding a specialist is particularly challenging for mental-health patients, who have trouble managing phone calls and e-mails.

Tania Tajirian, chief health information officer at Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, spoke at the briefing about a female patient living with schizophrenia who needed to see a cancer specialist. “Unfortunately her phone has been disconnected. After a few missed calls … no one in the system is responsible for following up, and her family doctor was never told.”

Questioned by reporters about the Oma’s concerns, Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones noted that the province already has a referral system for family doctors. “The next step, of course, is making sure that on the specialist side, we do the same thing.”

She would not say when a specialists’ referral system would be in place. “I’m not going to give you a timeline because it is something that physicians have to make the decision if they want to participate.”

Quebec doesn’t have a central referral system either, but there are dispatch centres in each health region, where requests for 26 main specialties are received, prioritized and directed to where service is available.
With files from Jeff Gray and Laura Stone

stories.title: Two youths charged after alleged hate-motivated threats at Woodstock park
stories.summary: Two youths have been charged following an alleged hate-motivated incident involving a replica firearm at a Woodstock park.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Two youths have been charged following an alleged hate-motivated incident involving a replica firearm at a Woodstock park.

Woodstock police say the incident happened at Southside Park on Oct. 27 at about 6 p.m., when a youth allegedly displayed what appeared to be a handgun to two other youths.

Investigators say the 14-year-old suspect approached the pair and started an argument, during which racial slurs were allegedly directed at them. The suspect then allegedly displayed the firearm and threatened to shoot them.

The two youths left the area safely and reported the incident. No physical injuries were reported.

Officers located and arrested the 14-year-old at the park. During the arrest, a second youth, 17, allegedly struck an officer and was also taken into custody.

Police seized a replica handgun and a folding pocketknife.

The 14-year-old faces two counts of hate-motivated uttering threats, possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose and resisting a peace officer.

The 17-year-old has been charged with assaulting a peace officer.

Both youths were released on undertakings with conditions and are scheduled to appear in court at a later date.

Their identities cannot be released under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

stories.title: Privacy commissioner calls for new curbs on government’s ‘lawful access’ bill
stories.summary: Privacy commissioner Philippe Dufresne says the government's "lawful access" bill should be amended to limit the sort of information available to authorities under a new production order.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Privacy commissioner Philippe Dufresne says the government’s “lawful access” bill should be amended to limit the sort of information available to authorities under a new production order.

Currently, police can obtain a general production order from a court to obtain subscriber information, such as the name, address and email linked to an account. The government says this can take time.

The new legislation, known as Bill C-22, would create a narrower court order that would allow police to seek subscriber information from a service provider.

Police would need to apply to a judge and establish that they have reasonable grounds to suspect criminal activity. They would also need to satisfy the court that subscriber information would assist their investigation.

The government says the measure is not particularly sensitive, since it is limited to information that identifies clients and services and does not include the contents of communications such as emails.

Dufresne told senators studying the bill Monday the proposed definition of “subscriber information” and the range of people from whom it could be sought under the new production order are broad relative to the reasonable suspicion threshold required to access it.

Depending on the nature of the services in question — which could include healthcare providers, lawyers, financial institutions and dating apps — such information could reasonably attract “a heightened expectation of privacy due to its sensitivity,” Dufresne said.

Dufresne recommended narrowing the definition of subscriber information to a finite list of discrete identifiers, and restricting the range of people or organizations from whom it May be compelled to “telecommunications service providers.”

Dufresne said if the government doesn’t make those changes, he would recommend adding a carve-out for medical or privileged information to the new production order.

The government says the bill — “An Act respecting lawful access” — will ensure law enforcement agencies have the legal tools to prevent, investigate and respond to modern crime and protect Canadians in a manner consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Opponents argue the legislation unnecessarily expands the powers of police and intelligence agencies, endangering the privacy of Canadians, flouting the Charter and making Canada a less attractive place to do business.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told the Senate committee Monday the bill is about ensuring that when a judge authorizes an investigation, law enforcement has the ability to carry out that authorization.

“The legislation before you today was shaped by significant engagement with stakeholders and parliamentarians, and that collaboration did not weaken the bill,” he said. “It actually made it stronger.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.summary: Vancouver - The man accused of killing 11 people in a vehicle-ramming attack at the Lapu Lapu Day festival in Vancouver has pleaded not guilty to all 42 charges he faces.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The man accused of killing 11 people in a vehicle-ramming attack at the Lapu Lapu Day festival in Vancouver has pleaded not guilty to all 42 charges he faces.

Damienne Darby, communications council with the BC Prosecution Service, said Adam Kai-Ji Lo pleaded not guilty on Monday to 11 counts of second-degree murder and 31 counts of attempted murder in the attack in April 2025.

stories.title: Students, staff at London’s Anderson College caught up in Osap fallout
stories.summary: There is more local fallout from the Ontario Student Assistance Program (Osap) controversy at Ontario’s private colleges.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
There is more local fallout from the Ontario Student Assistance Program (Osap) controversy at Ontario’s private colleges.

Late last week the London campus for Anderson College let 10 of its staff go because of the pause on Osap payments.

It has students like sisters Jorgia, Charly and Emma Gullons worried about making tuition payments. In their 20s and in the same class, the Dental Assistant students each have to come up with $6,300 within one week for their next installment.

“It’s very uneasy. Especially if we do end up going to get a student line of credit. If we do pay the school and they do shut down, do we get that back. We don’t know what to do,” said Emma.

On top of that, the teacher they’ve bonded with has been let go.

“It’s hard for us to want to continue when our teacher’s not here. But they’re trying to continue with the program,” explained Jorgia.

“Are the doors going to be locked tomorrow, is our next teacher going to go, is our class the next to go. We have no idea,” added Charly.

The provincial government announced last month Osap payments are paused for students at all private post-secondary institutions after audit findings raised concerns about financial aid usage at some career colleges.

Anderson has ten locations across Ontario, with more than 450 students currently enrolled at the London campus. And for many, the fate of their academic futures remains in limbo.

Mother of seven, 50-year-old Crystal Mellon is halfway through the Medical Lab program.

“So, I’m solely reliant on Osap as a mother of seven. It’s absolutely heartbreaking, and I’m terrified because I don’t know what I’m going to do,” she said.

Medical Laboratory Assistant Technician lead instructor Christy Bruinink was one of 10 staff members let go last Friday.

“Unfortunately, this has come to a head and we’re starting to see the layoffs with my fellow co-workers and staff. Oh, it’s just devastating,” she said.

Anderson College President and CEO Heather Yang says she understands the need to get to the bottom of Osap irregularities, but she worries about students.

“Protecting the students and catching the bad players, they are not in conflict. Both can happen simultaneously,” she said.

In the meantime, mid-terms are scheduled for next week. The three sisters are hoping to make the grade.

“It’s kind of a catch-22. There’s really no winning in this situation,” said Charly.

stories.title: Global investors step up for Canadian infrastructure because it’s predictable
stories.summary: LNG Canada’s new backers regard the facility as a reliable, cash-spinning business, despite the risks that come with aggressive growth plans
stories.author: Andrew Willis
stories.content:
Back in June, the head of Korea Gas Corp. travelled to the port city of Incheon to make the case for a massive investment in another port: LNG Canada’s planned $33-billion terminal expansion in Kitimat, B.C.

Choi Yeon-hye, then the company’s chief executive, stood in front of a tanker from Canada as it fed natural gas into the main pipelines that fuel Seoul and praised the reliability of a “strategic energy asset we can control ourselves.”

Korea Gas, a 5-per-cent stakeholder, and its partners lived through 13 years of cost overruns and delays before the $18-billion LNG Canada facility began shipping. The experience didn’t stop Ms. Choi from making an upbeat pitch for her company to invest in a buildout that will double capacity.

Duplicating equipment and suppliers from the first phase of the project is expected to shorten the construction schedule and cut costs, said Ms. Choi, who retired in July.

Some of the largest asset managers in the world are buying into the argument that Korea Gas is making.

On Monday, New York-based Blackstone Inc. teamed up with four major Canadian pension funds to purchase a minority stake in LNG Canada from Mitsubishi Corp. for US$3.1-billion. The investment means the asset managers are on the hook for the cost of expanding the terminal.

Mitsubishi owns a 15-per-cent stake in LNG Canada, and is selling half the holding to both raise money from a long-held project and offset part of the expansion costs.

State-controlled Korea Gas backs LNG Canada for strategic reasons. The utility wants to diversify away from Middle East producers such as Qatar, which historically supplied 15 per cent of South Korea’s natural gas.

Prime Minister Mark Carney gave the Major Projects Office responsibility for speeding up the LNG Canada expansion on economic grounds. The facility is part of a strategy to realize the country’s potential as an energy superpower.

Patriotism and geopolitics have nothing to do with the LNG Canada investment from Blackstone and some of the largest domestic funds: the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System, Investment Management Corp. of Ontario and Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

The money managers are investing because they regard LNG Canada as a reliable, cash-spinning business, despite the risks that come with the facility’s aggressive growth plans. The Blackstone consortium view this infrastructure asset as a substitute for bonds and other fixed-income investments in credit portfolios they run for insurers and pensioners.

LNG Canada is a source of predictable double-digit returns in a world where returns on credit and equity investments are increasingly unpredictable.

The largest shareholder in LNG Canada, Shell PLC, is also showing increased faith in the project’s prospects.

Earlier this year, London-based Shell signalled that the Canadian natural gas industry is central to its future growth by dropping US$16.4-billion to acquire Calgary-based ARC Resources Ltd.

Like Mitsubishi, Shell considered selling down its 40-per-cent stake in LNG Canada over the past year. The energy company hired an investment bank and ran an auction that lasted several months.

Shell recently shut down that process, according to sources familiar with the company’s strategy. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources because they are not authorized to speak for the company.

The spike in oil prices in the wake of the conflict in Iran is boosting Shell’s balance sheet and making it easier to pay for projects such as the Kitimat facility. Analysts estimate over the next 18 months, Shell will spend at least US$10-billion buying back its own stock.

Less than two months after asset managers, including Blackstone, spent a day listening to Mr. Carney pitch opportunities at the Canada Investment Summit, the deals are coming.

Kitimat joins Manitoba’s Port of Churchill as a target for global capital. In October, Dubai-based port operator DP World Ltd. signed a memorandum of understanding with the port’s owner to expand the northern shipping corridor, potentially adding container terminals to a facility that only ships commodities such as grain and potash.

The mindset around Canada as a place where things don’t get done has shifted. If the likes of Korea Gas, Shell, Blackstone and domestic pension plans now view large domestic infrastructure projects as low risk, Mr. Carney is on his way to achieving what was initially seen a stretch goal of attracting $500-billion in new investment to Canada over the next five years.

stories.title: B.C. First Nations file legal challenges to feds’ Pacific Link pipeline decision
stories.summary: The pipeline was the first project to receive the national interest designation under the Building Canada Act during an announcement last month.
stories.author: Chuck Chiang
stories.content:
First Nations in British Columbia have filed eight separate legal challenges to the federal government’s decision to list the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline between Alberta to B.C.’s coast as a project of national interest, fast-tracking its review.

Among them is Tsartlip First Nation on Vancouver Island, which said it filed a Federal Court application for judicial review on Friday, asserting Ottawa had not “given sufficient information about the project and its potential impacts.”

Adam Olsen, a spokesman for the nation, called the pipeline decision “reckless” and “rushed,” saying in an interview on Monday that Ottawa had failed in its duty to consult Indigenous communities.

“Tsartlip has a responsibility, as has been expressed by our chief and council, to look after its territory, stand up for those places for the past, present, and future,” said Olsen, who is a former B.C. Green legislator.

“These are incredibly important fishing areas for our people, and so the process was rushed. It was through the middle of summer and the government failed its basic test.”

The pipeline was the first project to receive the national interest designation under the Building Canada Act during an announcement by Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last month.

It means the project would be subject to a fast-tracked, streamlined regulatory process conducted by the federal major projects office.

Olsen said the process is moving too fast.

“The national interest designation concerns a multibillion-dollar publicly funded project that is not expected to be completed until 2032,” he said in the Tsartlip statement. “Yet the consultation and decision-making process happened in less than three months.”

The proposed pipeline would largely follow the path of the existing Trans Mountain pipeline to an export terminal in Metro Vancouver, with an estimated price tag between $35.2 billion and $42.7 billion.

The nine nations involved in challenging Ottawa’s decision are located along the proposed pipeline and tanker routes or use the Fraser River for fishing.

The Boston Bar, Cheam, Lower Nicola, Kwantlen and Kwikwetlem First Nations and the Skeetchestn Indian Band filed their own legal challenges, while the St’at’imc Nation and T’Sou-ke First Nation filed a joint application.

The St’at’imc Chiefs Council, which represents 11 communities along the Lillooet and Fraser rivers, issued a statement on Monday saying it had launched legal action in Federal Court to the government’s designation of the pipeline.

Approving the Pacific Link project without full assessment of risks to salmon and fishing rights, and without deep consultation to ensure the consent of all affected First Nations, is unacceptable and unlawful, the statement said.

The council said its members rely on Fraser River salmon, and the risk of an oil spill from the proposed pipeline’s river crossings was a “heinous” threat to the communities’ fishing rights and way of life.

“The collusion of the federal and provincial governments along with a few industry and corporate elites, who cloak themselves as economic saviours, will force First Nations further into third-world conditions contributed to by the extinction of the Fraser River wild salmon and the collapse of First Nations’ culture and traditions relating to wild salmon,” St’at’imc elder Art Adolph said in the statement.

The statement said the pipeline proposal involves more than 500 river crossings, including two new crossings along the Fraser River.

It would also increase tanker traffic in the Salish Sea, the group said.

The Tsartlip application asks the court to confirm the Canadian government must “meaningfully consult” the nation before deciding whether the pipeline is in the national interest.

Olsen said there is concern there May be more projects of national interest affecting First Nations, pointing to last week’s announcement that the Port of Vancouver’s Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion has also been added to the list.

Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said the existing port facility is approaching the limit of its capacity and the expansion would add 2.4 million containers of capacity annually.

He said the national interest listing provided certainty for a project that’s a key part of Ottawa’s drive to expand and diversify trade, including a goal to double exports to markets other than the United States by 2035.

MacKinnon said the project, which has an estimated capital cost of $5.9 billion, would “fit gently into the ecosystem,” with Ottawa committing funding to protect the habitat of fish, marine mammals and endangered southern resident killer whales.

Olsen, however, wasn’t convinced, saying Tsartlip “has the same level of concern” for the terminal expansion as it does for the new pipeline.

“How these decisions are made are going to shape decisions going forward, not just for First Nations, but for all Canadians,” Olsen said.

“I think that it’s important that we understand the implications of those laws, and in this case, the Government of Canada has a duty to consult Tsartlip, and we believe they failed in that duty.”

The pipeline was the first project to receive the national interest designation under the Building Canada Act during an announcement by Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last month.
It means the project would be subject to a fast-tracked, streamlined regulatory process conducted by the federal major projects office.
Olsen said the process is moving too fast.

“The national interest designation concerns a multibillion-dollar publicly funded project that is not expected to be completed until 2032,” he said in the Tsartlip statement. “Yet the consultation and decision-making process happened in less than three months.”

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Pacific Link pipeline receives national interest designation'

content_blocks.text: The proposed pipeline would largely follow the path of the existing Trans Mountain pipeline to an export terminal in Metro Vancouver, with an estimated price tag between $35.2 billion and $42.7 billion.
The nine nations involved in challenging Ottawa’s decision are located along the proposed pipeline and tanker routes or use the Fraser River for fishing.

The Boston Bar, Cheam, Lower Nicola, Kwantlen and Kwikwetlem First Nations and the Skeetchestn Indian Band filed their own legal challenges, while the St’at’imc Nation and T’Sou-ke First Nation filed a joint application.

The St’at’imc Chiefs Council, which represents 11 communities along the Lillooet and Fraser rivers, issued a statement on Monday saying it had launched legal action in Federal Court to the government’s designation of the pipeline.

Approving the Pacific Link project without full assessment of risks to salmon and fishing rights, and without deep consultation to ensure the consent of all affected First Nations, is unacceptable and unlawful, the statement said.

The council said its members rely on Fraser River salmon, and the risk of an oil spill from the proposed pipeline’s river crossings was a “heinous” threat to the communities’ fishing rights and way of life.

“The collusion of the federal and provincial governments along with a few industry and corporate elites, who cloak themselves as economic saviours, will force First Nations further into third-world conditions contributed to by the extinction of the Fraser River wild salmon and the collapse of First Nations’ culture and traditions relating to wild salmon,” St’at’imc elder Art Adolph said in the statement.
The statement said the pipeline proposal involves more than 500 river crossings, including two new crossings along the Fraser River.
It would also increase tanker traffic in the Salish Sea, the group said.
The Tsartlip application asks the court to confirm the Canadian government must “meaningfully consult” the nation before deciding whether the pipeline is in the national interest.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Pacific Link: New west coast pipeline project receives ‘national interest’ designation'

content_blocks.text: Olsen said there is concern there May be more projects of national interest affecting First Nations, pointing to last week’s announcement that the Port of Vancouver’s Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion has also been added to the list.
Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said the existing port facility is approaching the limit of its capacity and the expansion would add 2.4 million containers of capacity annually.

He said the national interest listing provided certainty for a project that’s a key part of Ottawa’s drive to expand and diversify trade, including a goal to double exports to markets other than the United States by 2035.

MacKinnon said the project, which has an estimated capital cost of $5.9 billion, would “fit gently into the ecosystem,” with Ottawa committing funding to protect the habitat of fish, marine mammals and endangered southern resident killer whales.
Olsen, however, wasn’t convinced, saying Tsartlip “has the same level of concern” for the terminal expansion as it does for the new pipeline.
“How these decisions are made are going to shape decisions going forward, not just for First Nations, but for all Canadians,” Olsen said.
“I think that it’s important that we understand the implications of those laws, and in this case, the Government of Canada has a duty to consult Tsartlip, and we believe they failed in that duty.”

stories.title: Industry enthusiasm for Galloway book ‘remarkable,’ publishing expert testifies
stories.summary: Sexual assault allegations against Galloway in 2015 affected the performance of his next novel, industry veteran Kevin Hanson believes
stories.author: Darryl Greer
stories.content:
A lawyer for the woman who accused author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway of sexual assault says his client could not have foreseen the “reckoning” that followed in the Canadian publishing industry.

Galloway is suing the woman, whose name is protected under a publication ban, and other defendants, alleging they defamed him by publishing the unproven allegations online and elsewhere after they surfaced in November 2015.

Galloway has denied the allegations, and a former judge hired by the university to investigate found them to be unsubstantiated.

The university fired Galloway, who has said the claims destroyed his career.

Arden Beddoes, who is representing Galloway’s accuser, known as A.B., said the fallout from the allegations “can’t all be put at the feet of our client.”

Beddoes said in his opening statement in B.C. Supreme Court on Monday that the case involves various events and “distinct publications” between 2015 and 2018, but the court will have to determine what can be legally attributed to A.B.

“There’s no dispute from us that allegations of rape and sexual assault are serious, and there’s no dispute that Mr. Galloway has described profound personal or professional impacts upon him,” Beddoes said.

“This became a big deal … and everything that happened after November 2015, it’s very complex, but we also say it is not proper and we’ll take the court through why we say that just can’t all be put at the feet of our client.”

Beddoes said the woman could not have foreseen Ubc’s handling of the situation and its investigation and public statements about Galloway, “let alone that it would become this extensive reckoning and controversy within the Canadian literary community.”

The court learned earlier this month that A.B. was no longer asserting in her defence that Galloway assaulted her, rather that she reported he had done so. The woman is not testifying in the case, citing mental health struggles.

Galloway’s lawyers closed their case Monday after weeks of testimony detailing the impacts on the bestselling author’s career and personal life after being accused and later fired by UBC.

His lawsuit was originally filed in 2018, alleging statements by A.B. and others on Twitter and elsewhere were defamatory, and he is seeking general and special damages.

A.B. is a former creative writing student who is years older than Galloway, and the court heard they had an extramarital affair for approximately two years more than a decade ago.

The court heard earlier on Monday from the last witness called by Galloway, a publishing industry expert who produced a report about Galloway’s potential earnings as an author, had his career not been derailed.

Kevin Hanson said that enthusiasm for Galloway’s novel “The Cellist of Sarajevo” was remarkable and rare, putting the author and former University of British Columbia creative writing chair in a “unique class.”

While sales of books published after such breakout successes often fall off, the industry veteran testified that he believed sexual assault allegations against Galloway in 2015 affected the performance of the author’s next novel.

Hanson recalled how “The Cellist of Sarajevo” was one of the “hot books” at the London Book Fair.

“From what I gather there were heated auctions in many territories for the rights to that book,” he told the court.

Hanson said he believed the alleged defamations resulted in the diminished performance of Galloway’s subsequent book, “The Confabulist.”

The court has heard that when the allegations surfaced in November 2015, Penguin Random House Canada shelved the paperback run of “The Confabulist.”

Several people originally named as defendants in Galloway’s lawsuit have settled with him and offered public apologies.

Galloway testified earlier in the trial that he could no longer write and now sells boats for a living.

Hanson said publishers determine how much to pay authors based on several factors, and his report sought to forecast Galloway’s earnings from 2016 until his 70th birthday.

Beddoes questioned Hanson about the report and its use of assumptions and comparisons to project earnings, including a comparison with Canadian author Miriam Toews, who also saw success abroad with her novel “A Complicated Kindness.”

“All I’m doing is looking at the numbers,” Hanson told the court under cross-examination. “But if you’re asking me, do I think that there is an impact of the defamations on the performance of ‘The Confabulist,’ I would say yes.”

Questioning Hanson, Beddoes said “The Confabulist,” Galloway’s fourth book, hadn’t performed as well as the author’s previous hit novel.

“The Cellist of Sarajevo” had earned more than $1 million in royalties, Beddoes said, while Galloway’s first two books and “The Confabulist” earned tens of thousands.

The defence lawyer said Galloway was “one for four” with successful books.

But Hanson’s report estimated the author’s potential earnings for six more books would range between more than $700,000 and $2 million each, he said.

“Your projection then showed that he would go after that six for six,” Beddoes said.

Hanson said it was “fairly typical” for writers not to find success until their third book.

“It takes them a few novels to be discovered and understood and for them to find their strengths. That’s a relatively common thing,” he told the court, while noting some first-time authors do see success at the outset.

“Third novels really establish the pre-eminence of the writer’s capabilities and that was certainly shown in how publishers around the world, not just Random House of Canada, interpreted what was happening. Because collectively, they saw something completely new,” he said of Galloway’s “The Cellist of Sarajevo.”

Justice Neena Sharma briefly excused Hanson, who was testifying by video, and told Beddoes his questions were improperly worded.

“His answer is basically saying no, I don’t agree with you. He wasn’t one for four,” Sharma said. “He didn’t agree with the underlying assumption in your question.”

Sharma said the question implied that a book earning tens of thousands of dollars in royalties was a “failure,” a characterization the expert witness refuted.

“I would mean no disrespect to Canadian authors who have published books. I know some personally myself and I consider them very successful,” Beddoes said.

“What I’m concerned about is the quantification of damages.”

Beddoes said “The Confabulist” didn’t live up to expectations and subsequent novels May also have underperformed.

“In terms of the numbers, it totally did not perform, and the question is why?” Hanson said. “There’s an infinity of possibilities, obviously.”

Hanson said the report was based on his experience with how writers across a number of genres perform.

“The numbers that I’m projecting for Mr. Galloway are not out of (the) question. It could be high, it could be low, but they’re a reasonable projection,” Hanson said.

Hanson was excused after Beddoes finished his cross-examination and Galloway’s lawyer, Daniel Burnett, said his client’s case was closed.

The trial continues in B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver on Tuesday.
