stories.title: Now up to a judge to decide if airport worker was in on Pearson gold heist or a fall guy
stories.summary: The Crown and defence agree the case against Parmpal Sidhu is circumstantial but differ on what it adds up to
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The case against Air Canada worker Parmpal Sidhu for helping steal more than $22.5 million in gold and cash from the airline’s cargo facility is entirely circumstantial, Crown and defence lawyers agree; their divergence on what that means leads either to “near impossible” he isn’t guilty or such an absence of evidence that “zero plus zero plus zero still equals zero.”

In closing submissions Monday, Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic said when the evidence presented at the Brampton, Ont., trial is added together it reveals Sidhu’s guilt for theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit theft.

“The Crown does not need to prove things to an absolute certainty, or negate every possible speculative inference,” she said. “The evidence is, of course, to be considered collectively.”

Court had heard that Sidhu, also known as Paul, was working at the Air Canada cargo processing facility at Toronto’s Pearson international airport on the evening of the gold heist in 2023, working a double shift, and was on a dinner break at the time the crate was collected by a driver.

Beyond that, she said, the evidence against Sidhu amounts to seven building blocks that together form a wall supporting a finding of guilt.

Vlacic said Sidhu, as an experienced employee at the facility, knew the airline’s internal systems; that he printed a legitimate air waybill inside the warehouse and then altered it to allow the crate of gold to be picked up by a crook; made a phone call to a colleague asking the crate be released; had a close relationship with Simran Preet Panesar, an Air Canada manager accused of masterminding the heist plot; had a connection to Archit Grover, another accused and was seen meeting with Grover afterwards; was implicated by Arsalan Chaudhary, an admitted heist planner; and is heard on police wiretaps angrily complaining of not being paid his “cut.”

The Crown’s submission to Ontario Superior Court Justice Gordon Cudjoe is that those factors make it “near impossible” that Sidhu was not part of the heist.

“Either those seven differing circumstantial factors have cosmically conspired to make Mr. Sidhu appear to be guilty of this theft, or he is guilty of this theft, and convictions of guilt should flow on each count,” she said.

Accused Toronto airport gold heist gang turned on each other in nasty fight for loot

'I did everything for nothing': Pearson Airport gold heist ringleader says fortune lost

Vlacic said the defence submissions don’t look at the completed picture, only present a piecemeal analysis of each piece and present a speculative, alternative explanation for it.

Shale Wagman, Sidhu’s lawyer, said it is the prosecutors, not defence, who are presenting speculative motive and meanings behind things.

“What is a collective reality when you put all the pieces together? Preet Panesar and Arsalan Chaudhary ran a strictly compartmentalized heist. On the inside, Panesar abused his 21-year workplace friendship with Paul Sidhu, or Parmal Sidhu. Panesar knew Paul’s user ID and password and used shared warehouse terminals to print the seafood waybill, just as he hijacked the accounts of two other innocent employees” to facilitate the heist.

He said his client was used as a go-between for simple messages between the two masterminds without knowing what was behind them. He said Sidhu was used without him knowing, just as Chaudhary had said he used others who unwittingly helped him get the truck and sell the gold.

He poked at Vlacic’s analogy of a series of bricks that form a wall.

“You cannot count the same brick five times and call it a wall,” he said. Most of the elements outlined by the Crown stemmed from the same fact: that Sidhu and Panesar were colleagues at Air Canada who were friendly outside of work.

“Zero plus zero plus zero still equals zero. Stacking disproven or innocent workplace facts on top of one another cannot manufacture proof of subjective criminal knowledge,” Wagman said.

“Turning an everyday chat between work friends about coffee, haircuts, slow ops, and an anniversary cake into a gold heist conspiracy is deeply unfair.”

As for the wiretaps heard at trial of an increasingly angry Sidhu seeking money, Wagman said that one explanation is that after the gold heist, Sidhu realized his boss and friend had used him without his knowledge and then fled the country leaving Sidhu as a scapegoat and his “life in ruins.” His anger and desire for money months after the heist does not retroactively prove he knew of the heist ahead of time or was involved.

Cudjoe said he would take time to weigh the evidence and make his decision. He said court would reconvene for his verdict in late January.

'We are very very clear. We are following the evidence as it becomes available,' said Chief Myron Demkiw on Monday

The group also called on the Liberals to renew and reform the government's National Strategy on Countering Radicalization to Violence

stories.title: ‘Cart before the horse’: Site prep work approved before development plans in HRM
stories.summary: 'It's really bad planning, because why clear a site before you have the final design?' said Karen McKendry, the Ecology Action Centre's senior wilderness outreach coordinator.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
Nova Scotia has approved work to begin in a handful of special planning areas in the Halifax Regional Municipality — including Sandy Lake in Bedford — where site preparation work was given the green light without development plans in place.

That work includes tree removal, blasting and earthwork.

While a multi-unit neighbourhood is planned for the area, there are no approved designs yet and further public consultation is needed.

“It’s really bad planning, because why clear a site before you have the final design?” said Karen McKendry, the Ecology Action Centre’s senior wilderness outreach coordinator.

“You end up destroying more old-growth forest and wetlands and streams than you have to.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "You end up destroying more old-growth forest and wetlands and streams than you have to."

The provincial government approved the projects last month, with a goal of increasing housing stock.

In the case of Sandy Lake, the approvals were also meant to ease traffic and congestion on Hammonds Plains Road.

But McKendry says she feels this isn’t good planning.

“Sandy Lake is one example of 16 where this ‘cart before the horse’ approach is being used. So destroy the environment first, figure out things later is terrible environmental planning,” she said.

“Also, not including the public in decision making about the city is wrong.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Also, not including the public in decision making about the city is wrong."

She added on top of the environmental impact, sprawling development is also more expensive.

Local councillor Kathryn Morse shares the sentiment, especially given the recent approval of a multi-unit development along Kearney Lake Road.

“With the special-planning areas, I don’t feel we’re just doing good community planning,” said Morse. “That we’re just building housing without all of the infrastructure and the social infrastructure that should be around it.”

Speaking to reporters last week, Housing Minister John White said the Sandy Lake project is about looking ahead to address traffic and housing struggles in the area.

“What we’re doing here is, we are looking at it from a community perspective overall and we’re looking at what is the future build of that area,” he said on Oct. 29.

But Morse notes planning and development should remain in the hands of the municipality.

“When the province overrides all these things, I think we’re getting more expensive development and not necessarily the best long-term development for the city and for residents,” she said.

stories.title: Pop-up veterinary clinic brings affordable pet care to London residents
stories.summary: A London initiative is bringing veterinary care directly to residents, helping pet owners overcome financial and transportation barriers to keeping their animals healthy.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A London initiative is bringing veterinary care directly to residents, helping pet owners overcome financial and transportation barriers to keeping their animals healthy.

Progressive Animal Welfare Services (Paws) partnered with East Village Animal Hospital to host a pop-up veterinary clinic at Village SoHo on Monday, offering subsidized services to cats and dogs living in the affordable housing community.

The clinic provided wellness examinations and core vaccinations, along with additional treatments and nail trims.

Among the pets receiving care was Chimmo, a four-month-old kitten whose owner, Crystal Kennedy, brought her in for a checkup and vaccinations.

“I brought Chimmo here for a checkup and to get her vaccinations done,” Kennedy said. “She needs her second vaccinations, and hopefully she’ll be able to get spayed.”

“We are examining dogs and kitties that live here at this apartment complex, doing physical exams, updating vaccines as needed, and just ensuring the overall health of the pets that live here that are very well loved by their owners, which is really important for both pet health and for the owners as well,” Denstedt said.

Paws board chair Linda Armstrong said bringing veterinary services directly into communities can help prevent the spread of disease, particularly in high-density housing where some residents May struggle to afford routine care.

“What’s super important is to protect not just a person’s pets, but the pets in a community,” Armstrong said. “When you have these high-density locations where some people have, unfortunately, not enough funding to pay to go and get their vaccines and their checkups, then you have the potential for rapid spread of disease.”

Armstrong said cost is not the only obstacle for some pet owners, with transportation also making it difficult to access veterinary services.

“We need to bring care into the community, and we need that because some people have barriers of not just cost but also transportation,” she said.

Paws helps pet owners overcome financial barriers to routine and emergency veterinary care. The organization also provides resources and education to individuals and community agencies.

Its broader goal is to reduce animal suffering, overpopulation and unnecessary euthanasia or surrender to already overburdened animal shelters.

The Nov. 2 initiative was made possible through support from the Lawson Foundation’s Miggsie Fund, with veterinary services provided by East Village Animal Hospital.

Among the pets receiving care was Chimmo, a four-month-old kitten whose owner, Crystal Kennedy, brought her in for a checkup and vaccinations.
“I brought Chimmo here for a checkup and to get her vaccinations done,” Kennedy said. “She needs her second vaccinations, and hopefully she’ll be able to get spayed.”

“We are examining dogs and kitties that live here at this apartment complex, doing physical exams, updating vaccines as needed, and just ensuring the overall health of the pets that live here that are very well loved by their owners, which is really important for both pet health and for the owners as well,” Denstedt said.

Paws board chair Linda Armstrong said bringing veterinary services directly into communities can help prevent the spread of disease, particularly in high-density housing where some residents May struggle to afford routine care.

“What’s super important is to protect not just a person’s pets, but the pets in a community,” Armstrong said. “When you have these high-density locations where some people have, unfortunately, not enough funding to pay to go and get their vaccines and their checkups, then you have the potential for rapid spread of disease.”
Armstrong said cost is not the only obstacle for some pet owners, with transportation also making it difficult to access veterinary services.
“We need to bring care into the community, and we need that because some people have barriers of not just cost but also transportation,” she said.
Paws helps pet owners overcome financial barriers to routine and emergency veterinary care. The organization also provides resources and education to individuals and community agencies.
Its broader goal is to reduce animal suffering, overpopulation and unnecessary euthanasia or surrender to already overburdened animal shelters.
The Nov. 2 initiative was made possible through support from the Lawson Foundation’s Miggsie Fund, with veterinary services provided by East Village Animal Hospital.

stories.title: U.S. air travel compensation is changing. What Canadians should know
stories.summary: The rules have been amended where 10 'events' are no longer under the airline's control, such as weather-related aircraft damage.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The U.S. is changing some rules around compensation for air travellers when flights are cancelled or delayed.

Two months ago, the U.S. Department of Transportation amended an existing rules about what “events” that cause disruptions can be considered outside the airline’s control. The change was to take effect Oct. 19, but was delayed until Feb. 1, 2027.

“These new rules that are coming into effect in the United States are actually just solidifying the reasons that airlines don’t have to compensate travelers,” said McKenzie McMillan, a managing partner at The Travel Group travel agency in Vancouver.

If you’re a Canadian, the question of whether the amended rules impact you will come down to where you’re travelling.

“So now for Canadian travellers, if you’re looking at flights to, from, or within Canada, we will remain covered by Canada’s own regulations,” said Amra Durakovic, head of communications for Flight Centre Canada. “In other words, we expect the impact to be very minimal.”

That means if you’re planning to take a trip to Florida from Canada for spring break, you’d be covered by Canadian rules if something occurred.

Durakovic cautioned that won’t apply if you decide to take an additional trip domestically in the U.S., such as from Orlando to Los Angeles.

“I think the biggest difference will likely be felt on travel that falls solely in the U.S.,” Durakovic said. “So I wouldn’t tell Canadians to worry about this, I would just tell them to understand what applies to their trip and to always ask why if their flight is delayed or cancelled.”

The amended U.S. rules means if your flight solely within the U.S. is affected by 10 events now deemed out of the airline’s control, that compensation May be more difficult to receive.

The 10 events include cyberattacks, weather-related aircraft damage, removal of an unruly passenger, or unscheduled maintenance.

In certain cases, travellers in the U.S. are able to receive a refund if the airline cancelled or significantly delayed or changed the flight and the customer chooses not to travel. Choosing not to accept a travel credit, voucher or other compensation, would also allow them to get a refund.

But the U.S. department says people aren’t entitled to a refund if they choose to take the delayed or changed flight, or take an alternative flight offered.

Several airlines like American, Delta and United could rebook you on a partner airline, offer complimentary hotel accommodations or provide a meal voucher if a “controllable” delay or cancellation occurs.

Canada’s rules differ, with delays of a certain length that’s under an airline’s control amounting to hundreds of dollars in monetary compensation. Should a delay be outside the airline’s control, they also must still work to rebook or even refund you depending on the situation and length of time.

There could be additional confusion that arises if you’re doing a flight in the U.S. that’s a part of your overall itinerary, McMillan said. This could be a WestJet flight to New York then a Delta flight to Los Angeles followed by a WestJet flight back to Vancouver.

“Generally the rule would be that you would be entitled to whatever Delta’s offering or whatever Delta is bound to within the United States,” he said. “You could definitely try to fight that with a Canadian airline, but chances are you would be spending a lot of time on the phone, a lot of time on emails, and probably would not get the result you want.”

Aviation management professor John Gradek said the changes to the rules are “more airline-friendly,” but it means travellers have more regulations to figure out.

“This rule is not going to make life any simpler, it’s going to make life more chaotic and a lot more confusion,” said Gradek. “It’s really going to be a situation where you’re going to have to walk around with your lawyer on your trip … before you go on your trip in order for you to understand under whose jurisdiction am I flying this flight from?”

stories.title: Construction begins on $11M Saugeen Hospice
stories.summary: More than a decade after the idea was conceived, construction is finally underway on the Saugeen Hospice in Walkerton.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
More than a decade after the idea was conceived, construction is finally underway on the Saugeen Hospice in Walkerton.

“This is amazing. We’ve been waiting for this for so long. It feels like an eternity. And today it’s happening,” said Julie Johnston, Fund Development and Operational Readiness manager with the Saugeen Hospice.

Johnston says seven end-of-life care beds will be part of the Saugeen Hospice, but only six will be operational when the facility opens by the Summer of 2028.

The $11 million project fills a geographical gap for hospice care with the closest hospice beds in Tiverton and Owen Sound.

“There is a huge radius that doesn’t have hospice care, and it’s certainly required in our region. To avoid the travel, and the winters, and the cost factors. We are so delighted to be able to be bringing such a facility to our region,” said Saugeen Hospice Board Chair, Carol Kraft.

While construction is underway, fundraising is far from over.

“We’ve raised $8.9 million to date. We still have a funding gap of $2.1 million. So, we’re busy behind the scenes trying to raise that money, so that we can finish the build, and open the doors,” said Johnston.

“Approximately 130 individuals and families will be served every year. So, it’s a wonderful place to be able to come closer to home, to receive end of life care,” said Kraft.

The anticipated construction of the Saugeen Hospice built atop the Eastridge Development in Walkerton, will be completed in 14 to 15 months. However, the doors aren’t likely to open until the summer of 2028 as government approvals to operate will need to be secured, once the bricks and mortar are complete.

“It’s wonderful to be able to see the machines on site and construction happening. And, our dream coming into reality,” said Johnston.

Once complete, $1.3 million will need to be raised each year to operate the Saugeen Hospice, as the government covers no more than 50% of operational costs for hospices in Ontario.

“We’ve been saying for a long time it’s built by the community, for the community. And, it really has been how it has unfolded that way through our journey. The community is behind us so incredibly much, and we would not be at this point without our community support,” said Johnston.

“It’s our dreams come true, but our goal has been achieved. It’s happening,” said Kraft.

stories.title: Where is Jennifer? After almost 2 years, rural B.C. mom of three still missing
stories.summary: Jennifer Provencal, 51, was last seen on Feb. 5, 2025, by her husband, Tom Boulding, who said they had an argument at their rural B.C. home.
stories.author: Kristen Robinson, Amy Judd
stories.content:
It has been a year and nine months since a mother of three vanished from her rural home near 100 Mile House.

Jennifer Provencal was last seen on Feb. 5, 2025, by her husband, Tom Boulding, who said they had an argument at home.

He said he left and returned to the rural Forest Grove property where they lived off-grid with their youngest son to find her gone.

Sunday marked one year since the first community-led walk for Provencal in Forest Grove.

Anita Coombe organized that first walk.

“It’s pretty emotional,” she said on Sunday.

“Very heartwarming. It’s also heartbreaking.”

Coombe said they do not believe Provencal just walked away.

“She wouldn’t walk away from her children,” she added.

Provencal’s sister, from Montreal, joined the walk to stand with everyone she says has been standing up for her missing sister.

“Every day is harm, every day is torment. Every day,” Johanne Provencal said.

“I feel heartbroken.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I feel heartbroken."

“There’s someone out there who knows what happened to Jennifer. There May be several people out there who know what happened to Jennifer and I just can’t believe it’s a year-and-a-half later and they’re still hiding the truth.”

Johanne reported her sister missing in April 2025, when she learned her 51-year-old sister had not been seen in two-and-a-half months.

She said this has been the most difficult time in her life but she is heartened by all the community support.

“We will not stop until the answers and the truth are uncovered,” she added.

Police suspect foul play. Boulding has denied any involvement in his wife’s disappearance, although he said police are investigating him .

BC RCMP said they were unable to accommodate an interview request on Monday.

stories.title: New Brunswick aims to become bigger player in Canada’s defence industry: premier
stories.summary: New Brunswick's provincial government has laid out a new strategy on how it aims to become a bigger player in Canada's defence sector.
stories.author: Johnny James, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
New Brunswick’s provincial government has laid out a new strategy on how it aims to become a bigger player in Canada’s defence sector.

Premier Susan Holt was on hand at CFB Gagetown Monday to release Defence Ready: New Brunswick’s Defence Growth Framework .

The framework outlines the province’s role as Canada invests in modernizing its armed forces.

Holt said the plan also includes creating jobs and growing the provincial economy by 10 per cent by 2030.

“There are two targets attached to this strategy: one is growing our GDP from the sector, you heard the minister mention it’s $762 million today. We want to get that up to a billion dollars,” she said.

According to the report, New Brunswick has the second highest military employment per capita in Canada, and the largest military training facility in Eastern Canada.

The strategy consists of four pillars: industry and investment; technology and innovation; infrastructure and resources; and base and community growth.

stories.title: Feds defend extradition treaty talks with UAE amid concerns
stories.summary: The Prime Minister's Office said last week's visit by the crown prince to Ottawa led to "significant progress" on the Uae’s commitment to invest in Canada.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
The federal government is defending its plan to start talks on an extradition treaty with the United Arab Emirates as civil society groups issue warnings over the country’s human-rights record.

Canada and the UAE signed a free-trade deal last week when the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed, met with Prime Minister Mark Carney during a visit to Ottawa.

They also announced plans to start negotiations on an extradition treaty and a mutual legal assistance treaty.

Amani Khalfan, a spokesperson for the social justice organization Inter Pares, asked what kind of message Canada would send to the world by signing extradition and defence treaties with the UAE, a country with a troubling human-rights record.

Khalfan said the Uae’s record of unlawful and arbitrary detentions is “appalling.”

She cited the case of Sudanese advocate Mohammed Farouk Salman Mahmoud, who she said was imprisoned for over a year and a half in the UAE without charges.

Authorities said he was under investigation for insulting the UAE head of state. Amnesty International said he was released on Aug. 22.

The UAE has taken on increasing importance in global politics and has been praised for work aimed at ending conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine.

But the country also has been accused of supporting a militia in Sudan that has been accused of genocide — a claim Abu Dhabi denies.

“While we recognize that diversifying trade and investment is an important goal, it is clear that the UAE is supporting a militia that has carried out genocide, and continues to do so,” Khalfan said.

“In the context of such massacres, prioritizing economic partnerships over human rights means that Canada is at risk of seeking blood money in the UAE.”

Kwame Bonsu, a spokesperson for the Department of Justice, said strengthening Canada’s foreign partnerships on investigating, prosecuting and preventing serious crime is critical to keeping Canadians safe.

Bonsu said an extradition treaty would help bring to justice individuals accused or convicted of serious crimes, such as money laundering, drug trafficking or cybercrime.

“The Uae’s increasing and successful international partnerships on extradition and mutual legal assistance with countries that take a similar approach to these matters as Canada, such as the United Kingdom, Ireland, Belgium, France, Italy, Sweden, and the Netherlands, makes this a suitable moment at which to revisit the Uae’s invitation to negotiate with Canada,” said Bonsu.

A mutual legal assistance treaty, Bonsu said, would facilitate the exchange of evidence and other forms of legal assistance in criminal investigations and prosecutions.

“This type of treaty helps authorities in both countries investigate and prosecute serious crimes,” Bonsu said.

An extradition treaty is an agreement between countries that allows one country to request the surrender and transfer by another country of an individual accused of crimes.

The federal government’s website says there are three key stages to Canada’s extradition process.

First, the justice minister must issue an “authority to proceed.” Next, Canadian courts need to say whether there is enough evidence to justify an individual’s extradition. The justice minister must also decide whether to order the individual’s surrender to the foreign state.

The individual can then seek judicial review of the minister’s order or appeal the decision.

“In all cases, the conduct for which extradition is sought must be considered criminal in both the requesting country and in Canada,” says the government website.

The Extradition Act says the minister should refuse to issue an extradition order if they believe it would be “unjust or oppressive,” or if the request for extradition is made to prosecute or punish someone for things like race, religion or nationality.

The act says the minister also can refuse to issue an extradition order if they think the conduct for which the request was made is punishable by death under the laws of the country requesting extradition.

Ketty Nivyabandi, secretary general of Amnesty International Canada’s English-speaking section, said in an email her organization is also concerned by the talk of an extradition treaty given the Uae’s “disturbing” record on human rights.

“Amnesty International has documented grossly unfair mass trials, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearances in the UAE, including the disappearance of poet Abdul Rahman Al-Qaradawi following his extradition in 2025,” she said. “Our global research has also found torture to be correlated with enforced disappearances.”

Nivyabandi said Canada should not rely on diplomatic assurances from the UAE. She said such promises can’t reliably prevent torture or erase Canada’s legal duty never to send someone where they face a real risk of abuse.

“If these talks move forward, Canadian officials must proceed with extreme caution and, ultimately, should not enter into an agreement unless and until they have evidence and full confidence that human rights will be upheld,” said Nivyabandi.

Seventeen civil society organizations signed an open letter earlier this year warning Canada against deeper ties to the UAE and arguing the country is perpetuating the war in Sudan. The letter said that as Canada looks to diversify its trade, it needs to assert support for human rights as a core Canadian value.

Carney travelled to the United Arab Emirates last year. At the end of that November visit, the prime minister said Ottawa was working on a $1-billion project to expand critical minerals processing capacity in Canada.

The UAE pledged to invest about $70 billion in Canada.

The Prime Minister’s Office said last week’s visit by the crown prince to Ottawa led to “significant progress” on the Uae’s commitment to invest in Canada.

— with files from Dylan Robertson

stories.title: St. Thomas police investigate razor blade found in Halloween candy
stories.summary: St. Thomas police are investigating after a reported razor blade was found inside a mini Mars bar received while trick-or-treating Saturday evening.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
St. Thomas police are investigating after a reported razor blade was found inside a mini Mars bar received while trick-or-treating Saturday evening.

Police say a person reported finding a piece of a razor blade inside the chocolate after visiting Margaret and Centre streets near the courthouse.

The specific address where the candy was obtained is unknown. The chocolate and suspected blade have been turned over to police for examination.

Police say the investigation is ongoing and no other similar reports have been received in St. Thomas.

Police are reminding parents and caregivers to carefully inspect Halloween candy before it is eaten.

Anyone who finds a suspicious item is asked not to consume it, and to keep the candy and packaging and contact police.

Anyone with information about the incident is asked to contact the St. Thomas Police Service.

stories.title: World-renowned seabird scientist Bill Montevecchi remembered in Newfoundland
stories.summary: ST. John's - Scientists, academics, friends and family gathered on Sunday to honour the life of world-renowned seabird biologist William Montevecchi, who died earlier this year at the age of 80.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Scientists, academics, friends and family gathered on Sunday to honour the life of world-renowned seabird biologist William Montevecchi, who died earlier this year at the age of 80.

Montevecchi was professor at Memorial University in Newfoundland and Labrador for more than 40 years. He was ranked by Stanford University among the top two per cent of the world’s scientists in 2020.

In almost every year of his career, he travelled to a remote, barren rock in the North Atlantic Ocean called Funk Island where he lived among more than a million seabirds for weeks on end. The island was home to one of the last colonies of the great auk, whose life and extinction Montevecchi studied.

In 2021, he took his last voyage to the island, which is about 65 kilometres off the northeast coast of Newfoundland. His two daughters, Gioia and Marina Montevecchi, went with him.

“Dad would make us walk behind him through the bird colonies, like Moses parting the sea,” Gioia Montevecchi said in an interview Monday.

“He was just in awe of the world. He really paid attention to the marine environment and the impacts of climate change in the North Atlantic, using seabirds as indicators,” she added. “The more he knew, the more he was interested in learning.”

Montevecchi was born in 1946, in Massachusetts. He first began studying chickens, but ultimately had an opportunity to focus on sea birds and move to Newfoundland and Labrador, where he’d have plenty of opportunity for field work, said his colleague, Pierre-Paul Bitton, an associate professor of psychology and chair of the school’s cognitive and behavioural ecology program studying animal behaviour.

“He never looked back,” Bitton said in an interview.

His daughter, Gioia Montevecchi, said she grew up in a house full of graduate students and oiled and injured birds her father was nursing back to health. He hitched rides on fishing boats to Funk Island, an ecological reserve atop a barren rock that is roughly 700 metres long.

There is nothing to see in any direction but open water, birds and their pungent excrement, and there is still equipment in her parents’ basement that carries its distinctive smell, his daughter said.

He gathered vast quantities of data about the birds and their behaviour, and he was always happy to share it, Bitton said.

Montevecchi retired in 2021, but he kept working with students and leading research projects well after he finished.

His daughter said she wrote a book chapter with him in the last six months of his life, and he was still working on another book when he died in July.

He was dedicated to teaching the next generation of scientists, Bitton said. Colleagues often joked that half the scientists now working for Environment Canada in Newfoundland and Labrador were once Montevecchi’s students, he added.

Montevecchi did countless media interviews, urging protection for wildlife and the environment as the province’s cod fishery collapsed in the early 1990s and the offshore oil industry took hold.

Chris O’Neill-Yates, a retired national reporter for Newfoundland and Labrador with CBC News, said Montevecchi’s passion and clarity helped residents understand the interwoven life in the ocean around them.

He saw it as part of his job to inform the public and he would do interviews in the field, surrounded by shrieking birds, she said.

Scientists and fish harvesters in the province often butt heads, but fishers loved Montevecchi, O’Neill-Yates said in an interview.

“He knew there were people who opposed what he was saying. He was taking on some really big heavy-hitters in the work that he did,” she said.

But he stuck to the facts and stayed composed, even when head-to-head with politicians on the evening news, she said.

”(He) understood that people had a right to information,” O’Neill-Yates said. “He did a tremendous service to the public of Newfoundland and Labrador.”

Montevecchi’s family and colleagues at Memorial University have established the Dr. William Montevecchi Memorial Scholarship to support a graduate student in the school’s cognitive and behavioural ecology program. They unveiled it to a crowd of more than 100 people gathered for Montevecchi’s memorial on Sunday, in a university building just outside St. John’s, N.L., that looks out over the ocean.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version incorrectly stated Montevecchi was born in 1964. In fact, he was born in 1946.

stories.title: Toronto police chief offended at suggestion they lost Bridle Path home invasion suspect
stories.summary: 'We are very very clear. We are following the evidence as it becomes available,' said Chief Myron Demkiw on Monday
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
The Toronto Police Service kickoff to crime prevention week on Monday quickly took a turn into questions about an already committed crime — the home invasion last week in the city’s Bridle Path that wounded local CEO David Morton and his family, and resulted in police searching for a suspect, Daijohn Richards, who was himself briefly admitted to hospital.

Asked by a reporter to “clarify for the public how (Richards) was let go and is now missing,” Police Chief Myron Demkiw responded: “I actually take umbrage with the way you frame that question. That’s not what has been said by the police at all. We are very very clear. We are following the evidence as it becomes available. Had there been evidence to allow us to do something different, that’s what would have happened. We are following the evidence as expeditiously as we can, and the investigation continues to unfold.”

He would not give further details, he said, “to preserve the integrity of the investigation, as it is very very dynamic and active as we speak here today.”

Demkiw was joined at the podium at 11 Division Headquarters by newly re-elected Mayor Olivia Chow, Ontario Solicitor General Michael Kerzner, Toronto Police Service Board Chair Councillor Shelley Carroll, Brian Callahan of the Toronto Police Association, and Dr. Jose Couto of the Ontario Association of Chiefs of Police.

They outlined a plan to set up designated buy-and-sell safe zones at or near police stations across the city, with camera surveillance and officers nearby, as a way to deter fraud and theft among online buyers when they meet to exchange money for goods.

However, all the speakers touched on the recent violence at the Morton home, in which David, his wife and two adult daughters were attacked by three masked individuals who forced their way in, armed with handguns and a hammer, which they used in the attack.

After the attack, a man now known to be Richards, age 23, of Toronto, was treated in hospital for a gunshot wound and then discharged. Police are now asking the public for help in finding him. The other two suspects were described as being in their 20s but have not been identified.

On Saturday, amid mounting criticism over Richards’ unknown whereabouts, police released a statement “to address some confusion surrounding the investigation.”

They noted: “Investigators immediately recognized the potential connection between the home invasion and the individual who showed up at hospital with a gunshot wound. But recognizing a potential suspect and having enough evidence to arrest them are two different things. Suspicion alone isn’t enough. Police need reasonable grounds, supported by evidence, to make an arrest.”

Asked by National Post what Toronto homeowners and residents can do to feel and be more safe in their homes, Demkiw replied: “I’d encourage everybody who has concerns to connect with their local division.”

He said the police run a program called Crime Prevention through Environmental Design , “where we can assist residents to examine the streetscape and immediate surroundings of their homes to make sure they’re as safe as they can be and as effectively protected as they can be, and consider the different things that can be put in place, whether it’s security systems or lighting or film on glass, locking mechanisms, etc.”

He added: “Connecting with your local division … would be very very important and will help everybody to address their unique circumstances on a case by case basis.”

To a followup as to whether police have noticed any patterns in home invasions in recent months, Demkiw replied: “Well, we’re always looking for what our data points will tell us regarding any geospatial patterning or time patterning, but you know that doesn’t quite line up that way all the time. And often, what we have to do is do our preventative work in a broader area.”

“I really want to reassure Torontonians,” he added. “We totally understand their concern, and we are sparing no resource. Every resource necessary is being brought to bear on this case, and we continue to do our work regarding home invasions, shootings and other violent crimes in the city. And our police officers, our investigators, have all the tools they need, and will be provided every opportunity to advance their investigations, supported by the city and the command as required.”

Kerzner, the Ontario Solicitor General, added: “Our government, led by Premier Ford, will never apologize for being tough on crime. We will be relentless, and we will always, always stand with Ontarians. Somebody needs to know there’s somebody on their side.”

stories.title: After re-election, Olivia Chow needs to ‘show up’ in order to gain Jewish community’s trust
stories.summary: 'People around the world are talking about the untenable situation for Toronto's Jews,' says CEO of advocacy group
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Mayor Olivia Chow’s re-election is not yet seen as a victory among many in Toronto’s Jewish community, but Jewish groups suggest she still has an opportunity to gain trust.

“Under her leadership to date, it is simply a fact that Toronto has emerged as an unacceptable flashpoint within a global crisis of antisemitism, and it’s not only Toronto’s community that’s noticing this,” B’nai Brith Canada CEO Simon Wolle, a Toronto resident, told National Post.

“People around the world are talking about the untenable situation for Toronto’s Jews.”

On Oct. 28, Chow was re-elected , beating city councillor Brad Bradford. The following day, speaking to media, Chow said she would be “mayor for everyone,” the Canadian Press reported.

“Well, I think that there is a large segment of the Jewish community that feels that so far, the mayor has not been one for them,” said Wolle.

Another Jewish advocacy group, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, said in a statement following the election that “attention now turns to the commitments made during the campaign and the work still ahead.”

Cija said Chow made promises “to build on policing investments, expand security funding for vulnerable institutions, and continue efforts to address antisemitism and hate.”

“The election May be over, but the responsibility to deliver results is just beginning. Statements condemning antisemitism and other forms of hate must be matched by concrete action.”

B’nai Brith Canada publishes an annual audit on antisemitic incidents across the country. Last year, there were a total of 6,800 incidents , ranging from vandalism to threats of violence.

In Toronto, synagogues have been shot at , events featuring Israeli speakers have been disrupted and Jewish-owned businesses have been targeted . Not far from Toronto, in Belleville, Ont., a gunman opened fire on a synagogue on Yom Kippur in late September, in an attempt to attack its congregants. A police officer stationed outside was severely injured.

Wolle added that there have been ongoing protests in a predominantly Jewish area of the city “with masked participants, sometimes waving flags of terrorist organizations, chanting hate, spewing division, and intimidating and harassing Jewish Torontonians.”

“(Chow’s) allowing for the incitement and division to fester here,” he said.

Chow was notably absent from a debate on antisemitism held at a synagogue in September. She also did not to attend Toronto’s March for Israel over the summer. However, she did attend events like Toronto Pride Parade and Caribana festival.

“When the mayor takes those types of calculated steps to show up for one community and not another, it sends a very clear signal to anyone who’s paying attention that one thing matters and another does not,” Wolle said.

“The inference from her choices and actions to date embolden those who would like to take a position that the Jewish community of Toronto simply does not matter.”

Chris Selley: What does Olivia Chow's 'progressive base' think it's defending?

Anthony Furey: Think Toronto is bad now? Wait till Chow's new left-wing council takes over

Olivia Chow keeps job as Toronto mayor with decisive victory over Brad Bradford

When asked how Chow could win over the approval of Jewish Torontonians, Wolle said all she had to do was show up.

“She needs to take the necessary and sufficient steps to protect public order,” he said. “We want the mayor to step up. We want the mayor to own any mistakes that she’s made to date, and to take the corrective measures to move this city in the right direction.”

B’nai Brith and other partners from the community are willing to help her, said Wolle. “With this election, the mayor should take a good look in the mirror and say, ‘I can do this. I can change course in the city.'”

“We look forward to addressing the challenges facing Torontonians, including the surge in antisemitism and extremism, and protecting human rights for everyone in the city,” it said.

The group also called on the Liberals to renew and reform the government's National Strategy on Countering Radicalization to Violence

B’nai Brith and other partners from the community are willing to help her, said Wolle. “With this election, the mayor should take a good look in the mirror and say, ‘I can do this. I can change course in the city.'”
“We look forward to addressing the challenges facing Torontonians, including the surge in antisemitism and extremism, and protecting human rights for everyone in the city,” it said.

stories.title: Montreal police to fire seven after allegations of discriminatory, racist conduct
stories.summary: Chief Fady Dagher promised action after series of scandals that led police service to suspend at least six officers in recent months
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal’s police chief said Monday that seven officers have been fired following allegations of discriminatory and racist conduct that have dogged the service in recent months.

Chief Fady Dagher told a news conference that the dismissals are unprecedented and involve allegations of “discrimination and racism” and “vulnerable people.”

Dagher confirmed that the dismissals were linked to ongoing criminal investigations into a series of scandals involving officers at two police stations that have made headlines since June.

“To the victims of unacceptable conduct by (Montreal) police officers, I promised you truth and consequences,” he said.

“You have truth, to the extent the investigation allows it, and you have consequences. In the end, we judge a police officer by the way they treat those who cannot defend themselves.”

Dagher had previously announced that six officers had been suspended as part of those probes. He did not confirm the identity of the dismissed officers, but said Monday’s announcement involved the “same individuals.”

Dagher said the force has also turned over its investigative files to the provincial Crown prosecutor’s office, which will decide whether to file criminal charges against the officers.

In the meantime, he said the force worked with the city’s lawyers to carry out what he described as an “administrative dismissal” that essentially meant revoking the officers’ security clearance and police accreditation over alleged failure to uphold the code of conduct.

“They will no longer wear the uniform or carry a weapon, and they will no longer serve the citizens of Montreal,” he said.

Montreal's police chief, Fady Dagher, has announced that seven officers are being fired following allegations of discriminatory and racist conduct that have dogged the force in recen…

The series of scandals that have rocked the force in recent months include allegations of criminal misconduct and racism by some officers, including members of a patrol unit in a multicultural neighbourhood of Montreal that police dismantled in June.

Dagher confirmed earlier this year that the allegations include claims that officers at the station in the Montréal-Nord borough cut the hair of racialized civilians to keep as trophies.

Police also announced last week that an officer linked to the investigation could face criminal charges after allegedly concealing evidence related to a situation involving domestic violence in 2025. Dagher did not confirm Monday whether the officer was one of the seven who was dismissed.

Radio-Canada reported last week that an officer responding to a call in connection with conjugal violence allegedly erased evidence on a smartphone that was provided by a complainant. The report suggested the officer knew the alleged perpetrator.

The Canadian Press has not independently verified the allegations in the news report.

The seven people who are being dismissed include five from the Montréal-Nord station as well as two from a downtown station. The downtown dismissals are linked to racism and conduct towards vulnerable people, Dagher said.

Montreal news outlet La Presse has reported that one of those officers allegedly urinated on a homeless person, while the second officer allegedly posed for photos mocking suspects under arrest in humiliating positions. The Canadian Press has not confirmed the details that led to the suspensions.

Dagher addressed the alleged urination incident on Monday, saying that his information concerns a “dishonourable act of a similar nature, but not on a human.” He said the information in the media report was being investigated by the province’s police watchdog, the Bureau des enquêtes independantes.

The police chief couldn’t confirm Monday that there would be no more officers sanctioned, but reiterated his belief that 99 per cent of officers do their jobs well and noted that some had spoken out against their colleagues.

“I think the kind of announcement that we’re doing today, it shows that the silence is broken, the omerta is broken and we’re taking action,” said Dagher.

Montreal’s mayor said Monday that the police force had taken an “unprecedented” step toward rebuilding citizens’ trust. “Nobody is above the rules,” Soraya Martinez Ferrada said in a statement.

The executive director of a civil-rights group called the Red Coalition called for an independent public inquiry into “systemic racism, racial profiling, discriminatory policing practices and institutional accountability” within the Montreal police force.

“Seven dismissals cannot be considered a sufficient institutional response to allegations of this magnitude,” Joel DeBellefeuille wrote in a statement.

“The public is entitled to know what the (Montreal police) knew, when concerns were brought to its attention, whether warnings were disregarded and whether institutional failures allowed misconduct to persist.”

stories.title: Expert insight: Does easier access to cannabis stores increase teen use? The answer is complicated
stories.summary: A Western-led study found that having cannabis retailers near schools was not associated with an overall increase in use among adolescents.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
When Canada legalized recreational cannabis in October 2018, one concern was that more legal stores would make cannabis easier for young people to access and encourage adolescent use. But does having more cannabis retailers near high schools actually mean more students use cannabis?

Our study suggests the relationship is more complicated. Across more than 419,000 student survey responses collected in four Canadian provinces, we found little consistent evidence that greater access to nearby cannabis retailers was associated with whether adolescents used cannabis.

However, accessibility was associated with more frequent use among existing users during the first year of legalization.

Our research team examined this question in a study published in the Drug and Alcohol Dependence journal. Our findings offer new insight into how cannabis retail accessibility relates to adolescent use as Canada’s legal market matures.

We examined student survey data collected between 2018–19 and 2023–24 through the Compass study in Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario and Québec. We measured accessibility using the distance to the nearest retailer, the number of nearby stores and a measure that gives greater weight to closer retailers.

Overall, greater retail accessibility was not consistently associated with ever using cannabis, past-year or past-month use, or daily and almost-daily use.

Cannabis use also declined in our study sample. Past-year use fell from 22.2 per cent in 2018 to 10.0 per cent in 2023. Past-month use declined from 13.0 per cent to 6.4 per cent, while almost-daily use fell from 4.2 per cent to 2.4 per cent. These figures describe students in participating schools, not a nationally representative sample.

For national context, Health Canada’s Canadian Student Alcohol and Drugs Survey reported that 18.3 per cent of students in Grades 7 to 12 used cannabis in 2023–24. This estimate comes from a separate survey and should not be directly equated with our findings.

However, our study did not examine where students obtained cannabis, so access through friends is one possible explanation for our findings, not something we directly tested.

A meta-analysis found associations with depression and suicidal ideation, while other research examined associations between cannabis use and poorer academic outcomes.

However, our findings suggest that store proximity alone May be insufficient to understand or prevent adolescent use. stories.title: When did kids’ sports become so serious?
stories.summary: Competition has invaded what I thought was the spirit of rec leagues. The days of healthy exploration and dabbling are gone
stories.author: Janna Harowitz
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

Where is the beer league for the kids?

I am a geriatric parent. I had kids “late.” I was 39 years old when I had my first child and 41 with my second. The doctors, seemingly fresh out of puberty, called my twilight pregnancy “high risk.”

There are a few of us older moms in the school yard. We reminisce about the days when after-school activities were meant for filling our free time with no end game. We’d make up games from discarded juice boxes, toss hockey cards down the hallway and create loud sounds with our armpits. All healthy alternatives to prank calling.

There was competitive play and there were year-end dance shows when I was growing up, but no one thought we would amount to anything in our respective activity. We were there for the fun, the connection and the park nights with kids from next door. Tap dancing one month and soccer the next. Each activity – one afternoon a week. A select few danced or played “competitively” – but they were in a separate stream. There were no after-school play dates for them.

These days are over. I have found no true “recreational stream” for kids. Rec leagues exist in name only. Competitive serious tendencies have invaded what I thought was the spirit of rec leagues. The days of healthy exploration and dabbling are gone. Kids must commit and do so early. With dedication. Rec hockey? Three times a week. Missing dance? Verbal reprimand from the teacher. Soccer is tiered into divisions. League-facilitated video calls are permeated by parent hopefuls desperate for tips to secure spots in coveted tiers. Me? I asked about how I could ensure my kid entered the lowest-division one-day-a-week team. I made no friends on the call.

The issue came to a head in our house in spring 2025. My then-eight-year-old’s little league baseball practice (three hours!) conflicted with his hip-hop class. It was a “crisis.” I had been confident that this would not be a problem. We’ll just switch teams. Nope. I pleaded my case to the league. Surely, in the days of celebrating diversity, we would accommodate a boy who wants to go to dance class? Again, no. My boy is sweet, curious and hilarious. Top athlete? No. He prefers the locker-room banter to the field.

In the serious iron-man-recreational-sport world we were living in, I was told that moving him would disrupt the delicate balance of the league teams. There is no way that such a move was going to disrupt anything. He’s not that bad and he’s definitely not that good. No amount of convincing could change the decision. This really was the Big Leagues.

The kids had been drafted by coaches based on 45-minute assessments that had occurred in the months prior to equalize the teams. Each group needed just the right amount of “apples” and “oranges” (my code names for athletic aptitude or lack thereof). Team rosters were locked in and we had to make a choice. There was no moving or trading. We said goodbye to hip hop. My son took the news well − not quite appreciating the absurdity of the situation. After all, he’s grown up observing parents who think their children are being scouted on the playground.

And for what? My son, like the other oranges, was relegated to what some parents might consider inconsequential positions on the field. I get it, him playing first base all the time would not have helped the final score. Yes, we all want our kids to experience the jubilation in winning. But are we capital “W” winning if we are taking this too seriously? In a time when we see mental-health issues rising in our kids, and difficulties with retention rates in sport, isn’t decreasing the intensity in favour of playing just for fun, in fact, winning?

Last spring, my son, again, went through the league’s assessment. At this stage, he was now eligible for two different levels – I’ll call it the “A” and “B” grade. About a month later we received an e-mail from the league. It read like a sympathy card or my doctor e-mailing to tell me I was dying. A league representative was reaching out “personally” to inform us of the terrible news – our child was a B.

We were elated. I don’t criticize the representative. She was being kind and I’m sure there were other parents that were distraught when they received the death notice. Therein lies the problem. Why should it matter?

Let’s reclaim the beer league spirit for our kids. No tequila shooters though, let’s just let them play. And have fun. So that they keep playing. And stay happy.

Janna Harowitz lives in Vancouver.

stories.title: How U.S. border state midterm races are shaping up amid ‘insane tariffs’
stories.summary: Nowhere has the trade war with Canada occupied the election cycle narrative than in the seven border states electing new senators on Tuesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Americans will head to the polls on Tuesday for the midterms , with U.S. President Donald Trump’s war in Iran and trade war with Canada looming large in the election cycle.

Many of the 33 out of 100 U.S. Senate seats are being fiercely contested between Democrats and Trump’s Republican Party.

The trade war with Canada has occupied a large part of the narrative this election cycle in the seven border states electing senators on Tuesday.

The Wolverine State is seeing a heated election campaign between Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers.

El-Sayed, a Muslim, has been the subject of several Islamophobic and racists attacks, including from Trump who called the Democrat a “jihadist” and said he should have to use a metal detector to enter the U.S. Senate.

On his part, El-Sayed has kept a focus on affordability and the high price of gas from the Iran war. When asked about the attacks against his name and faith, El-Sayed turned the conversation towards the high cost of the trade war with Canada.

“My name is not the reason you can’t afford your gas or groceries or to go see a doctor. Their war in Iran is the reason why. Their insane tariffs on Canada is the reason why,” he told reporters last month.

“If you’re picking a fight with Canada, you’re the asshole,” he said.

Michigan and Ontario have deeply integrated auto and steel manufacturing supply chains, with Trump’s trade war causing economic pain on both sides of the border. Canada has become a sticking point in the Michigan Senate election, with even Rogers distancing himself from Trump’s trade policy.

“Canada is not our enemy,” Rogers said in a campaign ad, in which he called for an end to the trade war despite supporting it months earlier.

El-Sayed appears to have the lead, although polls diverge on how sizeable his lead is.

A Beacon Research and Shaw & Company poll conducted for Fox News in September found he had a slight one-point lead, and a Marist University poll found him ahead by a thin two-point margin.

However, more recent polls suggest he May have surged. A CNN/Ssrs poll conducted between Oct. 20 and 27 giving him a seven-point lead, while the latest New York Times/Siena Poll released on Sunday put him ahead by 11 points.

The Democratic campaign in Michigan, though, has had its share of hiccups with Congresswoman Haley Stevens’s shock decision to endorse Rogers, who she once said was a “fraud” and a “rubber stamp” for Trump.

Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed in August, broke with El-Sayed after asking him to disavow an ad from an outside group that was critical of American aid to Israel. El-Sayed said he had nothing to do with the ad.

Appearing at a campaign event with Rogers, Stevens said her endorsement was “about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country.”

The Democratic establishment rallied around El-Sayed, with Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer calling Stevens’s move a “despicable betrayal.”

During the Senate candidates’ debate last month, Republican incumbent Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson sparred in a heated exchange over Canada.

“I was successful in getting road salt removed from the tariff list,” Collins said, referring to Trump’s decision to exempt certain Canadian goods from his sweeping 50 per cent tariffs.

“What about everything else? We can’t eat road salt,” Jackson hit back, arguing that Trump’s tariffs have not only hit Maine’s lumber and fishing industries, but also put a dent in the tourism sector with visits from Canadians taking a nosedive.

Collins, who has been the senator from Maine since she was first elected in January 1997, has distanced herself from the Trump administration’s trade policies.

In a letter to U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in August, Collins warned that Trump’s trade war against Canada would mean “higher costs, risk, and uncertainty for Maine families, small and large businesses and our communities.”

Jackson appears to have a slight edge in the polls, with the latest New York Times/Sienna poll putting him six points ahead. The same poll in September had Collins ahead with three points in September.

The latest University of New Hampshire Poll said he was nine points ahead while the CNN/Ssrs poll gave him a narrow four-point lead.

Collins, however, is known to be a bit of a political survivor who has proven the polls wrong before. In 2020, some polls had Collins trailing by as much as 12 points when she came back from behind to win the seat.

The race for traditionally ruby-red Alaska looks to be in contention this year.

Democrat Mary Peltola still leads Republican Dan Sullivan in the polls, but her lead in the New York Times/Sienna poll has narrowed from seven points in September to a single point in the latest poll released on Sunday.

The state’s Senate election is in Trump’s crosshairs after the New York Times reported a secret effort to stack the ballot to favour Peltola. It was reported that the Peltola campaign allegedly recruited another candidate called Dan J. Sullivan Jr., who has a similar name to the Republican nominee Dan S. Sullivan, to run to deliberately confuse voters.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said this was “Voter Fraud at the Highest Level” and called for Peltola to be “removed from the Ballot and prosecuted.”

Alaska’s Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an inquiry into what he called “an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections.”

There is no Democrat on the ballot for the Senate in Idaho, where the Democratic nominee withdrew in July. Instead, three-term Republican senator Jim Risch is facing independent candidate and U.S. Army veteran Todd Achilles, who has previously served as a Democrat in the Idaho House of Representatives.

Despite a spirited campaign that has focused on the anger around affordability and data centre development in the state, Achilles is trailing in the polls. Even a Nexus poll commissioned by his own campaign has him down six points, while a Republican-sponsored poll puts Risch ahead by 27 points.

Montana is seeing a three-horse race, with Republican Kurt Alme facing Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead and independent candidate Seth Bodnar.

While Bankhead won the primary, polls show she has been trailing in third place with Alme the favourite to win the race. This has prompted several prominent Democrats, including former Transport Secretary Pete Butteigeg to endorse Bodnar over the official party nominee.

Democrat Chris Pappas, who became the first openly gay member to represent New Hampshire in 2018, is heavily favoured in the polls win the race for senate.

The most recent New York Times/Sienna poll had Pappas up by 12 points over Republican John Sununu, who has Trump’s endorsement, while the most recent UMass Lowell poll had him up by seven.

Polls are divided on how wide Democrat Peggy Flannigan’s lead is in Minnesota, with the New York Times/Sienna poll putting her ahead by 14 points.

On the other hand, a Mason-Dixon poll conducted for the Minnesota Star Tribune in October had Flannigan, the state’s Lt. Gov., leading Republican conservative commentator and Republican candidate Michele Tafoya by four points.

stories.title: ‘No amendment was done’: Ridesharing issue back in St. Thomas, two years after council asked staff to amend 2013 taxi bylaw
stories.summary: After seven months driving the citizens of St. Thomas for a flat rate of $12, Bob Pate is being told he’s no longer allowed to do so.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
After seven months driving the citizens of St. Thomas for a flat rate of $12, Bob Pate is being told he’s no longer allowed to do so.

“I got a phone call on Friday from the bylaw officer, and he said I have to stop everything by Friday, Nov. 6,” said Pate – the owner of Easy Ride – who created a ridesharing app, bought a Cadillac, and has multiple drivers.

The city received a complaint about his service and is now threatening to shut him down.

“All rideshare services right now would fall under the current taxi bylaw,” said Thomas Thayer, St. Thomas’ city clerk.

“Any vehicle participating in rideshare would fall under the definition of a taxicab.”

This issue came up two years ago in November 2024.

At the request of rideshare driver Malachi Male, St. Thomas City Council asked staff to amend their 2013 Taxi bylaw to include ride shares .

It was never done.

“They didn’t pass any law or anything and no amendment was done,” said Pate.

“It is still lingering from last two years.”

Thayer said the city is looking at options.

“But as I understand it, the provincial government is looking to potentially upload rideshare enforcement and authorization regulation to their level, which would take it away from the municipalities,” said Thayer.

“To put staff effort right now into developing and amending our taxi bylaw for rideshare services, we’re going to wait until the province determines what they ultimately want to do. We’re taking a similar stance to what other medium-sized cities are currently doing.”

Pate has been told he needs to comply by either obtaining a taxi licence or be shut down.

“This is not a taxi, this is a ride sharing business,” said Pate.

“The same as Uber, Lyft, and other platforms.”

Pate says he has all the safety precautions in place to be a rideshare driver and business owner.

“I have to get the venerable sector check from the police,” said Pate.

“We get that report and after that I will hire them as a driver. I am driving [a], like, $100,000 worth car and all the cars we are having a proper insurance and plus I have additional insurance for my passengers.”

Pate has started a petition asking for “Fair Recognition, Regulation, and Support of Easy Ride.”

He is hoping to get the issue before council on Nov. 9.

“You can make it official for every ride share and apply the rules and regulations,” said Pate.

“What kind of license do you need? What kind of other stuff do we need to get? We will get it done and we will get legalized and we will get everything running.”

stories.title: Prenatal program expands in London thanks to funding from London Food Bank
stories.summary: Multiple agencies, including the London Food Bank (LFB) and the Middlesex-London Health Unit (MLHU), have expanded services for expecting people in London.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Multiple agencies, including the London Food Bank (LFB) and the Middlesex-London Health Unit (MLHU), have expanded services for expecting people in London.

The partners hope the growth of the Smart Start for Babies program will go a long way towards reducing food insecurity and improving nutrition.

The program, which already operates in six locations around London, is being expanded to the Boys and Girls Club of London and the Highbury and Huron location of London Intercommunity Health Centre.

Melina Rimtebaye, a mother of a six-month-old son, has already been helped through SSB services.

“Even just changing a diaper, trying to know what the baby needs, helps,” she said during an interview with CTV News.

The program offers insight and information to pregnant people facing social or economic barriers. Programs include classes on a range of topics, including preparing for labour and cooking affordable snacks to keep themselves and their baby healthy.

“While they’re here, they’ll be preparing food together and learning about healthy nutrition and also receiving supports like grocery cards,” said Jennifer Proulx, the director of family and community health at MLHU.

The expansion of the Smart Start program was made possible by a $180,000 donation from the LFB.

Thanks to cash donations, the agency has expanded its footprint beyond traditional food donations.

“We often don’t know the people we serve, so we wanted to work with groups like the resource centers as well, that work with people on the deeper issues and in the causes of food insecurity”, said Jane Roy of the London Food Bank.

Melina says the help has given her a chance to care for her son while preparing to enter the workforce with a nearly acquired business law degree.

More information on the Smart Start for Babies program can be found here: Prenatal Health – Middlesex-London Health Unit

stories.title: Difficult and unpopular decisions ahead, B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says the Conservative caucus of 63 legislators is united to lead the province but he warns of difficult and unpopular decisions ahead.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - The British Columbia Conservative caucus of 63 newly elected legislators is united to lead the province, premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said Monday, but he warned there would be difficult and unpopular decisions ahead.

Doerkson made the comments as Conservative legislators gathered for their first caucus meeting in Victoria, where he said their job now would be to govern on behalf of all constituents, no matter which party people voted for in the Oct. 24 election.

He said Conservatives owe every British Columbian the same effort and respect.

“That is the responsibility, of course, that comes from winning, but it makes making difficult decisions somewhat, maybe unpopular.”

He said B.C. residents don’t expect perfection, but they do want honesty, effort and integrity from their government, and elected Conservatives must put the public ahead of their own party’s interests every time.

Doerkson said people would be watching to see if his caucus would splinter as it did under the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

“I know that there will be a lot of commentary about this caucus, and a lot of people watching to see whether or not we can hold it together,” he said.

“So, let me save everyone the suspense: this caucus is unified,” Doerkson said to cheers from the crowd.

Jaime Stein, the Conservative just elected in the riding of Vancouver-Langara, was asked about caucus unity Monday and said in an interview that his main concern was getting things done for B.C. residents.

“We left the caucus meeting this morning with a message, which is one team, and that is what we are going forward with as a team,” Stein said.

UBC political science lecturer Stewart Prest said the caucus is united for now.

“But I don’t know that it will be true for the duration,” he said. “We have in many ways a deeply divided caucus here, two parties present within the single B.C. Conservative caucus.”

Prest said the party still has a populist faction.

“On the other side, we know there are a number of MLAs, who had left to join CentreBC, who were looking for a moderate version of conservatism.”

While the caucus is united through the “promise of power,” decisions around cabinet appointments and the legislative agenda May lead to disharmony, Prest said.

Several Conservative members quit or were fired from the caucus just months into Findlay’s leadership before she resigned two days before the NDP under David Eby set off an election.

The members came back after Doerkson was appointed and he led the party to the election win.

Prest said the large size of the caucus gives Doerkson more of a cushion.

“He can afford to alienate a couple of individual MLAs,” he said. “If anyone is in a mood to be completely uncompromising, they May find themselves left in the cold.”

He said if there was a perception that one side of the party was not being listened to, then a number of members — particularly if they are left out of cabinet — were free to speak their minds, becoming like a minor opposition from the backbench.

Doerkson said Monday that B.C. residents could count on the Conservatives to stay focused on what they were elected to do.

He said a Conservative government would deliver a better economy, health care system and public safety.

“That is what we are going to do, and it is absolutely my intention to do it as quickly as possible,” he said.

The incoming premier says legislators are to be sworn in Nov. 19 and the new cabinet would be announced Nov. 20.

Former Conservative leader John Rustad said the toughest job of any premier is to build a cabinet.

No matter how many people Doerkson appoints to cabinet, he will disappoint others, he said.

“So, does he go with 12 people in cabinet, and have 50 people not in cabinet?” Rustad said in an interview last week.

Claire Rattee, who previously served as critic for mental health and addictions, said nobody has heard anything about cabinet.

“I have every confidence and faith in his ability to choose an excellent cabinet,” she said. “I’m just happy to be here to serve (the riding of) Skeena and the residents I represent and anywhere that he would see fit for me or for any of my colleagues.”

Doerkson did not say whether he would recall the legislature for a fall session, but repeated previous promises made on the campaign trail.

“That means putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working British Columbians,” he said. “It means treating taxpayers with respect and saying no to new taxes. It means giving small businesses room to grow with a (provincial sales tax) exemption that will help them to invest, hire and succeed.”

Doerkson also said his government would repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, while continuing to “build strong relationships” with First Nations in the province.

“I am committed that we will do that also as soon as we can,” he said.

B.C. First Nations chiefs have warned against repealing the legislation, urging instead to use it as a framework for reconciliation.

Doerkson also signalled a change in housing legislation.

“We will return housing decisions to the people and the communities, who know their neighbourhoods so much better than Victoria.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version misspelled the first name of Jaime Stein.

stories.title: Survivor of Belleville, Ont., synagogue shooting cites need for extensive security
stories.summary: The vice-president of the Belleville synagogue that was attacked by a gunman in September says costly, enhanced security measures are needed to ensure the safety of congregants.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — One of the leaders of the Belleville, Ont., synagogue that was targeted by a gunman in September says costly enhanced security measures are needed to ensure the safety of congregants.

Police have described the Sept. 20 attack as a thwarted attempt at a mass killing of Jewish worshippers at the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

Police say the shooter had multiple guns, large amounts of ammunition and gasoline and the motive to carry out an extended attack when he opened fire on an officer stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue.

Shima Vigodda, vice-president of the synagogue, told a news conference on Parliament Hill on Monday that before the shooting, the institution’s security priorities were things like replacing windows broken in acts of vandalism and installing burglar alarms.

An existing federal program that helps places of worship make security improvements was adequate for such modest expenses, he indicated.

But Vigodda, who survived the gunman’s assault, said it has become clear that more expensive measures are necessary — improvements the Canada Community Security Program would not fully cover.

He said those measures include things like installing bullet-resistant glass, replacing inner and outer doors, building a safe room, installing fencing to slow or halt a would-be attacker, and having security personnel or armed police on site.

“These measures are necessary not only to ensure our physical security, but to deter would-be attackers,” Vigodda said. “For many in our congregation who were there on Yom Kippur, it is also a necessity for them to feel comfortable enough to return to the synagogue.”

Approved proposals under the federal security program are eligible for funding to cover up to 70 per cent of project costs, with a maximum Public Safety Canada contribution of $5 million per project.

Vigodda said that even with the program, smaller communities struggling to ensure adequate security while trying to cover other expenses face “an agonizing and sometimes impossible choice.”

Noah Shack, chief executive of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, told the news conference the federal budget, being tabled Thursday, is an opportunity for the Liberal government to build on its new national security strategy by investing in counter-radicalization, intelligence and counterterrorism.

He said the centre is working closely with Public Safety Canada to strengthen the Canada Community Security Program, “so that every institution can access the support it needs, and that the program is intended to provide, regardless of its financial circumstances.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

— With files from Alyssa Wheeler in Ottawa and Paola Loriggio in Toronto

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press
