“These measures are necessary not only to ensure our physical security, but to deter would-be attackers,” Vigodda said. “For many in our congregation who were there on Yom Kippur, it is also a necessity for them to feel comfortable enough to return to the synagogue.”
Approved proposals under the federal security program are eligible for funding to cover up to 70 per cent of project costs, with a maximum Public Safety Canada contribution of $5 million per project.
Vigodda said that even with the program, smaller communities struggling to ensure adequate security while trying to cover other expenses face “an agonizing and sometimes impossible choice.”

Noah Shack, chief executive of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, told the news conference the federal budget, being tabled Thursday, is an opportunity for the Liberal government to build on its new national security strategy by investing in counter-radicalization, intelligence and counterterrorism.

He said the centre is working closely with Public Safety Canada to strengthen the Canada Community Security Program, “so that every institution can access the support it needs, and that the program is intended to provide, regardless of its financial circumstances.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.
— With files from Alyssa Wheeler in Ottawa and Paola Loriggio in Toronto
Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Experts suggest Canada lock in gains with EU amid rise in far-right movements
stories.summary: Experts in European Union policy say Canada should try solidifying gains with the EU in legal frameworks as right-wing movements gain ground on the continent.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Experts in European Union policy say Canada should try solidifying gains with the EU in legal frameworks as right-wing movements gain ground on the continent.

Academics studying EU relations are testifying to the House foreign-affairs committee after a Montreal summit last week which officials praised as a historic partnership.

Carleton University professor Achim Hurrelmann says that recent talk of Canada becoming an EU “associate member” attracts symbolic attention but officials could easily drop that language.

He says Canada should focus on getting wins encoded into European law, and consider restructuring the EU trade deal to increase economic gains.

University of Toronto professor Mark Manger says there are few concrete outcomes from last week’s summit and that many of the agreements match what Mexico already has with the EU.

He suggested Ottawa could allow European mobile networks to set up shop in Canada in exchange for European countries dropping restrictions on importing Canadian food.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

By Owen Schuller Nov 2, 2026 | 2:14 PM

Conflicting messages from Washington and Ottawa are raising questions about the state of Canada-U.S. trade talks, with U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting a deal is near while Canadian officials say little progress has been made.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has acknowledged that trade talks with the U.S. have become more intense. American officials have suggested a deal could be possible before the U.S. midterm elections.

A Canadian government official with knowledge of the negotiations, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said discussions have continued but that limited progress has been made.

The current dispute began in early 2025 when President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Over time, some tariffs were paused and exemptions were introduced. However, the trade dispute has continued to escalate, affecting steel, automotive, lumber and aluminum industries.

Matt Farrell, a political science professor at Fanshawe College, describes the main obstacle to reaching a trade agreement. “In short, it is the President. If Trump doesn’t like something that Canada is doing, he will add tariffs.”

Image 15 Photo credit: reuters

Farrell explained that tariffs could potentially be dropped,but only if Canada offers something in return.

To make significant progress or a trade deal, Farrell believes, “it’s just political convenience and optics. If there’s a reason where President Trump wants to make a deal, then he will. That’s it.”

Farrell said any breakthrough may ultimately depend on political priorities in Washington, leaving the timing and outcome of a potential agreement uncertain.

stories.title: Flu season hit early this year. Ask us your questions on how to stay healthy
stories.summary: Experts say rates this fall are several times higher than the numbers recorded in previous years
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
The influenza virus is hitting harder and earlier this year across Canada, prompting an early start to flu season.

Rates this fall are several times higher than the numbers recorded in previous years, experts say, and some provinces are offering flu shots earlier than usual, as vulnerable populations seek to protect themselves.

In an ever-changing situation, it can be hard to know what’s best to keep you and your family safe. Health editor Caroline Alphonso and health reporter Alanna Smith answered reader questions on this year’s flu season, what infection rates and vaccination plans look like in your region and how you can prevent and manage symptoms.

Submit your questions in the box below, or send us an e-mail at audience@globeandmail.com .

stories.title: Cija calls for more power and resources for police to protect Jews ahead of federal budget
stories.summary: The group also called on the Liberals to renew and reform the government's National Strategy on Countering Radicalization to Violence
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — A leading Jewish group is asking the federal government to boost police and intelligence agencies’ abilities to fight antisemitic crimes as a Liberal MP says there is still more work to be done to protect Canadian Jews.

Speaking to reporters before the Liberals table their 2026 budget on Thursday, Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs head Noah Shack called on the government to ensure proper funding for counter-radicalization programs to stem the rapid rise of antisemitism in Canada.

“The common thread among youth in particular who are susceptible to violent extremism, the common thread across all the different ideological vectors, is conspiracy theories and hate towards Jews,” Shack said Monday.

“We know that in confronting antisemitism, we are getting at the root of a larger problem, or at least a significant manifestation of a larger problem,” he added.

On Sept. 20, a gunman fired at police officers stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., while congregants met inside for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

Reports state that the assailant opened fire on police constables Jeff Smith and Michael McCurdy while yelling “you are going to die for the Jews.”

The shooting was the latest in a rising number of antisemitic violent attacks against Jewish individuals or their meeting spaces across Canada.

Shack was accompanied on Parliament Hill on Monday with Douglas Lobel and Shima Vigodda, two survivors of the shooting last month at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue.

“For those of us at the synagogue on Yom Kippur, though we were shocked at what occurred, none of us were surprised. I hope that what occurred in Belleville is a wake-up call as to just how high the stakes are at the moment,” said Vigodda, vice-president of Sons of Jacob Congregation.

In a memo to Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree on Oct. 22, Cija called on the government to further invest and expand “Charter-compliant” powers of the RCMP and Csis in order to fight antisemitism and radicalization.

Shack also called on the Liberals to renew and reform the government’s National Strategy on Countering Radicalization to Violence.

“Antisemitism has become the glue by which different extremist ideologies, from far-left radicals to neo-Nazis and Islamists come together,” Shack noted.

Liberal MP Chris Malette, who represents the riding containing Belleville and lives just two blocks from the synagogue, said there is proof that the government’s recent changes to anti-hate speech legislation are working.

“Do I agree that more needs to be done? Absolutely,” said Malette, assuring that the government was listening to the Jewish community’s concerns.

“I’m confident that that we can help adjust our security systems and our legislation to meet the changing realities and severity and the seriousness of the threats against our faith communities, because we’re seeing it at unseen levels,” he added.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter with National Post in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government.

stories.content:
Burnaby - Two family members have been charged in the death of an 11-year-old boy who was reported missing in Burnaby, B.C., more than a year ago.

Police received a report in September 2025 to check on the well-being of Kai Pavlovic, who was last known to be living with his family in Burnaby.

stories.title: Unseasonably warm temperatures expected across southern Ontario this week
stories.summary: A low-pressure system is expected to influence the region’s weather pattern, drawing moisture northward and bringing periodic chances of light showers.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Southern Ontario is set to experience unseasonably warm temperatures this week, with daytime highs climbing into the upper teens and low 20s, according to CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Atchison said mild conditions will persist through much of the week, with overnight temperatures remaining relatively warm and daytime highs ranging from 18 C to 21 C in many areas.

“We’re taking a run at some records over the next couple of days with temperatures in the upper teens and low 20s,” Atchison said.

A low-pressure system is expected to influence the region’s weather pattern, drawing moisture northward and bringing periodic chances of light showers.

Atchison said there is about a 40 per cent chance of scattered showers Monday evening into early Tuesday morning. Any rainfall that develops is expected to be light and spotty.

Cloud cover is forecast to clear Tuesday afternoon, giving way to a mix of sun and cloud.

“Tuesday is going to be gorgeous,” Atchison said, noting temperatures are expected to reach between 20 C and 21 C across much of southern Ontario, with Windsor forecast to be the warm spot at 22 C.

Another 40 per cent chance of showers is forecast for Wednesday, although temperatures are expected to remain near 21 C. Highs are expected to cool slightly to around 16 C on Thursday, which also carries a chance of showers.

The warm spell is expected to come to an end by the weekend as cooler air moves into the region. Temperatures are forecast to fall to about 8 C on Saturday, accompanied by a 40 per cent chance of rain.

Sunday is expected to bring a mix of sun and cloud with a high near 8 C.

stories.title: Canada on the minds of American voters ahead of the U.S. midterm elections
stories.summary: As Americans are preparing to cast their ballots in their midterm election on Tuesday, their northern neighbours are in the back of their mind as Canadians are paying close attention to what the outcome could mean on this side of the border. For the Republican Party, they are looking to hold onto their slim majorities in […]
stories.author: Caryn Ceolin
stories.content:
As Americans are preparing to cast their ballots in their midterm election on Tuesday, their northern neighbours are in the back of their mind as Canadians are paying close attention to what the outcome could mean on this side of the border.

For the Republican Party, they are looking to hold onto their slim majorities in both chambers of Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate, and whether or not they will continue to control the legislative agenda for the last two years of Donald Trump’s second presidency.

Meanwhile, the Democrats are hoping to flip the House and Senate to attempt to restrain Trump’s unprecedented use of presidential powers.

Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority.

The future of the Senate is less clear. Democrats need a net gain of four seats for a majority, and some polling shows that is within reach.

Trump has largely governed through executive orders in order to get around Congress to further his tariff and trade agenda.

Canada was an early target of Trump’s tariffs and Canadians were shocked and appalled by the president’s repeated threats of annexation.

Tensions escalated further in August when trade talks collapsed and Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had a good conversation with Trump about a trade deal, but did not provide any details.

CityNews is in Washington ahead of the elections where some voters have told us that Canada will be in the back of their minds when they cast their ballots on Tuesday, many who said they were opposed to his treatment of their northern neighbour.

“It’s the closest embassy to the capital,” said one voter. When asked about what he thought of Trump’s treatment of Canada, he said, “It’s the horror story. It’s horrible. They’re our best neighbours.”

“I think it’s unfortunate that one of our biggest allies and trade partners, we’re now in this situation in which we, the American people, don’t agree with. We didn’t ask for it, and here we are having to bear the brunt of the bad news,” said another voter.

Another said they believe the former North American Free Trade Agreement hurt the manufacturing sector in the U.S.

“My perspective is that there needs to be fair trade across … I personally like our northern neighbours tremendously. But in the same sense, I’m not a fan of tariffs either way with a country as long as they’re treating each other fair,”

The top issue to most voters CityNews spoke with was the affordability and the cost of living, with some saying the economic impacts of Trump’s policies acting as major motivators in the midterms.

CityNews 24/7 will provide live coverage of the U.S. midterm elections throughout Tuesday evening. You can watch it the CityNews website here .

With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Canadian dollar steadies as investors weigh officials’ trade comments
stories.summary: Bond yields fall across the curve
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar steadied near a six-week ​high against its U.S. counterpart on ‌Monday as oil prices tumbled and investors weighed positive signals on prospects of a trade deal between the U.S. and Canada.

The loonie was ⁠trading nearly ​unchanged at 1.3975 per US dollar, or 71.56 US cents, after touching on Friday its strongest intraday level since September 16 at 1.3940.

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday ​that his administration has the “concept” of a ‌new trade deal with Canada while Prime Minister Mark Carney said the two leaders had a good conversation on the future of trade between their countries.

The imposition of tariffs on Canada has emerged as an issue ‌in some ​northern U.S. border ‌states like Michigan and Maine before U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.

“Headlines ​have been constructive, following positive comments from ⁠both U.S. and Canadian officials on the topic of trade,” ⁠Shaun Osborne and Eric Theoret, FX strategists at Scotiabank, said in a ​note.

“Fundamentally, the CAD remains well supported by narrowing U.S.-Canada yield spreads which have delivered the bulk of its recent gains,” the strategists said.

The gap between Canada’s 2-year yield and the U.S. equivalent was trading at about 129 ⁠basis points in favor of the U.S. note. Last month, the gap was as wide as 161 basis points.

The Bank of Canada last week raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.50 per cent, its first hike in three ⁠years, out of concern that soaring energy ​prices could drive broader inflation.

U.S. crude oil futures fell 7.8 per cent ⁠to $96.01 a barrel as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials lifted hopes for an end to ‌the US-Israeli war with Iran and stabilization of Middle East crude supply. ​Oil is one of Canada’s major exports.

Canadian bond yields fell across the curve, tracking moves in U.S. Treasuries. The 10-year was down 5.5 basis points at 3.744 per cent, after ​earlier touching its lowest level since September 3 at 3.740 per cent.

stories.title: Toronto police didn’t know hospital patient was home invasion suspect: Demkiw
stories.summary: Investigators didn’t know a man who showed up to a Toronto hospital last Thursday with a gunshot wound was wanted in a violent home invasion, Chief Myron Demkiw says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Investigators didn’t know a man who showed up to a hospital last with a gunshot wound Thursday was wanted for a violent home invasion, Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw says.

Demkiw told reporters Monday officers later learned that patient was allegedly one of three suspects involved in the break-in that sent four members of the same family to hospital .

“The home invasion happens in the middle of the night and a very short time later, an individual shows up at a hospital with a gunshot wound,” Demkiw said.

“What’s important to note is that in the home invasion investigation, there is no information that suggested to investigators an assailant had been shot.”

Police were first called to a home on Hyde Park Circle, near Bayview and Lawrence avenues, around 3:45 a.m. on Oct. 29.

Three masked men in their 20s allegedly forced their way into the home and eventually confronted the family inside, police said. The men were armed with handguns. One suspect had a hammer.

Police have not disclosed any arrests.

Daijohn Richards , 23, was identified Saturday as a suspect; police said he took himself to the hospital later that same day with a gunshot wound to his right shoulder.

Officers “responded to the hospital as they would when people walk into the hospital with a gunshot wound, which happens in the city from time to time,” Demkiw said.

“They continue to advance the investigation, gather evidence and made an announcement publicly that they’ve identified a suspect in the coming hours after that.”

Demkiw wouldn’t comment further, but said the investigators assigned to the case are “some of the best in the business.”

“Had I been a victim of this type of horrible set of circumstances, these are precisely the people I would want chasing and apprehending the offenders and bringing them to justice,” he said.

“I have complete confidence in their abilities, and we will create an opportunity for them to continue to advance their investigation, respecting the integrity of the investigative process.”

Richards is wanted on four counts of discharge of a firearm with intent to wound, four counts of robbery with a firearm, three counts of aggravated assault, break and enter, possession of a prohibited device and disguise with intent.

Four people were inside the home at the time: a man, his wife and their two adult daughters.

All four people were taken to hospital. Three of the victims were shot and two were struck in the head with a hammer, police said. Some have since been released from hospital.

Global News has learned the two adult daughters are Maggie and Cristina Zohil-Morton. Their parents are listed on business profiles as David Morton and Doriana Zohil.

David, CEO of Toronto-based real estate company MAC Group, said in a statement Friday the family is focused on recovery but is becoming more concerned with increasing violence associated with home invasions.

“No family should ever have to experience this,” he said.

“People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives.”

— with files from Rachel Morgan and Alessia Simona Maratta

stories.title: Canada presenting itself as climate leader at COP31, despite policy rollbacks
stories.summary: Ottawa - Despite its rollbacks of climate policy, the Carney government will lead a delegation to the COP31 conference in Turkey next week presenting itself as an international climate leader.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canada will present itself as an international climate leader when it sends a delegation to the annual UN climate talks next week in Turkey, despite its rollbacks of climate policy under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Government officials held a technical briefing for journalists Monday ahead of the annual two-week COP31 conference, the main forum for the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the 2015 Paris climate pact.

That pact committed signatories to reducing emissions sharply to keep global warming below 2 C and as close as possible to 1.5 C above pre-industrial levels by the end of this century. A UN report last month said that goal is now out of reach because emissions have not come down fast enough.

That report will be a key feature of the upcoming COP31, where discussions will address how to reduce emissions to keep warming below 2 C by 2100.

Government officials told the briefing on Monday that Canada remains a “credible international actor on climate change” that other countries are keen to engage with.

But Patrick Bonin, the Bloc Québécois environment critic who will attend COP31 as part of the Canadian delegation, said Canada’s track record of rolling back climate policy has harmed its international reputation.

“I can’t see how they can pivot over a few days during COP to have any credibility on climate change,” Bonin told The Canadian Press in French.

“We’re no longer in an era where Canada can lend itself to any credibility with its action plan on climate, since Canada is in the middle of completely halting its short-term goals and can’t meet its 2030 emission reduction goals until at least 2050.”

The government’s own numbers show Canada is nowhere close to meeting its international commitment to reduce emissions by at least 40 per cent from 2005 levels by 2030.

Since taking office Carney has rolled back a number of climate policies initiated by the former government under Justin Trudeau, including eliminating the consumer carbon price, adjusting standards for the industrial carbon price, repealing a mandate for electric vehicle sales, and cancelling a planned emissions cap on oil and gas production.

In a video released in June, Carney said federal climate policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau was too expensive and divisive.

That same month a number of Canada’s most prominent environmental groups, including the David Suzuki Foundation, Ecojustice, Greenpeace Canada, Nature Canada and Environmental Defence, pushed for meetings with Carney’s aides and MPs to discuss what they called “urgent concerns about the government’s moves to eviscerate environmental laws and procedures and to undermine Canada’s nature, climate and clean energy goals.”

Canada won the “fossil of the day” title at last year’s COP30 in Brazil. Climate Action Network International, which has handed out the satirical award since 1999, said Canada was singled out for the first time in more than a decade for “flushing years of climate action down the drain.”

Carney will not attend the leaders’ summit at the start of the summit but Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin will be in Turkey for the first week of talks. Officials said she will convene a ministerial meeting with the European Union of the Global Methane Pledge, a group of 159 countries committed to collectively reducing global methane emissions by 30 per cent from 2020 levels by 2030.

In June, UN Secretary-General António Guterres launched a global call to action on methane during an address at the London Climate Action Week.

Canadian officials on Monday said Canada will be “promoting” methane mitigation at COP31 as a “high-impact, cost-effective” way to address emissions.

In its latest annual national emissions report last month, the Canadian Climate Institute credited “fugitive methane emission reductions” as the main driver behind a lower level of emissions from Canada’s oil and gas sector in 2025, despite boosts in production.

But even on methane things have been slowed down as Canada delayed the implementation of its methane regulations.

Canada is also in the spotlight after the environment commissioner last week issued a report which found in 2024 the government abandoned work on a 2021 pledge to ban the export of thermal coal, without any record of having a directive to do so.

Government officials have since said the work is only “paused,” though the report said Ottawa formalized the end of the work in August 2025 as part of budget cuts.

Canada and the United Kingdom are the co-leaders of the Powering Past Coal alliance, which seeks to accelerate the transition off coal power around the world.

Government officials refused to say during Monday’s technical briefing whether Canada informed any of its international partners that its work to ban thermal coal exports had ended or was paused.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta’s Justice Minister rejects request to drop proposed electoral map, postpone vote
stories.summary: New boundaries set to be released Monday afternoon
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta’s proposed new provincial electoral boundaries would result in major changes to ridings in Calgary and Lethbridge, expanding their footprints into more rural areas, a prospect that drew accusations of gerrymandering when the maps were released publicly on Monday.

The chair of the independent panel that created the map dismissed concerns that the proposed boundaries would violate the Constitution. But Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi promised to file a legal challenge if Premier Danielle Smith’s government adopts the map, saying the new boundaries would hand an electoral edge to Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party.

Shortly after exiting Question Period, Mr. Nenshi pointed to the U.S.-style practice of manipulating electoral maps to create unfair advantages for a party.

“If the UCP has the nerve to pass this Trump-style, Maga gerrymandered map, if they have the nerve to cheat to win … we’ll see them in court,” Mr. Nenshi said at a news conference after the report containing the map was tabled in the legislature.

A redrawn electoral map has been the subject of intense debate and scrutiny since April when Ms. Smith rejected the proposed boundaries of a first independent commission.

Alberta’s political boundaries are revised every eight to 10 years by an independent panel, a process designed to foster compromise and limit political influence. For decades, provincial legislatures have routinely adopted the recommendations without question.

Ms. Smith’s decision to upend tradition, however, has fuelled accusations of gerrymandering.

After rejecting the first panel’s proposed map, Ms. Smith’s government formed a UCP-dominated committee that created a new independent panel charged with making a second attempt at drawing the electoral map. It was chaired by retired Alberta judge Brian O’Ferrall, selected by the UCP, and included two members tapped by the NDP and two by the UCP.

The new report shows the five-person panel was sharply divided on how to proceed with the map, mirroring tensions among the previous group tasked with the redrawing.

The proposed map was drawn by Mr. O’Ferrall and the two members selected by the UCP: Monte Solberg, a former cabinet minister under prime minister Stephen Harper, and Darwin Durnie, who previously co-authored a submission recommending map changes that would see several ridings in Calgary blend with neighbouring rural communities.

In the report, the three jointly write that the panel’s “time and energy were taken up with responding to the indictments of the panel’s minority who suggest that the process of the advisory panel was constitutionally reckless, an abuse of process, and that the panel’s proposals infringed the Charter.”

The two remaining committee members named by the NDP – University of Alberta law professor Gerard Kennedy and former Okotoks, Alta., town councillor Brent Robinson – wrote in a separate report that some of the new recommended ridings would be “constitutionally fraught” and will likely be challenged in court.

It is unclear how long it will take for the government to pass the new map if it decides to adopt it, but it’s expected to be approved before the fall session ends on Dec. 3.

If adopted, the map would most dramatically change the boundaries of Lethbridge, which is currently split into two ridings mostly contained within the city’s borders. One is represented by the NDP, the other by the UCP.

The new map would split Lethbridge into four, with one urban riding encompassing a chunk of the city and three massive urban-rural hybrids surrounding it.

In the report, the three authors in the majority reason that hybrid ridings can “help cities receive the representation they need” and “help rural electoral divisions obtain the population they need to be relatively compact and manageable.”

Prof. Kennedy and Mr. Robinson, meanwhile, charged the other commissioners with packing voters into the highly condensed Lethbridge riding while diluting the city’s remaining residents in rural areas that extend hundreds of kilometres beyond city limits.

“This makes it easier for the party who drew the boundaries to win additional seats,” the two wrote, adding that while they accept the panelists believe they’re improving effective representation, they are concerned the public won’t believe them.

In Calgary, the three-person majority recommended creating new boundaries that amalgamate three urban ridings in west Calgary with neighbouring rural constituencies.

Much of the Ucp’s political support is based in rural Alberta, while the Ndp’s strength lies in Calgary and Edmonton.

The panelists also disagreed on how much they should edit the proposed map recommended by the chair of the previous panel, Court of King’s Bench judge Dallas K. Miller.

The majority authors wrote that Mr. Miller’s recommendation “does not deserve deification,” while Prof. Kennedy and Mr. Robinson argued the panel didn’t have a mandate to overhaul parts of Alberta’s boundaries.

The new map is expected to be the subject of debate in the Alberta Legislature on Tuesday. So far, Ms. Smith’s government has rejected calls to reverse course.

On Sunday, Alberta’s Justice Minister batted away Elections Alberta’s request for the government to either not approve the new electoral maps or postpone next year’s provincial election to give the agency sufficient time to prepare.

The government “has no intention” of shifting next year’s Oct. 18 fixed election date, Justice Minister Mickey Amery wrote in a statement.

Mr. Amery was responding to a letter from provincial chief electoral officer Gordon McClure, who on Friday circulated a letter to MLAs imploring them to reconsider implementing the new electoral boundaries.

Mr. McClure said Elections Alberta’s resources are strained and that the agency would need 12 to 18 months to implement the new map with 91 ridings, up from 87.

stories.title: Parts of Florida and B.C on the same time zone after Daylight saving change
stories.summary: Although they're on opposite sides of North America, some clocks in Florida and B.C. are synched for the next six months
stories.author: National Post staff
stories.content:
Parts of Canada’s westernmost province, British Columbia, and the sunshine state, Florida, now share the same time.

That means, although Pensacola, Fla. and Cranbrook, B.C. are on opposite sides of North America with vastly different climates and environments, their clocks are synched for the next five months.

That’s because B.C. decided to stick to daylight time permanently, and did not gain an hour over the weekend.

On Nov. 1, most of Canada returned to standard time.

Meanwhile, B.C., Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories have decided against it. Yukon has been on permanent daylight time since 2021 and Saskatchewan since 1966, with the exception of Lloydminster, which straddles the border with Alberta and stopped changing its time this year.

While Pensacola is a balmy 23 degrees Celsius on Monday, Cranbrook is a cool 0 degrees — so for now, it seems that time is all they have in common.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Brilliant Maps (@brilliantmaps)

Most of B.C. has adopted permanent year-round daylight time, staying on Pacific Time. The government shared information online about certain locations that would remain on Mountain Time.

Residents of parts of Southeastern B.C., including Cranbrook, Fernie and Elkford, will “remain aligned with Alberta” and use Mountain Time year round.

It said the change was “to improve people’s overall health, reduce disruptions for families, simplify scheduling and provide an extra hour of evening light during the winter months.”

Pensacola, located in the Florida Panhandle northwest of Miami and Tampa, switched from Central Daylight Time to Central Standard Time over the weekend, as it normally does this time of year.

There are two time zones in Florida — Eastern and Central. Nine of the state’s 67 counties operate completely on Central Time, according to the Pensacola News Journal . Pensacola is located in Escambia County, one of the nine on Central Time.

The time zones in B.C. and Florida won’t stay matched up for too long, though. In March, Pensacola and other cities within the nine counties will revert to daylight time again.

stories.title: Huron County paramedics vote in favour of strike mandate amid contract talks
stories.summary: Paramedics represented by Cupe Local 4513 have voted overwhelmingly in favour of a strike mandate as contract negotiations with Huron County continue.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Paramedics represented by Cupe Local 4513 have voted overwhelmingly in favour of a strike mandate as contract negotiations with Huron County continue.

The union said 99 per cent of members who cast ballots voted to authorize strike action. According to Cupe 4513, all 112 members participated in the vote.

In a news release, local president Kelsy Long said the vote reflects concerns among paramedics about wages, benefits and mental health supports.

The union said paramedics have traditionally relied on arbitration to resolve contract disputes, making the strike vote a departure from past bargaining approaches.

Cupe 4513 argues wages and benefits have fallen behind those offered by neighbouring paramedic services and says staffing levels have become a concern. The union said four paramedics have left the service since the summer and seven have left since the previous collective agreement expired.

The union said progress has been made on several issues during negotiations, including float provisions, job posting language and leave for family-related responsibilities. However, it says significant differences remain on wages, benefits and mental health supports.

According to the union, management has proposed wage increases that would leave Huron County paramedics behind neighbouring services, including Perth and Bruce counties. The union also said no improvements to benefits have been offered.

The union also said it has requested conciliation, although a conciliator has not yet been appointed.

Bargaining between the two sides is scheduled to resume Nov. 23 and 24.

The union said paramedics have traditionally relied on arbitration to resolve contract disputes, making the strike vote a departure from past bargaining approaches.

Cupe 4513 argues wages and benefits have fallen behind those offered by neighbouring paramedic services and says staffing levels have become a concern. The union said four paramedics have left the service since the summer and seven have left since the previous collective agreement expired.

The union said progress has been made on several issues during negotiations, including float provisions, job posting language and leave for family-related responsibilities. However, it says significant differences remain on wages, benefits and mental health supports.

According to the union, management has proposed wage increases that would leave Huron County paramedics behind neighbouring services, including Perth and Bruce counties. The union also said no improvements to benefits have been offered.
The union also said it has requested conciliation, although a conciliator has not yet been appointed.
Bargaining between the two sides is scheduled to resume Nov. 23 and 24.

stories.title: Gas odour prompts partial evacuation at St. Joseph’s Hospital
stories.summary: A portion of the building was evacuated Monday after a gas odour was detected during roof construction.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The “all clear” has been given after a Code Green at St. Joseph’s Hospital.

A portion of the building was evacuated Monday after a gas odour was detected during roof construction.

Hospital officials said the odour was detected in Zone D and the area was evacuated out of an abundance of caution.

As a result, appointments in several clinics had to be cancelled, including the Breast Care Program, Rheumatology, Hand and Upper Limb, Hand Therapy and the Wsib clinic.

Patients with appointments in those programs were being asked to wait for a call to reschedule.

Officials said appointments in all other programs at St. Joseph’s Hospital are proceeding as scheduled.

No injuries or additional safety concerns were immediately reported.

stories.title: Nine more First Nations file court challenges to Pacific Link pipeline
stories.summary: The nine applicants include First Nations located along the proposed pipeline and tanker shipping routes
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — Nine more First Nations have filed court challenges against the federal government’s decision to designate the West Coast pipeline a project of national interest under Bill C-5, the Building Canada Act.

First Nations argue cabinet did not discharge its duty to consult and provide adequate accommodation, before deciding to fast-track the Pacific Link pipeline on Oct. 1.

The nine applicants from B.C. also argue the federal government erred by failing to exercise its powers under the BCA consistently with the statutory imperatives arising from the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (Unda), which was passed by Parliament in 2021.

“This project being pre-approved does not meet the standard not only of free, prior, and informed consent, but the minimum standard of consultation,” said Terry Teegee, regional chief of the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations, during a press conference in Richmond, B.C., ON Monday.

“We are very concerned about not only this project but other projects, and other First Nations should all be concerned across this country,” he added.

The legal challenges were filed in Federal Court last week, bringing the total number of First Nations challenging Pacific Link’s national interest designation to 10, after Cold Lake First Nation in Alberta was the first to file on Oct. 8.

The nine applicants include First Nations located along the proposed pipeline and tanker shipping routes, as well as those not geographically located close to the pipeline, but argue their fishing rights and livelihood rely on Fraser River salmon.

The Pacific Pipeline is the first project to be designated as a project of national interest under the government’s new major projects legislation. The legislation allows Cabinet to give projects in the national interest a fast-tracked regulatory process.

The proposed route will run 1,200 kilometres from Bruderheim, Alta., to a proposed large-tanker port in Delta, B.C.

The newly formed Major Projects Office undertook consultations with over 130 Indigenous communities between July 3 to Sept. 18, before the designation was announced.

The MPO will begin its review of the project in early 2027, with public hearings held by the commission of the Canada Energy Regulator. The MPO is expected to finalize a conditions document by Sept. 1, 2027.

The applicants argue the consultation process was inadequate and took place during the busy summer months.

“We were reached out to be engaged in late July with the deadline, and my community, we had a wildfire right above our community where it was two, five kilometers away and the letters came in,” said St’át’imc Chiefs Council Chairperson Chief Justin Kane.

Calgary-based Pembina Pipeline has so far agreed to take a minority 10 per cent private stake in the development, the publicly owned Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission is also a proponent. The Trans Mountain Corporation is leading the project.

Indigenous communities have been offered a 10 per-cent ownership stake in the pipeline project. The pipeline, once completed, is expected to generate over $20 billion in GDP per year and $100 billion in government revenue by 2060.

Government officials have acknowledged and are prepared for potential court challenges. Last week, Justice Minister Sean Fraser said Bill C-5 respects First Nations’ rights.

“We believe that we’ve met the constitutional obligations that we have to act within the spheres of authorities that we have, while respecting importantly the rights of First Nations communities and Indigenous rights holders more broadly,” said Fraser, before a caucus meeting on Oct. 28. “To the extent that there are concerns, my hope is that we can work through them through negotiation.”

Teegee said the prime minister should be held accountable for taking advantage of the uncertainty of a trade war with the U.S. to pass Bill C-5 and its successor, Bill C-39, which is currently being studied by a legislative committee.

“It’s a process that Prime Minister Carney should be called out for,” he said. “He is utilizing taking advantage of a crisis for a bill that they’ve always wanted to pass, it’s nothing new.”

Robert Banks Terminal 2, a proposed project in Delta, B.C., that would increase the Port of Vancouver’s container capacity by approximately 50 per cent, was also designated a project of national interest by the federal government last Friday.

Robert Banks is the endpoint of the proposed Pacific Link pipeline.

“I can only project that this is just going to heat up more and more and more as more massive projects are approved without proper consultation with First Nations people, as was the port and the pipeline, and without any recognition of the real needs of reconciliation, this is not ending today,” said Hugh Baker, a political executive at the First Nations Summit.

Jordan Gowling joined National Post's parliamentary bureau in 2026 after two years as Financial Post's economics reporter on Parliament Hill. She previously worked as a producer at CTV News in Ottawa.

stories.title: Ontario doctors call for reform, central intake, ON access to specialized care
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's doctors are calling on the province to reform access to specialist care, drop the use of fax machines and launch a provincewide central intake so they can end their patchwork process of finding specialized care for patients through group chats and social media.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario’s doctors are calling on the province to reform access to specialist care, drop the use of fax machines and launch a provincewide central intake so they can end their patchwork process of finding specialized care for patients through group chats and social media.

The Ontario Medical Association said a recent survey shows one third of patients with a chronic condition are waiting six months or longer to see a specialist.

The problem has become so pervasive that doctors say they now reach out to physicians in some ad hoc group chats or on social media to find a specialist with reasonable wait times to see their patients.

“These delays have real consequences and people are growing frustrated,” OMA president Dr. Rebecca Hicks said on Monday.

Problems accessing specialist care have led patients to hospital emergency departments instead, she said.

The association said it wants the province to expand team-based care within specialist practices, something the province has had success with for its primary care initiative.

The province is using the team-based model to link every Ontarian to primary care, rather than trying to link everyone to a family doctor. The team-based model combines family physicians with nurses and a number of other health-care providers like nurse practitioners, physiotherapists and occupational therapists.

“Giving doctors access to nurses, allied health professionals and administrative support can increase capacity, improve co-ordination, and help more patients receive treatment sooner,” Hicks said.

The OMA also wants to see a provincewide central intake system for specialist care and diagnostics.

“Patients should be connected to the right provider or service as quickly as possible, regardless of where they live,” Hicks said.

Patients are now also waiting longer to get an MRI scan, the association said.

“Since 2022, waits for a non-urgent adult MRI have increased from approximately 70 days to 100 days, and the provincial target is just 28 days,” Hicks said. “Every day spent waiting for a diagnostic test can delay the start of treatment.”

Health Minister Sylvia Jones said the province will work on a centralized intake system for specialized care once they have completed their central intake project for primary care.

“I’m not going to give you a timeline because it is something that physicians have to make the decision that they want to participate in the central referral,” Jones said. “What I can tell you is, ON the family physician side, the primary care side, they’re very excited about it, as are we.”

Hicks said OMA is compiling a list of specialists to be able “to do e-referrals instead of e-fax referrals, joining the 21st century.”

Jones said in 2023 the province would eliminate faxes in the medical system within five years. On Monday she said they’re “working on it,” but refused to provide a timeline.

There are centralized intakes in some regions of Ontario for hip and knee replacements, the OMA noted.

“We’d like to see what has worked in those systems and bring it forward as we expand outward,” Hicks said.

The situation for specialist referrals has become so untenable that doctors have begun looking elsewhere for help.

“Our physicians are using Facebook groups, WhatsApp groups, to actually find the community-based specialists to connect patients to care,” said Dr. Zainab Abdurrahman, a pediatric allergist and immunologist who is a former president of the OMA.

“We need a centralized system that’s going to allow for patients to be able to, if they can, go further to get faster care, to be able to know that these opportunities are there, and just to also know who is in practice and where. There’s no great way to know when there’s a new specialist in your region.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto police chief defends decision not to arrest Bridle Path home invasion suspect in hospital
stories.summary: Chief Myron Demkiw says police had no information at the time to suggest any of the attackers were shot
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
The Toronto Police chief says there was “no failure” when officers did not detain a man in hospital with a gunshot wound who was later identified as a suspect in a violent home invasion that injured a family of four.

The man, who left the hospital, is now the subject of a Canada-wide warrant in connection with the early-morning robbery last Thursday in Toronto’s Bridle Path neighbourhood, one of the city’s wealthiest areas. Police say masked assailants shot three members of the family and attacked them with a hammer.

Police revealed over the weekend that the suspect ended up in hospital just hours after the attack. Officers confronted the man in hospital but did not detain or arrest him. Investigators say they now believe he was accidentally shot by one of the other home invasion suspects.

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw said the officers could not have detained the man because they lacked evidence and did not know at the time that any of the suspects in the home invasion had a gunshot wound. The man was in the hospital for just a few hours before he was discharged.

“From my perspective, there has been no failure,” Chief Demkiw told reporters at a news conference on Monday. “There has been nothing but exceptional policework.”

Police now say the man who was in hospital, identified as 23-year-old Daijohn Richards, is wanted and should be considered armed and dangerous. He has a gunshot wound to the right shoulder, police said.

Chief Demkiw said there was no information in the hours after the attack that any of the suspects had been shot.

“The home invasion happens in the middle of the night and a short time – a very short time – later an individual shows up in the hospital with a gunshot wound,” the chief said.

“What’s important to note is that in the home invasion investigation there is no information that suggested to investigators an assailant had been shot.”

The home invasion robbery has drawn attention to an increase in such crimes in Toronto. Shootings and homicides have dramatically declined in the city in 2025 and 2026. But police say Toronto has had 119 home invasions in 2026, up 35 per cent from the same time last year.

The victims are real estate executive David Morton, 75; his wife Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64; and the couple’s two adult daughters in their 20s, Cristina and Maggie.

Police were called to the hospital because that is the standard protocol when someone is treated for gunshot wounds.

In Ontario, such ground rules are spelled out in the 2005 Mandatory Gunshot Wounds Reporting Act. But one legal expert said the law only gives police notifications about hospitalized people, and no heightened ability to detain or interview anyone.

“It doesn’t give police new powers – it doesn’t say that if someone is reported, police can arrest them on reasonable suspicion,“ said Andrew Flavelle Martin, a law professor at Dalhousie University’s Schulich School of Law.

Police previously said they were looking for three suspects. Investigators have said the assailants entered the house through its back entrance while the family was sleeping. The masked men attacked the family as they demanded valuables, police said.

Chief Demkiw said the investigation remains “very active” and is being handled by the force’s best investigators.

“We are following the evidence as it becomes available,” he said. “Had there been evidence to allow us to do something different, that’s what would have happened.”

Police were called to the family’s home on Hyde Park Circle shortly before 4 a.m. on Thursday.

Investigators have said they did not develop grounds for an arrest warrant until Friday evening. On Saturday morning, police publicly identified Mr. Richards as a suspect. He is now wanted for four counts of discharging a firearm with intent to wound, four counts of robbery with a firearm and three counts of aggravated assault.

With files from Kelly Grant

stories.title: Inside man or patsy? Crown, defence pitch narratives at trial of man accused in heist
stories.summary: Was a then-Air Canada employee an inside man who helped carry out one of the biggest gold heists in Canadian history, or a scapegoat exploited by a longtime friend and left to shoulder the blame?
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Was a then-Air Canada employee an inside man who helped carry out one of the biggest gold heists in Canadian history, or a scapegoat exploited by a longtime friend and left to shoulder the blame?

Those were the two competing scenarios presented to a Brampton, Ont., court Monday as prosecutors and defence lawyers made their closing submissions in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu.

Sidhu has pleaded not guilty to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in connection with the April 2023 heist at Toronto’s Pearson airport.

Court has heard Sidhu’s profile was used to print a doctored air waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency, but that it wasn’t uncommon for employees to use someone else’s profile on shared computers.

Prosecutors allege Sidhu was the one who printed the fraudulent waybill and who made the call to release the shipment. He also has a close relationship with Simran Preet Panesar, who worked for the airline at the time and is still wanted in the case, as well as a link to Archit Grover, another accused, they argued.

Sidhu was implicated by Arsalan Chaudhary, who is considered one of the architects of the plan, and made a “very explicit comment about the loss of his cut” in wiretaps from February 2024, Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic argued.

“For these following factors to exist ... and for Mr. Sidhu not to have been involved in the planning and the execution of the theft is near impossible,” she said.

The defence, meanwhile, argued the evidence points to a different narrative: that Sidhu was taken advantage of by Panesar, his then-colleague and friend of roughly two decades, who they allege actually orchestrated the heist from the inside.

Panesar resigned in the months that followed the heist and left Canada with his family after being interviewed by police, the trial has heard. He has never returned and a Canada-wide warrant has been issued for his arrest.

Panesar “hijacked” Sidhu’s user ID and password as well as that of two other employees, while Chaudhary used Sidhu as a “blind telephone switchboard” to reach his alleged co-conspirator when he wasn’t answering his phone, defence lawyer Shale Wagman argued.

“And then when the police closed in, Panesar and Chaudhary fled abroad, leaving Mr. Sidhu in the ditch with a ruined career, mounting legal bills and broken promises to fix the mess they caused,” he argued.

“That is not piecemeal speculation. That single unified explanation connects every dot in this courtroom,” he said, adding investigators did not find any heist money in Sidhu’s home or bank accounts.

In reply, the Crown noted there is no evidence Panesar used Sidhu’s username and password, nor that Panesar and Chaudhary made “hollow promises” from abroad, and that those should only be considered as hypotheticals.

Chaudhary was one of the Crown’s key witnesses in the case.

Chaudhary was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai and has since pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000. He was sentenced to four years in prison and given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

On the stand last month, Chaudhary testified that he’d planned the heist with Panesar and ended up taking 30 per cent of the boxes full of gold bars. He then melted some of the gold and sold it for cash before fleeing to Pakistan, he said.

Chaudhary said he communicated with Sidhu on the day of the theft but couldn’t remember what he said.

He told the court he let Sidhu know the truck and driver were ready on the day of the heist and Sidhu replied, “OK.”

But as his testimony continued, Chaudhary mostly said he did not remember details of conversations he’d mentioned in previous court statements — including one from July when he said he spoke to Sidhu on the phone three times on the day of the heist.

When asked about his previous statement that he’d discussed the logistics of the plan with Sidhu, Chaudhary said he couldn’t remember doing so.

He attributed his memory lapses to post-traumatic stress disorder linked to his alleged abduction in Pakistan.

The case is being heard by a judge alone and a ruling is expected in late January 2027.

In the leadup to the trial, prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case: Ali Raza and Amit Jalota.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Small business tax troubles a target of federal budget: Champagne
stories.summary: Champagne acknowledged that one of the barriers to investment, particularly among Canada's small businesses, is the complexity of the tax code.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Thursday’s federal budget will look to make life easier for Canada’s small- and medium-sized businesses, says Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne.

Champagne provided business leaders a preview of the government’s fiscal plan in a breakfast speech at the Canadian Club Toronto on Monday.

The budget — the second to be delivered under Prime Minister Mark Carney — is expected to support the Liberal government’s push to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States by building up the domestic economy.

In a brief fireside chat after Monday’s speech, Champagne told the crowd Ottawa’s ambitions to stoke private investment and improve productivity are not limited to Canada’s largest companies.

He acknowledged that one of the barriers to investment, particularly among Canada’s small businesses, is the complexity of the tax code.

“We had a number of boutique things and things which might be difficult if you’re small and medium-sized businesses, unless you have a tax adviser to figure out what’s the best way forward,” Champagne told CBC News journalist Peter Armstrong during a fireside chat after his speech.

“I think you will see in this budget a journey to fixing a number of things, to make things more simple, to simplify the life of small and medium-sized businesses. And I think that on Thursday, those who represent small businesses will see themselves in that budget.”

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has called on Ottawa to use the Nov. 5 budget to lower the small business tax rate and fix gaps in the federal tariff relief regime that box out smaller firms.

“Small businesses tell us they don’t want handouts. They want broad policies that would help them reinvest in their businesses and plan for the future,” said Corinne Pohlmann, Cfib executive vice-president of advocacy, in a statement on Oct. 29.

“While major project investments usually get the spotlight, we also need to be building the foundation of our economy by making it more attractive to start and grow a small business.”

Champagne would not offer specific examples of what the federal government is proposing in Thursday’s budget. He did suggest Ottawa is considering more changes to the Scientific Research and Experimental Development program, which encourages firms to invest in themselves to develop innovative technologies.

One of the big-ticket measures accounted for in this upcoming budget is the productivity mega-deduction, which the government announced in September and has continued to highlight as a cornerstone of its investment policy. It’s estimated to cost $36 billion over five years.

The mega-deduction allows businesses to immediately write off the full value of an eligible capital investment in its first year, rather than over the lifetime of its use. The government argues deferring tax payments in this way will encourage firms to invest more in technology and tools that can make their workers more productive.

Champagne said the productivity mega-deduction isn’t just for large firms that want to break ground on pipelines and other nation-building projects. He said it could also help a local café buy a new coffee machine, for example.

“It’s our government’s signal to Canadians to use their capital right here in Canada, to invest in new machinery and technology, to expand their enterprises and to support a Canadian economy that nurtures and develops more workers and innovators,” he said.

The minister did not answer directly when asked whether the budget will offer further details about a planned sovereign wealth fund or a proposal to open Canada’s airports up to private investment.

The Liberal government has set an ambitious goal of attracting $1 trillion in private investment over the next five years. Since Carney took office, the federal budget framework has pivoted sharply away from day-to-day government spending and toward a capital-focused agenda that prioritizes infrastructure and other nation-building projects.

“At its core, our plan is about changing Canada’s growth model. We are building one Canadian economy, unlocking private investment, raising productivity, expanding our productive capacity, and diversifying our trade,” Champagne said in his speech.

Armstrong asked Champagne how renewed momentum in U.S. trade talks could affect Ottawa’s spending plans. The finance minister brushed off the question.

“It’s not about them,” he said. “This is about us, regaining our ability to build.”

stories.title: B.C. First Nations file legal challenges of federal decision on Pacific Link pipeline
stories.summary: Vancouver - Several First Nations in British Columbia have filed legal challenges to the federal government's decision to list the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline between Alberta to B.C.'s coast as a project of national interest, fast-tracking its review.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - First Nations in British Columbia have filed eight separate legal challenges to the federal government’s decision to list the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline between Alberta to B.C.‘s coast as a project of national interest, fast-tracking its review.

Among them is Tsartlip First Nation on Vancouver Island, which said it filed a Federal Court application for judicial review on Friday, asserting Ottawa had not “given sufficient information about the project and its potential impacts.”

Adam Olsen, a spokesman for the nation, called the pipeline decision “reckless” and “rushed,” saying in an interview on Monday that Ottawa had failed in its duty to consult Indigenous communities.

“Tsartlip has a responsibility, as has been expressed by our chief and council, to look after its territory, stand up for those places for the past, present, and future,” said Olsen, who is a former B.C. Green legislator.

“These are incredibly important fishing areas for our people, and so the process was rushed. It was through the middle of summer and the government failed its basic test.”

The pipeline was the first project to receive the national interest designation under the Building Canada Act during an announcement by Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last month.

It means the project would be subject to a fast-tracked, streamlined regulatory process conducted by the federal major projects office.

Olsen said the process is moving too fast.

“The national interest designation concerns a multibillion-dollar publicly funded project that is not expected to be completed until 2032,” he said in the Tsartlip statement. “Yet the consultation and decision-making process happened in less than three months.”

The proposed pipeline would largely follow the path of the existing Trans Mountain pipeline to an export terminal in Metro Vancouver, with an estimated price tag between $35.2 billion and $42.7 billion.

The nine nations involved in challenging Ottawa’s decision are located along the proposed pipeline and tanker routes or use the Fraser River for fishing.

The Boston Bar, Cheam, Lower Nicola, Kwantlen and Kwikwetlem First Nations and the Skeetchestn Indian Band filed their own legal challenges, while the St’at’imc Nation and T’Sou-ke First Nation filed a joint application.

The St’at’imc Chiefs Council, which represents 11 communities along the Lillooet and Fraser rivers, issued a statement on Monday saying it had launched legal action in Federal Court to the government’s designation of the pipeline.

Approving the Pacific Link project without full assessment of risks to salmon and fishing rights, and without deep consultation to ensure the consent of all affected First Nations, is unacceptable and unlawful, the statement said.

The council said its members rely on Fraser River salmon, and the risk of an oil spill from the proposed pipeline’s river crossings was a “heinous” threat to the communities’ fishing rights and way of life.

“The collusion of the federal and provincial governments along with a few industry and corporate elites, who cloak themselves as economic saviours, will force First Nations further into third-world conditions contributed to by the extinction of the Fraser River wild salmon and the collapse of First Nations’ culture and traditions relating to wild salmon,” St’at’imc elder Art Adolph said in the statement.

The statement said the pipeline proposal involves more than 500 river crossings, including two new crossings along the Fraser River.

It would also increase tanker traffic in the Salish Sea, the group said.

The Tsartlip application asks the court to confirm the Canadian government must “meaningfully consult” the nation before deciding whether the pipeline is in the national interest.

Olsen said there is concern there May be more projects of national interest affecting First Nations, pointing to last week’s announcement that the Port of Vancouver’s Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion has also been added to the list.

Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said the existing port facility is approaching the limit of its capacity and the expansion would add 2.4 million containers of capacity annually.

He said the national interest listing provided certainty for a project that’s a key part of Ottawa’s drive to expand and diversify trade, including a goal to double exports to markets other than the United States by 2035.

MacKinnon said the project, which has an estimated capital cost of $5.9 billion, would “fit gently into the ecosystem,” with Ottawa committing funding to protect the habitat of fish, marine mammals and endangered southern resident killer whales.

Olsen, however, wasn’t convinced, saying Tsartlip “has the same level of concern” for the terminal expansion as it does for the new pipeline.

“How these decisions are made are going to shape decisions going forward, not just for First Nations, but for all Canadians,” Olsen said.

“I think that it’s important that we understand the implications of those laws, and in this case, the Government of Canada has a duty to consult Tsartlip, and we believe they failed in that duty.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version incorrectly said the St’át’imc Chiefs Council represented nine nations. In fact, it represents 11 communities.

stories.title: Chief says not enough evidence to arrest Toronto home invasion suspect in hospital
stories.summary: Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw says officers did not arrest a suspect in the violent Bridle Path home invasion after he showed up in a hospital with a gunshot wound because not all evidence was available to them yet.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - As Toronto’s police chief defended the police response after a suspect in the violent Bridle Path home invasion showed up in a hospital and then left, one expert said arresting the man without solid evidence and reasonable grounds would not have held up in court.

Chief Myron Demkiw said Monday that not all evidence was available to officers responding to reports of a person who walked into St. Joseph’s Health Centre with a gunshot wound just hours after the home invasion last Thursday.

Investigators had no information at the time to suggest any of the suspects were shot during the attack on a family of four in the affluent neighbourhood, he said.

“They responded to the hospital as they would when people walk into the hospital with a gunshot wound, which happens in the city from time to time,” Demkiw said at an unrelated press conference. “They advanced the investigation with the speed and flow that was available to them given the circumstances.”

He would not comment on the specific steps police took in their investigation before they identified 23-year-old Daijohn Richards as one of three suspects in the home invasion.

They believe he was accidentally shot in his right shoulder by one of the other suspects. He later walked into the west-end hospital where he had interactions with police officers, Toronto police Insp. Kristy Smith told a news conference Saturday morning.

Richards was discharged from the hospital early Thursday morning and a Canada-wide warrant was later issued for his arrest.

Police said in a social media post on Saturday that investigators “immediately” recognized the potential connection between the home invasion and the person who showed up at the hospital, but suspicion alone was not enough for them to make an arrest.

Along with the other two unidentified suspects, Richards remains at large and police said all three are considered armed and dangerous.

Patrick Watson, an assistant professor at the Centre for Criminology and Sociolegal Studies at the University of Toronto, said if police had arrested the suspect before they had all the necessary evidence, it would jeopardize the case and criminal proceedings.

“Being shot isn’t a crime,” he said. “It doesn’t necessitate any sort of form of criminal intervention.”

It was also unlikely that police had gathered solid evidence in the short hours between the home invasion and the suspect’s arrival at the hospital, said Watson.

“At that stage of the investigation, it would peak the curiosity of investigators but it would be very hard to envision a scenario where they would have had very solid evidence to enact an arrest,” he said in an interview.

He said while Toronto police May have asked the right questions, it’s also up to the person being interviewed to provide the information.

“If the individual who is alleged to have been involved with this was simply not willing to co-operate, that really does hamstring (the police),” he said. “The Charter protects you from unreasonable search and seizure, it protects you from participating in your own conviction.”

Police have said that a mother, father and their two adult daughters were injured when masked intruders forced their way into the home through the rear door, armed with guns and a hammer.

David Morton, CEO of real estate firm MAC Group, said in a statement on Friday that three members of his family were shot and all four were attacked with the hammer.

Morton said the family is focused on recovery and supporting one another.

“No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives,” he wrote in his statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa defends extradition treaty talks with UAE as civil society group sounds alarm
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government is defending its plan to start talks on an extradition treaty with the United Arab Emirates as a civil society group issues a warning over the country's human-rights record.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The federal government is defending its plan to start talks on an extradition treaty with the United Arab Emirates as civil society groups issue warnings over the country’s human-rights record.

Canada and the UAE signed a free-trade deal last week when the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed, met with Prime Minister Mark Carney during a visit to Ottawa.

They also announced plans to start negotiations on an extradition treaty and a mutual legal assistance treaty.

Amani Khalfan, a spokesperson for the social justice organization Inter Pares, asked what kind of message Canada would send to the world by signing extradition and defence treaties with the UAE, a country with a troubling human-rights record.

Khalfan said the Uae’s record of unlawful and arbitrary detentions is “appalling.”

She cited the case of Sudanese advocate Mohammed Farouk Salman Mahmoud, who she said was imprisoned for over a year and a half in the UAE without charges.

Authorities said he was under investigation for insulting the UAE head of state. Amnesty International said he was released on Aug. 22.

The UAE has taken on increasing importance in global politics and has been praised for work aimed at ending conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine.

But the country also has been accused of supporting a militia in Sudan that has been accused of genocide — a claim Abu Dhabi denies.

“While we recognize that diversifying trade and investment is an important goal, it is clear that the UAE is supporting a militia that has carried out genocide, and continues to do so,” Khalfan said.

“In the context of such massacres, prioritizing economic partnerships over human rights means that Canada is at risk of seeking blood money in the UAE.”

Kwame Bonsu, a spokesperson for the Department of Justice, said strengthening Canada’s foreign partnerships on investigating, prosecuting and preventing serious crime is critical to keeping Canadians safe.

Bonsu said an extradition treaty would help bring to justice individuals accused or convicted of serious crimes, such as money laundering, drug trafficking or cybercrime.

“The Uae’s increasing and successful international partnerships on extradition and mutual legal assistance with countries that take a similar approach to these matters as Canada, such as the United Kingdom, Ireland, Belgium, France, Italy, Sweden, and the Netherlands, makes this a suitable moment at which to revisit the Uae’s invitation to negotiate with Canada,” said Bonsu.

A mutual legal assistance treaty, Bonsu said, would facilitate the exchange of evidence and other forms of legal assistance in criminal investigations and prosecutions.

“This type of treaty helps authorities in both countries investigate and prosecute serious crimes,” Bonsu said.

An extradition treaty is an agreement between countries that allows one country to request the surrender and transfer by another country of an individual accused of crimes.

The federal government’s website says there are three key stages to Canada’s extradition process.

First, the justice minister must issue an “authority to proceed.” Next, Canadian courts need to say whether there is enough evidence to justify an individual’s extradition. The justice minister must also decide whether to order the individual’s surrender to the foreign state.

The individual can then seek judicial review of the minister’s order or appeal the decision.

“In all cases, the conduct for which extradition is sought must be considered criminal in both the requesting country and in Canada,” says the government website.

The Extradition Act says the minister should refuse to issue an extradition order if they believe it would be “unjust or oppressive,” or if the request for extradition is made to prosecute or punish someone for things like race, religion or nationality.

The act says the minister also can refuse to issue an extradition order if they think the conduct for which the request was made is punishable by death under the laws of the country requesting extradition.

Ketty Nivyabandi, secretary general of Amnesty International Canada’s English-speaking section, said in an email her organization is also concerned by the talk of an extradition treaty given the Uae’s “disturbing” record on human rights.

“Amnesty International has documented grossly unfair mass trials, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearances in the UAE, including the disappearance of poet Abdul Rahman Al-Qaradawi following his extradition in 2025,” she said. “Our global research has also found torture to be correlated with enforced disappearances.”

Nivyabandi said Canada should not rely on diplomatic assurances from the UAE. She said such promises can’t reliably prevent torture or erase Canada’s legal duty never to send someone where they face a real risk of abuse.

“If these talks move forward, Canadian officials must proceed with extreme caution and, ultimately, should not enter into an agreement unless and until they have evidence and full confidence that human rights will be upheld,” said Nivyabandi.

Seventeen civil society organizations signed an open letter earlier this year warning Canada against deeper ties to the UAE and arguing the country is perpetuating the war in Sudan. The letter said that as Canada looks to diversify its trade, it needs to assert support for human rights as a core Canadian value.

Carney travelled to the United Arab Emirates last year. At the end of that November visit, the prime minister said Ottawa was working on a $1-billion project to expand critical minerals processing capacity in Canada.

The UAE pledged to invest about $70 billion in Canada.

The Prime Minister’s Office said last week’s visit by the crown prince to Ottawa led to “significant progress” on the Uae’s commitment to invest in Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.
