They also announced plans to start negotiations on an extradition treaty and a mutual legal assistance treaty.

Amani Khalfan, a spokesperson for the social justice organization Inter Pares, asked what kind of message Canada would send to the world by signing extradition and defence treaties with the UAE, a country with a troubling human-rights record.
Khalfan said the Uae’s record of unlawful and arbitrary detentions is “appalling.”
She cited the case of Sudanese advocate Mohammed Farouk Salman Mahmoud, who she said was imprisoned for over a year and a half in the UAE without charges.
Authorities said he was under investigation for insulting the UAE head of state. Amnesty International said he was released on Aug. 22.
The UAE has taken on increasing importance in global politics and has been praised for work aimed at ending conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine.
But the country also has been accused of supporting a militia in Sudan that has been accused of genocide — a claim Abu Dhabi denies.
“While we recognize that diversifying trade and investment is an important goal, it is clear that the UAE is supporting a militia that has carried out genocide, and continues to do so,” Khalfan said.
“In the context of such massacres, prioritizing economic partnerships over human rights means that Canada is at risk of seeking blood money in the UAE.”

Kwame Bonsu, a spokesperson for the Department of Justice, said strengthening Canada’s foreign partnerships on investigating, prosecuting and preventing serious crime is critical to keeping Canadians safe.
Bonsu said an extradition treaty would help bring to justice individuals accused or convicted of serious crimes, such as money laundering, drug trafficking or cybercrime.

“The Uae’s increasing and successful international partnerships on extradition and mutual legal assistance with countries that take a similar approach to these matters as Canada, such as the United Kingdom, Ireland, Belgium, France, Italy, Sweden, and the Netherlands, makes this a suitable moment at which to revisit the Uae’s invitation to negotiate with Canada,” said Bonsu.
A mutual legal assistance treaty, Bonsu said, would facilitate the exchange of evidence and other forms of legal assistance in criminal investigations and prosecutions.
“This type of treaty helps authorities in both countries investigate and prosecute serious crimes,” Bonsu said.
An extradition treaty is an agreement between countries that allows one country to request the surrender and transfer by another country of an individual accused of crimes.
The federal government’s website says there are three key stages to Canada’s extradition process.

First, the justice minister must issue an “authority to proceed.” Next, Canadian courts need to say whether there is enough evidence to justify an individual’s extradition. The justice minister must also decide whether to order the individual’s surrender to the foreign state.
The individual can then seek judicial review of the minister’s order or appeal the decision.
“In all cases, the conduct for which extradition is sought must be considered criminal in both the requesting country and in Canada,” says the government website.

The Extradition Act says the minister should refuse to issue an extradition order if they believe it would be “unjust or oppressive,” or if the request for extradition is made to prosecute or punish someone for things like race, religion or nationality.

The act says the minister also can refuse to issue an extradition order if they think the conduct for which the request was made is punishable by death under the laws of the country requesting extradition.

Ketty Nivyabandi, secretary general of Amnesty International Canada’s English-speaking section, said in an email her organization is also concerned by the talk of an extradition treaty given the Uae’s “disturbing” record on human rights.

“Amnesty International has documented grossly unfair mass trials, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearances in the UAE, including the disappearance of poet Abdul Rahman Al-Qaradawi following his extradition in 2025,” she said. “Our global research has also found torture to be correlated with enforced disappearances.”

Nivyabandi said Canada should not rely on diplomatic assurances from the UAE. She said such promises can’t reliably prevent torture or erase Canada’s legal duty never to send someone where they face a real risk of abuse.

“If these talks move forward, Canadian officials must proceed with extreme caution and, ultimately, should not enter into an agreement unless and until they have evidence and full confidence that human rights will be upheld,” said Nivyabandi.

Seventeen civil society organizations signed an open letter earlier this year warning Canada against deeper ties to the UAE and arguing the country is perpetuating the war in Sudan. The letter said that as Canada looks to diversify its trade, it needs to assert support for human rights as a core Canadian value.

Carney travelled to the United Arab Emirates last year. At the end of that November visit, the prime minister said Ottawa was working on a $1-billion project to expand critical minerals processing capacity in Canada.
The UAE pledged to invest about $70 billion in Canada.
The Prime Minister’s Office said last week’s visit by the crown prince to Ottawa led to “significant progress” on the Uae’s commitment to invest in Canada.

stories.title: WestJet CEO calls for national aviation strategy, saying U.S. airlines have it easier
stories.summary: WestJet CEO Alexis von Hoensbroech is calling for a national aviation strategy as a path to a more competitive — and affordable — industry.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
WestJet chief executive Alexis von Hoensbroech has called for a national aviation strategy to rein in mounting costs and level a “tilting” market balance set askew by government aid.

In an interview, the head of the country’s second-largest carrier said current labour laws, passenger rights, taxes and fees hinder growth and chip away at Canadian carriers’ bottom lines.

Domestic airlines face higher costs than their U.S. competitors in areas ranging from air navigation to emissions offsets and customer compensation, von Hoensbroech said.

“We want a healthy industry which is competitive, which is growing, which is creating new connections and which provides affordable and reliable air service for Canadians,” he said in a phone interview from Calgary, WestJet’s home city.

“Right now we have an over-regulated system which is overly expensive and that does not meet those objectives.”

Von Hoensbroech qualified that he was “thankful” the current federal government has turned its eye to reforms around airport governance, labour rules and consumer protections, but that they must be weighed as part of a broader vision.

“I’m a bit concerned that they May be looking at them in isolation. This needs to be viewed in a holistic way,” the CEO told The Canadian Press.

The country’s airline industry has consolidated over the past three years, as budget carrier Lynx Air collapsed and WestJet folded its low-cost Swoop subsidiary into its mainline service and bought Sunwing Airlines.

The carriers that remain on the tarmac face big hurdles.

The cost of fuel has skyrocketed due to the global oil shock sparked by the Iran war, adding more than $1 billion to WestJet’s expense sheet this year — a year-over-year jump of more than 60 per cent — von Hoensbroech said. The crisis also prompted Porter Airlines, Air Transat owner Transat A.T. Inc. and Flair Airlines to successfully seek more than $630 million in emergency aid from Ottawa.

Despite arguing for a stronger industry, von Hoensbroech has denounced that move, saying a slice of those low-interest loans are liable to wind up as gifts from the taxpayer, amounting to an even heavier federal finger on the scale.

He cited the example of Transat, whose COVID-era government loans were restructured last year such that nearly half of its $772-million debt was forgiven and another chunk converted to five years of no-interest credit.

“This money actually turns into grants,” he said. “This is really tilting the marketplace.”

Von Hoensbroech also said airlines can use that cash to fund growth and lower ticket prices, which in turn undermines the sector’s ability to recover fuel costs.

Geraint Harvey, an employment relations professor at Western University, said any national industrial strategy would need to incorporate the views of consumers and the 265,000 workers directly employed in aviation, according to International Air Transport Association figures.

“Everyone’s in favour of strengthening the industry, but to what end?” Harvey asked, saying that strength can be a byword for profitability.

“What is the impact on the workers, what’s the impact on passengers?” he asked.

“A national aviation strategy is not necessarily a bad thing. It’s just got to be a strategy that is based on multiple stakeholder input, not simply something that is determined by airlines,” he said.

Despite Canada’s airline aid packages, the country remains a pricey place both to fly and to run a travel business, according to a World Economic Forum study.

Its 2024 travel and tourism competitiveness index ranked Canada 101st out of 116 countries on price competitiveness, which measures how “costly it is to travel or operate in a country.”

However, Canada also placed 11th overall, and beat out the 22 other North and South American countries in the business environment category.

WestJet has pointed to airport improvement fees — paid for by the passenger — that can top $40 in Canada while staying capped at US$4.50 in the United States. Canadian carriers also pay for air navigation costs, while the U.S. model hinges on subsidies.

Airlines north of the border compensate passengers for flight disruptions that are within their control, whereas American carriers face no such obligation.

Over the past three and a half years, strikes by Air Canada flight attendants and WestJet flight attendants and mechanics have briefly brought operations at the country’s two biggest airlines to a halt, and the threat of job action from pilots at WestJet and Air Transat was a real possibility during contract talks. The United States has not seen a major strike in the sector since 1993, as federal laws severely curtail unions’ ability to walk off the job.

However, experts say the disparities are not as vast as they appear.

Some jurisdictions fold airport improvement costs into landing fees more broadly instead of laying them out as a line item in the ticket purchase, said John Gradek, who teaches aviation management at McGill University.

“The Canadian model makes it explicit. Other models around the world hide it,” he said. “I’d rather see it and manage it and hold people accountable for it, rather than bury it.”

Other skeptics ask why taxpayers should subsidize air navigation costs. As for consumer protections, Europeans enjoy even more rigorous passenger rights than Canadians, even if Americans don’t.

“I think we’re OK as a country in terms of our national aviation strategy,” Gradek said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:TRZ)

stories.title: Canadian police urge caution after reports of tampered Halloween candy
stories.summary: Police across Canada are urging caution after several reports of families finding tampered Halloween candy.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Police across Canada are urging caution after several reports of families finding tampered Halloween candy.

The RCMP in Nova Scotia and Alberta, provincial police in Quebec and Durham Regional Police are just some of the police services putting out public notices advising people to check trick-or-treat hauls from Oct. 31.

Barry Horn, a father of three, told Global News Monday they found five candies five pieces of candy that appeared to have been tampered with after going trick-or-treating in Toronto’s Beaches neighbourhood.

“You hear of these things happening, but you never think it’s going to happen to you or your family or your kids,” he said.

Police in Durham said Sunday they’re investigating after sewing needles were found in Halloween candy in Oshawa.

Meanwhile, Quebec provincial police said they’ve gotten two calls about needles found in chocolate or candy in Drummondville, about 100 kilometres northeast of Montreal.

Nova Scotia RCMP said a parent found a syringe in a child’s bag after trick-or-treating in Beaver Bank.

RCMP in Blackfalds, Alta. say a needle was found in Halloween candy after a child was trick-or-treating in the town’s northeast, specifically:

Cedar Square

Cedar Crescent

Crimson Court

Cambridge Close

Pioneer Way

Churchill Place

Coachman Way

Each investigation is ongoing. No injuries were reported.

“Be diligent, check the candy,” Horn said.

“Celebration is a big part of what our kids enjoy … but it’s definitely going to make us more aware of the houses we’re going to, what they’re getting.”

stories.title: Calgary police investigating death of toddler who was hit by taxi in parking lot
stories.summary: Calgary police say they're investigating the death of a two-year-old boy who was hit in a northeast parking lot late Sunday afternoon.
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
Calgary police are investigating the death of a two-year-old boy who was hit in a northeast parking lot.

They say it happened late Sunday afternoon.

Police say the boy was with his parents just prior to the accident but had wandered away.

He was struck by a taxi.

The taxi driver took both the child and his parents to hospital, but the boy did not survive.

It is Calgary’s 10 pedestrian fatality of the year.

stories.title: Three people hurt, driver charged following single-vehicle crash
stories.summary: Grey Bruce OPP say emergency services responded on Oct. 31 after a vehicle left Bruce Road 14 and struck a tree.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 69-year-old Allenford resident is facing impaired driving and other charges following a single-vehicle collision in the Town of South Bruce Peninsula.

Grey Bruce OPP say emergency services responded on Oct. 31 after a vehicle left Bruce Road 14 and struck a tree.

Police said three occupants suffered non-life-threatening injuries and were transported to hospital.

Following an investigation, the driver was charged with:

Operation while impaired - alcohol (over 80)

Dangerous operation causing bodily harm

Operation causing bodily harm

Police said the accused was also issued a 90-day driver’s licence suspension and a seven-day vehicle impoundment.

No further details were released.

stories.title: Budget 2026 is about ‘us,’ not the U.S. trade war, finance minister says
stories.summary: Champagne is set to unveil the Carney government’s sophomore budget Thursday, as Trump’s trade war continues to loom over Canada’s economy.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
It’s about us, not the U.S.

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said Monday that this week’s federal budget will focus more on the government’s efforts to build up Canada’s economy and trade than the ongoing trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump.

“We have seen in trade, we have seen how the world has been changing, and for me this has been a moment for us as Canadians to … talk about building, investing in growth, (making) sure we’re more sovereign, supporting Canadians at a time of need, diversifying our trade,” Champagne said at a pre-budget event at the Canadian Club of Toronto Monday.

“Whatever May happen in these discussions (around Canada-U.S. trade), we will see. But one thing is true, everything I just said that we need to do for ourselves.”

Champagne is set to deliver the Liberal government’s sophomore budget on Thursday, the next major policy document in Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to diversify Canada’s trade relationships, strengthen domestic industries, dramatically ramp up defence spending and address continuing affordability concerns amid geopolitical turmoil.

While Champagne was quick to note the budget is not about the trade relationship with the U.S., the issue continues to loom large over both the Canadian economy and in voters’ minds.

There have been signs in recent days — in addition to a flurry of news reports citing unnamed sources — that negotiations between Canada and the Trump administration could soon resume after talks broke down in late August.

Carney issued a statement Sunday that said he had a “good” discussion with Trump that built “on recent constructive discussions on the outlines of a mutually beneficial trade deal.” Carney added that teams from the two countries will “be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome.”

Over the weekend, Trump added that the two sides have a “concept” of an agreement and said he believes a deal is close.

stories.title: Investigators recover cockpit recorder from Ontario air ambulance that crashed off Massachusetts coast
stories.summary: The early October flight, which went down off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., after departing Bermuda, was carrying six people, including four Canadian crew members.
stories.author: Raju Mudhar
stories.content:
Transportation Safety Board (TSB) investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder and other parts of Heartbeat 104, the Latitude Air Ambulance jet that crashed in early October, killing all six people on board, including four Canadian crew members .

The Ontario-based company’s flight — a Gulfstream G100 aircraft numbered C-Grjp — was carrying a patient and her son, en route to Boston, in the early morning hours of Oct. 3 .

The Canadian TSB has been leading the investigation and working with their U.S. counterparts and Massachusetts authorities to recover the plane and investigate why it went down.

“The TSB, working in co-ordination with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Canadian Coast Guard, has recovered the upper third of the occurrence aircraft’s cockpit, as well as the cockpit voice recorder. Both will be transported to Tsb’s Engineering Laboratory in Ottawa for further examination,” said a statement issued by the organization on Monday morning. “The investigation is ongoing.”

Latitude Air Ambulance captain Philip Childerhose, left, and first officer Thomas Farquhar are among the missing after the jet crashed over the Atlantic Ocean en route to Boston from Bermuda.

The tragic flight left Bermuda at 11:42 p.m. Oct. 2, and reported apparent problems at 12:46 a.m. Oct. 3 as it approached Nantucket, Mass., with the pilots telling air traffic control they were “coming in blind,” according to audio posted online.

After its departure from Bermuda, Flight Aware data shows the plane climbing for 10 minutes to 24,000 feet at 11:51 p.m., and remaining at that altitude until 1:04 a.m. The jet then apparently descended over several minutes to 11,000 feet and continued there until it disappeared.

After the U.S. Coast Guard called off the search and rescue — which took days and spanned more than 60,000 square miles, or about 155,400 square kilometres — the TSB took over the investigation because the aircraft was Canadian.

Hamilton-based Latitude Air Ambulance’s Gulfstream G100 jets. The U.S. Coast Guard is searching for jet C-Grjp, second from the bottom.

The goal of the investigation was to find the jet’s black boxes — the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder — and now the latter is in the hands of officials, who May be able to discover exactly what happened in the flight’s final minutes.

This is one of the most challenging recovery operations that the organization has had to deal with in recent years, according to Ewan Tasker, manager of international operations and major investigations at the TSB.

“This last trip down, the Canadian Coast Guard along with the RCMP and combined with some vessels that were chartered by the insurance company went out there, so a myriad of different organizations and vessels have been involved,” said Tasker, saying the U.S. Coast Guard and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration also aided with the recovery operation.

Both of the black boxes are equipped with underwater location beacons, and the search did find that both of them were active and pinging their locations, but recovery is difficult.

” So you’ve got the swells and the waves that drop, but then you also have a tide. And then underwater, there’s a very strong, what’s called rotary current in that area,” said Tasker.

That current swirls on the ocean floor, stirring up silt and making it difficult for divers. There are only a few short 45 minute windows a day to dive and reach the debris. They spent several days trying to get to the voice recorder and while they were successful, while they can hear the flight data recorder’s beacon, they haven’t been able to get to it.

TSB also recovered part of the cockpit, a large 7 foot by 7 foot by 3 foot (2.13 meters by 2.13 meters by 0.91 meters) piece that shows several instruments that will help the investigation piece together what happened. Tasker confirmed that no remains of the flight crew have been found yet.

The cockpit voice recorder is now in Ottawa where it is being examined, while the other recovered parts of the plane are in the U.S. still, but will be transported for further investigation. The TSB will examine what they found and depending on what they learn, that will help determine if another recovery trip will be undertaken.

The crew have been identified as pilots Philip Gregory Childerhose and Thomas Henry Farquhar and medical staff Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir, all from the Greater Toronto and Hamilton areas.

The two passengers they were escorting were Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore, a senior vice-president with a Bermudian insurance firm.

The tragic flight left Bermuda at 11:42 p.m. Oct. 2, and reported apparent problems at 12:46 a.m. Oct. 3 as it approached Nantucket, Mass., with the pilots telling air traffic control they were “coming in blind,” according to audio posted online.

After its departure from Bermuda, Flight Aware data shows the plane climbing for 10 minutes to 24,000 feet at 11:51 p.m., and remaining at that altitude until 1:04 a.m. The jet then apparently descended over several minutes to 11,000 feet and continued there until it disappeared.

After the U.S. Coast Guard called off the search and rescue — which took days and spanned more than 60,000 square miles, or about 155,400 square kilometres — the TSB took over the investigation because the aircraft was Canadian.
Hamilton-based Latitude Air Ambulance’s Gulfstream G100 jets. The U.S. Coast Guard is searching for jet C-Grjp, second from the bottom.

The goal of the investigation was to find the jet’s black boxes — the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder — and now the latter is in the hands of officials, who May be able to discover exactly what happened in the flight’s final minutes.

This is one of the most challenging recovery operations that the organization has had to deal with in recent years, according to Ewan Tasker, manager of international operations and major investigations at the TSB.

“This last trip down, the Canadian Coast Guard along with the RCMP and combined with some vessels that were chartered by the insurance company went out there, so a myriad of different organizations and vessels have been involved,” said Tasker, saying the U.S. Coast Guard and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration also aided with the recovery operation.
Both of the black boxes are equipped with underwater location beacons, and the search did find that both of them were active and pinging their locations, but recovery is difficult.
” So you’ve got the swells and the waves that drop, but then you also have a tide. And then underwater, there’s a very strong, what’s called rotary current in that area,” said Tasker.

That current swirls on the ocean floor, stirring up silt and making it difficult for divers. There are only a few short 45 minute windows a day to dive and reach the debris. They spent several days trying to get to the voice recorder and while they were successful, while they can hear the flight data recorder’s beacon, they haven’t been able to get to it.

The cockpit voice recorder is now in Ottawa where it is being examined, while the other recovered parts of the plane are in the U.S. still, but will be transported for further investigation. The TSB will examine what they found and depending on what they learn, that will help determine if another recovery trip will be undertaken.
The crew have been identified as pilots Philip Gregory Childerhose and Thomas Henry Farquhar and medical staff Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir, all from the Greater Toronto and Hamilton areas.
The two passengers they were escorting were Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore, a senior vice-president with a Bermudian insurance firm.

stories.title: One Canadian among 69 dead in last week's Spanish train crash
stories.summary: Ottawa - Spanish authorities have confirmed one Canadian is among those killed in last week's high-speed rail collision in Spain.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Global Affairs Canada has confirmed one Canadian is among those killed in last week’s high-speed rail collision in Spain.

Sixty-nine people died when one train slammed into another train parked on the tracks on Oct. 28.

Spanish authorities issued a statement Sunday listing a Canadian among the 66 victims who have been identified, and Global Affairs Canada on Monday confirmed the report.

Global Affairs Canada last week said six Canadians were injured in the crash but did not provide an update on their status Monday.

“Canadian officials are providing consular assistance and are in contact with local authorities to gather more information. Due to privacy considerations, no further information can be disclosed,” Global Affairs Canada said in a statement.

Spanish officials say 54 of those killed were Spanish nationals, four were Americans and one victim each came from France, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Portugal, Tunisia and the Czech Republic.

Authorities are working to identify three other bodies and three people are still reported missing — two Australians and one from Japan.

More than 100 people were treated for injuries.

Spain’s rail system operator Adif said the crash occurred in the province of Toledo. It involved two high-speed trains carrying more than 500 passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.

A train operated by the state-owned Renfe company struck the rear of another train operated by private company Iryo that was stopped. The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the Iryo train and the front of the Renfe train.

Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called an “inexplicable” order from a central command centre for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.

Puente said the train never should have been told to start moving again, since there was still a “stop signal” active on that line, and that it should at least have been told to go at a reduced speed.

Until this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992. Now there have been two in just 10 months.

In January a high-speed train derailed, and a second train crashed into it, killing 46 people, and injuring 292 others.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press.

stories.title: Federal budget is about ‘changing Canada’s growth model,’ finance minister says
stories.summary: Toronto — Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne says the federal budget he will table later this week is about "changing Canada's growth model."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Thursday’s federal budget will look to make life easier for Canada’s small- and medium-sized businesses, says Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne.

Champagne provided business leaders a preview of the government’s fiscal plan in a breakfast speech at the Canadian Club Toronto on Monday.

The budget — the second to be delivered under Prime Minister Mark Carney — is expected to support the Liberal government’s push to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States by building up the domestic economy.

In a brief fireside chat after Monday’s speech, Champagne told the crowd Ottawa’s ambitions to stoke private investment and improve productivity are not limited to Canada’s largest companies.

He acknowledged that one of the barriers to investment, particularly among Canada’s small businesses, is the complexity of the tax code.

“We had a number of boutique things and things which might be difficult if you’re small and medium-sized businesses, unless you have a tax adviser to figure out what’s the best way forward,” Champagne told CBC News journalist Peter Armstrong during a fireside chat after his speech.

“I think you will see in this budget a journey to fixing a number of things, to make things more simple, to simplify the life of small and medium-sized businesses. And I think that on Thursday, those who represent small businesses will see themselves in that budget.”

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has called on Ottawa to use the Nov. 5 budget to lower the small business tax rate and fix gaps in the federal tariff relief regime that box out smaller firms.

“Small businesses tell us they don’t want handouts. They want broad policies that would help them reinvest in their businesses and plan for the future,” said Corinne Pohlmann, Cfib executive vice-president of advocacy, in a statement on Oct. 29.

“While major project investments usually get the spotlight, we also need to be building the foundation of our economy by making it more attractive to start and grow a small business.”

Champagne would not offer specific examples of what the federal government is proposing in Thursday’s budget. He did suggest Ottawa is considering more changes to the Scientific Research and Experimental Development program, which encourages firms to invest in themselves to develop innovative technologies.

One of the big-ticket measures accounted for in this upcoming budget is the productivity mega-deduction, which the government announced in September and has continued to highlight as a cornerstone of its investment policy. It’s estimated to cost $36 billion over five years.

The mega-deduction allows businesses to immediately write off the full value of an eligible capital investment in its first year, rather than over the lifetime of its use. The government argues deferring tax payments in this way will encourage firms to invest more in technology and tools that can make their workers more productive.

Champagne said the productivity mega-deduction isn’t just for large firms that want to break ground on pipelines and other nation-building projects. He said it could also help a local café buy a new coffee machine, for example.

“It’s our government’s signal to Canadians to use their capital right here in Canada, to invest in new machinery and technology, to expand their enterprises and to support a Canadian economy that nurtures and develops more workers and innovators,” he said.

The minister did not answer directly when asked whether the budget will offer further details about a planned sovereign wealth fund or a proposal to open Canada’s airports up to private investment.

The Liberal government has set an ambitious goal of attracting $1 trillion in private investment over the next five years. Since Carney took office, the federal budget framework has pivoted sharply away from day-to-day government spending and toward a capital-focused agenda that prioritizes infrastructure and other nation-building projects.

“At its core, our plan is about changing Canada’s growth model. We are building one Canadian economy, unlocking private investment, raising productivity, expanding our productive capacity, and diversifying our trade,” Champagne said in his speech.

Armstrong asked Champagne how renewed momentum in U.S. trade talks could affect Ottawa’s spending plans. The finance minister brushed off the question.

“It’s not about them,” he said. “This is about us, regaining our ability to build.”

At a Canadian Club Ottawa event on Monday evening, Champagne would not directly answer whether the budget would include information on immigration levels. He also dodged a question about whether the budget would include information on Canada’s federal ban on foreign homebuyers.

“It’s something you have to look at,” he said. “We’re going to reflect carefully as to what is the best course of action.”

Champagne said Canada has the fiscal capacity and discipline to support Canadians at a time of need while also investing in the country’s future.

“We have had the discipline to reduce our expenses so that we can invest in the kind of things that are going to make a real difference in the lives of Canadians,” he told the Canadian Club of Ottawa.

Asked how high energy prices affected the upcoming budget and the Canadian economy, Champagne acknowledged the level of volatility is “quite unprecedented.” However, he also said Canada is working to build a more resilient and more independent country.

“There is no quick answer to that, because the kind of volatility you’ve seen there and the nature of war today certainly is going to make any straits, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, complex for years to come,” he said. “You need to make sure that you can develop your resources responsibly and sustainably.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

— By Craig Lord in Ottawa

Champagne said the productivity mega-deduction isn’t just for large firms that want to break ground on pipelines and other nation-building projects. He said it could also help a local café buy a new coffee machine, for example.

“It’s our government’s signal to Canadians to use their capital right here in Canada, to invest in new machinery and technology, to expand their enterprises and to support a Canadian economy that nurtures and develops more workers and innovators,” he said.
The minister did not answer directly when asked whether the budget will offer further details about a planned sovereign wealth fund or a proposal to open Canada’s airports up to private investment.

The Liberal government has set an ambitious goal of attracting $1 trillion in private investment over the next five years. Since Carney took office, the federal budget framework has pivoted sharply away from day-to-day government spending and toward a capital-focused agenda that prioritizes infrastructure and other nation-building projects.

“At its core, our plan is about changing Canada’s growth model. We are building one Canadian economy, unlocking private investment, raising productivity, expanding our productive capacity, and diversifying our trade,” Champagne said in his speech.
Armstrong asked Champagne how renewed momentum in U.S. trade talks could affect Ottawa’s spending plans. The finance minister brushed off the question.
“It’s not about them,” he said. “This is about us, regaining our ability to build.”

At a Canadian Club Ottawa event on Monday evening, Champagne would not directly answer whether the budget would include information on immigration levels. He also dodged a question about whether the budget would include information on Canada’s federal ban on foreign homebuyers.
“It’s something you have to look at,” he said. “We’re going to reflect carefully as to what is the best course of action.”
Champagne said Canada has the fiscal capacity and discipline to support Canadians at a time of need while also investing in the country’s future.

“We have had the discipline to reduce our expenses so that we can invest in the kind of things that are going to make a real difference in the lives of Canadians,” he told the Canadian Club of Ottawa.

Asked how high energy prices affected the upcoming budget and the Canadian economy, Champagne acknowledged the level of volatility is “quite unprecedented.” However, he also said Canada is working to build a more resilient and more independent country.

“There is no quick answer to that, because the kind of volatility you’ve seen there and the nature of war today certainly is going to make any straits, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, complex for years to come,” he said. “You need to make sure that you can develop your resources responsibly and sustainably.”

stories.title: Canadian national, 4 Americans among 69 dead in Spain train collision
stories.summary: Other foreigners among the fatalities who have been identified include one each from France, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Portugal, Tunisia and the Czech Republic.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A Canadian and four Americans were among the 69 people killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.

So far, 66 of the dead have been identified, authorities said late Sunday.

Most of those killed — 54 of the 69 victims — were Spanish nationals. The crash took place last Wednesday when a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks.

Other foreigners among the fatalities who have been identified include one each from France, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Portugal, Tunisia and the Czech Republic.

Authorities said they have three bodies still to identify and three people reported missing — two Australians and one Japanese.

The crash in the province of Toledo came just nine months after another collision farther south on the same Madrid-Seville line killed 46 people. The collisions have shaken confidence in the Spanish rail network that has long been hailed for its speed and safety.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged an investigation and improvements to restore trust in the system that carried some 45 million travelers last year, including millions of tourists.

The crash happened one month before a Nov. 29 general election in which Sánchez is seeking to extend his eight-year premiership. He is now facing questions about the safety of the railways and investments under his governments in Spanish infrastructure.

stories.title: Knights rally late, edge Greyhounds in overtime
stories.summary: London tied the game late in regulation before Zocco netted the winner despite the Knights being outshot 31-27.
stories.content:
Thomas Zocco scored 1:53 into overtime as the London Knights rallied for a 5-4 victory over the Soo Greyhounds on Sunday.

London tied the game late in regulation before Zocco netted the winner despite the Knights being outshot 31-27.

Ryan Brown scored the tying goal and added three assists for a four-point performance, while Cooper McAslan recorded three assists. Jacob Vandeven also scored his first goal of the season.

Brian Cooke made 27 saves on 31 shots for London (10-3-1-1).

Christopher Brown scored twice for the Greyhounds (10-5-2-0), who earned a point in the loss. David Vermirovsky stopped 22 of 27 shots for Soo.

stories.title: Kingston, Ont. woman dead after fiery 3-vehicle crash on Highway 401
stories.summary: Two of the vehicles involved in the crash burst into flames, and the 43-year-old woman was pronounced dead at the scene. Two others were taken to hospital with minor injuries.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A woman from Kingston, Ont., died Sunday after a three-vehicle collision on Highway 401 in Whitby.

Ontario Provincial Police said its officers responded to the crash, near Thickson Road, around 7:10 p.m. Nov. 1.

Two of the vehicles involved in the crash burst into flames, and the 43-year-old woman was pronounced dead at the scene. The OPP said two others were taken to hospital with minor injuries.

A 20-year-old man from Lincoln, Ont., was arrested and charged with dangerous driving causing death, impaired driving causing death and operation of a vehicle with excess blood over 80mg/alc in 100ml/blood.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Carney to meet with King Charles and Commonwealth heads of government
stories.summary: Commonwealth members include large countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, India and Nigeria, and many of the world’s smallest countries, such as Tuvalu.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading to Antigua and Barbuda on Monday, where he will have a chance to engage with heads of government from other Commonwealth countries — and with King Charles III.

Much of the meetings taking place this week will focus on trade and investment. But the gathering also offers a chance for Carney to meet with representatives from a wide variety of countries he might not otherwise visit, said retired Canadian diplomat Patricia Fortier.

“Fifty-six countries, Caribbean, Europe, Africa, North America, Indo-Pacific — this is like a diplomatic feast,” she said.

Commonwealth members include large countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, India and Nigeria, and many of the world’s smallest countries — such as Tuvalu, a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean with a population of about 10,000.

Fortier described it as an “extraordinary gathering.”

Carney has spent much of his time in office travelling to shore up multilateral relationships as he attempts to pivot Canada away from dependence on the United States.

Canada’s ties with the Commonwealth, especially with smaller states, could help with that effort. Multilateral organizations like the United Nations give each member country one vote, regardless of size, Fortier noted.

“If you’re trying to move things through a multilateral organization, it is very, very important that you pay attention to smaller states,” she said.

“The Caribbean and Africa and some of the Pacific Island states can make or break your initiatives.”

Michael Manulak, an associate professor of international affairs at Carleton University, said Canada has used this strategy successfully in the past, when it was an influential multilateral player under Prime Minister Lester Pearson, and in the 1980s.

“One of the kind of core constituencies that Canada often operated on was the Commonwealth,” he said.

Canada had good relations with a large number of African and Caribbean countries, which meant Ottawa could call on those leaders to support Canada’s position on international issues, he added.

Ronald Sanders, Antigua’s high commissioner to Canada, said there was a time in the past when “Canada put up a candidate for a post in the UN and it knew it had 14 votes behind it automatically.”

That relationship changed as various Canadian governments moved toward closer relations with the United States and Mexico and away from those relationships in the Caribbean.

“We would hope that we can rebuild that relationship now,” he said.

The modern Commonwealth was established in 1949 and most of its members have ties to the British Empire. Together, they represent a large chunk of the world’s population — 2.7 billion people.

“It’s a legacy of British imperialism but it’s now a consensual association,” said Manulak.

He said the Commonwealth gives Canada a platform to augment bilateral relations with “a whole set of countries that we might not have a whole lot to do with on an everyday basis. And I think that can be a really valuable thing.”

Manulak said trade and investment will be the top issue at the gathering. He said it’s something Commonwealth Secretary General Shirley Botchwey has been pushing for since she stepped into the role in 2025.

“There’s going to be a lot of discussion about concrete ways of reducing barriers to trade,” he said.

Carney will spend just one day at the gathering, attending a lunch hosted by the King for new leaders in the Commonwealth and a formal dinner — also hosted by the King — as well as executive sessions and other meetings.

Carney is also expected to hold bilateral meetings, but officials declined to say in advance who he will meet with.

Sanders said Carney will meet with Antigua and Barbuda’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne.

Browne will propose a bilateral agreement with Canada that “could see joint ventures and activities that promote economic growth and create commercial opportunities for Canadian enterprises,” Sanders said.

Canadian government officials described the Commonwealth meeting as a platform for Canada to expand trade, investment and strategic co-operation.

They noted Canada currently has $100 billion in trade with Commonwealth countries.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand will join Carney at the meeting. She told The Canadian Press in an interview that Canada “supports practical Commonwealth initiatives that strengthen supply chains and improve market access, that advance trade diversification.”

She added the Commonwealth has “ambitious targets” to increase trade among Commonwealth countries to $2 trillion by 2030.

The officials said in the briefing there will be a focus at the meeting on resilience and mitigation related to climate change — a major priority for states witnessing the effects of rising oceans firsthand.

“Given that many of these smaller states are islands and are most affected by climate change, I think that will also be something that will come up,” Fortier said.

Sanders noted the Commonwealth was where early discussions about climate change began. He said the Commonwealth has acted collectively on big issues in the past, such as helping to end apartheid in South Africa.

King Charles is expected to address the legacy of slavery at the meeting in Antigua. Officials did not answer directly when asked whether Carney will participate in any of those discussions.

Manulak said while the British are very reluctant to accept blame for slavery and colonialism — and the potential financial implications of that — Caribbean countries “naturally feel differently about this issue. Being in the Caribbean, this is going to be a really live issue.”

Tamanisha John, assistant professor at York University’s department of politics, predicted Canada will choose to stay quiet and, if pressed, will support the position of the U.K. government. She noted that even if King Charles apologizes, the U.K. government opposes reparations.

Before the opening ceremony on Tuesday, Carney will host a working breakfast with Caribbean leaders.

Government officials said that will be an opportunity for Carney to discuss trade and investment, climate action and regional security.

“The Caribbean and Canada have long had a kind of a special relationship, partly through the shared British colonial heritage, but also through trade with the maritime provinces going down to the Caribbean islands,” Fortier said.

John said Canada’s banks have a strong presence in the region, which gives Canada a voice in guiding their development prospects.

“The financial system that Canada sets up in the Caribbean acts in these very sort of discriminatory ways that end up empowering … North American corporations,” she said.

John said Canada’s banks have a strong presence in the region, which gives Canada a voice in guiding their development prospects.
“The financial system that Canada sets up in the Caribbean acts in these very sort of discriminatory ways that end up empowering … North American corporations,” she said.

stories.title: Canadian woman caught in Syria on trial over alleged role in Isis
stories.summary: The case against Ammara Amjad is the first terrorism prosecution of a Canadian woman accused of living under Isis.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
As Isis fighters and their families were surrounded and making their last stand in Syria in late 2018, a Canadian woman who was allegedly there with them sent a defiant text to her mother.

“Allah has written that victory is near,” Ammara Amjad wrote, according to the RCMP, which found her messages on a phone seized during a search of her parents’ home north of Toronto.

Eight years later, the 32-year-old mother of two sat in a courtroom in Brampton, Ont., last week while a jury heard evidence of her alleged involvement in the Islamic State terror group.

The Canadian government brought Amjad back from a Syrian detention camp in 2023, along with her children, both born after she allegedly left home and made her way to Isis territory.

She now faces a charge of participating in the activities of a terrorist group. It is the first prosecution of a Canadian woman accused of living under Isis as it committed untold atrocities.

To violently to impose its bleak ideology, the jihadist group massacred and enslaved Iraq’s Yazidis , executed captives on video and facilitated attacks in Western countries, including Canada.

As a result, security agencies have warned that Isis members returning to Canada following the group’s defeat in Syria are likely to pose a threat, and could either commit attacks or radicalize others.

Two other women, B.C. resident Kimberly Polman and Montreal’s Oumaima Chouay , have pleaded guilty. Canada repatriated six more Isis women from Syrian camps, but they have not been charged.

Since Amjad’s trial began on Oct. 22, much of the evidence has consisted of messages she exchanged with her mother — so many that it took the RCMP a year to translate them from Urdu, Pakistan’s national language.

In some of the estimated 10,000 texts and audio files, Amjad repeatedly pleaded with her family in Milton, Ont. to send money, and spoke of her decision to leave Canada as a religious duty.

“This is in the cause of Allah,” she wrote in an April 2018 message, according to RCMP Const. Ragiv Chaudhary, who translated most of the messages.

“You deceived us all, left us in tears,” her mother countered.

“I did not deceive,” Amjad responded. “Everyone should have taken this step.”

The Canadian courts have convicted a growing number of men who fought with Isis or plotted attacks, most recently in Ontario and B.C. But Amjad’s case is a test of whether Canada can bring to justice the women who were also part of Isis.

The trial focused initially on the role of women in the Islamic State, with an expert testifying they were mainly housewives and mothers to the next generation of jihadist fighters.

Prof. Guido Steinberg said some foreign Isis women were also given weapons training, and an all-female fighting unit was later established, but added that those caught trying to flee were often punished.

The trial also turns on the reliability of “battlefield evidence,” also called Collected Exploitable Material, which is the information taken from documents and electronic devices found in Syria.

But the Crown’s case appears to hinge largely on Amjad’s own statements in the text messages and voice recordings she sent to her mother from Syria, while the defence is challenging the accuracy of RCMP translations.

Read aloud in court by the multilingual RCMP officer who translated most of them, they allegedly chronicle Amjad’s journey through the rise and fall of Isis.

They also show how Amjad’s exasperated mother tried again and again to appeal to her headstrong daughter to get out of Syria after her first child was born.

“You are not using your brain,” her mother wrote at one point, according to the messages read into the court record by the RCMP officer. “Parents come before anyone else.”

“Parents do not come before Allah,” Amjad replied.

Like many of the dozens of radicalized Canadians who flew to Turkey and crossed into Syria to live under Isis, Amjad had a privileged upbringing, the messages suggest.

“You were living in peace and joy, you had everything,” her mother wrote to her in August 2018.

“You guys don’t understand,” Amjad wrote. “This was very important work for me and all the Muslims. But not everyone will do it. Not everyone will support the right.”

“We are here for the law to apply.”

Amjad’s messages suggest she followed her first husband to Syria. In the texts, she named him as Bilal. The Canadian military has confirmed that a former reservist by that name joined Isis.

Bilal Khan was a private in the Royal Hamilton Light Infantry in Hamilton, Ont. but was released from the army in October 2014, the Canadian Armed Forces told Global News.

Despite his military training, he did not last long in Syria, dying within months of arriving in Isis-controlled territory. Amjad appears to have then married another Isis fighter named Hamza.

The court heard testimony that Hamza Parvez was a British-Pakistani Isis member who, according to the terror group’s own extensive paperwork, entered Isis territory from Turkey in 2014.

Calling himself Abu Hamza al-Britani, he posted anti-Western screeds on social media. His online posts about missing junk food made him fodder for the British tabloids, which dubbed him “Hungry Hamza.”

The Daily Mail described him as a “cat-obsessed Isis fighter from London who dreams about KFC and Nando’s while waging jihad,” adding that fellow jihadists had “advised him to stop eating so much ice cream.”

“I travelled to Syria to make jihad. I won’t lie,” Parvez told Sky News last year from the prison where he was then held by Kurdish forces. Asked if he had been an Isis fighter, he reportedly smiled.

In her messages to her mother, Amjad said Hamza liked cooking in the clay oven in their backyard. “He’s a wonderful husband, exactly the kind I wanted. Intelligent, funny and caring,” she wrote.

But he was apparently upset by talk of Amjad’s first husband. “You shouldn’t mention Bilal over and over again,” Amjad told her mother. “Hamza and I always listen to all the voice messages together, and he doesn’t like it.”

Many of Amjad’s messages to her mother were requests for money, which she framed in religious terms, suggesting that if her family didn’t pay now, they would pay in the afterlife.

“Please send me dollars,” she wrote in one message, explaining that she needed a new phone and wanted to get internet service installed in her home.

“You have savings, you have been spending money on shopping for a long time. Father has savings, where else will he spend it?” she wrote.

She said she deserved it because her parents didn’t have to pay for her wedding. But her mother responded that it was risky to send money and “everyone is worried about getting caught.”

“How long will this go on,” her mother wrote in a response to one of Amjad’s pleas for cash. “You have to keep asking for money again and again.”

“This is the last time.”

Amjad wanted her family to send the money through South Africa, and spoke about going to Pakistan. She rejected returning to Canada, writing that authorities would put her son into foster care with “white people.”

Her mother encouraged her to contact Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, whom she said was a “kind person” who might give her asylum. “Tell him what you have done wrong.”

But even as Isis was headed for certain defeat in late 2018, Amjad stuck to the far-fetched belief that victory was assured, writing that the challenges they were enduring were only a test from God and that only “hypocrites” fled.

She said they were surrounded but that God was protecting them and had created a sandstorm that had forced the U.S.-backed anti-Isis Kurdish forces to temporarily pause their offensive.

“Allah turned around everything,” she wrote.

In early 2019, U.S.-backed Syrian Kurdish fighters pinned the remnants of Isis against the Iraqi border, an offensive known as the Battle of Baghuz. Routed, the surviving Isis fighters and their families were captured.

Amjad was among the thousands of foreign citizens sent to the Al Hol and Al Roj detention camps for Isis women and their kids in Kurdish-controlled northeast Syria.

“I have arrived in the camp now,” she wrote to her mother on March 28, 2019. “I’m in the Al Hol camp and Hamza is somewhere else.”

When the British tabloids found out Parvez had been imprisoned, the headline in the Mirror read, “Brit Isis fanatic Hungry Hamza who moaned about missing KFC captured in Syria.”

Amjad had spent more than four years in the crowded detention camps when a Global Affairs Canada delegation finally travelled to northeast Syria to secure her release.

She landed in Montreal in April 2023, along with three other women and their children who had been freed at the same time and repatriated at significant public expense .

Released on bail, Amjad was ordered to obey a list of conditions that included house arrest at her parents’ home. She was also banned from contacting Hamza Parvez and five other Canadian Isis women.

Her trial resumes on Monday.

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.CA

“Parents do not come before Allah,” Amjad replied.
Married two Isis fighters

content_blocks.alt: Screenshot from ISIS propaganda video.
content_blocks.caption: Screenshot from ISIS propaganda video.

content_blocks.text: Like many of the dozens of radicalized Canadians who flew to Turkey and crossed into Syria to live under Isis, Amjad had a privileged upbringing, the messages suggest.
“You were living in peace and joy, you had everything,” her mother wrote to her in August 2018.
“You guys don’t understand,” Amjad wrote. “This was very important work for me and all the Muslims. But not everyone will do it. Not everyone will support the right.”
“We are here for the law to apply.”
Amjad’s messages suggest she followed her first husband to Syria. In the texts, she named him as Bilal. The Canadian military has confirmed that a former reservist by that name joined Isis.
Bilal Khan was a private in the Royal Hamilton Light Infantry in Hamilton, Ont. but was released from the army in October 2014, the Canadian Armed Forces told Global News.
content_blocks.html: Bilal Khan was a private in the Royal Hamilton Light Infantry in Hamilton, Ont. but was released from the army in October 2014, the Canadian Armed Forces told Global News.

content_blocks.text: Despite his military training, he did not last long in Syria, dying within months of arriving in Isis-controlled territory. Amjad appears to have then married another Isis fighter named Hamza.
The court heard testimony that Hamza Parvez was a British-Pakistani Isis member who, according to the terror group’s own extensive paperwork, entered Isis territory from Turkey in 2014.

Calling himself Abu Hamza al-Britani, he posted anti-Western screeds on social media. His online posts about missing junk food made him fodder for the British tabloids, which dubbed him “Hungry Hamza.”

The Daily Mail described him as a “cat-obsessed Isis fighter from London who dreams about KFC and Nando’s while waging jihad,” adding that fellow jihadists had “advised him to stop eating so much ice cream.”
content_blocks.html: The Daily Mail described him as a “cat-obsessed ISIS fighter from London who dreams about KFC and Nando’s while waging jihad,” adding that fellow jihadists had “advised him to stop eating so much ice cream.”

content_blocks.text: “I travelled to Syria to make jihad. I won’t lie,” Parvez told Sky News last year from the prison where he was then held by Kurdish forces. Asked if he had been an Isis fighter, he reportedly smiled.
content_blocks.html: “I travelled to Syria to make jihad. I won’t lie,” Parvez told Sky News last year from the prison where he was then held by Kurdish forces. Asked if he had been an ISIS fighter, he reportedly smiled.

content_blocks.text: In her messages to her mother, Amjad said Hamza liked cooking in the clay oven in their backyard. “He’s a wonderful husband, exactly the kind I wanted. Intelligent, funny and caring,” she wrote.

But he was apparently upset by talk of Amjad’s first husband. “You shouldn’t mention Bilal over and over again,” Amjad told her mother. “Hamza and I always listen to all the voice messages together, and he doesn’t like it.”
‘Send me dollars’

content_blocks.alt: British ISIS member Hamza Parvez, left, in Mosul, Iraq, 2014.
content_blocks.caption: British ISIS member Hamza Parvez, left, in Mosul, Iraq, 2014.

content_blocks.text: Many of Amjad’s messages to her mother were requests for money, which she framed in religious terms, suggesting that if her family didn’t pay now, they would pay in the afterlife.
“Please send me dollars,” she wrote in one message, explaining that she needed a new phone and wanted to get internet service installed in her home.
“You have savings, you have been spending money on shopping for a long time. Father has savings, where else will he spend it?” she wrote.
She said she deserved it because her parents didn’t have to pay for her wedding. But her mother responded that it was risky to send money and “everyone is worried about getting caught.”
“How long will this go on,” her mother wrote in a response to one of Amjad’s pleas for cash. “You have to keep asking for money again and again.”
“This is the last time.”

Amjad wanted her family to send the money through South Africa, and spoke about going to Pakistan. She rejected returning to Canada, writing that authorities would put her son into foster care with “white people.”
Her mother encouraged her to contact Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, whom she said was a “kind person” who might give her asylum. “Tell him what you have done wrong.”

But even as Isis was headed for certain defeat in late 2018, Amjad stuck to the far-fetched belief that victory was assured, writing that the challenges they were enduring were only a test from God and that only “hypocrites” fled.
She said they were surrounded but that God was protecting them and had created a sandstorm that had forced the U.S.-backed anti-Isis Kurdish forces to temporarily pause their offensive.
“Allah turned around everything,” she wrote.
'Everything is finished

content_blocks.caption: Member of Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces directs woman waiting to be searched after leaving last ISIS holdout of Baghouz, Syria, March 1, 2019. (Photo by Delil SOULEIMAN / AFP).

content_blocks.text: In early 2019, U.S.-backed Syrian Kurdish fighters pinned the remnants of Isis against the Iraqi border, an offensive known as the Battle of Baghuz. Routed, the surviving Isis fighters and their families were captured.
Amjad was among the thousands of foreign citizens sent to the Al Hol and Al Roj detention camps for Isis women and their kids in Kurdish-controlled northeast Syria.
content_blocks.html: Amjad was among the thousands of foreign citizens sent to the Al Hol and Al Roj detention camps for ISIS women and their kids in Kurdish-controlled northeast Syria.

content_blocks.text: “I have arrived in the camp now,” she wrote to her mother on March 28, 2019. “I’m in the Al Hol camp and Hamza is somewhere else.”
When the British tabloids found out Parvez had been imprisoned, the headline in the Mirror read, “Brit Isis fanatic Hungry Hamza who moaned about missing KFC captured in Syria.”
Amjad had spent more than four years in the crowded detention camps when a Global Affairs Canada delegation finally travelled to northeast Syria to secure her release.
She landed in Montreal in April 2023, along with three other women and their children who had been freed at the same time and repatriated at significant public expense .
content_blocks.html: She landed in Montreal in April 2023, along with three other women and their children who had been freed at the same time and repatriated at significant public expense.

content_blocks.text: Released on bail, Amjad was ordered to obey a list of conditions that included house arrest at her parents’ home. She was also banned from contacting Hamza Parvez and five other Canadian Isis women.
Her trial resumes on Monday.

stories.title: Blackstone, Canadian pension funds invest $3.1-billion for minority interest in Mitsubishi’s LNG Canada stake
stories.summary: Acquired stake valued at $1.6-billion; total investment includes planned capital expenditures for phase 2 expansion project
stories.author: James Bradshaw
stories.content:
Blackstone Inc. BX-N and four major Canadian pension funds are paying US$1.6-billion to buy a minority stake in a Mitsubishi Corp. subsidiary that owns a share of LNG Canada’s liquefaction business, and investing a further US$1.5-billion to help fund expansion plans as part of the deal.

Mitsubishi owns a 15-per-cent stake in LNG Canada through a subsidiary and will stay the controlling partner of that entity. The investor group is acquiring a 49.9-per-cent interest in the Mitsubishi subsidiary, and committing to $3.1-billion in total investment.

Blackstone is leading the investor group that includes Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System, Investment Management Corp. of Ontario and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

LNG Canada operates the country’s first natural-gas export terminal, an $18-billion facility in Kitimat, B.C., that opened in June, 2025. Under the deal announced Monday, Mitsubishi will continue its agreement to offtake 2.1 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas annually from LNG Canada.

Earlier this year, both Mitsubishi and LNG Canada’s largest shareholder, Shell PLC, considered reducing their stakes to raise funds for expansion plans.

Mitsubishi hired Royal Bank of Canada’s capital markets arm to pursue a deal and both shareholders were reportedly fielding bids as early as this summer from U.S.-based asset managers such as Blackstone and Apollo Global Management Inc.

However, Shell is no longer pursuing a similar transaction, at least in the near term, three sources with knowledge of the process said.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources because they are not authorized to discuss confidential discussions.

Shell declined to comment.

The transaction marks the first investment by Canadian funds in LNG Canada. In addition to Mitsubishi’s 15-per-cent interest, Shell owns a 40-per-cent stake, Malaysia’s state-owned Petronas has 25 per cent, PetroChina owns 15 per cent and the Korea Gas Corp. (Kogas) holds 5 per cent.

It is also a sign of heightened interest among Canada’s largest pension funds and global investors such as Blackstone to invest in Canadian infrastructure and energy projects.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has set a target to attract $500-billion in new private-sector investment over five years, and some of the largest Canadian pension plans have made multibillion-dollar commitments to boost their domestic investments over the next few years .

“We see this as a compelling opportunity to invest at scale here in Canada,” Geoff Souter, Cppib’s head of real assets credit, said in a statement.

At the Canada Investment Summit, held in Toronto in mid-September, Blackstone president and chief operating officer Jon Gray called Canada “a bit of a sleeping giant, economically.”

An expansion plan to build a second phase of the LNG Canada terminal, confirmed in late September, would double the terminal’s annual output to 28 million tonnes from 14 million, making it one of the largest LNG facilities in the world.

The second phase was one of the first five projects referred to Canada’s Major Projects Office as a national priority.

LNG Canada’s shareholders announced a final investment decision on the expansion plan in September, reaching a key milestone that gave investors greater confidence in the project’s viability. Institutional investors have shown interest in LNG Canada because it is a large asset that can ship low-cost gas to Asia, where demand is increasing, and is capable of producing stable, long-term cash flows that produce steady returns.

The stake in Mitsubishi’s subsidiary that Blackstone and the pension funds are acquiring is valued at US$1.6-billion. The total $3.1-billion investment includes the new investors’ proportional share of planned capital expenditures for the phase 2 expansion project.

Though the Blackstone-led group is buying an equity stake in Mitsubishi’s subsidiary, the deal is being financed by the participating investors’ credit divisions.

It is an example of a type of transaction that has been gaining in popularity, often called “capital solutions” or “corporate solutions.” Using a mix of equity and debt, it provides provide large corporations a way to unlock cash from assets they own, and offers investors relatively predictable returns.

Blackstone has led similarly structured investments in Canada such as a $7-billion deal to acquire a portion of Rogers Communications Inc.’s wireless infrastructure, and a $2.5-billion investment in the Aeroplan loyalty program.

“This announcement builds on our deep conviction in Canada, our partnership with the country’s leading institutional investors and our ability to provide large corporates with flexible solutions to unlock value from their most critical assets,” said Zachary Rubenstein, managing director for Blackstone Credit & Insurance, in a statement.

Blackstone manages US$1.3-trillion, while Cppib, PSP, Omers and Imco collectively manage a total of more than $1.4-trillion in pension assets for Canadian workers and retirees.

Two climate-focused advocacy groups – Shift Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health, as well as Stand.Earth – released statements on Monday opposing the Canadian pension funds’ decision to invest in LNG Canada with Blackstone, citing risks to the environment and to pension savings.

“We are digging ourselves deeper into an incredibly risky project,” Shift Action director Adam Scott said in a statement.

LNG Canada will remain a strategic priority for Mitsubishi, which sells gas from the project into Asia, mostly in Japan, and allows it to secure a reliable supply of a key energy source. Disruptions to global energy flows from the United States war in Iran and Russia’s war in Ukraine have prompted governments and companies around the world to look to diversify their access to energy.

RBC advised Mitsubishi on the transaction, while Goldman Sachs and Scotiabank advised Blackstone. Kirkland & Ellis and Stikeman Elliott served as legal counsel to Blackstone.

With a report from Andrew Willis

stories.title: Parents cheer, businesses brace as Western Canada ditches the time change
stories.summary: Canadians woke up Sunday to a new time zone map after B.C., Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories opted to stay on daylight time year-round
stories.author: Ashley Joannou and Fakiha Baig
stories.content:
Jenn Irwin-Greer never looked forward to the routine gong show at her Edmonton dayhome business that came with the twice-annual time change as children struggled to adjust to a new pattern.

“(Children) show up a little bit irritable, as we all do when we’re tired,” she said. “Nap times get thrown out of whack.”

She’s hopeful things will be a little bit easier this year.

Canadians woke up Sunday to a new time zone map after British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories opted to stay on daylight time year-round rather than have clocks fall back one hour.

Saskatchewan already doesn’t adjust its clocks.

At a recreation centre in Edmonton’s south end on Sunday, some parents said not having to adjust their children’s sleep schedule felt refreshing.

“I’m going to be honest, I do kind of like it,” said Amanda Petrie after her seven-year-old son’s hockey game. “It’s just easier with kids when you don’t have to adjust their schedule.”

Siva Sivabalan, another resident, said he felt the Alberta government had made the right call by not changing the time.

“I rather have more daylight in the evening time rather than the morning,” he said as his daughter played nearby.

“Especially the November time change, I just didn’t like it at all.”

In Calgary, hairstylist Jordan Janovcik said he feels anxious about the work week ahead.

He said he spent the entire summer double- and sometimes triple-checking with clients to make sure they knew Alberta was not falling back.

Hairstylists like him have busy but by-the-book schedules, and missed appointments or delays could mean lost time and money.

“I am really concerned for this week,” he said in a phone interview.

“I think this is going to be really hard for a lot of businesses.”

Technology experts have said the change could cause problems for scheduling systems and older computer software.

Online, some Canadians reported Sunday that their cellphones displayed the incorrect time.

A statement from Telus says the issue is related to how some phones update their time zone information, rather than the service provider.

“Customers experiencing this issue can check their phone’s settings to ensure that ‘set time zone automatically’ is selected, then restart their phone to help apply any available time zone updates,” the company says.

A Rogers spokesperson said the company experienced no issues with its network, and referred questions to an industry group that posted instructions for updating phones and tablets.

In the skies, Air Canada said Sunday its operations were normal, noting that all flights use the internationally recognized time standard and that time changes are managed using established industry data sources.

Tech giant Google responded to an inquiry about how new time zones are affecting its services by linking to a blog post with instructions on how to make sure devices and services stay on schedule.

“From morning alarms to critical calendar invites, we know how much you rely on your devices to stay organized and on time,” the post said.

“Our teams are working to ensure these updates reach all Canadian users as quickly as possible.”

Back in Edmonton, Irwin-Greer said she’s curious how no time change might affect life on the Prairies.

She noted darker mornings in the months ahead and whether they would affect commutes for students and workers.

“I don’t love that it’s going to be darker for longer when the kids are going to school,” she said. “My teenage son is not overly worried about it, but it is a little bit concerning when they’re trying to travel.

“Crossing the street and it’s hard enough for traffic to see, so hopefully there are not more accidents.”
