stories.title: Prime Minister Mark Carney calls six federal byelections for December
stories.summary: Voters in six federal ridings in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan will be heading to the polls Dec. 7, after Prime Minister Mark Carney called byelections Sunday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Voters in six federal ridings in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan will be heading to the polls Dec. 7, after Prime Minister Mark Carney called byelections Sunday.

A press release from the Prime Minster’s Office says byelections will take place in three Quebec ridings, including Laurier—Sainte-Marie, Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton, where seats were previously held by the Liberals, the NDP and the Bloc Québécois respectively.

The remaining byelections are for Ontario ridings Brantford—Brant South and Scarborough North, along with Saskatchewan riding Yorkton—Melville.

The Conservatives held seats in Yorkton—Melville and Brantford—Brant South, while the seat in Scarborough North belonged to the Liberals.

Carney’s Liberals currently have a majority government after winning three byelections earlier this year.

In a tweet Sunday, Conservative Leader Pierre Pollievre asked that Canadians choose a different path, saying that his party’s plan will save money, protect jobs and reform the immigration system.

“I think it’s an opportunity for hard-working Canadians who think it’s unacceptable for Mark Carney to drive up their cost of gas, groceries and housing to vote for a for a party that will fight to save you money,” he said at a news conference later Sunday.

The byelections come after members of Parliament quit the House of Commons for diplomatic appointments, provincial politics or retirement.

Since the 2025 election, 13 of 343 members of Parliament have decided to step down.

The prime minister must call an election between 11 and 180 days after a member’s resignation.

A pastor and longtime Conservative is running as an independent candidate in Brantford-Brant South in Ontario after the party chose to bypass a local nomination contest and appoint Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis as its candidate.

Dave Carrol’s decision to run independently adds intrigue to the byelection, as it could draw votes from the Conservatives, who were already expected to face a tough challenge from the Liberals.

“Party leadership chose to appoint another candidate, skipping the process we have valued for decades,” Carrol, who previously sought the Conservative nomination, said on social media. “That decision, while legal, has been received poorly, and rightfully so.”

In the Saskatchewan riding of Yorkton-Melville, the Liberals are running candidate Aaron Kienle, the mayor of Yorkton, against Conservative Nelson Pohl, a farmer who owns a furnace cleaning company.

That riding has been held by the Conservatives and its predecessors, the Reform Party and Canadian Alliance, for more than 30 years. The Liberals have not won there since the riding was first created in 1968.

Cathay Wagantall, who was elected as a Conservative MP in 2015, won Yorkton-Melville with more than 77 per cent of the vote in 2025. She resigned in August.

The Laurier-Sainte-Marie riding was previously held by former environment minister Steven Guilbeault who left in the summer after a public disagreement with Carney over environment policy.

On Sunday, the Liberals announced that Guy Cormier, former president and CEO of Desjardins Group, will be their candidate in the byelection in Laurier–Sainte-Marie.

The Bloc is fielding Zumretay Arkin, the former vice-president of the World Uyghur Congress while the NDP has nominated epidemiologist Nima Machouf.

The St-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton byelection is needed because Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay quit the Bloc caucus in June ahead of a successful run provincially for the separatist Parti Québécois.

The Liberals are running former provincial politician Chantal Soucy, who represented the Coalition Avenir Québec in the National Assembly for eight years before choosing not to run again in the election this fall. The Bloc has nominated Caroline Emond, the former director general of the International Dairy Federation.

Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie was the only riding the NDP won east of Manitoba in the last federal election, and it was opened in August when MP Alexandre Boulerice resigned ahead of his successful provincial run for Québec solidaire.

The Liberals are running human rights advocate Jean-Sébastien Vallée, while the NDP are fielding Pierre Céré, a Quebec activist who made a brief bid for the leadership of the Parti Québécois in 2015.

The sixth byelection is to be held in Scarborough North, which former Liberal Shaun Chen vacated in August citing ongoing medical issues related to a vehicle crash in 2025.

The Liberals are seeking to hold onto the seat with accountant James Li.

Carney has had a string of byelection successes already this year.

Byelections were held in April in the Quebec riding of Terrebonne — a vote the Supreme Court ordered redone after issues with mail-in ballots during the 2025 election — along with the Liberal strongholds of University-Rosedale and Scarborough Southwest in Toronto. The three Liberal wins coming on the heels of five MPs who crossed the floor to the Liberals, cemented Carney’s majority government.

The Liberals swept another three ridings on Aug. 31, flipping a Conservative seat in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord and holding seats in Beaches-East York and North Vancouver-Capilano.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

With files from Tori Fitzpatrick in Halifax

That riding has been held by the Conservatives and its predecessors, the Reform Party and Canadian Alliance, for more than 30 years. The Liberals have not won there since the riding was first created in 1968.
Cathay Wagantall, who was elected as a Conservative MP in 2015, won Yorkton-Melville with more than 77 per cent of the vote in 2025. She resigned in August.
The Laurier-Sainte-Marie riding was previously held by former environment minister Steven Guilbeault who left in the summer after a public disagreement with Carney over environment policy.
On Sunday, the Liberals announced that Guy Cormier, former president and CEO of Desjardins Group, will be their candidate in the byelection in Laurier–Sainte-Marie.
The Bloc is fielding Zumretay Arkin, the former vice-president of the World Uyghur Congress while the NDP has nominated epidemiologist Nima Machouf.
The St-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton byelection is needed because Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay quit the Bloc caucus in June ahead of a successful run provincially for the separatist Parti Québécois.

The Liberals are running former provincial politician Chantal Soucy, who represented the Coalition Avenir Québec in the National Assembly for eight years before choosing not to run again in the election this fall. The Bloc has nominated Caroline Emond, the former director general of the International Dairy Federation.

Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie was the only riding the NDP won east of Manitoba in the last federal election, and it was opened in August when MP Alexandre Boulerice resigned ahead of his successful provincial run for Québec solidaire.
The Liberals are running human rights advocate Jean-Sébastien Vallée, while the NDP are fielding Pierre Céré, a Quebec activist who made a brief bid for the leadership of the Parti Québécois in 2015.
The sixth byelection is to be held in Scarborough North, which former Liberal Shaun Chen vacated in August citing ongoing medical issues related to a vehicle crash in 2025.
The Liberals are seeking to hold onto the seat with accountant James Li.
Carney has had a string of byelection successes already this year.

Byelections were held in April in the Quebec riding of Terrebonne — a vote the Supreme Court ordered redone after issues with mail-in ballots during the 2025 election — along with the Liberal strongholds of University-Rosedale and Scarborough Southwest in Toronto. The three Liberal wins coming on the heels of five MPs who crossed the floor to the Liberals, cemented Carney’s majority government.
The Liberals swept another three ridings on Aug. 31, flipping a Conservative seat in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord and holding seats in Beaches-East York and North Vancouver-Capilano.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.
With files from Tori Fitzpatrick in Halifax

stories.title: OPP release details of victims, injured in fatal collision near Guelph
stories.summary: OPP said investigators continue to gather and preserve evidence in what she calls a complex investigation, but it is too soon to determine the exact details of what occurred.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
One of the people injured in a fatal early morning single-vehicle crash Saturday has life-altering injuries, with police saying the second received non-life-threatening injuries.

Wellington OPP, fire and paramedic services responded to reports of the collision shortly after 1:30 a.m. Saturday on Watson Road South between Maltby Road East and Wellington Road 34, south of Guelph, Ont.

Six people were in the vehicle, police said. Four were pronounced dead at the scene, while two were transported to hospital.

“Our investigation has determined that six occupants were travelling in the vehicle when it left the roadway, struck a guardrail and entered the ravine,” said Insp. Karen Medeiros, detachment commander for Wellington OPP.

No names were released but OPP said the victims include a 19-year-old man from Mississauga, 19-year-old man from Brampton, a 17-year-old girl from Mississauga and a 15-year-old girl from Milton. A 17-year-old female remains in hospital with life-altering injuries as does a 16-year-old who received non-life-threatening injuries. Both teens in hospital are from Mississauga, according to police.

Medeiros said investigators continue to gather and preserve evidence in what she calls a complex investigation, but said it is too soon to determine exactly what happened. Anyone who May have been travelling in the area early Saturday, or who has surveillance or dashcam footage, is asked to contact OPP.

Asked about seatbelt use, Medeiros cautioned that the investigation is looking into whether speed or seatbelt use were contributing factors. But she said she did not believe there were enough seatbelts for the number of people in the vehicle.

— with files from Global News’ Rachel Morgan

stories.title: Four teens from Mississauga, Brampton, Milton killed in early morning crash near Guelph, police say
stories.summary: Police said that it is too early to determine the cause of the crash and that the investigation is ongoing.
stories.author: Megan Mills Devoe
stories.content:
Four teens, including two from Mississauga, one from Brampton and another as young as 15 from Milton, were killed in a single-vehicle crash early Saturday morning in Puslinch, Ont., just south of Guelph, police say.

The Ontario Provincial Police said first responders were called to the site of the crash at Watson Road South, just north of Wellington Road 34, around 1:30 a.m.

stories.title: Carney calls 6 byelections for December in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan
stories.summary: By-elections will be held in three Quebec ridings, two in Ontario and a sixth in Saskatchewan after their MPs left to return to previous jobs or run in another election.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced six by-elections to be held just before the holidays.

The votes will take place Dec. 7 to fill six vacancies caused by the departures of MPs from multiple parties in recent months.

Ontario voters will be deciding who to send to the House of Commons for the ridings of Brantford-Brant South and Scarborough North.

The former was vacated by Conservative MP Larry Brock, who returned to the Crown prosecutor’s office.

The Liberals have put forward certified financial planner Joy O’Donnell, with the Conservatives nominating Brantford’s former mayor Kevin Davis. His nomination caused some criticism after Brock endorsed local pastor Dave Carroll as his successor. Carroll is now planning to run as an independent.

In Scarborough North, Liberal MP Shaun Chen stepped down, citing health concerns following a car crash in October 2025.

Next door in Quebec, three ridings are up for grabs.

Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie became vacant when long-time NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice resigned to run for Quebec solidaire in the 2026 provincial election, which he won.

Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, a Bloc Quebecois riding, was previously represented by Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay. He also stepped down to run for the Parti Quebecois in the 2026 election and won.

The Liberals have put forward a relatively high-profile candidate in Laurier-Sainte-Marie, the third Quebec riding up for grabs, naming former Desjardins CEO Guy Cormier. The party confirmed his nomination in a news release Sunday. The riding was previously held by Liberal MP and former environment minister Steven Guilbeault, who resigned in August. The Bloc Quebecois have nominated human rights activist Zumretay Arkin, while the NDP have nominated Nima Machouf.

The Prairies will also see a by-election in Yorkton-Melville, which had been held by Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall since the 2015 federal election. She announced this summer she did not plan to run in the next federal election and resigned Aug. 31.

Yorkton Mayor Aaron Kienle has been named as the Liberals’ nominee, with Nelson Pohl representing the Conservatives. The NDP have not yet named a nominee.

stories.title: ‘He’s a leader’: Ben Casselman blossoms as Western Mustangs advance to OUA semifinal vs Windsor
stories.summary: The Western Mustangs picked the perfect time to end a four-game losing streak against their rival Wilfrid Laurier Golden Hawks.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Western Mustangs picked the perfect time to end a four-game losing streak against their rival Wilfrid Laurier Golden Hawks. Seven different players scored touchdowns as Western beat the Hawks 58-41 in the OUA quarterfinal at Alumni Field in London, Ont. on Saturday, Oct.

31, 2026. IN Photos: Western Mustangs vs. Wilfrid Laurier Western quarterback Ben Casselman threw for 405 yards and two scores and added a rushing touchdown in the win. “I think we really leaned into our running attack a bit more,” said Casselman after a 55-39 defeat to those same Hawks last week.

“It’s safe to say we had the training wheels on him early on,” said Faulds. ”He’s gained the confidence of our coaching staff and of our players. He’s a leader within the group and everyone trusts him.” Western ran for 274 yards, led by Ethan Dolby who had 18 carries for 155 yards and a touchdown.

He also had a big first down run late in regulation to seal the victory. “We’ve got to lean on our offensive line, especially in playoff football, whether it was Dolby, whether it was Jack Kelly,” said Faulds. “It didn’t matter who was touching the ball.

Even Geoff Clubine there at the end and Ben Casselman had a couple big carries. We’re a fully balanced attack, so it keeps them guessing whether it’s through the air or it’s on the ground.” The biggest difference between Saturday’s win and the loss in the final game of the regular season was the play of Western’s defence.

They had key third-down stops and forced turnovers which lead directly to Western scores. “He (Faulds) just he fired us up in the locker room,” said Dylan Tharby, who had a forced fumble and was in on nine tackles for Western.

“He was kind of like, you know, last week was a fluke. It was kind of like now it’s do or die for us. He told us to walk in in a sense and be better.” Western did surrender 41 points, but Faulds says other than a few long scores, he was thrilled with his defence.

“In the first half, our defense only gave up 14 points,” said Faulds. “Laurier in that second half is kind of knowing based on us, we kept scoring that they had to throw the ball around and do all that. So, you call the game a little bit differently that way,” he added.

“We’ve got a lot of trust and confidence in our defense and our defense played so much better. We got pressure on their quarterback and we made it tougher on them. So sure, Laurier scores 41 points versus 55. But the 41 they scored was a lot tougher.

It wasn’t one big play here or one big play there, they scored it was eight, nine or ten play drives.” Western will now face Windsor at Alumni Field next Saturday in the OUA Semifinal. They haven’t faced the Lancers since back in Week 2 when Casselman wasn’t the starting quarterback.

“It should be a physical game and it should be a good one,” said Casselman. “Every time we play them it’s a physical one. We’re going to have to establish the run early and get back to the pass late. You know it’s another game.” Faulds says he didn’t even take part in Halloween because it was right back to the film room with the coaches to prepare for the Lancers.

They’ve got some great running backs and a defense that flies around. We haven’t watched film on them for about eight weeks or seven weeks. So, it’ll be getting acclimated with them in the film room.” Kickoff is scheduled for 1 p.m. on Saturday, Nov.

7, 2026, at Alumni Field. The other semifinal features Ottawa at Queen’s.

stories.title: Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:

Earnings and the stock market

The steady stream of third-quarter earnings reports from the biggest names in corporate Canada continues this week. The financial results come after technology stocks sold off on Friday amid worries about the billions being spent on AI and concerns the money being spent on chips and data centres may not be worth it.

Macklem at committee

Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers looks on as Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem responds to a question during a news conference in Ottawa, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem and senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers are at the House of Commons standing committee on finance on Tuesday. The appearance comes after the central bank raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent.

Trade numbers

Truck traffic is shown on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, that connects Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Michigan, is shown on Monday, Aug. 24, 2026.

Statistics Canada will report September merchandise trade figures on Wednesday. The data comes after trade talks between Canada and the United States fell apart in August and the U.S. imposed a fresh round of tariffs, followed by counter-tariffs by Canada.

Federal budget

Minister of Finance Francois-Philippe Champagne gives remarks at a luncheon ahead of the Canada-EU Summit, in Montreal, on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026.

Federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will deliver his budget on Thursday. Prime Minister Mark Carney has been focused on an aggressive infrastructure agenda to build the economy in the face of U.S. tariffs and geopolitical changes.

stories.title: Federal byelections to be held in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan on Dec. 7
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has called byelections in six ridings, including three in Quebec, for next month.
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
Voters in six federal ridings in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan will be heading to the polls Dec. 7, after Prime Minister Mark Carney called byelections Sunday.

A press release from the Prime Minster’s Office says byelections will take place in three Quebec ridings, including Laurier—Sainte-Marie, Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton, where seats were previously held by the Liberals, the NDP and the Bloc Québécois respectively.

The remaining byelections are for Ontario ridings Brantford—Brant South and Scarborough North, along with Saskatchewan riding Yorkton—Melville.

The Conservatives held seats in Yorkton—Melville and Brantford—Brant South, while the seat in Scarborough North belonged to the Liberals.

Carney’s Liberals currently have a majority government after winning three byelections earlier this year.

In a tweet Sunday, Conservative Leader Pierre Pollievre asked that Canadians choose a different path, saying that his party’s plan will save money, protect jobs and reform the immigration system.

“I think it’s an opportunity for hard-working Canadians who think it’s unacceptable for Mark Carney to drive up their cost of gas, groceries and housing to vote for a for a party that will fight to save you money,” he said at a news conference later Sunday.

The byelections come after members of Parliament quit the House of Commons for diplomatic appointments, provincial politics or retirement.

Since the 2025 election, 13 of 343 members of Parliament have decided to step down.

The prime minister must call an election between 11 and 180 days after a member’s resignation.

A pastor and longtime Conservative is running as an independent candidate in Brantford-Brant South in Ontario after the party chose to bypass a local nomination contest and appoint Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis as its candidate.

Dave Carrol’s decision to run independently adds intrigue to the byelection, as it could draw votes from the Conservatives, who were already expected to face a tough challenge from the Liberals.

“Party leadership chose to appoint another candidate, skipping the process we have valued for decades,” Carrol, who previously sought the Conservative nomination, said on social media. “That decision, while legal, has been received poorly, and rightfully so.”

In the Saskatchewan riding of Yorkton-Melville, the Liberals are running candidate Aaron Kienle, the mayor of Yorkton, against Conservative Nelson Pohl, a farmer who owns a furnace cleaning company.

That riding has been held by the Conservatives and its predecessors, the Reform Party and Canadian Alliance, for more than 30 years. The Liberals have not won there since the riding was first created in 1968.

Cathay Wagantall, who was elected as a Conservative MP in 2015, won Yorkton-Melville with more than 77 per cent of the vote in 2025. She resigned in August.

The Laurier-Sainte-Marie riding was previously held by former environment minister Steven Guilbeault who left in the summer after a public disagreement with Carney over environment policy.

On Sunday, the Liberals announced that Guy Cormier, former president and CEO of Desjardins Group, will be their candidate in the byelection in Laurier–Sainte-Marie.

The Bloc is fielding Zumretay Arkin, the former vice-president of the World Uyghur Congress while the NDP has nominated epidemiologist Nima Machouf.

The St-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton byelection is needed because Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay quit the Bloc caucus in June ahead of a successful run provincially for the separatist Parti Québécois.

The Liberals are running former provincial politician Chantal Soucy, who represented the Coalition Avenir Québec in the National Assembly for eight years before choosing not to run again in the election this fall. The Bloc has nominated Caroline Emond, the former director general of the International Dairy Federation.

Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie was the only riding the NDP won east of Manitoba in the last federal election, and it was opened in August when MP Alexandre Boulerice resigned ahead of his successful provincial run for Québec solidaire.

The Liberals are running human rights advocate Jean-Sébastien Vallée, while the NDP are fielding Pierre Céré, a Quebec activist who made a brief bid for the leadership of the Parti Québécois in 2015.

The sixth byelection is to be held in Scarborough North, which former Liberal Shaun Chen vacated in August citing ongoing medical issues related to a vehicle crash in 2025.

The Liberals are seeking to hold onto the seat with accountant James Li.

Carney has had a string of byelection successes already this year.

Byelections were held in April in the Quebec riding of Terrebonne — a vote the Supreme Court ordered redone after issues with mail-in ballots during the 2025 election — along with the Liberal strongholds of University-Rosedale and Scarborough Southwest in Toronto. The three Liberal wins coming on the heels of five MPs who crossed the floor to the Liberals, cemented Carney’s majority government.

The Liberals swept another three ridings on Aug. 31, flipping a Conservative seat in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord and holding seats in Beaches-East York and North Vancouver-Capilano.

stories.title: Six federal by-elections to be held on Dec. 7
stories.summary: Prime Minister announced voting dates for the six ridings in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan.
stories.author: Marie Woolf
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sunday announced that six by-elections will be held on Dec. 7 in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan, days after Elections Canada figures showed the Liberals outstripping the Conservatives in fundraising.

The slew of by-elections follows a number of resignations by MPs, including former environment minister Steven Guilbeault, who stood down from his seat in the Montreal riding of Laurier—Sainte-Marie in August after expressing concerns about the direction of climate-change policy.

The New Democratic Party will be campaigning to retain its only federal seat in Quebec after veteran MP Alexandre Boulerice stood down to run for the province’s National Assembly as a Québec solidaire candidate. He was elected to the provincial legislature last month.

Mr. Carney will be hoping to bolster his slim majority in the Commons after his party raised nearly $1-million more than the Conservatives in the third quarter of 2026. This marks a reversal of fortune for the Tories , who traditionally outstrip other parties in political donations.

The Liberals secured three victories in by-elections in August. Support for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party was consolidated by voters concerned about the trade war with the U.S.

Worries over tariffs, and their impact on jobs and the cost of living, are expected to be among the issues influencing voters’ choices in the December by-elections.

In a social-media post on Sunday, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said immigration, crime and affordability would be key issues in the coming votes.

He has angered some party members by appointing Kevin Davis as his party’s candidate to replace frontbench Conservative Larry Brock, who resigned his Brantford-Brant South seat this fall, rather than holding an open nomination race. Mr. Poilievre visited Brantford, Ont., ON Friday.

Sarah Fischer, Conservative communications director, said in an e-mail Sunday that “to ensure a candidate was in place and ready to hit the ground running, the Conservative Party exercised its authority under the party’s rules to select Kevin Davis as our candidate for Brantford–Brant South.”

She said he was “overwhelmingly endorsed by local grassroots Conservatives, including riding association president Caine Chapman, Larry Brock’s former campaign manager Phil Gillies, nomination opponent Josh Wall, and two candidates for mayor.”

Local Conservative Dave Carrol, whom Mr. Brock had said he would back to run in the riding, has announced that he will now run in the by-election as an independent.

His move could split the traditional Conservative vote, and raise questions about whether Mr. Poilievre’s party can hold onto the seat.

Other by-elections will be held in Yorkton—Melville in Saskatchewan; Scarborough North in Ontario; and Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie, and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton, in Quebec.

Scarborough North became vacant after Liberal Shaun Chen stepped down in August, citing health concerns and travel limitations after a motor-vehicle accident in late 2025. The Liberals last week selected former Toronto District School Board trustee James Li as their candidate for the Ontario seat.

Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall resigned from her Yorkton-Melville seat on Aug. 31, 2026, earlier than she had previously planned. She had represented the southeastern Saskatchewan riding since 2015. The Liberals are running Aaron Kienle, mayor of Yorkton, against Conservative Nelson Pohl, a Yorkton-area farmer who owns a furnace and duct-cleaning company.

The NDP will be working to retain the Montreal riding of Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, which the party held until Mr. Boulerice decided to run for provincial office.

Mr. Boulerice had represented the riding since 2011. His new provincial riding encompasses a portion of his old federal constituency.

The Ndp’s standing was greatly diminished in the previous federal election when the party sent back only 7 MPs to the Commons. The by-election will be a test of new party Leader Avi Lewis.

NDP spokesman Sam Hersh said that in Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Laurier—Sainte-Marie, party candidates Pierre Céré and Nimâ Machouf have “been knocking on doors for months.” The party this weekend announced Mathieu Boisvert would run in Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton.

Well-known local politician Brad Ward, who used to represent Brantford in Ontario’s legislative assembly, will be announced as NDP candidate in Brantford—Brant South at a meeting on Nov. 7, he said.

The Bloc Québécois, which now has three times as many MPs as the NDP, will be striving to retain the federal riding of Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton, which was represented in the House of Commons by Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay before he opted to swap federal for provincial politics.

He quit his Commons seat in the spring and was recently elected to the Quebec Assembly for Saint-Hyacinthe. A member of the Wendat Nation, he has been appointed Quebec’s minister responsible for relations with the First Nations and Inuit.

Another by-election is expected soon in Parry Sound-Muskoka, a riding held by the Conservatives for more than two decades. Sitting MP Scott Aitchison has announced his intention to resign his Ontario seat at the end of the fall sitting.

paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sunday announced that six by-elections will be held on Dec. 7 in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan, days after Elections Canada figures showed the Liberals outstripping the Conservatives in fundraising.

The slew of by-elections follows a number of resignations by MPs, including former environment minister Steven Guilbeault, who stood down from his seat in the Montreal riding of Laurier—Sainte-Marie in August after expressing concerns about the direction of climate-change policy.

The New Democratic Party will be campaigning to retain its only federal seat in Quebec after veteran MP Alexandre Boulerice stood down to run for the province’s National Assembly as a Québec solidaire candidate. He was elected to the provincial legislature last month.

Mr. Carney will be hoping to bolster his slim majority in the Commons after his party raised nearly $1-million more than the Conservatives in the third quarter of 2026. This marks a reversal of fortune for the Tories , who traditionally outstrip other parties in political donations.
The Liberals secured three victories in by-elections in August. Support for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party was consolidated by voters concerned about the trade war with the U.S.
Worries over tariffs, and their impact on jobs and the cost of living, are expected to be among the issues influencing voters’ choices in the December by-elections.
In a social-media post on Sunday, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said immigration, crime and affordability would be key issues in the coming votes.

He has angered some party members by appointing Kevin Davis as his party’s candidate to replace frontbench Conservative Larry Brock, who resigned his Brantford-Brant South seat this fall, rather than holding an open nomination race. Mr. Poilievre visited Brantford, Ont., ON Friday.

Sarah Fischer, Conservative communications director, said in an e-mail Sunday that “to ensure a candidate was in place and ready to hit the ground running, the Conservative Party exercised its authority under the party’s rules to select Kevin Davis as our candidate for Brantford–Brant South.”

She said he was “overwhelmingly endorsed by local grassroots Conservatives, including riding association president Caine Chapman, Larry Brock’s former campaign manager Phil Gillies, nomination opponent Josh Wall, and two candidates for mayor.”
Local Conservative Dave Carrol, whom Mr. Brock had said he would back to run in the riding, has announced that he will now run in the by-election as an independent.
His move could split the traditional Conservative vote, and raise questions about whether Mr. Poilievre’s party can hold onto the seat.
Other by-elections will be held in Yorkton—Melville in Saskatchewan; Scarborough North in Ontario; and Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie, and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton, in Quebec.

stories.title: Driver charged after vehicle crashes into Brockton home: OPP
stories.summary: A 56-year-old Brockton resident is facing multiple charges after allegedly crashing a vehicle into a house on Main Street in Elmwood, Ont.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
A 56-year-old Brockton resident is facing multiple charges after allegedly crashing a vehicle into a house on Main Street in Elmwood, Ont.

The incident happened on Oct. 28 at about 10:30 p.m.

South Bruce OPP say officers responding to the collision observed signs of impairment and arrested the driver.

The accused is charged with:

Impaired operation (alcohol and drugs)

Impaired operation with a blood-alcohol concentration over 80 mg

Dangerous operation

Failure or refusal to comply with a demand

Police say the vehicle was impounded for one week and the driver’s licence was suspended for 90 days.

The accused was released from custody and is scheduled to appear in court at a later date.

stories.title: Virginia Hicks selected 2026 National Silver Cross Mother
stories.summary: Virginia Hicks from Frankford, Ont., has been named this year’s National Silver Cross Mother by the Royal Canadian Legion.
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
Virginia Hicks from Frankford, Ont., has been named this year’s National Silver Cross Mother by the Royal Canadian Legion.

Hicks served in the Royal Canadian Air Force for close to 29 years, working in supply and logistics, in a military career that took her to the Persian Gulf, Afghanistan and Italy. After retiring from the regular forces in 2008, she became a full-time reservist and served in that role in 2017.

“It’s a little overwhelming,” she tells Legion.CA , calling it an unexpected honour.

On November 11, Hicks will place a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on behalf of all Canadian mothers and families who have lost a son or daughter in the line of duty. Her presence will have some added significance this year in the wake of the tragedy that struck military personnel at CFB Wainwrigh t in Alberta last month.

Hicks’ daughter, Sapper Mariebeth Short, was herself killed during a training exercise on the Matawa Plains in Petawawa in 2002 when the light armoured vehicle she was travelling in rolled over. A subsequent investigation concluded that a defect in the wheel assembly of the vehicle was to blame for the accident.

“She watched what we did. She saw the experiences that we had, and she wanted to do the same,” said Hicks, while recalling the day military officials showed up at her home to deliver the tragic news.

“I was stunned and asked him to repeat himself. Brian was beside himself with grief and I knew then I had lost my little girl.”

Hicks was presented with the Silver Cross in 2009 following her daughters death, and admits she did not realize it was given to all those who have lost a child in service to Canada, not just those who have died in combat.

“I had more people ask me what it was…they didn’t know what it was for,” she said, adding she hopes to educate others about the honour during her year as Canada’s National Silver Cross Mother.

stories.title: The federal budget is coming. Here’s how to find the important stuff among hundreds of pages
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s first budget in 2025 tilted the scales at a fleshy 406 pages
stories.author: Mick Gzowski
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s first budget in 2025 tilted the scales at a fleshy 406 pages. If you’re economically fascinated and the pundit parade, breaking news and deep dive features aren’t in-the-trenches enough for you, we present a video guide to reading this year’s Budget 2026. Up until last year, these things arrived in the Spring like tulips. But this one is due to be released on Nov. 5. What can we expect from it? Let’s spell it out.

Budget 2025 was titled Canada Strong. Before the cover page for Budget 2026 was released on Oct. 29, we cheekily predicted that this year’s title would be either the Carney catchphrases Controlling What We Can or Canada Strong Elbows.

Governments need to carefully consider the stock photo on the cover. Is it Canadian? Is it legit? Mistakes have been made.

Under leader Jagmeet Singh, the NDP stumbled into controversy for releasing a video with stock footage of seniors at a computer that was actually Russian in origin.

Eleven years ago, the Canadian Space Agency was busted photoshopping a Canadian logo onto a photo of the International Space Station’s Canadarm.

Something that hopefully won’t be on the cover are these faux iconic Canadian stereotype photos created for free use by the Canadian Internet Registry Association or Cira if properly credited.

So here is the cover they’ve actually chosen, and they chose well. The stock photo shows transmission lines from the Churchill Falls Generating Station in Labrador.

Carney budget to focus on taxes, shift from Trudeau era

Carney's second budget will aim to help small businesses cut costs and invest more, sources say

Now let’s dig into what will be inside.

First off, there are always pages and pages of platitudes and promises that, while they do contain some figures, are enough wind to power a turbine project. You can read it if you enjoy reading press releases, but the real action is in the tables.

Jump right to the summary tables and focus on the main fiscal overview. This is where you’ll find the headline numbers of revenues, expenditures and whether we’re in surplus or deficit. Spoiler: It’s going to be a big deficit. That will make 2027 the 12th year of deficit in a row since the Liberals took power in 2015.

The Finance Minister has promised a balanced budget by 27-28. His spring fiscal update said we were ahead of fiscal goals because of revenues resulting from surging oil prices thanks to the war in Iran .

Then check out the government’s economic assumptions. Focus specifically on the economic growth forecasts (such as GDP growth, inflation, and interest rate projections) that underpin the budget. If the government assumes a stronger economy than independent forecasters do, you might catch a whiff of the sour smell of overly — BULLish optimism.

Next, look for some cuts or quiet sunsetting of previously announced programs. Both the carbon tax and the digital services tax, for example, are on their way out after they were cancelled this year. Finance ministers often find it convenient that it’s harder to spot something they’ve quietly removed — and this requires detective work.

The book begins with a summary and then breaks up into chapters on fiscal priorities. Read the “roll up” table at the end of each section to scan where and when money is being spent. Because you’re looking at just numbers, there’s no spin possible. Advance reports suggest the Foreign Affairs department and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation are targeted for big cuts.

stories.title: Canada’s trucking industry racked by non-compliance, training and safety concerns
stories.summary: In the depths of winter more than 20 years ago, Kate Shingler set off on the Plaster Rock Highway, a remote two-lane route cutting east-west through the dense wilderness of central New Brunswick.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
In the depths of winter more than 20 years ago, Kate Shingler set off on the Plaster Rock Highway, a remote two-lane route cutting east-west through the dense wilderness of central New Brunswick.

It was 2005 and so snowy and slippery that the young driver behind the wheel of a Toyota Tercel had to pull over on the side of the road. She May not have reached her destination without the help of a trucker who shepherded her through the treacherous conditions to safety.

“It was safe harbour in a terrible storm,” Shingler said, recalling the unknown truck driver who helped her on the icy roadway.

He let her use his radio and carefully drove her in the cab of his 18-wheeler up the highway until her boyfriend — now her husband — could pick her up.

“The conditions were so bad and I had no reception, but the driver made me feel safe,” she said. “I felt like truck drivers were the best drivers on the roads.”

The 21-year transition

Canada’s trucking industry has changed in the years since Shingler made that wintry drive in 2005.

Decades of deregulation, intensifying competition and uneven government oversight have reshaped the sector.

Recent government audits, roadside inspections and police investigations have uncovered significant shortcomings in how trucks are maintained and drivers are licensed.

Industry representatives say limited commercial truck-driver training and regulatory non-compliance by some operators have raised questions about worker exploitation and public safety.

“I’ve seen a great decline in the quality and the treatment of drivers,” Ken Adams, chairman of the Truck Training Schools Association of Ontario, told a House of Commons standing committee last October.

“We’ve seen carriers buy or influence schools to fast-track them through bare-bones programs, undermine the provincial licensing standards and shift the training liability away from these carriers.”

A review of the trucking industry by The Canadian Press reveals a sector increasingly divided between companies that invest in properly trained drivers and safe equipment, and those that cut corners to gain a competitive edge.

“We’re seeing two industries emerging,” said Jonathan Blackham, director of policy and public affairs with the Canadian Trucking Alliance.

“One makes investments in their people and equipment and another growing segment has little regard for labour practices, tax compliance, safety and training.”

The consequence for some truckers is a loss of training and support, employment misclassification, unpaid time and pressure to accept unsafe conditions, he said.

For the public, the situation raises broader safety concerns.

“You can’t just throw the keys at somebody and say, ‘Head out in this blizzard for the first time,’” Blackham said.

The transformation of Canada’s trucking industry can be traced back to the ’80s when the United States reduced its trucking regulations to boost competition and lower freight rates.

Canada followed with similar reforms in 1987, easing restrictions on who could operate a trucking company, where they could transport freight and in some cases, what they could charge.

“It led to a cutthroat level of competition, a massive oversupply in the trucking industry,” he said. “That drove rates trucking companies charged to shippers way down.”

Monette said older, established carriers — often the companies that paid workers top dollar and invested heavily in driver training, safety and maintenance — were slowly driven out of business.

“These were the firms that created this image of truckers as knights of the highway, professional drivers you could drive behind in a snowstorm, truckers who might stop on the side of the road to help out a stranded driver,” he said.

“As these firms started disappearing, it started a downward spiral and wages started stagnating and working conditions declined.”

First-hand trucker experience

It’s an evolution Bryon Slade witnessed first hand.

He entered the trucking industry in 1976, following in the footsteps of his dad, a delivery driver for the now-defunct Canadian department store Simpsons.

The 19-year-old spent years learning the ropes before getting behind the wheel of a big rig.

He served as a dock worker loading and unloading freight, moved on to shunting trucks short distances around a yard and eventually drove small trucks on city runs.

It would take years before Slade was allowed to drive a tractor-trailer on a highway.

“They wouldn’t turn you loose until they were satisfied you could do the job safely and properly,” he said. “All that started to change when they deregulated the industry.”

Slade retired in 2020 from a trucking industry he didn’t recognize.

He said new drivers lacked training, trucks weren’t properly maintained, and road safety had deteriorated with more distracted and dangerous driving behaviour.

“It wasn’t fun driving anymore.”

Industry representatives say stagnant wages, demanding working conditions and long stretches away from home have made trucking less attractive to younger workers.

They say this has prompted employers to increasingly turn to temporary foreign workers to fill positions.

The number of truck-driver positions approved through the federal temporary foreign worker program rose more than five-fold between 2018 and 2024 — to 8,101 from 1,584 — before dropping in 2025.

Labour advocates allege some trucking companies favour temporary foreign workers and recent immigrants who are more likely to accept lower pay and less likely to speak out against poor working conditions.

“They turn to vulnerable newcomers,” Monette said. “They turn to people who might be afraid to speak out, to turn to a union, or to go to the labour board with safety concerns.”

He said newcomers are also particularly vulnerable to being misclassified as independent contractors rather than employees.

Under the so-called Driver Inc. model, some trucking companies reduce labour costs by treating drivers as independent contractors. This avoids responsibilities such as employer payroll contributions and benefits they would otherwise be required to provide.

While hiring legitimate independent contractors is legal, misclassifying employees as contractors to avoid employment obligations goes against federal labour law.

“It reduces their workforce costs by 20 to 30 per cent compared with an employer that’s following the rules,” Monette said.

Training standards and enforcement have also come under scrutiny.

A report by Ontario’s auditor general in May found serious gaps in the training provided by some private career colleges.

The auditor general’s office sent undercover students to six truck-driver training schools and found that two delivered just 59.5 and 81 hours of instruction, well below the required minimum of 103.5 hours.

Two students were also not taught essential driving manoeuvres, including left turns at major intersections, reverse parking and emergency stopping.

The report came after 24 criminal charges were laid against eight people in January after an Ontario Provincial Police investigation into alleged fraudulent commercial driving exams in Kingston, Ont., and the Toronto area.

Police said bribes were allegedly exchanged for favourable treatment during road tests.

Kim Richardson, senior adviser with the Professional Truck Training Alliance of Canada, said the problem isn’t necessarily a lack of training standards but a failure to ensure schools follow them.

“The problem is compliance, regulation and enforcement,” he said.

Richardson said penalties are often too small to discourage repeat violations, allowing some companies to treat fines as a business expense.

“If the fines are just the cost of doing business, we’re in trouble.”

Trucking experts say critical fixes to address the industry’s problems include improving driver training, strengthening enforcement and recognizing truck driving as a skilled profession.

Some provinces are already taking steps in that direction.

In September, Ontario announced plans to introduce a standardized curriculum for entry-level truck drivers, with additional instruction under consideration on subjects such as fatigue management and driving in northern and remote areas.

Quebec introduced mandatory training for new truck drivers in December 2025, while Alberta adopted an apprenticeship-style licensing system that requires additional training before drivers can operate outside the province.

Nova Scotia has committed to introducing mandatory entry-level training, while Manitoba has strengthened enforcement measures targeting unsafe carriers and companies attempting to evade regulatory oversight.

Industry recommendations

Industry observers welcome these efforts but say more needs to be done.

“You don’t need to invent new laws or pass new legislation to make an impact in this industry,” Monette said. “Once you start enforcing the law as it’s written, you can have a huge impact.”

Blackham said if trucking companies are not held responsible for how they train and treat workers, the operators following the rules are at a disadvantage.

“We want the trucking industry to compete on a level playing field,” Blackham said.

Ultimately, Richardson said restoring professionalism and rebuilding public confidence in the trucking industry will require recognizing commercial truck driving as a skilled trade.

He said the training and qualifications need to reflect the responsibility of operating some of the largest vehicles on Canadian roads.

“Let’s legitimize the profession of these highway pilots.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

Ultimately, Richardson said restoring professionalism and rebuilding public confidence in the trucking industry will require recognizing commercial truck driving as a skilled trade.
He said the training and qualifications need to reflect the responsibility of operating some of the largest vehicles on Canadian roads.
“Let’s legitimize the profession of these highway pilots.”

stories.title: The working theory of legendary lawyer Earl Cherniak
stories.summary: 'I don't have to like my client. I just have to think they have an arguable case,' says Toronto lawyer who just released his memoirs
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
After a long legal career that saw him stand up in court for many of Canada’s most notorious litigants and defendants — Conrad Black, Tim Hortons owner Ron Joyce, Imperial Tobacco, the Canadian Red Cross in the tainted blood inquiry, even the National Hockey League in a case about player pensions that saw him cross-examine Gordie Howe and then immediately ask for his autograph — Earl Cherniak’s most famous client remains his most controversial, Shylock, the villain in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice.

In 2010, Cherniak, 91, who has just published his memoirs, appeared as counsel for the fictional stereotyped Jewish moneylender in a University of Western Ontario production of an appeal of his trial in the play. This was later reprised in 2013 at the Stratford Festival with then Chief Justice Beverley McLachlin and former justice Ian Binnie as judges.

“I thought Portia was a fraud and that vitiated the conviction,” Cherniak said in an interview, about the scheming heroine who delivers the “quality of mercy” speech.

Shylock was, among other things, a victim of the antisemitism Cherniak has seen evolve from the “subtle” bigotry of his early years at the Ontario bar, when he appeared before judges “who wouldn’t have much use for a young Jewish punk lawyer like me,” and the Toronto Lawyers Club did not admit Jews, who had their own organization called the Lord Reading Club, to the more activist “1930s kind” he sees around him in Canada now.

Much has changed. The Toronto Lawyers Club merged with the Lord Reading Club, and later admitted women. The Ontario bar went from a collegial, clubby assortment of 5,000 lawyers to a vast industry of 60,000. Cherniak lamented the lost collegiality of lawyers who would gown at the courthouse rather than at the office, and engage in a chummy professional lifestyle he said is now “mostly gone. I miss it, but I got to the point that that’s what I did too.”

“I had an advocacy practice that is not repeatable in today’s world,” he writes in his memoir, released on Oct. 13.

In The Courts: A Counsel’s Memoir, published by University of Toronto Press for the Osgoode Society for Canadian Legal History, recounts Cherniak’s career since being called to the bar in 1960, and clerking for Chief Justice of the High Court of Justice for Ontario John C. McRuer.

To call him a senior lawyer is an understatement. Cherniak is so senior he went to Osgoode Hall in Osgoode Hall. (The law school is of course now at York University, and the actual building next to Toronto’s City Hall houses the Court of Appeal and Law Society, but no law school anymore.)

“I’m old school,” he said.

In the memoir, he describes the stutter that, as a child, “hampered me from answering the telephone or responding in class, even when I knew the answer… While I have largely overcome that disability, it has never fully left me.”

He writes that he became a litigator “despite, or perhaps because of, my speech disability.”

The stutter remains barely noticeable, audible and visible in his jaw within the first few words of a recent interview, in a boardroom with a CN Tower view at Lerner’s LLP, the only firm he has ever worked for and for which he still works. His portrait by the prominent Canadian painter Joanne Tod hangs in the reception area.

One curiosity about this interview was that both subject and reporter have a stutter, similar speech impediments that are not much noticeable today but were serious in youth, and had to be overcome in the social, academic and professional worlds.

Two stutterers saying hello to each other is potentially humorous in principle. But Cherniak got a surprise laugh with a perfectly fluent opening quip. Told it was a pleasure to meet him, he said dryly, “We’ll see.”

It was. He spoke with good humour and nostalgia about a career in which he, for example, successfully argued a matter that redefined personal injury law, allowing for vastly higher damages to plaintiffs. This case, and other successes in civil law, inspired the nickname on the cover of Canadian Lawyer in 1985, “King of Torts — the Intransigent Earl Cherniak.”

“Better publicity would be hard to come by,” he writes. It was so good, in fact, that he was hauled before the Law Society on a complaint that he was improperly promoting himself, though he had not sought out the attention and said he only gave interviews if he thought it was in his client’s interest. The complaint went no further, but it reminded him “that having a public reputation does engender professional jealousy in some colleagues.”

Thereafter, most cases came to him by referral from other lawyers, which he cultivated on the principle that “nobody refers cases to a jerk.”

“I was well brought up,” he said. “I’m the kind of guy who would never ever leave an elevator before a woman. I just wouldn’t do it. And when I see people do it, I’m offended.”

He reflected on the ethical tensions that can face a lawyer in highly controversial matters involving all sorts of people, and the principles that allow him to give sound advice without being drawn on the question of whether his client is ultimately right or wrong.

“I was my client’s counsel, not their judge,” he writes, quoting the late defence counsel Edward Greenspan.

Asked if any client had especially tested him on this point, he reflects, then says if there was, he probably would not reveal it in a newspaper interview.

“I don’t have to like my client. I just have to think they have an arguable case. I would defend a Nazi if they had an arguable defence,” he said. (On the other hand, his memoir also tells the story of him punching an actual Nazi, a former German pilot called Martin Weiche, who was leader of the Canadian Nazi Party in the 1950s and also landlord to people Cherniak represented in a rental dispute. His clients tried to move out, Weiche blocked them, Cherniak showed up, and Weiche “grabbed me by the collar, ripped my white dress shirt, and shouted that the Nazis should have finished the job against people like me — meaning Jews. I slugged him.” Weiche wanted to press assault charges, but none were ever filed, and to this day Cherniak thinks he would have beaten them.)

Imperial Tobacco, which he represented for many years, “wasn’t my more popular retainers with my kids,” he said. “But I wasn’t their judge, I was their lawyer, and the question was were they liable in these lawsuits. It was one of the longest retainers I’ve ever had, and it was intensely interesting, and very well paid.”

Other clients were more sympathetic, such as the Canadian Red Cross, which he represented at the Krever Inquiry into the 1980s tainted blood disaster.

“They had to supply blood all across the country every day while this completely unknown crisis was going on, so they did the best they could,” Cherniak said.

He maintains the American criminal case against Conrad Black, whom he represented in Canadian civil matters, was “a crock,” and that his infamous removal of 13 file boxes from his Toronto office was perfectly innocent because he had been evicted, and the contents of the boxes were available to prosecutors anyway.

In the Walkerton water contamination inquiry, he acted for the medical officer of health. He also represented the lawyer Joseph Groia, whose successful defence of a key player in the Bre-X Minerals gold mining scandal led to misconduct charges of incivility, which Groia and Cherniak fought all the way to vindication in the Supreme Court of Canada.

“We lost all the way up,” Cherniak said.

Chris Selley: Canada's law schools, law societies have incinerated their reputations

He represented the late Ron Joyce in litigation brought by Lori Horton, widow of Tim Horton, for half the value of the iconic coffee shop company.

“That was a great case, so interesting,” he said.

He acted for Kpmg in the Garth Drabinsky and Livent fraud scandal, over a collapsed entertainment business, and for developer Tridel in the Patti Starr affair, a political controversy involving illegal political contributions to the Ontario Liberal Party.

He never wished to follow the traditional path from successful lawyer to a judge on the bench. He was moved by another lawyer’s comment that to be a respected counsel is “a sufficient calling,” and unlike in the United States, he said, in Canada you cannot go back to the bar once you join the bench.

“I didn’t have a calling. I mean, a lot of my friends had a calling, they wanted to be judges, they thought they should be judges,” he said. “I never did… If I’d have gone into journalism, I would have been a writer, I wouldn’t have been an editor. Even though I’m a pretty good editor.”

He probably would have been a good judge too. He was named a Queen’s Counsel in the 1970s, a designation that ended in 1985 and brought back in 2023, now as King’s Counsel. He writes that he has “known and appeared before every Chief Justice of Canada from John Cartwright to Richard Wagner, and every chief justice of Ontario from Dana Porter to Michael Tulloch.”

stories.title: Family of man who went missing on Quebec ski trip turns to digital clues
stories.summary: The family of an Ontario man is making a deeper technological dive to fish out clues on what happened to their son, who went missing in Mont-Tremblant, Que., 21 months ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal — The family of an Ontario man is making a deeper technological dive to fish out clues on what happened to their son, who went missing in Mont-Tremblant, Que., 21 months ago.

Metadata linked to Liam Toman’s phone the night the 22-year-old disappeared from the Laurentian ski resort might offer fresh information on his whereabouts, said his father Chris Toman.

“We’ve been mining that data with a digital forensic expert in conjunction with the SQ,” Chris said, referring to the Sûreté du Québec, the provincial police force.

He said cell tower pings, router data and other signal metrics could further help searchers home in on where in the sprawling mountain resort or beyond to look.

“Those are kernels, or data packs, that we have requested — some production orders through the SQ to retain that from some of the third-party apps — and that allows us to narrow that search area a little tighter,” the father said.

Toman vanished at around 3 a.m. on Feb. 2, 2025, after leaving a bar in the ski village north of Montreal following a night of dinner and drinks with friends on a ski trip in Mont-Tremblant.

Liam’s parents and stepmother have said he was last seen on camera walking back toward his hotel, but there was no footage of him heading inside. A last call and text were sent from his phone at around 3:15 a.m., with no activity on his bank account, social media or phone since.

“If you see the video surveillance, he’s walking with purpose,” said Chris. “He’s not lost ... he’s not stumbling. He’s obviously had something to drink, which they all do, but he’s got his faculties, he’s multitasking ... phoning, texting.”

His disappearance prompted provincial police to carry out searches by land, helicopter and in nearby bodies of water.

After his wallet was found in a nearby parking lot seven weeks later, police dispatched more helicopters, dogs, ATVs and searchers on horseback while volunteer groups combed the surrounding hills.

Authorities have not ruled out criminal activity.

The family has also launched a blue wristband campaign, inviting visitors to wear the bracelets as a sign of support and to help keep attention on Liam’s disappearance.

A $50,000 reward remains in place for information leading to his location, as his parents continue to work with police, forensics analysts and the community to find their son.

This weekend marked the 18th or 19th visit Liam’s parents had made to the resort since February 2025, they said.

Since then, new lighting and upgrades to cameras — more now record footage rather than offering only a livestream, for example — have given a small measure of solace to Chris as well as Kathleen Toman, Liam’s mother, and Lara Toman, his stepmother.

“Now if this happened, he would be on camera,” said Lara. “They’ve really taken those steps,” she said, while noting that a security audit at the resort is ongoing.

“If anything positive comes out of this, it’s that we don’t want another family to go through this,” said Chris, who lives in Whitby, Ont.

The couple described Liam as kind, quick-witted and risk-averse.

“He was an old, sensitive soul. He loved his outdoors. He made friends easily, he was very sociable,” Chris said of his son, who graduated from Niagara College with an electronics technician diploma in 2024.

Chris recalled teaching his boy to swim, skate and grill a good steak, while Lara remembers Liam’s close relationship with her own son.

“I was lucky to be a bonus mom,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Poilievre says Carney must keep fiscal promises in upcoming budget
stories.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is pushing for the federal government to eliminate all federal taxes on diesel until Canada Day, part of a list of demands ahead of the budget being tabled on Nov. 5.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is pushing for the federal government to eliminate all federal taxes on diesel until Canada Day, part of a list of demands ahead of the budget being tabled on Nov. 5.

In a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, Poilievre says suspending the GST on fuel until summer and permanently scrapping the fuel standard tax would save Canadians money whether they’re buying groceries or toys for Christmas.

The letter also calls for the Liberal government to cut wasteful and inflationary spending and fulfil promises to reduce both the debt-to-GDP ratio and deficit-to-GDP.

Poilievre says keeping his word to reduce the debt and deficit as a share of the economy is the bare minimum Carney can do.

The Parliamentary Budget Office has predicted that the government will not meet its fiscal anchor of maintaining a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio; instead, the office expects the measure to rise in 2027-28 and 2029-30.

The office also expects a $63.3-billion deficit in fiscal 2026-27, down from a forecast of $71.8 billion in its June outlook. It sees annual deficit levels peaking at $70.2 billion the following year.

Poilievre says Carney’s government has the biggest deficit ever outside of the COVID-19 pandemic and the highest spending as a share of GDP since the 1990s debt crisis

He says the prime minister has helped drive up the cost of basic living expenses that people can’t afford.

“You promised affordability. Yet everything is more expensive since you took office. While you cannot control things outside Canada, your decisions at home have only made things worse,” the letter says.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said the budget will “outline the next steps in our plan to build a stronger, more resilient and more affordable Canada.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 1, 2026

The Canadian Press

stories.title: At 14, Clifford Robinson Oulton fibbed about his age to enlist. He was the youngest Canadian serviceman to sacrifice his life
stories.summary: "How does a 14-year-old end up in France?” asks his great-nephew now.
stories.author: Edward Brown
stories.content:
The day after attending a rousing recruiting meeting at the Grand Opera House in Moncton, N.B., ON February 1, 1916, 14 volunteers visited the Moncton Barracks to enlist in the 145th Battalion. Two were deemed medically unfit. Another was sent home when it was discovered he was underage at 15. The remaining 11 swore an oath to defend his majesty against all enemies.

Among that day’s recruits, Clifford Robinson Oulton fibbed about his age on his attestation papers, then crossed the muddy Petitcodiac River back to his home in Bridgedale and told his mother, stepfather and sisters that he was bound for war in Europe.

No one questioned the youngster’s decision to enlist. “They could have stopped it,” Oulton’s great-nephew, Jamie Heffer, 59, says now. “How does a 14-year-old end up in France?”

The question has haunted Heffer for ages.

Clifford Robinson Oulton’s time in uniform would make him the answer to a dark trivia question: According to the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, he was the youngest Canadian serviceman to sacrifice his life for the cause in the First World War.

With the minimum enlistment age at 18, recruiting officers in Moncton were instructed to watch for adolescents attempting to answer the call of duty. Officers of the 145th Battalion, in which Oulton had signed up, complained publicly about the number of youngsters attempting to enlist and the financial cost to the battalion when they were discharged.

Clifford Robinson Oulton, teen First World War soldier for Canada.

An estimated 20,000 underage soldiers enlisted in the Canadian Expeditionary Force during the First World War. If discovered before going overseas, they were sent home. If found out in Europe, they’d either be returned to Canada or placed in noncombat outfits like the Canadian Forestry Battalion or in special units formed to handle underage enlistees, including the Young Soldiers Battalion, which provided military training and education.

So how did Oulton slip through?

Heffer, now mayor of Morris-Turnberry in Ontario’s Huron County, grew up with a black-and-white portrait of Private Oulton prominently displayed on the mantelpiece of his childhood home. Asked if he thought Oulton could pass for 18, Heffer is adamant: “Absolutely not.” He struggles to understand how the youngster duped recruitment officers.

His great-uncle Clifford, born in 1901, was the fifth of six children of Dora and George Oulton. He was named after barrister Clifford W. Robinson, an associate of his father’s, the future mayor of Moncton, premier of New Brunswick and senator. Clifford’s older brother Frank died of consumption in 1909. Records indicate Clifford was an above-average student at Bridgedale Public School.

Heffer says the family appears not to have struggled financially, telling the Star, “They weren’t at the worst end of society.” The 1911 census bears that out. A male servant lived in the family residence, which boasted a telephone, a rare utility in rural New Brunswick at the time.

George Oulton operated a farm in addition to working in the boiler shop at the Intercolonial Railway until his untimely death in April 1912. His widow received a sizable inheritance.

“I am still alive and well hoping you are the same.” Private Clifford Oulton’s last letter home to New Brunswick from his place in the First World War fighting. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission considers Oulton to be the youngest Canadian serviceman to die in war.

Heffer was unaware before the Star told him that eight months later, the Oulton household took a turn when Heffer’s great-grandmother Dora wed John Hyslop, the man previously listed on the census as a servant 17 years her senior, ON New Year’s Eve.

Hyslop, twice widowed, had seven adult children. Changing family dynamics May have contributed to Oulton’s decision to enlist.

Wilmot, John Hyslop’s youngest child from his first marriage, enlisted in October 1915. The day after Clifford Oulton enlisted, in an inexplicable move, his stepbrother William, the married father of four, visited the barracks, claimed to be 34 instead of his actual age of 41, and enlisted in the same battalion as Clifford.

Before departing for training camp in Valcartier, Que., family and friends lauded Clifford and William at a soiree and presented them with matching rings engraved with their battalion number. In Oulton’s official portrait, still displayed in his great-nephew’s home today, the private’s hand is positioned to draw the viewer’s eye to the commemorative piece of jewellery. “I often wondered about the peculiar placement of his hand showing the ring finger,” Heffer explains.

On a separate occasion, Dora gave her son a wristwatch.

At the end of August, 41-year-old William Hyslop was deemed medically unfit and discharged from the 145th. Then, eight days before Oulton boarded the troopship S.S. Tuscania, a telegram arrived stating that his stepbrother Wilmot Hyslop had died at the First Battle of the Somme.

Arriving in England in October 1916, Oulton transferred to the 9th Reserve Battalion and was in France by month’s end. Next, he was allocated to the 5th Canadian Mounted Regiment, bound for the front. After two months on the continent, Oulton celebrated his 15th birthday participating in trench raids in northern France.

Oulton saw action at the Somme, Vimy Ridge, and the Battle of Hill 70, nearby in northern France.

His mother sent parcels, and he wrote home often. One letter informed his family of a close call resulting in his wristwatch — a gift from his mother — being shattered by shrapnel, noting the ring he was given remained in his possession.

Heffer has a few artifacts once belonging to Oulton, including the final letter the private wrote home. The Albert County Museum in Hopewell Cape, N.B., also holds two of Oulton’s medals. “The letter is something our family considers very precious,” Heffer explains to the Star. “It gives me a real sense of what his life was like day to day.”

In the correspondence, Oulton wrote about the gruelling monotony of digging trenches, of the mud, cold and fatigue. He also confessed he was homesick, writing, “I hope to be back again soon.”

A week later, Clifford Oulton was machine-gunned to death at Passchendaele and died on Nov. 1, 1917, a month shy of his 16th birthday.

The Death Penny, officially called the Memorial Plaque, is a bronze commemorative disc issued after the First World War to the next of kin of British and Commonwealth service members who died in the war. This is the penny honouring Oulton.

Noting his great-uncle made the ultimate sacrifice so young, Heffer says, “I have a hard time even understanding it.

Clifford Robinson Oulton is interred at Nine Elms British Cemetery in Belgium. Though other records point to Frederick Freeman Laing, of Halifax, as being even younger when he was killed by an enemy shell in May 1916, the Commonwealth War Graves Commission gives that claim to Oulton. Modern birth records being rather better, it’s not a record that seems to be in jeopardy.

On Remembrance Day, Jamie Heffer reflects on his great-uncle’s sacrifice at such a tender age. Unable to comprehend decisions that placed a boy at the front, Heffer concludes, “We always need to be reminded of those who went before … we need to really understand and respect that.”
