stories.title: Matthews, Nylander lead Leafs to 4-2 win over struggling Canucks
stories.summary: Auston Matthews collected his team-leading 11th goal of the season as the Toronto Maple Leafs defeated the Vancouver Canucks 4-2 Saturday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Auston Matthews collected his team-leading 11th goal of the season as the Toronto Maple Leafs defeated the Vancouver Canucks 4-2 Saturday to snap a two-game NHL skid.

William Nylander and Teddy Blueger both had a goal and an assist, while Zack MacEwen also scored for Toronto (8-6-2), which wrapped up a four-game road trip with two wins and two losses.

Brock Boeser, ON the power play, and Max Sasson scored for the Canucks (3-12-1) who have one win in their last 13 games.

Canucks goaltender Leevi Merilainen made 24 saves.

Leafs goalie Anthony Stolarz stopped 26 shots and also earned an assist on Blueger’s empty net goal.

Sasson made things interesting early in the third, drawing the Canucks to within a goal by scoring off the rebound of a Brendan Gallagher shot.

Matthews gave the Leafs a 2-1 lead at 3:47 of the second period, beating Merilainen on the short side after a pretty back-and-forth pass with defenceman Darren Raddysh.

McEwen put Toronto up two goals during a scramble at 12:34.

The teams exchanged first-period breakaway goals.

Nylander opening the scoring with the game just 83 seconds old. He scooped up a puck that bounced off Canuck defenceman Jamie Oleksiak’s stick, skated in alone and lifted a backhand past Merilainen.

Boeser tied the game about nine minutes later. With the Canucks on a power play he got behind the Toronto defence, he took a long pass on the fly from defenceman Filip Hronek and beat Stolarz.

Canucks: Merilainen robbed rookie Gavin McKenna on a power play in the first period. Parked at the side of the net McKenna took a cross-ice pass from centre Jack Roslovic but Merilainen got a pad on his shot. … Centre Jacob Quillan, acquired Oct. 15 in a trade from Toronto, was inserted into the lineup after being recalled from Abbotsford of the AHL on Friday to replace Filip Chytil who was placed on injured reserve after reaggravating a shoulder injury in a 3-2 loss at the San Jose Sharks on Thursday. … Centre Elias Pettersson saw a six-game point streak end (2G, 5A).

Leafs: Roslovic earned an assist on Matthews goal, extending his points streak to six games (3G, 7A). … Toronto has just 28 wins in 86 games playing in Vancouver. … Former Canuck defenceman Chris Tanev and forward Dakota Joshua returned to the lineup. Joshua was playing his first game of the season after suffering a core injury late last year. Tanev missed nine games with an upper-body injury sustained Oct. 10 at Colorado. … Blueger, who spent three seasons with the Canucks, played in his first game in Vancouver since signing a two-year contract with the Leafs.

McEwan was awarded Toronto’s third goal but replays seemed to show defenceman Morgan Rielly’s shot went off Merilainen’s glove, hit defenceman Luke Schenn on the back, then rolled into the net.

Matthews has points in six of his last seven games (5G, 5A).

Maple Leafs: Host the Utah Mammoth on Tuesday.

Canucks: Host the Anaheim Ducks on Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

stories.title: Endangered North Atlantic right whale entangled in gear spotted in the Gulf of St. Lawrence
stories.summary: If located again, officials plan to tag the gear with a satellite tracker and try to disentangle the animal
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Federal officials say they’ve spotted a critically endangered North Atlantic right whale entangled in gear in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada says a surveillance flight spotted the whale on Oct. 21 between New Brunswick’s Acadian Peninsula, P.E.I. and Quebec’s Îles-de-la-Madeleine.

The department says the entanglement in the Bradelle Bank region wasn’t spotted until scientists and experts reviewed footage this week.

If the whale is located again, officials plan to tag the gear with a satellite tracker and try to disentangle the animal.

The department says it has not been able to identify the whale or the type of gear it’s caught in.

The entire North Atlantic right whale population is estimated at just 384 animals.

stories.title: Lions roar back, oust Roughriders from playoffs
stories.summary: Nathan Rourke passed for 366 yards and the B.C. Lions came all the way back to beat the Saskatchewan Roughriders 33-26 in the CFL's West Division semifinal on Saturday.
stories.author: Gemma Karstens-Smith
stories.content:
Vancouver – Nathan Rourke passed for 366 yards and the B.C. Lions came all the way back to beat the Saskatchewan Roughriders 33-26 in the CFL’s West Division semifinal on Saturday.

The Lions fell behind 17-3 midway through the second quarter before rallying in the third and taking over the game in the fourth.

Rourke connected on 21 of his 32 attempts, including a pair of touchdown passes to Jevon Cottoy and another to Stanley Berryhill III.

Kicker Sean Whyte added four field goals — his longest was a 48-yard kick — as B.C. eliminated the reigning Grey Cup champions from the playoffs.

Trevor Harris logged 255 passing yards with one interception for the Riders, who bounced the Lions from the post-season in both 2024 and 2025.

Saskatchewan QB Tommy Stevens rushed for a four-yard major in the second quarter and Brett Lauther made six field goals, including two from 55 yards.

The Lions will travel to face the Edmonton Elks (13-5) in the West Division final on Nov. 7.

The East semifinal earlier on Saturday saw the Winnipeg Blue Bombers stun the Argonauts with a 25-22 comeback victory in Toronto.

The Bombers will take on the host Montreal Alouettes in the East final on Nov. 7. Calgary hosts the Grey Cup on Nov. 15.

The Riders and Lions came in with identical 10-8 regular-season records, but B.C. earned the right to host by winning the season head-to-head series 2-1.

The two sides traded field goals over the first quarter on Saturday, starting with Lauther booting the ball 55 yards through the uprights to open the scoring for Saskatchewan.

Each side followed with a 26-yard field goal to make it 6-3 at the end of the opening frame before Lauther scored on another 55-yard kick early in the second quarter.

A turnover on downs proved costly for the Lions midway through the second.

The Riders got the ball at their own 49-yard line and worked it up the field over six plays, capping the drive with Stevens muscling his way into the end zone. Saskatchewan opted to go for the two-point convert and Harris made good, connecting with Samuel Emilus to give his side a 17-3 advantage.

B.C. replied with Rourke scrambling out of the pocket and lobbing a rainbow up the field to an unmarked Berryhill, who dashed over the goal line for the major. Whyte’s kick for the extra point was good, cutting the Lions’ deficit to 17-10.

The home side’s other chance to put up points came late in the first half after defensive back Robert Carter Jr. made a flying grab to pick off Harris’ pass to Emilus midfield, but B.C. couldn’t turn the interception into points.

Keon Hatcher Sr. had a prime opportunity to add points with just seconds left on the clock, too, but dropped the ball inches from the goal line and the Lions settled for a 48-yard field goal that made it 17-13 for Saskatchewan heading into the locker rooms.

Another field goal from Lauther — this time a 34-yard strike — boosted the Riders’ lead to 20-13 early in the third quarter.

B.C. was quick to answer.

Rourke sent a quick dish to Cottoy, who split the Saskatchewan defence and sprinted up the field for a 70-yard touchdown. Whyte added the extra point to level the score at 20-20.

The Riders added another three points with Lauther’s fifth field goal of the night before Rourke found an open Cottoy steps from the end zone.

The Canadian receiver reeled in the pass and took a few strides in for his second major of the game, putting the Lions up 27-23 at the end of the quarter.

The teams once again traded field goals across the fourth and final frame.

Whyte’s 34-yard kick boosted B.C.’s lead to seven points midway through the quarter and the veteran kicker added another from 24 yards with three minutes left on the game clock.

The Riders clawed three points back in the final two minutes of the game when Lauther made a 44-yard field goal to put the score at 33-26.

Whyte’s 49-yard attempt field goal fell short with 49 seconds to go, giving Saskatchewan’s offence one last chance, but the green and white stalled out at B.C.’s 34-yard line.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

stories.title: Joly seeks Competition Bureau probe of Stelco as more layoffs loom
stories.summary: The federal government is asking the competition commissioner to 'thoroughly examine' if Stelco owner Cleveland-Cliffs breached the Competition Act.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
With the deadline for Cleveland-Cliffs ‘ layoffs at Stelco fast approaching, Industry Minister Melanie Joly is asking the commissioner of the Competition Bureau to investigate whether the company’s U.S.-based owner is breaking Canadian competition law.

The federal government is asking the competition commissioner to “thoroughly examine whether Cleveland-Cliffs’ conduct in the Canadian marketplace warrants enforcement action under the Competition Act,” Joly said in a statement Friday.

In her letter to the commissioner, Joly said she cited remarks by Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves, who said he “bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the determinant of my own company.”

Ottawa has issued several warnings to the steel company, which has already started issuing layoff notices to employees at its Hamilton, Ont., steel plant.

In a letter dated Oct. 29 obtained by Global News and addressed to Stelco’s president, Paul Simon, Joly said she expects a “concrete and credible plan for re-engagement with these workers.”

Stelco began issuing layoff notices to about 500 employees at the beginning of October following an announcement of its plans to pull back on operations at its Hamilton plant.

The company has said some of the employees laid off in Hamilton will be offered jobs at their Lake Erie facility but the union representing Stelco workers told Global News only 40 jobs have been offered to the impacted employees.

In a letter sent last month, Joly warned Stelco that if they do not reverse the layoffs within 15 days, the federal government will start legal action against the company that could ultimately lead to the parent company Cleveland-Cliffs being forced to divest of the Canadian steel firm.

Cleveland-Cliffs has maintained its position that one of the reasons for the layoffs is the 50 per cent tariff on aluminum and steel imposed by the U.S., which the company’s leadership has publicly supported.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last month that Cleveland-Cliffs would be making a “mistake” by not respecting its obligations and commitments.

The comments came at an event in Ottawa when Carney was asked by a reporter if, given what has transpired in recent weeks, the federal government felt it was a mistake to allow Cleveland-Cliffs to acquire Stelco in 2024.

“The mistake here would be Cleveland-Cliffs not respecting the obligations, the commitments that they made in the acquisition,” Carney said in response.

–with files from Global’s Rachel Morgan and Ari Rabinovitch

stories.title: Ontario businesses gain ‘fragile’ optimism on trade after U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Economic uncertainty due to Trump’s tariff regime has lead to upheaval for Ontario's businesses that has required increased resilience.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
The Republican Party’s disastrous performance in the U.S. midterm elections has injected some fragile hope into the Ontario business community, according to some business advocacy organizations eager to see Canada step into a strengthened position in its trade relationship with the U.S.

“(Optimism) is higher, certainly, than it was a year ago, despite all the challenges that we’ve been in,” said Daniel Tisch, the president and CEO of the Ontario Chamber of Commerce , a non-profit group representing around 60,000 businesses.

“After the midterms and the indisputable weakening of (U.S. President) Donald Trump and his agenda, our strategic position has improved…modestly but meaningfully, because we are less vulnerable,” he said, describing the optimism as “very fragile right now.”

As the results of the U.S. midterm elections began to trickle in Tuesday night, it was clear the Democratic Party achieved a decisive victory, taking control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in a rebuke of the Trump administration.

“It’s pretty clear that Trump’s approach to Canada has widespread opposition in the U.S.,” said Tisch.

An increased alignment has also emerged between the federal government, Ontario and the business community, he said, while much of the last decade saw those three pillars in a “gridlock.”

“We’re working together,” he said. “We’ve started to invest in our economy, we’ve diversified our trade relationships, you see really positive measures that are incentivizing businesses to invest in themselves.”

But economic uncertainty due to Trump’s tariff regime on Canada, first levelled less than two weeks after he was inaugurated, has led to upheaval for Ontario’s businesses that has required increased resilience, according to surveys of owners published since 2025 by the Ontario Chamber of Commerce.

The organization’s most recent data published Oct. 1 shows some increased optimism, even before the midterm results, amid continued worries about the trade war.

The survey of 851 businesses across Ontario showed that while 44 per cent lacked confidence in the economy, business confidence rose over the course of 2026, from 23 to 34 per cent.

Yet, the majority did expect economic uncertainty due to the trade war with the U.S. to continue to hurt their businesses. Fifty-seven per cent reported they expect tariffs, trade policies and economic uncertainty to negatively affect their investment or expansion plans.

As a result, business owners reported they were increasing prices, reducing trade with the U.S., expanding domestic sales and diversifying suppliers.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford expressed similar optimism about the midterm results earlier this week, telling media he was “doing cartwheels” when he saw the Democrats’ blue wave. But the premier also voiced caution, citing that it will be up to Prime Minister Mark Carney to continue to try to make a trade deal with the president.

The Ford government also watched closely as Ottawa released its fall budget on Thursday. It featured an additional $151 billion over five years in “supports” for Canadian households, businesses and other levels of government.

Ontario Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy said the government welcomed the budget as it provided “further tax relief for businesses,” stating that it aligned with “Ontario’s own focus on attracting investment and cutting taxes for workers and businesses.” He cited the province’s $8 billion Ontario Competitiveness Tax Cut and $1.1 billion small business tax cut as examples.

However, both the federal government and Ontario have been criticized for not providing enough support for small businesses amid the trade war.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business said Thursday’s federal budget is a “mega disappointment,” as small businesses with less than $1 million in annual sales do not qualify for any tariff support programs.

In the legislature Thursday, Ontario NDP MPP Kristyn Wong-Tam criticized the Ford government for allowing small businesses in Toronto to languish without protection from corporate landlords while they deal with what the opposition described as unfair lease terms, eviction threats and communities losing stalwart small businesses.

In response to Wong-Tam’s comments, Progressive Conservative MPP Doug Downey said the Ford government has cut “so many taxes” for businesses and removed bike lanes, which he said were hurting small businesses.

The Ontario Chamber of Commerce study, conducted in partnership with Leger, is based on a survey of 851 businesses across Ontario between July 27 and Aug. 17, 2026.

“We’re working together,” he said. “We’ve started to invest in our economy, we’ve diversified our trade relationships, you see really positive measures that are incentivizing businesses to invest in themselves.”

But economic uncertainty due to Trump’s tariff regime on Canada, first levelled less than two weeks after he was inaugurated, has led to upheaval for Ontario’s businesses that has required increased resilience, according to surveys of owners published since 2025 by the Ontario Chamber of Commerce.
The organization’s most recent data published Oct. 1 shows some increased optimism, even before the midterm results, amid continued worries about the trade war.
The survey of 851 businesses across Ontario showed that while 44 per cent lacked confidence in the economy, business confidence rose over the course of 2026, from 23 to 34 per cent.

Yet, the majority did expect economic uncertainty due to the trade war with the U.S. to continue to hurt their businesses. Fifty-seven per cent reported they expect tariffs, trade policies and economic uncertainty to negatively affect their investment or expansion plans.
As a result, business owners reported they were increasing prices, reducing trade with the U.S., expanding domestic sales and diversifying suppliers.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford expressed similar optimism about the midterm results earlier this week, telling media he was “doing cartwheels” when he saw the Democrats’ blue wave. But the premier also voiced caution, citing that it will be up to Prime Minister Mark Carney to continue to try to make a trade deal with the president.

The Ford government also watched closely as Ottawa released its fall budget on Thursday. It featured an additional $151 billion over five years in “supports” for Canadian households, businesses and other levels of government.

Ontario Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy said the government welcomed the budget as it provided “further tax relief for businesses,” stating that it aligned with “Ontario’s own focus on attracting investment and cutting taxes for workers and businesses.” He cited the province’s $8 billion Ontario Competitiveness Tax Cut and $1.1 billion small business tax cut as examples.
However, both the federal government and Ontario have been criticized for not providing enough support for small businesses amid the trade war.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business said Thursday’s federal budget is a “mega disappointment,” as small businesses with less than $1 million in annual sales do not qualify for any tariff support programs.

In the legislature Thursday, Ontario NDP MPP Kristyn Wong-Tam criticized the Ford government for allowing small businesses in Toronto to languish without protection from corporate landlords while they deal with what the opposition described as unfair lease terms, eviction threats and communities losing stalwart small businesses.

In response to Wong-Tam’s comments, Progressive Conservative MPP Doug Downey said the Ford government has cut “so many taxes” for businesses and removed bike lanes, which he said were hurting small businesses.
The Ontario Chamber of Commerce study, conducted in partnership with Leger, is based on a survey of 851 businesses across Ontario between July 27 and Aug. 17, 2026.

stories.title: Patron death leaves Toronto bar facing liquor licence suspension
stories.summary: The patron was served 14 beers over a five-and-a-half-hour period, which is the equivalent of more than 21 standard drinks, said the Agco in a news release.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
A bar in midtown Toronto is facing the loss of its liquor licence after a patron who was served more than 21 standard drinks died following a fall down a stairwell at the establishment.

The Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario (Agco) announced Thursday it issued a 60-day suspension to St. Louis Bar & Grill at 11 St. Clair Avenue West after concluding its investigation of the incident. The bar is one of dozens of St. Louis franchises across Canada. Individual locations are owned by franchise owners and the brand is owned by Aegis Brands Inc., according to the chain’s website.

On April 11, 2026, the patron was served 14 beers over a five-and-a-half-hour period. The beers were 23 ounces each, which is the equivalent of more than 21 standard drinks, said the Agco in a news release. The patron then fell in a stairwell leading to a washroom, it said.

The investigation found the bar “permitted the patron to remain on the premises and continued to serve them alcohol after becoming intoxicated,” it said. Due to this, the commission is alleging the bar broke the law. The Agco is the province’s alcohol regulator.

Under Ontario’s Liquor Licence and Control Act, it’s illegal to sell liquor to a person who appears to be drunk.

“Responsible alcohol service requirements are designed to protect people from harm. Licenced establishments must monitor alcohol service, recognize signs of intoxication, and stop serving alcohol to anyone who is or appears to be intoxicated,” the commission said.

Karin Schnarr, the chief executive officer and registrar of the Agco, said in the news release that the “tragic loss of life” has devastated family, friends and the community. It underscores “why responsible alcohol service matters,” they said.

The bar has the right to appeal the suspension within 15 days of it being issued.

Global News has reached out to St. Louis Franchise Limited to respond to the allegations.

stories.title: Crossing guard hit in Richmond Hill crash following string of pedestrian collisions
stories.summary: York Regional Police confirm a crossing guard was one of four pedestrians, including two children, struck by an SUV in Richmond Hill, north of Toronto, ON Thursday afternoon.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
York Regional Police confirm a crossing guard was one of four pedestrians, including two children, struck by an SUV in Richmond Hill, north of Toronto, ON Thursday afternoon.

Officers first responded to reports of multiple pedestrians struck near Major Mackenzie Drive East and Essex Avenue at around 3:15 p.m., where they found two women and two children injured.

They say a 61-year-old Richmond Hill woman was working as a crossing guard at the time of the collision.

Police say she was transported to a trauma centre in life-threatening condition.

They say a 36-year-old woman, also from Richmond Hill, and two children, ages seven and one, suffered non-life-threatening injuries and were transported to hospital.

Investigators say the driver stayed on the scene and was co-operating with investigators.

They say there is no indication this was an intentional act of violence.

The investigation remains ongoing and no charges have been laid.

Anyone who witnessed the crash or has dashcam footage is asked to contact the investigators.

The City of Toronto has issued several warnings and an educational campaign around daylight saving time and the risks of reduced visibility for road users after the clocks rolled back by an hour on Nov. 1.

The city says pedestrian collisions increase by more than 30 per cent from November to March during the evening commute.

Several police agencies across Ontario, including Toronto, York and Peel police, have launched similar campaigns.

There have been several pedestrian collisions across the Greater Toronto Area this week, including a 20-year-old woman who was fatally struck in Newmarket on Wednesday and a man in his 70s who was struck in Toronto’s east end early Thursday morning.

stories.title: DNA expert likens B.C. bear attack investigation to human crime scene
stories.summary: A forensic DNA expert says investigators assessing the scene of this week's deadly bear attack in Bella Coola, B.C., will likely use techniques to identify the culprit animal very similar to those used on a human crime scene.
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A forensic DNA expert said investigators assessing the scene of this week’s deadly bear attack in Bella Coola, B.C., will likely use techniques to identify the culprit animal very similar to those used at a crime scene involving human DNA.

“It is pretty much exactly the same techniques. It’s just we’re reading a different book,” said Dean Hildebrand, who oversees the accredited forensic DNA lab at the British Columbia Institute of Technology.

stories.title: U of T’s dentistry dean to step down following antisemitic images in course material
stories.summary: The University of Toronto says its dean of dentistry will be stepping down immediately, following an investigation into his use of antisemitic imagery in February.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
The University of Toronto says its dean of dentistry will be stepping down immediately, following an investigation into his use of antisemitic imagery in February.

Trevor Young, the university’s vice-president and provost, says Anil Kishen voluntarily resigned as dean of the Faculty of Dentistry.

The investigation found that Kishen did not intend to promote antisemitism and had limited knowledge of the images’ history.

Young says Kishen has committed to learning more about antisemitism and has already undergone training.

Kishen will remain at the university as a tenured faculty member and will return to his full duties in the 2027-28 academic year.

The university says acting dean Laura Tam will continue in her role as they look for a new dean.

stories.title: Needles did not come from resident handing out candy in Strathroy: police
stories.summary: Strathroy-Caradoc police are investigating after needles were found in a Halloween treat bag.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein, Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Strathroy-Caradoc police are updating the public about an investigation involving needles in a Halloween treat bag.

Earlier on Friday, officers said they believed the treat bag was given out by a resident in a neighbourhood off Head Street in Strathroy on Oct. 31.

In an updated post on social media Friday afternoon, police said that the source of the needles in the ziploc bag did not come from a resident handing out candy in Strathroy.

Police say as a matter of safety, parents should always check their children’s Halloween candy as a precaution, however, this occurrence has been solved and police have isolated this incident.

Anyone with information can contact the Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service with reference number SC26008863.

Public Service Announcement

[](https://london.ca/newsroom/public-service-announcement/temporary-closure-colonel-talbot-road-construction-private)

Thursday, November 5, 2026

Colonel Talbot Road will be closed north of Southdale Road from Monday, November 9 to Friday, November 13 to facilitate private construction work at a residential development in the area.

A map showing the road closure on Colonel Talbot Road.

A signed detour will direct drivers around the closure. Drivers should follow posted signs and directions.

Traffic will be detoured along Byron Baseline Road, Boler Road, and Southdale Road. Drivers are encouraged to plan ahead, use Google maps or Waze to help navigate, and please drive safely following posted detour signs.

The City’s improvements on Boler Road are mostly complete, and the road reopened earlier this week. Some work will continue through the rest of the year. Boler Road will provide an alternate route for traffic detouring around the closure on Colonel Talbot Road.

For more information about construction projects in London, visit theRenew London map.

Thursday, November 5, 2026
Colonel Talbot Road will be closed north of Southdale Road from Monday, November 9 to Friday, November 13 to facilitate private construction work at a residential development in the area.
A map showing the road closure on Colonel Talbot Road.
A signed detour will direct drivers around the closure. Drivers should follow posted signs and directions.

Traffic will be detoured along Byron Baseline Road, Boler Road, and Southdale Road. Drivers are encouraged to plan ahead, use Google maps or Waze to help navigate, and please drive safely following posted detour signs.

The City’s improvements on Boler Road are mostly complete, and the road reopened earlier this week. Some work will continue through the rest of the year. Boler Road will provide an alternate route for traffic detouring around the closure on Colonel Talbot Road.

stories.summary: The Oxford County teams in the Provincial Junior Hockey League will be getting lots of miles on their skates this weekend.
stories.author: Kyle Freel
stories.content:
News Home

Friday, 6 November 2026 at 10:42

By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The Oxford County teams in the Provincial Junior Hockey League will be getting lots of miles on their skates this weekend.

PJHL - It will be a busy weekend for the Oxford County teams in the Provincial Junior Hockey League.

The Norwich Merchants will look to improve their 8-8-0-0 record as they will hit the ice twice this weekend, starting tonight. The Merchants welcome the Wellesley Applejacks to Nor-Del Arena, with puck drop scheduled for 8 p.m. Then tomorrow, it is a road trip to the Flight Exec Centre in Dorchester to take on the Dolphins at 7:30 p.m.

The other Oxford County team in the Doherty Division, the Tavistock Braves, will be the busiest as they are in for a three-game weekend. They will try to further their lead atop the standings, as they currently have a record of 10-2-2-0. It gets underway tonight as they welcome the Dorchester Dolphins to the Tavistock and District Recreation Centre for puck drop at 7:30 p.m. Tomorrow, the Braves travel to Paris to take on the Mounties at the Brant Sports Complex, and game time is set for 7:30 p.m. To round out the weekend, the Braves make their way to Hespeler for a 3:30 p.m. puck drop against the Shamrocks at the Hespeler Memorial Arena.

Finishing in the Yeck Division, the Thamesford Trojans are looking to make up ground in the standings as they are sitting 6th with a record of 5-6-3-0. The Trojans are on home ice at the Thamesford Recreation Centre tonight at 7:30 p.m. as they welcome the Mount Brydges Bulldogs. Tomorrow, the Trojans make their way to Parkhill to battle the North Middlesex Stars at the North Middlesex and District Arena, and game time is set for 8 p.m.

Navy Vets Preview - Nov. 6th The Woodstock Navy Vets hit the ice once this weekend, and there will be a special ceremony at the game tonight.

Fall Book Sale Supporting WPL The Friends of the Woodstock Public Library will host their biannual book sale this Saturday.

West Region OPP Release Project Safe Haul Results A total of 325 CMV inspections were completed through 22 safety blitzes, resulting 226 charges and 119 unsafe vehicles taken off the road.

Liberals Table Federal Budget Prime Minister Mark Carney says the budget builds a stronger Canada, while the opposition leaders say it falls short.

Oxford OPP Briefs - Nov. 5th, 2026 A pair of impaired drivers were caught in Oxford County over the past couple of days.

Stair Climb Results Released The United Way Stair Climb took over Reeves Community Complex to support United Way Oxford.

Winners Announced for Business Awards The Woodstock District Chamber of Commerce held the Business Awards of Excellence.

Citizen Applications Open for Oxford County Committees Those selected will serve for the 2026-2030 council term.

Oxford Tourism Award Recipients Announced The recipients were selected by a panel of external judges with representatives from provincial tourism organizations outside of Oxford.

United Way Student Stair Climb Returns Today The school that raised the most funds for United Way will be presented with a trophy.

Woodstonian Wins in Lotto Max Draw One Woodstock resident has all the reasons to smile after winning a Max Plus prize.

SWPH Set to Move in Oxford County The Board of Health at Southwestern Public Health has made the decision to move operations in Woodstock.

Seniors Centres in Oxford Receive Funding Three Seniors Centres in Oxford County are set to receive funding from the provincial government.

CO Awareness Week Underway Carbon monoxide is a colourless and odourless gas that could be deadly if its found inside the home.

The Greatest Debuts on Prime Video Video A parade scene featured in the The Greatest was filmed in downtown Woodstock in May of 2025.

Big Night Out Raises Over $100,000 for BBBS Oxford The Big Night Out Halloween Bash raised over $100,000 for youth mentorship programs in our community.

Deadline Looms for RRHS Online Survey You have until tomorrow to provide input for the next strategic plan for Rural Roads Health Services.

Charity of Choice Applications Open for 2027 WITAAR would like to support another local cause through the Charity of Choice program next year.

SUV Stolen in Waterford The Norfolk OPP is asking for the public's help tracking down an SUV that was stolen in Waterford.

Ingersoll Church Looking for Affordable Housing Partnership St. James Anglican Church would like to convert its second story into affordable housing units.

The Woodstock Navy Vets hit the ice once this weekend, and there will be a special ceremony at the game tonight.

WOODSTOCK - It will be a light weekend for the Woodstock Navy Vets in the Greater Ontario Hockey League.

The Vets only have one game on the schedule, and that will be tonight as they welcome the Strathroy Rockets to Southwood Arena. Tonight's game is a special one, as they will be honouring those who have fought for our freedoms and country. Woodstock and Strathroy have only met once so far this season, and that was back on Friday, October 9th at Southwood Arena. The Rockets skated away with the 5-4 victory.

The Vets sit 9th in the Western Conference with a record of 7-9-0-0 and 14 points. They are currently tied in points with the LaSalle Vipers, who have played one less game than the Vets. Woodstock could leapfrog their opponent tonight with a victory, as the Rockets are in 7th with a record of 6-9-2-1, which is good for 15 points.

Tonight's game is scheduled for 7:45 p.m.

stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The University of Toronto says its dean of dentistry will be stepping down immediately, following an investigation into his use of antisemitic imagery in February.

Nov. 6, 2026

Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press file photo[](https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/u-of-t-s-dentistry-dean-to-step-down-following-antisemitic-images-in-course-material/article_2f6a29e9-120e-53d6-8ed6-5c438dfc8355.html)

By Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press

Trevor Young, the university’s vice-president and provost, says Anil Kishen voluntarily resigned as dean of the Faculty of Dentistry.

The investigation found that Kishen did not intend to promote antisemitism and had limited knowledge of the images’ history.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

Image 9Image 10Image 11

Young says Kishen has committed to learning more about antisemitism and has already undergone training.

Kishen will remain at the university as a tenured faculty member and will return to his full duties in the 2027-28 academic year.

The university says acting dean Laura Tam will continue in her role as they look for a new dean.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

stories.title: U.S. midterm results spark joy among Canadians but trust in America remains shaky
stories.summary: Toronto - Many Canadians welcome the Democratic sweep of U.S. Congress, but have mixed views on whether voters' strong rebuke of President Donald Trump's administration will change their attitude toward America amid the ongoing trade war.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Many Canadians welcome the Democratic sweep of U.S. Congress, but have mixed views on whether voters’ strong rebuke of President Donald Trump’s administration will change their attitude toward America amid the ongoing trade war.

Trump’s punishing tariffs on Canadian goods, repeated musings about making Canada the 51st state and escalating tensions that include changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America have had a profound impact on the relationship between the two countries.

stories.title: Court certifies class action alleging negligence at LTC home led to COVID-19 deaths
stories.summary: Toronto - A lawsuit alleging that gross negligence at a Toronto long-term care home led to hundreds of deaths from COVID-19 has been certified as a class action.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A lawsuit alleging that gross negligence at a Toronto long-term care home led to more than 60 deaths from COVID-19 has been certified as a class action.

An Ontario Superior Court judge granted the certification last week with the consent of the defendants, the Downsview Long-Term Care Centre Limited and the company that owns it, Gem Healthcare Group Limited.

The lawsuit alleges Downsview and Gem were grossly negligent in their response to the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in multiple outbreaks at the home between late January 2020 and early May 2023.

It alleges those outbreaks caused at least 191 residents to get COVID-19 and at least 65 to die from it.

The plaintiffs include residents, people receiving care and visitors who contracted COVID-19 at the home during that period or their estates, as well as their family members.

The allegations have not been tested at trial. Downsview and Gem have said they intend to defend themselves against the allegations.

Billy Powell, whose mother Zellora Graham lived at Downsview until she died from COVID-19 in May 2020, is named as a representative plaintiff in a statement of claim filed a year ago.

Graham moved to Downsview in September 2017, a few months after suffering a hip fracture, the document said. She had arthritis and used a walker to get around. She had no other chronic conditions, it said.

By the time the pandemic hit the province, Graham was living in a private room but ate and watched TV in communal areas, the statement of claim said.

Powell last visited his mother in early March 2020, about a week before the Ontario government imposed restrictions on visits to long-term care homes, the document said. After that, he received “little to no information” about his mother or her health, it said.

He only learned of the possible risk to his mother after his wife saw a news article in late April about a COVID-19 outbreak at Downsview, the statement of claim said. When he called the home, a nurse told him Graham was doing well and the virus had not spread to her section, the statement of claim said.

He asked to speak with his mother but was told she had gone to bed, and received the same answer when he called again in the following days, it said.

On May 1, 2020, Powell returned a missed call from the home and was told his mother was not doing well and was suspected to have COVID-19, the document said. Staff asked if he wanted Graham to stay at Downsview or get transferred to hospital, and Powell and his siblings agreed she should go to a hospital, it said.

Once she arrived, Graham tested positive for COVID-19, the statement of claim said. A doctor called Powell that evening, saying his mother was severely dehydrated and struggling to breathe, and that she had a 20 per cent chance of survival, it said. A call the next day confirmed she was not improving, it said.

Graham died two days later.

The lawsuit alleges that long-standing deficiencies — including overcrowding, inadequate infection prevention and control practices, systemic failures to ensure compliance with regulatory, legal and industry standards, as well as understaffing — made the facility vulnerable to outbreaks.

It also alleges Downsview and Gem didn’t act quickly or proactively to impose infection prevention and control measures, and those they did implement did not reflect the state of knowledge on the virus and the risk it posed for elderly people.

The lawsuit further alleges the outbreaks were preventable had Downsview and Gem not breached their common law obligations.

In his ruling, Justice Edward Morgan said there is some factual basis to support those allegations for the purpose of certification.

“Given the number of class members and the economics of pursuing a claim of this nature requiring expert evidence, a class proceeding is the preferable procedure for ensuring their just and expeditious determination, promoting judicial economy, and seeking behaviour modification,” he wrote.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

Note to readers:This a corrected story. An earlier version had the wrong number of infected residents and deaths from COVID-19, based on figures cited in the court document that has since been corrected.
paragraphs: TORONTO - A lawsuit alleging that gross negligence at a Toronto long-term care home led to more than 60 deaths from COVID-19 has been certified as a class action.

An Ontario Superior Court judge granted the certification last week with the consent of the defendants, the Downsview Long-Term Care Centre Limited and the company that owns it, Gem Healthcare Group Limited.
The lawsuit alleges Downsview and Gem were grossly negligent in their response to the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in multiple outbreaks at the home between late January 2020 and early May 2023.
It alleges those outbreaks caused at least 191 residents to get COVID-19 and at least 65 to die from it.
The plaintiffs include residents, people receiving care and visitors who contracted COVID-19 at the home during that period or their estates, as well as their family members.
The allegations have not been tested at trial. Downsview and Gem have said they intend to defend themselves against the allegations.
Billy Powell, whose mother Zellora Graham lived at Downsview until she died from COVID-19 in May 2020, is named as a representative plaintiff in a statement of claim filed a year ago.

Graham moved to Downsview in September 2017, a few months after suffering a hip fracture, the document said. She had arthritis and used a walker to get around. She had no other chronic conditions, it said.
By the time the pandemic hit the province, Graham was living in a private room but ate and watched TV in communal areas, the statement of claim said.

Powell last visited his mother in early March 2020, about a week before the Ontario government imposed restrictions on visits to long-term care homes, the document said. After that, he received “little to no information” about his mother or her health, it said.

He only learned of the possible risk to his mother after his wife saw a news article in late April about a COVID-19 outbreak at Downsview, the statement of claim said. When he called the home, a nurse told him Graham was doing well and the virus had not spread to her section, the statement of claim said.
He asked to speak with his mother but was told she had gone to bed, and received the same answer when he called again in the following days, it said.

On May 1, 2020, Powell returned a missed call from the home and was told his mother was not doing well and was suspected to have COVID-19, the document said. Staff asked if he wanted Graham to stay at Downsview or get transferred to hospital, and Powell and his siblings agreed she should go to a hospital, it said.

Once she arrived, Graham tested positive for COVID-19, the statement of claim said. A doctor called Powell that evening, saying his mother was severely dehydrated and struggling to breathe, and that she had a 20 per cent chance of survival, it said. A call the next day confirmed she was not improving, it said.
Graham died two days later.

The lawsuit alleges that long-standing deficiencies — including overcrowding, inadequate infection prevention and control practices, systemic failures to ensure compliance with regulatory, legal and industry standards, as well as understaffing — made the facility vulnerable to outbreaks.

It also alleges Downsview and Gem didn’t act quickly or proactively to impose infection prevention and control measures, and those they did implement did not reflect the state of knowledge on the virus and the risk it posed for elderly people.
The lawsuit further alleges the outbreaks were preventable had Downsview and Gem not breached their common law obligations.
In his ruling, Justice Edward Morgan said there is some factual basis to support those allegations for the purpose of certification.

“Given the number of class members and the economics of pursuing a claim of this nature requiring expert evidence, a class proceeding is the preferable procedure for ensuring their just and expeditious determination, promoting judicial economy, and seeking behaviour modification,” he wrote.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 5, 2026.

By Fakiha Baig The Canadian Press

EDMONTON - Two more soldiers injured in a deadly fire at an Alberta military base have been discharged from hospital.

The Department of National Defence also says four of the 25 soldiers who remain hospitalized have been relocated to centres in British Columbia and Ontario, so they can receive treatment closer to their families.

The update comes a little more than two weeks after a fierce wind whipped a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright onto troops in a training exercise.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Smart glasses are showing up in Toronto nightclubs. Not everyone’s ok with it

The Oct. 17 blaze killed four and left 39 wounded, many with serious burns.

Officials previously said 13 were in critical condition.

“Recovery will look different for each injured person and their family. Some may face a long journey ahead, but they will not face it alone,” said a news release.

“Ongoing support and services remain available to injured personnel, their families, and all CAF members as they continue to navigate the effects of this tragedy.”

Three separate investigations are looking into the fire.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Spy watchdog flags privacy risk from military’s online intelligence activities
stories.summary: A national spy watchdog report says the military's policy on the collection of information about Canadians doesn't sufficiently address the privacy risks posed by online searches.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A national spy watchdog report says the military’s policy on the collection of information about Canadians doesn’t sufficiently address the privacy risks posed by online searches.

The National Security and Intelligence Review Agency found the Defence Department and the Canadian Armed Forces have the legal authority to collect publicly available information from the internet for intelligence purposes, but the watchdog noted shortcomings on privacy protection and oversight.

The review agency says information publicly available online can still raise privacy concerns when it’s collected and analyzed by government organizations.

It says Canadians should be able to trust that intelligence collection has a clear, lawful purpose and that their privacy rights are respected.

The watchdog found the military does not systematically record the link between open-source collection activities on the internet and the approved operation or defence activity.

It also says policies and record-keeping do not adequately address all privacy risks or demonstrate that collection involving Canadians is necessary.

stories.title: Amazon breaks ground on 200,000-square metre fulfilment warehouse in the Halifax area
stories.summary: Dartmouth - American e-commerce giant Amazon held a ground-breaking ceremony in the Halifax area today for a massive new warehouse that will use robots and more than 1,000 full-time employees to fulfil orders.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
DARTMOUTH - American e-commerce giant Amazon held a groundbreaking ceremony in the Halifax area Wednesday for a massive new warehouse that will use robots and more than 1,000 full-time employees to fulfil orders.

The online retailer said the warehouse in Dartmouth, N.S., will cover more than 200,000-square metres in the Burnside industrial park. It’s slated to open in 2029.

Brooks Barnett, head of economic development for Amazon Canada, declined to say how much the project will cost.

He said Halifax’s port, growing customer base and openness to investment were reasons Amazon chose the area for the new facility.

Barnett said the new site should offer more products and speed up deliveries for customers in the region, but he would not commit to same-day delivery.

“The second you click ‘buy,’ a robot in this building will be moving to satisfy your order,” Barnett said, adding that the facility will complement Amazon’s existing Dartmouth delivery facility.

Barnett said employee wages will start at $26 per hour. Benefits will include health, dental and a retirement savings plan.

He declined to say if the new site will replace a warehouse in Quebec that the company shuttered in January 2025 after employees there formed a union.

“All I’ll say is that we respect our employees’ right to have their voice heard and to make whatever decisions they want around unionization. But today we’re really talking about a new investment here in this region,” he said.

About 240 Amazon workers at the company’s warehouse in Laval, Que., unionized in May 2024, becoming the first of the tech company’s Canadian warehouses to do so.

The company had challenged the union drive before the province’s labour tribunal, but their case was rejected in October 2024. The tribunal’s ruling was upheld by Quebec Superior Court last month.

Amazon also faced anti-union allegations at a now-closed warehouse in the Montreal borough of Lachine. In August 2024, the labour tribunal ordered Amazon to stop interfering in union affairs and pay the union $30,000.

In January 2026, Amazon Canada announced it would close all seven of its Quebec warehouses within two months, eliminating 1,700 permanent jobs and 250 temporary ones.

At the time, the company said the move was aimed at cutting costs and improving service, and it insisted the closures had nothing to do with unionization.

Amazon isn’t the only major U.S. tech firm growing its operations in Nova Scotia. Artificial intelligence firm Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease to set up in a proposed $10-billion data centre in Cape Breton, slated to open late next year.

Meanwhile, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said there’s no government money in the Amazon project. While the province does have economic development programs that the Jeff Bezos-led company can apply for, Houston said Amazon is driving the investment on its own.

“This is a company investing in our province, like the data centre as well. That’s not government money either,” the premier told reporters Wednesday. “So these are good statements from international companies about the prospects that they see for Nova Scotia.”

Barnett declined to comment on how Democrats taking control of the U.S. Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections could impact Amazon’s business, which has sought close ties to U.S. President Donald Trump, a Republican, in his second term.

In his first term, Trump accused Bezos of using The Washington Post, which he owns, to persuade politicians not to tax Amazon. Trump also criticized the Post and Bezos over coverage of his campaign and presidency.

In 2019, Amazon sued after the Pentagon awarded a $10-billion cloud computing contract to Microsoft, alleging Trump’s interference harmed Amazon’s chances of winning.

Both sides have been friendlier since Trump won the 2024 election. In December 2024, Amazon said it planned to donate US$1 million to Trump’s inauguration fund. The company also and said it would stream the event on Prime Video, a separate in-kind donation worth another US$1 million.

The following month, Amazon acquired the licensing rights for a documentary about First Lady Melania Trump. In March 2025, it began streaming the first seven seasons of Trump’s reality show “The Apprentice.”

In November 2025, Amazon was among the 37 donors the government said were helping to pay for Trump’s US$300-million White House ballroom.

stories.title: Ford says Osap auditors will clear low-risk career colleges first; no timeline given
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario Premier Doug Ford says an audit firm that is investigating student financial aid usage at career colleges is making it a priority to clear lower-risk schools first so their funding can be unfrozen, but he was not clear on a timeline.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - An audit firm that is investigating student financial aid usage at Ontario career colleges is making it a priority to clear lower-risk schools first so their funding can be unfrozen, Premier Doug Ford said Wednesday, but he was not clear on a timeline.

Ford’s government paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all career colleges and private post-secondary institutions while KPMG is conducting an audit looking at serious concerns with the integrity of the system.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has said the audit’s preliminary findings include concerns about inadequate student validation and verification of course enrolment, and unusually high concentrations of OSAP from the same geographic locations. He has referred those preliminary findings to the Ontario Provincial Police.

Quinn has said he paused OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institutions while that audit is ongoing because concerns are systemic and he wants to ensure the integrity of the system.

But colleges, students and critics say it is too blunt of an instrument and is making students pay the price even at schools where no concerns have been raised. Many students say they don’t know how they will pay their rent and living expenses, let alone tuition, without their OSAP funding that had been previously approved.

Ford said Wednesday that his government has asked KPMG to look at the most reliable colleges first, but he did not give a specific idea of timing.

“We’ve asked KPMG to prioritize low-risk colleges,” he said. “Let’s get them back up and moving as quickly as possible, and that’s our goal.”

Bianca Giacoboni, a spokesperson for Quinn, later said the ministry is “working as quickly as possible to restore integrity to the private post-secondary OSAP system” and renew institutions’ access to OSAP.

Tatiana Bramnik, a vice-president at APlus Institute, said students at her dental hygienist career college are already having to withdraw and she is facing the prospect of having to consider layoffs with OSAP-funded students unable to pay their tuition.

Quinn should not have enacted a blanket OSAP pause in the first place, Bramnik said.

“This is a crisis they created, and now they don’t know how to deal with it,” she said.

Bramnik and her business partner came to Canada 33 years ago as immigrants from the former Soviet Union and many of their students are immigrants, she said, people who were professionals in their home country and want the accelerated education a career college can provide so they can start working and support their families.

“Dental hygiene is a good opportunity, still in high demand, and very well paid, so it’s a chance,” she said. “It’s a chance to have a normal life, to be able to live your life fully and give this to your children.”

Career Colleges Ontario said in a statement that it is hopeful that OSAP will be restored “without delay” for students at compliant institutions.

“Our position has been consistent: concerns about some institutions should not result in students at compliant colleges losing access to the financial assistance they rely on,” the association wrote in a statement.

“For many students, OSAP helps cover not only tuition, but also rent, food, transportation, books and other essential living costs. Restoring access for students at compliant institutions is urgent.”

Quinn has said the OSAP pause will last until the government puts a new and strengthened approval process in place for career colleges, and he expects that to be done in the new year.

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said students at institutions who have always followed the rules should never have been caught up in this in the first place.

“Students did all the right things,” she said. “They are pursuing careers in professions that we desperately need in Ontario, and they are being punished for this minister’s incompetence.”

Quinn has also said the government is reaching out to banks to try to secure third-party loans for students while OSAP is paused, but he has not given any updates on that in the month since making the announcement.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said students can’t wait until the new year.

“People live paycheque to paycheque,” he said. “The premier doesn’t understand that.”

Ford also said the KPMG report will “eventually” be released, but he doesn’t want to jeopardize a potential OPP investigation. That is counter to what Quinn said Tuesday, when he said the audit would not be made public.

Quinn’s office said later that day that they will “consider” releasing information from the audit if it doesn’t compromise a potential police investigation, a potential future auditor general investigation, “or the ministry’s efforts to obtain evidence, recover funds and hold bad actors accountable.”

The government is in panic mode, Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner suggested.

“I think the government knows they have completely mismanaged the OSAP file, and they don’t know what to do about it,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: 'A victory across the world,' Ontario Premier Doug Ford says after U.S. midterms
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he was "doing cartwheels" after the Democrats took control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in the U.S. midterm elections.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he was “doing cartwheels” after the Democrats took control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in the U.S. midterm elections.

Ford cautioned the trade war is not over, but said he is buoyed by the rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump by the American electorate.

“I was doing cartwheels down the street,” Ford said at Queen’s Park on Wednesday.

“But it’s very simple, the American people spoke on a couple issues: cost of living, cost of gas, the war in Iran, but most important is tariffs, because that’s all tied into the cost of living.”

On Tuesday, Democrats flipped long-held Republican Senate seats in Texas, Maine and South Carolina while also taking over House seats.

Trump has begun backpedalling following the losses, shifting blame elsewhere but also pledging to work with the Democrats in a rare moment of bipartisanship.

Ford called out Trump for lambasting some of his supporters after the loss, including Texas Governor Greg Abbott.

“The cheese has slipped off the cracker with this guy totally,” Ford said of Trump. “Like there is no cracker, there’s no more cheese, and I think the Republican Party are going to start moving forward without him.”

Ford and Trump traded barbs in late August after Trump said he would implement stiff tariffs on the auto sector on Jan. 1. Ford told Trump to “kiss my ass” in response, which enraged Trump, who responded by saying Ford was the less charismatic and less intelligent brother to the late Rob Ford, the former mayor of Toronto.

Trump has imposed 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion of Canadian goods, which came into effect in early September, and the Mark Carney government responded with its own suite of tariffs on U.S. goods.

Ford said the midterms give the Canadians “a little more leverage” in talks over a new trade deal.

“I want to emphasize the war is not over, and we’re going to have to keep fighting,” he said.

Ford said he has directed his cabinet to head to the United States once the new members are sworn in to build relationships in an effort to de-escalate the trade war with the U.S.

He praised Canadians, many of whom have boycotted travel to the U.S. or changed shopping habits to support Canadian businesses.

“It’s not just a victory for the people in the U.S., I think it’s a victory across the world, and most importantly, it’s a victory for the people of Canada because they played a strong voice.”

Interim Ontario Liberal leader John Fraser said Ford needs to stay in his lane on negotiations with the U.S.

“What we need is a plan,” he said. “The prime minister is leading that plan, and I think that the premier of this province and premiers in this country should take the lead from the prime minister. That’s Team Canada.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

stories.title: AFN chief says no one besides Carney, Kinew talked about abolishing Indian Act
stories.summary: The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the only leaders to discuss abolishing the Indian Act during a landmark meeting last week were Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Prime Minister Mark Carney.
stories.content:
Ottawa — The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the only leaders to discuss abolishing the Indian Act during a landmark meeting last week were Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Kinew, who is Anishinaabe, called for the act to be abolished during the historic gathering of federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in Ottawa.

The prime minister said he was “very open to” the idea but later said it could be reformed rather than abolished.

The Indian Act, which dates from 1876, gives Ottawa sweeping powers over First Nations communities and people, including the authority to decide who qualifies for status and what reserves can and can’t do.

Both Kinew and Carney said the idea to change or abolish the Indian Act was raised and supported by some chiefs in the room, but AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak says that’s not true.

Woodhouse Nepinak says the chiefs were focused more on the major projects legislation they say threatens their rights, and those conversations “went to the wayside” after Kinew and Carney made their remarks.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: McGill confirms convicted murderer no longer enrolled as a law student
stories.summary: Montreal - Montreal's McGill University says a man who was convicted of murder and attempted murder for attacks committed in 1984 is no longer a student.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Montreal’s McGill University says a man who was convicted of murder and attempted murder for attacks committed in 1984 is no longer a student.

McGill’s provost, Angela Campbell, informed students and staff about the news in a statement sent on Monday.

“McGill’s principal obligation is our duty of care to everyone who learns, works and lives on our campuses,” Campbell wrote.

Campbell sent the message after news from October about Jeffrey George Ewart’s enrolment in law classes while on parole sparked concern about student safety and debate over whether or not he should be allowed to attend.

Ewert, now in his 60s, was sentenced to two life sentences after he sexually assaulted and strangled two women in British Columbia in separate 1984 incidents that left one victim dead and the other severely disabled.

Campbell’s note did not identify Ewart by name, but said a person on day parole who was admitted to its law faculty this fall is no longer enrolled.

“Each student and colleague deserves a learning and research environment that is safe, respectful, inclusive, and conducive to their flourishing and success’” Campbell said.

Campbell said the university has launched an independent review of admissions processes and protocols that will take several months to complete.

“The goal of this review is to make sure existing procedures are sufficiently rigorous, set clearly defined responsibilities, and reflect our values, our academic mission, and our duty of care,” she wrote.

Campbell said the school is also committed to “dignity and second chances.”

“We believe in rehabilitation and in education’s power to transform lives,” the statement read. “Accordingly, past convictions do not, on their own, bar anyone from studying here.”

Campbell also acknowledged that students have been under strain due to media attention generated by the case, and that “differing views about recent events have created tensions within our community.”

The statement did not say whether Ewert’s enrolment was revoked by the school or whether he withdrew. The Canadian Press could not immediately reach his lawyer for comment.

Correctional Service Canada confirmed that it had issued a warrant to suspend Ewert’s conditional release and said he has returned to custody while the situation is being reviewed.

The agency said it can move to return someone to custody “when there are reasonable grounds to believe that the offender has breached a condition of release or that the risk they present can no longer be safely managed in the community.”

The agency said it can either cancel the suspension within 30 days or refer the case to the Parole Board of Canada for a post-suspension review.

McGill said it could not comment on specific cases for privacy reasons. However, it said that while criminal background checks are not typically part of Canadian universities’ admissions processes, the school “would act quickly and decisively should concerning information be brought forward about a student’s background or behaviour on campus.”

McGill said its procedures also include consulting relevant government bodies and its own policies to remove the individual from campus and to review its admission processes to ensure the situation isn’t repeated.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Head of UN relief praises Canada, calls for accountability in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan
stories.summary: The United Nations’ global head of humanitarian issues is praising Canada for helping the world’s most vulnerable even as he calls for accountability for the wars driving suffering worldwide. “Canada has become a humanitarian superpower,” Tom Fletcher said in an exclusive interview with The Canadian Press during a Monday visit to Ottawa. “I really hope […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The United Nations’ global head of humanitarian issues is praising Canada for helping the world’s most vulnerable even as he calls for accountability for the wars driving suffering worldwide.

“Canada has become a humanitarian superpower,” Tom Fletcher said in an exclusive interview with The Canadian Press during a Monday visit to Ottawa.

“I really hope that Canada continues to hold the line.”

Fletcher leads the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. For two years he has visited the front lines in Ukraine and Gaza while urging the world not to forget about ongoing crises in Sudan, Afghanistan and Mali.

His term started just weeks before the U.S. made deep cuts to foreign aid — though Fletcher praised the United States for restoring some of that funding over the past year.

Pointing to the conflicts in Sudan and Gaza, Fletcher said the funding shortfall is being compounded by wars that are spreading hunger and blocking humanitarian relief.

Roughly 19 million people in Sudan are living with acute hunger and Fletcher warns their plight could be made worse by changing weather patterns and the U.S. war in Iran blocking supply routes.

Sudan’s warring parties in the now three-year-old civil war have banned aid workers from certain areas based on how they perceive the local population’s loyalties.

Fletcher said he worries about normalizing practices the Israeli government has implemented in Gaza, such as barring journalists from the territory and drastically restricting aid flows.

“It’s sort of infectious, in the way that it undermines international law elsewhere, and creates or adds to this climate of impunity that we’re seeing across all the crises we work in,” he said.

Fletcher has faced sustained criticism from supporters of Israel who say the UN is downplaying groups like Hamas diverting aid or embedding themselves among civilians.

Fletcher said it’s important not to bow to that pressure, which he said comes from people who don’t want the world to see the extent of suffering inside Gaza.

“We’re being told, ‘Well, you’ll get more access if you change your reporting, or if you reduce your criticism, or your advocacy, or, if you spend less time talking about international law,’ and so on,” he said. “We just have to be consistent here.”

Technology is also making wars easier to fight. Fletcher said drones are being used more frequently against civilians in Sudan, Ukraine, Gaza and Lebanon.

“The way in which humans are using their ingenuity to find new ways to kill civilians is terrifying,” he said. “We need the member states to be holding themselves and each other to account.”

Fletcher praised Canada for its advocacy and its foreign aid funding, which he said “is saving millions of lives every year from Sudan to Afghanistan, to Gaza, to Ukraine, to Haiti and beyond.”

“We’re in a world right now where we’re underfunded, we’re overstretched, we’re literally under attack — a thousand dead humanitarians in three years,” he said.

“And at each point at which I’ve felt particularly exposed and where we as humanitarians feel exposed, we do look behind us and we find that Canada does have our back. And that means a huge amount.”

Fletcher met Tuesday with Randeep Sarai, Canada’s secretary of state for international development, who announced the renewal of $6 million in federal funding to help co-ordinate global emergency responses.

But Canada has changed its approach to foreign aid since Prime Minister Mark Carney took office. It cut funding for global health programs, is pushing for more private-sector investments in aid programs and spinoffs for Canadian companies, and dropped the “feminist” label from its foreign policy.

The aid sector has criticized this shift. They argue it prioritizes domestic growth over aid intended to address the issues which drive migration and conflict, and does not support the world’s most vulnerable people.

Ottawa has insisted it can fight poverty abroad while boosting Canadian companies at home.

Co-operation Canada, a coalition of most Canadian aid groups operating abroad, said the sector supports reforms but is urging Ottawa not to cut development and humanitarian funding further.

Coalition head Kate Higgins said during a Monday reception for Fletcher that the government’s recent national security strategy called for “strong international partnerships and a disciplined foreign policy.”

“Canada can give practical expression to that ambition through sustained humanitarian funding, principled diplomacy, and consistent leadership in upholding international humanitarian law,” she said.

Next July, Canada will chair a donor support group which consults with other rich countries on how the UN uses its humanitarian funding.

Fletcher said that’s an opportunity for a “reimagination” of what humanitarian aid looks like in an era when governments aren’t meeting the needs.

“I’d like to reach out beyond just traditional humanitarian development partners, actually towards technology companies, to the private sector, to really get their sense of how we can together deal with these crises,” he said.

Fletcher said UN agencies and large organizations have a crucial role to play in addressing complex problems like the hunger crisis in Darfur.

But he said places with internet connectivity and a functioning market might benefit more from cash transfers to individuals, or from health care programs where private companies can help while making a profit.

stories.title: Peel school board 'deeply saddened' after current, former students killed in crash
stories.summary: The Peel District School Board says it's "deeply saddened" after four young people, three of whom had ties to the school district, died when the car they were travelling in fell into a ravine in Puslinch, Ont., just outside Guelph.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Peel District School Board says it’s “deeply saddened” after four young people, three of whom had ties to the school district, died when the car they were travelling in fell into a ravine in Puslinch, Ont., just outside Guelph.

The school board in the region west of Toronto says one current and two former students were among those who died in the single-vehicle crash over the weekend.

stories.title: Toronto’s child hunger rates nearly double as city sees 4.1M food bank visits: report
stories.summary: When Volodymyr Kravchuk visits the Daily Bread Food Bank, he’s constantly thinking about his two young sons.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
When Volodymyr Kravchuk visits the Daily Bread Food Bank, he’s constantly thinking about his two young sons.

The Toronto resident is often looking for milk, eggs and vegetables such as potatoes or carrots, to make sure his children get the nutrition they need.

Kravchuk and his family moved to Canada from Ukraine in September 2023 and he remembers having to start his life over from scratch. While he holds degrees in psychology and marketing, Kravchuk said it’s been difficult finding stable employment and there are essentials that he has to turn to food banks for.

“Sometimes, somebody can lose their job (and) need more money to feed his family,” Kravchuk, who sometimes volunteers at Daily Bread, said. “In one day, everything can change.”

A new report from Daily Bread Food Bank says the number of children struggling with food insecurity in Toronto has risen, as food bank visits held steady at more than 4.1 million visits for the second year.

The non-profit’s latest Who’s Hungry report, released Tuesday, says more than one in eight children living in Toronto rely on food banks, which is nearly double the rate from 2022, when one in 15 children relied on them.

The report says 67 per cent of parents have given up a meal to make sure their children had enough food to eat while 17 per cent had a child in their household go hungry at least once a week in 2026.

Neil Hetherington, CEO of Daily Bread, said this rise in child hunger is “alarming,” as children became the most overrepresented group in food bank clients across the city. He says the roughly 220 food banks his organization services across the city have been feeling the strain.

“The fact that it’s more children than ever before is what’s changing and that it is the working poor,” he said. “It’s a horrific tax on each of the food banks.”

One in 10 Torontonians are still regularly relying on food banks but Hetherington said the city has “risen to the occasion to be able to meet the need.”

However, there are ongoing challenges, especially with the U.S.-Canada tariff war and the cost-of-living crisis.

One in four food bank clients spent all of their income on housing, an increase from one in five clients in 2025.

“We know why they’re coming to food banks and we just have to have the courage and leadership and fortitude to be able to make those policy changes,” Hetherington said.

The report includes several policy recommendations aimed at all three levels of government to address growing food insecurity, such as a provincial establishment of a Shelter Allowance Reserve Fund to help social assistance recipients regain housing and a municipal investment of $100 million to preserve Toronto’s affordable housing.

Kitty Raman Costa, executive director of the Parkdale Community Food Bank, said they’re serving more than 15,000 food clients through delivery and community drop-ins since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Many members of the Parkdale community who are employed still rely on the food bank because of the cost-of-living crisis, Raman Costa said. She’s also seen an influx of families with two working parents come in, who are struggling to balance rent and increasing food costs.

“We need to prioritize items like school lunch supplies, snacks, easy meals that young or older kids can prepare when parents are working,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.
