stories.title: Osap pause hits paramedic students bound to work in underserved areas
stories.summary: Paramedic students at a career college in northern Ontario who were approved to receive funding through a signature government program aiming to boost health-care staffing have been swept up in the provincewide pause on student aid.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — Paramedic students at a career college in northern Ontario who were approved to receive funding through a signature government program aiming to boost health-care staffing have been swept up in the provincewide pause on student aid.

More than 40 affected students have already dropped out, their school says.

Members of Premier Doug Ford’s government have often boasted about their Learn and Stay Grant, which covers the cost of tuition for nursing, paramedic and medical lab technology students who agree to work in underserved areas.

But it is funded through the Ontario Student Assistance Program, which Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has paused for all career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions.

Quinn has tasked Kpmg with auditing Osap usage in career colleges and said that preliminary findings were of such concern that he enacted the Osap pause sector-wide to protect the integrity of the system until the audit is completed.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial Osap grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year, a previous freedom-of-information request by The Canadian Press showed.

A second FOI shows skyrocketing usage at a relatively small number of schools, and the ministry says it now has broad concerns about the integrity of the system.

Only one career college is eligible for the Learn and Stay Grant – CTS Canadian Career College, which offers a paramedic diploma program in North Bay, Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury.

Some of the career colleges under suspicion saw increases in Osap usage of more than 1,000 per cent over three years. CTS saw a 14 per cent increase over that time, according to the data obtained through FOI.

Aaron Madgett is at the CTS campus in Sault Ste. Marie, trying to become a paramedic after getting laid off from Algoma Steel. He said his stomach dropped when he heard the funding was paused, and wondered if he would have to quit school.

“It kind of ripped away all the goals and aspirations that I had for me and my family, and I was gutted at the time,” he said.

Madgett said the school is helping, such as giving students chapters of textbooks they need, but he is now behind on property tax and electricity payments and has been making use of food bank services. Still, he said he is trying to stay positive.

“I have a positive outlook that things will work out,” he said. “I believe the government — there’s got to be something that they can do. There’s always something. That’s my belief.”

Quinn’s office said in a statement that “work is underway to reassess” Learn and Stay Grant eligibility at CTS Canadian Career College.

“As the Olsg has a separate, rigorous accountability process in place, including in-person instruction and return-of-service commitments, work is underway to reassess Olsg eligibility at this institution,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.

Quinn touted Monday in the legislature that the Learn and Stay Grant is “supporting students pursuing in-demand health-care careers in communities that need them the most.”

He was speaking to the broader Osap pause in responding to an NDP motion calling on the government to provide a plan within 14 days for relief for affected students.

Quinn said his message to “impacted, legitimate students” is that he is working efficiently to bring forward a stronger Osap for all.

“You deserve an education that is free from fraudulent, abusive, and malicious actors, so that you can get the high-quality, legitimate skills you need to launch successful, fulfilling careers,” he said.

CTS said that 41 students who were supposed to be receiving the Learn and Stay Grant have already dropped out, while 115 grant-funded students are left.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the government is making students pay for a problem they did not cause.

“The government’s failing,” he said. “It is cutting its nose off to spite its face.”

Fyonna Vanderwerf is in the CTS paramedic program in North Bay. The Learn and Stay Grant was supposed to pay her tuition and other school costs, and she intended to rely on an Osap loan for living expenses while she studied.

“Mortgage, food, gas, money — there’s nothing there, and there won’t be anything there for the foreseeable future,” she said.

“I really want everything investigated. I really do. But I also want accountability for the employment commitment that we signed for.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government should be transparent about the funding streams affected by the Osap pause and the impacts they are having.

“These communities desperately need those students,” she said. “We need those paramedics, and we need those workers out there.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

Allison Jones, The Canadian Press

stories.title: In new memoir, Harper says he offered Carney a job — but not finance minister
stories.summary: Ottawa - Former prime minister Stephen Harper says he offered Mark Carney, then the governor of the Bank of Canada, a role in his Conservative government in 2012 — though not as finance minister. Not right away, at least.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Former prime minister Stephen Harper says he offered Mark Carney, then the governor of the Bank of Canada, a role in his Conservative government in 2012 — though not as finance minister. Not right away, at least.

In his new book “Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister,” Harper says he told Carney the finance position was already taken but indicated that he would be next in line for the job when it became vacant.

“Obviously, I did not offer him the post of minister of finance, as it was then not available. However, I indicated that, if he chose to join the government, he would be the leading candidate should the post come open,” Harper writes.

Carney said in an interview on CBC during the 2025 Liberal leadership race that Harper had “asked me if I would be his finance minister in 2012.” He said at the time it wouldn’t be appropriate to go directly from the Bank of Canada governorship to party politics.

In ‘Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister,’ Harper disputes a claim about Mark Carney from 2012 and reflects on his decade in power.

In his book, released Tuesday, Harper says while Carney was “highly effective” as bank governor, his finance minister Jim Flaherty was “increasingly” worried in the wake of the 2011 election that Carney was nurturing political ambitions and might wish to seek the Liberal party leadership — something widely rumoured at the time.

“This was a serious concern for us,” Harper writes.

Harper says he brought it up with Nigel Wright, his chief of staff, who suggested a job offer would either secure Carney’s services for the government or force him to rule out a Liberal leadership bid, since he was in the non-partisan role of bank governor.

“Mark took some time to reflect on the opportunity, ultimately declaring that he should stay out of partisan politics,” he said, noting Carney left soon after for the top job at the Bank of England.

The mention of Carney is just a small aside in the nearly 650-page memoir. Harper says he felt he should address the issue since it has “occasionally cropped up in the media.”

The book offers Harper’s perspective on his tenure in Canadian politics from start to finish, from uniting the right under the modern Conservative party through a decade in government.

It also contains a rare first-person account of Harper’s final election campaign and the defeat of his government in 2015.

The former prime minister writes that he debated stepping down from the leadership in the summer of 2014 to rejuvenate the party.

Harper says after deciding to remain at the helm and lead his party into what he knew would be a tough race, he decided he would serve until just after the 150th anniversary of Confederation on July 1, 2017, then call a leadership race.

Harper also says he only learned of one of the most controversial episodes of the 2015 election — his party’s embrace of a “barbaric cultural practices hotline” — during his preparation for the French leaders’ debate in Montreal when the news “flashed across my screen.”

The announcement of the proposed tip line — which frustrated Red Tories and hindered the party’s outreach efforts with multicultural communities years after the fact — was fronted at the time by former cabinet ministers Kellie Leitch and Chris Alexander.

Harper writes he was “furious” upon learning about the policy, which he says he was not consulted on and had to defend on the campaign trail.

The book spans decades of Canadian political history. It includes Harper’s description of face-to-face standoffs with Russian President Vladimir Putin at G8 meetings, his reaction to the 2008 parliamentary crisis — when opposition parties attempted and failed to form a coalition government to oust the Conservatives — and Harper’s personal experience during the 2014 shooting on Parliament Hill, which happened when he was without his normal personal protective detail.

The former prime minister also offers up occasional reflections on current matters. While he attended the World Economic Forum in Davos twice during in his time in office, he now says he opposes it.

If he were prime minister today, Harper writes, he would end the Canadian government’s participation in the WEF, an event he describes as a once-useful forum that has become a club for advancing the “narrow interests of its globalist, elitist attendees.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Osap pause hits paramedic students bound to work in underserved areas
stories.summary: Toronto - Paramedic students at a career college in northern Ontario who were approved to receive funding through a signature government program aiming to boost health-care staffing have been swept up in the provincewide pause on student aid.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Paramedic students at a career college in northern Ontario who were approved to receive funding through a signature government program aiming to boost health-care staffing have been swept up in the provincewide pause on student aid.

More than 40 affected students have already dropped out, their school says.

Members of Premier Doug Ford’s government have often boasted about their Learn and Stay Grant, which covers the cost of tuition for nursing, paramedic and medical lab technology students who agree to work in underserved areas.

But it is funded through the Ontario Student Assistance Program, which Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has paused for all career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions.

Quinn has tasked KPMG with auditing OSAP usage in career colleges and said that preliminary findings were of such concern that he enacted the OSAP pause sector-wide to protect the integrity of the system until the audit is completed.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial OSAP grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year, a previous freedom-of-information request by The Canadian Press showed.

A second FOI shows skyrocketing usage at a relatively small number of schools, and the ministry says it now has broad concerns about the integrity of the system.

Only one career college is eligible for the Learn and Stay Grant – CTS Canadian Career College, which offers a paramedic diploma program in North Bay, Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury.

Some of the career colleges under suspicion saw increases in OSAP usage of more than 1,000 per cent over three years. CTS saw a 14 per cent increase over that time, according to the data obtained through FOI.

Aaron Madgett is at the CTS campus in Sault Ste. Marie, trying to become a paramedic after getting laid off from Algoma Steel. He said his stomach dropped when he heard the funding was paused, and wondered if he would have to quit school.

“It kind of ripped away all the goals and aspirations that I had for me and my family, and I was gutted at the time,” he said.

Madgett said the school is helping, such as giving students chapters of textbooks they need, but he is now behind on property tax and electricity payments and has been making use of food bank services. Still, he said he is trying to stay positive.

“I have a positive outlook that things will work out,” he said. “I believe the government — there’s got to be something that they can do. There’s always something. That’s my belief.”

Quinn’s office said in a statement that “work is underway to reassess” Learn and Stay Grant eligibility at CTS Canadian Career College.

“As the OLSG has a separate, rigorous accountability process in place, including in-person instruction and return-of-service commitments, work is underway to reassess OLSG eligibility at this institution,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.

Quinn touted Monday in the legislature that the Learn and Stay Grant is “supporting students pursuing in-demand health-care careers in communities that need them the most.”

He was speaking to the broader OSAP pause in responding to an NDP motion calling on the government to provide a plan within 14 days for relief for affected students.

Quinn said his message to “impacted, legitimate students” is that he is working efficiently to bring forward a stronger OSAP for all.

“You deserve an education that is free from fraudulent, abusive, and malicious actors, so that you can get the high-quality, legitimate skills you need to launch successful, fulfilling careers,” he said.

CTS said that 41 students who were supposed to be receiving the Learn and Stay Grant have already dropped out, while 115 grant-funded students are left.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the government is making students pay for a problem they did not cause.

“The government’s failing,” he said. “It is cutting its nose off to spite its face.”

Fyonna Vanderwerf is in the CTS paramedic program in North Bay. The Learn and Stay Grant was supposed to pay her tuition and other school costs, and she intended to rely on an OSAP loan for living expenses while she studied.

“Mortgage, food, gas, money — there’s nothing there, and there won’t be anything there for the foreseeable future,” she said.

“I really want everything investigated. I really do. But I also want accountability for the employment commitment that we signed for.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government should be transparent about the funding streams affected by the OSAP pause and the impacts they are having.

“These communities desperately need those students,” she said. “We need those paramedics, and we need those workers out there.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Former Alberta junior hockey executive charged with sex offences against players
stories.summary: Okotoks - A former junior hockey executive in Alberta has been arrested and charged with sexually exploiting three players.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OKOTOKS - A former junior hockey executive in Alberta has been charged with sexually exploiting three players.

Tyler King, 39, was arrested Friday at a U.S. border crossing in Ontario, RCMP announced Monday.

He had been working with the State University of New York campus at Oswego in New York state.

RCMP said the 39-year-old is to be returned later this week to Alberta to face charges of luring, sexual exploitation and making child pornography.

“We are still actively investigating the span of the time that (these offences) happened,” Cpl. Daniel Campbell said during a virtual news conference.

“Given the seriousness of the accusations and to protect the integrity of the investigation, it was important that we proceed carefully and thoroughly at every stage.”

King had worked with various teams across Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia, including the Okotoks Oilers with the British Columbia Hockey League.

Mounties said the Alberta-based Oilers reported in June 2024 that a former employee had allegedly solicited and compensated players for intimate images and sexual videos.

A statement published on the team’s website around the same time announced King was leaving his job.

“The Okotoks Oilers would like to thank Tyler King for his tireless efforts during his three seasons in our organization as Assistant GM, Business Operations,” said the June 2024 statement.

It said King had been in charge of overseeing all off-ice operations.

“During his second and third seasons with the Oilers, Tyler served as the main play-by-play voice of the team on The Eagle 100.9 FM in Okotoks and online streaming platforms,” it added.

The Oilers said in a statement Monday that it became aware of the allegations against King after he left the team.

“After his departure, we received information that, while unverified at the time, raised enough concern that we felt it needed a closer look,” said Brent Lauinger, the team’s chairman and governor

“We reviewed it carefully and passed it to the RCMP.”

The university in New York state said King joined the school in 2025 as a professor of practice with its communications studies department.

“We are aware of the arrest in Canada and are co-ordinating with law enforcement,” it said in an email. “Because this is an ongoing criminal matter involving a university employee, we cannot comment further at this time.”

Campbell said the Oilers have also been co-operative with investigators.

“They’re obviously very concerned for their players,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

— By Fakiha Baig and Daniela Germano in Edmonton

stories.title: Survivor of Belleville, Ont., synagogue shooting cites need for extensive security
stories.summary: Ottawa - The vice-president of the Belleville, Ont., synagogue that was attacked by a gunman in September says costly, enhanced security measures are needed to ensure the safety of congregants.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - One of the leaders of the Belleville, Ont., synagogue that was targeted by a gunman in September says costly enhanced security measures are needed to ensure the safety of congregants.

Police have described the Sept. 20 attack as a thwarted attempt at a mass killing of Jewish worshippers at the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

Police say the shooter had multiple guns, large amounts of ammunition and gasoline and the motive to carry out an extended attack when he opened fire on an officer stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue.

Shima Vigodda, vice-president of the synagogue, told a news conference on Parliament Hill on Monday that before the shooting, the institution’s security priorities were things like replacing windows broken in acts of vandalism and installing burglar alarms.

An existing federal program that helps places of worship make security improvements was adequate for such modest expenses, he indicated.

But Vigodda, who survived the gunman’s assault, said it has become clear that more expensive measures are necessary — improvements the Canada Community Security Program would not fully cover.

He said those measures include things like installing bullet-resistant glass, replacing inner and outer doors, building a safe room, installing fencing to slow or halt a would-be attacker, and having security personnel or armed police on site.

“These measures are necessary not only to ensure our physical security, but to deter would-be attackers,” Vigodda said. “For many in our congregation who were there on Yom Kippur, it is also a necessity for them to feel comfortable enough to return to the synagogue.”

Approved proposals under the federal security program are eligible for funding to cover up to 70 per cent of project costs, with a maximum Public Safety Canada contribution of $5 million per project.

Vigodda said that even with the program, smaller communities struggling to ensure adequate security while trying to cover other expenses face “an agonizing and sometimes impossible choice.”

Noah Shack, chief executive of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, told the news conference the federal budget, being tabled Thursday, is an opportunity for the Liberal government to build on its new national security strategy by investing in counter-radicalization, intelligence and counterterrorism.

He said the centre is working closely with Public Safety Canada to strengthen the Canada Community Security Program, “so that every institution can access the support it needs, and that the program is intended to provide, regardless of its financial circumstances.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

— With files from Alyssa Wheeler in Ottawa and Paola Loriggio in Toronto

stories.title: Experts suggest Canada lock in gains with EU amid rise in far-right movements
stories.summary: Ottawa - Experts in European Union policy say Canada should try solidifying gains with the EU in legal frameworks as right-wing movements gain ground on the continent.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Experts in European Union policy say Canada should try solidifying gains with the EU in legal frameworks, particularly as talk of becoming an EU “associate member” continues to cause confusion.

Academics studying EU relations testified Monday to the House foreign-affairs committee after a summit in Montreal last week.

Canadian and European officials praised the EU plan as a historic partnership. The experts were less enthusiastic.

“A lot of these agreements are essentially expressions of intent more than anything,” University of Toronto professor Mark Manger testified.

“I’m still waiting for a concrete announcement, of something that is more than more co-operation, better relations, etc., etc.,” he said.

Manger argued Mexico already has many of the arrangements with the EU that Canada is now gaining or seeking.

The testimony comes after weeks of confusion over nomenclature, with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pitching Canada as an “associate member” of the EU.

Prime Minister Mark Carney originally avoided that phrasing for weeks and instead spoke of an “alliance for the future.” He switched last Thursday, saying the goal was associate EU membership — a term that has no official definition.

Achim Hurrelmann, co-director of the Centre for European Studies at Carleton University, said the phrasing was “a bit of a distraction from the policy work leading up to the summit — mainly because the EU, frankly, hadn’t really done its homework in defining what this status would mean, and how it could be integrated into EU law.”

Still, Hurrelmann said Carney and von der Leyen are “keen to maintain” the buzz around the phrasing.

“I don’t think they are really fully attached to the concept of associate membership, but stick to it now because it brings this symbolic attention. Everyone’s talking about this,” he testified.

Hurrelmann said both sides will need to settle on an arrangement that is somewhere between a mere political declaration and some formal status — which would require complicated amendments to EU treaties and votes in the Canadian Parliament.

“The proposals that we have heard do not require associate membership at all to be realized,” he said.

Hurrelmann suggested thinking of associate membership as the “symbolic affirmation” of moving from a common-law relationship to marriage.

Anand Sundar, a transatlantic defence adviser at the European Council on Foreign Relations, testified that “associate membership” seems to be something Brussels is pushing despite strong objections from countries such as Germany.

“It’s a very political sort of game that we’re seeing,” he said. “This might be something in interest of the commission, but not of certain member states.”

As MPs on the committee raised concerns about rising far-right movements in Europe that are skeptical of partnering with other countries, Hurrelmann said Canada should move fast to nail down a deal with the EU.

“On the Canadian side it’s going to be important to ask how quickly can this agreement be put fully in legal force on the European side,” Hurrelmann said.

Hurrelmann also suggested Ottawa consider restructuring its EU trade deal to increase economic gains by changing its status from the current “mixed agreement” that requires individual ratification by each member state.

Of the bloc’s 27 members, nine still haven’t put the Canadian deal in full force despite the agreement operating for a decade.

Canadians chafe at food regulations that bar many Canadian imports. Europeans complain about Canada’s dairy quota and protected-origin phrasing, Hurrelmann noted, such as whether cheeses called feta can originate from anywhere outside a specific region of Greece.

Hurrelmann noted the deal was praised at the time it was signed for innovative clauses on aligning regulations, assessing conformity with rules and recognizing professional qualifications — and that all these have had limited success, resulting in less trade than what was envisioned.

“The joint statement from the summit has some very vague language on that. But I would really encourage both sides to look at the CETA governance structure,” he said.

Manger suggested Canada and the EU enhance the existing trade deal with “economic and legal parameters” that make it more appealing for exports and investments.

“In international agreements, it’s desirable to have something that is locking in a certain trade relationship, that makes it clear for Canadian firms … that this is a long-term relationship,” he said.

“If we were to fully replace a lot of the imports (to) the European Union in terms of raw materials that came before from, say, Russia and parts of the (Persian) Gulf, where we can offer something instead — we can probably double our trade with the EU over 10 years,” Manger added.

He suggested Ottawa could allow European mobile networks to set up in Canada in exchange for European countries dropping restrictions on Canadian food imports.

Hurrelmann added that any agreements between Canada and the EU will face complex negotiations to achieve consensus among the provinces and the EU’s 28 member states.

He suggested Ottawa focus on projects in areas where the EU has clear jurisdiction, such as research and academic exchanges, while working directly with countries on key issues where they have power, such as defence and energy.

Hurrelmann also said closer ties to Europe will only work if there is cross-party collaboration.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre argues the government has not been clear on its deal with Europe, that the Montreal summit was a waste of time meant to distract from domestic issues, and that Canada risks losing sovereignty to Europe and control of its borders.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said the European Union has 28 member states.

stories.title: Prime Minister Mark Carney calls six federal byelections for December
stories.summary: Ottawa - Voters in six federal ridings in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan will be heading to the polls Dec. 7, after Prime Minister Mark Carney called byelections Sunday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Voters in six federal ridings in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan will be heading to the polls Dec. 7, after Prime Minister Mark Carney called byelections Sunday.

A press release from the Prime Minister’s Office says byelections will take place in three Quebec ridings, including Laurier—Sainte-Marie, Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton, where seats were previously held by the Liberals, the NDP and the Bloc Québécois respectively.

stories.title: Parents cheer, businesses brace as Western Canada ditches the time change
stories.summary: Jenn Irwin-Greer never looked forward to the routine gong show at her Edmonton dayhome business that came with the twice-annual time change as children struggled to adjust to a new pattern.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Jenn Irwin-Greer never looked forward to the routine gong show at her Edmonton dayhome business that came with the twice-annual time change as children struggled to adjust to a new pattern.

“(Children) show up a little bit irritable, as we all do when we’re tired,” she said. “Nap times get thrown out of whack.”

She’s hopeful things will be a little bit easier this year.

Canadians woke up Sunday to a new time zone map after British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories opted to stay on daylight time year-round rather than have clocks fall back one hour.

Saskatchewan already doesn’t adjust its clocks.

At a recreation centre in Edmonton’s south end on Sunday, some parents said not having to adjust their children’s sleep schedule felt refreshing.

“I’m going to be honest, I do kind of like it,” said Amanda Petrie after her seven-year-old son’s hockey game. “It’s just easier with kids when you don’t have to adjust their schedule.”

Siva Sivabalan, another resident, said he felt the Alberta government had made the right call by not changing the time.

“I rather have more daylight in the evening time rather than the morning,” he said as his daughter played nearby.

“Especially the November time change, I just didn’t like it at all.”

In Calgary, hairstylist Jordan Janovcik said he feels anxious about the work week ahead.

He said he spent the entire summer double- and sometimes triple-checking with clients to make sure they knew Alberta was not falling back.

Hairstylists like him have busy but by-the-book schedules, and missed appointments or delays could mean lost time and money.

“I am really concerned for this week,” he said in a phone interview.

“I think this is going to be really hard for a lot of businesses.”

Technology experts have said the change could cause problems for scheduling systems and older computer software.

Online, some Canadians reported Sunday that their cellphones displayed the incorrect time.

A statement from Telus says the issue is related to how some phones update their time zone information, rather than the service provider.

“Customers experiencing this issue can check their phone’s settings to ensure that ‘set time zone automatically’ is selected, then restart their phone to help apply any available time zone updates,” the company says.

A Rogers spokesperson said the company experienced no issues with its network, and referred questions to an industry group that posted instructions for updating phones and tablets.

In the skies, Air Canada said Sunday its operations were normal, noting that all flights use the internationally recognized time standard and that time changes are managed using established industry data sources.

Tech giant Google responded to an inquiry about how new time zones are affecting its services by linking to a blog post with instructions on how to make sure devices and services stay on schedule.

“From morning alarms to critical calendar invites, we know how much you rely on your devices to stay organized and on time,” the post said.

Back in Edmonton, Irwin-Greer said she’s curious how no time change might affect life on the Prairies.

She noted darker mornings in the months ahead and whether they would affect commutes for students and workers.

“I don’t love that it’s going to be darker for longer when the kids are going to school,” she said. “My teenage son is not overly worried about it, but it is a little bit concerning when they’re trying to travel.

“Crossing the street and it’s hard enough for traffic to see, so hopefully there are not more accidents.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

With files from Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman in Montreal

Ashley Joannou and Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Thousands of Osap applications came from a single IP address, ministry alleges
stories.summary: Toronto - At two career colleges now under the Ontario government's microscope, more than half of the thousands of student financial aid applications last year came from a single IP address, officials allege in documents filed in court.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - At two career colleges now under the Ontario government’s microscope, more than half of the thousands of student financial aid applications last year came from a single IP address, officials allege in documents filed in court.

The government has also received more than 200 tips about that network of schools, including allegations that certain recruiters were submitting students’ Ontario Student Assistance Program applications at those schools, which is not allowed, and completing their coursework, those same documents show.

The Academy of Learning did not provide comment on the new court filings in response to a request from The Canadian Press, but has previously denied allegations of wrongdoing. They say the schools have implemented a long list of corrective actions, including cutting ties with some recruiters and bolstering admissions practices. The ministry’s allegations have not been proven in court.

The newly filed allegations against the schools come as Premier Doug Ford’s government is under increasing fire for its handling of OSAP. Critics say alleged misuse of the system was allowed to fester under lax oversight, then when it was brought to light Ford left innocent students paying the price.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn says his government acted on tips and conducted in-depth inspections that ultimately led to barring the schools from OSAP eligibility and launching a broader probe.

Quinn earlier this year drastically reduced the amount of OSAP grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive in the name of “sustainability” as the program was facing rising costs.

Those costs were later revealed by The Canadian Press to largely be due to activity at a small number of career colleges. Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial OSAP grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year.

The Academy of Learning operates as franchises but the three schools barred from OSAP share a parent company, Opulence Education Group. Its campuses in Toronto on Bay Street and in North York, and one in Brampton East, accounted for one-fifth of that spending.

The three schools were among six that in May the province made ineligible for OSAP, citing an “inability to reliably determine bona fide studies,” a decision the schools are challenging in court. As part of that case, the province issued a final decision in August and added that to the court record in October.

“The ministry is not satisfied that the institutions have adequate processes in place to ensure that its records and processes can be relied on for the proper administration and disbursement of OSAP funding to eligible students,” the decision says.

Ministry officials who last year inspected the campuses at issue looked at a sampling of student accounts and found evidence of shared IP address activity across students referred by the same recruiter, the government alleges.

In completing its final decision to deny the schools OSAP eligibility this year, the ministry appears to have taken a closer look at IP address activity.

There were 6,001 OSAP applications from students at the Brampton East campus for the 2025-26 year and 3,136 of them — 52 per cent — came from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. There were five more IP addresses responsible for 100 or more applications, they allege.

At the North York campus, 3,460 out of 6,070 OSAP applications for that year — 57 per cent — came from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. Two other IP addresses were responsible for another 255 applications, they allege.

The Bay campus saw 6,966 OSAP applications that year, with 1,736 — 25 per cent — coming from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. Five other IP addresses submitted 100 or more applications, they allege.

The Academy of Learning argued in an earlier letter to the ministry that shared IP addresses may be due to multiple people living at the same address, but the ministry is calling that into question.

“While patterns of shared IP addresses among students attending the same physical school campus space accessing their student accounts may be expected, patterns of shared IP address activity among the institution’s asynchronous learners referred to the institution by the same recruiter is significant and renders the institution’s proposed explanation unlikely in this case,” the ministry wrote in the court filing.

In its letter to the province to rebut any nefarious assumptions about students’ logins, the Academy of Learning also wrote, “the presence of the same IP address among different users does not, by itself, establish misconduct, misrepresentation, or unauthorized activity.”

Quinn has tasked KPMG with an audit of OSAP payments to career colleges and in October referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police, while pausing such payments to all private post-secondary institutions. It is not known if the referral contains specific allegations relating to the Academy of Learning.

It comes after warnings from Career Colleges Ontario, the federal government, and hundreds of tips and complaints about possible misuse of the OSAP system.

The new ministry court filings reveal that since Jan. 1, 2024 it has received more than 220 tips, complaints, referrals and investigations relating to the three Academy of Learning campuses, with the volume and consistency of the concerns “significant,” the government alleges.

“The ministry received related third-party complaints and tips alleging that certain recruiters were acting on behalf of students, including in submitting OSAP applications, in uploading supporting documentation on students’ OSAP accounts, and in completing coursework on behalf of students, and that recruiters were using OSAP funding as a recruitment or marketing tool,” the ministry wrote.

The schools have since cut off ties with some recruiters, they have said.

Academy of Learning did not directly respond to a request for comment by The Canadian Press on the allegation that recruiters were completing students’ coursework, but has noted in a corrective action plan last year that it added enhanced IP tracking to identify possible third-party access and added two-factor authentication “to safeguard against third-party completion of assignments.”

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said given all the information that is now public about what the government knew or should have known about the skyrocketing OSAP usage at some career colleges, it is shocking they did not act with more urgency.

“I think the more details that we learn through these court proceedings, the clearer it is that the minister was completely incompetent at doing his job,” she said. “It is stunning that these five-alarm fires were being ignored by the government.”

Liberal critic Tyler Watt also said the new revelations reflect poorly on Quinn.

“Minister Nolan Quinn keeps insisting he’s taken this scandal seriously, but every new revelation raises more questions about what his ministry knew, when they knew it, and why they failed to act,” he wrote in a statement.

Quinn’s office said when serious concerns are identified, they do not hesitate to cut an institution off from OSAP entirely, as was done with the Academy of Learning locations in this court case.

“Any misuse of OSAP is unacceptable,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement. “We have zero tolerance for bad actors who threaten the integrity of our post-secondary system.”

Quinn has indicated he will introduce further legislation this fall to enhance accountability in the system.

There were 6,001 OSAP applications from students at the Brampton East campus for the 2025-26 year and 3,136 of them — 52 per cent — came from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. There were five more IP addresses responsible for 100 or more applications, they allege.

At the North York campus, 3,460 out of 6,070 OSAP applications for that year — 57 per cent — came from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. Two other IP addresses were responsible for another 255 applications, they allege.

The Bay campus saw 6,966 OSAP applications that year, with 1,736 — 25 per cent — coming from a single IP address, the ministry alleges. Five other IP addresses submitted 100 or more applications, they allege.
The Academy of Learning argued in an earlier letter to the ministry that shared IP addresses may be due to multiple people living at the same address, but the ministry is calling that into question.

“While patterns of shared IP addresses among students attending the same physical school campus space accessing their student accounts may be expected, patterns of shared IP address activity among the institution’s asynchronous learners referred to the institution by the same recruiter is significant and renders the institution’s proposed explanation unlikely in this case,” the ministry wrote in the court filing.

In its letter to the province to rebut any nefarious assumptions about students’ logins, the Academy of Learning also wrote, “the presence of the same IP address among different users does not, by itself, establish misconduct, misrepresentation, or unauthorized activity.”

Quinn has tasked KPMG with an audit of OSAP payments to career colleges and in October referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police, while pausing such payments to all private post-secondary institutions. It is not known if the referral contains specific allegations relating to the Academy of Learning.
It comes after warnings from Career Colleges Ontario, the federal government, and hundreds of tips and complaints about possible misuse of the OSAP system.

The new ministry court filings reveal that since Jan. 1, 2024 it has received more than 220 tips, complaints, referrals and investigations relating to the three Academy of Learning campuses, with the volume and consistency of the concerns “significant,” the government alleges.

“The ministry received related third-party complaints and tips alleging that certain recruiters were acting on behalf of students, including in submitting OSAP applications, in uploading supporting documentation on students’ OSAP accounts, and in completing coursework on behalf of students, and that recruiters were using OSAP funding as a recruitment or marketing tool,” the ministry wrote.
The schools have since cut off ties with some recruiters, they have said.

Academy of Learning did not directly respond to a request for comment by The Canadian Press on the allegation that recruiters were completing students’ coursework, but has noted in a corrective action plan last year that it added enhanced IP tracking to identify possible third-party access and added two-factor authentication “to safeguard against third-party completion of assignments.”

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said given all the information that is now public about what the government knew or should have known about the skyrocketing OSAP usage at some career colleges, it is shocking they did not act with more urgency.

“I think the more details that we learn through these court proceedings, the clearer it is that the minister was completely incompetent at doing his job,” she said. “It is stunning that these five-alarm fires were being ignored by the government.”
Liberal critic Tyler Watt also said the new revelations reflect poorly on Quinn.

“Minister Nolan Quinn keeps insisting he’s taken this scandal seriously, but every new revelation raises more questions about what his ministry knew, when they knew it, and why they failed to act,” he wrote in a statement.
Quinn’s office said when serious concerns are identified, they do not hesitate to cut an institution off from OSAP entirely, as was done with the Academy of Learning locations in this court case.
“Any misuse of OSAP is unacceptable,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement. “We have zero tolerance for bad actors who threaten the integrity of our post-secondary system.”
Quinn has indicated he will introduce further legislation this fall to enhance accountability in the system.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Parents cheer, businesses brace as Western Canada ditches the time change
stories.summary: Jenn Irwin-Greer never looked forward to the routine gong show at her Edmonton dayhome business that came with the twice-annual time change as children struggled to adjust to a new pattern.
stories.author: Ashley Joannou and Fakiha Baig The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Jenn Irwin-Greer never looked forward to the routine gong show at her Edmonton in-home daycare business that came with the twice-annual time change as children struggled to adjust to a new pattern.

“(Children) show up a little bit irritable, as we all do when we’re tired,” she said. “Nap times get thrown out of whack.”

She’s hopeful things will be a little bit easier this year.

Canadians woke up Sunday to a new time zone map after British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and the Northwest Territories opted to stay on daylight time year-round rather than have clocks fall back one hour.

As more provinces and territories move away from twice-yearly clock changes, they face a choice between permanent daylight time and standard time. Canadian Press Reporter Sandra Ezekwesili explains how health experts, public opinion and economic considerations are shaping the debate over which one to keep. (Oct. 30, 2026)

Saskatchewan already doesn’t adjust its clocks.

At a recreation centre in Edmonton’s south end on Sunday, some parents said not having to adjust their children’s sleep schedule felt refreshing.

“I’m going to be honest, I do kind of like it,” said Amanda Petrie after her seven-year-old son’s hockey game. “It’s just easier with kids when you don’t have to adjust their schedule.”

Siva Sivabalan, another resident, said he felt the Alberta government had made the right call by not changing the time.

“I rather have more daylight in the evening time rather than the morning,” he said as his daughter played nearby.

“Especially the November time change, I just didn’t like it at all.”

In Calgary, hairstylist Jordan Janovcik said he feels anxious about the work week ahead.

He said he spent the entire summer double- and sometimes triple-checking with clients to make sure they knew Alberta was not falling back.

Hairstylists like him have busy but by-the-book schedules, and missed appointments or delays could mean lost time and money.

“I am really concerned for this week,” he said in a phone interview.

“I think this is going to be really hard for a lot of businesses.”

Technology experts have said the change could cause problems for scheduling systems and older computer software.

Online, some Canadians reported Sunday that their cellphones displayed the incorrect time.

A statement from Telus says the issue is related to how some phones update their time zone information, rather than the service provider.

“Customers experiencing this issue can check their phone’s settings to ensure that ‘set time zone automatically’ is selected, then restart their phone to help apply any available time zone updates,” the company says.

A Rogers spokesperson said the company experienced no issues with its network, and referred questions to an industry group that posted instructions for updating phones and tablets.

In the skies, Air Canada said Sunday its operations were normal, noting that all flights use the internationally recognized time standard and that time changes are managed using established industry data sources.

Tech giant Google responded to an inquiry about how new time zones are affecting its services by linking to a blog post with instructions on how to make sure devices and services stay on schedule.

“From morning alarms to critical calendar invites, we know how much you rely on your devices to stay organized and on time,” the post said.

“Our teams are working to ensure these updates reach all Canadian users as quickly as possible.”

Back in Edmonton, Irwin-Greer said she’s curious how no time change might affect life on the Prairies.

She noted darker mornings in the months ahead and whether they would affect commutes for students and workers.

“I don’t love that it’s going to be darker for longer when the kids are going to school,” she said. “My teenage son is not overly worried about it, but it is a little bit concerning when they’re trying to travel.

“Crossing the street and it’s hard enough for traffic to see, so hopefully there are not more accidents.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

— With files from Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman in Montreal
